latin: Aeque stationes nostras, ut indignas; quasdam vero et in serum constitutas, novitatis nomine incusant, hoc quoque munus et ex arbitrio obeundum esse dicentes, et non ultra nonam detinendum, de suo scilicet more. Sed quod pertineat ad interdictionis quaestionem, semel pro omnibus caussis respondebo. Nunc ad proprium hujus speciei articulum, de modo temporis dico, de ipsis prius expostulandum, unde hanc formam nova dirimendis stationibus praescribant. Si, quia Petrus, et qui cum eo, ad horam nonam orationis templum introgressi leguntur, quis mihi probabit illos ea die statione functos, ut horam nonam ad clausulam et expunctionem stationis interpretetur? Atqui facilius invenias Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi caussa, prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse, quo magis sexta diei finiri officio huic possit, quae illud absolutura post orationem videbatur. Porro, cum in eodem commentario Lucae, et tertia hora orationis demonstretur, sub qua Spiritu Sancto initiati, pro ebriis habebantur; et sexta, qua Petrus ascendit in superiora; et nona, qua templum sunt introgressi, cur non intelligamus salva plane indifferentia semper et ubique et omni tempore orandi, tamen tres istas horas ut insigniores in rebus humanis, quae diem distribuunt, quae negotia distinguunt, quae publice resonant, ita et solemniores fuisse in orationibus divinis? Quod etiam suadet Danielis quoque argumentum ter die orantis, utique per aliquarum horarum exceptionem, non aliarum autem quam insigniorum, exinde Apostolicorum, tertiae, sextae, nonae. Hinc itaque et Petrum dicam ex vetere potius usu nonam observasse, tertio orantem supremae orationis munere. Haec autem propter illos, qui se putant ex forma Petri agere, quam ignorant; non quasi respuamus nonam, cui et quarta sabbati, et sexta plurimum fungimur: sed quia eorum quae ex traditione observantur, tanto magis dignam rationem afferre debemus, quanto carent Scripturae auctoritate, donec aliquo coelesti charismate aut confirmentur, aut corrigantur. Et si qua, inquit, ignoratis, Dominus vobis revelabit. Itaque, seposito confirmatore omnium istorum Paracleto, duce universae veritatis, an indignior apud vos ratio afferatur in nonam observandi requiro, ut etiam Petro ea ratio deputanda sit, si statione tunc functus est. Venit enim de exitu Domini, quem etsi semper commemorari oportet sine differentia horarum, impressius tamen tum ei secundum ipsum stationis vocabulum addicimur: nam et milites nunquam immemores sacramenti, magis stationibus parent. Itaque in eam usque horam celebranda pressura est, in qua a sexta contenebratus orbis defuncto domino lugubre fecit officium, ut tunc et nos revertamur ad jucunditatem, cum et mundus recepit claritatem. Hoc si magis ad religionem sapit christianam, dum magis Christi gloriam celebrat, possum aeque serae stationis ex eodem rei ordine statum figere, ut jejunemus ad serum, exspectantes tempus Dominicae sepulturae cum Joseph postulatum detulit corpus, et condidit. Inde et irreligiosum est ante famulorum carnem refrigerare, quam domini. Sed hoc ex argumentationum provocatione commiserim, conjecturas conjecturis, et tamen puto fidelioribus, repercutiens. Videamus an aliquid tale nobis de vetustatibus quoque patrocinetur. In Exodo, habitus ille Moysis adversus Amalech orationibus praeliantis usque in occasum perseverans, nonne statio fuit sera? Jesum Nave debellantem Amorrhaeos, prandisse illa die existimamus, qua ipsis elementis stationem imperavit? Stetit sol in Gabaon, et luna in Aialon: stetit sol et luna instructione, donec ultus est populus de inimicis suis; et stetit sol medio coelo, et non accedebat in occasum, et in finem diei unius. Non fuit dies talis retro et in novissimo, utique tam prolixus; ut, inquit, exaudiret Deus hominem, parem scilicet solis, instantem tamdiu in officio, stationem etiam sera longiorem. Certe Saul et ipse in praelio constitutus, manifeste munus istud indixit: Maledictus homo qui ederit panem ad vesperam usque dum ulciscur de inimico meo; et non gustavit totus populus ejus, et tota terra non prandebat. Tantam autem Deus praestitit auctoritatem edicto stationis illius, ut Jonathan filius Saulis, quanquam ignarus jejunationis in serum definitae gustum mellis admiserat, et sorte mox de delicto sit traductus, et vix per precem populi periculo exemptus, gulae enim, licet simplicis, reus fuerat. Sed et Daniel, anno primo regis Darii, cum jejunans in sacco et cinere exomologesin Deo ageret, et adhuc, inquit, loquente me in oratione, ecce vir quem videram in somnis initio, velociter volans adpropinquavit mihi quasi hora vespertini sacrificii. Haec erit statio sera, quae ad vesperam jejunans, pinguiorem orationem Deo immolat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We know their suspicions here perfectly well. They suspect that the apostle Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, granted forgiveness to the very same fornicator whom, in his first letter, he had handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:5) — an impious heir to his father's marriage bed. They act as if Paul then changed his tune, writing: "If anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure — not to put it too severely — to all of you. For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough. So you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. That is why I beg you to reaffirm your love for him. I wrote for this very purpose: to test you and see whether you are obedient in everything. Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs" (2 Corinthians 2:5-11).

But what is actually understood here about the fornicator, about the defiler of his father's bed, about the Christian who outdid the very shamelessness of the Gentiles? Since Paul had absolved with special mercy the very man he had condemned with special wrath. His pity is obscure; his severity is open. Yet anger is more easily turned aside than indulgence; we hesitate longer over harsh things than joyful ones. We are dealing with a moderate indulgence — which, if it were assessed today, when even the greatest gifts are not usually given without proclamation, would be all the more impossible without some sign.

And you — dragging the adulterer's penance into the church to exhort the brotherhood — you throw him down in the middle, a spectacle composed of shame and horror, before widows, before presbyters, invading every lap, licking every footstep, clutching every knee. And with every lure of mercy you can muster, you preach — good shepherd, blessed Pope — and in the parable of the sheep you go hunting for your goats, pleading for your own sheep lest it wander from the flock again, as if what was never lawful even once has now become lawful. You strike the rest with fear even while you are at your most indulgent.

Yet the apostle so openly forgave the criminal lust of fornication, weighted with incest, that he did not even demand from him that habit of penance which he ought to have learned from Paul himself. He threatened nothing about the future; he addressed nothing further. On the contrary, he actually begged them to establish love toward the man, as if making satisfaction rather than granting forgiveness — and yet I hear only of love, not of communion. Paul says the same to the Thessalonians: "If anyone does not obey what we say in this letter, take note of that person, and have nothing to do with him, that he may be ashamed. Do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:14-15). So he could have said to the fornicator that love alone was conceded, not communion. But to the incestuous man — neither love, since he had ordered him removed from their midst, much less from their hearts.

Paul feared, however, that they might be cheated by Satan over the loss of this man's person — the very man Satan himself had cast out — or that he might be swallowed by excessive sorrow, the man Paul had handed over to the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:5). Now they reinterpret that destruction of the flesh as a penitential function: as if fasts, filth, total neglect, and dedication to abusing the body — exterminating the flesh — could satisfy God. From this they argue that the fornicator, that incestuous man, was not handed over by the apostle to Satan for destruction, but for correction — as if he would later obtain forgiveness because of that destruction, that is, the conflict of the flesh, and therefore had already obtained it.

The same apostle handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). Yet Paul himself says a thorn was given him, a messenger of Satan, to buffet him and keep him from becoming conceited. If they press this parallel — that those handed over to Satan by Paul were for correction, not destruction — what similarity exists between blasphemy and incest, and a soul kept intact, indeed elevated from the highest sanctity and all innocence, which, if restrained in the apostle at all, was restrained by buffets, through pain, as they say, of ear or head? Incest and blasphemy handed whole men over to the possession of Satan himself, not merely to his messenger. And this matters greatly: we read that those men were handed over to Satan by the apostle; but the apostle himself was given a messenger of Satan.

Finally, when Paul pleads with the Lord, what does he hear? "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness." Those who are handed over to Satan cannot hear that. But if the crime of Hymenaeus and Alexander is irremissible even in the age to come — namely blasphemy — then certainly the apostle did not hand them over to Satan against the Lord's limit, in hope of forgiveness, men already sunk from faith into blasphemy. Therefore he pronounced them shipwrecked regarding the faith, having no comfort from the ship of the Church: for forgiveness is denied to those who have plunged from faith into blasphemy. Yet Gentiles and heretics emerge daily from blasphemy.

But if Paul said, "I handed them over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Timothy 1:20), he spoke of the others — those handed over to Satan, that is, cast out of the Church — that they should be rebuked not to blaspheme. So therefore the incestuous fornicator was not handed over to Satan for correction, but for destruction — a man who had already gone beyond the Gentiles in sinning — that they might learn not to fornicate. In the end, Paul says, "for the destruction of the flesh, not for torment" — condemning the very substance by which he had fallen, which had already perished from that point on, baptism having been lost — "that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 5:5).

The question is asked: will that man's spirit itself be saved? Therefore the spirit, polluted by so great a crime, will be saved on account of the lost flesh, so that it may be saved in punishment. A contrary interpretation would have punishment without flesh, if we lose the resurrection of the flesh. It remains, then, that Paul meant the spirit which is recognized in the Church — saved, that is, kept intact, to be presented on the day of the Lord, free from the contagion of impurities, the incestuous fornicator having been cast out. For he adds: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" And yet incestuous fornication was not a little leaven, but a great one.

latin: Novimus plane et hic suspiciones eorum. Revera enim suspicantur apostolum Paulum, in secunda ad Corinthios, eidem fornicatori veniam dedisse, quem in prima dedendum Satanae in interitum carnis pronuntiarit, impium patris de matrimonio haeredem; quasique ipsum postea stylum verterit scribens: Si quis autem contristavit, non me contristavit, sed ex parte, ne vos onerem omnes. Satis est talis increpatio quae a multis fit. Uti e contrario magis vos donare et advocare, ne forte abundantiore tristitia devoretur ejusmodi. Propter quod oro vos, constituatis in eum dilectionem. In hoc enim et scripsi, uti cognoscam probationem vestram quod in omnibus obauditis mihi. Si cui autem donaveritis, et ego. Nam et ego si quid donavi, donavi in persona Christi, ne fraudemur a Satana: quoniam non ignoramus injectiones ejus. Quid hic de fornicatore, quid de paterni thori contaminatore, quid de christiano ethnicorum impudentiam supergresso intelligitur? cum proinde utique speciali venia absolvisset, quem speciali ira damnasset. Obscurius miseretur, quam indignatur; apertior est in austeritate, quam in lenitate: atquin facilius ira quam indulgentia obliqua est; magis tristiora cunctantur, quam laetiora. De modica scilicet indulgentia agebatur; quae si forte nunc aestimaretur, quando maxima quaeque non soleant etiam sine praedicatione donari, tanto abest sine significatione. Et tu quidem poenitentiam moechi ad exorandam fraternitatem in ecclesiam inducens, conciliciatum et concineratum cum dedecore et horrore compositum prosternis in medium ante viduas, ante presbyteros, omnium lacinias invadentem, omniunt vestigia lambentem, omnium genua detinentem, inque cum hominis exitum quantis potes misericordiae inlecebris, bonus pastor et benedictus Papa concionaris, et in parabola ovis, capras tuas quaeris, tua ovis ne rursus de grege exiliat, quasi non exinde jam liceat quod nec semel licuit, caeteras etiam metu comples, cum maxime indulgens. Apostolus vero sceleratam libidinem fornicationis incesto onustam tam projecte ignovisset, ut nec hunc saltem habitum legatum poenitentiae quem ab ipso didicisse deberes, ab eo exegerit, nihil de postero sit comminatus, nihil de caetero allocutus? Quin imo, et ultro obsecrat, constituerent in cum dilectionem, quasi satisfaciens, non quasi ignoscens: et tamen dilectionem audio, non communicationem. Quod et ad Thessalonicenses: Si quis autem non obaudit sermoni nostro per epistolam, hunc notate, nec commisceamini illi, ut revereatur, non quasi inimicum deputantes, sed quasi fratrem objurgantes. Adeo potuisset dicere et fornicatori dilectionem solummodo concessam, non et communicationem. Incesto vero nec dilectionem, quem scilicet auferri jussisset de medio ipsorum, multo magis utique de animo. Sed verebatur ne fraudarentur a Satana circa ejus personae amissionem, quem Satanae ipse projecerat; aut ne abundantia moeroris devoraretur, quem in interitum carnis addixerat. Hic jam carnis interitum in officium poenitentiae interpretantur, quod videatur jejuniis et sordibus et incuria omni et dedita opera malae tractationis carnem exterminando satis Deo facere; ut ex hoc argumententur fornicatorem, imo incestum illum, non in perditionem Satanae ab Apostolo traditum, sed in emendationem, quasi postea veniam ob interitum, id est conflictationem carnis, consecuturum, igitur et consecutum. Plane idem apostolus Hymenaeum et Alexandrum Satanae tradidit, ut emendarentur non blasphemare, sicut Timotheo suo scribit. Sed et ipse datum sibi ait sudem, angelum Satanae, a quo colaphizaretur ne se extolleret.. Si et hoc tangunt ut traditos Satanae ab illo, in emendationem, non in perditionem intelligamus, quid simile blasphemia et incestum et anima ab his integra, imo non aliunde quam ex summa sanctitate et ex omni innocentia elata, quae in apostolo colaphis si forte cohibebatur, per dolorem, ut aiunt, auriculae vel capitis. Incestum vero atque blasphemia totos homines in possessionem ipsi Satanae, non angelo ejus tradidisse meruerunt. Et de hoc enim interest, imo et ad hoc plurimum refert, quod illos traditos ab Apostolo legimus Satanae; Apostolo vero angelum datum Satanae. Postremo, cum deprecatur Dominum Paulus, quid audit? Satis habe gratiam meam; virtus enim in infirmitate perficitur. Hoc, qui Satanae deduntur, audire non possunt. Hymenaei autem et Alexandri crimen si et in isto et in futuro aevo irremissibile est, blasphemia scilicet; utique Apostolus non adversus terminum Domini sub spe veniae dedisset Satanae, jam a fidei in blasphemiam mersos. Unde et naufragos eos juxta fidem pronuntiavit, non habentes jam solatium navis Ecclesiae: illis enim venia negatur, qui de fide in blasphemiam impegerunt. Caeterum, ethnici et haeretici quotidie ex blasphemia emergunt. Sed etsi dixit: Tradidi eos Satanae, uti disciplinam acciperent non blasphemandi; de caeteris dixit qui, illis traditis Satanae, id est extra Ecclesiam projectis, crudiri haberent blasphemandum non esse. Sic igitur et incestum fornicatorem non in emendationem, sed in perditionem tradidit Satanae, ad quem jam super ethnicos delinquendo transierat, ut discerent fornicandum non esse. Denique in interitum, inquit, carnis, non, in cruciatum; ipsam substantiam damnans per quam exciderat, quae exinde jam perierat, baptismate amisso; ut spiritus, inquit, salvus sit in die Domini. Et de hoc enim quaeratur si spiritus hominis ipsius salvus erit. Ergo salvus erit spiritus tanto scelere pollutus, propter hoc perdita carne, ut salvus sit in poena. Ergo poenam sine carne censebit contraria interpretatio, si resurrectionem carnis amittimus. Superest igitur ut eum spiritum dixerit, qui in Ecclesia censetur, salvum, id est integrum, praestandum in die Domini ab immunditiarum contagione, ejecto incesto fornicatore; siquidem subjungit: Non scitis quod modicum fermentum totam desipiat conspersionem? Et tamen fornicatio incesta non erat modicum, sed grande fermentum.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: All who believe and are certain that grace and truth came to be through Jesus Christ, and who know that Christ is truth — just as he himself said, "I am the truth" (John 14:6) — receive the knowledge that provokes people to live well and blessedly from nowhere else than from Christ's own words and teaching. When we speak of Christ's words, we do not mean only those he taught as a man made flesh; for Christ was the Word of God in Moses and the prophets even before that. Without the Word of God, how could they have prophesied about Christ? It would not be difficult to show from the divine scriptures how Moses and the prophets were filled with the Spirit of Christ and spoke and did everything they did, but my aim is to finish this present work with all possible brevity. So I consider it enough to use this one testimony of Paul from the letter he wrote to the Hebrews, where he says: "By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt" (Hebrews 11:24-26). And after his assumption into heaven, Paul indicates that Christ spoke in him: "Or do you seek a proof of Christ, who speaks in me?" (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since many who profess to believe in Christ disagree not only in small and minor matters but also in great and major ones — that is, about God, or about the Lord Jesus Christ himself, or about the Holy Spirit, and not only about these but also about other creatures, whether dominions or holy virtues — it seems necessary first to lay down a certain and clear rule about each of these, and then to investigate the rest. Just as we stopped seeking the truth among all those Greeks and barbarians who promised it but asserted it with false opinions, once we believed that the Son of God, Christ, is the truth and became persuaded that we must learn it from him, so now, when there are many who think they hold the mind of Christ and some of them differ from their predecessors, the ecclesiastical preaching that has been preserved through the succession of the apostles and remains in the churches to the present day — that alone is to be believed as truth which in nothing disagrees with the ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.

One must know that the holy apostles, preaching the faith of Christ, handed down to all believers — even to those who seemed slower in inquiring into divine knowledge — the things they believed necessary, most clearly, while leaving the reason for their assertions to be investigated by those who would merit the excellent gifts of the Spirit and especially the grace of speech, wisdom, and knowledge through the Holy Spirit. About other matters they did say that they exist, but they were silent about how or from where they exist, precisely so that the more studious among their successors, lovers of wisdom, might have an exercise in which to show the fruit of their genius — those, namely, who prepare themselves to be worthy and capable of receiving wisdom.

The items handed down openly through apostolic preaching are these: First, that there is one God, who created and ordered all things, and who, when nothing existed, brought all things into being — the God of the first creation and constitution of the world, the God of all the righteous, of Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets; and that this God, in the last days, as he had promised through his prophets, sent the Lord Jesus Christ, first to call Israel, and then also the Gentiles after the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel. This God is just and good, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the law, the prophets, and the Gospels, and who is the God of the apostles and of the Old and New Testaments. Next, that Jesus Christ, the one who came, was born from the Father before all creation. Having served the Father in the constitution of all things — "for through him all things were made" (John 1:3) — in the last times he emptied himself, became man, was incarnate, and, being God, remained what he was, God. He assumed a body like our own, differing only in that he was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. And since this Jesus Christ was born and suffered in truth, and not in appearance, he truly died this common death; for he truly rose from the dead, and after the resurrection conversed with his disciples and was taken up. Then they handed down that the Holy Spirit is associated with the Father and the Son in honor and dignity. In this matter it is not yet clearly discerned whether he is begotten or unbegotten, or whether he should even be considered the Son of God; but these things must be investigated from Holy Scripture and sought out by sagacious inquiry. Certainly it is preached most clearly in the Church that the Holy Spirit inspired every saint, prophet, and apostle, and that there is not one Spirit in the Old Testament and another in those who were inspired at the advent of Christ.

After these things, it is held that the soul, having its own substance and life, when it departs from this world will be dispensed according to its merits — either to inherit eternal life and blessedness, if its deeds have deserved it, or to be handed over to eternal fire and punishment, if the guilt of sins has turned it that way. But there will also be a time of resurrection of the dead, and this body, which is now "sown in corruption, will rise in incorruption, and what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory" (1 Corinthians 15:42-43). It is also defined in ecclesiastical preaching that every rational soul possesses free will and volition; and that it has a struggle against the devil and his angels and contrary powers, because they try to burden it with sins, but we, if we live rightly and wisely, try to strip ourselves of such stain. From this it follows that we understand we are not subject to necessity so as to be forced in every way, even against our will, to do either evil or good. For if we are masters of our own choice, perhaps some powers can assault us toward sin and others help us toward salvation, yet we are not compelled by necessity to act either rightly or wrongly — which is what those think who say the course and movements of the stars are the cause of human actions, not only of those that happen outside the freedom of our will, but also of those that lie within our power. Concerning the soul, however — whether it is derived from the seed, so that its reason or substance is inserted into the bodily seeds, or whether it has another beginning, and if this beginning is generated or ungenerated, or if it is put upon the body from outside — the preaching does not clearly distinguish.

The ecclesiastical preaching also taught that the devil and his angels and contrary powers exist, but it did not clearly explain what they are or how they are. Among many, however, the opinion is held that the devil was an angel and, having become apostate, persuaded many angels to fall away with him, who are now called his angels. There is also this in ecclesiastical preaching: that this world was made and began at a certain time, and will be dissolved on account of its own corruption. But what was before this world, or what will be after the world, has not become clearly known to many. For the teaching about these things is not evident in ecclesiastical preaching. Then, that the scriptures were written by the Spirit of God and have a sense not only the one that is on the surface, but also another, hidden one, accessible to very many. For these are the forms that are described as sacraments of certain divine things and images of divine realities. On this the whole Church holds one view: that the whole law is spiritual, yet what the law breathes is not known to all, but only to those to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit is granted in the word of wisdom and knowledge. The term "incorporeal" is unusual and unknown not only among many others, but even in our own scriptures. If someone wishes to bring forward against us that little book called the Teaching of Peter, where the Savior seems to say to the disciples, "I am not an incorporeal demon," one must first answer that the book itself is not counted among the ecclesiastical books, and show that neither is the writing Peter's nor that of anyone else inspired by the Spirit of God. Even if it were conceded, the sense indicated there by that saying is not the same as the one shown by Greek or Gentile authors when they dispute the incorporeal nature in philosophy. For in that little book — "incorporeal demon" — he said it to mean that that being, whoever he is, does not have a habit or circumscription of a demon's body similar to this our grosser and visible body; but according to the sense of the one who composed that writing, it is to be understood that he said: he does not have such a body as demons have (which is naturally a certain subtle thing, like a thin breath, and for that reason is thought or called incorporeal by many), but he has a solid and tangible body. In human usage, everything that is not of that sort is called incorporeal by the simpler or less instructed — as if someone were to call this air we enjoy incorporeal, because it is not such a body as can be grasped and held and resist when pressed.

We will inquire, however, whether the very thing that Greek philosophers call "incorporeal" is found in Holy Scripture under another name. How God himself ought to be understood must also be sought: whether corporeal and deformed in some shape, or of another nature than bodies are — which is certainly not openly designated in our preaching. The same must be inquired also about Christ and the Holy Spirit, and no less about every soul and every rational nature. It is also in ecclesiastical preaching that there are certain angels of God and good powers who minister to him for the accomplishment of human salvation; but when these were created, or of what sort, or how they are, is not clearly distinguished. About the sun, moon, and stars, whether they are animate or without soul, is not handed down clearly. Therefore one must use such things as elements and foundations, according to the command that says: "Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge" (cf. Psalm 36:9), so that anyone who wishes may complete a series and a body of knowledge from the reasoning of all these, investigating what is true about each thing, and make one body out of examples and affirmations — either those found in Holy Scriptures, or those discovered through investigation of the consequences and the right line of thought.

latin: Omnes qui eredunt et certi sunt quod gratia et veritas per lesum Christum facta sit, et Christum esse veritatem norunt, secundum quod ipse dixit: “Ego sum veritas”, scientiam quae provocat homines ad bene beateque vivendum non aliunde quam ab ipsis Christi verbis doetrinaque suscipiunt. Christi autem verbis dieimus non his solum, quae homo factus atque in carne positus docuit; et prius namque Christus dei verbum in Moyse atque in prophetis erat. Nam sine verbo dei quomodo poterant prophetare de Christo? Ad cuius rei probationem non esset difficile ex divinis seripturis ostendere, quomodo vel Moyses vel prophetae spiritu Christi repleti vel locuti sunt vel gesserunt omnia quae gesserunt, nisi studii nobis esset, praesens hoc opus omni qua possumus brevitate suecingere. Unde sufficere aestimo uno hoc Pauli testimonio debere nos uti ex epistula, quam ad Hebraeos scribit, in qua ita ait: “Fide magnus factus Moyses negavit se dici filium filiae Pharaonis, magis eligens afflietari cum populo dei quam temporalem habere peccati iueunditatem, maiores divitias aestimans Aegyptiorum thesauris inproperium Christi”. Sed et post adsumptionem eius in caelos quod in apostolis suis loeutus sit, hoc modo indicat Paulus: “Aut numquid probamentum quaeritis eius, qui in me loquitur Christus?” 2. Quoniam ergo multi ex his, qui Christo se credere profitentur, non solum in parvis et minimis discordant, verum etiam in magnis et maximis, id est vel de deo vel de ipso domino lesu Christo vel de spiritu sancto, non solum autem de his, sed et de alus creaturis, id est vel de dominationibus vel de virtutibus sanctis: propter hoc necessarium videtur prius de his singulis certam lineam manifestamque regulam ponere, tum deinde etiam de ceteris quaerere. Sicut enim, multis apud Graecos et barbaros pollicentibus veritatem, desivimus apud omnes eam quaerere, qui eam falsis opinionibus asserebant, posteaquam eredidimus fihum esse dei Christum et ab ipso nobis hane discendam esse persuasimus: ita eum multi sint, qui se putant sentire quae Christi sunt, et nonnulh eorum diversa a prioribus sentiant, servetur vero ecclesiastica praedicatio per successionis ordinem ab apostolis tradita et usque ad praesens in ecclesiis permanens, illa sola credenda est veritas, quae in nullo ab ecclesiastica et apostolica traditione discordat. 3. Illud autem scire oportet, quoniam sancti apostoli fidem Christi praedieantes de quibusdam quidem, quaecumque necessaria crediderunt, p omnibus eredentibus, etiam his, qui pigriores erga inquisitionem divinae scientiae videbantur, manifestissime tradiderunt, rationem seilicet assertioms eorum relinquentes ab his inquirendam, qui spiritus dona excellentia mererentur et praecipue sermonis, sapientiae et scientiae gratiam per ipsum sanctum spiritum percepissent; de aliis vero dixerunt quidem quia sint, quomodo autem aut unde sint, siluerunt, profecto ut studiosiores quique ex posteris suis, qui amatores essent sapientiae, exercitium habere possent, in quo ingenii sui fructum ostenderent, hi videlicet, qui dignos se et capaces ad recipiendam sapientiam praepararent. 4. Species vero eorum, quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo, quod unus est deus, qui omnia creavit atque composuit, quique, cum nihil esset, esse fecit universa, deus a prima creatura et conditione mundi, omnium iustorum deus, Adam Abel Seth Enos Enoch No? Sem Abraham Isaac lacob duodecim patriarcharum Moysei et prophetarum; et quod hie deus in novissimis diebus, sicut per prophetas suos ante promiserat, misit dominum lesum Christum, primo quidem vocaturum Israhel, secundo vero etiam gentes post perfidiam populi Israhel. Hie deus iustus et bonus, pater domini nostri lesu Christi, legem et prophetas et evangelia ipse dedit, qui et apostolorum deus est et veteris ac novi testamenti. Tum deinde quia Christus lesus, ipse qui venit, ante omnem creaturam natus ex patre est. Qui cum in omnium conditione patri ministrasset, “per ipsum” namque “omnia facta sunt”, novissimis temporibus se ipsum exinaniens homo factus est, incarnatus est, cum deus esset, et homo factus mansit quod erat, deus. Corpus assumsit nostro corpori simile, eo solo differens, quod natum ex virgine et spiritu sancto est. Et quoniam hie lesus Christus natus et passus est in veritate, et non per phantasiam, communem hanc mortem vere mortuus; vere enim et a mortuis resurrexit et post resurrectionem conversatus cum diseipulis suis assumtus est. Tum deinde honore ac dignitate patri ac filio sociatum tradiderunt spiritum sanctum. In hoe non iam manifeste discernitur, utrum natus aut innatus, vel filius etiam ipse dei habendus sit, neene; sed inquirenda iam ista pro viribus sunt de sancta scriptura et sagaci perquisitione investiganda. Sane quod iste spiritus sanctus unumquemque sanctorum vel prophetarum vel apostolorum inspiraverit, et non alius spiritus in veteribus, alius vero in his, qui in adventu Christi inspirati sunt, fuerit, manifestissime in ecclesia praedicatur. 9. Post haec iam quod anima substantiam vitamque habens propriam, cum ex hoe mundo discesserit, pro suis meritis dispensabitur, sive vitae aeternae ac beatitudinis hereditate potitura, si hoc ei sua gesta praestiterint, sive igni aeterno ac supplieus mancipanda, si in hoc eam scelerum culpa detorserit; sed et quia erit tempus resurrectionis mortuorum, eum corpus hoc, quod nune “in corruptione seminatur, surget in incorruptionec, et quod “seminatur in ignominia, surget in gloria”. Est et illud definitum in eeclesiastica praedicatione, omnem animam rationabilem esse liberi arbitru et voluntatis; esse quoque ei certamen adversum diabolum et angelos eius contrariasque virtutes, ex eo quod ili peccatis eam onerare contendant, nos vero si recte consulteque vivamus, ab huiuscemodi labe exuere nos conemur. Unde et consequens est intellegere, non nos necessitati esse subiectos, ut omni modo, etiamsi nolimus, vel mala vel bona agere cogamur. Si enim nostri arbitri! sumus, inpugnare nos fortasse possint aliquae virtutes ad peccatum et aliae iuvare ad salutem, non tamen necessitate cogimur vel recte agere vel male; quod fieri arbitrantur hi, qui stellarum cursum et motus causam dieunt humanorum esse gestorum, non solum eorum, quae extra arbitrii accidunt libertatem, sed et eorum, quae in nostra sunt posita potestate. De anima vero utrum ex seminis traduce ducatur, ita ut ratio ipsius vel substantia inserta ipsis corporalibus seminibus habeatur, an vero aliud habeat initium, et hoc ipsum initium si genitum est aut non genitum, vel certe si extrinsecus corpori inditur, necne: non satis manifesta praedicatione distinguitur. 6. De diabolo quoque et angelis eius contrarüsque virtutibus ecelesiastica praedicatio docuit quoniam sint quidem haec, quae autem sint vel quomodo sint, non satis clare exposuit. Apud plurimos tamen ista habetur opinio, quod angelus fuerit iste diabolus, et apostata effectus quam plurimos angelorum secum declinare persuaserit, qui et nune usque angel ipsius nuncupantur. 7. Est praeterea et illud in eeclesiastiea praedicatione, quod mundus iste factus sit et a certo tempore coeperit et sit pro 1psa sui corruptione solvendus. Quid tamen ante hunc mundum fuerit, aut quid post mundum erit, jam non pro manifesto multis innotuit. Non enim evidens de his in ecclesiastica praedicatione sermo profertur. 8. Tum deinde quod per spiritum dei seripturae conscriptae sint et sensum habeant non eum solum, qui in manifesto est, sed et alium quendam latentem quam plurimos. Formae enim sunt haec quae descripta sunt sacramentorum quorundam et divinarum rerum imagines. De quo totius eeclesiae una sententia est, esse quidem omnem legem spiritalem, non tamen ea, quae spirat lex, esse omnibus nota nisi his solis, quibus gratia spiritus sancti in verbo sapientiae ac scientiae condonatur. Appellatio autem (id est incorporei) non solum apud multos alios, verum etiam apud nostras scripturas inusitata est et incognita. Si vero quis velt nobis proferre ex illo libello, qui Petri Doctrina appellatur, ubi salvator videtur ad discipulos dieere: “Non sum daemonium incorporeum”, primo respondendum est ei quoniam liber ipse inter libros eeclesiasticos non habetur, et ostendendum quia neque Petri est ipsa scriptura neque alterius cuiusquam, qui spiritu dei fuerit inspiratus. Quod etiamsi ipsum concederetur, non idem sensus inibi ex isto sermone indicatur, qui a graecis vel gentilibus auctoribus ostenditur, eum de incorporea natura a philosophis disputatur. In hoc enim libello -incorporeum daemonium: dixit pro eo, quod ipse ille quicumque est habitus vel eircumscriptio daemoniei corporis non est similis huie nostro crassiori et visibili corpori; sed secundum sensum eius, qui composuit illam scripturam, intellegendum est quod dixit, id est non se habere tale corpus quale habent daemones (quod est naturaliter subtile quoddam et velut aura tenue, et propter hoe vel putatur a multis vel dicitur incorporeum), sed habere se corpus solidum et palpabile. In consuetudine vero hominum omne, quod tale non fuerit, incorporeum a simplicioribus vel imperitioribus nominatur; velut si quis aérem istum quo fruimur incorporeum dieat, quoniam quidem non est tale corpus, ut conprehendi ac teneri possit urgentique resistere. 9. Quaeremus tamen si vel alio nomine res ipsa, quam graeci philosophi (id est ineorporeum) dicunt, in sanctis scripturis invenitur. Deus quoque ipse quomodo intellegi debeat requirendum est, corporeus et secundum aliquem habitum deformatus, an alterius naturae quam corpora sunt, quod utique in praedicatione nostra manifeste non designatur. Eadem quoque etiam de Christo et de saneto spiritu requirenda sunt, sed et de omni anima atque omni rationabili natura nihilominus requirendum est. Est etiam illud in eeclesiastica praedicatione, esse angelos dei quosdam et virtutes bonas, qui ei ministrant ad salutem hominum con- "^" summandam; sed quando isti creati sint, vel quales, aut quomodo sint, non satis in manifesto distinguitur. De sole autem et luna et stellis, utrum animantia sint an sine anima, manifeste non traditur. Oportet igitur velut elementis ac fundamentis huiusmodi uti secundum mandatum, quod dicit: “Inluminate vobis lumen scientiae”, omnem qui eupit seriem quandam et corpus ex horum omnium ratione perficere, ut manifestis et necessarüs assertionibus de singulis quibusque quid sit in vero rimetur, et unum, ut diximus, corpus efficiat exemplis et affirmationibus, vel his, quas in sanctis scripturis invenerit, vel quas ex consequentiae ipsius indagine ac recti tenore reppererit.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: We hold that certain teachings about God's promises must be grasped when we turn our understanding toward the contemplation of that endless, eternal age of praise, fixing our gaze on its indescribable joy and blessedness.

Yet because the Church's preaching also includes faith in the future judgment of God — a judgment whose certainty stirs people and urges them to live well and blessedly and to flee every kind of sin — it is plainly shown that it lies within our power to commit ourselves either to a praiseworthy life or a blameworthy one. For this reason I consider it necessary to say something, too, about the freedom of our will, since this question is being debated by very many people, and not without dignity.

So that we may more easily understand what freedom of will is, we must ask what the very nature of will and choice desires. Among all things that are moved, some carry the causes of their motion within themselves, while others receive them from outside. For example, everything without life — stones, wood, and whatever consists solely in the disposition of its matter or bodies — is moved only from without. We may set aside for now the question whether the motion of corruption, when bodies dissolve, counts as motion at all, because it does not serve our present purpose.

Other things, however, possess the cause of movement within themselves: animals, trees, and everything that subsists either through natural life or through a soul. Some have thought that even veins of metal, and perhaps the motion of fire and the sources of water, belong in this class. Among these self-moved things, some are said to move from themselves, others from themselves; thus they distinguish those that move from themselves because they live but are not animate, from animate things that move from themselves when fantasy — that is, a certain will or impulse — is present, provoking and urging them to move toward something.

Indeed, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, a will or sense, which by a natural instinct stirs and incites them to ordered and composite movements. We see this in spiders, which are roused to the work of weaving in a remarkably orderly way by a fantasy, that is, by a certain will or zeal for weaving, a natural movement that prompts the intention of this work; yet the animal itself is found to possess no other sense than this natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to fashion honeycombs and honey.

The rational animal, since it also has these natural movements within itself, nevertheless possesses something more than the other animals: the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern among natural movements, rejecting and casting away some, approving and accepting others, so that human movements may be directed and governed toward a worthy life by the judgment of this reason. It follows that, because the nature of this reason in man has within itself the power to distinguish good and evil, and once it has distinguished, there is also in it the faculty of choosing what it has approved. In choosing what is good it is praiseworthy; in following what is base or evil it is justly blameworthy.

We must not overlook the fact that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in others — as in clever dogs or war horses — so that they appear to be moved by a kind of rational sense. But this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain impulse and natural movement, more abundantly granted for such uses.

But to return to our starting point: since the rational animal is so constituted, certain things can befall us from outside and occur — whether to sight, hearing, or other senses — which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements. Because these things happen from outside, it is not in our power to prevent them from happening or occurring. But to judge and determine how we ought to use these things that befall us is the work of nothing other than the reason that is in us, that is, our own judgment. By the judgment of this reason we employ the external incitements toward whatever reason itself has approved, and we govern our natural movements by its nod either toward good or toward contrary things.

If someone should claim that the external occurrences which provoke our movements are such that it is impossible to resist them, whether they incite us to good or to evil: let him turn his mind to himself for a little while and examine his own movements more closely. He will find that when the allurements of some desire strike him, nothing is done before the assent of his mind is given and the nod of his mind yields to the wicked suggestion — so that even in the tribunals of our heart, as it were, with the judge presiding, an argument seems to be made from both sides, that a sentence about the judgment of reason may be pronounced after the causes have been laid out.

For, to take an example, a man who has decided to live continently and chastely and to keep himself from all sexual contact is not forced into sin simply because a woman appears who provokes and entices him to act against his purpose. She is not a perfect and absolute cause or necessity of transgression for him, since he can certainly remember his resolve, restrain the incitements of lust, and curb the delights of the alluring pleasure with the stricter precepts of virtue, so that the firmness and constancy of his purpose may endure with every sense of luxury banished.

Finally, when such incitements come upon more learned men and those strengthened in divine institutions, they, mindful of themselves, immediately recall to memory what they have meditated on and been taught, and, fortifying themselves with the supports of a holier doctrine, they reject and repel every allurement of incitement and drive away contrary desires by the objection of the reason innate to them.

latin: Talia quaedam de repromissionibus divinis credimus sentienda, cum intellegentiam nostram ad contemplationem aeterni illius et nullo fine elaudendi saeculi iaculamur atque ineffabilem eius laetitiam ae beatitudinem contemplamur. Verum quoniam in ecclesiastica praedicatione inest etiam de futuro ‚15 dei (iusto) iudicio fides, quae iudieii eredulitas provocat homines et suadet ad bene beateque vivendum et omni genere refugere peccatum, et per hoc sine dubio indieatur quod in nostra sit positum potestate vel laudabili nos vitae vel culpabili dedere: propterea necessarium reor pauca etiam de arbitrii nostri libertate disserere, eo quod non ignobiliter (20 haee quoque quaestio a quam plurimis agitetur. Ut autem facilius quid sit libertas arbitrii cognoscamus, quid sibi velit natura ipsius arbitrii voluntatisque requiramus. 2. Omnium quae moventur alia in semet ipsis causas motuum suorum gerunt, alia extrinsecus accipiunt: ut puta extrinsecus tantummodo moventur omnia, quae sine vita sunt, ut lapides vel ligna et quaeeumque huiusmodi sunt, quae solo habitu materiae suae vel corporum constant. Omittenda sane nune est illa quaestio, quae etiam illum motum putat esse, cum per corruptelam corpora dissolvuntur; nihil enim nunc haee ad propositum conducunt. Alia vero in semet ipsis habent movendi causam, ut animalia vel arbores et omnia, quae vel per naturalem vitam vel per animam constant; inter quae etiam metallorum venas deputari aliquibus visum est, sed et ignis sui motus esse putandus est, fortassis autem etiam fontes aquarum. Haec autem, quae in semet ipsis causam suorum motuum habent, quaedam dieunt ex se, quaedam ab se moveri; et ita dividunt quod ex se moveantur ea, quae vivunt quidem non tamen animantia sunt, a se autem moveantur animantia, cum eis fantasia, id est voluntas quaedam vel incitamentum, adfuerit, quae ea moveri ad aliquid vel incitari provocaverit. Denique etiam in quibusdam animalibus inest talis fantasia, id est voluntas vel sensus, qui ea natural quodam instinctu provocet et concitet ad ordinatos et conpositos motus; sieut videmus araneas facere, quae fantasia, id est voluntate quadam vel studio textrinae, ad opus texendi ordinatissime concitantur, sine dubio naturali quodam motu intentionem huiuscemodi operis provocante, nec tamen ultra alium ahquem sensum quam texendi naturale studium habere ipsum animal invenitur, sicut et apis fingendi favos ac mella, ut aiunt, aöria congre3. Rationabile vero animal cum habeat in se et hos naturales motus, habet tamen amplius ceteris animalibus etiam rationis vim, qua ludicare et discernere de motibus naturalibus possit et alios quidem reprobare et abicere alios vero probare atque suscipere, cuius rationis iudicio dirigi et gubernari hominis motus ad vitam probabilem possint. Unde consequens est ut, quoniam natura rationis huius, quae est in homine, habet in se vim dinoscendi boni vel mali, idque cum discreverit, inest ei facultas etiam eligendi quod probaverit, in eligendo quidem quod bonum est laudabilis, in sequendo vero quod turpe vel malum est iure culpabilis iudicetur. Illud sane nequaquam latere nos debet, quod in nonnullis mutis animalibus ordinatior quidam motus a ceteris animalibus invenitur, ut in sagacibus canibus vel bellatoribus equis, ita ut videantur aliquibus velut rationabili quodam sensu moveri; sed id non tam ratione quam incentivo quodam et naturah motu, pro huiuscemodi usibus largius indulto, fieri credendum est. Verum ut dieere eoeperamus, cum ita se habeat rationabile animal, nobis hominibus incidere quidem extrinsecus possunt aliqua et occurrere sive ad visum sive ad auditum vel ad alios sensus, quae nos concitent ac provocent ad bonos vel contrarios motus; quae utique quia extrinsecus incidunt, non est in nostra positum potestate ne incidant vel occurrant: iudieare vero et probare, qualiter uti debeamus his, quae incidunt, nullius alterius res est vel opus nisi rationis eius, quae est in nobis, id est nostri iudicii; euius rationis iudicio ineidentibus extrinsecus concitamentis abutimur ad id, quodcumque ipsa ratio probaverit, naturalibus motibus nostris nutu eius vel ad bona vel ad contraria guber4. Si vero quis dicat ea, quae extrinsecus incidunt motus nostros provocantia, talia esse, ut possibile non sit adversari eis, sive ad bonum nos sive ad malum concitantibus: in semet ipsum paulisper qui haee aestimat convertat animum et proprios diligentius introspieiat motus, nisi invenerit, cum alicuius desideri pulsat inlecebra, nihil prius geri quam animi accommodetur assensus et suggestioni pravae nutus mentis indulgeat; ita ut etiam verisimilibus quibusdam causis intra cordis nostri tribunalia velut iudici residenti ex utraque parte adhiberi videatur assertio, ut causis prius expositis gerundi sententia de rationis ludicio proferatur. Non enim, ut verbi gratia dixerim, hule, qui statuit continenter et easte vivere atque ab omni se muliebri contagio continere, si forte apparuerit mulier provocans eum et inliciens aliquid contra propositum gerere, causa ei (perfecta et absoluta) vel necessitas praevaricandi mulier extitit, cum possit utique statuti sui memor libidinis incitamenta refrenare et inritantis inlecebrae delectamenta austerioribus virtutis inerepationibus cohercere, ut omni luxuriae sensu fugato propositi firmitas et constantia perseveret. Denique si eruditioribus quibusque viris et in divinis insütutionibus roboratis huiuscemodi inritamenta provenerint, memores continuo sui, ea quae dudum meditati sunt et in quibus eruditi sunt in memoriam revocantes et sanctioris se doctrinae adminieulis munientes, respuunt ac refellunt omnem incitamenti inleeebram atque adversas concupiscentias insitae sibi rationis obiectione depellunt. 9.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Since we are examining matters of such magnitude, we are not guided by common opinions or by the obviousness of what is seen. Instead, we bring in as additional support for the apparent proof of what we are saying the testimonies drawn from the writings we believe to be divine — both the so-called Old Covenant and the one called the New — and we attempt to reinforce our faith by means of reason. We have not yet spoken of these writings as divine; come then, let us take up a few points about them in summary, setting forth the considerations that move us concerning divine Scripture.

First of all, before we draw on the writings themselves and the statements they contain, we must understand the figures of Moses and Jesus Christ: Moses, the lawgiver of the Hebrews, and Jesus Christ, the expounder of the saving doctrines of Christianity. For among the many lawgivers who have arisen among Greeks and barbarians, and among the many teachers who have proclaimed doctrines promising truth, we find no lawgiver who was able to kindle zeal in other nations to accept his words. Many have brought forward an elaborate preparation accompanied by what seems to be logical proof, promising to philosophize about truth; yet not one has succeeded in planting the truth he himself believed among diverse nations, or even among significant multitudes of a single nation.

And indeed the lawgivers would have wished, if it were possible, to make the laws that appeared good prevail among the whole human race, and the teachers would have wished — or at least imagined — their truth to spread everywhere in the inhabited world. But because they were unable to summon people of other languages and many nations to the observance of their laws and the acceptance of their teachings, they did not even attempt such a thing from the outset, having shrewdly recognized the impossibility of it for themselves.

Yet the whole of Greece and the barbarian world throughout our inhabited world now possess countless zealots who have abandoned their ancestral laws and the gods they once revered, devoting themselves to the observance of the laws of Jesus Christ and to discipleship to his words — even though they are hated by those who venerate idols and by those who adhere to the law of Moses, and even though they face the danger of death because of the hatred directed at those who have received the word of Jesus Christ.

excerpts.citation: Origen — On First Principles Translated from the Latin of Rufinus
excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.locus: Translated from the Latin of Rufinus
english: Since human senses and common understanding are not enough to commit the whole matter to them and, so to speak, to pronounce visibly on invisible things, we must also take up the testimonies of divine scriptures for the proof of what we say. It seems necessary first to show that the scriptures themselves are divine — that is, inspired by the Spirit of God — so that these testimonies may have certain and undoubted authority, whether in what we must still say or in what has already been said. We will therefore briefly set this out from the divine scriptures themselves, which have fittingly moved us, bringing forward the witness of Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and of the words of Jesus Christ, the author and prince of the Christian religion and doctrine (Matthew 10:18; Matthew 24:14; Matthew 7:22-23).

Many lawgivers have existed among Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers or philosophers have promised to assert the truth; yet we recall no lawgiver who could instill any affection or zeal into the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either receive his laws willingly or defend them with all their heart’s intent. No one could insinuate the truth that seemed true to him, not even to a single nation, so that its knowledge or belief would reach everyone. It cannot be doubted that lawgivers wished their laws to be observed by all people, if possible, and that teachers wished the truth they saw to become known to all. But knowing they could not do this at all, and that no such great virtue existed in them to provoke foreign nations to observe their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try or begin, lest they be marked as imprudent and their undertaking prove ineffectual and unending.

Yet in the whole world, in all Greece, and in all foreign nations, innumerable multitudes have abandoned their fathers’ laws and the gods they thought were gods, and have given themselves to the observance of Moses’ law and the discipleship of Christ. They have done this despite great hatred stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are often afflicted by torments and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard the word of Christ’s teaching with all affection. It is evident how the religion itself has grown in a short time, profiting from the punishments and deaths of its adherents, and also from the plundering of goods and every kind of suffering they endured. And it is all the more wonderful that the teachers themselves are neither sufficient nor numerous enough: ‘the sermon is preached in the whole world’, so that ‘Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish’ receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From this there is no doubt that ‘these things are not done by human strength or power’, so that the sermon of Christ Jesus may prevail with all power and credibility in the minds and souls of all.

For it is manifest that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that ‘you will be led before governors and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations’; and again: ‘This gospel will be preached in all nations’; and again: ‘Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you’ (Matthew 10:18; Matthew 24:14; Matthew 7:22-23). If these things had been said by him but had not yet reached the fulfillment of what was predicted, they might seem less true and carry no authority. But now, since the things he predicted have come to pass, and were predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God is truly he who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men.

What then must be said of the fact that the prophets foretold of him beforehand: ‘The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs, and until the expectation of the nations arrives’? It is manifest from history itself and from what is seen today that since the time of Christ no kings have existed among the Jews. All those Jewish boasts in which they gloried and exulted — whether about the temple’s beauty, the altar’s distinction, or all those priestly vestments and high-priestly garments — have been utterly destroyed at once. For the prophecy has been fulfilled that said: ‘For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince; there shall be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood, no oracle’ (Genesis 49:10). We use these testimonies against those who seem to assert that what was said of Judah in Genesis still applies, claiming a ruler from Judah’s line still remains — namely, the one they call their patriarch — and that his line cannot fail until the coming of the Christ they describe for themselves. But if the prophet’s word is true — ‘For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince; there shall be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood’ — and certainly since the temple was overthrown sacrifices are not offered, no altar is found, no priesthood stands: it is certain that ‘the scepter has departed from Judah’ and ‘the ruler’s staff from between his feet’, just as scripture says, until he comes to whom it belongs. Therefore it is established that ‘he has come, to whom it belongs, in whom also the expectation of the nations’ resides. This is manifestly fulfilled in the multitude of those who through Christ have believed in God from diverse nations.

Even in the Song of Deuteronomy it is marked out by prophecy that for the sins of the former people there would be a future election of a foolish nation — none other than this one, which has come about through Christ. For it says: ‘They provoked me to jealousy with their idols; I will provoke them to jealousy with a foolish nation’ (Deuteronomy 32:21). It is therefore sufficiently evident to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have ‘provoked’ God by things that are not gods and to have angered him ‘with their idols,’ have themselves been provoked to jealousy ‘by a foolish nation,’ which God ‘chose’ through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For the apostle says: ‘Consider your calling, brothers; not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that were before’. Therefore let not ‘carnal Israel glory’.

english: In the church's proclamation, the message about God's righteous anointing is contained; once it is believed to be true, it also provokes people to live well and to flee from sin in every way, so that we, having been reconciled to God, may grasp the most necessary problem. To grasp what free will is, we must unfold its concept so that, once clarified, the question at hand may be set out clearly. Some things that are moved have the cause of their movement within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried — wood, stones, and all matter held together by habit alone — are moved only from outside. Let us set aside from the discussion the motion of bodies as such, since it is not needed for our present topic. Animals, plants, and in short all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of movement within themselves; they say that metals belong among these, and that fire is self-moving, and perhaps springs as well. Among the things that have the cause of movement within themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves: the inanimate things are moved from outside themselves, the animate things from themselves. Animate things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs that provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals, fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with their imaginative nature moving the impulse in an orderly way — as in the spider, where a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, because its imaginative nature provokes it to this very thing in an orderly way, and the animal believes nothing else after that nature; and in the bee, toward the shaping of wax. But the rational animal also possesses reason alongside its imaginative nature — reason that judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since the nature of reason contains starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, and by following them we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. Still, we must not ignore that the greater part of the nature ordered to all things exists in animals, and for the most part, or for the lesser part, so that the work of reason in tracking dogs and war horses is, so to speak, close at hand. To undergo something from outside that stirs a fantasy in us, one way or another, is, to be sure, not within our power; but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us — whether it acts in us through the starting points that provoke us toward the good and toward duty, or turns us away toward the opposite.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Jesus therefore turns his disciples away not from simply ignoring magicians and those who promise to perform spectacular feats by whatever means (for his disciples had no need of such a warning) but from those who proclaim themselves to be the Christ of God and try, through certain pretenses, to draw Jesus' disciples to themselves. He does this in the passage where he says: "Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ,' or 'There he is,' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. See, I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out; 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man" (Matt 24:24, 24:26-27). And in the passage where he says: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name and drink in your name and cast out demons in your name and do many mighty works?' And then I will declare to them, 'Depart from me, for you are workers of lawlessness'" (Matt 7:22-23).

Celsus, however, wants to assimilate Jesus' mighty works to the magic practiced among men, and he puts it in these very words: "Oh light and truth," he openly confesses with his own voice, just as you also have written, that others will come to you with similar powers, evil men and magicians, and he names a certain Satan who contrives such things; so that he is not himself uncondemned, as if these works were not divine but the deeds of evil men. Yet, compelled by the truth, he has disclosed both the deeds of others and convicted himself. How then is it not wicked to judge the one as God and the others as magicians based on the same works? For why should the others be deemed evil rather than this one, when he uses the very same testimony? These things he himself has acknowledged are not marks of a divine nature but of certain deceivers and thoroughly wicked men.

Look, then, and see whether Celsus is not clearly refuted as one who corrupts the word, attributing one thing to Jesus when he speaks of those who will perform 'signs and wonders,' and another to the Jew in Celsus's narrative. For if Jesus had simply told his disciples to beware of those who promise mighty works without specifying what they claim to be, his suspicion might have had some foothold. But since Jesus warns us to beware of those who promise to be 'the Christ' — which magicians do not do — and also says that some living wickedly in the name of Jesus will perform mighty works and cast out demons, rather, if one must put it this way, magic and every suspicion about them is proclaimed false, and the divinity of Christ and the divinity of his disciples is vindicated. For it is possible that someone, using his name and I know not how energized by some power to pretend that he himself is the Christ, might seem to accomplish things similar to Christ, and that others, in the name of Jesus, might do things resembling those of his genuine disciples.

greek: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Ἰησοῦς ἐπιστρέφων τοὺς μαθητὰς οὐχὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ [μὴ] προσέχειν ἁπαξαπλῶς γόησι καὶ τοῖς ἐπαγγελλομένοις δι᾿ οἱασδήποτε ὁδοῦ ποιεῖν τεράστια (οὐ γὰρ ἐδέοντο τούτου οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ) ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ τοῦ τοῖς ἀναγορεύουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πειρωμένοις διά τινων φαντασιῶν πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιστρέφειν τοὺς Ἰησοῦ μαθητὰς ὅπου μὲν εἶπε· „τότε ἐάν τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ· ἰδοὺ ὧδε ὁ Χριστὸς ἢ ὧδε, μὴ πιστεύετε. ἐγερθήσονται γὰρ ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται καὶ δώσουσι σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα μεγάλα. ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς. ἰδοὺ προείρηκα ὑμῖν. ἐὰν οὖν εἴπωσιν ὑμῖν· ἰδοὺ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ἐστὶ, μὴ ἐξέλθητε· ἰδοὺ ἐν τοῖς ταμείοις, μὴ πιστεύσητε. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ ἀστραπὴ ἐξέρχεται ἀπ᾿ ἀνατολῶν καὶ φαίνεται ἕως δυσμῶν, οὕτως ἔσται ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου“· ὅπου δέ· „πολλοὶ ἐροῦσί μοι ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ· κύριε, κύριε, οὐ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐφάγομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐπίομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου δαιμόνια ἐξεβάλομεν καὶ δυνάμεις πολλὰς ἐποιήσαμεν; καὶ ἐρῶ αὐτοῖς· ἀποχωρεῖτε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ. ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐργάται ἀδικίας.“ ὁ δὲ Κέλσος κοινοποιῆσαι βουλόμενος τὰ τεράστια τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις γοητείαν φησὶν αὐταῖς λέξεσιν· ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια, τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει, καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε, διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν καὶ ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες, καὶ σατανᾶν τινα τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζει· ᾥστ᾿ οὐδὲ αὐτὸς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. βιαζόμενος δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπεκάλυψε καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ αὑτὸν ἤλεγξε. πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν θεὸν τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων τοὺς ἄλλους πονηροὺς ἢ τοῦτον νομιστέον αὐτῷ χρωμένους μάρτυρι; ταῦτα μέν γε καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησεν οὐχὶ θείας φύσεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπατεώνων τινῶν καὶ παμπονήρων εἶναι γνωρίσματα. ὅρα δὴ εἰ μὴ ἐν τούτοις σαφῶς ὁ Κέλσος ἐλέγχεται κακουργῶν τὸν λόγον, ἄλλο μὲν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λέγοντος περὶ τῶν ποιησόντων „σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα,“ ἄλλο δὲ τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου φάσκοντος. καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὲν ἁπλῶς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἔλεγεν Ἰησοῦς φυλάσσεσθαι τοὺς τὰ τεράστια ἐπαγγελλομένους οὐ παρατιθέμενος, τί φήσουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι, τάχα χώραν εἶχεν ἂν ἡ ὑπόνοια αὐτοῦ· ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἀφ᾿ ὧν θέλει ἡμᾶς φυλάσσεσθαι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπαγγέλλονται εἶναι „ὁ Χριστὸς,“ ὅπερ οὐ ποιοῦσιν οἱ γόητες, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ βιοῦντας κακῶς φησι τινὰς δυνάμεις ποιήσειν καὶ δαίμονας ἀποβαλεῖν ἀνθρώπων· μᾶλλον δ᾿, εἰ δεῖ οὕτως εἰπεῖν, ἀποκηρύσσεται μὲν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἡ γοητεία καὶ πᾶσα ἡ κατ᾿ αὐτῶν ὑπόνοια, εἰσάγεται δὲ ἡ θειότης τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θειότης τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, ὅτι δυνατόν τινα τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ χρησάμενον καὶ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἐνεργηθέντα ὑπό τινος δυνάμεως πρὸς τὸ προσποιήσασθαι, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ Χριστὸς, δοκεῖν τὰ παραπλήσια ἐπιτελεῖν τῷ Χριστῷ καὶ ἄλλους τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὰ ὡσπερεὶ παραπλήσια τοῖς γνησίοις αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: It is a most shameful claim that some Christians and some Jews assert that a certain god or son of a god—described as the justifier of those here—has already come down to earth or will come down, and this charge does not require a lengthy refutation. The text appears to speak accurately concerning Jews, not merely some but all of them, in that they expect a certain figure to come down to earth, while concerning Christians it says that some of them claim he has already come down. It makes clear those who, drawing from Jewish scriptures, construct the sojourn of Christ as something that has already taken place, and it seems aware that there are heresies denying that Jesus Christ is the one who was prophesied. We have already addressed in the earlier sections the matter of Christ having been prophesied, doing so to the best of our ability; therefore we do not repeat most of what could be said on this topic, so as not to be redundant. Consider then that if someone wanted to overturn the faith concerning the prophecies—or concerning Christ's sojourn or his having sojourned—with even a semblance of logical sequence, he ought to have set forth the prophecies themselves, the very ones we Christians and Jews use when debating with each other. Only in that way could he have hoped to overturn, even if it merely seemed plausible, those who are being drawn away by what he thinks is a plausible argument from their assent to the prophetic writings and the faith in Jesus as the Christ that comes through those prophecies. As it stands, however, either he is unable to answer the prophecies about Christ, or he does not even know the first thing about what has been prophesied concerning him; he puts forward not a single prophetic word, even though there are countless such prophecies about Christ, yet he presumes to accuse the prophetic writings without even stating the plausibility he would claim for them. He does not seem to know, moreover, that not all Jews say that the Christ who will come down is God or the Son of God, as we have also said in the preceding passages.

greek: Ὅτι δὲ καὶ Χριστιανῶν τινες καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι, οἱ μὲν καταβεβηκέναι (λέγουσιν,) οἱ δὲ καταβήσεσθαι εἰς τὴν γῆν τινα θεὸν ἢ θεοῦ υἱὸν τῶν τῇδε δικαιωτὴν, τοῦτ᾿ αἴσχιστον, καὶ οὐδὲ δεῖται μακροῦ λόγου ὁ ἔλεγχος. καὶ δοκεῖ γε ἀκριβῶς περὶ μὲν Ἰουδαίων οὐ τινῶν ἀλλὰ πάντων λέγειν ὅτι οἴονταί τινα καταβήσεσθαι ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, περὶ δὲ Χριστιανῶν οτι τινὲς αὐτῶν καταβεβηκέναι λέγουσιν. ἐμφαίνει γὰρ τοὺς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαϊκῶν γραφῶν κατασκευάζοντας τὴν Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίαν ὡς ἤδη γεγενημένην, καὶ ἔοικεν εἰδέναι ὅτι εἰσί τινες αἱρέσεις ἀρνούμεναι Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν εἶναι τὸν πεπροφητευμένον. ἤδη μὲν οὖν καὶ ἐν τοῖς προτέροις περὶ τοῦ πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Χριστὸν κατὰ δύναμιν διειλήφαμεν, διὸ τὰ πολλὰ τῶν δυναμένων λέγεσθαι εἰς τὸν τόπον οὐκ ἐπαναλαμβάνομεν, ἵνα μὴ παλιλλογῶμεν. ὅρα δὴ ὅτι, εἴπερ μετά τινος κἂν δοκούσης ἀκολουθίας ἐβούλετο ἀνατρέπειν τὴν περὶ τῶν προφητειῶν (ἢ) περὶ τοῦ ἐπιδημήσειν ἢ ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τὸν Χριστὸν πίστιν, ἐχρῆν αὐτὸν αὐτὰς ἐκθέσθαι τὰς προφητείας. αἷς ἐν τῷ διαλέγεσθαι πρὸς ἀλλήλους χρώμεθα Χριστιανοὶ καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι· οὕτως γὰρ ἂν κἂν ἔδοξε τοὺς περισπωμένους ὑπὸ τῆς, ὡς οἴεται, πιθανότητος [δοκεῖν] ἀνατρέπειν ἀπὸ τῆς πρὸς τὰ προφητικὰ συγκαταθέσεως καὶ τῆς διὰ τὰ προφητικὰ εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὡς ὄντα Χριστὸν πίστεως· νυνὶ δὲ ἤτοι μὴ δυνάμενος ἀπαντῆσαι πρὸς τὰς περὶ Χριστοῦ προφητείας (ἢ) μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς, τίνα ἐστὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ προφητευόμενα, οὐδεμίαν μὲν λέξιν τίθησι προφητικὴν, καίτοι γε μυρίαι ὅσαι εἰσὶ περὶ Χριστοῦ, κατηγορεῖν δὲ οἴεται τῶν προφητικῶν, μηδ᾿ ἣν εἴποι ἂν ἐκεῖνος πιθανότητα αὐτῶν ἐκθέμενος. οὐκ οἶδε μέντοι γε ὅτι οὐ πάνυ τι Ἰουδαῖοι λέγουσι θεὸν ὄντα τὸν Χριστὸν καταβήσεσθαι ἢ θεοῦ υἱὸν, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρήκαμεν.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Since Celsus dismisses what is said about the so-called antichrist, having read neither Daniel nor Paul nor the Savior's own prophecies in the Gospels about his coming, a brief word on the subject is needed. As the proverb goes, "Just as faces are not alike, so also hearts are not like the hearts of men" (Prov 24:16 LXX). Clearly, then, there are differences among human hearts—some turned toward the good, others toward its opposite through neglect of the good—and among the latter, evil is poured out to a greater degree in some, to a lesser degree in others. So what is so absurd about the existence of two extremes in humanity, as I might call them: one of the good, the other of its opposite? The extreme of the good is found in the man conceived according to Jesus, from whom so great a turning, healing, and betterment of the human race has flowed; the extreme of the opposite resides in the one called antichrist. God, foreknowing all things and seeing the destinies of both, chose to make them known through the prophets, so that those who understand their words might attach themselves to the better and guard against the opposite (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). It was fitting that the one extreme—the best—be proclaimed Son of God because of his excellence, and the other, diametrically opposed to him, be the son of the evil demon, Satan, and the devil. And precisely because evil is most intensely characterized by its outpouring and extremity when it counterfeits the better, signs and wonders and false powers accompany the worse one through the cooperation of his father, the devil. For a cooperation from the devil himself arises—beyond the demonic cooperations that deceive the most worthless of men—in order to deceive the human race. Paul speaks of this so-called antichrist, teaching and setting forth the matter with a certain reserve: how he will appear, when he will come to humankind, and why. And one must ask whether Paul does not treat these things with the utmost dignity, in no way deserving even the slightest contempt.

greek: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ καλουμένου ἀντιχρίστου παραῤῥιπτεῖ ὁ Κέλσος. ουτε τὰ ἐν τῷ Δανιὴλ οὔτε τὰ παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ ἀναγνοὺς περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰρημένα οὔτε τὰ ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις ὑπὸ τοῦ σωτῆρος προφητευθέντα περὶ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ, ὀλίγα καὶ περὶ τούτου λεκτέον. ὅτι „ὥσπερ οὐχ ὅμοια πρόσωπα προσώποις. οὕτως οὐδὲ αἱ καρδίαι ὅμοιαι ταῖς καρδίαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων.“ δῆλον ὅτι εἶεν ἂν ἐν „ταῖς καρδίαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων“ διαφοραὶ καὶ τῶν πρὸς τὸ καλὸν νενευκότων, οὐκ ἐπ᾿ ἴσης καὶ παραπλησίως ἀλλήλοις πάντων τυπωθέντων καὶ μορφωθέντων πρὸς αὐτὸ, καὶ τῶν δι᾿ ἀμέλειαν τοῦ καλοῦ ἐπὶ τὰ ἐναντία ᾀττόντων· καὶ ἐν τούτοις γὰρ ἐν οἷς μέν ἐστι σφόδρα κεχυμένη ἡ κακία ἐν οἷς δ᾿ ἐπ᾿ ἔλαττον· τί οὖν ἄτοπον δύο, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, ἀκρότητας. τὴν μὲν τοῦ καλοῦ τὴν δὲ τοῦ ἐναντίου, ἐν ἀνθρώποις γίνεσθαι, ὥστε τὴν μὲν τοῦ καλοῦ ἀκρότητα εἶναι ἐν τῷ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν νοουμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ, ἀφ᾿ ου ἡ τοσαύτη ἔῤῥευσε τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιστροφὴ καὶ θεραπεία καὶ βελτίωσις, τὴν δὲ τοῦ ἐναντίου ἐν τῷ κατὰ τὸν ὀνομαζόμενον ἀντίχριστον; πάντα δὲ τῇ ἑαυτοῦ προγνώσει ἐκπεριλαβὼν ὁ θεὸς καὶ ἰδὼν τὰ περὶ ἀμφοτέρων τούτων ἐβουλήθη περὶ τούτων γνωρίσαι διὰ τῶν προφητῶν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ἵνα οἱ συνιέντες τῶν λόγων αὐτῶν οἰκειωθῶσι μὲν τῷ κρείττονι. φυλάξωνται δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐναντίου. ἐχρῆν δὲ τὸν μὲν ἕτερον τῶν ἄκρων καὶ βέλτιστον υἱὸν ἀναγορεύεσθαι τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ τὴν ὑπεροχὴν, τὸν δὲ τούτῳ κατὰ διάμετρον ἐναντίον υἱὸν τοῦ πονηροῦ δαίμονος καὶ Σατανᾶ καὶ διαβόλου. εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ τότε μάλιστα τὸ φαῦλον ἐν τῇ χύσει τῆς κακίας καὶ τῇ ἀκρότητι αὐτῆς εἶναι χαρακτηρίζεται, ὅτε ὑποκρίνεται τὸ κρεῖττον, διὰ τοῦτο περὶ τὸν χείρονα γίνεται ἐκ συνεργίας τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ διαβόλου σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα καὶ δυνάμεις ψεύδους. ὑπὲρ γὰρ τὰς εἰς τοὺς γόητας γινομένας ἀπὸ δαιμόνων συνεργίας πρὸς τὰ φαυλότατα τῶν ἀνθρώπους ἀπατώντων γίνεται συνεργία ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐπὶ ἀπάτῃ τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων. Λέγει δὲ ὁ Παῦλος περὶ τούτου τοῦ καλουμένου ἀντιχρίστου διδάσκων καὶ παριστὰς μετά τινος ἐπικρύψεως, τίνα τρόπον ἐπιδημήσει καὶ πότε τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ διὰ τί· καὶ ὅρα εἰ μὴ σεμνότατα περὶ τούτων ὁ Παῦλος ἐκτίθεται καὶ οὐκ ἀξίως χλεύης τινὸς κἂν ἐλαχίστης·

excerpts.author: Origen
english: It is thus that the apostle expresses himself: We beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ , and by our gathering together unto Him, that you be not soon shaken in mind , or be troubled, neither by word, nor by spirit, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of the Lord is at hand. Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come , except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition; who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God , or that is worshipped; so that he sits in the temple of God , showing himself that he is God . Do you not remember that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things? And now you know what withholds, that he might be revealed in his time.

For the mystery of iniquity does already work: only he who now lets will let , until he be taken out of the way. And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of His mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of His coming: even him , whose coming is after the working of Satan , with all power, and signs, and lying wonders, and with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth , that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie ; that they all might be damned who believed not the truth , but had pleasure in unrighteousness. To explain each particular here referred to does not belong to our present purpose.

The prophecy also regarding Antichrist is stated in the book of Daniel, and is fitted to make an intelligent and candid reader admire the words as truly divine and prophetic; for in them are mentioned the things relating to the coming kingdom, beginning with the times of Daniel, and continuing to the destruction of the world. And any one who chooses may read it. Observe, however, whether the prophecy regarding Antichrist be not as follows: And at the latter time of their kingdom, when their sins are coming to the full, there shall arise a king, bold in countenance, and understanding riddles. And his power shall be great, and he shall destroy wonderfully, and prosper, and practise; and shall destroy mighty men, and the holy people.

And the yoke of his chain shall prosper: there is craft in his hand, and he shall magnify himself in his heart, and by craft shall destroy many; and he shall stand up for the destruction of many, and shall crush them as eggs in his hand. What is stated by Paul in the words quoted from him, where he says, so that he sits in the temple of God , showing himself that he is God , is in Daniel referred to in the following fashion: And on the temple shall be the abomination of desolations, and at the end of the time an end shall be put to the desolation.
