greek: Δεῖ οὖν ἡμᾶς περὶ τῶν ἐνεστώτων ἐπιπολὺ ἐραυνῶντας ἐκζητεῖν τὰ δυνάμενα ἡμᾶς σώζειν. φύγωμεν οὑν τελείως ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων τῆς ἀνομίας, μήποτε καταλάβῃ ἡμᾶς τὰ ἔργα τῆς ἀνομίας: καὶ μισήσωμεν τὴν πλάνην τοῦ νῦν καιροῦ, ἵνα εἰς τὸν μέλλοντα ἀγαπηθῶμεν. μὴ δῶμεν τῇ ἑαυτῶν ψυχῇ ἄνεσιν, ὥστε ἔχειν αὐτὴν ἐξουσίαν μετὰ ἁμαρτωλῶν καὶ πονηρῶν συντρέχειν, μήποτε ὁμοιωθῶμεν αὐτοῖς. τὸ τέλειον σκάνδαλον ἤγγικεν, περὶ οὖ γέγραπται, ὡς Ἐνὼχ λέγει. Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ὁ δεσπότης συντέτμηκεν τοὺς καιροὺς καὶ τὰς ἡμέρας, ἵνα ταχύνῃ ὁ ἠγαπημένος αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν κληρονομίαν ἥξῃ, λέγει δὲ οὕτως καὶ ὁ προφήτης: Βασιλεῖαι δέκα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς βασιλεύσουσιν, καὶ ἐξαναστήσεται ὄπισθεν μικρὸς βασιλεύς, ὃς ταπεινώσει τρεῖς ὑφ̓ ἓν τῶν βασιλέων. ὁμοίως περὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λέγει Δανιήλ: Καὶ εἶδον τὸ τέταρτον θηρίον τὸ πονηρὸν καὶ ἰσχυρὸν καὶ χαλεπώτερον παρὰ πάντα τὰ θηρία τῆς θαλάσσης, καὶ ὡς ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἀνέτειλεν δέκα κέρατα, καὶ ἐξ αὐτῶν μικρὸν κέρας παραφυάδιον, καὶ ὡς ἐταπείνωσεν ὑφ̓ ἓν τρία τῶν μεγάλων κεράτων. συνιέναι οὖν ὀφείλετε. ἔτι δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἐρωτῶ ὑμᾶς ὡς εἶς ἐξ ὑμῶν ὤν, ἰδίως δὲ καὶ πάντας ἀγαπῶν ὑπὲρ τὴν ψυχήν μου, προσέχειν νῦν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ μὴ ὁμοιοῦσθαί τισιν ἐπισωρεύοντας ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν λέγοντας, ὅτι ἡ διαθήκη ἐκείνων καὶ ἡμῶν. ἡμῶν μέν: ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνοι οὕτως εἰς τέλος ἀπώλεσαν αὐτὴν λαβόντος ἤδη τοῦ Μωϋσέως. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή: Καὶ ἦν Μωϋσῆς ἐν τῷ ὄρει νηστεύων ἡμέρας τεσσαράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσαράκοντα, καὶ ἔλαβεν τὴν διαθήκην ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου, πλάκας λιθίνας γεγραμμένας τῷ δακτύλῳ τῆς χειρὸς τοῦ κυρίου. ἀλλὰ ἐπιστραφέντες ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα ἀπώλεσαν αὐτήν. λέγει γὰρ οὕτως κύριος. Μωϋσῆ Μωϋσῆ, κατάβηθι τὸ τάχος, ὅτι ἠνόμησεν ὁ λαός σου, οὓς ἐξήγαγες ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου, καὶ συνῆκεν Μωϋσῆς καὶ ἔριψεν τὰς δύο πλάκας ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ: καὶ συνετρίβη αὐτῶν ἡ διαθήκη, ἵνα ἡ τοῦ ἠγαπημένου Ἰησοῦ ἐγκατασφραγισθῇ εἰς τὴν καρδίαν ἡμῶν ἐν ἐλπίδι τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ. πολλὰ δὲ θέλων γράφειν, οὐχ ὡς διδάσκαλος, ἀλλ’ ὡς πρέπει ἀγαπῶντι ἀφ̓ ὧν ἔχομεν μὴ ἐλλείπειν, γράφειν ἐσπούδασα, περίψημα ὑμῶν. διὸ προσέχωμεν ἐν ταῖς ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις: οὐδὲν γὰρ ὠφελήσει ἡμᾶς ὁ πᾶς χρόνος τῆς πίστεως ἡμῶν, ἐὰν μὴ νῦν ἐν τῷ ἀνόμῳ καιρῷ καὶ τοῖς μέλλουσιν σκανδάλοις, ὡς πρέπει υἱοῖς θεοῦ, ἀντιστῶμεν, ἵνα μὴ σχῇ παρείσδυσιν ὁ μέλας. φύγωμεν ἀπὸ πάσης ματαιότητος, μισήσωμεν τελείως τὰ ἔργα τῆς πονηρᾶς ὁδοῦ. μὴ καθ̓ ἑαυτοὺς ἐνδύνοντες μονάζετε ὡς ἤδη δεδικαιωμένοι, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνερχόμενοι συνζητεῖτε περὶ τοῦ κοινῇ συμφέροντος. λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή: Οὐαὶ οἱ συνετοὶ ἑαυτοῖς καὶ ἐνώπιαν ἑαυτῶν ἐπιστήμονες. γενώμεθα πνευματικοί, γενώμεθα ναὸς τέλειος τῷ θεῷ. ἐφ̓ ὅσον ἐστὶν ἐν ἡμῖν, μελετῶμεν τὸν φόβον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ φυλάσσειν ἀγωνιζώμεθα τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ, ἵνα ἐν τοῖς δικαιώμασιν αὐτοῦ εὐφρανθῶμεν. ὁ κύριος ἀπροσωπολήμπτως κρινεῖ τὸν κόσμον. ἕκαστος καθὼς ἐποίησεν κομιεῖται. ἐὰν ᾖ ἀγαθός, ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ προηγήσεται αὐτοῦ: ἐὰν ᾖ πονηρός, ὁ μισθὸς τῆς πονηρίας ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ: ἵνα μήποτε ἐπαναπαύομενοι ὡς κλητοὶ ἐπικαθυπνώσωμεν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν, καὶ ὁ πονηρὸς ἄρχων λαβὼν τὴν καθ̓ ἡμῶν ἐξουσίαν ἀπώσηται ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ κυρίου. ἔτι δὲ κἀκεῖνο, ἀδελφοί μου, νοεῖτε: ὅταν βλέπετε μετὰ τηλικαῦτα σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα γεγονότα ἐν τῷ Ἰσραήλ, καὶ οὕτως ἐγκαταλελεῖφθαι αὐτούς: προσέχωμεν, μήποτε, ὡς γέγραπται, πολλοὶ κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοὶ εὑρεθῶμεν.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Justin: Further, to persuade you that you have not understood anything of the Scriptures , I will remind you of another psalm, dictated to David by the Holy Spirit , which you say refers to Solomon, who was also your king. But it refers also to our Christ. But you deceive yourselves by the ambiguous forms of speech. For where it is said, 'The law of the Lord is perfect,' you do not understand it of the law which was to be after Moses , but of the law which was given by Moses , although God declared that He would establish a new law and a new covenant. And where it has been said, 'O God , give Your judgment to the king,' since Solomon was king, you say that the Psalm refers to him, although the words of the Psalm expressly proclaim that reference is made to the everlasting King, i.e., to Christ .

For Christ is King, and Priest, and God , and Lord, and angel , and man, and captain, and stone, and a Son born, and first made subject to suffering, then returning to heaven, and again coming with glory , and He is preached as having the everlasting kingdom: so I prove from all the Scriptures . But that you may perceive what I have said, I quote the words of the Psalm; they are these: O God , give Your judgment to the king, and Your righteousness unto the king's son, to judge Your people with righteousness, and Your poor with judgment. The mountains shall take up peace to the people, and the little hills righteousness. He shall judge the poor of the people, and shall save the children of the needy, and shall abase the slanderer. He shall co-endure with the sun, and before the moon unto all generations.

He shall come down like rain upon the fleece, as drops falling on the earth. In His days shall righteousness flourish, and abundance of peace until the moon be taken away. And He shall have dominion from sea to sea, and from the rivers unto the ends of the earth. Ethiopians shall fall down before Him, and His enemies shall lick the dust. The kings of Tarshish and the isles shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Seba shall offer gifts; and all the kings of the earth shall worship Him, and all the nations shall serve Him: for He has delivered the poor from the man of power, and the needy that has no helper. He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the needy: He shall redeem their souls from usury and injustice , and His name shall be honourable before them.

And He shall live, and to Him shall be given of the gold of Arabia, and they shall pray continually for Him: they shall bless Him all the day. And there shall be a foundation on the earth, it shall be exalted on the tops of the mountains: His fruit shall be on Lebanon, and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth. His name shall be blessed forever. His name shall endure before the sun; and all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in Him, all nations shall call Him blessed. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel , who only does wondrous things; and blessed be His glorious name for ever, and for ever and ever; and the whole earth shall be filled with His glory . Amen , amen .

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Trypho said, "Overwhelmed by so many passages, I do not know what to say about the passage Isaiah spoke, in which God declares He will not give His glory to another, putting it like this: 'I am the Lord God; this is My name. I will not give My glory to another, nor My virtues' (Isaiah 42:8)." I replied, "If you have spoken these words simply and without malice — having kept silent about what precedes them and without connecting what follows — you are excusable. But if you do it to make it seem you can throw the argument into confusion so that I would say the Scriptures contradict each other, you are deceived. I will never dare to think or say such a thing. Rather, if some passage appears to have a pretext of being contrary, since I am convinced that no Scripture contradicts another, I will admit that I do not understand what has been said, and I will strive to persuade those who think the Scriptures contradict each other to think as I do. How you have framed the problem, God knows. As has been said, I will remind you of the passage so that you may also know from it that God gives His glory to His Christ alone. I will take up a few brief words, men, that are connected with what Trypho said and that follow in the same sequence; for I will not cite them from another section, but as they are joined together under one heading. So attend with your minds. They are these: 'Thus says the Lord God, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and what comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it and spirit to those who walk on it' (Isaiah 42:5). 'I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness; I will take hold of your hand and keep you; I have given you as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations, to open eyes that are blind, to bring out prisoners from the dungeon and those who sit in darkness from the prison house' (Isaiah 42:6-7). 'I am the Lord God; that is My name. I will not give My glory to another, nor My virtues to carved idols' (Isaiah 42:8). 'See, the former things have come to pass, and new things I declare; before they spring up I tell you of them' (Isaiah 42:9). 'Sing to the Lord a new song, His praise from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea and all that is in it, you islands and all who live in them' (Isaiah 42:10). 'Let the wilderness and its towns raise their voices; let the settlements where Kedar lives rejoice. Let the people of Sela sing for joy; let them shout from the mountaintops. Let them give glory to the Lord and proclaim His praise in the islands' (Isaiah 42:11-12). 'The Lord will march out like a champion, like a warrior He will stir up His zeal; with a shout He will raise the battle cry and will triumph over His enemies' (Isaiah 42:13)." Having said these things, I said to them, "Have you perceived, friends, that God says He will give glory to this One, whom He has appointed as a light to the nations, and not to another? Not, as Trypho said, as though God were keeping His glory for Himself?" And Trypho answered, "We have perceived this too; proceed then with the rest of the argument."

greek: Καὶ ὁ Τρύφων ἔφη· Ὑπὸ τῶν τοσούτων γραφῶν δυσωπούμενος οὐκ οἶδα τί φῶ περὶ τῆς γραφῆς ἣν ἔφη Ἡσαΐας, καθ᾿ ἣν ὁ θεὸς οὐδενὶ ἑτέρῳ δοῦναι τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ λέγει, οὕτως εἰπών· Ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεός, τοῦτό μου ὄνομα, τὴν δόξαν μου ἑτέρῳ οὐ μὴ δώσω οὐδὲ τὰς ἀρετάς μου . Κἀγώ· Εἰ μὲν ἁπλῶς καὶ μὴ μετὰ κακὶας τούτους τοὺς λόγους εἰπὼν ἐσίγησας, ὦ Τρύφων, μήτε τοὺς πρὸ αὐτῶν προειπὼν μήτε τοὺς ἐπακολουθοῦντας συνάψας, συγγνωστὸς εἶ, εἰ δὲ χάριν τοῦ νομίζειν δύνασθαι εἰς ἀπορίαν ἐμβάλλειν τὸν λόγον, ἵνα εἴπω ἐναντίας εἶναι τὰς γραφὰς ἀλλήλαις, πεπλάνησαι· οὐ γὰρ τολμήσω τοῦτό ποτε ἢ ἐνθυμηθῆναι ἢ εἰπεῖν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐὰν τοιαύτη τις δοκοῦσα εἶναι γραφὴ προβληθῇ, καὶ πρόφασιν ἔχῃ ὡς ἐναντία οὖσα, ἐκ παντὸς πεπεισμένος ὅτι οὐδεμία γραφὴ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ἐναντία ἐστίν, αὐτὸς μὴ νοεῖν μᾶλλον ὁμολογήσω τὰ εἰρημένα, καὶ τοὺς ἐναντίας τὰς γραφὰς ὑπολαμβάνοντας τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν μᾶλλον ἐμοὶ πεῖσαι ἀγωνίσομαι. Ὅπως δ᾿ ἂν ᾖς προτεθεικὼς τὸ πρόβλημα, θεὸς ἐπίσταται. Ἐγὼ δὲ ὡς εἴρηται ὁ λόγος ἀναμνήσω ὑμᾶς, ὅπως καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τούτου γνωρίσητε ὅτι ὁ θεὸς τῷ Χριστῷ αὐτοῦ μόνῳ τὴν δόξαν δίδωσιν. Ἀναλήψομαι δὲ βραχεῖς τινας λόγους, ὦ ἄνδρες, τοὺς ἐν συναφείᾳ τῶν εἰρημένων ὑπὸ τοῦ Τρύφωνος καὶ τοὺς ὁμοίως συνημμένους κατ᾿ ἐπακολούθησιν· οὐ γὰρ ἐξ ἑτέρας περικοπῆς αὐτοὺς ἐρῶ, ἀλλ᾿ ὑφ᾿ ἓν ὥς εἰσι συνημμένοι· καὶ ὑμεῖς τὸν νοῦν χρήσατέ μοι. Εἰσὶ δὲ οὗτοι· Οὕτως λέγει κύριος ὁ θεός, ὁ ποιήσας τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ πήξας αὐτόν, ὁ στερεώσας τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ, καὶ διδοὺς πνοὴν τῷ λαῷ τῷ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς καὶ πνεῦμα τοῖς πατοῦσιν αὐτήν. Ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἐκάλεσά σε ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, καὶ κρατήσω τῆς χειρός σου καὶ ἰσχύσω σε, καὶ ἔδωκά σε εἰς διαθήκην γένους, εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, ἀνοῖξαι ὀφθαλμοὺς τυφλῶν, ἐξαγαγεῖν ἐκ δεσμῶν πεπεδημένους καὶ ἐξ οἴκου φυλακῆς καθημένους ἐν σκότει. Ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεός, τοῦτό μου ὄνομα, τὴν δόξαν μου ἑτέρῳ οὐ μὴ δώσω οὐδὲ τὰς ἀρετάς μου τοῖς γλυπτοῖς. Τὰ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ἰδοὺ ἥκει, καινὰ ἃ ἐγὼ ἀναγγέλλω. καὶ πρὸ τοῦ ἀναγγεῖλαι ἐδηλώθη ὑμῖν. Ὑμνήσατε τῷ θεῷ ὕμνον καινόν· ἀρχὴ αὐτοῦ ἀπ᾿ ἄκρου τῆς γῆς· οἱ καταβαίνοντες τὴν θάλασσαν καὶ πλέοντες, αἱ νῆσοι καὶ οἱ κατοικοῦντες αὐτάς. Εὐφράνθητι ἔρημος καὶ αἱ κῶμαι αὐτῶν καὶ αἱ ἐπαύλεις, καὶ οἱ κατοικοῦντες Κηδάρ εὐφρανθήσονται, καὶ οἱ κατοικοῦντες πέτραν ἀπ᾿ ἄκρου τῶν ὀρέων βοήσονται, δώσουσι τῷ θεῷ δόξαν, τὰς ἀρετάς αὐτοῦ ἐν ταῖς νήσοις ἀναγγελοῦσι. Κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῶν δυνάμεων ἐξελεύσεται, συντρίψει πόλεμον, ἐπεγερεῖ ζῆλον καὶ βοήσεται ἐπὶ τοὺς ἐχθροὺς μετ᾿ ἰσχύος . Καὶ ταῦτα εἰπὼν ἔφην πρὸς αὐτούς· Νενοήκατε, ὧ φίλοι, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς λέγει δώσειν τούτῳ, ὃν εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν κατέστησε, δόξαν καὶ οὐκ ἄλλῳ τινί, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ, ὡς ἔφη Τρύφων, ὡς ἑαυτῷ κατέχοντος τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν δόξαν; Καὶ ὁ Τρύφων ἀπεκρίνατο· Νενοήκαμεν καὶ τοῦτο· πέραινε τοιγαροῦν καὶ τὰ ἐπίλοιπα τοῦ λόγου.

english: I said, "I will do as you wish." They removed this explanation from the commentaries in which Ezra interpreted the law concerning the Passover: Ezra told the people, "This Passover is our Savior and our refuge. If you reflect and it enters your heart that we are going to humble him by a sign, and after these things we hope in him, this place will not be deserted for all time, says the God of hosts. But if you do not believe in him nor listen to his proclamation, you will be a laughingstock to the nations." They also cut out these words spoken through Jeremiah: "I was like an innocent lamb led to be sacrificed. They devised a plot against me, saying, 'Come, let us put wood into his bread and let us eradicate him from the land of the living, and his name will not be remembered anymore'" (Jer. 11:19). Since this pericope from the words of Jeremiah is still written in some copies of the Jewish synagogues (for they cut these things out a short time ago), it is demonstrated even from these words that the Jews plotted to kill Christ by crucifying him after planning it, and he himself is indicated as the one who was prophesied through Isaiah to be led like a sheep to slaughter, and here he is revealed as an innocent lamb; thus, being at a loss, they proceed to blaspheme. Similarly, they cut out these words from the same Jeremiah: "And the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, remembered his dead who had fallen asleep in the earth of dust, and he went down to them to proclaim the good news of his salvation to them" (cf. 1 Pet. 3:19; 4:6).

greek: Κἀγὼ εἶπον· Ὡς ὑμῖν φίλον, πράξω. Ἀπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἐξηγήσεων, ὧν ἐξηγήσατο Ἔσδρας εἰς τὸν νόμον τὸν περὶ τοῦ πάσχα, τὴν ἐξήγησιν ταύτην ἀφείλοντο· Καὶ εἶπεν Ἔσδρας τῷ λαῷ· Τοῦτο τὸ πάσχα ὁ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν καὶ ἡ καταφυγὴ ἡμῶν. Καὶ ἐὰν διανοηθῆτε καὶ ἀναβῇ ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν, ὅτι μέλλομεν αὐτὸν ταπεινοῦν ἐν σημείῳ, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ἐλπίσωμεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτόν, οὐ μὴ ἐρημωθῇ ὁ τόπος οὗτος εἰς τὸν ἅπαντα χρόνον, λέγει ὁ θεὸς τῶν δυνάμεων· ἂν δὲ μὴ πιστεύσητε αὐτῷ μηδὲ εἰσακούσητε τοῦ κηρύγματος αὐτοῦ. ἔσεσθε ἐπίχαρμα τοῖς ἔθνεσι [Esdr. ?]. Καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν διὰ Ἱερεμίου λεχθέντων ταῦτα περιέκοψαν· Ἐγὼ ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον. φερόμενον τοῦ θύεσθαι. Ἐπ᾿ ἐμὲ ἐλογίζοντο λογισμόν, λέγοντες· Δεῦτε, ἐμβάλωμεν ξύλον εἰς τὸν ἄρτον αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκτρίψωμεν αὐτὸν ἐκ γῆς ζώντων, καὶ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ οὐ μὴ μνησθῇ οὐκέτι [JÉR., XI, 19]. Καὶ ἐπειδὴ αὕτη ή περικοπή, ἡ ἐκ τῶν λόγων τοῦ Ἱερεμίου, ἔτι ἐστὶν ἐγγεγραμμένη ἔν τισιν ἀντιγράφοις τῶν ἐν συναγωγαῖς Ἰουδαίων (πρὸ γὰρ ὀλίγου χρόνου ταῦτα ἐξέκοψαν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ ἐκ τούτων τῶν λόγων ἀποδεικνύηται ὅτι ἐβουλεύσαντο Ἰουδαῖοι περὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀναιρεῖν αὐτὸν σταυρώσαντες βουλευσάμενοι, καὶ αὐτὸς μηνύεται, ὡς καὶ διὰ τοῦ Ἡσαΐου προεφητεύθη, ὡς πρόβατον ἐπὶ σφαγὴν ἀγόμενος , καὶ ἐνθάδε ὡς ἀρνίον ἄκακον δηλοῦται· ὥστ᾿ ἀπορούμενοι ἐπὶ τὸ βλασφημεῖν χωροῦσι. Καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων τοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἱερεμίου ὁμοίως ταῦτα περιέκοψαν· Ἐμνήσθη δὲ κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἅγιος Ἰσραὴλ τῶν νεκρῶν αὐτοῦ, τῶν κεκοιμημένων εἰς γῆν χώματος, καὶ κατέβη πρὸς αὐτοὺς εὐαγγελίσασθαι αὐτοῖς τὸ σωτήριον αὐτοῦ [JÉR. ? cf. I Pierre, III, 19, et IV. 6].

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Consider that we said these things on your behalf, because it is in our power to deny the charges when we are examined. Yet we do not wish to live by speaking falsely; for we, desiring the eternal and pure life, are imitators of the communion with God, the Father of all and Creator, and we hasten to confess. We are convinced and believe that those who have persuaded God through their works are able to obtain these things, because they followed Him and loved His communion, where evil does not stand against them. In short, these are the things we expect, have learned through Christ, and teach. Plato likewise said that Rhadamanthus and Minos would punish the unjust who came before them; we say the same thing will happen, but through Christ, and that in the same bodies together with their souls they will be punished with eternal punishment, not only a thousand-year period as he said. If someone declares this unbelievable or impossible, this error lies with us, not with another, until we are convicted by deed while doing no wrong.

greek: Λογίσασθε δ᾿ ὅτι ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ταῦτα ἔφημεν ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν εἶναι ἀρνεῖσθαι ἐξεταζομένους. Ἀλλ᾿ οὐ βουλόμεθα ζῆν ψευδολογοῦντες· τοῦ γὰρ αἰωνίου καὶ καθαροῦ βίου ἐπιθυμοῦντες τῆς μετὰ θεοῦ τοῦ πάντων πατρὸς καὶ δημιουργοῦ διαγωγῆς ἀντιποιούμεθα, καὶ σπεύδομεν ἐπὶ τὸ ὁμολογεῖν, οἱ πεπεισμένοι καὶ πιστεύοντες τυχεῖν τούτων δύνασθαι τοὺς τὸν θεὸν δι᾿ ἔργων πείσαντας, ὅτι αὐτῷ εἵποντο καὶ τῆς παρ᾿ αὐτῷ διαγωγῆς ἤρων, ἔνθα κακία οὐκ ἀντιτυπεῖ. Ὡς μὲν οὖν διὰ βραχέων εἰπεῖν, ἅ τε προσδοκῶμεν καὶ μεμαθήκαμεν διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ διδάσκομεν, ταῦτά ἐστι. Πλάτων δ᾿ ὁμοίως ἔφη Ῥαδάμανθυν καὶ Μίνω κολάσειν τοὺς ἀδίκους παρ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἐλθόντας· ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ πρᾶγμά φαμεν γενήσεσθαι, ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, κἀν τοῖς αὐτοῖς σώμασι μετὰ τῶν ψυχῶν γινομένων καὶ αἰωνίαν κόλασιν κολασθησομένων, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχὶ χιλιονταετῆ περίοδον, ὡς ἐκεῖνος ἔφη, μόνον. Εἰ μὲν οὖν ἄπιστον ἢ ἀδύνατον τοῦτο φήσει τις, πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἥδε ἡ πλάνη ἐστὶν ἀλλ᾿ οὐ πρὸς ἕτερον, μέχρις οἷ ἔργῳ μηδὲν ἀδικοῦντες ἐλεγχόμεθα.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Trypho responded, "I told you, my friend, that you strive to make your position secure in every way by intertwining yourself with the Scriptures. But tell me this: do you truly confess that this place Jerusalem will be rebuilt, and that your people will be gathered and will rejoice with the Christ, together with the patriarchs, the prophets, and the saints of our race—or even those proselytes who converted before your Christ came? Do you expect this, or did you only agree to confess these things so that you might appear to overcome us in these debates?" I answered, "I am not so foolish, Trypho, as to say things other than what I actually think. I have already confessed to you that I and many others hold this view, fully convinced that it will certainly happen. Yet I also made it clear to you that many who are pure and pious Christians do not share this knowledge. I pointed out to you that those who are called Christians but are actually atheists and impious heretics teach things that are blasphemous, godless, and senseless."

"You know from all the words that have passed between us, as far as my ability allows, that I am not saying these things only about you. I will compile an account in which I will also write, confessing these very things that I now confess to you. For I choose to follow not human teachings more than divine ones, but God and the teachings that come from Him. Even if you have encountered some so-called Christians who do not confess these things, but even dare to blaspheme the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—who also say there is no resurrection of the dead, but that their souls are taken up into heaven the moment they die—do not suppose them to be Christians. Just as, if someone examines the matter correctly, they would not acknowledge the Sadducees or similar sects of Genistae, Meristae, Galilaeans, Hellenians, Pharisees, and Baptists to be true Jews—(please do not be annoyed at hearing all that I think and say)—but only so-called Jews and children of Abraham who confess God with their lips, as God Himself has cried out, yet have their hearts far from Him."

"But as for me, and any who are orthodox Christians in every respect, we know that there will be a resurrection of the flesh, and that Jerusalem will be built, adorned, and enlarged for a thousand years, just as the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah and the others confess." (Ezekiel; Isaiah)

greek: Καὶ ὁ Τρύφων πρὸς ταῦτα ἔφη· Εἶπον πρός σε, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, ὅτι ἀσφαλὴς ἐν πᾶσι σπουδάζεις εἶναι ταῖς γραφαῖς προσπλεκόμενος. Εἰπὲ δέ μοι. ἀληθῶς ὑμεῖς ἀνοικοδομηθῆναι τὸν τόπον Ἱερουσαλὴμ τοῦτον ὁμολογεῖτε, καὶ συναχθήσεσθαι τὸν λαὸν ὑμῶν καὶ εὐφρανθῆναι σὺν τῷ Χριστῷ, ἅμα τοῖς πατριάρχαις καὶ τοῖς προφήταις καὶ τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῦ ἡμετέρου γένους ἢ καὶ τῶν προσηλύτων γενομένων πρὶν ἐλθεῖν ὑμῶν τὸν Χριστόν, προσδοκᾶτε, ἤ, ἵνα δόξῃς περικρατεῖν ἡμῶν ἐν ταῖς ζητήσεσι, πρὸς τὸ ταῦτα ὁμολογεῖν ἐχώρησας; Κἀγὼ εἶπον· Οὐχ οὕτω τάλας ἐγώ, ὦ Τρύφων, ὡς ἕτερα λέγειν παρ᾿ ἃ φρονῶ. Ὡμολόγησα οὖν σοι καὶ πρότερον ὅτι ἐγὼ μὲν καὶ ἄλλοι πολλοὶ ταῦτα φρονοῦμεν, ὡς καὶ πάντως ἐπίστασθαι τοῦτο γενησόμενον· πολλοὺς δ᾿ αὖ καὶ τῶν τῆς καθαρᾶς καὶ εὐσεβοῦς ὄντων Χριστιανῶν γνώμης τοῦτο μὴ γνωρίζειν ἐσήμανά σοι. Τοὺς γὰρ λεγομένους μὲν Χριστιανούς, ὄντας δὲ ἀθέους καὶ ἀσεβεῖς αἱρεσιώτας, ὅτι κατὰ πάντα βλάσφημα καὶ ἄθεα καὶ ἀνόητα διδάσκουσιν, ἐδήλωσά σοι. Ὅτι δ᾿ οὐκ ἐφ᾿ ὑμῶν μόνων τοῦτο λέγειν με ἐπίστασθε, τῶν γεγενημένων ἡμῖν λόγων ἁπάντων, ὡς δύναμίς μου, σύνταξιν ποιήσομαι, ἐν οἷς καὶ τοῦτο ὁμολογοῦντά με, ὃ καὶ πρὸς ὑμᾶς ὁμολογῶ, ἐγγράψω. Οὐ γὰρ ἀνθρώποις μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρωπίνοις διδάγμασιν αἱροῦμαι ἀκολουθεῖν, ἀλλὰ θεῷ καὶ τοῖς παρ᾿ ἐκείνου διδάγμασιν. Εἰ γὰρ καὶ συνεβάλετε ὑμεῖς τισι λεγομένοις Χριστιανοῖς. καὶ τοῦτο μὴ ὁμολογοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλασφημεῖν τολμῶσι τὸν θεὸν Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τὸν θεὸν Ἰσαὰκ καὶ τὸν θεὸν Ἰακώβ. οἳ καὶ λέγουσι μὴ εἶναι νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν, ἀλλὰ ἅμα τῷ ἀποθνήσκειν τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, μὴ ὑπολάβητε αὐτοὺς Χριστιανούς, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ Ἰουδαίους, ἄν τις ὀρθῶς ἐξετάσῃ, ὁμολογήσειεν εἶναι τοὺς Σαδδουκαίους ἢ τὰς ὁμοίας αἱρέσεις Γενιστῶν καὶ Μεριστῶν καὶ Γαλιλαίων καὶ Ἑλληνιανῶν καὶ Φαρισαίων καὶ Βαπτιστῶν (καὶ μὴ ἀηδῶς ἀκούσητέ μου πάντα ἃ φρονῶ λέγοντος), ἀλλὰ λεγομένους μὲν Ἰουδαίους καὶ τέκνα Ἀβραάμ, καὶ χείλεσιν ὁμολογοῦντας τὸν θεόν, ὡς αὐτὸς κέκραγεν ὁ θεός, τὴν δὲ καρδίαν πόρρω ἔχειν ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ . Ἐγὼ δέ, καὶ εἴ τινές εἰσιν ὁρθογνώμονες κατὰ πάντα Χριστιανοί, καὶ σαρκὸς ἀνάστασιν γενήσεσθαι ἐπιστάμεθα καὶ χίλια ἔτη ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ οἰκοδομηθείσῃ καὶ κοσμηθείσῃ καὶ πλατυνθείσῃ. ὡς οἱ προφῆται Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ Ήσαΐας [voy. ch. suivant] καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι ὁμολογοῦσιν.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: For Isaiah spoke thus concerning this millennium: The heaven will be new and the earth new, and they will not remember the former things nor will these come to mind; instead they will find joy and gladness in what I create. For behold, I make Jerusalem a gladness and my people a joy, and I will rejoice over Jerusalem and be glad over my people. No longer will the sound of weeping be heard in it, nor the sound of crying. No longer will a youth die before his time, nor an old man who has not filled his days; for the boy will be a hundred years old, and the sinner who dies at a hundred years will be accursed. They will build houses and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They will not build for others to inhabit, nor plant for others to eat; for as the days of the tree of life, so will be the days of my people, and the works of their hands will wear out. My chosen ones will not labor in vain, nor bear children for a curse; for they are a righteous and blessed seed of the Lord, and their offspring with them. Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will say, 'What is it?' Then wolves and lambs will graze together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, and dust will be the serpent's food. They will not do evil or destroy on all my holy mountain, says the Lord (Isaiah 65:17-25).

Concerning what was said in these words — 'As the days of the tree, so will be the days of my people, and the works of their labors will wear out' — we have understood that it signifies a thousand years in a mystery. For as it was said to Adam, 'On the day you eat from it you will die' (Genesis 2:17), we know that he did not complete a thousand years. We also understood the saying, 'A day of the Lord is like a thousand years' (Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8), as pointing to this. And later, among us, a man named John, one of Christ's apostles, prophesied in a revelation that those who believe in our Christ will spend a thousand years in Jerusalem. And after these things the universal and, in a word, eternal resurrection of all will take place together with judgment. Our Lord also said this: 'They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven, being children of God, children of the resurrection' (Luke 20:35-36).

greek: Οὕτως γὰρ Ἡσαΐας περὶ τῆς χιλιονταετηρίδος ταύτης εἶπεν· Ἔσται γὰρ ὁ οὐρανὸς καινὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ καινή, καὶ οὐ μὴ μνησθῶσι τῶν προτέρων οὐδὲ μὴ ἐπέλθῃ αὐτῶν ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν, ἀλλ᾿ εὐφροσύνην καὶ ἀγαλλίαμα εὑρήσουσιν ἐν αὐτῇ, ὅσα ἐγὼ κτίζω· ὅτι ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ποιῶ τὴν Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἀγαλλίαμα καὶ τὸν λαόν μου εὐφροσύνην, καὶ ἀγαλλιάσομαι ἐπὶ Ἰερουσαλὴμ καὶ εὐφρανθήσομαι ἐπὶ τῷ λαῷ μου. Καὶ οὐκέτι οὐ μὴ ἀκουσθῇ ἐν αὐτῇ φωνὴ κλαυθμοῦ οὐδὲ φωνὴ κραυγῆς, καὶ οὐ μὴ γένηται ἔτι ἐκεῖ ἄωρος ἡμέραις καὶ πρεσβύτης ὃς οὐκ ἐμπλήσει τὸν χρόνον αὐτοῦ· ἔσται γὰρ ὁ νέος υἱὸς ἑκατὸν ἐτῶν, ὁ δὲ ἀποθνήσκων ἁμαρτωλὸς υἱὸς ἑκατὸν ἐτῶν καὶ ἐπικατάρατος ἔσται. Καὶ οἰκοδομήσουσιν οἰκίας καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐνοικήσουσι, καὶ καταφυτεύσουσιν ἀμπελῶνας καὶ αὐτοὶ φάγονται τὰ γεννήματα αὐτῶν. Οὐ μὴ οἰκοδομήσωσι καὶ ἄλλοι κατοικήσουσι, καὶ οὐ μὴ φυτεύσωσι καὶ ἄλλοι φάγονται· κατὰ γὰρ τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἔσονται, τὰ ἔργα τῶν πόνων αὐτῶν παλαιώσουσιν. Οἱ ἐκλεκτοί μου οὐ μὴ πονέσουσιν εἰς κενὸν οὐδὲ τεκνοποιήσουσιν εἰς κατάραν· ὅτι σπέρμα δίκαιον καὶ εὐλογημένον ὑπὸ κυρίου ἔσονται, καὶ ἔγγονα αὐτῶν μετ᾿ αὐτῶν. Καὶ ἔσται πρὶν ἢ κεκράξαι αὐτοὺς ἐγὼ ἐπακούσομαι αὐτῶν· ἔτι λαλούντων αὐτῶν ἐρῶ· Τί ἐστι; Τότε λύκοι καὶ ἄρνες ἅμα βοσκηθήσονται, καὶ λέων ὡς βοῦς φάγεται ἄχυρα, ὄφις δὲ γῆν ὡς ἄρτον. Οὐκ ἀδικήσουσιν οὐδὲ λυμανοῦνται ἐπὶ τῷ ὄρει τῷ ἁγίῳ, λέγει κύριος . Τὸ οὖν εἰρημένον ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τούτοις, ἔφην· Κατὰ γὰρ τὰς ἡμέρας τοῦ ξύλου αἱ ἡμέραι τοῦ λαοῦ μου ἔσονται, τὰ ἔργα τῶν πόνων αὐτῶν παλαιώσουσι , νενοήκαμεν ὅτι χίλια ἔτη ἐν μυστηρίῳ μηνύει. Ὡς γὰρ τῷ Ἀδὰμ εἴρητο, ὅτι ᾗ δ᾿ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ ξύλου, ἐν ἐκείνῃ ἀποθανεῖται , ἔγνωμεν αὐτὸν μὴ ἀναπληρώσαντα χίλια ἔτη. Συνήκαμεν καὶ τὸ εἰρημένον, ὅτι Ἡμέρα κυρίου ὡς χίλια ἔτη , εἰς τοῦτο συνάγειν. Καὶ ἔπειτα καὶ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀνήρ τις, ᾧ ὄνομα Ἰωάννης, εἷς τῶν ἀποστόλων τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐν ἀποκαλύψει γενομένῃ αὐτῷ χίλια ἔτη ποιήσειν ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ τοὺς τῷ ἡμετέρῳ Χριστῷ πιστεύσαντας προεφήτευσε . καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα τὴν καθολικὴν καί, συνελόντι φάναι, αἰωνίαν ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἅμα πάντων ἀνάστασιν γενήσεσθαι καὶ κρίσιν. Ὅπερ καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἶπεν, ὅτι Οὔτε γαμήσουσιν οὔτε γαμηθήσονται, ἀλλὰ ἰσάγγελοι ἔσονται, τέκνα τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ὄντες .

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We cannot know God by measuring his magnitude, because the Father cannot be measured; but his love draws us to him through his Word, and as we obey that Word we keep learning just how great God truly is. He himself, in his own person, establishes, chooses, and adorns all things in a way that relates to us, and we ourselves have been made from what he contains. This is what Scripture declares: "Then the Lord God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Angels did not make us, nor did they shape us; angels could not fashion the image of God, nor could anyone else except the Word of the Lord, and certainly no power that stands far removed from the Father. God did not need such beings to carry out what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present to him; through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things. He speaks to them, saying, "Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness" (Genesis 1:26), himself drawing the substance of creatures, the pattern of his works, and the form of the world's adornments from his own being.

Et nos igitur cum his que continentur ab eo, factisumus. Et hic est de quo Scriptura ait; Ht plasmavit Deus hominem, limum terre accipiens, et insufflavit in faciem ejus Jjlatum vite. Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis preter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre uniNec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quie ipse apud se preefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ipse a semetipso substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: For this reason he came to his passion: to preach the gospel to Abraham and those with him, opening the inheritance. Having given thanks, he took the cup, drank from it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, "Drink from it, all of you. This is my blood of the new Testament, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:27-28). I tell you, from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom (Matt 26:29). Indeed, he himself will renew the inheritance of the earth and restore the mystery of the glorification of the sons; just as David says: "Who promised to drink of the fruit of the vine with his disciples," showing both the inheritance of the earth in which the new fruit of the vine is drunk, and the bodily resurrection of the disciples (Ps 110:1; Acts 2:30-31). For the new flesh that rises is the very flesh that also receives the drink from the vine; it is proper to the flesh, not the spirit, to receive what comes from the vine. Neither can it be understood that he drinks the fruit of the vine up in a super-celestial place, seated there with his disciples; nor again are those who drink it without flesh, for it belongs to the flesh, not the spirit, to receive drink from the vine.

And for this reason the Lord said: "When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite the rich, nor your friends, brothers, or relatives, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But invite the lame, the blind, the poor, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just" (Luke 14:12-14). And again he says: "Whoever leaves fields, or houses, or parents, or brothers, or children for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the age to come" (Matt 19:29; Mark 10:30). For in this age there are a hundredfold — meals given to the poor, and suppers that are returned. These belong to the times of the Kingdom, that is, the seventh day, which is sanctified, in which God rested from all the works he made (Gen 2:2-3) — which is truly the Sabbath of the just, in which they will not do every work for God, while he feeds them with every delight.

Just as Isaac contains the blessing by which he blessed the younger Jacob: "Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field, which God has blessed" (Gen 27:27). The field is the world, and therefore he added: "May God give you the dew of heaven, and the richness of the earth; may peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you" (Gen 27:28-29). If anyone does not receive these things according to the appointed times of the Kingdom, they will fall into great contradiction and contrariety, just as the Jews fall into every difficulty. For not only in this life did the nations not serve this Jacob; but after the blessing he went and served his uncle Laban the Syrian for twenty years (Gen 29-31). And not only was he not made lord over his brother, but Esau bowed down to his brother when he returned from Mesopotamia to his father, and offered him many gifts (Gen 33:3-11). How then did he inherit a multitude of wheat and wine, he who, because of the famine in the land where he lived, migrated to Egypt, subject to Pharaoh who then reigned in Egypt (Gen 46-47)? Therefore the aforementioned blessing pertains to the times of the Kingdom without contradiction, when the just, rising from the dead, will reign: when also the creation, renewed and set free, will produce an abundance of fruit from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth (Rom 8:21). Just as the presbyters remembered, those who saw John the disciple of the Lord and heard from him how he taught about those times, saying: "Days will come when vines will grow, each having ten thousand branches, and on one branch ten thousand shoots, and on one shoot ten thousand clusters, and on each cluster ten thousand grapes, and each grape pressed will give twenty-five measures of wine. And when one of the saints takes hold of a cluster, another will cry out: 'I am a better cluster; take me, and through me bless the Lord.' Likewise a grain of wheat will produce ten thousand ears, and each ear will have ten thousand grains, and each grain will yield five pounds of the purest flour; and the rest of the fruits, seeds, and herbs will follow in like proportion. And all animals, feeding on these foods taken from the earth, will become peaceful and harmonious with one another, subject to humans in all subjection."

Papias, hearer of John and companion of Polycarp, an old man, bears witness in writing in the fourth of his five books. He adds: "These things are credible to those who believe. And Judas," he says, "the betrayer, not believing, asked: 'How then will the Lord accomplish such harvests?' The Lord said: 'Those who come into those times will see.'" Therefore Isaiah prophesies about these times: "The wolf will feed with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the kid; the calf and the young lion and the fatling together, and a little child will lead them" (Isaiah 11:6). "The cow and the bear will graze together; their young will lie down together; the lion will eat straw like the ox. The nursing child will play by the cobra's hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper's den. They will not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain" (Isaiah 11:7-8). And again, recapitulating, he says: "Then the wolf and the lamb will feed together, the lion will eat straw like the ox, and the serpent will eat dust like bread. They will not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, says the Lord" (Isaiah 65:25). I am not unaware that some, believing these things to refer to wild beasts and diverse nations and various works, and having believed, consenting with the just, try to transfer them. Although this may happen now in some people, from diverse nations coming into one faith, nevertheless in the resurrection of the just, over these animals, as has been said — for God is rich in all things — it is necessary, the condition having been restored, that all animals obey and be subject to humans, and return to the first food given by God, just as they were subject to Adam in obedience, the fruit of the earth. But it is also shown now that the lion eats straw. This signifies the greatness and richness of the fruits. For if the lion, an animal, eats straw, what kind of wheat will it be, whose straw will be suitable food for lions?

Non ignoro autem, quoniam quidam hee in feros et ex diversis gentibus, et variis operibus credentes, et cum crediderint consentientes justis, tentent transferre. etsi nunc hoc sit in quibusdam hominibus, ex variis gentibus in unam sententiam fidei venientibus, nihilominus in rejustorum super iis animalibus, quemadmodum dictum est: Dives enim in omnibus Deus. excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: If some try to allegorize these things, they will not be able to square their readings with themselves on every point; the very words will convict them. For when the cities of the nations have been deserted, the houses left empty because no one lives in them, and the earth abandoned, see what Isaiah says: "The day of the Lord is coming, incurable, full of fury and wrath, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it" (Isaiah 13:9; Isaiah 13:19). And again he says: "Let him be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord." When these things have come to pass, God will prolong the days of men, and those left behind will multiply on the earth. They will build houses and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit. These words were spoken without controversy about the resurrection of the just, which takes place after the coming of the Antichrist and the destruction of all the nations that exist under heaven. In that time the just will reign on the earth, growing from the vision of the Lord, and through him they will become accustomed to taking the glory of God; the unity of spiritual things they will take up in the kingdom. They are those whom the Lord finds on the earth, waiting for him from heaven, who have endured tribulation and escaped the hands of the wicked. These are the ones of whom the prophet says: "And those who have been left behind will multiply on the earth." As many believers as God has prepared for this—to be left on the earth and to serve under the Kingdom of the Saints, ministering to this Jerusalem and the kingdom in it—Jeremiah the prophet has signified, saying: "Look toward the East, Jerusalem, and see the joy that comes to you from God himself. Behold, your sons whom you sent away will come, gathered from East to West by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the glory that is from your God. Put off, Jerusalem, the garment of your mourning and affliction, and put on forever the beauty of the glory from your God. Wrap yourself in the double garment of righteousness from your God; set upon your head the mitre of eternal glory. For God will show to her all your splendor under heaven. Your name will be called by God forever: Peace of Righteousness and Glory of God's Worship. Arise, Jerusalem, stand on the height; look toward the East, and see your children gathered from the rising of the sun to its setting by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of God. For they went out on foot, led away by enemies; but God will bring them back to you, carried in glory as on a royal throne. For God has decreed that every high mountain be humbled and the ancient hills brought low, that the valleys be filled to make the ground level, so that Israel may walk securely in the glory of God. The woods have shaded the sycamores, and the sweet-smelling wood, by God's command, for Israel. For God will lead them with joy, in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness that proceed from him.

But all these things cannot be understood as belonging to a super-celestial realm; for God says he will show to her what is under heaven, your splendor. Rather, they belong to the times of the Kingdom, when the earth has been recalled by Christ and Jerusalem rebuilt according to the pattern that is above—Jerusalem about which the prophet Isaiah says: "Behold, I have engraved your walls on my palms; you are continually before me." And the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says the same: "But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother" (Galatians 4:26)—not from the fantasy of an erratic Aeon, nor by any virtue that flowed out of the Pleroma and the Prunicus, but from the Jerusalem that is described in the hands of God. And John saw her descending upon the earth, new, in the Apocalypse. For after the times of the Kingdom, he says: "I saw a great white throne and him who sat on it; from his face earth and heaven fled away, and no place was found for them" (Revelation 20:11). And he describes the things of the general resurrection and judgment: "The sea gave up the dead that were in it, Death and Hades gave up the dead that were in them, and the books were opened. The book of life was opened, and the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to their deeds. Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire, the second death" (Revelation 20:12-14). This is what is called Gehenna, which the Lord called eternal fire. "And if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire" (Revelation 20:15). After these things he says: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: 'Behold, the dwelling of God is with men; he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away'" (Revelation 21:1-4). And Isaiah says the same: "They shall obtain joy and gladness." This is what the Apostle said: "The fashion of this world is passing away." Likewise the Lord says: "Heaven and earth will pass away." When these things have passed away, the Lord's disciple John says that the new and higher Jerusalem will be on the earth, as a bride adorned for her husband; and this is the tabernacle of God in which God will dwell with men. The image of this Jerusalem is the Jerusalem that existed on the former earth, in which the just are prepared for incorruption and made ready for salvation. Moses received the type of this tabernacle on the mountain; and nothing can be allegorized, but all things are firm, true, and substantial, made by God for the enjoyment of the just. For just as God truly raises man, so he truly rose from the dead, not allegorically, as we have shown through so many proofs. And just as he truly rose, so he will truly be prepared for incorruption, and will increase and flourish in the times of the kingdom, that he may become capable of the glory of the Father. Then, when all things have been renewed, he will truly dwell in the city of God. For he who sits on the throne says: "Behold, I make all things new." And the Lord says: "Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true." And he said to me: "It is done." And this accords with reason.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: In this world some run toward the light and, through faith, join themselves to God, while others turn away from the light and separate themselves from him. The Word of God comes bringing a dwelling suited to everyone: for those who are in the light, that they may enjoy it and the good things within it; for those who are in darkness, that they may share in the calamities that belong to them. Therefore he says that those on the right are called into the kingdom of the Father, but those on the left are sent into eternal fire, because they have deprived themselves of every good (Matt 25:34, 41).

For this reason the Apostle declares: because they did not receive the love of God so as to be saved, God will send them a working of error, so that they believe a lie, so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged (2 Thess 2:10-12). When that one comes, he will recapitulate the apostasy in himself by his own sentence, and by his own will and choice he will do whatever he does, and he will sit in the temple of God so that those he deceives may worship him as Christ; therefore they will justly be thrown into the lake of fire (2 Thess 2:4; Rev 19:20). Yet God, according to his providence, foreknows all things and at the fitting time sends the one who is to be such a person, so that they may believe falsehood, so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged.

John signified his coming in the Apocalypse: the beast I saw was like a leopard, its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth like a lion's mouth; the dragon gave it his power, his throne, and great authority (Rev 13:1-2). One of its heads seemed to have been slain to death, but its death wound was healed, and the whole earth marveled and followed the beast; they worshiped the dragon because he had given authority to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, 'Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?' (Rev 13:3-4). A mouth speaking great things and blasphemies was given to it, and authority to act for forty-two months (Rev 13:5). It opened its mouth to blaspheme God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling place, and those who dwell in heaven (Rev 13:6). Authority was given it over every tribe, people, language, and nation, and all who dwell on the earth worshiped it—everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain (Rev 13:7-8). If anyone has an ear, let him hear. If anyone is to be taken captive, to captivity he goes; if anyone is to be killed with the sword, with the sword he must be killed. Here is the endurance and faith of the saints (Rev 13:9-10).

Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth, the one he calls the false prophet. It spoke like a dragon and exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and it made the earth and its inhabitants worship the first beast, whose death wound had been healed (Rev 13:11-12). It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth before people, and by these signs it deceives the inhabitants of the earth (Rev 13:13-14). No one should think it does these signs by divine power, but by magical operation; it is no wonder, since demons and apostate spirits serve it and through them it performs signs and deceives the earth's inhabitants (Rev 13:14; 16:13-14). It will order an image of the beast to be made, give breath to the image so that it can speak, and cause all who refuse to worship the image to be killed (Rev 13:15). It will also cause a mark to be put on the right hand or forehead of everyone, so that no one can buy or sell unless they have the mark, that is, the name of the beast or the number of its name (Rev 13:16-17). The number is six hundred sixty-six: six times one hundred, plus ten times seven, plus six; this sums up the whole apostasy that has taken place over six thousand years (Rev 13:18).

For as many days as the world was made, so many thousands of years it will be completed. Therefore Scripture says: 'And the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their host. And on the sixth day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done' (Gen 2:1-2). This is both a narrative of past things and a prophecy of future things. For the day of the Lord is like a thousand years (Ps 90:4); in six days the things that were made were finished, so it is clear that their completion comes in the sixth thousandth year.

For this reason, at every time the human being, formed at the beginning by the hands of God—that is, by the Son and the Spirit—is made according to the image and likeness of God, casting away the chaff, which are the apostasies, but gathering the wheat into the storehouse, which are those who bear fruit in faith toward God (Matt 3:12). Therefore tribulation is necessary for those who are saved, so that—being in a sense broken, refined, and sprinkled with patience by the Word of God, and kindled—they may become fit for the banquet of the King. As one of ours said, when he was condemned to the beasts for the testimony of God: 'I am the wheat of Christ, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of God' (Ignatius, Romans 4:1). All things were made for the benefit of humanity; and the snares of the Antichrist, his wickedness, and apostate power were prefigured from the flood onward, and afterward in the persecution of Ananias, Azarias, and Misael (Dan 3).

excerpts.author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: No human can fully explain the narrative and the entire ordering of the six days, not even if they possessed countless mouths and tongues; nor would they succeed even if they lived countless years in this life, because the surpassing greatness and the wealth of God's wisdom contained in those six days exceed any capacity to speak worthily.

Many writers have imitated and attempted to produce an account of these matters, drawing their starting points from the creation of the world or human nature, yet they have not uttered a single word worthy of the truth.

The statements of philosophers, writers, and poets appear trustworthy because of their polished phrasing, but their discourse is shown to be foolish and empty, for it contains a great abundance of nonsense and no truth; even when something true seems to be spoken through them, it is mixed with error, just as a poisonous drug mixed with honey or wine makes the whole mixture harmful and useless, so their verbosity proves a useless and harmful pursuit for those who believe it.

Concerning the seventh day, which all people name but most ignore, the Hebrews call it Sabbath, which translates into Greek as 'seventh day'; it is named among all generations, yet they do not know why it is called that.

The poet Hesiod's claim that Chaos gave birth to Erebus, Earth, and Eros, who rules over gods and humans according to him, is shown to be vain, cold, and alien to all truth, for God should not be overcome by pleasure, whereas even self‑controlled people avoid all shameful pleasure and evil desire.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The highest antiquity claims the first authority for these writings. Among you, too, asserting faith from the records of time is a kind of religious standard.

Consider Moses, the first prophet. He began with the creation of the world, the multiplication of the human race, and the avenging force of the flood that punished the wickedness of that age. Through prophecy he sketched images of future events up to his own day, and through his own actions thereafter. He also arranged the chronological order from the beginning, providing a calculation of the world's age that predates your earliest records by about three hundred years — earlier than Danaus who sailed to Argos in the Argo, and roughly a thousand years before the Trojan War, from which you even trace Saturn himself. Thallus' history corroborates this: it records the war of the Assyrians and the battle of Saturn, king of the Titans, against Jupiter, showing that this war preceded the fall of Ilium by 302 years. Through Moses, God also gave the Law proper to the Jews.

After him came many other prophets, older than your literature. Even the last of them, Zechariah — who either slightly anticipated or at least coincided with your sages and lawgivers — prophesied under Cyrus and Darius. In that era, Thales, the prince of physicists, could give Croesus no certain answer about the Divine, clearly unsettled by the prophets' voices. Solon likewise warned that same king to look to the end of a long life, in terms no different from the prophets'. Thus it is evident that both your laws and your philosophical studies have drawn their conception from the Law and divine teaching. What comes first must be the seed; from it you hold certain things in common with us, or at least near us. The love of wisdom was named philosophy; the emulation of prophecy refined poetic prophecy into something purer. Famous men, when they discovered something, adulterated it to claim it as their own, and the fruits degenerated from the seed. I could press many more arguments for the antiquity of the divine writings, but a greater authority supports faith in their truth than mere annals: the daily testimony of the whole age. The dispositions of kingdoms, the falls of cities, the exits of nations, the conditions of the times — all answer to what was predicted thousands of years ago. From this our hope — which you mock — is encouraged, and our confidence — which you call presumption — is strengthened. Knowledge of the past is the proper basis for confidence in the future: the same voices foretold both, the same writings recorded them. There is a single timeline in Scripture that appears divided to us. Therefore we reject everything that remains unfulfilled, because those things were predicted as future alongside the ones already verified.

You also possess, as far as I know, the Sibyl — insofar as the title of the true prophet of the true God has been usurped by her above all others who seemed to prophesy, just as your Sibyl's name is a lie from the truth, and so are your gods. Therefore the archive of a single prophet — Moses — surpasses all substances, all materials, origins, orders, and veins of every ancient style of yours, most nations and notable cities, the hoary records of histories and memories, the very images of writings, the indices and guardians of facts, and (I think we understate it) even your gods themselves, their temples, oracles, and sacred rites. In that archive lies the treasure of the entire Jewish sacrament, and from it, ours as well. If you have heard of Moses, know that he is coeval with Argive Inachus; he precedes Danaus by nearly four hundred years — seven years short — and the fall of Priam by about a thousand. I could even say he predates Homer by more than five hundred years, and I have authorities to follow. The other prophets, though later than Moses, are still not more recent than your earliest sages, lawgivers, and historians. Demonstrating the chronological orders that prove this is not so much difficult as enormous — not arduous, but long. It requires many instruments, with finger-reckoning and calculations. The archives of the most ancient nations — Egyptians, Chaldeans, Phoenicians — must be opened; their own citizens must be summoned, through whom knowledge was transmitted: Manetho the Egyptian, Berosus the Chaldean, and Iromus the Phoenician king of Tyre; also their followers — Ptolemy Mendesius, Menander of Ephesus, Demetrius of Phalerum, King Juba, Apion, Thallus, and the Jew Josephus, native defender of Jewish antiquities, who either confirms or refutes them. Greek censuses must be compared, and the dates of events correlated, so that the concatenations of time are revealed and the numbers of annals clarified. One must traverse the histories and writings of the world. And yet we have already introduced a portion of the proof, by merely touching on the means by which it can be proven. But it is better to defer the rest, lest in haste we pursue it insufficiently, or in thoroughness we wander too long.

[Primus enim prophetes Moyses, qui mundi conditionem et generis humani pullulationem et mox ultricem iniquitatis illius aevi vim cataclysmi de praeterito exorsus est, per vaticinationem usque ad suam aetatem et deinceps per res suas futurorum imagines edidit, penes quem et temporum ordo digestus ab initio supputationem saeculi praestitit: superior invenitur annis circiter trecentis, quam ille antiquissimus penes vos Danaus in Argo transvenisset; Trojano denique praelio ad mille annos ante est, unde et ipso Saturno. Secundum enim historiam Thalli, qua relatum est bellum Assyriorum et Saturnum Titanorum regem cum Jove dimicasse, ostenditur bellum CCCXX. et duobus annis Iliacum exitium antecessisse. Per hunc Moysen etiam illa lex propria Judaeis a Deo missa est. Deinceps multa et alii prophetae vetustiores litteris vestris. Nam et qui ultimo cecinit, aut aliquantulo praecucurrit, aut certe concurrit aetate sapientiae auctoribus, etiam latoribus legis. Cyri enim et Darii regno fuit Zacharias, quo in tempore Thales physicorum princeps, sciscitanti Croeso nihil certum de Divinitate respondit, turbatus scilicet vocibus prophetarum, Solon eidem regi finem longae vitae intuendum praedicavit non aliter, quam Prophetae; adeo respici potest, tam jura vestra quam studia de lege deque divina doctrina concepisse. Quod prius est, hoc sit semen necesse est. Inde quaedam nobiscum vel prope nos habetis. De sophia amor ejus philosophia vocitatus est, de prophetia affectatio ejus poeticam vaticinationem depuravit. Gloriae homines, si quid invenerant, ut proprium facerent, adulteraverunt; etiam fructibus a semine degenerare contigit. Multis adhuc de vetustate modis consisterem divinarum litterarum, si non major auctoritas illis ad fidem de veritatis suae viribus, quam aetatis annalibus suppetisset. Quid enim potentius patrocinabitur testimonio earum, nisi dispunctio quotidiana saeculi totius, cum dispositiones regnorum, cum casus urbium, cum exitus gentium, cum status temporum ita omnibus respondent, quemadmodum ante millia annorum praenuntiabantur? Unde et spes nostra, quam ridetis, animatur, et fiducia, quam praesumptionem vocatis, corroboratur. Idonea est enim recognitio praeteritorum ad disponendam fiduciam futurorum: eadem voces praedicaverunt utramque partem, eadem litterae notaverunt. Unum est tempus apud illas, quod apud nos separari videtur. Ita omnia quae supersunt improbata sunt nobis, quia cum illis, quae probata sunt, tunc futuris praedicabantur. Habetis, quod sciam, et vos Sibyllam, quatenus appellatione ita vera vates dei veri passim super caeteros, qui vaticinari videbantur, usurpata est, sicut vestrae Sibyllae nomen de veritate mentitae, quemadmodum et dei vestri.] Omnes itaque substantias, omnesque materias, origines, ordines, venas veterani cujusque styli vestri, gentes etiam plerasque et urbes insignes, historiarum canas, et memoriarum, ipsas denique effigies litterarum, indices custodesque rerum, et (puto adhuc minus dicimus) ipsos inquam deos vestros, ipsa templa et oracula et sacra unius interim prophetae scrinium saeculis vincit, in quo videtur thesaurus collocatus totius Judaici sacramenti, et inde etiam nostri. Si quem audistis interim Moysen, Argivo Inacho pariter aetate est; quadringentis pene annis, nam et septem minus, Danaum, et ipsum apud vos vetustissimum, praevenit, mille circiter cladem Priami antecedit; possem etiam dicere, quingentis amplius et Homerum, habens quos sequar. Caeteri quoque prophetae, etsi Moysi posthumant, extremissimi tamen eorum non retrosiores deprehenduntur primoribus vestris sapientibus et legiferis et historicis. Haec quibus ordinibus probari possint, non tam difficile est nobis exponere, quam enorme, nec arduum, sed interim longum. Multis instrumentis, cum digitorum supputariis gesticulis assidendum est. Reseranda antiquissimarum etiam gentium archiva, Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Phoenicum; advocandi etiam municipes eorum, per quos notitia subministrata est; aliqui Manethon Aegyptius, et Berosus Chaldaeus, sed et Iromus Phoenix Tyri rex; sectatores quoque eorum Mendesius Ptolemaeus, et Menander Ephesius, et Demetrius Phalereus, et rex Juba, et Appion, et Thallus, et qui istos aut probat aut revincit, judaeus Josephus antiquitatum Judaicarum vernaculus vindex. Graecorum etiam censuales conferendi, et quae quando sint gesta, ut concatenationes temporum aperiantur, per quae luceant annalium numeri. Peregrinandum est in historias et litteras orbis. Et tamen quasi partem jam probationis intulimus, quum per quae probari possint, aspersimus. Verum differre praestat, ne vel minus persequamur festinando, vel diutius evagemur persequendo.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I have, I think, sufficiently proven the distinction between false and true divinity by showing that the proof rests not merely on debates and arguments, but also on the testimonies of the very beings you call gods, so that nothing further remains to be retracted on this point. Yet since the Roman name has been formally invoked, I will not pass over the challenge raised by the presumption that the Romans were elevated to such heights of world domination as a reward for their diligent religiosity — indeed, that they have become gods themselves, flourishing beyond all others because they render those others a service beyond all others. A fine reward the gods have paid the Romans for their gratitude: Sterculius, Mutunus, and Larentina advanced the empire. I hardly think foreign gods chose to favor a foreign nation over their own, handing over the native soil where they were born, grew up, were ennobled, and buried to men who crossed the sea. Let Cybele judge whether she loved the Roman city as a memorial of the Trojan race — her own people, shielded against the arms of the Achaeans — if she looked to the avengers she knew would subdue Greece, the conqueror of Phrygia. And so she has offered our own age a grand testament of her majesty bestowed upon the city: when Marcus Aurelius was away from the capital at Sirmium, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that most holy Archigallus, on the ninth day before those same Kalends — the very day he was offering impure blood and even castrating himself — issued the usual orders for the salvation of the Emperor Marcus, already dead. O slow messengers, o sleepy dispatches, whose fault it was that Cybele did not learn of the emperor's death beforehand, lest Christians ridicule such a goddess. But Jupiter would not immediately allow his Cretan land to be shaken by the Roman rods, forgetting that Idaean cave, the Corybantic bronze, and the most pleasant odor of his nurse there. Would he not have preferred that tomb of his to the whole Capitol, so that the earth might rather excel in the ashes that cover Jupiter? Would Juno have wished the Punic city, setting aside Samos, to be destroyed — the city beloved by the race of the Aeneadae? What if these were her arms, this her chariot, this the kingdom of the goddess among the nations — if the fates allow, even then she was striving and fostering it. That wretched wife and sister of Jupiter could not prevail against the fates: Jupiter himself is established by fate. Nor did the fates, yielding to themselves, devote as much honor to the Roman name as to the most prostituted she-wolf Larentina, against the destined vow and will of Juno. It is certain that many of your gods have reigned. Therefore, if they hold the power of conferring empire, from whom did they receive that grace when they themselves reigned? Whom did Saturn and Jupiter worship? Some Sterculius, I think — but later in Rome, with their own indigenous people. Even if some did not reign, they were still ruled by others who were not yet their worshipers, so that they were not yet considered gods. It is therefore the province of others to give the kingdom, because the kingdom was ruled long before these gods were encountered. But how vain to attribute the heights of the Roman name to the merits of religiosity, when religion progressed only after the empire — or even the kingdom — had grown. For even if the curiosity of superstition was conceived by Numa, the divine was still not established among the Romans either by statues or by temples; religion was frugal, rites were poor, there were no Capitols competing with the sky, only reckless altars of turf, Samian vessels, the smell from them, and God himself was nowhere. For the ingenuity of the Greeks and Tuscans had not yet flooded the city with fabricated statues. Therefore the Romans were not religious before they were great; and so they were not great because they were religious. But how can they be great because of religion when their greatness springs from irreligion? For, if I am not mistaken, every kingdom or empire is sought by wars and propagated by victories. And wars and victories consist in the capture and destruction of countless cities. This business is not without injury to the gods: the same massacres of walls and temples, the same slaughter of citizens and priests, the same plundering of sacred and profane wealth. So many Roman sacrileges, so many trophies; so many triumphs over gods as over nations; so many spoils, as many statues of captured gods still remain. And they are worshiped by their enemies, and they decree endless empire to those whose injuries they ought to have avenged rather than flattered. But those who feel nothing are injured as impunely as they are worshiped in vain. It certainly cannot be consistent with faith that they appear to have grown by the merits of religion, when, as we have suggested, they either increased religion by injuring it, or injured it by increasing. Even those whose kingdoms were gathered into the sum of the Roman empire, when they lost them, were not without religions of their own.

latin: Satis mihi quidem videor probasse de falsa et vera divinitate, cum demonstravi, quemadmodum probatio consistat, non modo disputationibus nec argumentationibus, sed ipsorum etiam testimoniis, quos deos creditis, ut nihil jam ad hanc caussam sit retractandum. Quoniam tamen Romani nominis proprie mentio occurrit, non omittam congressionem, quam provocat illa praesumptio dicentium Romanos pro merito religiositatis diligentissimae in tantum sublimitatis elatos, ut orbem occuparint, et adeo deos esse, ut praeter caeteros floreant, qui illis officium praeter caeteros faciant. Scilicet ista merces Romanis a diis pro gratia expensa est, Sterculius, et Mutunus, et Larentina provexit imperium. Peregrinos enim deos non putem extraneae genti magis fautum voluisse quam suae, et patrium solum, in quo nati, adulti, nobilitati, sepultique sunt, transfretanis dedisse. Viderit Cybele, si urbem romanam ut memoriam Trojani generis adamavit, vernaculi sui scilicet adversus Achivorum arma protecti, si ad ultores transire prospexit, quos sciebat Graeciam Phrygiae debellatricem subacturos. Itaque majestatis suae in urbem collatae grande documentum nostrae etiam aetati proposuit, cum Marco Aurelio apud Sirmium reipublicae exempto, die decimo sexto Kalendarum Aprilium, Archigallus ille sanctissimus, die nono Kalend. earumdem, quo sanguinem impurum, lacertos quoque castrando libabat, pro salute imperatoris Marci jam intercepti solita aeque imperia mandavit. O nuntios tardos, o somniculosa diplomata, quorum vitio excessum imperatoris non ante Cybele cognovit, ne deam talem riderent Christiani. Sed non statim et Jupiter Cretam suam Romanis fascibus concuti sineret, oblitus antrum illud Idaeum, et aera Corybantia, et jucundissimum illic nutricis suae odorem. Nonne omni Capitolio tumulum illum suum praeposuisset, ut ea potius orbi terra praecelleret, quae cineres Jovis texit? Vellet Juno Punicam urbem posthabita Samo dilectam ab Aeneadarum utique genere deleri? Quod si Hic illius arma, Hic currus fuit, hoc regnum dea gentibus esse, Si qua fata sinant, jam tum tenditque fovetque. Misera illa conjux Jovis et soror adversus fata non valuit plane: Fato stat Jupiter ipse. Nec tantum tamen honoris Romani dicaverunt fatis dedentibus sibi Carthaginem adversus destinatum votumque Junonis, quantum prostitutissimae lupae Larentinae. Plures deos vestros regnasse certum est. Igitur si conferendi imperii tenent potestatem, cum ipsi regnarent, a quibus acceperant eam gratiam? quem coluerat Saturnus et Jupiter? aliquem opinor Sterculium [sed Romae postea], cum indigenis suis. Etiam si qui non regnarunt, tamen regnabatur ab aliis nondum cultoribus suis, ut qui nondum dii habebantur. Ergo aliorum est regnum dare, quia regnabatur multo ante quam isti dii inciderentur. Sed quam vanum est fastigium Romani nominis religiositatis meritis deputare, cum post imperium sive adhuc regnum [auctis jam rebus] religio profecerit. Nam etsi a Numa concepta est curiositas superstitiosa, nondum tamen aut simulacris aut templis res divina apud Romanos constabat; frugi religio et pauperes ritus, et nulla capitolia certantia coelo, sed temeraria de cespite altaria, et vasa adhuc Samia, et nidor ex illis, et Deus ipse nusquam. Nondum enim tunc ingenia Graecorum atque Tuscorum fingendis simulacris urbem inundaverant. Ergo non ante religiosi Romani, quam magni; ideoque non ob hoc magni, quia religiosi. Atqui quomodo ob religionem magni, quibus magnitudo de irreligiositate provenit? Ni fallor enim, omne regnum vel imperium bellis quaeritur et victoriis propagatur. Porro bella et victoriae captis et eversis plurimum urbibus constant. Id negotium sine deorum injuria non est. Eaedem strages moenium et templorum, pares caedes civium et sacerdotum, nec dissimiles rapinae sacrarum divitiarum et profanarum. Tot igitur sacrilegia Romanorum, quot trophaea; tot de diis, quot de gentibus triumphi; tot manubiae, quot manent adhuc simulacra captivorum deorum. Et ab hostibus ergo suis sustinent adorari, et illis imperium sine fine decernunt, quorum magis injurias quam adulationes remunerasse debuerant. Sed qui nihil sentiunt, tam impune laeduntur, quam frustra coluntur. Certe non potest fidei convenire, ut religionis meritis excrevisse videantur, qui, ut suggessimus, religionem aut laedendo creverunt, aut crescendo laeserunt. Etiam illi, quorum regna conflata sunt in imperii Romani summam, cum ea amitterent, sine religionibus non fuerunt.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: I must now return to the topics that follow and demonstrate more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they claim the soul is; you will find all these assertions plainly stated in the scriptures. Do not suppose that I now treat their allegories as the gnosis delivers the truth, for if they point to something other than what they appear to say—much like the ancient wise wrestlers who feint one way and strike another—they signal a different meaning entirely. The Stoics say that God permeates all existence, but we call Him only the Creator, the Maker by His Word. The statement in Wisdom—‘He passes through and fills all things because of His purity’—misled them, since they failed to grasp that these words refer to the primal Wisdom created by God. They object that the philosophers—Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic alike—posit matter as a first principle, not a single one. Let them acknowledge, then, that this so-called matter is described by them as qualityless and formless, and even more boldly, that it does not exist according to Plato. And lest they claim to know the one truly existing principle in the most mystical sense from the Timaeus, he speaks in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: the question concerning all things, whether there is one principle or many or whatever they suppose, is not to be discussed at present, for no other reason than the difficulty of explaining what appears plausible by our current method. Besides, the prophetic utterance, ‘the earth was invisible and unformed,’ gave them an opening for the notion of material substance. Epicurus, failing to follow the sense of the text, let the idea of chance slip in, ending in ‘vanity of vanities, all is vanity.’ Aristotle, drawing providence down only as far as the moon from the psalm ‘Lord, your mercy is in the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds’ (Psalm 36:5), did so because the revelation of the prophetic mysteries had not yet come before the Lord’s advent. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire were borrowed from barbarian philosophy by the entire poetic tradition and by Greek philosophy itself. Plato, in the final book of the Republic, says in these very words: ‘Here wild men, fiery to behold, stand by, discerning the sound; taking some aside privately they lead them away, but binding the hands, feet, and head of Aridaeus and the others, throwing them down and flaying them, they drag them along the road outside, striking them on asphodels.’ The fiery wild men, he says, represent angels who seize the wicked to punish them—‘He who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire.’ It follows for them that the soul is immortal, for what is punished or instructed while possessing sensation lives on, even if it is said to suffer.

greek: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται.

english: We will examine shortly the fact that the philosophers' doctrines appeared among the Hebrews, but first, as the proper order requires, we must discuss the times of Moses. Through that discussion it will be demonstrated conclusively that Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, our own account also obliges us to run through the relevant chronological statements. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Pleistonices, addresses them in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*. Although he is an Egyptian by birth and displays a decided hostility toward the Hebrews—going so far as to compose a treatise against the Jews—he still cites Amosis, the Egyptian king, and the events of his reign, and he calls Ptolemy of Mendes as his witness. Ptolemy's words run as follows: "Amosis, who became king in the time of the Argive Inachus, laid waste Avaris," as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, and he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic, that is, those traced from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Compared with these, the Attic traditions deriving from Cecrops—the two‑natured, autochthonous figure, to use Tatian's exact phrase—are forty generations younger; the Arcadic traditions from Pelasgus, who is also said to be autochthonous, are nine generations younger; and the Phthiotic traditions from Deucalion are younger by two generations. By the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are counted from Inachus, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years. If, as Ctesias asserts, Assyrian history is far older than the Greek, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian Amosis and the Argive Inachus falls in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire and the thirty‑second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. Meanwhile in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, occurred the flood of Ogygus and the early Sicyonian kingdom—first Aegialeus, then Europs, then Telchin—along with the Cretan dynasty in Crete. greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει·

english: Since you wished to learn the precise details of the topics you proposed to us, my beloved brother Theophilus, I considered it reasonable to set the matters you seek before your eyes, drawing abundantly from the divine Scriptures themselves as from a holy spring. I did this so that you would not only delight in these things by hearing them with your ears, but also, having been instructed by the power of the realities themselves, you might be able to glorify God in every way.
