excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You say you hope that He will Himself act as a testimony to the diversity of God's kingdom — the eternal, heavenly possession. Your Christ, meanwhile, promises the Jews their original state: a restored land, and after life ends, refreshment in Abraham's bosom among the dead. God Most Good — if He gives back what He took away in anger, now that He is placated. Oh, your God who both strikes and heals, creates evil and makes peace! (Isaiah 45:7) Oh, a God merciful even to the underworld! But we will return to Abraham's bosom at the proper time.

As for the restoration of Judea — which the Jews themselves hope for, exactly as described, led on by the names of places and regions — tracing how an allegorical interpretation applies spiritually to Christ and the Church, its character and its fruit, would take too long; it is treated in another work, titled *On the Hope of the Faithful*. Here it would be idle, because the question is not about an earthly promise but a heavenly one. We do confess a kingdom promised to us on earth — but before heaven, and in another state: after the resurrection, for a thousand years, in the city of God's work, Jerusalem, lifted up from heaven. The Apostle calls her our mother above (Galatians 4:26), and declares our citizenship — our municipality — to be in heaven, assigning it to a certain heavenly city. Ezekiel knows this city (Ezekiel 40–48), the apostle John has seen it (Revelation 21:10), and the word of the new prophecy among our faith testifies to it, even predicting the city's image as a sign before it appears.

Finally, it was recently confirmed by an eastern expedition. Pagan witnesses agree: in Judea, for forty days, at morning moments, a city hung from heaven, every appearance of the moon vanishing as the day advanced, and at other times none visible from nearby. We say this city is for receiving the resurrection of the saints, and for renewing every spiritual good in compensation for what we have despised or lost in the world, as foreseen by God. For it is just, and worthy of God, that His servants should rejoice there, where they were also afflicted in His name. This is the rationale for the earthly kingdom: after its thousand years, within which the resurrection of the saints is completed — sooner or later, according to the merits of those rising — then, with the world's destruction and the conflagration of judgment, changed in an instant into angelic substance, clothed with that garment of incorruptibility, we will be transferred into the heavenly kingdom. This kingdom is now discussed as if it had not been predicted by the Creator — and thus Christ is proved to belong to another God, from whom alone it was first and only revealed.

latin: Imo, inquis, spero ab illo quod et ipsum faciat ad testimonium diversitatis regnum Dei aeternae et coelestis possessionis. Caeterum, vester Christus pristimum statum Judaeis pollicetur, ex restitutione terrae, et post decursum vitae, apud inferos in sinu Abrahae refrigerium. Deum optimum! si reddit placatus, quod et abstulerat iratus. O Deum tuum qui et caedit et sanat, condit mala et facit pacem! O Deum etiam ad inferos usque misericordem! Sed de sinu Abrahae suo tempore. De restitutione vero Judaeae, quam et ipsi Judaei, ita ut describitur, sperant, locorum et regionum nominibus inducti, quomodo allegorica interpretatio in Christum et in Ecclesiam, et habitum et fructum ejus spiritaliter competat, et longum est persequi, et in alio opere digestum, quod inscribimus, De spe fidelium; et in praesenti vel eo otiosum, quia non de terrena, sed de coelesti promissione sit quaestio. Nam et confitemur in terra nobis regnum repromissum; sed ante coelum, sed alio statu; utpote post resurrectionem in mille annos, in civitate divini operis Hierusalem coelo delata, quam et Apostolus matrem nostram sursum designat, et politeuma nostrum, id est, municipatum in coelis esse pronuntians, alicui utique coelesti civitati eum deputat. Hanc et Ezechiel novit, et apostolus Joannes vidit, et qui apud fidem nostram est, novae prophetiae sermo testatur, ut etiam effigiem civitatis ante repraesentationem ejus conspectu futuram in signum praedicarit. Denique proxime expunctum est orientali expeditione. Constat enim, ethnicis quoque testibus, in Judaea per dies quadraginta matutinis momentis civitatem de coelo pependisse, omni meoniorum habitu evanescente de profectu diei, et alias de proximo nullam. Hanc dicimus excipiendis resurrectione sanctis, et refovendis omnium bonorum utique spiritalium copia in compensationem eorum quae in saeculo vel despeximus, vel amisimus, a Deo prospectam. Siquidem et justum, et Deo dignum, illic quoque exultare famulos ejus, ubi sunt et afflicti in nomine ipsius. Haec ratio regni terreni, post cujus mille annos, intra quam aetatem concluditur sanctorum resurrectio, pro meritis maturius vel tardius resurgentium, tunc et mundi destructione, et judicii conflagratione commissa, demutati in atomo in angelicam substantiam, scilicet per illud incorruptelae superindumentum, transferemur in coeleste regnum, de quo nunc sic ideo retractatur, quasi non praedicato apud Creatorem, ac per hoc, alterius Dei Christum probante, a quo primo et solo sit revelatum.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — A Treatise on the Soul 30
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So what do we say to the rest of the objections? First: if the living come from the dead just as the dead come from the living, one single, identical headcount of all humanity would have stayed frozen forever—the exact number that first stepped into life. The living come first, then the dead from the living, then the living again from the dead. While this cycle spins from the same pool, the tally coming out always matches the tally going in; not one more, not one fewer would have exited than returned. But the records of human antiquity tell a different story: the race has steadily swollen. Indigenous peoples, wanderers, exiles, and glorious conquerors alike have seized territories—Scythians in Parthia, Amyclae in the Peloponnese, Athenians in Asia, Phrygians in Italy, Phoenicians in Africa. Organized migrations, the so-called apoikiai, deliberately poured surplus populations into new frontiers. The original inhabitants still hold their ground, yet they have also loaned their stock abroad. The world itself lies open before us, more cultivated and better mapped with each passing day. Every route is passable, every region known, every corner open for business. Famous wildernesses have vanished under pleasant estates; forests have yielded to fields; wild beasts have fled before cattle; sands are sown, rocks planted, marshes drained. Cities now rise where not even huts once stood. Islands no longer repel, cliffs no longer terrify; everywhere houses, everywhere people, everywhere government, everywhere life. The supreme proof of human density: we are a burden on the world. The elements barely cover our needs, necessities pinch tighter, complaints rise on all sides, because nature no longer sustains us. Pestilence, famine, wars, the swallowing of cities—these count as remedies, a pruning of the overgrown human race. Yet when such axes once hack down the greatest mass of mortals, they never bring it back by raising the living from the dead; after a thousand years the world once shuddered at depopulation. If the living were made from the dead, that equal force of loss and restoration would have been palpable. Why, then, a thousand years later and not at once? If what is paid out is not instantly replenished, the whole stock risks being consumed, since restoration would be pre-empted by the collapse; the provisions of this life could never stretch to a thousand years—far too short a span, and therefore easier to extinguish than to rekindle. So what would have collapsed in that scenario, if the living came from the dead, has not collapsed; therefore it will not be believed that the living come from the dead.

latin: Quid autem ad caetera respondebimus? Primo enim, si ex mortuis vivi, sicut mortui ex vivis, unus omnino et idem numerus semper haesisset omnium, ille scilicet numerus qui primus vitam introisset, priores enim mortuis vivi, dehinc mortui ex vivis, et rursus ex mortuis vivi. Et dum hoc semper ex iisdem, ita totidem semper qui ex iisdem; neque plures aut pauciores exissent, quam redirent. Invenimus autem apud commentarios etiam humanarum antiquitatum, paulatim humanum genus exuberasse, dum aborigines, vel vagi, vel extorres, vel gloriosi quique occupant terras, ut Scythae Parthicas, ut Amyclae Peloponesum, ut Athenienses Asiam, ut Phryges Italiam, ut Phoenices Africam, dum solennes etiam migrationes, quas ἀποικίας appellant, consilio exonerandae popularitatis, in alios fines examina gentis eructant. Nam et aborigines nunc in suis sedibus permanent, et alibi amplius gentilitatem foeneraverunt. Certe quidem ipse orbis in promptu est, cultior de die, et instructior pristino. Omnia jam pervia, omnia nota, omnia negotiosa; solitudines famosas retro fundi amoenissimi obliteraverunt; sylvas arva domuerunt; feras pecora fugaverunt; arenae seruntur, saxa panguntur, paludes eliquantur; tantae urbes jam, quantae non casae quondam. Jam nec insulae horrent, nec scopuli terrent; ubique domus, ubique populus, ubique respublica, ubique vita. Summum testimonium frequentiae humanae, onerosi sumus mundo, vix nobis elementa sufficiunt, et necessitates arctiores, et querelae apud omnes, dum jam nos natura non sustinet. Revera lues, et fames, et bella, et voragines civitatum, pro remedio deputanda, tanquam tonsura inolescentis generis humani; et tamen cum ejusmodi secures maximam mortalium vim semel caedant, nunquam restitutionem ejus vivos ex mortuis reducentem, post mille annos, semel orbis expavit. Et hoc enim sensibile fecisset aequa vis amissionis et restitutionis, si vivi ex mortuis fierent. Cur autem mille annis post, et non statim, ex mortuis vivi? cum si non statim supparetur quod erogatur, in totum absumi periclitetur, praeveniente restitutionem defectione, quia nec pariasset commeatus hic vitae milliario tempori, longe scilicet brevior, et idcirco facilior ante extingui quam redaccendi. Igitur quae hoc modo intercidisset, si vivi ex mortuis fierent, quando non intercidit, non erit credendum vivos ex mortuis fieri.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — A Treatise on the Soul 31
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If the living come from the dead, they must come one-to-one. That means each individual soul ought to return to its own individual body. But if two, three, or five souls are crammed back into a single womb, the living are no longer coming from the dead, because the one-to-one rule is broken. This whole theory forces the primordial pattern into a singleton mold, even though right now multiple souls are born from one mother. Then there is the age problem: souls die at every stage of life, so why do they all come back as infants? Everyone starts from infancy. What sense does it make for an old man to die and return as a baby? If the soul shrinks outward with age going in reverse, it should have been even more fitting for it to come back more advanced a thousand years later. At minimum, it should have retrieved the exact age it left, returning as a contemporary of its own death.

Even granting that the same souls recycle, they ought to carry their old character traits, pursuits, and passions with them, even if their bodies change. Without those markers, they would be declared the same arbitrarily, lacking the very evidence that would prove identity. You ask how I know this does not happen secretly, since the sheer length of time destroys the ability to recognize returning strangers? I know it does not happen, and Exhibit A is your own star witness: Pythagoras and Euphorbus. Euphorbus was a military, warlike soul, well attested by the fame of his dedicated shields. Pythagoras, by contrast, was so sedentary and unwarlike that he fled the wars of Greece for the quiet of Italy, devoting himself to geometry, astrology, and music, utterly alien to Euphorbus' pursuits and passions. Then there is Pyrrhus, who made a practice of tricking fish; Pythagoras would not even eat them, abstaining from animals. Aethalides and Hermotimus dove into common fare like beans; Pythagoras forbade his disciples even to walk through bean fields. How can the same souls be recovered when they fail to match in character, in training, or in diet?

Right now, out of the vast population of Greece, only four souls are claimed to have recycled. But why stop at Greece? If metempsychosis and transmigration happen daily across every nation, every age, every rank, and both sexes, why does only Pythagoras recognize his past selves, and not me? If this is a philosophers' privilege, and a Greek one at that, as if Scythians and Indians do not philosophize, why do Epicurus, Chrysippus, Zeno, and even Plato himself recall nothing? We might have believed Plato was Nestor reincarnated, given the honey of his eloquence.

latin: Jam vero si ex mortuis vivi, utique singuli ex singulis. Singulorum ergo corporum animas, ut singulas in singula corpora reverti oportuerat. Porro si et binae et trinae et quinae usque uno utero resumuntur, non erunt ex mortuis vivi, quia non singuli ex singulis. Et hoc autem modo primordii forma singulatur, cum et nunc plures animae de una proferuntur. Item, cum varia aetate decedant animae, cur una revertuntur? omnes enim ab infantia imbuuntur. Quale est autem ut senex defunctus, infans revertatur? si decrescit foris anima retrograda aetate, quanto magis erat ut progressior reverteretur mille post annis? Certe vel coaetanea suae mortis, ut aevum quod reliquisset, iterum recepisset. Sed etsi eaedem semper revolverentur, licet non corporum quoque formas easdem, tamen vel ingeniorum et studiorum et adfectionum pristinas proprietates secum referre deberent; quoniam temere eaedem haberentur, carentes iis per quae eaedem probarentur. Unde scias, inquis, an ita quidem fiat occulte, sed conditio milliarii aevi interimat facultatem recensendi, quia ignotae tibi revertuntur? Atquin scio non ita fieri, cum Pythagoram, Euphorbum mihi opponis. Ecce enim Euphorbum militarem et bellicam animam satis constat vel de ipsa gloria clypeorum consecratorum; Pythagoram vero tam residem et imbellem, ut praelia tunc Graeciae vitans, Italiae maluerit quietem, geometricae et astrologiae et musicae devotus, alienus studio et adfectu Euphorbi. Sed et Pyrrhus ille fallendis piscibus agebat; Pythagoras contra nec edendis, ut animalibus abstinens. Aethalides autem et Hermotimus fabam quoque in pabulis communibus inruerat; Pythagoras vero ne per fabalia quidem transeundum discipulis suis tradidit. Quomodo ergo eaedem animae recuperantur, quae nec ingeniis, nec institutis jam, nec victibus eaedem probabuntur? Jam nunc, de tanto Graeciae censu quatuor solae animae recensentur. Sed et quid utique de solo Graeciae censu, ut non ex omni gente, ex omni aetate ac dignitate, ex omni denique sexu, et μετεμψυχώσεις μετενσωματώσεις quotidie existant, cur solus Pythagoras alium atque alium se recognoscat, non et ego? aut si privilegium philosophorum est, et utique graecorum, quasi non et scythae et indi philosophentur, cur neminem se retro meminit Epicurus, neminem Chrysippus, neminem Zeno, ne ipse quidem Plato, quem forsitan Nestorem credidissemus, ob mella facundiae?

excerpts.author: Dionysius of Alexandria
english: 1. But as they produce a certain composition by Nepos, on which they insist very strongly, as if it demonstrated incontestably that there will be a (temporal) reign of Christ upon the earth, I have to say, that in many other respects I accept the opinion of Nepos, and love him at once for his faith , and his laboriousness, and his patient study in the Scriptures , as also for his great efforts in psalmody, by which even now many of the brethren are delighted. I hold the man, too, in deep respect still more, inasmuch as he has gone to his rest before us. Nevertheless the truth is to be prized and reverenced above all things else. And while it is indeed proper to praise and approve ungrudgingly anything that is said aright, it is no less proper to examine and correct anything which may appear to have been written unsoundly. If he had been present then himself, and had been stating his opinions orally, it would have been sufficient to discuss the question together without the use of writing, and to endeavour to convince the opponents, and carry them along by interrogation and reply. But the work is published, and is, as it seems to some, of a very persuasive character; and there are unquestionably some teachers, who hold that the law and the prophets are of no importance, and who decline to follow the Gospels , and who depreciate the epistles of the apostles , and who have also made large promises regarding the doctrine of this composition, as though it were some great and…

2. After certain other mailers, he adds the following statement : — Being then in the Arsinoitic prefecture — where, as you are aware, this doctrine was current long ago, and caused such division, that schisms and apostasies took place I in whole churches — I called together the presbyters and the teachers among the brethren in the villages, and those of the brethren also who wished to attend were present. I exhorted them to make an investigation into that dogma in public. Accordingly, when they had brought this book before us, as though it were a kind of weapon or impregnable battlement, I sat with them for three days in succession from morning till evening, and attempted to set them right on the subjects propounded in the composition. Then, too, I was greatly gratified by observing the constancy of the brethren, and their love of the truth , and their docility and intelligence, as we proceeded, in an orderly method, and in a spirit of moderation, to deal with questions, and difficulties, and concessions. For we took care not to press, in every way and with jealous urgency, opinions which had once been adopted, even although they might appear to be correct. Neither did we evade objections alleged by others; but we endeavoured as far as possible to keep by the subject in hand, and to establish the positions pertinent to it. Nor, again, were we ashamed to change our opinions, if reason convinced us, and to acknowledge the fact; but rather with a good conscience , and in all…

3. Then, a little further on, he speaks of the Revelation of John as follows : — Now some before our time have set aside this book, and repudiated it entirely, criticising it chapter by chapter, and endeavouring to show it to be without either sense or reason. They have alleged also that its title is false; for they deny that John is the author. Nay, further, they hold that it can be no sort of revelation, because it is covered with so gross and dense a veil of ignorance . They affirm, therefore, that none of the apostles , nor indeed any of the saints , nor any person belonging to the Church , could be its author; but that Cerinthus , and the heretical sect founded by him, and named after him the Cerinthian sect , being desirous of attaching the authority of a great name to the fiction propounded by him, prefixed that title to the book. For the doctrine inculcated by Cerinthus is this: that there will be an earthly reign of Christ; and as he was himself a man devoted to the pleasures of the body, and altogether carnal l in his dispositions, he fancied that that kingdom would consist in those kinds of gratifications on which his own heart was set — to wit, in the delights of the belly, and what comes beneath the belly, that is to say, in eating and drinking, and marrying, and in other things under the guise of which he thought he could indulge his appetites with a better grace , such as festivals, and sacrifices , and the slaying of victims. But I, for my part, could not…

4. After this, he examines the whole book of the Revelation; and having proved that it cannot possible be understood according to the bald, literal sense, he proceeds thus :— When the prophet now has completed, so to speak, the whole prophecy , he pronounces those blessed who should observe it, and names himself, too, in the number of the same: For blessed, says he, is he that keeps the words of the prophecy of this book; and I John who saw and heard these things. Revelation 22:7-8 That this person was called John, therefore, and that this was the writing of a John, I do not deny. And I admit further, that it was also the work of some holy and inspired man. But I could not so easily admit that this was the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the brother of James, and the same person with him who wrote the Gospel which bears the title according to John , and the catholic epistle. But from the character of both, and the forms of expression, and the whole disposition and execution of the book, I draw the conclusion that the authorship is not his. For the evangelist nowhere else subjoins his name, and he never proclaims himself either in the Gospel or in the epistle. And a little further on he adds : — John, moreover, nowhere gives us the name, whether as of himself directly (in the first person), or as of another (in the third person). But the writer of the Revelation puts himself forward at once in the very beginning, for he says: The Revelation of Jesus Christ , which He gave to him…

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: You who are to be inhabitants of the heavens with God-Christ, hold fast the beginning, look at all things from heaven. Let simplicity, let meekness dwell in your body. Be not angry with your devout brother without a cause , for you shall receive whatever you may have done from him. This has pleased Christ, that the dead should rise again, yea, with their bodies; and those, too, whom in this world the fire has burned, when six thousand years are completed, and the world has come to an end. The heaven in the meantime is changed with an altered course, for then the wicked are burnt up with divine fire. The creature with groaning burns with the anger of the highest God.

Those who are more worthy, and who are begotten of an illustrious stem, and the men of nobility under the conquered Antichrist , according to God's command living again in the world for a thousand years , indeed, that they may serve the saints , and the High One, under a servile yoke, that they may bear victuals on their neck. Moreover, that they may be judged again when the reign is finished. They who make God of no account when the thousandth year is finished shall perish by fire, when they themselves shall speak to the mountains. All flesh in the monuments and tombs is restored according to its deed: they are plunged in hell ; they bear their punishments in the world; they are shown to them, and they read the things transacted from heaven; the reward according to one's deeds in a perpetual tyranny.

I cannot comprehend all things in a little treatise; the curiosity of the learned men shall find my name in this. I know nothing of the second poem of our author, and am indebted for the following particulars to Dr. Schaff. It is an apologetic poem against Jews and Gentiles , written in uncouth hexameters, and discusses in forty-seven sections the doctrine concerning God and the Redeemer and mankind . It treats of the names of Son and Father; and here, probably, he lays himself open to the charge of Patripassian heresy . He passes to the obstacles encountered by the Gospel , warns the Jews and the Gentiles to forsake their unprofitable devotions, and enlarges on the eschatology, as he conceives of it. Let me now quote textually, as follows:— The most interesting part of the second poem is the conclusion.

It contains a fuller description of Antichrist than the first poem. The author expects that the end of the world will come with the seventh persecution . The Goths will conquer Rome and redeem the Christians ; but then Nero will appear as the heathen Antichrist , reconquer Rome, and rage against the Christians three years and a half. He will be conquered in turn by the Jewish and real Antichrist from the East, who, after the defeat of Nero and the burning of Rome, will return to Judea , perform false miracles , and be worshipped by the Jews . At last Christ appears, that is, God himself (from the Monarchian stand-point of the author) with the lost Twelve Tribes [?] as his army, which had lived beyond Persia in happy simplicity and virtue .

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: The trumpet sounds its signal to heaven, the lion lifted up. Suddenly darkness falls with heaven's crash. The Lord lowers his eyes so that the earth trembles. He cries out so that all in the world may hear: Look, I have kept silent a long time, enduring what you have done. Together they scream, weeping, groaning too late. Howling rises, weeping rises, and no room is given to the wicked. What can a nursing mother do, when she herself is burning? The Lord will judge the wicked in the flame of fire, but fire will not touch the righteous — rather it will cleanse them. They linger under one judgment, yet part of the sentence has already wept. The heat will be so great that even stones melt. Winds gather into lightning; heaven's rage roars, so that wherever the impious flees, fire seizes him. No refuge will exist, no ship's stern to save them. The nations blaze; the Medes and Parthians burn in the thousand years, as John's sealed words declare. For after the thousand years they are handed over to Gehenna, and the very structure they belonged to burns while they themselves burn.

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: The city will descend from heaven in the first resurrection; we must speak of such a great heavenly structure. We who were devoted will rise again, incorruptible, already then living without death. No pain, no groaning will exist in that place. Those who come under the Antichrist and overcome strong martyrdoms will also live for the whole time. They will receive good things because they suffered evil, and they themselves will produce offspring for a thousand years, marrying. All the revenues of the earth are compared there, because the earth, renewed without end, produces abundantly. In the golden camp there will be no rain, no cold, no sieges as now, no plundering. The city will not need the light of lamps; it shines from its Author. It is also visible there, for it spans twelve thousand stadia wide, long, and thus high. Its root rests on the earth, but its head equals the heaven. In the city, instead of gates, the sun and moon will shine. The evil one is shut up in anguish for the sake of nourishing the just. But after the thousand years God will destroy all things.

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: Adam, the first to sin, wanted to dodge God's commands, so Belial tempted him out of envy for paradise. Adam passed on to us everything he did, good or bad. As the leader of the human race, we die because of him and through him. He himself became an exile, retreating from the divine Word. When six thousand years are complete, we will become immortal. Death entered the world when the wood of the tree was tasted; by this wood of death we are born for the life to come. Life hangs on the wood, bearing fruit and commandments. So beware now, you who believe, of those life-giving fruits. The law was given to the first man from the wood, a law to be feared, for death springs from neglecting that primal law. Now reach out your hand and take from the wood of life. The best law of the Lord came forth from the wood for those who follow it. The first law is lost; he tastes because permission is granted to him. Whoever worships forbidden gods possesses the evil joys of life. Reject the taste; knowing what it was will suffice. If you want to live, surrender yourselves to the second law. Shun the cults of temples and the doom of demons. Turn to Christ, and you will become companions of God. The law of God is Xanta, which teaches the dead to live. The Lord alone commanded that his name be proclaimed; completely avoid the law of Zabolicam.

excerpts.citation: Victorinus of Pettau — On the Creation of the World On the Creation of the World (Victorinus)
excerpts.author: Victorinus of Pettau
excerpts.work: On the Creation of the World
excerpts.locus: On the Creation of the World (Victorinus)
english: Because a seven‑day cycle governs both heavenly and earthly things, I take this seventh day as my starting point and, as far as I am able, I will measure from it to every septenary region and try to set forth the day of virtue to its consummation.

In the beginning God made light (Genesis 1:3), and He divided it into a twelve‑hour measure of day and night so that night might give rest a place after human labor, and day might overcome night again; thus labor is refreshed by alternating rest, and rest is tempered by the exercise of day.

On the fourth day He made two luminaries in the heavens, a greater and a lesser, that one might preside over the day and the other over the night—the sun and the moon (Genesis 1:14-19)—and He set the other stars in the heavens to shine on the earth and to mark off seasons, years, months, days, and hours by their courses.
Now the reason of truth is shown: why the fourth day is called tetras, why we fast until the ninth hour, until evening, or why a superposition is kept until the next day.
This world consists of four elements—fire, water, heaven, earth—and these four elements make a tetrad of times.
The sun and the moon also produce four seasons through the course of a year—spring, summer, autumn, winter—and those seasons make a tetrad.

To speak more fully from this point: behold, four living creatures before the throne of God (Revelation 4:6-8), four Gospels, four rivers flowing in paradise, four generations of peoples from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to Moses, from Moses to Christ the Lord, the Son of God; and four living creatures of man—the calf, the lion, the eagle; and four rivers—Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, Euphrates.
Christ Jesus, the author of the things mentioned above, was seized by the tetrad of the impious.

Therefore, because of His captivity, we observe a tetrad; because of the majesty of His works, and because the wholesome times of humanity, joyful with fruits and tranquil with seasons, run their course, we make a superposition.
On the fifth day the earth and water brought forth their offspring.
On the sixth day the things that were still lacking were created; and so God formed man from the dust, the lord of all things that He had created on the earth and in the water (Genesis 2:2-3).
Nevertheless, He created angels and archangels before He formed man, preferring spiritual things to earthly ones, for light existed before heaven and earth.
This sixth day is called Parasceve, that is, a preparation of the kingdom; for Adam was completed in God's own image and likeness.

latin: Idcirco igitur, quoniam septenario numero dierum et coelestia et terrestria reguntur, principii loco, de hac septimam ad omnium septimanarium rigionum metibor, et prout potuero, virtutis diem in eam consummationem conabor exprimere. In principio fecit Deus lucem, eamque duodenario mero horarum, die noctuque, divisit, idcirco videlicet, ut laboribus hominum requies locum noctem dies superduceret, rursus dies supervinceret; hac se alterna vice labor quetis refoveretur, quies exercitatione rursus diei temperaretur. Quarto die fecit duo luminaria in coelo, majus et minus, ut alterum praeesset diei, alterum nocti, solis et lunae; caeteraque sidera posuit in coelo, ut lucerent super terram, et discernerent tempora et annos et menses et dies et horas per stationes. Nunc ratio veritatis ostenditur, quare dies IIII, tetras nuncupatur; quare usque ad horam nonam jejunamus , usque ad vesperam, aut superpositio usque in alterum diem fiat. Mundus itaque iste ex quatuor elementis constat, igne, aqua, coelo, terra. Haec igitur quator elementa temporum tetradem faciunt. Sol quoque et luna per anni spatium quatuor tempora efficiunt, veris, aestatis, autumni, hyemis; et haec tempora tetradem faciunt. Et ut ex ea re longius enarrem, ecce quatuor animalia ante thronum Dei. quatuor evangelia, quatuor flumina in paradiso fluentia, quatuor generationes populorum, ab Adam usque ad Noe, a Noe usque ad Abraham, ab Abraham usque ad Moysem, a Moyse usque ad Christum Dominum, Filium Dei; et quatuor animalia hominis, vituli, leonis, aquilae; et quatuor flumina, Fyson, Geon, Tygris, Euphrates. Homo Christus Jesus auctor eorum, quae supra memoravimus, tetrade ab impiis comprehensus est. Itaque ob captivitatem ejus tetradem ob majestatem operum suorum, et tempora humanitatis salubria, frugibus laeta, tempestatibus tranquilla, decurrant, ideo aut superpositionem facimus. Die quinto terra et aqua foetus suos ediderunt. Die sexto creata sunt, quae deerant; ac sic Deus hominem de humo instruxit, dominum omnium rerum, quae super terram et super aquam creavit. Prius tamen angelos atque archangelos creavit, quam hominem finxit, spiritalia terrenis anteponens. Prius enim lux, quam coelum et terram. Hic dies sextus parasceve appellatur, praeparatio scilicet regni; Adam enim quem ad imaginem et similitudinem suam consummavit.

excerpts.citation: Methodius — Banquet of the Ten Virgins Discourse 9
excerpts.author: Methodius of Olympus
english: For this reason I declare that those who are eager for the contests and exercise great wisdom should especially hasten to possess and honor purity as the most beneficial and approved virtue. In the new and painless creation, whoever is not found adorned with the branches of purity will not attain rest, because they have not fulfilled God's command according to the law; nor will they sojourn in the land of promise, since they have not first celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles. Only those who have celebrated the tabernacle are led into the holy land: they depart from the so-called tabernacles and continue until they reach the temple and the city of God, advancing to greater and more glorious joy, just as the types that occurred among the Jews also show. For just as the Israelites, after leaving the borders of Egypt, journeyed first to the tabernacles and then, departing from there, entered the promised land, so it is with us. Having journeyed from here and departed from this present life as from Egypt, I come first to the resurrection, the true tabernacle, and there I pitch my tent, adorned with the fruits of virtue, on the first day of the resurrection feast, the day of judgment. On that day I celebrate with Christ the millennium of rest — the so-called seven days, the true Sabbaths. Then, following Jesus who has passed through the heavens, I come again to the promised land, the heavens, just as they did after the rest of the tabernacle — not remaining in tabernacles, which means my mortal body does not remain as it is, but after the millennium is transformed from human frailty and corruption into angelic magnitude and beauty. From that wondrous tent, O virgins, once the feast of resurrection is completed, we proceed to greater and better things, ascending into the very house of God above the heavens, with a voice of rejoicing and the sound of confession, celebrating as the psalmist says (Psalm 42:4). Accordingly, O Arete, I gift you with this robe according to my own power.

EUOULIS: I am deeply anxious, Gregory, as I consider what turmoil Domnina must now be in — her heart troubled and fearing she may be at a loss for words and utter something inferior to the other virgins, after so many varied things have already been spoken on the subject. If it is clear that she has been moved, then come, let this also be brought to completion; for I wonder whether, having been called last, she has anything left to say.

GREGORY: 'She was indeed troubled, Euboulis, and very much so,' Theopatra told me, 'but not at a loss for words.' After Arete fixed her gaze on her and said, 'Come, daughter, give your speech, that we may fulfill the banquet completely.'

excerpts.citation: Arnobius — Against the Nations Against the Heathen, Book I (Arnobius)
excerpts.author: Arnobius
english: Some people imagine themselves wise, yet they rave like oracles: ever since the Christian faith appeared, they claim the world has perished, humanity has been overwhelmed by countless evils, and even the heavenly powers have abandoned their ancient care for our affairs and been driven from the earth. I have decided, within the limits of my ability and my plain speech, to confront this envy and dismantle these slanderous charges. Otherwise, these accusers will congratulate themselves on their popular rhetoric, thinking they have said something profound, or — if we stay silent — they will boast that they have won a case that collapses from its own emptiness, not from any lack of defenders.

I do not deny that the accusation sounds formidable, nor that we would deserve hatred — if it could be proved that among us exist causes that made the world stray from its laws, drove the gods far away, and imported such massive miseries into the ages. So let us examine the substance of this opinion. Setting aside all partisan zeal that usually obscures the truth, let us weigh the claim on an even scale. The chain of reasoning will show that we are not the impious ones; rather, those who boast of cultivating the divine and clinging to ancient rites will be found guilty of the very crime they charge us with.

First, I ask them calmly: since the name of the Christian religion began to be spoken on earth, what has nature — the thing itself, called and known as nature — sensed or suffered that is unseen, unknown, or contrary to the fundamental laws? Have the primary elements, from which all things are composed, changed into opposite qualities? Has any part of the cosmic machine that covers and contains us been loosened or dissolved? Does the world's rotation, which governs the primordial motion, now drag or race, or has it been seized by a headlong spin? Have the stars begun to rise in the west and set in the east? Has the sun, prince of the stars, which clothes all things in light and animates them with heat, flared up, gone cold, or corrupted the temperaments of its usual moderation? Has the moon stopped renewing itself, ceasing its constant return to former phases? Have cold, heat, and the moderate temperatures of the seasons perished in confusion? Does winter now bring long days and recall the late lights of summer? Have the winds breathed their last? Have the lightning flashes died out so that heaven is no longer driven into clouds, and rain-moistened fields no longer follow? Does the earth refuse the seeds entrusted to it? Do trees refuse to leaf? Has the taste of edible fruits and the juice of the vine been altered? Does oil pressed from olives no longer feed the lamp? Do land and water animals fail to conceive and give birth? Do embryos in the womb not develop according to their own laws? Do humans — scattered by the first navigation to the earth's uninhabitable shores — still contract marriages with proper solemnities? Do they not beget beloved offspring, conduct public and private business, manage households? Do they not direct their talents through every art and discipline as they please, and reap the rewards of their studies? Do they not rule and command, those to whom the lot of affairs has fallen? Are they not daily advanced in dignity and power? Do they not preside over courts, interpret laws, administer justice? Do they not celebrate all the other customs that sustain human life, each nation in its own land?

Since all this is so, and no novelty has broken the perpetual course of things, what is this stain that the Christian religion is said to have brought upon the earth when it entered the world and revealed the hidden mysteries of truth? They answer: pestilences, droughts, wars, crop failures, locusts, mice, hail, and other scourges that afflict human affairs — these the gods inflict, enraged by your injuries and offenses. If it were not foolish to linger over facts so clear they need no defense, I would prove by reviewing earlier centuries that these evils are neither unknown nor sudden; they did not erupt only after our people received the honor of this calling. If we are the cause, and these plagues were devised as punishment for our crime, how did antiquity even know the names of these misfortunes? How did it have words for war, pestilence, hail — concepts it could not have formed for things it had never experienced, nor learned from ancestors? Famine and grain shortages, they say, grip us tight. Were not the ancient and most ancient centuries acquainted with this necessity? Do not the very names of these evils testify that no mortal has ever been immune? If testimony is needed, I can cite authors recording how many nations, how often, have felt horrific famine and perished in vast numbers. Hailstorms are frequent and universal; ancient writings record rocky rains destroying entire regions. Excessive rains rot crops and signal sterility. Was antiquity exempt? We know great rivers have dried up in cracked mud. Pestilence burns through the human race. Run through the annals written in many languages: you will learn that all nations have often been desolated and stripped of their peoples. Locusts and mice devour every crop. Consult your own histories: see how often earlier ages were afflicted and reduced to misery. Cities shake with the strongest earthquakes, trembling on the brink of ruin. Have earlier times not seen cities swallowed by great chasms, or fortunes secured from such disasters? When was the human race wiped out by floods? Not before us? When was the world burned to ashes and embers? Not before us? When were the greatest cities submerged by the sea? Not before us? When were wars waged with wild beasts and battles fought with lions? Not before us? When did poisonous snakes destroy peoples? Not before us?

You habitually throw at us the causes of frequent wars, the devastation of cities, the invasions of Germans and Scythians — and I say this with peace and good will: you do not see the absurdity of your own calumny. Ten thousand years ago, as Plato shows, a great force erupted from the island of Atlantis and wiped out innumerable nations — were we the cause? Among Assyrians and Bactrians under Ninus and Zoroaster, war was waged not only with iron but with magical and Chaldean arts — was that our envy? When Helen was abducted by divine impulse, becoming a dire fate for her time and future ages — was that our religion's crime? When Xerxes poured the sea onto the land and marched across the waters — was that the effect of our name? When a single youth from Macedonia subjugated the East to slavery — did we stir up those causes? When the Romans, like a torrent, submerged and overwhelmed all nations — did we drive the gods into fury? If no one dares impute those ancient events to our times, how can we be the cause of present miseries, when nothing new is happening — everything is old, and nothing is unheard of in antiquity?

latin: Quoniam comperi nonnullos, qui se plurimum sapere suis persuasionibus credunt, insanire, bacchari, et velut quiddam promptum ex oraculo dicere: postquam esse in mundo christiana gens coepit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum; ipsos etiam coelites, derelictis curis solemnibus, quibus quondam solebant invisere res nostras, terrarum ab regionibus exterminatos: statui pro captu, ac mediocritate sermonis contraire invidiae, et calumniosas dissolvere criminationes, ne aut illi sibi videantur, popularia dum verba depromunt, magnum aliquid dicere; aut, si nos talibus continuerimus a litibus, obtinuisse se causam putent, victam sui vitio, non assertorum silentio destitutam. Neque enim negaverim validissimam esse accusationem istam, hostilibusque condignos odiis nos esse, si apud nos esse constiterit causas, per quas suis mundus aberravit ab legibus, exterminati sunt dii longe, examina tanta moerorum mortalium importata sunt saeculis. Inspiciamus igitur opinionis istius mentem, et hoc quod dicitur, quale sit: summotisque omnibus contentionum studiis, quibus obscurari et contegi contemplatio rerum solet, an sit istud quod dicitur verum, momentorum parium examinatione pendamus. Efficietur enim profecto rationum consequentium copulatu, ut non impii nos magis, sed illi ipsi reperiantur criminis istius rei, qui se numinum profitentur esse cultores, atque inveteratis religionibus deditos. Ac primum ab his illud familiari et placida oratione perquirimus: postquam esse nomen in terris christianae religionis occoepit, quidnam invisitatum, quid incognitum, quid contra leges principaliter institutas, aut sensit aut passa est rerum ipsa quae dicitur appellaturque natura? Numquid in contrarias qualitates prima illa elementa mutata sunt, ex quibus res omnes consensum est esse concretas? Numquid machinae hujus, et molis, qua universi tegimur, et continemur inclusi, parte est in aliqua relaxata, aut dissoluta constructio? Numquid vertigo haec mundi, primigenii motus moderaren excedens, aut tardius repere, aut praecipiti coepit volubilitate raptari? Numquid ab occiduis partibus attolere se astra, atque in ortus fieri signorum coepta est inclinatio? Numquid ipse siderum sol princeps, cujus omnia luce vestiuntur, atque animantur calore, exarsit, intepuit, atque in contrarios habitus moderaminis soliti temperamenta corrupit? Numquid luna desivit redintegrare se ipsam, atque in veteres formas novellarum semper restitutione traducere? Numquid frigora, numquid calores, numquid tepores medii inaequalium temporum confusionibus occiderunt? Numquid longos habere dies bruma, revocare tardissimas luces nox coepit aestatis? Numquid suas animas expiraverunt venti? emortiusque flaminibus neque coelum coactatur in nubila, nec madidata ex imbribus arva succedunt? Commendata semina tellus recusat accidere, aut frondescere arbores nolunt? sapor frugibus esculentis, et vitis liquoribus mutatus est? olearum ex bacculis cruor teter exprimitur, nec lumini subministratur extincto? Animalia terris sueta, atque in aquis degentia non suriunt, nec concipiunt? foetus non in uteris sumptos suis moribus, et sua lege custodiunt? Ipsi homines denique, quos per inhabitabiles oras terrae sparsit prima incipiensque navitas, non matrimonia copulant nuptiarum solennibus justis? non dulcissimas procreant liberorum stirpes, non negotia publica, non privata, et familiares res agunt? non, ut cuique libitum est, per diversas artium, disciplinarumque rationes ingenia dirigunt, et studiosae referunt navitatis usuras? Non regnant, non imperant, quibus sors rerum attributa est talium? non auctiores quotidie dignitatibus et potestatibus fiunt? judiciorum disceptationibus praesunt? leges interpretantur et jura? Nonne omnia caetera, quibus vita succingitur et continetur humana, suis omnes in gentibus patriorum celebrant institutionibus morum? Cum igitur haec ita sint, neque ulla irruperit novitas, quae tenorem perpetuum rerum dissociata continuatione diduxerit: quid est istud, quod dicitur invectam esse labem terris, postquam religio christiana intulit se mundo, et veritatis absconditae sacramenta patefecit? Sed pestilentias, inquiunt, et siccitates, bella, frugum inopiam, locustas, mures, et grandines, resque alias noxias, quibus negotia incursantur humana, dii nobis important injuriis vestris atque offensionibus exasperati. Si in rebus perspicuis, et nullam desiderantibus defensionem, non stoliditatis esset diutius immorari, ostenderem profecto, replicatis prioribus saeculis, mala ista, quae dicitis, non esse incognita, non repentina; nec postquam gens nostra felicitate donari hujus vocaminis meruit, irrupisse has labes, et infestari coepisse discriminum varietate mortalia. Si enim nos sumus in causa, et in nostri criminis meritum excogitatae sunt hae pestes, unde novit antiquitas miseriarum haec nomina? unde bellis significatum dedit? pestilentiam, grandines, qua potuit notione signare, aut inter suas voces, quibus oratio explicabatur, assumere? Nam si novella sunt haec mala, et ab recentibus ducunt offensionibus causas, qui potuit fieri ut eis rebus verba formaret, quas nec ipsa sciebat expertam se esse, neque ullis comperisset majorum in temporibus factitatas? Penuria, inquit, frugum, et angustiae frumentariae arctius nos habent. Antiqua enim et vetustissima saecula necessitatis istius aliquando fuerunt expertia? nonne ipsa nomina, quibus censentur haec mala, testificantur et clamant, nullum ab his umquam immunem abisse mortalium? Quod si ad credendum difficilis res esset, testimoniis agere possemus auctorum, quantae, quoties, et quae gentes famem senserint horridam, et aggerata interierint vastitate. Casus frequentissimi grandinis accidunt, atque adierunt cuncta. In litteris enim priscis comprehensum et compositum non videmus, etiam imbres saxeos totas saepe comminuisse regiones? Difficiles pluviae sata faciunt emori, et sterilitatem indicunt terris. Immunis enim antiquitas malis ab his fuit? cum etiam flumina cognoverimus ingentia limis inaruisse siccatis. Pestilentiae contagia urunt genus humanum. Annalium scripta percurrite linguarum, fol. 3, diversitatibus scripta, universas discetis gentes saepenumero desolatas, et viduatas suis esse cultoribus. A locustis, a muribus, genus omne acciditur atque arroditur frugum. Historias ite per vestras, et ab istis pestibus instruemini, quoties prior aetas affecta sit, et paupertatis ad miserias venerit. Terrarum validissimis motibus tremefactae nutant usque ad periculum civitates. Quid, hiatibus maximis interceptas urbes cum gentibus superiora tempora non viderunt, aut ab hujusmodi casibus fortunas habuere securas? Quando est humanum genus aquarum diluviis interemptum? non ante nos? Quando mundus incensus in favillas et cineres dissolutus est? non ante nos? Quando urbes amplissimae marinis coopertae sunt fluctibus? non ante nos? Quando cum feris bella, et praelia cum leonibus gesta sunt? non ante nos? Quando pernicies populis venenatis ab anguibus data est? non ante nos? Nam quod nobis objectare consuestis bellorum frequentium causas, vastationes urbium. Germanorum et Scythicas irruptiones, cum pace hoc vestra et cum bona venia dixerim: quale sit istud quod dicitur, calumniarum libidine non videtis. Ut ante millia annorum decem, ab insula quae perhibetur Atlantica Neptuni, sicut Plato demonstrat, magna erumperet vis hominum, et innumeras funditus deleret atque extingueret nationes, nos fuimus causa? ut inter Assyrios et Bactrianos, Nino quondam Zoroastreque ductoribus, non tantum ferro dimicaretur et viribus, verum etiam Magicis et Chaldaeorum ex reconditis disciplinis, invidia nostra haec fuit? ut Helena diis ducibus atque impulsoribus rapta, et suis esset dirum et venturis temporibus fatum, religionis nostrae attributum est crimini? ut ille immanis Xerxes mare terris immitteret, et gressibus maria transiret, nostri nominis effectum est causa? ut ex Macedoniae finibus unus exortus adolescens Orientis regna et populos captivitati et servitio subjugaret, nos fecimus, atque excitavimus causas? ut modo Romani, velut aliquod flumen torrens, cunctas submergerent atque obruerint nationes, nos videlicet numina praecipitavimus in furorem? Quod si hominum nullus est, qui, quae dudum gesta sunt, nostris audeat temporibus imputare, quemadmodum possimus miseriarum esse praesentium causae, cum novi fiat nihil, sed sunt omnia vetera, et nullis antiquitatibus inaudita?

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Who is so foolish as to think that this one reigns in heaven, when he ought not even to have reigned on earth? A certain poet did not foolishly write of the triumph of Cupid; in that work he makes Cupid not only the most powerful of the gods, but also their victor. Having enumerated the loves of individuals by which they fell under Cupid's power and dominion, he describes the procession in which Jupiter, together with the other gods, is led in chains before the chariot of the triumphant one. The poet figured this elegantly, yet it does not stray far from the truth. For the one who lacks virtue, who is conquered by desire and evil lusts, is subject not to Cupid as the poet imagined, but to eternal death. But let us omit speaking of morals; let us consider the matter, so that men may understand in what errors they are miserably entangled.

The common people believe that Jupiter reigns in heaven; this has persuaded both the learned and the unlearned alike, as demonstrated by the religion itself and its prayers, hymns, temples, and statues. Yet they confess that he was born of Saturn and Rhea. How can he be regarded as a god, or, as the poet says, the discoverer of human and worldly things, when before his birth there were countless thousands of men—namely, those who lived under Saturn's reign and who enjoyed the light before Jupiter possessed it? It is therefore clear that there was one divine king in the earliest times, another in the ages that followed. Hence it is possible that another will arise in the future. For if the kingdom was changed once, why should we despair that it might be changed again? Unless, perhaps, Saturn could generate a stronger son, but Jupiter cannot. Yet the divine empire is either always unchangeable, or, if it is changeable—which cannot happen—it is always changeable. Can Jupiter therefore lose his kingdom, just as his father lost it? Yes, certainly. For though he spared neither virgins nor married women, he nevertheless abstained from Thetis alone, because it was prophesied that whoever would be born of her would be greater than his father. This reveals, first, imprudence unworthy of a god: unless Themis had foretold the future, he himself would not have known it; but if he is not divine, he is not a god at all, since divinity takes its name from the divine just as humanity takes its name from man. Second, it reveals a consciousness of weakness: he certainly feared a greater power. Whoever does this knows full well that he is not the greatest, since something greater can exist. This same Jupiter swears most sacredly by the Stygian marsh—the one superstition rendered to the gods above.

latin: Quis est igitur tam excors qui hunc regnare in caelo putet, qui ne in terra quidem debuit? non insulse quidam poeta triumphum Cupidinis scripsit, quo in libro non modo potentissimum deorum Cupidinem, sed etiam uictorem facit. enumeratis enim amoribus singulorum, quibus in potestatem Cupidinis dicionemque uenissent, instruit pompam, in qua Iuppiter cum ceteris diis ante currum triumphantis ducitur catenatus. eleganter id quidem a poeta figuratum, sed tamen non multum distat a uero. qui enim uirtutis est expers, qui cupiditate ac libidinibus malis uincitur, non Cupidini ut ille finxit, sed morti subiectus est sempiternae. sed omittamus de moribus dicere, rem consideremus, ut intellegant homines in quibus miseri uersentur erroribus. regnare in caelo Iouem uulgus existimat: id et doctis pariter et indoctis persuasum est, quod et religio ipsa et precationes et hymni et delubra et simulacra demonstrant. eundem tamen Saturno et Rhea genitum confitentur. quomodo potest deus uideri aut, ut ait poeta, hominum rerumque repertor, ante cuius ortum infinita hominum milia fuerunt? eorum scilicet, qui Saturno regnante uixerunt et priores luce quam Iuppiter sunt potiti. nideo alium deum regem fuisse primis temporibus, alium consequentibus. potest ergo fieri ut alius postea sit futurus. si enim prius regnum mutatum est, cur desperemus etiam posterius posse mutari? nisi forte Saturnus generare potuit fortiorem, Iuppiter non potest. atquin diuinum imperium aut semper inmutabile est aut si est mutabile, quod fieri non potest, semper utique mutabile est. potest ergo Iuppiter regnum amittere, sicut pater eius amisit? ita plane. nam cum idem neque uirginibus neque maritatis umquam pepercisset, abstinuit se tamen una Thetide, quod responsum fuit maiorem patre suo futurum quisquis ex ilia natus esset. et primum mprudentia in eo non dei, cui nisi Themis futura dixisset, ipse nesciret; si autem diuinus non sit, ne deus quidem sit, unde ipsa diuinitas nominatur, ut ab homine humanitas; deinde conscientia inbecillitatis, qui timuit utique maiorem. quod qui facit, scit profecto non esse se maximum, quandoquidem potest aliquid maius existere. idem per Stygiam paludem sanctissime iurat, una superstitio superis quae reddita diuis.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: When God saw that the earth was filled with malice and crimes, He decided to destroy the human race by a flood; yet, to restore the multitude, He chose one man, because among all the corrupted a single example of justice remained (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

This man, when he was six hundred years old, built an ark just as God had commanded him, and in it he himself was preserved together with his wife, his three sons, and their three wives, when the waters covered all the highest mountains (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

After the earth dried, God cursed the injustice of the former age, so that the length of life would not again become a cause for devising evils; He gradually diminished the human lifespan through successive generations and set a limit at one hundred and twenty years, which it was not permitted to exceed (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

When he had come out of the ark, as the Holy Scriptures teach, he diligently cultivated the ground and planted a vineyard with his own hand; when it first bore fruit, he rejoiced, drank to drunkenness, and lay naked (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

One of his sons, named Ham, saw his father's nakedness but did not cover it; instead he went out and told his brothers, while they, taking a cloak, entered with faces turned away and covered their father (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

When the father learned what had been done, he disowned and expelled that son; the fugitive settled in the part of the earth now called Arabia, and the land was named Canaan from his name, and his descendants were called Canaanites (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

This was the first nation that ignored God, because its leader and founder did not receive the worship of God from his father but was cursed by him, and so he bequeathed ignorance of the divine to his descendants; from this nation the neighboring peoples flowed forth as their multitude increased (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

The descendants of the father himself, however, were called Hebrews, among whom the religion of God resided; but when their number later grew immensely and their own lands could no longer contain them, young men — whether sent by their parents or acting on their own, driven by scarcity — fled to seek new homes, dispersed hither and thither, filled all the islands and the whole world, and, torn from the holy root, established new customs and institutions according to their own will (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

The first of all who occupied Egypt began to suspect and worship celestial things; because they were not sheltered by houses due to the climate, nor was the sky ever veiled by clouds in that region, they noted the courses of the stars and their effects while venerating them and gazing at them more curiously and freely (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

Afterwards they invented portentous animals to worship, led by certain prodigies, whose authors we shall soon reveal; the other peoples dispersed throughout the land, admiring the elements of the world — heaven, sun, earth, sea — worshiped them without any images or temples and celebrated sacrifices to them in the open, until, as time passed, the most powerful kings built temples and statues and instituted their worship with victims and incense (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

Thus the nations began to stray from the knowledge of God; therefore they are wrong who contend that the worship of gods existed from the beginning of things and that paganism is prior to the religion of God, which they think was invented later, because they are ignorant of the source and origin of truth; now we return to the beginning of the world (Genesis 6:9-9:29).

latin: Deus autem postea cum uideret orbem terrae malitia et sceleribus obpletum, statuit humanum genus diluuio perdere. sed tamen ad multitudinem reparandam delegit unum, quod corruptis omnibus singulare iustitia supererat exemplum. hic cum sescentorum esset annorum, fabrica-uit arcam, sicut ei praeceperat deus, in qua ipse cum coniuge ac tribus filiis totidemque nuribus reseruatus est, cum aqua uniuersos montes altissimos operuisset. deinde orbe siccato exsecratus iniustitiam prioris saeculi deus, ne rursus longitudo uitae causa esset excogitandorum malorum, paulatim per singulas progenies deminuit hominis aetatem atque in centum et uiginti annis metam conlocauit, quam transgredi non liceret. ille uero cum egressus esset ex arca, sicuti sanctae litterae docent, terram studiose coluit ac uineam sua manu seuit. unde arguuntur qui auctorem uini Liberum putant. ille enim non modo Liberum, sed etiam Saturnum atque Uranum multis antecessit aetatibus. qua ei uinea cum primum fructum cepisset, laetus factas bibit usque ad ebrietatem iacuitque nudus. quod cum uidisset unus ei filiis, cui nomen fuit Cham, non texit patris nuditatem, sed egressus etiam fratribus indicauit. at illi sumpto pallio intrauerunt auersis uultibus patremque texerunt. quae facta cum pater recognosset, abdicauit atque expulit filium. at ille profugus in eius terrae parte consedit quae nunc Arabia, nominatur, eaque terra de nomine eius Chanaan dicta est et posteri eius Chananaei. haec fuit prima gens quae deum ignoranit, quoniam princeps eius et conditor cultum dei a patre non accepit maledictus ab eo: itaque ignorantiam diuinitatis minoribus suis reliquit. ab hac gente proximi quique populi multitudine increscente fluxerunt. ipsius autem patris posteri Hebraei dicti: penes quos religio dei resedit. sed et ab his postea multiplicato in inmensum numero cum eos angustiae locorum suorum capere non possent, tum adulescentes uel missi a parentibus uel sua sponte, cum rerum penuria cogeret, profugi ad quaerendas sibi nouas sedes huc atque illuc dispersi omnes insulas et orbem totum repleuerunt et a stirpe sanctae radicis auulsi nouos sibi mores atque instituta pro arbitrio condiderunt. sed omnium primi qui Aegyptum occupauerant caelestia. suspicere atque adorare coeperunt. et quia neque domiciliis tegebantur propter aeris qualitatem nec ullis in ea regione nubibus subtexitur caelum, cursus siderum et effectus nota-uerunt, dum ea saepe uenerantes curiosius ac liberius intuentur. postea deinde portentificas animalium Sguras quas colerent commenti sunt quibusdam prodigiis inducti, quorum mox auctores aperiemus. ceteri autem qui per terram dispersi fuerant admirantes elementa mundi, caelum solem terram mare, sine ullis imaginibus ac templis uenerabantur et his sacrificia in aperto celebrabant, donec processu temporum potentissimis regibus templa et simulacra fecerunt eaque uictimis et odoribus colere instituerunt. sic aberrantes a notitia dei gentes esse coeperunt. errant igitur qui deorum cultus ab exordio rerum fuisse contendunt et priorem esse gentilitatem quam dei religionem, quam putant posterius inuentam, quia. fontem atque originem ueritatis ignorant. nunc ad principium mundi reuertamur.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Since we have spoken of the soul's immortality, we must now teach to what extent and when that gift is granted to humanity, so that those who imagine certain mortals were made gods by mortal decrees and judgments may see their own perversity and folly exposed here as well — whether because they discovered arts, taught the use of certain crops, bestowed useful gifts for human life, or slaughtered savage beasts. How far such merits fall short of immortality we have shown in the earlier books and will show again now, so that it becomes clear that justice alone begets eternal life for man, and God alone bestows the reward of eternal life. For those who are said to have become immortals by their own merits — since neither justice nor any true virtue dwelt in them — did not win immortality for themselves, but death through sins and lusts; they earned not a heavenly reward but infernal punishments, which hang over them and over all who worshiped them. I will demonstrate that the time of this judgment is drawing near, so that a worthy recompense may be paid to the just and a deserved penalty inflicted on the impious.

Plato and many other philosophers, ignorant of the origin of things and of the supreme moment when the world was made, declared that many thousands of ages had elapsed since this most beautiful ordering of the world came into being — perhaps following the Chaldeans, who, as Cicero reports in the first book of On Divination, delude themselves by claiming to possess records embracing 470,000 years. Because they thought they could never be called to account, they believed themselves free to lie. But we, whom the divine scriptures instruct in the knowledge of truth, know both the beginning and the end of the world. We will now treat the end at the close of this work, since we explained the beginning in the second book. Let the philosophers who count thousands of ages from the world's beginning understand that the sixth millennium has not yet run its course. When that number is complete, the consummation must come and the condition of human affairs be reformed for the better. The argument for this must be set forth first, so that the reason may shine forth.

God completed this admirable work of nature, the world, in the space of six days, as the secrets of sacred scripture contain it, and hallowed the seventh day on which he rested from his labors. This is the Sabbath day, which in Hebrew takes its name from the number, and from this the number seven is legitimate and full. There are seven days by which the orbits are completed in their turn, seven stars that never set, and seven planets called wandering, whose unequal courses and motions are believed to produce the varieties of things and times. Therefore, since all God's works were perfected in six days, the world must remain in this present state for six ages — that is, six thousand years. For the great day of God is bounded by a circle of a thousand years, as the prophet declares: "Before your eyes, Lord, a thousand years are like one day" (Psalm 90:4). And just as God labored during those six days in fashioning so many things, so his religion and truth must labor through these six thousand years while malice prevails and dominates. And again, because he rested on the seventh day after perfecting his works and blessed it, at the close of the sixth millennium all malice must be abolished from the earth, and justice must reign for a thousand years, with tranquility and rest from the labors the world has long endured. How this will come to pass I will explain in due order.

We have often said that lesser and fleeting things are figures and foreshadowings of greater things, so that this present day of ours — bounded by the sun's rising and setting — bears the image of the great day, which is determined by a circuit of a thousand years. In the same way the figure of the earthly man prefigured the formation of the heavenly people. For just as God, after completing all things made for man's use, fashioned man himself on the sixth day and led him into this world as into a house already carefully prepared, so now on the sixth great day the true man is fashioned by the Word of God — that is, the holy people are formed by God's doctrine and precepts unto righteousness. And just as then a mortal and imperfect man was formed from the earth to live a thousand years in this world, so now the perfect man is fashioned from this earthly age, that, vivified by God, he may rule in this same world for a thousand years. But how the future consummation will be, and what outcome awaits human affairs, anyone who searches the divine letters will discover. The voices of secular prophets, harmonious with the heavenly ones, also announce the end of things and the downfall after a brief time, describing as it were the final old age of a weary and decaying world. Whatever the prophets and seers declare will happen before that final consummation arrives, I will gather from all sources and link together.

latin: Quoniam de immortalitate animae diximus, sequitur ut doceamus quatenus homini et quando tribuatur, ut in hoc quoque prauitatis ac stultitiae suae perspiciant errores qui mortales quosdam decretis placitisque mortalium deos esse factos opinantur, uel quod artes inuenerant uel quod usum I quarundam frugum docuerant uel quod utilia uitae hominum , prodiderant uel quod inmanes bestias interemerant. quae, merita quam longe ab inmortalitate semota sint, et docuimus in prioribus libris et nunc docebimus, ut appareat solam esse iustitiam quae uitam homini pariat aeternam, et solum deum qui aeternae uitae praemium largiatur. nam illi qui suis meritis inmortales facti esse dicuntur, quia nec iustitia nec ulla in his uera uirtus fuit, non inmortalitatem sibi, sed mortem\' peccatis ac libidinibus quaesierunt neque caeleste praemium, sed inferna supplicia meruerunt, quae pendent simul cum iis omnibus qui eos coluerunt. cuius iudicii propinquare tempus ostendam, ut et iustis merces digna soluatur et poena merita inpiis inrogetur. Plato et multi alii philosophorum cum ignorarent originem rerum supremumque illut tempus quo mundus esset effectus, multa milia saeculorum fluxisse dixerunt, ex quo hic pulcherrimus mundi extiterit ornatus, secuti fortasse Chaldaeos, qui, ut Cicero tradit in libro de diuinatione primo, quadringenta septuaginta milia annorum monumentis conprehensa se habere delirant: in quo se quia posse argui non putabant, liberum sibi crediderunt esse mentiri. nos autem, quos diuinae litterae ad scientiam ueritatis erudiunt, principium mundi, finemque cognouimus: de quo nunc in fine operis disseremus, quoniam de principio in secundo libro explicauimus. sciant igitur philosophi qui ab exordio mundi saeculorum milia enumerant, nondum sextum millesimum annum esse conclusum. quo numero expleto consummationem fieri necesse est et humanarum rerum statum in melius reformari: cuius rei argumentum prius enarrandum est, quo ratio eluceat. Mundum deus et hoc rerum naturae admirabile opus, sicut arcanis sacrae scripturae continetur, sex dierum spatio consummauit diemque septimum, quo ab operibus suis requieuerat, sanxit. hic est autem dies sabbati, qui lingua Hebraeorum a numero nomen accepit, unde septenarius numerus legitimus ac plenus est. nam et dies septem sunt quibus per uicem reuolutis orbes conficiuntur annorum et septem stellae quae non occidunt et septem sidera quae uocantur errantia, quorum dispares cursus et inaequabiles motus rerum ac temporum uarietates efficere creduntur. ergo quoniam sex diebus cuncta dei opera perfecta sunt, per saecula sex id est annorum sex milia manere in hoc statu mundum necesse est. dies enim magnus dei mille annorum circulo terminatur, sicut indicat propheta, qui dicit: ante oculos tuos, domine, mille anni tamquam dies unus. et sicut deus sex illos dies in tantis rebus fabricandis laborauit, ita et religio eius et ueritas in his sex milibus annorum laboret necesse est, malitia praeualente atque dominante. et rursus quoniam perfectis operibus requieuit die septimo eumque benedixit, necesse est ut in fine sexti millesimi anni malitia omnis aboleatur e terra et regnet per annos mille iustitia sitque tranquillitas et requies a laboribus quos mundus iam diu perfert. uerum quatenus id eueniat, ordine suo explicabo. saepe diximus minora et exigua magnorum figuras et praemonstrationes esse, ut hunc diem nostrum, qui ortu solis occasuque finitur, diei magni speciem gerere, quem circuitus annorum mille determinat. eodem modo etiam figuratio terreni hominis caelestis populi praeferebat in posterum fictionem. nam sicut perfectis omnibus quae in usum hominis molitus est deus ipsum hominem sexto die ultimum fecit eumque induxit in hunc mundum tamquam in domum iam diligenter instructam, ita nunc sexto die magno uerus homo uerbo dei fingitur, id est sanctus populus doctrina et praeceptis dei ad iustitiam figuratur. et sicut tunc mortalis atque inperfectus e terra fictus est, ut mille annis in hoc mundo uiueret, ita nunc ex hoc terrestri saeculo perfectus homo fingitur, ut uiuificatus a deo in hoc eodem mundo per annos mille dominetur. quomodo autem consummatio futura sit et qualis exitus humanis rebus inpendeat, si quis diuinas litteras fuerit scrutatus, inueniet. sed et saecularium prophetarum congruentes cum caelestibus uoces finem rerum et occasum post breue tempus adnuntiant describentes quasi fatigati et dilabentis mundi ultimam senectutem. quae uero a prophetis et uatibus futura esse dicantur, priusquam superueniat extrema illa conclusio, collecta ex omnibus et coaceruata subnectam.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Some dismiss these accounts as mere poetic fictions, ignorant of the source from which the poets drew them, and deny that such things can happen. It is no wonder they see it that way. The poets transmit reality in a distorted form. Although they are far older than historians, orators, and other writers, they knew nothing of the mystery of the divine sacrament. The news of a future resurrection reached them only as an obscure rumor, and they rashly passed on what they had lightly heard as if it were a fabricated tale. Yet the poets themselves testified that they followed no single authoritative source, but general opinion — as Vergil says: 'May it be right for me to speak what I have heard.' Consequently, though they corrupted the secrets of truth in part, the matter itself proves more true because it agrees in part with the prophets; that partial agreement is sufficient for us as proof.

Nevertheless, a not insignificant reason underlies their error. The prophets had ceaselessly proclaimed that the Son of God would judge the dead, and this announcement was not hidden. Because the poets believed the ruler of heaven, God, was none other than Jupiter, they handed down that Jupiter's son would judge in the underworld. Yet they did not assign this role to Apollo, Liber, or Mercury, who are considered heavenly, but to one who was both mortal and just — either Minos, Aeacus, or Rhadamanthus. Thus poetic license corrupted what they had received, or opinion altered the truth after it had been dispersed through various mouths and speeches. They sang that after a thousand years souls would be restored to life again, Vergil saying: 'When a thousand years have rolled around, God calls them all in a great throng to the river Lethe, so that, forgetful, they may revisit the upper world and begin to wish to return to bodies.' This reasoning deceived them, because the dead will rise not after a thousand years of their death, but, once restored, will reign with God for a thousand years. God will come to purify this world from every stain and raise the revived souls of the just, with bodies renewed, to eternal blessedness. So, except for the water of forgetfulness, the other details are true. The poets invented that water for a reason: lest anyone object, 'Why then do they not remember that they once lived, or who they were, or what they did?' Even so, the whole account is not thought to resemble the truth and is rejected as if it were a licentious, fictional fabrication.

But when we affirm and teach that souls are not forgetful of themselves, but will return to another life in the same sense and figure, the objection is raised: 'So many ages have passed: who has ever risen from the underworld, that we might believe it can happen by his example?' Yet resurrection cannot happen while injustice still reigns. In this age men are killed by force, iron, ambushes, and poisons, and are afflicted by injuries, poverty, prisons, torments, and proscriptions. To this is added that justice is hated: all who wish to follow God are not only hated but harassed by every insult and tortured by multiple kinds of punishments, and are forced into the impious worship of handmade gods — not by reason or truth, but by nefarious laceration of their bodies. Should men therefore rise again or return to a life in which they cannot be safe? When the just are held so vile and so easily removed, what do we think would happen if someone returning from the underworld received life again by restoration? He would certainly be taken from the eyes of men, lest, seeing or hearing him, all would abandon their gods and convert to the worship and religion of the one God. Therefore resurrection must happen once, when evil has been removed, since it is not right that those who have risen should die again or be violated in any way, so that they may lead a blessed life whose death has been annulled.

The poets, since they knew this age abounds with every evil, introduced the river of forgetfulness so that souls, mindful of evils and labors, would not refuse to return to the world above. Hence Vergil: 'O father, is it to be thought that some souls go from here to heaven and return again to sluggish bodies? What dire desire for light is this for wretched men?' They were ignorant of how or when this should happen, and so they thought souls were reborn and returned again to the womb and regressed to infancy. Hence also Plato, discussing the soul, argues from this that souls can be known to be immortal and divine, because in children talents are mobile and easily perceived, and because they seize what they learn so quickly that they seem not to be learning it for the first time, but recognizing and remembering it. In this, a wise man most foolishly believed the poets.
