latin: Figmenta haec esse poetarum quidam putant ignorantes unde illa poetae acceperint, ac negant haec fieri posse: nec mirum est ita illis uideri. aliter enim quam res habet traditur a poetis: qui licet sint multo antiquiores quam historici et oratores et cetera genera scriptorum, tamen quia mysterium diuini sacramenti nesciebant et ad eos mentio resurrectionis futurae obscuro rumore peruenerat, eam uero temere ac leuiter auditam in modum commenticiae fabulae prodiderunt. et tamen idem testati sunt non auctorem se certum, sed opinionem sequi, ut Maro qui ait: sit mihi fas audita loqui. quamuis igitur ueritatis arcana in parte corruperint, tamen ipsa res eo uerior inuenitur, quod cum prophetis in parte consentiunt: quod nobis ad probationem rei satis est. errori tamen eorum subest ratio non nulla. nam cum prophetae adsiduis contionibus praedicarent iudicaturum esse de mortuis filium dei et haec adnuntiatio non lateret, quoniam rectorem caeli deum non alium putabant esse quam Iouem, iudicare aput inferos Iouis filium tradiderunt, sed tamen non Apollinem aut Liberum aut Mercurium, qui caelestes putantur, sed eum, qui et mortalis fuerit et iustus, uel Minoem uel Aeacum uel Rhadamanthum. corruperunt igitur poetica licentia quod acceperant, uel opinio ueritatem per diuersa ora sermonesque uarios dissipatam mutauit. nam quod peractis ad inferos mille annis rursus ad uitam restitui cecinerunt, Marone ita dicente: has omnis, ubi mille rotam uoluere per annos, Lethaeum ad fluuium deus euocat agmine magno, scilicet inmemores supera ut conuexa reuisant rursus et incipiant in corpora uelle reuerti, haec eos ratio fefellit, quod resurgent defuncti non post mille annos mortis suae, sed ut restituti rursus in uitam mille annis cum deo regnent. deus enim ueniet, ut orbe hoc ab omni labe purgato rediuiuas iustorum animas corporibus innouatis ad sempiternam beatitudinem suscitet. itaque praeter aquam obliuionis uera sunt cetera; quam idcirco finxerunt, ne quis illis opponeret: \'cur ergo non meminerint se aliquando uixisse aut qui fuerint aut quae gesserint?\' sed nihilominus tamen ueri simile non putatur et res tota uelut licenter ac fabulose ficta respuitur. nobis autem de resurrectione adfirmantibus et docentibus animas ad alteram uitam non oblitas sui, sed in eodem sensu ac figura esse redituras illut opponitur: \'tot iam saecula transierunt: quis umquam unus ab inferis resur- rexit, ut exemplo eius fieri posse credamus?\' at enim resurrectio fieri non potest dominante adhuc iniustitia. hoc enim saeculo necantur homines ui ferro insidiis uenenis et adficiuntur iniuriis egestate carceribus tormentis proscriptionibus. eo accedit quod iustitia inuisa est, quod omnes, qui deum sequi uolunt, non tantum odio habentur, sed uexantur omnibus contumeliis et excruciantur multiplici genere poenarum et ad inpios cultus manu factorum deorum non ratione aut ueritate, sed nefanda corporum laceratione coguntur. num lgitur oportet ad haec eadem resurgere aut reuerti homines ad uitam, in qua tuti esse non possunt? cum ergo iusti tam uiles habeantur, tam facile tollantur, quid putemus futurum fuisse, si & quis ab inferis rediens uitam postliminio recepisset? auferretur profecto ab oculis hominum, ne uiso eo uel audito deos uniuersi relinquerent et ad unius se dei cultum religionemque conuerterent. ergo semel fieri resurrectionem necesse est, cum malum fuerit ablatum, quoniam eos qui resurrexerint nec mori iam ulterius nec uiolari ullo modo fas est, ut beatam possint agere uitam quorum mors resignata est. poetae uero cum scirent hoc saeculum malis omnibus redundare, obliuionis amnem induxerunt, ne malorum ac laborum memores animae reuerti ad superos recusarent. unde Vergilius: o pater, anne aliquas ad caelum hinc ire putandum est sublimis animas iterumque ad tarda reuerti corpora? quae lucis miseris tam dira cupido? ignorabant enim quomodo aut quando id fieri oporteret, itaque ] renasci eas putauerunt et denuo ad uterum reuolui atque ad infantiam regredi. unde etiam Plato de anima disserens ex hoc ait posse cognosci animas esse inmortales atque diuinas, quod in pueris mobilia sint ingenia et ad percipiendum facilia, quod ea quae discant ita celeriter rapiant, ut non tunc primum discere illa uideantur, sed recognoscere atque reminisci: in quo uir sapiens poetis ineptissime credidit.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: I now append the rest. The Son of the highest and greatest God will come to judge the living and the dead, as the Sibyl testifies and declares: there shall be a mingling of mortals across the whole earth when the Almighty Himself arrives to judge the souls of the living and the dead and the entire world. After He has destroyed injustice, executed the great judgment, and restored to life the just who existed from the beginning, He will dwell among men for a thousand years and govern them with the most just rule. Another Sibyl, prophesying in ecstatic frenzy, proclaims: "Listen to me, mortals; the Eternal King reigns." Then those who are alive in their bodies will not die; instead, throughout those same thousand years they will produce an innumerable multitude, and their offspring will be holy and dear to God. Those raised from the underworld, however, will preside over the living as judges. The nations will not be utterly exterminated; some will be spared for God's victory, so that the just may triumph over them and reduce them to perpetual servitude. At the same time the prince of demons, the author of all evils, will be bound in chains and held in custody for a thousand years of the heavenly reign, so that justice may rule on earth and he may plot no evil against God's people. After His coming the just will be gathered from every land, and when judgment is complete the holy city will be established in the middle of the earth, where the Founder God Himself will dwell with the just who reign. The Sibyl identifies this city when she says: "The city that God desired, He made brighter than the stars, the sun, and the moon." Then the darkness that veils the world and obscures heaven will be removed; the moon will receive the sun's brightness and wane no more, while the sun will become seven times brighter than it is now. The earth will unlock its fertility and yield most abundant crops of its own accord; mountain rocks will sweat honey, wine will run through the streams, and rivers will overflow with milk. The world itself will rejoice, and all nature will be glad, snatched free from the dominion of evil, impiety, crime, and error. During this time no beast will be nourished by blood, no bird by prey; all will be quiet and peaceful. Lions and calves will stand together at the manger; the wolf will not seize the sheep, the dog will not hunt, hawks and eagles will not harm, and an infant will play with serpents. At last those things will happen which the poets claimed occurred in the golden age under Saturn's reign. Their error arose because the prophets of future events set forth and declare most things as if already accomplished. Visions were presented to their eyes by the divine Spirit, and they saw those things in their sight as if happening and being completed. When these prophecies gradually spread by report, the profane, ignorant of the mystery and not knowing how they were spoken, supposed all those things had already been fulfilled in ancient ages—things which could not possibly be fulfilled while man was ruling. But when impious religions have been destroyed and wickedness suppressed, the earth will be subject to God; the sea also will yield, ships will not change their cargo, and the earth will produce all things. The soil will not endure the hoe, the vine will not endure the sickle; even the sturdy plowman will unyoke his oxen. Then the field will gradually turn golden with soft grain, the uncultivated vine will hang red with grapes, and hard oaks will sweat dewy honey. Wool will not learn to feign varied colors; the ram itself will change its fleece in the meadows, now to a sweet purple-red, now to saffron-yellow; lambs will be clothed with their own sandyx as they graze. She-goats will return home with udders distended with milk, and flocks will not fear great lions. The poet spoke these things following the songs of the Cumaean Sibyl. The Erythraean Sibyl says likewise: "Wolves and lambs will eat grass together on the mountains; leopards will graze with kids; bears will be together with calves and all mortals; the flesh-eating lion will eat straw beside the manger; dragons will sleep with infants and shields." In another place concerning the fertility of creation: "Then indeed God will give great joy to men. For earth, trees, and the untamed animals of the earth will yield true fruit to men: wine, sweet honey, white milk, and wheat—which is the fairest of all things for mortals." And another in the same strain: "The holy earth of the pious alone will bring forth all these things; a stream of honey-dripping water will flow from the rock and the spring, and the milk of ambrosia will flow to all the just." Men will therefore live a most tranquil and abundant life and reign with God as equals. Kings of the nations will come from the ends of the earth with gifts and offerings to adore and honor the great King, whose name will be famous and venerable to all nations under heaven and to the kings who rule on earth.

latin: Nunc reliqua subnectam. ueniet igitur summi et maximi dei filius, ut uiuos ac mortuos iudicet, Sibylla testante atque dicente: , πάσης γὰρ γαίης τότε θνητῶν σύγχυσις ἔσται, αὐτὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ὅταν ἐλθῃ βήματι κρῖναι ζώντων καὶ νεκύων ψυχὰς καὶ κόσμον ἅπαντα. uerum ille cum deleuerit iniustitiam iudiciumque maximum fecerit ac iustos qui a principio fuerunt ad uitam instaurauerit. mille annos inter homines uersabitur eosque iustissimo imperio reget. quod alia Sibylla uaticinans furensque proclamat: κλῦτε δέ μου, μέροπες, βασιλεὺς αἰώνιος ἄρχει. tum qui erunt in corporibus uiui, non morientur, sed per eosdem mille annos infinitam multitudinem generabunt et erit suboles eorum sancta et deo cara: qui autem ab inferis suscitabuntur, hi praeerunt uiuentibus uelut iudices. gentes uero non extinguentur omnino, sed quaedam relinquentur in uictoriam dei, ut triumphentur a iustis ac subiugentur perpetuae seruituti. sub idem tempus etiam princeps daemonum, qui est machinator omnium malorum, catenis uincietur et erit in custodia mille annis caelestis imperii, quo iustitia in orbe regnabit. ne quod malum aduersus populum dei moliatur. post cuius aduentum congregabuntur iusti ex omni terra peractoque iudicio ciuitas sancta constituetur in medio terrae, in qua ipse conditor deus cum iustis dominantibus commoretur. quam ciuitatem Sibylla designat, cum dicit: καὶ πόλιν, ἥν ἐπόθησε θεὸς, ταύτην ἐποίησεν λαμπροτέραν ἄστρων ἠδ\' ἡλίου ἠδὲ σελήνης. tunc auferentur a mundo tenebrae illae quibus obfundetur atque occaecabitur caelum, et luna claritudinem solis accipiet nec minuetur ulterius, sol autem septies tanto quam nunc est clarior fiet. terra uero aperiet fecunditatem suam et uberrimas fruges sua sponte generabit, rupes montium melle sudabunt, per riuos uina decurrent et flumina lacte inundabunt: mundus denique ipse gaudebit et omnis rerum natura laetabitur erepta et liberata dominio mali et impietatis et sceleris et erroris. non bestiae per hoc tempus sanguine alentur, non aues praeda, sed quieta et placida erunt omnia. leones et uituli ad praesepe simul stabunt, lupus ouem non rapiet, canis non uenabitur, accipitres et aquilae non nocebunt, infans cum serpentibus ludet. denique tum fient illa quae poetae aureis temporibus facta esse iam Saturno regnante dixerunt. quorum error hinc ortus est, quod prophetae futurorum pleraque sic proferunt et enuntiant quasi iam peracta. uisiones enim diuino spiritu offerebantur oculis eorum et uidebant illa in conspectu suo quasi fieri ac terminari. quae uaticinia eorum cum paulatim fama uulgasset, quoniam profani a sacramento ignorabant quatenus dicerentur, conpleta esse iam ueteribus saeculis illa omnia putauerunt, quae utique fieri conplerique non poterant homine regnante. cum uero deletis religionibus impiis et scelere compresso subiecta erit deo terra, cedet et ipse mari uector nec nautica pinus mutabit merces, omnis feret omnia tellus. non rastros patietur humus, non uinea falcem; robustus quoque iam tauris iuga soluet arator. tunc et molli paulatim flauescet campus arista incultisque rubens pendebit sentibus uua et durae quercus sudabunt roscida mella. nec uarios discet mentiri lana colores, ipse sed in pratis aries iam suaue rubenti- murice, iam croceo mutabit uellera luto, sponte sua sandyx pascentis uestiet agnos. ipsae lacte domum referent distenta capellae ubera nec magnos metuent armenta leones. quae poeta secundum Cymaeae Sibyllae carmina prolocutus est. Erythraea uero sic ait: οἱ δὲ λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ἐν οὔρεσιν ἄμμιγ\' ἔδονται χόρτον παρδάλιες τ᾽ ἐρίφοις ἄμα βοσκήσονται· ἄρκτοι σὺν μόσχοισιν ὁμοῦ καὶ πᾶσι βροτοῖσιν σαρκοβόρος τε λέων φάγεται ἄχυρον παρὰ φάτνῃ, σὺν βρέφεσίν τε δράκοντες ἄμ\' ἀσπίσι κοιμήσονται. et alio loco de ubertate rerum: καὶ τότε δὴ χάρμην μεγάλην θεὸς ἀνδράσι δώσει. καὶ γὰρ γῆ καὶ δένδρα καὶ ἄσπετα θρέμματα γαίης δώσουσι καρπὸν τὸν ἀληθινὸν ἀνθρώποισιν οἴνου καὶ μέλιτος γλυκεροῦ λευκοῦ τε γάλακτος καὶ σίτου, ὅπερ ἐστὶ βροτοῖς κάλλιστον ἁπάντων. et alia eodem modo: εὐσεβέων δὲ μόνων ἁγία χθὼν πάντα τάδ᾽ οἴσει, νᾶμα μελισταγέης ἀπὸ πέτρης ἠδ᾽ ἀπὸ πηγῆς καὶ γάλα τ᾽ ἀμβροσίης ῥεύσει πάντεσσι δικαίοις. uiuent itaque homines tranquillissimam et copiosissimam uitam et regnabunt cum deo pariter, reges gentium uenient a finibus terrae cum donis ac muneribus, ut adorent et honorificent regem magnum, cuius nomen erit praeclarum ac uenerabile uniuersis nationibus quae sub caelo erunt et regibus qui dominabuntur in terra.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: These are the things the prophets foretell: I did not think it necessary to set forth their testimonies and words, because that would be endless, and the scope of a book cannot contain so vast a multitude of matters, with so many speaking in similar ways by one Spirit; moreover I wished to avoid wearying readers by collecting and translating everything. My further purpose was to confirm and teach the very things I say not only among us, but even among those who attack us, that the confirmed truth stands firm, though they refuse to recognize it. If anyone wishes to know these matters more diligently, let him draw from the very source, and he will find wonders beyond what we have embraced in these books.

Perhaps someone now asks when the things we spoke of will come to pass. I have already shown that this transformation must occur when six thousand years are completed, and that the final day of the ultimate consummation is already drawing near. We may recognize the signs the prophets foretold; they announced signs by which the consummation of the ages is to be expected and feared by us day by day. As for when this full measure is completed, those who wrote on chronology teach us, gathering from the sacred writings and from various histories how great the number of years is from the world's beginning. Though they vary and their totals disagree somewhat, every expectation nevertheless appears to be no more than two hundred years. The reality itself also declares that the collapse and ruin of all things will come soon, unless the fact that Rome still stands means nothing of this seems to be feared. But when that head of the world has fallen and the stream has begun to flow, as the Sibyls say it will, who doubts that the end of human affairs and of the world itself has already arrived? That city is the one that still sustains all things, and the God of heaven must be prayed to and adored by us, if indeed His decrees and plans can be delayed, lest that abominable tyrant come sooner than we think, who is plotting so great a crime and digging out that light by whose extinction the world itself will be ruined. Now let us return to the remaining matters that must be carried out, which will follow in due course.

latin: Haec sunt quae a prophetis futura dicuntur: quorum testimonia et uerba ponere opus esse non duxi, quoniam esset infinitum nec tantam rerum multitudinem mensura libri caperet tam multis uno spiritu similia dicentibus simulque ne fastidium legentibus fieret, si ex omnibus collecta et translata congererem, praeterea ut ea ipsa quae dicerem non nostris, . sed alienis potissimum litteris confirmarem doceremque non \' modo aput nos, uerum etiam aput eos ipsos qui nos insectantur, ueritatem consignatam teneri, quam recusent adgnoscere. si quis autem diligentius haec uoluerit scire, ex ipso fonte hauriat et plura quam nos in his libris conplexi sumus admirabilia reperiet. Fortasse quispiam nunc requirat quando ista quae diximus sint futura. iam superius ostendi conpletis annorum sex milibus mutationem istam fieri oportere et iam propinquare summum illum conclusionis extremae diem. de signis quae praedicta sunt a prophetis licet noscere: praedixerunt enim signa, quibus consummatio temporum et expectanda sit nobis in dies singulos et timenda. quando tamen conpleatur haec summa, docent ii qui de temporibus scripserunt, colligentes ex litteris sanctis et ex uariis historiis quantus sit numerus annorum ab exordio mundi. qui licet uarient et aliquantum numeri eorum summa dissentiant, omnis tamen expectatio non amplius quam ducentorum uidetur annorum. etiam res ipsa declarat lapsum ruinamque rerum breui fore, nisi quod incolumi urbe Roma nihil istius uidetur esse metuendum. at uero cum caput illut orbis occiderit et ῥύμη esse coeperit, quod Sibyllae fore aiunt, quis dubitet uenisse iam finem rebus humanis orbique terrarum? illa est ciuitas quae adhuc sustentat omnia, precandusque nobis et adorandus est deus caeli, si tamen statuta eius et placita differri possunt, ne citius quam putamus tyrannus ille abominabilis ueniat, qui tantum facinus moliatur ac lumen illut effodiat, cuius interitu mundus ipse lapsurus est. nunc ad cetera exequenda redeamus quae deinceps secutura sunt.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: We mentioned a short while ago that at the outset of the holy kingdom the prince of demons would be conquered by God. Yet once the thousand years of that kingdom — in other words, seven thousand years — begin to draw to a close, he will be released once more, let loose from custody, and will go out to incite all the nations then living under the rule of the just, so that they wage war against the holy city. An innumerable multitude of peoples will be gathered from the whole earth; they will besiege and encircle the city. Then the final wrath of God will fall upon the nations, and He will war against them until not a single one remains. First He will shake the earth with utmost violence; at its convulsion the mountains of Syria will split apart, valleys will plunge abruptly downward, and the walls of every city will collapse. God will then command the sun to stand still for three days so that it does not set, and He will set it ablaze. An overwhelming heat and a great scorching will descend upon the perverse and impious peoples: showers of sulfur, hailstones, and drops of fire. Their spirits will melt in the heat, their bodies will be crushed by the hail, and they will turn their swords against one another. Mountains will be filled with corpses, fields covered with bones. Meanwhile, for those three days the people of God will be hidden in the hollows of the earth until God's wrath against the nations and the final judgment have run their course. Then the just will emerge from their hiding places to find everything blanketed with corpses and bones. The entire race of the impious will perish root and branch, and no nation will remain in this world except the one nation of God.

For seven years thereafter the forests will stand untouched; no tree will be felled on the mountains. Instead, the weapons of the nations will be burned, and war will be no more — only everlasting peace and rest. When the thousand years are completed, God will renew the world: the heavens will be rolled up, the earth transformed. God will refashion human beings into the likeness of angels; they will be white as snow and will live forever in the presence of the Almighty, offering sacrifice and service to their Lord for all eternity. At that same moment the second, public resurrection of all will take place, and the unjust will be raised for everlasting torment. These are the ones who worshiped things made by hand, who either did not know or denied the Lord of the world and Father. Their own lord, together with his ministers, will be seized for punishment and condemned; along with him the whole throng of the impious will be burned in eternal fire before the angels and the just, each for their own deeds.

This is the teaching of the holy prophets, which Christians follow; this is our wisdom. Those who worship fragile things or defend empty philosophy mock it as foolishness and vanity, because we are not accustomed to defend and proclaim it publicly. God commands that we keep His mystery in silence and hidden within our own conscience, and not engage in stubborn contention with those profane people who attack God and His religion not to learn but to argue and scoff. The mystery must be hidden and concealed most faithfully, especially by us who bear the name of faith. Yet they criticize our silence as if it were a guilty conscience, and from that they invent execrable accusations against chaste and innocent people, readily believing their own fabrications.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Some who are thought to have believed rightly nevertheless overstep the order of the just's promotion and ignore the modes of meditation that lead to incorruptibility, because they harbor heretical notions. Heretics despise God's creation and refuse to accept the salvation of their own flesh; they also scorn God's promise and presume to overstep God in their thinking. As soon as they die, they claim they will overstep the heavens and the Demiurge and go to the Mother, or to the Father whom they have fabricated. Since they reject the resurrection entirely and, as far as they can, remove it from the picture, why should it surprise us that they do not know the order of the resurrection or understand it? For if things were as they say, the Lord himself, in whom they claim to believe, would not have risen on the third day; instead, expiring on the cross, he would have gone up at once, leaving his body to the earth.

But he spent three days among the dead, just as the prophet says of him: "The Lord is mindful of his holy ones, who slept before on the earth of burial, and he descended to them, to draw them out and save them" (cf. Ps 16:10). The Lord himself said: "As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth" (Jonah 1:17). The Apostle also says: "He ascended -- what does this mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?" (Ephesians 4:9). And David, prophesying about him, said: "You have rescued my soul from the lowest hell" (Ps 16:10). Rising on the third day, he appeared to Mary, who saw him first; she worshiped him, but he said, "Do not hold on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father. Go instead to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father" (John 20:17).

If the Lord kept the law of the dead so that he might become the firstborn from the dead, staying until the third day among the dead of the earth, then rising bodily to show the disciples the nail marks, and only then ascending to the Father, how can those not be confounded who claim the lower world is this present world, while their inner self, leaving the body here, ascends to a supercelestial place? When the Lord went into the midst of death's shadow, where the souls of the dead were, he afterward rose bodily, and after the resurrection he was taken up. It is therefore clear that the souls of his disciples, for whose sake the Lord did all these things, will go to an invisible place appointed for them by God, and there they will remain until the resurrection, awaiting it. Then, receiving bodies and rising perfectly -- that is, bodily, just as the Lord rose -- they will come into God's sight. No disciple is above the master; the fully trained will be like the master. Since our Master did not fly away at once but waited for the resurrection time appointed by the Father, revealed through Jonah, and rose after three days before being taken up, we too must wait for the resurrection time appointed by God, announced by the prophets, and so, rising, be taken up -- as many as the Lord deems worthy.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: If some have tried to allegorize these matters, they will not be found consistent with themselves in every respect, and the very words they discuss will convict them. For when the cities of the nations have been deserted, because they are not inhabited, and the houses, because there are no men, and the earth has been left desolate — behold, Isaiah says: the day of the Lord is coming, incurable, full of fury and anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it (Isaiah 13:9). And again he says: Let him be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord (Isaiah 13:19); and when these things have come to pass, God will remove men far away, and the forsaken will multiply on the earth. And they will build houses and inhabit them; they will plant vineyards and eat the fruit. These things are spoken without controversy concerning the resurrection of the just, which takes place after the coming of the Antichrist and the destruction of all nations under heaven, in which the just will reign on the earth, growing through the vision of the Lord, and through him becoming accustomed to receive the glory of God, the unity of spiritual things, in the kingdom. And those whom he finds in the flesh, waiting for him from heaven and having endured tribulation, who have also escaped the hands of the wicked — these are the ones of whom the prophet says: the forsaken will multiply on the earth. And as many as God has prepared from among believers for this purpose, to be left on the earth and to be under the Kingdom of the Saints, and to minister to this Jerusalem, and the kingdom within it, the prophet Jeremiah has signified, saying: Look toward the east, O Jerusalem, and see the joy that comes to you from God himself. Behold, your sons whom you sent away shall come; they shall come gathered from east to west by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the glory that comes from your God (Jeremiah 31:8–9). Put off, Jerusalem, the garment of your mourning and affliction, and put on the beauty of the glory from your God forever. Wrap yourself in the double mantle of righteousness from your God; set upon your head the mitre of eternal glory. For God will show your splendor to every eye under heaven. Your name shall be named by God forever: Peace of Righteousness and Glory of God's Worship. Arise, Jerusalem, stand on the height; look toward the east and see your children gathered from the rising of the sun to its setting by the word of the Holy One, rejoicing in the remembrance of God. For they went out on foot, led away by enemies; but God will bring them back to you, borne in glory as on a royal throne. For God has decreed that every high mountain shall be humbled and the everlasting hills, and the valleys filled up, to make the ground level, so that Israel may walk safely in the glory of God. The woods and every fragrant tree have shaded Israel at God's command. For God will lead Israel with joy in the light of his glory, with mercy and righteousness that proceed from him (Baruch 5:1–9).

Now such things as these cannot be understood as belonging to a super-celestial realm; for God, he says, will show her your splendor under the whole heaven — but in the times of the Kingdom, when the earth has been reclaimed by Christ and Jerusalem rebuilt according to the pattern of the Jerusalem which is above, of which the prophet Isaiah says: I have engraved your walls upon my palms; you are ever before me (Isaiah 49:16). And the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says the same: But the Jerusalem above is free; she is our mother (Galatians 4:26) — not speaking from the fantasy of errant Aeons, nor from any virtue that fell from the Pleroma, nor from Prunicus, but from the Jerusalem depicted in God's hands. And John saw this Jerusalem descending upon the earth, new, in the Apocalypse. For after the times of the Kingdom, he says: I saw a great white throne, and him who sat upon it; from his face earth and heaven fled away, and no place was found for them (Revelation 20:11). And he describes the general resurrection and judgment: I saw the dead, great and small. The sea gave up the dead in it; Death and Hades gave up the dead in them; and books were opened. Also the book of life was opened, and the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to their works. And Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire — this is the second death, the Gehenna of which the Lord spoke, eternal fire. And if anyone was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:12–15). And after this he says: I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. And I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (Revelation 21:1–2). And I heard a loud voice from the throne: Behold, the dwelling of God is with men; he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes; death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain any more, for the former things have passed away (Revelation 21:3–4). And Isaiah says the same: they shall find joy and exultation in it (Isaiah 65:18). This is what the Apostle said: The form of this world is passing away (1 Corinthians 7:31). Likewise the Lord says: Heaven and earth will pass away (Matthew 24:35). When these things have passed away, the Lord's disciple John says there will be a new Jerusalem above, like a bride adorned for her husband; and this is the tabernacle of God, in which God will dwell with men. The image of this Jerusalem is that Jerusalem on the former earth, in which the just are prepared for incorruption and made ready for salvation. And Moses received the pattern of this tabernacle on the mountain. Nothing here can be allegorized; all is firm, true, and substantial, made by God for the enjoyment of the just. For just as God truly raises man, so he truly rises from the dead — not allegorically, as we have shown at length. And just as he truly rises, so he will truly put on incorruption, and increase, and flourish in the times of the kingdom, that he may become the glory of the Father. Then, when all things are renewed, he will truly dwell in the city of God. For he who sits upon the throne says: Behold, I make all things new (Revelation 21:5). And the Lord says: Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true. And he said to me: It is done. And this is according to reason.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Because they are true human beings, their planting must also be genuine, yet it must not stretch beyond what is real; it must advance only in what truly exists. The substance and the matter of our condition are not annihilated — for the One who established them is true and steadfast — but the present form of this world passes away, that is, the order in which the transgression occurred, since humanity has grown old within it. Precisely because God foresaw everything, this temporal form was instituted; we have already demonstrated this in the preceding book, explaining as far as possible the reason for the world's temporal fabrication. When this form is joined with a renewed humanity that lives toward incorruptibility and can no longer grow old, there will be a new heaven and a new earth in which the new human being perseveres, forever speaking fresh words to God. Since these realities endure without end, Isaiah declares: "For just as the new heavens and the new earth which I make shall remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name remain" (Isaiah 65:17). The Presbyters teach that those deemed worthy of heavenly fellowship will pass into the heavens; others will enjoy the delights of Paradise; still others will possess the beauty of the city. God will be seen everywhere, yet each will behold Him in proportion to their worthiness. There is a distinction among the dwellings of those who have borne fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold: some will be taken up into heaven, others will dwell in Paradise, others will inhabit the city. That is why the Lord said there are many mansions with the Father. All things belong to God, who supplies a fitting habitation for everyone. As His Word says, the Father apportions all things according to what each person is or will be worthy of. This is the banqueting hall where those invited to the wedding feast recline. The Presbyters, disciples of the Apostles, affirm that this is the ordering and arrangement of the saved, who advance through such grades: by the Spirit to the Son, and by the Son to the Father. The Son then hands over His work to the Father, just as the Apostle said: "For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). In the days of the Kingdom, the righteous person living on earth will forget how to die. When it is said that all things have been subjected, this plainly excludes the One who subjected all things to Him. But when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be subjected to the One who subjected all things to Him, so that God may be all in all. John therefore carefully foresaw the first resurrection of the just and their inheritance in the earthly Kingdom, and the prophets prophesied in harmony about it. The Lord Himself taught this, promising to share a new cup with His disciples in the Kingdom. The Apostle also confessed that creation will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. In all these things and through them all, the same God the Father is revealed: He who formed humanity, promised the inheritance of the earth to the fathers, brought that promise to fulfillment in the resurrection of the just, and completes the promises in His Son's Kingdom — afterward bestowing paternally those things which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have never entered the human heart. For there is one Son who brings the Father's work to perfection, and one human race in which the mysteries of God are perfected — mysteries angels long to see and strive to fathom, the wisdom of God by which the very substance of His creation is perfected, conformed to the Son. Thus the offspring of His Word descends into the creation, that is, into the formed substance, and is received by it; and the creation in turn receives the Word and ascends to Him, surpassing the angels, and is made according to the image and likeness of God.

latin: 1. Cum sint enim veri homines, veram esse oportet et plantationem ipsorum, sed non excedere in ea quee non sunt; sed in iis quee sunt, proficere. Non enim substantia, neque materia conditionis exterminatur; (verus enim et firmus qui constituit illam:) sed Jigura transit mundi hujus, hoc est, in quibus transgressio facta est ; quoniam veteratus est homo in ipsis. Et propter hoe figura hee temporalis facta est, preesciente omnia Deo; quemadmodum ostendimus ®in eo libro qui ante hune est, et causam temporalium mundi fabricationis, secundum quod potuit, ostendimus. autem figura hac, et renovato homine, et vigente ad incorruptelam, ut non possit jam veterascere, erit coelum novum et terra nova, in quibus novus perseverabit homo, semper nova confabulans Deo. Et quoniam hee semper perseverabunt sine fine, Esaias ait sic: Quemadmodum enim caelum novum et terra nova, que ego facio, dicit Dominus, sic stabit semen perseverant in conspectu meo, vestrum et nomen vestrum. Et quemadmodum Presbyteri dicunt, tune qui digni fuerint ccelorum conversatione, illue transibunt, id est, in coelos; alii %tute Paradisi deliciis utentur; alii autem speciositatem civitatis possidebunt: ubique autem Deus videbitur, set quemadmodum digni erunt videntes eum. Esse autem distantiam hance habitationis eorum qui centum fructificaverunt, et eorum qui sexaginta, et eorum qui triginta: quorum quidam in celum assumentur, alii in paradiso conversabuntur, alii in civitate inhabitabunt: et propter hoc dixisse Dominum, multas esse apud Patrem mansiones. Omnia enim Dei sunt, qui omnibus aptam habitationem prestat. Quemadmodum ° Verbum ejus ait, omnibus divisum esse a Patre secundum quod quis est dignus, aut erit. Et hoe est triclinium, in quo recumbent ii, qui epulantur yocati ad nuptias. Hance esse adordinationem et dispositionem eorum qui Salvantur, dicunt Presbyteri Apostolorum discipuli, et per hujusmodi gradus proficere, et per Spiritum quidem ad Filium, per Filium autem ascendere ad Patrem; Filio deinceps cedente Patri opus suum, quemadmodum et ab Apostolo dictum est: Quoniam oportet regnare eum, quoadusgque ponat omnes inimicos sub pedibus sejus. Novissima inimica destruetur mors. In temporibus enim Regni justus homo super terram exsistens, obliviscetur mori jam. Quando autem dixerit, inquit, omnia subjecta sunt, scilicet absque co qui subjecit omnia. Cum autem ei fuerint subdita omnia, tune tpse Filius subjectus erit ei, qui sibi subjecit omnia, ut sit Deus loomnia in omnibus. Diligenter ergo Johannes previdit primam justorum resurrectionem, et in Regno terree heereditatem: consonanter autem et prophetee prophetaverunt de ea. Hee enim et Dominus docuit, mixtionem calicis novam in regno cum discipulis habiturum se pollicitus. Et Apostolus autem liberam futuram creaturam a servitute corruptelz in libertatem gloriz filiorum Dei confessus est. Et in omnibus iis et per omnia idem Deus Pater ostenditur, qui plasmavit hominem, et heereditatem terree promisit patribus, qui eduxit illam in resurrectione justorum, et promissiones adimplet in Filii sui regnum: postea preestans illa paternaliter, que neque oculus vidit, neque auris audivit, neque in cor hominis ascendit. Etenim unus Filius, qui tatem Patris perfecit; et unum genus humanum, in quo perficiuntur mysteria Dei, guem concupiscunt angeli videre, et prevalent investigare sapientiam Dei, per quam plasma ejus conet concorporatum Filio perficitur: ut progenies ejus Verbum descendat in facturam, hoe est in plasma, et capiatur ab eo; et factura iterum capiat Verbum, et ascendat ad eum, supergrediens angelos, et fiet secundum imaginem et similitudinem Dei.

excerpts.author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: God caused every tree that is pleasing to the sight and good for food to spring from the earth. At the beginning only the vegetation created on the third day existed—plants, seeds, and grasses—yet the growth in Paradise was fashioned with a distinct beauty and loveliness, so that the very planting was called by God a planting of His own. The rest of the plants are like those the world possesses, but the two trees, the tree of life and the tree of knowledge, are found nowhere else but in Paradise alone. Scripture teaches that Paradise is a land planted on the earth, for it says that God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, set the man there, and made every tree pleasing to the sight and good for food rise from the earth (Genesis 2:8-10). The phrase “from the earth” and “toward the east” shows that Paradise lies beneath this heaven, under which both east and earth exist. Eden, in Hebrew, means luxury. A river flows out of Eden to water Paradise and then splits into four branches; two of them, Phison and Geon, irrigate the eastern regions, especially Geon, which encircles all the land of Ethiopia and is identified with the Nile in Egypt. The other two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, are well known to us because they reach our own lands. God placed the man in Paradise, as previously noted, to cultivate and guard it, commanding him to eat from every fruit—including the tree of life—but forbidding him to taste of the tree of knowledge. God transferred the man from the earth from which he was formed into Paradise, granting him a chance for advancement so that, as he grew and became perfect and even divine, he might ascend to heaven; for man was created as a middle being, neither wholly mortal nor wholly immortal, but capable of both, and Paradise itself, in its beauty, stands midway between the world and heaven, possessing eternity. The command “to work” signifies no labor other than keeping God’s commandment, so that by not disobeying he would not destroy himself, as he ultimately did through sin.

greek: Ἐξανατείλας οὖν ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἔτι πᾶν ξύλον, ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν. Ἐν γὰρ πρώτοις μόνα ᾖν τὰ ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ γεγενημένα, φυτὰ καὶ σπέρματα καὶ χλόαι· τὰ δὲ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ ἐγενήθη διαφόρῳ καλλονῇ καὶ ὡραιότητι, ὅκου γε καὶ φυτεία ὠνόμασται ὑπὸ θεοῦ πεφυτευμένη. Καὶ τὰ μὲν λοιπὰ φυτὰ ὅμοια καὶ ὁ κόσμος ἔσχηκεν· τὰ δὲ δύο ξύλα, τὸ τῆς ζωῆς καὶ τὸ τῆς γνώσεως, οὐκ ἔσχηκεν ἑτέρα γῆ ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἐν μόνῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ.Ὅτι δὲ καὶ ὁ παράδεισος γῆ ἐστιν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς πεφύτευται, ἡ γραφὴ λέγει· Καὶ ἐφύτευσεν ὁ θεὸς παράδεισον ἐν Ἐδὲμ κατὰ ἀντολάς, καὶ ἔθετο ἐκεῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον· καὶ ἐξανέτειλεν ὁ θεὸς ἔτι ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς πᾶν ξύλον, ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν. Τὸ οὖν ἔτι ἐκ τῆς γῆς καὶ κατὰ ἀνατολὰς σαφῶς διδάσκει ἡμᾶς ἡ θεία γραφὴ τὸν παράδεισον ὑπὸ τοῦτον τὸν οὐρανόν, ὑφ᾿ ὃν καὶ ἀνατολαὶ καὶ· γῆ εἰσιν. Ἐδὲμ δὲ ἑβραϊστὶ τὸ εἰρημένον ἑρμηνεύεται τρυφή. Ποταμὸν δὲ σεσήμακεν ἐκπορεύεσθαι ἐξ Ἐδὲμ ποτίζειν τὸν παράδεισον, κἀκεῖθεν διαχωρίζεσθαι εἰς τέσσαρας ἀρχάς· ὧν δύο, οἱ καλούμενοι Φεισὼν καὶ Γεών, ποτίζουσιν τὰ ἀνατολικὰ μέρη, μάλιστα ὁ Γεών, ὁ κυκλῶν πᾶσαν γῆν Αἰθιοπίας, ὅν φασιν ἐν τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ ἀναφαίνεσθαι τὸν καλούμενον Νεῖλον. Οἱ δὲ ἄλλοι δύο ποταμοὶ φανερῶς γινώσκονται παρ᾿ ἡμῖν, οἱ καλούμενοι Τίγρις καὶ Εὐφράτης· οὗτοι γὰρ γειτνιῶσιν ἕως τῶν ἡμετέρων κλιμάτων.Θεὶς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, καθὼς προειρήκαμεν, ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ εἰς τὸ ἐργάζεσθαι καὶ φυλάσσειν αὐτόν, ἐνετείλατο αὐτῷ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν καρπῶν ἐσθίειν, δηλονότι καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ τῆς ζωῆς, μόνου δὲ ἐκ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ τῆς γνώσεως ἐνετείλατο αὐτῷ μὴ γεύσασθαι. Μετέθηκεν δὲ αὐτὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῆς γῆς, ἐξ ἧς ἐγεγόνει, εἰς τὸν παράδεισον, διδοὺς αὐτῷ ἀφορμὴν προκοπῆς, ὅπως αὐξάνων καὶ τέλειος γενόμενος, ἔτι δὲ καὶ θεὸς ἀναδειχθείς, οὕτως καὶ εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀναβῇ (μέσος γὰρ ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐγεγόνει, οὔτε θνητὸς ὁλοσχερῶς οὔτε ἀθάνατος τὸ καθόλου, δεκτικὸς δὲ ἑκατέρων· οὕτως καὶ τὸ χωρίον ὁ παράδεισος, ὡς πρὸς καλλονήν, μέσος τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ γεγένηται), ἔχων ἀϊδιότητα. Τὸ δὲ εἰπεῖν ἐργάζεσθαι οὐκ ἄλλην τινὰ ἐργασίαν δηλοῖ ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τὸ φυλάσσειν τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅκως μὴ παρακούσας ἀπολέσῃ ἑαυτόν, καθὼς καὶ ἀπώλεσεν διὰ ἁμαρτίας.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We must now restore what follows and demonstrate more clearly the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy. The Stoics claim that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they also claim the soul is. You will find all these points plainly in the Scriptures. Do not mistake their allegorical interpretations for the truth that the gnosis now delivers, for even if they appear to show something, they actually signal something else, much like the ancient wise wrestlers. They assert that God permeates all existence, but we call Him only the Creator and the Creator by the Word. They were misled by the passage in Wisdom — 'it passes through and penetrates all things because of its purity' — since they did not understand that these words refer to the primordial Wisdom created by God. True, they reply, but the philosophers — Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic alike — posit matter as a first principle, not a single one. Let them therefore acknowledge the so-called matter, described by them as unqualified and formless, and even more boldly, as non-being, according to Plato's own statement. And although he knew the most mystical truth — that there is only one truly existing principle — he speaks of it in the Timaeus in those very words. For now, let our position stand thus: the question concerning all things, whether of one principle or many or whatever they suppose about them, is not to be discussed at present, for no other reason than the difficulty of explaining what seems plausible in the present mode of exposition. Besides, that prophetic saying — 'the earth was invisible and unformed' (Genesis 1:2) — has furnished them with a starting point for material substance. In Epicurus's case, the notion of chance arose because he did not attend to the literal sense, resulting in 'vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' As for Aristotle, he limited providence only as far as the moon, drawing from this psalm: 'Lord, your mercy reaches to the heavens, your truth to the clouds' (Psalm 36:6). For the prophetic revelation of mysteries had not yet been unveiled before the Lord's coming. Both the punishments after death and the penal fire were borrowed from barbarian philosophy by the entire poetic tradition, and by Greek philosophy as well. Plato, in the final book of the Republic, puts it in these very words: 'Here are wild men, fiery to behold, standing by, discerning the cry; taking some aside privately, they led them away, but binding Aridaeus and the others hand and foot and head, throwing them down and flaying them, they dragged them along the road outside, beating them with thorns.' He intends the fiery wild men to represent angels who seize the wicked and punish them — 'He makes His angels spirits, His ministers a flame of fire.' It follows from this that the soul is immortal; for that which is punished or corrected, existing in sensation, continues to live, even if it is said to suffer.

greek: τὰ δ’ ἑξῆς προςαποδοτέον καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας Ελληνικὴν κλοπὴν σαφέστερον ἤδη παραστατέον. Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Just as the preaching arrived at the appointed moment, so the law and the prophets were given in their season to the barbarians, and philosophy to the Greeks, to prepare their hearing for the gospel. The Lord who redeemed Israel declares: "In an acceptable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you; I gave you as a covenant to the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit the desolate heritages," saying to the prisoners, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Be revealed" (Isaiah 49:8). If the Jews are the prisoners to whom the Lord said, "Come out of the bonds," then the ones who want to leave are those who bound themselves voluntarily and loaded themselves with unbearable burdens through human contrivance; clearly, those in darkness are the ones who have idolatry rooted in their governing faculty. For those who were righteous according to the law lacked faith, so the Lord healed them as well, saying, "Your faith has saved you"; but for those who were righteous according to philosophy, not only was faith in the Lord lacking, but also the turning away from idolatry. The moment the truth was disclosed, they too repented of their former deeds; therefore the Lord preached the gospel even to those in Hades. Scripture says: "Hades says to Destruction, 'We have not seen his form, but we have heard his voice'" (Psalm 107:20). It was not the place itself that received a voice and spoke those words, but the souls consigned to Hades who gave themselves over to destruction — like men who willingly throw themselves from a ship into the sea — and these are the ones who heard the divine power and voice. Who in their right mind would suppose that in a single condemnation the souls of the righteous and the wicked are lumped together, charging providence with injustice? What then? Does this not show that the Lord preached the gospel to those lost in the flood — or rather, to those who were bound — and to those held in prison and under guard (1 Peter 3:19)? It has also been demonstrated in the second Stromata that the apostles, following the Lord, preached the gospel to those in Hades as well; for it was necessary, I think, that just as the best disciples imitated the Teacher here, so they would do the same there, so that some would bring the Hebrews and others the nations to repentance — that is, those who had lived righteously according to the law and according to philosophy, yet not perfectly, but who passed through life in a sinful manner.

greek: Ἀλλ’ ὡς κατὰ καιρὸν ἥκει τὸ κήρυγμα νῦν, οὕτως κατὰ καιρὸν ἐδόθη νόμος μὲν καὶ προφῆται βαρβάροις, φιλοσοφία δὲ Ἕλλησι, τὰς ἀκοὰς ἐθίζουσα πρὸς τὸ κήρυγμα. λέγει γοῦν κύριος ὁ ῥυσάμενος Ἰσραήλ· καιρῷ δεκτῷ ἐπήκουσά σου καὶ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σωτηρίας ἐβοήθησά σοι, ἔδωκά σε εἰς διαθήκην ἐθνῶν τοῦ κατασκηνῶσαι τὴν γῆν καὶ κληρονομῆσαι κληρονομίαν ἐρήμου, λέγοντα τοῖς ἐν δεσμοῖς· ἐξέλθετε, καὶ τοῖς ἐν τῷ σκότει ἀνακαλυφθῆναι. εἰ γὰρ δέσμιοι μὲν Ἰουδαῖοι, ἐφ’ ὧν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἐξέλθετε εἶπεν ἐκ τῶν δεσμῶν οἱ θέλοντες, τοὺς ἑκουσίως δεδεμένους καὶ τὰ δυσβάστακτα φορτία (φησὶν) αὑτοῖς διὰ τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης παρεγχειρήσεως ἐπαναθεμένους λέγων, δῆλον ὡς οἱ ἐν σκότει οὗτοι ἂν εἶεν οἱ ἐν τῇ εἰδωλολατρείᾳ κατορωρυγμένον ἔχοντες τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. τοῖς μὲν γὰρ κατὰ νόμον δικαίοις ἔλειπεν ἡ πίστις, διὸ καὶ τούτους ἰώμενος ὁ κύριος ἔλεγεν· ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· τοῖς δὲ κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν δικαίοις οὐχ ἡ πίστις μόνον ἡ εἰς τὸν κύριον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἀποστῆναι τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ἔλειπεν. αὐτίκα ἀποκαλυφθείσης τῆς ἀληθείας καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς προπεπραγμένοις μεταμέλονται· διόπερ ὁ κύριος εὐηγγελίσατο καὶ τοῖς ἐν Ἅιδου. φησὶ γοῦν ἡ γραφή· λέγει ὁ Ἅιδης τῇ ἀπωλείᾳ· εἶδος μὲν αὐτοῦ οὐκ εἴδομεν, φωνὴν δὲ αὐτοῦ ἠκούσαμεν. οὐχ ὁ τόπος δή που φωνὴν λαβὼν εἶπεν τὰ προειρημένα, ἀλλ’ οἱ ἐν Ἅιδου καταταγέντες καὶ εἰς ἀπώλειαν ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδεδωκότες καθάπερ ἔκ τινος νεὼς εἰς θάλασσαν ἑκόντες ἀπορρίψαντες, οὗτοι τοίνυν εἰσὶν οἱ ἐπακούσαντες τῆς θείας δυνάμεώς τε καὶ φωνῆς· ἐπεὶ τίς ἂν εὖ φρονῶν ἐν μιᾷ καταδίκῃ καὶ τὰς τῶν δικαίων καὶ τὰς τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν ὑπολάβοι εἶναι ψυχάς, ἀδικίαν τῆς προνοίας καταχέων; τί δ’; οὐχὶ δηλοῦσιν εὐηγγελίσθαι τὸν κύριον τοῖς τε ἀπολωλόσιν ἐν τῷ κατακλυσμῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ πεπεδημένοις, καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ τε καὶ φρουρᾷ συνεχομένοις; δέδεικται δὲ κάν τῷ δευτέρῳ Στρωματεῖ τοὺς ἀποστόλους ἀκολούθως τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ τοὺς ἐν Ἅιδου εὐηγγελισμένους· ἐχρῆν γάρ, οἶμαι, ὥσπερ κἀνταῦθα, οὕτως δὲ κἀκεῖσε τοὺς ἀρίστους τῶν μαθητῶν μιμητὰς γενέσθαι τοῦ διδασκάλου, ἵν’ ὃ μὲν τοὺς ἐξ Ἑβραίων, οἳ δὲ τὰ ἔθνη εἰς ἐπιστροφὴν ἀγάγωσι, τουτέστιν τοὺς ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ τῇ κατὰ νόμον καὶ κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν βεβιωκότας μέν, οὐ τελείως δέ, ἀλλ’ ἁμαρτητικῶς διαπεραναμένους τὸν βίον·

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — An Answer to the Jews 2
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let us now move forward and define the heart of the matter with precision. Why should anyone think that God—the Founder of the universe, the Governor of the world, the Shaper of man, the Sower of all nations—gave his law through Moses to a single people and withheld it from the rest? If he had not given it to everyone, he would never have allowed Gentile proselytes to approach it at all. But because it fits both the goodness and the equity of the One who shaped the human race, he gave the same law to every nation, ordering it to be kept at the specific times, through the specific people, and in the specific manner he chose.

At the very beginning, he gave Adam and Eve a law: do not eat from the tree planted in the middle of Paradise. Disobedience meant certain death. That one command would have been enough, had they kept it. In that law given to Adam we already recognize every commandment that later sprouted through Moses: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul. You shall love your neighbor as yourself. You shall not kill, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness. Honor your father and mother. You shall not covet what belongs to another (Genesis 2:16-17; Exodus 20:1-17). This primordial law, given in Paradise, is the matrix of all God's commandments.

Had they loved the Lord their God, they would not have broken his command. Had they loved their neighbor—that is, themselves—they would have rejected the serpent's lie. They would not have committed suicide by cutting themselves off from immortality through disobedience. They would have avoided theft, since they would not have secretly tasted the fruit. They would not have hid from the Lord their God among the trees. They would not have become accomplices to the devil's false claim that they would become like God. They would not have offended their Father, who formed them from the clay of the earth as from a mother's womb. Had they not coveted another's property, they would never have touched the forbidden fruit.

Thus in this universal, primordial law—which God sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree—we find every commandment of the later law already implanted, waiting to be published and to sprout in its appointed season. The God who later teaches the law is the same One who first sent the commandment; it belongs to him to instruct later those he first formed as righteous. Why should it surprise us that the One who instituted discipline also increases it, or that the One who began the work also perfects it?

I maintain that long before Moses received the written law on stone tablets, an unwritten law existed—naturally understood and kept by the fathers. How else was Noah found righteous, unless the justice of natural law had gone before him? How was Abraham called God's friend, except through the equity and justice of that same natural law? How was Melchizedek named priest of God Most High, unless there were already those who offered sacrifices to God before the Levitical priesthood existed? The law came to Moses only after the Exodus, after a long interval of time—four hundred and thirty years after Abraham.

From this we see that God's law did not begin with Moses, or at Horeb, Sinai, or the desert. It began earlier, first in Paradise, then with the patriarchs, and only later was it reformed for the Jews at set times. We must therefore stop treating the Law of Moses as the principal law. It is a subsequent law, which God gave to the nations at a specific moment, promised through the prophets to reform for the better, and foretold would be observed only temporarily—just as it was given at a specific time through Moses. We cannot strip God of his power to reform the law's precepts according to the condition of the times for the salvation of humanity.

Anyone who insists the Sabbath must still be kept as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day under threat of death (Genesis 17:10-14), must prove that the righteous of the past kept the Sabbath or were circumcised, and so became God's friends. If circumcision purifies a man, why did God not circumcise Adam when he created him, or after he sinned? God established him in Paradise as uncircumcised and appointed him its keeper. Since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or Sabbath-keeping, it follows that he also praised Abel—uncircumcised, not keeping the Sabbath—accepting his sacrifice offered in simplicity of heart, while rejecting Cain's, who did not offer rightly.

God also delivered Noah, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, from the Flood. He translated Enoch, the most righteous, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, from this world before he tasted death—showing us that we too can please God without the burden of the Mosaic law. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, was drawn into the priesthood of God. And Lot, Abraham's brother, proves that a man can be rescued from the burning of Sodom without observing the law, purely on the merit of his own justice.

latin: Igitur gradum conferamus, et summam quaestionis ipsius certis lineis determinemus. Cur etenim Deus, universitatis conditor, mundi totius gubernator, hominis plasmator, universarum gentium sator, legem per Moysen uni populo dedisse credatur, et non omnibus gentibus attribuisse dicatur? Nisi enim omnibus eam dedisset, nullo pacto ad eam etiam proselytos ex gentibus accessum habere permitteret: sed, ut congruit bonitati Dei et aequitati ipsius, utpote plasmatoris generis humani, omnibus gentibus eamdem legem dedit: quam certis et statutis temporibus observari praecepit, quando voluit, et per quos voluit, et sicut voluit. Namque in principio mundi, ipsi Adae et Evae legem dedit, ne de fructu arboris plantatae in medio paradisi ederent; quod si contra fecissent, morte morerentur: quae lex eis sufficeret, si esset custodita. In hac enim lege Adae data, omnia praecepta condita recognoscimus quae postea pullulaverunt data per Moysen, id est, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum de toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua; et, Diliges proximum tibi tanquam te; et, Non occides, non moechaberis, non furaberis, falsum testimonium non dices. Honora patrem tuum et matrem: et, Alienum non concupisces. Primordialis lex est enim data Adae et Evae in paradiso, quasi matrix omnium praeceptorum Dei. Denique, si Dominum Deum suum dilexissent, contra praeceptum ejus non fecissent: si proximum diligerent, id est semetipsos, persuasioni serpentis non credidissent; atque ita in semetipsos homicidium non commisissent, excidendo de immortalitate, faciendo contra Dei praeceptum; a furto quoque abstinuissent, si de fructu arboris clam non degustassent, nec a conspectu Domini Dei sui sub arbore delitescere gestissent: nec falsum asseveranti diabolo participes efficerentur, credendo ei quod similes Dei essent futuri: atque ita nec Deum offendissent, ut patrem, qui eos de limo terrae quasi ex utero matris figuraverat: si alienum non concupissent, de fructu illicito non gustassent. Igitur in hac generali et primordiali Dei lege, quam in arboris fructu observari Deus sanxerat, omnia praecepta legis posterioris specialiter indita fuisse cognoscimus, quae suis temporibus edita germinaverunt Ejusdem est enim postea subdocere legem, qui ante praemiserat praeceptum, quoniam et ipsius est erudire postea qui ante justos formare instituerat. Quid enim mirum, si is auget disciplinam qui instituit? si is perfecit qui coepit? Denique ante legem Moysi scriptam in tabulis lapideis legem fuisse contendo non scriptam, quae naturaliter intelligebatur, et a patribus custodiebatur. Nam unde Noe justus inventus, si non illum naturalis legis justitia praecedebat? unde Abraham amicus Dei deputatus, si non de aequitate et justitiae legis naturalis? unde Melchisedech sacerdos Dei summi nuncupatus, si non ante Leviticae legis sacerdotium Levitae fuerunt, qui sacrificia Deo offerebant? Sic enim post supra scriptos patriarchas data lex est Moysi eo tempore posteaquam ab Aegypto excesserunt, post intervallum multorum temporum et spatia Denique, post quadringentos et triginta annos Abrahae data est lex. Unde intelligimus Dei legem etiam ante Moysen, nec in Horeb tantum, aut in Sina et in cremo, sed antiquiorem primum in paradiso, post patriarchis, atque ita et Judaeis certis temporibus reformatam; ut non jam ad Moysi legem ita attendamus, quasi ad principalem legem, sed ad subsequentem, quam certo tempore Deus et gentibus exhibuit, et repromissam per prophetas in melius reformavit, et praemonuit futurum ut, sicuti certo tempore data est lex per Moysen, ita temporaliter observata et custodita credatur: nec adimamus hanc Dei potestatem, pro temporum conditione legis praecepta reformantem in hominis salutem. Denique, qui contendit et sabbatum adhuc observandum quasi salutis medelam, circumcisionem octavi diei propter mortis comminationem, doceat in praeteritum justos sabbatizasse aut circumcidisse, et sic amicos Dei effectos. Nam, si circumcisio purgat hominem, Deus Adam incircumcisum cum faceret, cur eum non circumcidit, vel posteaquam deliquit, si purgat circumcisio? Certe in paradiso constituens eum incircumcisum, colonum paradisi praefecit. Igitur, cum neque circumcisum neque sabbatizantem Deus Adam instituerit, consequenter quoque sobolem ejus Abel offerentem sibi sacrificia, incircumcisum nec sabbatizantem laudavit, accepto ferens quae offerebat in simplicitate cordis, et reprobans sacrificium fratris ejus Cain, qui non offerebat, non recte dividebat. Noe quoque incircumcisum Deus, sed et non sabbatizantem, de diluvio liberavit. Nam et Enoch justissimum non circumcisum, nec sabbatizantem, de hoc mundo transtulit; qui necdum mortem gustavit, ut aeternitatis candidatus, jam nobis ostenderet nos quoque sine legis onere Moysi, Deo posse placere. Melchisedech quoque summi Dei sacerdos incircumcisus, et non sabbatizans, ad sacerdotium Dei allectus est. Probat et Loth frater Abrahae, quod pro meritis justitiae suae sine legis observatione de Sodomitarum incendio sit liberatus.

excerpts.citation: Hippolytus — On Christ and Antichrist On Christ and Antichrist (Hippolytus)
excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: Since you wanted to learn accurately the topics you proposed to us, my beloved brother Theophilus, I considered it right to set before your eyes the matters you seek, drawing abundantly from the divine Scriptures as from a holy spring, so that you might rejoice not only by hearing with your ears, but also, having been instructed by the power of the realities themselves, you might be able to glorify God in every way. For this will be a safeguard for you in the present life, free from danger, that you may bring forth from prepared words the things hard for many to know and hard to grasp, sow them in the breadth of your heart as in fertile and pure soil, and overthrow those who contradict and speak against the saving word. But be afraid lest these things be entrusted to unbelieving and blaspheming tongues, for the danger is no ordinary one; rather entrust them to cautious and faithful men who wish to live holily and righteously with fear. For not in vain did the blessed apostle warn Timothy, writing: "Guard the deposit, turning away from profane and empty talk and the contradictions of the falsely named knowledge, which some, by professing it, have missed the faith" (2 Timothy 1:14). And again: "You, therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you heard from me through many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2).

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We return now to the resurrection. I have already taken on every heretic in my own volume and satisfied them on this point, but I will not leave it alone here, not when some still ignore that earlier work. "What will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise?" (1 Corinthians 15:29). Let that practice answer for itself; perhaps the February Kalends will speak up for those who petition on behalf of the dead. So do not make the apostle the author or confirmer of that rite, as if he used it to prop up the resurrection of the flesh — as if those who are baptized in vain for the dead do so only because they believe in the resurrection. We have him somewhere defining one baptism. Therefore, to be baptized for the dead is to be baptized for bodies, since we have shown the body to be dead. What will those do who are baptized for bodies, if bodies do not rise?

And so we rightly plant this step: the apostle also introduced a second argument, equally about the body. "How will the dead rise? With what body will they come?" (1 Corinthians 15:35). Once the resurrection — which was being denied — was defended, it followed naturally to discuss the quality of the body, which was not yet seen. But that discussion belongs with others. Marcion, who refuses the resurrection of the flesh altogether and promises salvation only to the soul, makes the issue one of substance, not quality. Furthermore, it is most clearly shown from these very passages what the apostle treats regarding the body's quality on account of those who ask, "How will the dead rise? With what body will they come?" He has already preached that the body will rise; otherwise he would not have treated the body's quality. Finally, if he offers examples like a grain of wheat or anything of that sort — to which God gives a body as he wishes — if he says each seed has its own body, so that there is one flesh of humans, another of animals and birds, and heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and another glory of the sun and another of the moon and another of the stars — does he not portend a fleshly, bodily resurrection, which he commends through fleshly, bodily examples?

Marcion enim in totum carnis resurrectionem non admittens et soli animae salutem repromittens, non qualitatis, sed substantiae facit quaestionem. porro et ex his manifestissime obducitur, quae apostolus ad qualitatem corporis tractat propter illos, qui dicunt: quomodo resurgent mortui? quo autem corpore uenient? iam enim praedicauit resurrecturum esse corpus, si de corporis qualitate tractauit. denique si proponit exempla grani tritici uel alicuius eiusmodi, quibus det corpus deus prout uolet, si unicuique seminum proprium ait corpus esse, ut aliam quidem carnem hominum, aliam uero pecudum et uolucrum, et corpora caelestia atque terrena, et aliam gloriam solis et lunae aliam et stellarum aliam, — nonne carnalem et corporalem portendit resurrectionem, quam per carnalia et corporalia exempla commendat?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ forbids divorce, saying that whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer — so that in this way too he blocks divorce by making the marriage of the repudiated woman illicit. Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife and lives with her, and it happens that he finds no favor in her because some indecent matter is found in her, he shall write a certificate of divorce, give it into her hand, and send her from his house (Deuteronomy). You see the difference between the law and the gospel, between Moses and Christ? Obviously. For you have not accepted that gospel of the same truth and the same Christ, in which, while prohibiting divorce, he answers his own question: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, commanded you to give a certificate of divorce; but from the beginning it was not so, for the one who made male and female said the two shall become one flesh; what God has joined together, let no one separate (Matthew). By that answer he both safeguarded Moses' statute as his own and upheld the Creator's institution as Christ himself. But to the extent you must be convicted from the texts you have accepted, I will meet you on your own ground, as if my Christ were yours: does he not, while forbidding divorce yet sharing the mind of the one who joined male and female, rather vindicate than demolish Moses' statute? But look — if your Christ teaches the opposite of Moses and the Creator, then he is mine if I do not prove the contrary. For I say he imposed the divorce prohibition conditionally: if a man dismisses his wife in order to marry another, he who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer, on the very ground for which she was dismissed — a ground on which dismissal is not lawful — so that another may be taken; for he who marries a woman illicitly dismissed, as though she were not dismissed, is an adulterer. The marriage remains, since it has not been lawfully dissolved; and while the marriage endures, to marry again is adultery. Thus, if he prohibited dismissing a wife only conditionally, he did not prohibit it entirely, and what he did not wholly prohibit he permitted in other cases where the cause for the prohibition ceases; and so he no longer teaches the opposite of Moses, whose precept he preserves somewhere, not to say confirms. Or if you deny outright that Christ permits divorce, how do you dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female nor admitting those already joined to the sacrament of baptism and the Eucharist, unless they have sworn against the fruit of marriage — that is, against the Creator himself? What will a husband do with you if his wife commits adultery? Keep her? But your own apostle does not allow the members of Christ to be joined to a prostitute. Therefore Christ too upholds the justice of divorce. Now this is confirmed by Moses on the same ground on which Christ also permits repudiation: if an indecent matter is found in a woman. For in Matthew's gospel: whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of adultery, makes her an adulteress; and thus the man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is also counted an adulterer (Matthew).

plane. non enim recepisti illud quoque euangelium eiusdem ueritatis et eiusdem Christi, in quo prohibens diuortium propriam quaestionem eius absoluit: Moyses propter duritiam cordis uestri praecepit libellum repudii dare; a primordio autem non fuit sic; quia scilicet qui marem et feminam fecerat, erunt duo, dixerat, in carne una; quod deus itaque iunxit, homo (non) disiunxerit. hoc enim responso et Moysi constitutionem protexit, ut sui, et creatoris institutionem direxit, ut Christus ipsius. sed quatenus ex his reuincendus es, quae recepisti, sic tibi occurram, ac si meus Christus (tuus:) nonne et ipse prohibens diuortium et parem tamen gestans eius, qui marem et feminam iunxit, excusauerit potius quam destruxerit Moysi constitutionem? sed ecce sic tuus sit iste Christus contrarium docens Moysi et creatori, ut, si non contrarium ostendero, meus sit. dico enim illum condicionaliter nunc fecisse diuortii prohibitionem, si ideo quis dimittat uxoiem, ut aliam ducat: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem et aliam duxerit, adulterium commisit, et qui a marito dimissam duxerit aeque adulter est, ex eadem utique causa dimissam, qua non licet dimitti, ut alia ducatur; inlicite enim dimissam pro indimissa ducens adulter est. manet enim matrimonium quod non rite diremptum est; manente (autem) matrimonio nubere adulterium est. ita si condicionaliter prohibuit dimittere uxorem, non in totum prohibuit, et quod non prohibuit in totum, permisit alias, ubi causa cessat, ob quam prohibuit; et iam non contrarium Moysi docet, cuius praeceptum alicubi conseruat, nondum dico confirmat. aut si omnino [non] negas permitti diuortium a \' Christo, quomodo tu nuptias dirimis, nec coniungens marem et feminam nec alibi coniunctos ad sacramentum baptismatis et eucharistiae admittens, nisi inter se coniurauerint aduersus fructum nuptiarum, ut aduersus ipsum creatorem? certe quid faciet apud te maritus, si uxor eius commiserit adulterium? habebitne illam? sed nec tuum apostolum sinere (scis) coniungi prostitutae membra Christi. habet itaque et Christum adsertorem iustitia diuortii. iam hinc confirmatur ab illo Moyses ex eodem titulo perhibens repudium, quo et Christus: si inuentum fuerit in muliere negotium impudicum. nam et in euangelio Mathei: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem suam praeter causam adulterii, facit eam adulterari. atque ita adulter censetur et ille, qui dimissam a uiro duxerit.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Resurrection of the Flesh VII
excerpts.author: Tertullian
excerpts.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
english: The flesh's authority seems weaker because the divine hand didn't handle it directly, as it did the clay. Yet when God worked the clay so that flesh would later come from it, he was already conducting the flesh's business. I still want you to learn when and how the flesh flowered from that clay. Some claim the skin tunics Adam and Eve put on after being expelled from Paradise represent the flesh's reformation from clay, but that's false. Adam had already recognized flesh in the woman formed from his substance long before that, declaring, "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Gen 2:23). That recognition of the male in the female, filled out with flesh, had to be supplemented by clay, I think, if Adam was still clay at that point. So the clay was obliterated and consumed into flesh. When? When man became a living soul by God's breath—a vapor suited to bake the clay into a different quality, as a potter fires clay into earthenware. Just as a potter reforms fire-tempered clay into stronger material, shaping one form into another more fitting than the first, now of its own kind and name. Scripture asks, "Will the clay say to the potter?"—meaning, will man challenge God? (Isa 64:8). And the Apostle calls us "earthen vessels" (2 Cor 4:7). Yet clay is also man, because it was clay first; and earthenware is flesh, because it comes from clay through the divine vapor breathed into it, which the skin tunics—meaning skins—later covered. To the point that if you strip off the skin, you lay the flesh bare. What becomes spoil when removed was a garment when put on. That's why the Apostle, calling circumcision a stripping of the flesh, confirmed the skin is a tunic. Given all this, you have clay made glorious by God's hand, and flesh made more glorious by God's breath—by which both laid aside the rudiments of clay and took on the soul's ornaments. You aren't more careful than God. You set Scythian and Indian gems, the glowing pearls of the Red Sea, not in lead, copper, iron, or even silver, but in the most select and painstakingly worked gold. You anoint vessels with the costliest wines and ointments. You match the dignity of perfectly forged swords to their sheaths. Yet God entrusted the shadow of his soul, the breeze of his spirit, the work of his mouth, to the vilest vessel—and by placing it so unworthily, condemned it, as it were. But he placed, or rather inserted and blended, the soul into flesh with such intimate concretion that it's uncertain whether flesh carries soul or soul carries flesh; whether soul appears to flesh or flesh to soul. Still, we must believe the soul is borne along and dominates, since it stands nearer to God. This too redounds to the flesh's glory: it lies closest to God, contains him, and shares in his dominion. For what use of nature, what fruit of the world, what taste of the elements does the soul not enjoy through the flesh? Through which the soul is served by every instrument of sense—sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch; through which the soul is sprinkled with divine power, accomplishing nothing without speech, even if silently permitted. Speech itself comes from the flesh's organ; arts through the flesh; studies, talents, through the flesh; works, business, duties, through the flesh. The soul's entire life is the flesh, so that not to live is nothing other than turning away from the flesh. Dying, too, belongs to the flesh, whose life it also is. If all things are subject to the soul through the flesh, they must also be subject to the flesh, through which you use them. So the flesh, though appointed minister and servant of the soul, is found to be partner and co-heir. If this holds for temporal things, why not for eternal ones?
