excerpts.author: Origen
english: He will say that the ecclesiastical proclamation contains the word about God's righteous anointing, and that this word—once believed to be true—also provokes us to live well and to flee sin in every way. Through it, once we have been consoled by the Lord, we may grasp the most necessary problem. In order to understand what the self-moved is, we must unfold its concept; once that concept is clarified, what we are seeking can be presented clearly.

Of the things that are moved, some have the cause of their movement within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Therefore, objects that are carried—such as wood, stones, and all matter held together by habit alone—are moved only from outside. Let the notion of the movement of bodies be set aside from the discussion for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals, plants, and all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of being moved within themselves. From this group, they say metals come; besides these, fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among the things that have the cause of being moved within themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves. The non-living things are moved from outside themselves; the living things are moved from themselves. Living things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs that provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals fantasies occur that provoke an impulse, with nature moving the impulse in an orderly way. For example, in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, the spider's imaginative nature moving it in an orderly way to this very thing, with no other thing being believed by the animal after its imaginative nature; and in the bee, the impulse is to shape wax.

The rational animal, however, also has reason alongside its imaginative nature—reason that judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since in the nature of reason there are starting-points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following these we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad. In doing so we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. It must not be overlooked, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered toward all things exists in animals, whether to a greater or a lesser degree, so that it comes near—as it were—to the rational work found in tracking dogs and war horses. To be subjected to this or that external thing, a fantasy moving us in such and such a way, is admittedly not in our power. But to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of nothing other than the reason within us—either operating in us according to the starting-points that provoke us toward the good and toward duty, or turning us away toward the opposite.

excerpts.citation: Gregory Thaumaturgus — Panegyric to Origen Argument 10.— Hence the Mere Word-Sages are Confuted, Wh
excerpts.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
excerpts.locus: Argument 10.— Hence the Mere Word-Sages are Confuted, Wh
english: I ask both the philosophers living today — those I know personally and those I have heard about from others — and everyone else to listen to what I am saying now without bias. Let no one think I speak this way because of friendship toward the man, or because I still depend on the other philosophers (I want to be, if anyone else is, a lover of them because of their words; I want to speak well of them and I am glad when I hear others speaking well of them). But these things are such that philosophy is almost despised by everyone and its very name is brought to an end, and I was about to choose to be a private person rather than learn anything from what these men proclaim — men to whom, because of the rest of their lives, it did not seem worthy to approach, perhaps not thinking this correctly). Let no one suppose that I say these things out of some ambition, either from praise toward the man or from another kind of ambition toward the outside philosophers. But also let us not seem to flatter by saying lesser things than their deeds deserve, and let us not speak empty words and names and clever expressions which they provide for themselves. For I, not even when I was a young man learning the common rhetoric of a rhetorician, endured willingly to praise or to give an encomium about something that was not true. So then not even now, when I am about to praise, do I think it necessary to extol him simply by the censures of others, or to speak badly of the man because of the faults of others so that I might have something greater to say about him by comparing his blessed life. We do not think in this way; but I will acknowledge what I have experienced, without any comparison or fabrication of words.

greek: ᾿Ἐξαιτοῦμαι δὲ παρά τε φιλοσόφων τῶν νῦν ὄντων, σοὺυς αὐτὸς ἔγνων καὶ ὃσους ἄλλων διηγουμένων ἤκουσα, καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων, ἀνεμεσήτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ νῦν ἡμῖν λεγόμενα. μηδέ μέ τις ἢ φιλίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα ἢ καὶ ἀπτεχϑανόμενον ἔτι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις (ὧν, εἴπτερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐραστής ve διὰ τοὺς λόγους εἶναι ϑέλω, καὶ εὐφημεῖν αὐτοὺς βούλομαι αὐτός τε καὶ ἑτέρων τὰ κάλλιστα λεγόντων περὶ αὐτῶν ἀκούεξιν᾽ ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτά ἐστιν, ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον περιϊβρίζεσϑαι μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων σχεδὸν καὶ τοὔνομα τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἐμὲ δὲ μικροῦ δεῖν ἰδιωτεύειν ἑλέσϑαι πτάντη, ἤπερ τι μαϑεῖν ὧν οὗτοι ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, οἷς διὰ τὸν λοιττὸν βίον οὐδὲ προσιέναι ἄξιον εἶναι ἐδόκουν, ἴσως οὐκ ὀρϑῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν), πλὴν μή μέ τις φιλοτιμίᾳ τινὶ ἤτοι τῶν εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἐπαίνων ἢ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω φιλοσόφους ἄλλῃ ταύτῃ φιλο- τὸ τιμίᾳ ταῦτα λέγειν ὑπονοησάτω" ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρότερα ἡμᾶς τῶν αὐτοῖ: ἔργων, μὴ κολακεύειν δοχοίημεν, λέγειν τεεττείσϑω οὐχὲ ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐντέχνους ἐγχωμίων ἑαυτοῖς ἐχποριζομένοις" ὃς οὐδ᾽ ὕτε μειράκιον ὧν τὴν δημώδη ῥητορικὴν ἔχ. ῥήτορος ἐδιδασκόμην, ἐπαινεῖν καὶ τὸ λέγειν περί του ἐγκώμιον, ὃ τι μὴ ἀληϑὲς ἦν, ἑκὼν ὑπέμενον. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ νῦν ἐπαινεῖν ττροϑέμενος, ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἑτέρων ψόγοις τοῦτον ἐξαίρειν οἶμαι δεῖν" ἢ κακῶς ἂν ἔλεγον τὸν ἄνδρα, τοῖς ἄλλων πταίσμασιν, ἵνα τι ττερὶ αὐτοῦ μεῖζον δὴ λέγειν ἔχοιμι, τταραβαλὼν τὸν μακάριον αὐτοῦ βίον" οὐχ οὕτως ἀφραίνομεν᾽ ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸ ὃ πέπονθα δίχα τινὸς παραβολῆς χαὶ τεανουργίας τῆς ἐν λόγοις ὁμολογήσω.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Since Celsus also ridicules the serpent narrative as contradicting God's commands to humanity, treating the account as merely another myth like those told to old women, he deliberately omits mention of God's "paradise" and the statement that God "planted a garden in Eden, toward the east" and "made every tree grow from the ground that is pleasant to the sight and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil" (Genesis 2:8-9), along with the subsequent details that could move a receptive reader, since all these matters are not treated without dignity. Let us therefore set against this the passages from Plato's Symposium concerning Eros as recounted to Socrates, and how Socrates' speech surpasses all others in the dialogue in dignity. Plato writes: "When Aphrodite was born, the gods held a feast, including Poros, son of Metis. After dinner, Penia arrived as if for a celebration and stood by the doors. Poros, drunk on nectar (for wine did not yet exist), entered the garden of Zeus and fell asleep, weighed down. Penia, plotting to have a child by Poros because of her poverty, lay beside him and conceived Eros. Thus Eros became Aphrodite's attendant and servant, born on her birthday and by nature a lover of beauty — and Aphrodite is beautiful. As the son of Poros and Penia, Eros finds himself in this condition: first, he is always poor and far from tender and fair, as most suppose, but hard, rough, barefoot, and homeless, always sleeping on the ground without bedding, in doorways and streets under the open sky, sharing his mother's nature of constant need. From his father, however, he schemes against the beautiful and the good. He is brave, enterprising, and intense, a mighty hunter, always weaving schemes, desiring wisdom, resourceful, philosophizing all his life, a terrible sorcerer, pharmacist, and sophist; neither immortal nor mortal by nature, but sometimes flourishing and living on the same day when he prospers, sometimes dying, then reviving again through his father's nature. What he acquires always slips away, so that Eros never lacks nor grows rich. And he stands midway between wisdom and ignorance." Consequently, those who encounter this myth, if they imitate Celsus' malice — which is alien to Christians — will mock the myth and bring shame upon the great Plato; but if, examining the mythic form philosophically, they can discern Plato's intention — how he managed to conceal his great doctrines from the many within a mythic framework while speaking as necessary to those who know how to find truth from myths. I have cited this Platonic myth because it seems to contain something akin to God's paradise, with Penia corresponding to the serpent there, and Poros, plotted against by Penia, corresponding to the man plotted against by the serpent. It is not entirely clear whether Plato hit upon these parallels by chance or, as some suppose, encountered them during his journey to Egypt and learned certain things from the Jewish philosophers, preserving some and adapting others while avoiding offense to Greeks by not openly preserving all Jewish wisdom — wisdom slandered among the many because of the strangeness of their laws and their distinctive polity. Neither was this the moment to narrate Plato's myth or the serpent and God's paradise and all written therein; for earlier, in the commentaries on Genesis, we treated these matters as thoroughly as possible.

greek: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ τὰ περὶ τὸν ὄφιν ὡς ἀντιπράσσοντα τοῖς τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον παραγγέλμασιν ὁ Κέλσος κωμῳδεῖ, μῦθόν τινα παραπλήσιον τοῖς παραδιδομένοις ταῖς γραυσὶν ὑπολαβὼν εἶναι τὸν λόγον, καὶ ἑκὼν οὔτε τὸν θεοῦ „παράδεισον“ ὠνόμασεν οὐδ᾿ ὡς πεφυτευκέναι λέγεται „ὁ θεὸς“ „ἐν Ἐδὲμ κατ᾿ ἀνατολὰς“ καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο ἐξανατεταλκέναι „ἐκ τῆς γῆς πᾶν ξύλον ὡραῖον εἰς ὅρασιν καὶ καλὸν εἰς βρῶσιν καὶ τὸ ξύλον τῆς ζωῆς ἐν μέσῳ τῷ παραδείσῳ καὶ τὸ γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ ξύλον“ καὶ τὰ ἐπὶ τούτοις εἰρημένα, δυνάμενα αὐτόθεν κινῆσαι τὸν εὐμενῶς ἐντυγχάνοντα, ὅτι πάντα ταῦτα οὐκ ἀσέμνως τροπολογεῖται· φέρε ἀντιπαραθῶμεν ἐκ τοῦ Συμποσίου Πλάτωνος τὰ εἰρημένα περὶ τοῦ Ἔρωτος τῷ Σωκράτει καὶ ὡς σεμνότερα πάντων τῶν ἐν τῷ Συμποσίῳ εἰπόντων περὶ αὐτοῦ τῷ Σωκράτει περιτεθέντα. οὕτω δ᾿ ἔχει ἡ Πλάτωνος λέξις· „ὅτ᾿ ἐγένετο ἡ Ἀφροδίτη, εἱστιῶντο οἱ θεοὶ, οἵ τε ἄλλοι καὶ ὁ τῆς Μήτιδος υἱὸς Πόρος. ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἐδείπνησαν, προσαιτήσουσα οἷον δὴ εὐωχίας οὔσης ἀφίκετο ἡ Πενία καὶ ἦν περὶ τὰς θύρας. ὁ οὖν Πόρος μεθυσθεὶς τοῦ νέκταρος (οἶνος γὰρ οὔπω ἦν) εἰς τὸν τοῦ Διὸς κῆπον εἰσελθὼν βεβαρημένος εὗδεν. ἡ οὖν Πενία ἐπιβουλεύουσα διὰ τὴν αὑτῆς ἀπορίαν παιδίον ποιήσασθαι ἐκ τοῦ Πόρου, κατακλίνεταί τε παρ᾿ αὐτῷ καὶ ἐκύησε τὸν Ἔρωτα. διὸ δὴ καὶ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης ἀκόλουθος θεράπων γέγονεν ὁ Ἔρως, γεννηθεὶς ἐν τοῖς ἐκείνης γενεθλίοις καὶ ἅμα φύσει ἐραστὴς ὢν περὶ τὸ καλὸν, καὶ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης καλῆς οὔσης. ἅτε οὖν Πόρου καὶ Πενίας υἱὸς ὢν ὁ Ἔρως ἐν τοιαύτῃ τύχῃ καθέστηκε. πρῶτον μὲν πένης ἀεί ἐστι καὶ πολλοῦ δεῖ ἁπαλός τε καὶ καλὸς, οἷον οἱ πολλοὶ οἴονται, ἀλλὰ σκληρὸς καὶ αὐχμηρὸς καὶ ἀνυπόδητος καὶ ἄοικος, χαμαιπετὴς ἀεὶ ὢν καὶ ἄστρωτος, ἐπὶ θύραις καὶ ἐν ὁδοῖς ὑπαίθριος κοιμώμενος, τὴν τῆς μητρὸς φύσιν ἔχων ἀεὶ ἐνδείᾳ ξύνοικος. κατὰ δ᾿ αὖ τὸν πατέρα ἐπίβουλός ἐστι τοῖς καλοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς. ἀνδρεῖος ὢν καὶ ἴτης καὶ σύντονος, θηρευτὴς δεινὸς, ἀεὶ προσπλέκων μηχανὰς καὶ φρονήσεως ἐπιθυμητὴς καὶ πόριμος, φιλοσοφῶν διὰ παντὸς τοῦ βίου, δεινὸς γόης καὶ φαρμακεὺς καὶ σοφιστής· καὶ οὔτε ὡς ἀθάνατος πέφυκεν οὔτε ὡς θνητὸς, ἀλλὰ τοτὲ μὲν τῆς αὐτῆς ἡμέρας θάλλει καὶ ζῇ, ὅταν εὐπορήσῃ, τοτὲ δ᾿ ἀποθνῄσκει [πάλιν], πάλιν δ᾿ ἀναβιώσκεται διὰ τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς φύσιν. τὸ δὲ ποριζόμενον ἀεὶ ὑπεκρεῖ, ὥστε οὔτ᾿ ἀπορεῖ Ἔρως ποτὲ οὔτε πλουτεῖ. σοφίας δ᾿ αὖ καὶ ἀμαθίας ἐν μέσῳ ἐστίν.“ ἄρα γὰρ οἱ ἐντυγχάνοντες τούτοις ἐὰν μὲν τὴν κακοήθειαν τοῦ Κέλσου μιμῶνται, ὅπερ Χριστιανῶν ἀπείη, καταγελάσονται τοῦ μύθου καὶ ἐν χλεύῃ θήσονται τὸν τηλικοῦτον Πλάτωνα· ἐὰν δὲ τὰ ἐν μύθου σχήματι λεγόμενα φιλοσόφως ἐξετάζοντες δυνηθῶσιν εὑρεῖν τὸ βούλημα τοῦ Πλάτωνος . . . ., τίνα τρόπον δεδύνηται τὰ μεγάλα ἑαυτῷ φαινόμενα δόγματα κρύψαι μὲν διὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐν τῷ τοῦ μύθου σχήματι, εἰπεῖν δ᾿ ὡς ἐχρῆν τοῖς εἰδόσιν ἀπὸ μύθων εὑρίσκειν τὸ περὶ ἀληθείας τοῦ ταῦτα συντάξαντος βούλημα. τοῦτον δὲ τὸν παρὰ Πλάτωνι μῦθον ἐξεθέμην διὰ „τὸν“ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ „τοῦ Διὸς κῆπον,“ παραπλήσιόν τι ἔχειν δοκοῦντα τῷ παραδείσῳ τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ τὴν Πενίαν, τῷ ἐκεῖ ὄφει παραβαλλομένην, καὶ τὸν ὑπὸ τῆς Πενίας ἐπιβουλευόμενον Πόρον τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐπιβουλευομένῳ ὑπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως. οὐ πάνυ δὲ δῆλον, πότερον κατὰ συντυχίαν ἐπιπέπτωκε τούτοις ὁ Πλάτων ἢ, ὡς οἴονταί τινες, ἐν τῇ εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἀποδημίᾳ συντυχὼν καὶ τοῖς τὰ Ἰουδαίων φιλοσοφοῦσι καὶ μαθών τινα παρ᾿ αὐτῶν τὰ μέν τινα τετήρηκε τὰ δὲ παρεποίησε, φυλαξάμενος προσκόψαι τοῖς Ἕλλησιν ἐκ τοῦ πάντῃ τὰ τῆς Ἰουδαίων τηρῆσαι σοφίας. διαβεβλημένων παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς διὰ τὸ ξενίζον τῶν νόμων καὶ τὴν ἰδιότροπον κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς πολιτείαν. οὔτε δὲ τὸν Πλάτωνος μῦθον οὔτε τὰ περὶ τὸν ὄφιν καὶ τὸν παράδεισον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ὅσα ἐν αὐτῷ ἀναγέγραπται γεγονέναι νῦν καιρὸς ἦν διηγήσασθαι· προηγουμένως γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ἐξηγητικοῖς τῆς Γενέσεως, ὡς οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν, εἰς ταῦτα ἐπραγματευσάμεθα.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — An Address to Demetrianus An Address to Demetrianus
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: I frequently despised you, Demetriane, because you kept opening your sacrilegious mouth and shouting impious words against the one true God. I judged it more proper to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence than to provoke the madness of a demented man by speaking, and I did not act without the authority of divine teaching. Scripture says: "Do not speak in the ears of a fool, lest he despise the wisdom of your words" (Prov. 23:9). It also says: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him yourself" (Prov. 26:4). We are also commanded to keep the holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, as the Lord says: "Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you" (Matt. 7:6). You often came to me more eager to contradict than to learn, and with loud voices you preferred to force your own opinions on me impudently rather than listen patiently to mine. It seemed foolish to engage you, since it would be easier and lighter to calm the turbulent waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussion. To offer light to the blind, a sermon to the deaf, or wisdom to a brute is useless labor with no effect, for a brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear. Considering these things, I often kept silent and overcame the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable nor restrain the impious with religion nor calm the furious with gentleness. But now you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plague and famine rage, and that rains and showers are withheld after long serenity, and you impute all this to us because your gods are not worshipped by us. It is no longer fitting to remain silent, lest our silence begin to look not like modesty but like diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false accusations we seem to acknowledge the crime. I answer you, Demetriane, and the others you may have stirred up against us by sowing hatred with your slanderous voices; you have gathered many companions for yourself from the root and origin of your own multitude. Yet I believe these people will accept the reason of our words, for whoever is moved to evil by deceit will be much more moved to good by compelling truth. Since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to truth, you should first know that the world has already grown old; it no longer stands with the strength it once had, nor does it prevail with its former vigor and power. The world itself testifies to this even when we are silent and produce no documents from the holy Scriptures and divine preaching; the world now speaks and proves its own decline by the evidence of its failing things. Winter no longer brings such abundance of rain to nourish seeds; summer no longer brings such burning heat to ripen crops; spring no longer makes the sown fields so fertile; autumn is no longer so fruitful with the yield of trees. Less marble is quarried from exhausted mountains; less silver and gold flow from depleted mines, and poor veins shrink and dwindle day by day. The farmer is lacking in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in judgment, concord in friendships, skill in arts, discipline in morals. Do you think a declining substance can possess the same greatness it had when it was still new and flourishing in youth? Whatever is nearing its end and turning toward the west must decrease. Thus the sun at its setting throws its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus the moon, as its course declines, is diminished with worn horns; thus the tree that was once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed in old age as its branches wither; and the spring that once flowed abundantly with overflowing veins now, in its old age, barely trickles with a scant flow. This is the sentence passed upon the world; this is the law of God: that all things that arise must decline, and all that grow must grow old, the strong must become weak, the great must diminish, and when they have become weak and diminished they must come to an end. You impute to Christians the fact that individual things are diminishing while the world grows old. What if the old also imputed to Christians that they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as they once did in hearing, walking, sight, strength, bodily vigor, and limb mass? Once human life lasted eight or nine hundred years; now it can hardly reach a hundred. We see gray hair in children, and hair falls out before it even grows; nor does age end in old age, but rather begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, humanity hastens to its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates because of the old age of the world itself, so that no one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail when the whole world is already in decline and at its end.

latin: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On Works and Alms On Works and Alms
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Many and great are the divine benefits by which God the Father and Christ have worked, and continue to work, for our salvation. The Father sent the Son to preserve us and give us life so that He might restore us, and the Son willingly allowed Himself to be sent and to become human so that He might make us children of God. He humbled Himself in order to raise up a people who had previously lain prostrate. He was wounded so that He might heal our wounds. He served so that He might lead servants into freedom. He endured death so that He might offer immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy.

But beyond this, consider what kind of providence and how great the mercy is by which we are watched over for our salvation, so that the person who has been redeemed might be more fully provided for. When the Lord came, He healed the wounds that Adam had borne and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent. He gave a law to the healthy and commanded them not to sin again, lest something worse befall the sinner. We were restricted and confined within a narrow prescription of innocence. Human frailty and weakness would have had no recourse unless divine piety came to our aid once more. By showing works of justice and mercy, it opened a way to preserve our salvation, so that we might wash away whatever filth we contract afterward through alms.

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: 'Sins are purified by alms and faith' (Proverbs 16:6). This does not refer, of course, to sins contracted beforehand; those are purified by the blood of Christ and by sanctification. Again He says: 'Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguishes sin' (Sirach 3:30). Here it is also shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so also the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. Because the remission of sins is given once in Baptism, a constant and daily practice that imitates Baptism again obtains God's indulgence.

The Lord teaches this also in the Gospel. When His disciples were rebuked for eating without first washing their hands, He responded: 'He who made what is inside also made what is outside. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you' (Luke 11:40-41). He was teaching and showing that it is not the hands but the heart that must be washed, and that the filth inside must be drawn out rather than what is outside. He showed that whoever purifies what is inside has also purified what is outside, and that with a cleansed mind, the skin and body also begin to be clean. Moreover, warning and showing from where we can be clean and purified, He added that alms are to be given. The Merciful One teaches and urges us to show mercy. Because He seeks to keep those whom He redeemed at a great price, He teaches that those stained after the grace of Baptism can be purified again.

Let us therefore recognize, brothers, the salutary gift of divine indulgence. Since we cannot be without some wound of conscience, let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies to cleanse and purify our sins. Let no one flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate heart, so that, trusting in his own innocence, he thinks medicine need not be applied to wounds. It is written: 'Who will boast that he has a chaste heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?' (Proverbs 20:9). And again John says in his Epistle: 'If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us' (1 John 1:8). If no one can be without sin, and whoever claims to be blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and how kind is divine mercy! Knowing that the healthy do not lack certain wounds afterward, God gave remedies to heal and save those wounds again.

Finally, brothers, divine admonition has never ceased or been silent, so that in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, always and everywhere, God's people are urged to works of mercy. With the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders Isaiah: 'Cry out with strength, do not hold back. Raise your voice like a trumpet. Announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their wicked deeds' (Isaiah 58:1). After commanding that their sins be rebuked and their wicked deeds be brought forth with a full impulse of indignation, He declared that they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers, supplications, and fasts, nor could they placate God's wrath even by rolling in sackcloth and ashes. Yet in the last part, showing that God can be placated only by alms, He added: 'Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh and blood' (Isaiah 58:7). 'Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will quickly appear. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will be your rear guard. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry for help, and He will say: Here I am' (Isaiah 58:8-9).

latin: MULTA et magna sunt, fratres charissimi beneficia divina quibus in salutem nostram Dei Patris et Christi larga et copiosa clementia et operata sit et semper operetur, quod conservandis ac vivificandis nobis Pater Filium misit, ut reparare nos posset, quodque Filius missus esse et hominis filius fieri voluit ut nos Dei filios faceret. Humiliavit se, ut populum qui prius jacebat erigeret: vulneratus est, ut vulnera nostra curaret: servivit, ut ad libertatem servientes extraheret: mori sustinuit, ut immortalitatem mortalibus exhiberet. Multa haec sunt et magna divinae misericordiae munera. Sed adhuc, qualis providentia illa et quanta clementia est quod nobis salutari ratione prospicitur, ut homini qui redemptus est reservando plenius consulatur! Nam, cum Dominus adveniens sanasset illa quae Adam portaverat vulnera, et venena serpentis antiqua curasset, legem dedit sano, et praecepit ne ultra jam peccaret, ne quid peccanti gravius eveniret. Coarctati eramus et in angustum innocentiae praescriptione conclusi. Nec haberet quid fragilitatis humanae infirmitas atque imbecillitas faceret, nisi iterum pietas divina subveniens, justitiae et misericordiae operibus ostensis, viam quamdam tuendae salutis aperiret, ut sordes postmodum, quascumque contrahimus, eleemosynis abluamus. Loquitur in Scripturis divinis Spiritus sanctus et dicit: Eleemosynis et fide delicta purgantur. Non utique illa delicta quae fuerant ante contracta, nam illa Christi sanguine et sanctificatione purgantur. Item denuo dicit: Sicut aqua extinguit ignem, sic eleemosyna extinguit peccatum. Hic quoque ostenditur et probatur quia, sicut lavacro aquae salutaris gehennae ignis extinguitur, ita et eleemosynis atque operationibus justis delictorum flamma sopitur. Et quia semel in Baptismo remissa peccatorum datur, assidua et jugis operatio Baptismi instar imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largitur. Hoc et in Evangelio Dominus docet. Nam cum denotarentur discipuli ejus quod ederent, nec prius manus abluissent, respondit et dixit: Qui fecit quod intus est, fecit et quod foris est. Verum date eleemosynam, et ecce vobis munda omnia: docens scilicet et ostendens non manus lavandas esse, sed pectus, et sordes intrinsecus potius quam extrinsecus detrahendas; verum qui purgaverit quod est intus, eum quoque id quod foris est repurgasse, et emundata mente, cute quoque et corpore mundum esse coepisse. Porro autem, monens et ostendens unde mundi et purgati esse possimus, addidit eleemosynas esse faciendas. Misericors docet et monet misericordiam fieri; et quia servare quaerit quos magno pretio redemit, post Baptismi gratiam sordidatos docet denuo posse purgari. Agnoscamus itaque, fratres charissimi, divinae indulgentiae munus salubre, et emundandis purgandisque peccatis nostris, qui sine aliquo conscientiae vulnere esse non possumus, medelis spiritalibus vulnera nostra curemus. Nec quisquam sic sibi de puro atque immaculato pectore blandiatur, ut, innocentia sua fretus, medicinam non putet adhibendam esse vulneribus, cum scriptum sit: Quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? et iterum in Epistola sua Joannes ponat et dicat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Si autem nemo esse sine peccato potest, et quisquis inculpatum se esse dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, quam necessaria, quam benigna est divina clementia, quae, cum sciat non deesse sanatis quaedam postmodum vulnera, dedit curandis denuo sanandisque vulneribus remedia salutaria! Numquam denique, fratres dilectissimi, admonitio divina cessavit et tacuit quominus in Scripturis sanctis tam veteribus quam novis semper et ubique ad misericordiae opera Dei populus provocaretur; et canente atque exhortante Spiritu sancto, quisquis ad spem regni coelestis instruitur, facere eleemosynas jubetur. Mandat et praecipit Esaiae Deus: Exclama, inquit, in fortitudine, et noli parcere. Sicut tuba exalta vocem tuam, et annuntia plebi meae peccata ipsorum et domui Jacob facinora eorum. Et cum peccata eis sua exprobrari praecepisset, cumque eorum facinora pleno indignationis impetu protulisset, dixissetque eos nec, si orationibus et precibus et jejuniis uterentur, satisfacere pro delictis posse, nec, si in cilicio et cinere volverentur, iram Dei posse lenire, in novissima tamen parte, demonstrans solis eleemosynis Deum posse placari, addidit dicens: Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos sine tecto induc in domum tuam. Si videris nudum, vesti eum, et domesticos seminis tui non despicias. Tunc erumpet temporaneum lumen tuum, et vestimenta tua cito orientur, et praeibit ante te justitia, et claritas Dei circumdabit te. Tunc exclamabis, et Deus exaudiet te. Dum adhuc loqueris dicet: Ecce adsum.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On the Mortality On the Mortality
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Although many of you, my dearest brothers, possess a steadfast mind, a firm faith, and a devoted soul that the present abundance of mortality does not shake, but which, like a strong and stable rock, breaks the world's turbulent attacks and the age's violent waves rather than being broken by them, and which is not conquered by temptations but proven by them, I nevertheless notice among the common people some who, whether through weakness of mind, smallness of faith, the sweetness of secular life, softness of sex, or, what is worse, error of truth, stand less firmly and do not exercise the divine and invincible strength of their hearts. This matter must not be hidden or left unspoken, so that, as far as my mediocrity suffices, a sermon conceived from the Lord's reading and delivered with full vigor may suppress the laziness of delicate minds, and that the one who has begun to be a man of God and of Christ may be deemed worthy of God and of Christ. For the one who serves God, who is stationed in the heavenly camp and already hopes for what is divine, ought to acknowledge himself so that no trepidation or disturbance exists in us amid the world's storms and whirlwinds, since the Lord has foretold these things with a provident voice, exhorting, teaching, preparing, and strengthening his Church's people for every endurance of future events. He announced that wars, fires, earthquakes, and pestilences would arise in various places, and he forewarned that adversities would increase more and more in the last times, so that we would not be shaken by the unexpected and new fear of threatening things. Behold, the things spoken are coming to pass; and as the things predicted beforehand happen, the things promised will also follow, the Lord himself promising and saying: "When you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near" (Luke 21:31). The kingdom of God, my dearest brothers, has begun to draw near. The reward of life, the joy of eternal salvation, perpetual security, and the possession of paradise, recently lost, now arrive as the world passes away; now heavenly things succeed earthly ones, great things succeed small ones, eternal things succeed transient ones. What room is here for anxiety and worry? Who is troubled and sad amid these things except the one who lacks hope and faith? For it belongs to the one who fears death to refuse to go to Christ. It belongs to the one who refuses to go to Christ to disbelieve that he will begin to reign with Christ. For it is written that the just man lives by faith. If you are just and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why do you not embrace the fact that you will be with Christ in the future, and why are you not secure in the Lord's promise, and why do you not rejoice that you will be free from the devil? Simeon, that just man who was truly just, who kept God's commands with full faith, when he had been divinely assured that he would not die before seeing Christ, and when Christ the infant came to the temple with his mother, recognized in the Spirit that Christ had already been born, the one foretold to him; and upon seeing him, he knew he would soon die. Therefore, rejoicing at his approaching death and secure in his near summons, he took the child in his hands, and blessing the Lord, he exclaimed: "Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation"; thereby proving and testifying that peace belongs to the servants of God then, a free peace then, a tranquil rest then, when, extracted from the world's turmoil, we seek the harbor of eternal rest and security, when, having finished this death, we come to immortality. For that is the true peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable, firm, and perpetual security. Moreover, what else is the world but a daily battle against the devil, a constant conflict against his darts and arrows? We contend with greed, impurity, anger, ambition, carnal vices, and worldly allurements in a continual and troublesome struggle. The human mind, besieged and hedged in on all sides by the devil's attacks, can hardly meet each assault, can hardly resist. If greed is cast down, lust rises; if lust is suppressed, ambition follows; if ambition is despised, anger inflames, pride puffs up, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, and jealousy severs friendship. You are forced to curse what the divine law forbids, compelled to swear what is not permitted.

latin: Etsi apud plurimos vestrum, fratres dilectissimi, mens solida est et fides firma et anima devota, quae ad praesentis mortalitatis copiam non movetur, sed tamquam petra fortis et stabilis turbidos impetus mundi et violentos saeculi fluctus frangit potius ipsa nec frangitur, et tentationibus non vincitur, sed probatur, tamen quia animadverto in plebe quosdam vel imbecillitate animi, vel fidei parvitate, vel dulcedine saecularis vitae, vel sexus mollitie, vel, quod majus est, veritatis errore minus stare fortiter nec pectoris sui divinum atque invictum robur exercere, dissimulanda res non fuit nec tacenda quo minus quantum nostra mediocritas sufficit, vigore pleno et sermone de dominica lectione concepto delicatae mentis ignavia comprimatur, et qui homo Dei et Christi esse jam coepit, Deo et Christo dignus habeatur. Agnoscere enim se debet, fratres dilectissimi, qui Deo militat, qui positus in coelestibus castris divinam jam sperat, ut ad procellas et turbines mundi trepidatio nulla sit in nobis, nulla turbatio, quando haec ventura praedixerit Dominus providae vocis hortatu instruens et docens et praeparans atque corroborans Ecclesiae suae populum ad omnem tolerantiam futurorum, bella et fumes et terrae motus et pestilentias per loca singula exsurgere praenuntiavit et cecinit. Et ne inopinatus nos et novus rerum infestantium metus quateret, magis ac magis in novissimis temporibus adversa crebrescere ante praemonuit. Fiunt ecce quae dicta sunt; et quando fiunt quae ante praedicta sunt, sequentur et quaecumque promissa sunt, Domino ipso pollicente et dicente: Cum autem videritis haec omnia fieri, scitote quoniam in proximo est regnum Dei.. Regnum Dei, fratres dilectissimi, esse coepit in proximo. Praemium vitae et gaudium salutis aeternae, et perpetua securitas, et possessio paradisi nuper amissa, mundo transeunte jam veniunt; jam terrenis coelestia et magna parvis et caducis aeterna succedunt. Quis hic anxietatis et sollicitudinis locus est? Quis inter haec trepidus et moestus est, nisi cui spes et fides deest? Ejus est enim mortem timere qui ad Christum nolit ire. Ejus est ad Christum nolle ire qui se non credat cum Christo incipere regnare. Scriptum est enim justum fide vivere. Si justus es, et fide vivis, si vere in Christum credis, cur non cum Christo futurus et de Domini pollicitatione securus quod ad Christum voceris amplecteris, et quod diabolo careas gratularis. Simeon denique ille justus, qui vere justus fuit, qui fide plena Dei praecepta servavit, dum ei divinitus responsum fuisset quod non ante moreretur quam Christum vidisset, et Christus infans in templum cum matre venisset, agnovit in Spiritu natum esse jam Christum, de quo sibi fuerat ante praedictum; quo viso, scivit se cito esse moriturum. Laetus itaque de morte jam proxima, et de vicina accersitione securus, accepit in manus puerum, et benedicens Dominum exclamavit et dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secuudum verbum tuum in pace, quoniam viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum; probans scilicet atque contestans tunc esse servis Dei pacem, tunc liberam, tunc tranquillam quietem, quando, de istis mundi turbinibus extracti, sedis et securitatis aeternae portum petimus, quando expuncta hac morte ad immortalitatem venimus. Illa est enim vera pax, illa fida tranquillitas, illa stabilis et firma et perpetua securitas. Caeterum, quid aliud in mundo, quam pugna adversus diabolum, quotidie geritur, quam adversus jacula ejus et tela conflictationibus assiduis dimicatur? Cum avaritia nobis, cum impudicitia, cum ira, cum ambitione congressio est, cum carnalibus vitiis, cum illecebris saecularibus assidua et molesta luctatio est. Obsessa mens hominis et undique diaboli infestatatione vallata vix occurrit singulis, vix resistit. Si avaritia prostrata est, exsurgit libido: si libido compressa est, succedit ambitio: si ambitio contempta est, ira exasperat, inflat superbia, vinolentia invitat, invidia concordiam rumpit, amicitiam zelus abscindit. Cogeris maledicere quod divina lex prohibet, compelleris jurare quod non licet.

excerpts.citation: Alexander of Alexandria — On the Soul and Body and the Passion of the Lord
excerpts.author: Alexander of Alexandria
excerpts.work: On the Soul and Body and the Passion of the Lord
english: 1. The Word which is ungrudgingly sent down from heaven, is fitted for the irrigation of our hearts, if we have been prepared for His power, not by speaking only, but by listening. For as the rain without the ground does not produce fruit, so neither does the Word fructify without hearing, nor hearing without the Word. Moreover, the Word then becomes fruitful when we pronounce it, and in the same way hearing, when we listen. Therefore since the Word draws forth its power, do you also ungrudgingly lend your ears, and when you come to hear, cleanse yourselves from all ill-will and unbelief. Two very bad things are ill-will and unbelief, both of which are contrary to righteousness; for ill-will is opposed to charity, and unbelief to faith ; just in the same way as bitterness is opposed to sweetness, darkness to light, evil to good, death to life, falsehood to truth . Those, therefore, who abound in these vices that are repugnant to virtue , are in a manner dead; for the malignant and the unbelieving hate charity and faith , and they who do this are the enemies of God .

2. Since therefore you know , brethren beloved, that the malignant and the unbelieving are the enemies of righteousness, beware of these, embrace faith and charity, by which all the holy men who have existed from the beginning of the world to this day have attained unto salvation . And show forth the fruit of charity, not in words only, but also in deeds , that is, in all godly patience for God's sake. For, see! The Lord Himself has shown His charity towards us, not only in words but also in deeds , since He has given Himself up as the price of our salvation . Besides, we were not created, like the rest of the world, by word alone, but also by deed. For God made the world to exist by the power of a single word, but us He produced by the efficacy alike of His word and working. For it was not enough for God to say, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, Genesis 1:26 but deed followed word; for, taking the dust from the ground, He formed man out of it, conformable to His image and similitude, and into him He breathed the breath of life, so that Adam became a living soul .

3. But when man afterwards by his fall had inclined to death, it was necessary that that form should be recreated anew to salvation by the same Artificer. For the form indeed lay rotting in the ground; but that inspiration which had been as the breath of life, was detained separate from the body in a dark place, which is called Hades. There was, therefore, a division of the soul from the body; it was banished ad inferos , while the latter was resolved into dust; and there was a great interval of separation between them; for the body, by the dissolution of the flesh, becomes corrupt; the soul being loosened from it, its action ceases. For as when the king is thrown into chains, the city falls to ruin; or as when the general is taken captive, the army is scattered abroad; or as when the helmsman is shaken off, the vessel is submerged; so when the soul is bound in chains, its body goes to pieces; as the city without its king, so its members are dissolved; as is the case with an army when its general is lost, they are drowned in death, even as happens to a vessel when deprived of its helmsman. The soul , therefore, governed the man, as long as the body survived; even as the king governs the city, the general the army, the helmsman the ship. But it was powerless to rule it, from the time when it was immoveably tied to it, and became immersed in error ; therefore it was that it declined from the straight path, and followed tempters, giving heed to fornication, idolatry , and…

4. Man went forth from paradise to a region which was the sink of unrighteousness, fornication, adultery , and cruel murder . And there he found his destruction; for all things conspired to his death, and worked the ruin of him who had hardly entered there. Meanwhile man wanted some consolation and assistance and rest. For when was it well with man? In his mother's womb? But when he was shut up there, he differed but little from the dead. When he was nourished with milk from the breast? Not even then, indeed, did he feel any joy . Was it rather while he was coming to maturity? But then, especially, danger's impended over him from his youthful lusts . Was it, lastly, when he grew old? Nay, but then does he begin to groan, being pressed down by the weight of old age, and the expectation of death. For what else is old age but the expectation of death? Verily all the inhabitants of earth do die, young men and old, little children and adults, for no age or bodily stature is exempt from death. Why, then, is man tormented by this exceeding grief? excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Later, when God saw the earth filled with malice and crimes, He decided to destroy the human race with a flood. Still, to restore the multitude, He chose one man, because among all the corrupted a singular example of justice remained. When he was six hundred years old, he built an ark, just as God had commanded him, and in it he himself was preserved with his wife, three sons, and three daughters-in-law, after water had covered all the highest mountains (Genesis 6:9–9:29).

After the earth dried, God cursed the injustice of the former age so that the length of life would not again become a cause for devising evils; He gradually diminished the span of human life through successive generations and set the limit at one hundred twenty years, which may not be exceeded (Genesis 6:3). When he came out of the ark, the man diligently cultivated the ground and planted a vineyard with his own hand, as the Holy Scriptures teach (Genesis 9:20). From this it is argued that those who consider Liber the author of wine are mistaken; for he preceded not only Liber but also Saturn and Uranus by many ages.

When his vineyard first bore fruit, he rejoiced, drank to drunkenness, and lay naked. One of his sons, whose name was Ham, saw his father's nakedness but did not cover it; instead he went out and told his brothers. The brothers, taking a cloak, entered with faces turned away and covered their father. When the father learned what had been done, he disowned and expelled the son (Genesis 9:21–27). The fugitive settled in the part of the earth now called Arabia, and that land was named Canaan after him, and his descendants were called Canaanites. This was the first nation to ignore God, because its leader and founder did not receive the worship of God from his father, having been cursed by him; thus he bequeathed ignorance of the divine to his offspring.

From this nation the nearest peoples spread as their numbers increased. The man's own descendants, however, were called Hebrews, and with them the religion of God remained. Later, when these Hebrews had multiplied immensely and the narrowness of their land could not contain them, young men — whether sent by their parents or acting on their own, driven by scarcity — scattered as fugitives here and there; they filled all the islands and the whole world, and, torn from the holy root, established new customs and institutions according to their own will.

The first who occupied Egypt began to observe and worship celestial bodies. Because they were not sheltered by houses on account of the climate, nor was the sky ever veiled by clouds in that region, they noted the courses of the stars and their effects while they frequently venerated them, watching them more curiously and freely. Afterwards they invented portentous animal figures to worship, led by certain prodigies, whose authors we will soon reveal. The other peoples dispersed through the land, admiring the elements of the world — heaven, sun, earth, sea — venerated them without images or temples and offered sacrifices to them in the open, until the passage of time brought the most powerful kings to build temples and statues and to institute their worship with victims and incense.

Thus the nations began to stray from the knowledge of God. They are wrong, therefore, who contend that the worship of gods existed from the beginning of things and that paganism is prior to the religion of God, which they think was invented later, because they ignore the source and origin of truth. Now we return to the beginning of the world.

progenies deminuit hominis aetatem atque in centum et uiginti annis metam conlocauit, quam transgredi non liceret. ille uero cum egressus esset ex arca, sicuti sanctae litterae docent, terram studiose fructum cepisset, laetus factas bibit usque ad ebrietatem iacuitque nudus. quod cum uidisset unus ei filiis, cui nomen fuit Cham, non texit patris nuditatem, sed egressus etiam fratribus indicauit. at nominatur, eaque terra de nomine eius Chanaan dicta est et posteri eius Chananaei. haec fuit prima gens quae deum ignoranit, quoniam princeps eius et conditor cultum dei a patre non accepit maledictus ab eo: itaque ignorantiam diuinitatis minoribus suis reliquit. ab hac gente proximi quique populi multitudine increscente fluxerunt. ipsius autem patris posteri Hebraei dicti: penes quos religio dei resedit. sed et ab his postea multiplicato in inmensum numero cum eos angustiae locorum suorum capere non possent, tum adulescentes uel missi a parentibus uel sua sponte, cum rerum penuria cogeret, profugi ad quaerendas sibi nouas sedes huc atque illuc dispersi omnes insulas et orbem totum repleuerunt et a stirpe sanctae radicis auulsi nouos sibi mores atque instituta pro arbitrio condiderunt. sed omnium primi qui Aegyptum occupauerant caelestia. suspicere atque adorare coeperunt. et quia neque domiciliis tegebantur propter aeris qualitatem nec ullis in ea regione nubibus subtexitur caelum, cursus siderum et effectus nota-uerunt, dum ea saepe uenerantes curiosius ac liberius intuentur. postea deinde portentificas animalium Sguras quas colerent commenti sunt quibusdam prodigiis inducti, quorum mox auctores aperiemus. ceteri autem qui per terram dispersi fuerant admirantes elementa mundi, caelum solem terram mare, sine ullis imaginibus ac templis uenerabantur et his sacrificia in aperto celebrabant, donec processu temporum potentissimis regibus templa et simulacra fecerunt eaque uictimis et odoribus colere instituerunt. sic aberrantes a notitia dei gentes esse coeperunt. errant igitur qui deorum cultus ab exordio rerum fuisse contendunt et priorem esse gentilitatem quam dei religionem, quam putant posterius inuentam, quia. fontem atque originem ueritatis ignorant. nunc ad principium mundi reuertamur.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: When the times that God has fixed for death reach their completion, death itself will come to an end. Since temporal death follows temporal life, it follows necessarily that souls will rise again to everlasting life, because temporal death has received its limit. Just as the life of the soul is eternal — in it the soul takes the divine and inexpressible fruits of its own immortality — so too its death must be perpetual, a state in which it pays perpetual punishments and infinite torments for its sins. The situation therefore stands thus: those who are blessed in this bodily and earthly life will always be miserable hereafter, because they have already obtained the good things they preferred; this is the lot of those who worship gods but neglect God. But those who pursued justice in this life and were miserable, despised, and needy, often vexed by insults and injuries on account of justice itself — for virtue cannot be held in any other way — will always be blessed hereafter, so that, having already borne evils, they may also enjoy good things. This certainly befalls those who, despising earthly and fragile goods, follow the heavenly religion of God, whose goods are eternal, just like the One who bestows them. Do not the works of body and soul show that the soul is exempt from death? Because the body is itself fragile and mortal, whatever works it undertakes are equally transitory. Tullius says there is nothing worked by human hands that is not sometime reduced to ruin, either by human violence or by the sheer aging of all things. Yet we see that the works of the soul are eternal. Whoever, despising present things, have left monuments of their genius and great deeds for posterity have clearly sought an indelible name for their mind and virtue. If bodily works are mortal because the body itself is mortal, it follows that the soul proves to be immortal, because we see that its works are not mortal. In the same way, the desires of body and soul declare the one to be mortal, the other everlasting. The body desires nothing but temporal things — food, drink, clothing, rest, pleasure — and yet it cannot even desire or attain these without the soul’s assent and aid. The soul, by itself, desires many things that do not pertain to the body’s duty or fruit, and these are not fragile but eternal: the fame of virtue, the memory of a name. The soul even desires the worship of God, which consists in abstaining from desires and lusts, enduring pain, and despising death — all against the body’s inclinations. From this it is credible that the soul does not perish but is separated from the body, because the body can do nothing without the soul, while the soul can do many and great things without the body. Consider also this: things visible to the eyes and tangible to the hand, because they can suffer external force, cannot be eternal; but things that come under neither touch nor sight, whose only power, reason, and effect appear, are eternal, because they suffer no external force. If the body is mortal because it is subject to sight and touch, then the soul is immortal because it can be neither touched nor seen.

latin: Inpletis igitur temporibus quae deus morti statuit terminabitur ipsa mors. et quia temporalem uitam temporalis mors sequitur, consequens est ut resurgant animae ad uitam perennem, quia finem mors temporalis accepit. rursus sicut uita animi sempiterna est, in qua diuinos et ineloquibiles inmortalitatis suae fructus capit, ita et mors eius perpetua sit necesse est, in qua perennes poenas et infinita tormenta pro peccatis suis pendit. ergo in ea condicione res posita est, ut qui beati sunt in hac uita corporali atque terrena, semper miseri sint futuri, quia iam bonis quae maluerunt potiti sunt, quod iis euenit qui deos adorant ac deum neglegunt, deinde qui iustitiam sequentes in hac uita miseri fuerint et contempti et inopes et ob ipsam iustitiam contumeliis et iniuriis saepe uexati, quia nec aliter uirtus teneri potest, semper beati sint futuri, ut quia mala iam pertulerunt, etiam bonis fruantur: quod iis utique contingit qui contemptis terrestribus diis et fragilibus bonis caelestem religionem dei secuntur, cuius bona sicut ipse qui tribuit sempiterna sunt. quid? opera corporis atque animi nonne indicant esse animam mortis expertem? nam corpus quia ipsum fragile est atque mortale, quaecumque opera molitur, aeque caduca sunt. nihil enim Tullius ait esse quod sit manibus humanis laboratum, quod non aliquando ad interitum redigatur uel iniuria hominum uel ipsa confectrice rerum omnium uetustate. at uero animi opera uidemus aeterna. nam quicumque contemptu praesentium studentes in memoriam monumenta ingeniorum factorumque magnorum reliquerunt, hi plane mentis ac uirtutis suae nomen indelebile quaesierunt. ergo si opera corporis ideo mortalia sunt, quia ipsum mortale est, sequitur ut anima ex eo inmortalis appareat, quia uidemus opera eius non esse mortalia. eodem modo desideria quoque corporis animique decarant alterum esse mortale, alterum sempiternum. corpus enim nihil nisi temporale desiderat id est cibum potum indumentum quietem uoluptatem, et tamen haec ipsa sine nutu et adminiculo animi nec cupere nec adsequi potest: animus autem per se multa desiderat quae ad officium fructumue corporis non redundent, eaque non fragilia, sed aeterna sunt, ut fama uirtutis, ut memoria nominis. nam cultum dei, qui constat abstinentia cupiditatum ac libidinum, patientia doloris, contemptu mortis, etiam contra corpus anima concupiscit. unde credibile est non interire animam, sed dissociari a corpore, quia corpus sine animo nihil potest, animus uero potest multa et magna sine corpore. quid quod ea quae uisibilia sunt oculis et tangibilia manu, quia externam uim pati possunt, aeterna esse non possunt, ea uero quae neque sub tactum neque sub uisum ueniunt, sed tantummodo uis eorum et ratio et effectus apparet, aeterna sunt, quia nullam uim patiuntur extrinsecus? corpus autem si ideo mortale est, quia uism pariter et tactui subiacet, ergo et anima idcirco inmortalis est, quia nec tangi potest nec uideri.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Let us now refute the arguments of those who argue against us, arguments that Lucretius set out in his third book. He says that since the soul is born with the body, it must necessarily perish with the body. But the reasoning for the two is not equal. The body is solid and tangible, perceived by both eyes and hand, while the soul is subtle and eludes both touch and sight. The body is fashioned and solidified from the earth; the soul has nothing concrete in itself, no earthly weight, as Plato used to say. For it could not possess such great skill, such great power, such great swiftness unless it drew its origin from heaven. Therefore, because the body is formed from a heavy and corruptible element, it is tangible and visible; it decays and dies and cannot repel force, since it falls under both sight and touch. But the soul, because by its subtlety it flees all touch, cannot be dissolved by any blow. Thus, although they are born connected and united, and the one formed from earthly concretion serves as a kind of vessel for the other derived from heavenly subtlety, when some force separates them—a separation called death—each returns to its own nature: what came from earth dissolves back into earth, and what came from the heavenly spirit endures and thrives forever, because the divine spirit is eternal.

Finally, Lucretius himself, forgetting what he was asserting and what dogma he was defending, wrote these lines: "It yields back to the earth what was from the earth before, but what was sent from the shores of the ether, the shining temples of heaven receive again." That was not something he ought to have said, he who argued that souls perish with bodies; but he was conquered by the truth, and true reason slipped in unawares. Moreover, the very conclusion he draws—that the soul is dissolved, that is, perishes at the same time as the body because they are born at the same time—is false and can be turned to the contrary. For the body does not perish at the same time; it remains intact for many days after the soul has departed, and often, when treated with medicine, it endures for a very long time. If, just as they are born together, they were to perish together, the soul would not suddenly depart and leave the body deserted; instead both would dissipate at the same moment, and the body would melt away and perish as quickly as the soul departs—indeed, with the body dissolved, the soul would vanish like liquid spilled from a broken vessel. But if the earthly and fragile body does not immediately dissolve into the earth and decay after the soul's departure, because it has that origin, then the soul, which is not fragile, remains forever, because its origin is eternal.

latin: Nunc argumenta eorum qui contra disserunt refellamus: quae Lucretius tertio libro executus est. quoniam cum corpore inquit anima nascitur, cum corpore intereat necesse est. at non est par utriusque ratio. solidum enim et conprehensibile corpus est et oculis et manu, anima uero tenuis et tactum uisumque fugiens. corpus e terra fictum atque solidatum est, anima nihil in se concreti, nihil ponderis terreni habet, ut Plato disserebat. nec enim tantam posset habere sollertiam, tantam uim, tantam celeritatem, nisi originem traheret e caelo. corpus igitur quoniam fictum ex ponderoso et corruptibili elemento et tangibile est et uisibile, corrumpitur atque occidit nec uim repellere potest, quia sub aspectum et sub tactum uenit, anima autem quia tenuitate sua omnem tactum fugit, nullo ictu dissolui potest. ergo quamuis inter se coniuncta et sociata nascantur et alterum, quod est de terrena concretione formatum, quasi uasculum sit alterius, quod est a caelesti suptilitate deductum, cum uis aliqua utrumque discreuerit, quae discretio mors uocatur, utrumque in naturam suam recedit: quod ex terra fuit, id in terram resoluitur, quod ex caelesti spiritu, id constat ac uiget semper, quoniam diuinus spiritus sempiternus est. denique idem Lucretius oblitus quid adsereret et quod dogma defenderet, hos uersus posuit: cedit item retro, de terra quod fuit ante, in terram, sed quod missum est ex aetheris oris, id rursum caeli fulgentia templa receptant. quod eius non erat dicere qui perire animas cum corporibus disserebat: sed uictus est ueritate et inprudenti ratio uera subrepsit. praeterea id ipsum quod colligit, dissolui animam, hoc est simul cum corpore interire, quoniam simul nascantur, et falsum est et in contrarium conuerti potest. non enim simul interit, sed anima discedente integrum per multos dies manet et plerumque medicatum diutissime durat. nam si ut simul nascuntur, simul interirent, non discederet repente anima corpusque desereret, sed uno temporis puncto utrumque pariter dissiparetur et tam celeriter etiam corpus adhuc spiritu in eo manente deliquesceret ac periret, quam celeriter anima secedit, immo uero dissoluto corpore anima uanesceret uelut umor fracto uase diffusus. nam si terrenum et tragile corpus post secessum animae non statim diffluit in terramque tabescit, ei qua illi origo est, ergo anima, quae fragilis non est, in aeternum manet, quoniam origo eius aeterna est.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: We must now explain why God created humanity. Had the philosophers grasped this, they would have defended the truths they did discover, or at least avoided the gravest errors. This point is the sum and hinge of everything; without it, all truth slips away, and reason itself fails to cohere. If this light had dawned on them—if they had known the full mystery of man—their disputes and the whole of philosophy would never have been cut down by the sword of Academic skepticism.

Just as God did not make the world for its own sake—He has no need of its benefits—but for the sake of man who uses it, so He made man for His own sake. Epicurus asks what usefulness man could have for God, that He should create him for Himself. The answer: so there would be someone able to understand God's works, to arrange providence, to reason out actions, to perfect virtue, to admire with the senses and proclaim with the voice. The sum of all these capacities is that man may worship God. For the one who understands these things worships; the one who, with due reverence, follows the true Father and Artificer of all, measuring the virtue of His majesty by the invention, beginning, and perfection of His works.

What plainer argument could show that God made both the world and man for His own sake than this: among all living creatures, man alone is formed with eyes directed toward heaven, a face looking toward God, a countenance that seems to share a likeness with his Parent? It appears that God has lifted man from the earth to the contemplation of Himself, as with an outstretched hand. What, then, does man's worship add to a blessed God who lacks nothing? Or if God honored man so highly that He created the world for him, instructed him with wisdom, made him lord of living things, and loved him like a son, why did He make him mortal and fragile? Why did He expose the one He loved to every evil, when it would have been fitting for man to be blessed—joined to and near God, perpetual as God Himself is—for whose worship and contemplation he was formed?

Although we have touched on these points scattered through the earlier books, the present subject—the discussion of the blessed life—properly demands them. Therefore they must be explained more diligently and fully, so that God's disposition, work, and will may be known.

latin: Reddamus nunc rationem quare hominem ipsum fecerit: quod si philosophi scissent, aut defendissent illa quae uera inuenerant aut in maximos errores non incidissent. haec enim summa, hic cardo rerum est, quem qui non tenuerit, ueritas illi omnis elabitur, hoc est denique, quod efficiat illis non quadrare rationem: quae illis si adfulsisset, si sacramentum hominis omne cognossent, numquam disputationes eorum et omnem philosophiam de transuerso Academia iugulasset. sicut ergo mundum non propter se deus fecit, quia commodis eius non indiget, sed propter hominem, qui eo utitur, ita ipsum hominem propter se. quae utilitas deo in homine, inquit Epicurus ut eum propter se faceret? scilicet ut esset qui opera eius intellegeret, qui prouidentiam disponendi, rationem faciendi, uirtutem consummandi et sensu admirari et uoce proloqui posset: quorum omnium summa haec est, ut deum colat. is enim colit qui haec intellegit, is artificem rerum omnium, is uerum patrem suum debita ueneratione prosequitur qui uirtutem maiestatis eius de suorum operum inuentione inceptione « perfectione metitur. quod planius argumentum proferri potest et mundum hominis et hominem sua causa deum fecisse, quam quod ex omnibus animantibus solus ita formatus est, ut oculi eius ad caelum directi, facies ad deum spectans, uultus cum suo parente communis sit uideaturque hominem deus quasi porrecta manu adleuatum ex humo ad contemplationem sui excitasse? quid ergo inquit deo cultus hominis confert beato et nulla re indigenti? uel si tantum honoris homini habuit, ut ipsius causa mundum fabricaret, ut instrueret eum sapientia, ut dominum uiuentium faceret eumque diligeret tamquam filium, cur mortalem fragilemque constituit? cur omnibus malis quem diligebat obiecit, cum oporteret et beatum esse hominem tamquam coniunctum ac proximum deo et perpetuum, sicut est ipse, ad quem colendum et contemplandum figuratus est? quamquam haec fere in prioribus libris sparsim docuimus, tamen quoniam: proprie id materia nunc exigit, qua de uita beata disserere propositum est, explicanda sunt ista diligentius et plenius, ut dispositio dei et opus uoluntasque noscatur.

excerpts.author: Didache
english: There are two ways — one of life, one of death — and the difference between them is vast. The way of life is this: first, love the God who made you; second, love your neighbor as yourself. And whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else.

This is the teaching of those words: bless those who curse you and pray for your enemies; fast for those who persecute you. After all, what credit is it if you love only those who love you? Even the nations do that. But you are to love those who hate you, and then you will have no enemy.

Keep clear of fleshly and bodily desires. If someone slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well, and you will be complete. If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two. If someone takes your coat, give him your shirt too. If someone takes what belongs to you, do not demand it back, because you are not able to. Give to everyone who asks you, and do not ask for it back, for the Father wants to give to all from his own gifts.

Blessed is the one who gives according to the command, for he is guiltless. Woe to the one who receives: if someone receives because he is in need, he will be guiltless; but the one who has no need and yet receives will give an account — why he took it and for what purpose. And while he is held in custody, he will be examined concerning what he did, and he will not get out until he has paid back the last quadrans. It has also been said about this: 'Let your charity sweat in your hands until you know to whom you give.' (Matthew 5:39-42; Matthew 6:14-15; Luke 6:27-31)

greek: Ὁδοὶ δύο εἰσί, μία τῆς ζωῆς καὶ μια τοῦ θανάτου, διαφορὰ δὲ πολλὴ μεταξὺ τῶν δύο ὁδῶν. Ἡ μὲν οὖν ὁδὸς τῆς ζωῆς ἐστιν αὕτη: πρῶτον ἀγαπήσεις τὸν θεὸν τὸν ποιήσαντά σε, δεύτερον τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν: πάντα δὲ ὅσα ἐὰν θελήσῃς μὴ γίνεσθαί σοι, καὶ σὺ ἄλλῳ μὴ ποίει. Τούτων δὲ τῶν λόγων ἡ διδαχή ἐστιν αὕτη: εὐλογεῖτε τοῦς καταρωμένους ὑμῖν καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὑμῶν, νηστεύετε δὲ ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς: ποία γὰρ χάρις, ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἀγαπῶντας ὑμᾶς; οὐχὶ καὶ τὰ ἔθνη τὸ αὐτὸ ποιοῦσιν; ὑμεῖς δὲ ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς μισοῦντας ὑμᾶς, καὶ οὐχ ἕξετε ἐχθρόν. ἀπέχου τῶν σαρκικῶν καὶ σωματικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν: ἐάν τίς σοι δῷ ῥάπισμα εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν σιαγόνα, στρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην, καὶ ἔσῃ τέλειος: ἐὰν ἀγγαρεύσῃ σέ τις μίλιον ἕν, ὕπαγε μετ’ αὐτοῦ δύο: ἐὰν ἄρῃ τις τὸ ἱμάτιόν σου, δὸς αὐτῷ καὶ τὸν χιτῶνα: ἐὰν λάβῃ τις ἀπὸ σοῦ τὸ σόν, μὴ ἀπαίτει: οὐδὲ γὰρ δύνασαι. παντὶ τῷ αἰτοῦντί σε δίδου καὶ μὴ ἀπαίτει: πᾶσι γὰρ θέλει δίδοσθαι ὁ πατὴρ ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων χαρισμάτων. μακάριος ὁ διδοὺς κατὰ τὴν ἐντολήν: ἀθῷος γάρ ἐστιν. οὐαὶ τῷ λαμβάνονται: εἰ μὲν γὰρ χρείαν ἔχων λαμβάνει τις, ἀθῷος ἔσται: ὁ δὲ μὴ χρείαν ἔχων δώσει δίκην, ἱνατί ἔλαβε καὶ εἰς τί: ἐν συνοχῇ δὲ γενόμενος ἐξετασθήσεται περὶ ὧν ἔπραξε, καὶ οὐκ ἐξελεύσεται ἐκεῖθεν, μέχρις οὗ ἀποδῷ τὸν ἔσχατον κοδράντην. ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τούτου δὲ εἴρηται: Ἱδρωσάτω ἡ ἐλεημοσύνη σου εἰς τὰς χεῖράς σου, μέχρις ἂν γνῷς, τίνι δῷς.

excerpts.author: Didache
english: The second commandment of the Teaching is this: you must not murder, you must not commit adultery, you must not corrupt children, you must not engage in sexual immorality, you must not steal, you must not practice magic, you must not use potions, you must not kill a child by abortion, nor may you kill a newborn, and you must not covet anything that belongs to your neighbor. You must not swear falsely, you must not give false testimony, you must not speak evil of anyone, and you must not hold a grudge. Do not be double‑minded or double‑tongued, because a double tongue is a snare of death. Let your word not be false or empty, but filled with action. You must not be greedy, or a robber, or a hypocrite, or evil‑minded, or arrogant. You must not plot evil against your neighbor. You must not hate every person; instead, rebuke some, pray for others, and love some more than your own life.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: Let us move on to another subject of knowledge and teaching. There are two ways of teaching and authority: one of light and one of darkness, and the difference between them is immense. On the one hand, light-guiding angels of God are stationed; on the other, angels of Satan. The one is Lord from ages past and into the ages to come, while the other is the ruler of the present age of lawlessness.

greek: Μεταβῶμεν δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ ἑτέραν γνῶσιν καὶ διδαχήν. Ὁδοὶ δύο εἰσὶν διδαχῆς καὶ ἐξουσίας, ἥ τε τοῦ φωτὸς καὶ ἡ τοῦ σκότους. διαφορὰ δὲ πολλὴ τῶν δύο ὁδῶν. ἐφ̓ ἧς μὲν γάρ εἰσιν τεταγμένοι φωταγωγοὶ ἄγγελοι τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐφ̓ ἦς δὲ ἄγγελοι τοῦ σατανᾶ. καὶ ὁ μέν ἐστιν κύριος ἀπὸ αἰώνων καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ὁ δὲ ἄρχων καιροῦ τοῦ νῦν τῆς ἀνομίας.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: This is the way of light: if anyone wants to travel the road to the appointed destination, let them hurry on with their deeds. The knowledge given to us so we may walk in it is as follows. You shall love the One who made you; you shall fear the One who formed you; you shall glorify the One who redeemed you from death. Be single-hearted and rich in spirit. Do not join yourself to those who walk on the path of death. Hate everything that is not pleasing to God; hate all hypocrisy. Do not abandon the Lord's commands. Do not exalt yourself; instead, be humble in every respect and do not seek glory for yourself. Do not plot evil against your neighbor, and do not give your soul over to arrogance. Do not commit sexual immorality, do not commit adultery, do not corrupt children. Do not let the word of God leave your lips in any impurity. Do not show partiality when correcting someone for a transgression. Be gentle, be peaceful, and tremble at the words you have heard. Do not hold a grudge against your brother. Do not be double-minded, wondering whether a thing will happen or not. Do not take the Lord's name in vain. Love your neighbor more than your own life (Matthew 22:37-40). Do not kill a child by abortion, nor kill a newborn infant. Do not withhold your hand from your son or daughter; rather, teach them the fear of God from their youth. Do not covet your neighbor's possessions, and do not be greedy. Do not associate with the arrogant, but keep company with the humble and the righteous. Accept whatever happens to you as good, knowing that nothing occurs without God. Do not be double-tongued or double-minded. Submit to your masters as to God's representatives, with reverence and fear (1 Peter 2:17). Do not command your slave or servant harshly, for they hope in the same God, lest they cease to fear the God who is over both of you; for He did not come to call people according to outward appearance, but those whom the Spirit has prepared. Share everything with your neighbor and do not claim anything as your own; for if you share in the imperishable, how much more should you share in the perishable? Do not be a gossip, for the mouth is a snare of death. As far as you are able, keep yourself pure for the sake of your soul. Do not stretch out your hands to receive only to clench them when it is time to give. Love everyone who speaks the word of the Lord to you as the apple of your eye. Remember the day of judgment night and day, and seek out the saints daily—either by laboring in word and going to encourage them, or by meditating on the word to save a soul, or by working with your hands to make amends for your sins. Do not hesitate to give, and do not grumble when you give; you will know who is the generous Rewarder. Guard what you have received, neither adding to it nor taking away. Hate evil to the end. Judge justly. Do not create division, but reconcile those who fight by bringing them together. Confess your sins. Do not approach prayer with a guilty conscience. This is the way of light.
