greek: Ἀλλ᾿ οἱ πονεῖν ἕτοιμοι ἐπὶ τοῖς καλλίστοις οὐ πρότερον ἀποστήσονται ζητοῦντες τὴν ἀλήθειαν πρὶν ἂν τὴν ἀπόδειξιν ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν λάβωσι τῶν γραφῶν. ἔστι μὲν οὖν κοινά τινα τῶν ἀνθρώπων κριτήρια καθάπερ τὰ αἰσθητήρια. τὰ δ᾿ ἄλλα τῶν βουληθέντων καὶ ἀσκησάντων τὰ ἀληθῆ. τὰ διὰ νοῦ καὶ λογισμοῦ τεχνικὰ λόγων ἀληθῶν τε καὶ ψευδῶν. μέγιστον δὲ τὸ καὶ τὴν οἴησιν ἀποθέσθαι. ἐν μέσῳ καταστάντας ἀκριβοῦς ἐπιστήμης καὶ προπετοῦς δοξοσοφίας, καὶ γνῶναι ὅτι ὁ τὴν αἰώνιον ἐλπίζων ἀνάπαυσιν γιγνώσκει καὶ τὴν εἴσοδον αὐτῆς ἐπίπονον οὖσαν καὶ »τεθλιμμένην«. ὁ δὲ ἅπαξ εὐαγγελισθεὶς καὶ »τὸ σωτήριόν« φησιν »ἰδών«, ἐν ᾗ ὥρᾳ ἂν ἐπιγνῷ, μὴ »ἐπιστρεφέσθω εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω καθάπερ ἡ Αὼτ γυνὴ« μηδὲ εἰς τὸν πρότερον βίον τὸν τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς προσανέχοντα, μηδὲ μὴν εἰς τὰς αἱρέσεις παλινδρομείτω· ἐρίζουσι γὰρ ἁμῇ γέ πῃ, τὸν ὄντα μὴ γινώσκουσαι θεόν. »ὁ γὰρ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμέ«, τὸν ὄντως πατέρα καὶ διδάσκαλον τῆς ἀληθείας, τὸν ἀναγεννῶντα καὶ ἀνακτίζοντα καὶ τιθηνούμενον τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἐξειλεγμένην, »οὐκ ἔστι μου ἄξιος«, ἄξιος λέγει τοῦ εἶναι υἱὸς θεοῦ καὶ μαθητὴς θεοῦ ὁμοῦ καὶ φίλος καὶ συγγενής. »οὐδεὶς γὰρ εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω βλέπων καὶ ἐπιβάλλων τὴν χεῖρα αὐτοῦ ἐπ᾿ ἄροτρον εὔθετος τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ.« Ἀλλ᾿. ὡς ἔοικεν. τοῖς πολλοῖς καὶ μέχρι νῦν δοκεῖ ἡ Μαριὰμ λεχὼ εἶναι διὰ τὴν τοῦ παιδίου γέννησιν, οὐκ οὖσα λεχώ (καὶ γὰρ μετὰ τὸ τεκεῖν αὐτὴν μαιωθεῖσάν φασί τινες παρθένον εὑρεθῆναι)· τοιαῦται δ᾿ ἡμῖν αἱ κυριακαὶ γραφαί, τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀποτίκτουσαι καὶ μένουσαι παρθένοι μετὰ τῆς ἐπικρύψεως τῶν τῆς ἀληθείας μυστηρίων. »τέτοκεν καὶ οὐ τέτοκεν«, φησὶν ἡ γραφή, ὡς ἂν ἐξ αὑτῆς. οὐκ ἐκ συνδυασμοῦ συλλαβοῦσα. διόπερ τοῖς γνωστικοῖς κεκυήκασιν αἱ γραφαί, αἱ δὲ αἱρέσεις οὐκ ἐκμαθοῦσαι ὡς μὴ κεκυηκυίας παραπέμπονται. πάντων δὲ ἀνθρώπων τὴν αὐτὴν κρίσιν ἐχόντων οἱ μὲν ἀκολουθοῦντες τῷ αἱροῦντι λόγῳ ποιοῦνται τὰς πίστεις, οἱ δὲ ἡδοναῖς σφᾶς αὐτοὺς ἐκδεδωκότες βιάζονται πρὸς τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τὴν γραφήν. δεῖ δ᾿, οἶμαι, τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐραστῇ ψυχικῆς εὐτονίας· σφάλλεσθαι γὰρ ἀνάγκη μέγιστα τοὺς μεγίστοις ἐγχειροῦντας πράγμασιν, ἢν μὴ τὸν κανόνα τῆς ἀληθείας παρ᾿ αὐτῆς λαβόντες ἔχωσι τῆς ἀληθείας. οἱ τοιοῦτοι δέ, ἅτε ἀποπεσόντες τῆς ὀρθῆς ὁδοῦ. κἀν τοῖς πλείστοις τῶν κατὰ μέρος σφάλλονται εἰκότως. διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ἀληθῶν καὶ ψευδῶν κριτήριον συγγεγυμνασμένον ἀκριβῶς τὰ δέοντα αἱρεῖσθαι. εἰ γὰρ ἐκέκτηντο, ταῖς θείαις ἐπείθοντο ἂν γραφαῖς.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The dignity of our philanthropy and our pure way of life, according to Clement, seeks the common good, whether it bears witness or educates through both deed and word, in a twofold manner: unwritten and written. This is love: to love God and one's neighbor. It raises us to an unspeakable height. "Love covers a multitude of sins" (Proverbs 10:12). Love endures all things, is patient in all things. Love binds us to God, doing all things in harmony. In love, all the elect of God have been perfected. Without love, nothing is pleasing to God. There is no explanation of its perfection, he says. Who is able to be found in it, except those whom God himself deems worthy? At once the apostle Paul says, even if I give my body to be burned, if I do not have love, I am a clanging cymbal (1 Corinthians 13:1-3). Even if I testify from an elect disposition, he says, I do so through knowledgeable love, but also with fear. If, then, I confess the Lord with my lips for a hoped-for reward, spurring myself on to the Lord's witness, I am a common man, sounding the Lord but not knowing Him. For there is a people who love with their lips, and there is another who gives up his body to be burned. Even if I distribute all my possessions, he says, I do not do so according to the principle of the fellowship of love, but according to the principle of recompense, whether from the benefited man or from the promising Lord. Even if I have all faith so as to move mountains and cast off the obscuring passions, yet if I am not made faithful to the Lord through love, I am nothing. In comparison with the one who witnesses knowledgeably, I am reckoned as a multitude and as nothing differing from nothing. All generations from Adam until this day have passed away; but those who have been perfected in love according to the grace of God possess a place among the godly. They will be revealed in the visitation of the kingdom of Christ. Love does not permit us to sin. But if we fall unwillingly into some such circumstance because of the assaults of the adversary, imitating David we sing: "I will confess to the Lord, and it will please Him more than a young bull that has horns and hooves. Let the poor see and be glad." For He says: "Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Lord; and call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify Me." "For a sacrifice to God is a broken spirit." Love, then, is also called God, since He is good. Where love toward one's neighbor is at work, it neither does wrong nor ever retaliates, but simply does good to all in the image of God. Love is therefore the fulfillment of the law, just as Christ is — that is, the presence of the Lord who loves us — and our loving teaching and way of life according to Christ. Through love, the command not to commit adultery and not to covet what belongs to one's neighbor is perfected, previously restrained by fear. The same action carries a difference, whether it is done from fear or completed from love, and whether it operates through faith or knowledgeably. It is reasonable, then, that the rewards for these are different: for the knowledgeable, those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered the heart of man have been prepared; for the one who has simply believed, a hundredfold of what he has left behind is witnessed, a promise that falls within human understanding.

At this point I recalled a certain man who claimed to be knowledgeable. Explaining the saying, "But I say to you, everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart," he maintained that not the bare desire, but only the completion within the desire of the act corresponding to it, should be judged. For if one has intercourse in the imagination as in a dream, he said, the body is already cooperating with the imagination. The compilers of histories, then, relate the judgment of Bocchoris the just judge as follows. A young man in love with a courtesan persuaded her servant with a fixed fee to bring the girl to him the next day. But when the servant arrived, the young man — having already satisfied his desire in a dream that anticipated the reality — refused to admit the courtesan, though she had come at the appointed time. She, however, demanded the fee, saying that she had already fulfilled the desire for him. They came before the judge. He ordered the young man to hold out the purse of the fee, and commanded the courtesan to take the payment in the sunlight, while the young man was to take the shadow — cleverly ordering her to give the image of the fee for the image of the embrace. One who dreams, then, with the imagination of the soul consenting, sins; so does the one who looks at a woman with desire — not only as that so-called knowledgeable man said, if one conceives the conversation at the same moment as the sight of the woman (for that is already an act of desire as desire), but if anyone looks at the beauty of a body and the flesh appears beautiful to him because of desire, he is judged carnally and sinfully through the very thing he admired. On the contrary, the one who looks upon beauty with pure love does not regard the flesh as beautiful, but the soul; he marvels at the body as a statue, and through it refers the beauty to the Craftsman and the truly Beautiful itself, displaying the luminous character of righteousness, the anointing of good pleasure — that is, the quality of the disposition added to the soul through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit — to the angels who attend the ascent. The people were not able to look upon the glory that shone on the face of Moses; therefore he took a veil to cover the glory from those who viewed it carnally. For those who are led away by worldly things are held fast by the passions that weigh them down, demanding the end; but the one who is stripped of the things that fall short of the end, full of knowledge and of righteousness from works — such a one those who pray with him send forward, blessing the man and his work. And his leaf shall not wither — the tree of life, nurtured by the channels of water. The righteous is likened to fruit-bearing trees, not only those according to the sacrifice of the transgressors; for there were also inspectors of blemishes for the priests at the approaches to the sacrifices according to the Law. The experts in these matters distinguish the reach of desire: they assign the desire for pleasures and licentiousness to the irrational, but the desire for things necessary by nature they deem a rational movement.

greek: Ἡ σεμνὴ οὖν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἡμῶν καὶ ἁγνὴ ἀγωγὴ κατὰ τὸν Κλήμεντα τὸ κοινωφελὲς ζητεῖ, ἐάν τε μαρτυρῇ ἐάν τε καὶ παιδεύῃ ἔργῳ τε καὶ λόγῳ, διττῷ δὲ τούτῳ, ἀγράφῳ τε καὶ ἐγγράφῳ. αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγάπη, τὸ ἀγαπᾶν τὸν θεὸν καὶ τὸν πλησίον, αὕτη εἰς τὸ ἀνεκδιήγητον ὕψος ἀνάγει· ›ἀγάπη καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν‹, ἀγάπη πάντα ἀνέχεται, πάντα μακροθυμεῖ, ἀγάπη κολλᾷ ἡμᾶς τῷ θεῷ, πάντα ποιεῖ ἐν ὁμονοίᾳ· ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ ἐτελειώθησαν πάντες οἱ ἐκλεκτοὶ τοῦ θεοῦ· δίχα ἀγάπης οὐδὲν εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῷ. τῆς τελειότητος αὐτῆς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐξήγησις, φησί. τίς ἱκανὸς ἐν αὐτῇ εὑρεθῆναι, εἰ μὴ οὓς ἂν αὐτὸς καταξιώσῃ ὁ θεός; αὐτίκα ὁ ἀπόστολος Παῦλος ἐὰν τὸ σῶμά μου ἐπιδῶ φησίν. ἀγάπην δὲ μὴ ἔχω, χαλκός εἰμι ἠχῶν καὶ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον· ἢν μὴ ἐκ διαθέσεως ἐκλεκτῆς, δἰ ἀγάπης γνωστικῆς μαρτυρήσω, λέγει, φόβῳ δέ. εἴπερ οὖν καὶ μισθῷ προσδοκωμένῳ ἐπικροτῶν τὰ χείλη εἰς μαρτυρίαν κυρίου ὁμολογήσω κύριον, κοινός εἰμι ἄνθρωπος, ἠχῶν τὸν κύριον, οὐ γινώσκων. ἔστι γὰρ καὶ ὁ λαὸς ὁ τοῖς χείλεσιν ἀγαπῶν, ἔστι καὶ ἄλλος ὁ παραδιδοὺς τὸ σῶμα, ἵνα καυθήσεται. κἂν ψωμίσω πάντα τὰ ὑπάρχοντά μου, φησίν, οὐ κατὰ τὸν τῆς κοινωνίας τῆς ἀγαπητικῆς λόγον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν τῆς ἀνταποδόσεως ἢ παρὰ τοῦ εὐεργετουμένου ἀνθρώπου ἢ παρὰ τοῦ ἐπηγγελμένου κυρίου· κἂν ἔχω πᾶσαν τὴν πίστιν ὥστε ὄρη μεθιστάναι καὶ τὰ ἐπισκοτοῦντα ἀποβαλεῖν πάθη, μὴ δἰ ἀγάπην δὲ πιστωθῶ τῷ κυρίῳ, οὐθέν εἰμι. ὡς πρὸς σύγκρισιν τοῦ γνωστικῶς μαρτυροῦντος, εἰς πλῆθος καὶ τὸ μηδὲν διαφέρον λογιζόμενος. αἱ γενεαὶ δὲ πᾶσαι ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ ἕως τῆσδε τῆς ἡμέρας παρῆλθον· ἀλλ’ οἱ ἐν ἀγάπῃ τελειωθέντες κατὰ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ χάριν ἔχουσι χώραν εὐσεβῶν· οἳ φανερωθήσονται ἐν τῇ ἐπισκοπῇ τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ. ἡ ἀγάπη ἁμαρτάνειν οὐκ ἐᾷ· ἢν δὲ καὶ περιπέσῃ ἄκων τοιαύτῃ τινὶ περιστάσει διὰ τὰς παρεμπτώσεις τοῦ ἀντικειμένου, μιμησάμενος τὸν Δαβὶδ ψαλεῖ· ›ἐξομολογήσομαι τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ ἀρέσει αὐτῷ ὑπὲρ μόσχον νέον, φέροντα κέρατα καὶ ὁπλάς. ἰδέτωσαν πτωχοὶ καὶ εὐφρανθήτωσαν.‹ λέγει γάρ· ›θῦσον τῷ θεῷ θυσίαν αἰνέσεως καὶ ἀπόδος τῷ κυρίῳ τὰς εὐχάς σου· καὶ ἐπικάλεσαί με ἐν ἡμέρᾳ θλίψεώς σου, καὶ ἐξελοῦμαί σε καὶ δοξάσεις με·‹ ›θυσία γὰρ τῷ θεῷ πνεῦμα συντετριμμένον.‹ ἀγάπη τοίνυν καὶ ὁ θεὸς εἴρηται, ἀγαθὸς ὤν. οὗ ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον οὐκ ἐργάζεται, μήτε ἀδικοῦσα μήτε ἀνταδικοῦσά ποτε, ἀγαθοποιοῦσα δὲ πρὸς πάντας ἁπαξαπλῶς κατ’ εἰκόνα θεοῦ. πλήρωμα οὖν νόμου ἡ ἀγάπη, καθάπερ ὁ Χριστός, τουτέστιν ἡ παρουσία τοῦ ἀγαπῶντος ἡμᾶς κυρίου, καὶ ἡ κατὰ Χριστὸν ἀγαπητικὴ ἡμῶν διδασκαλία τε καὶ πολιτεία. ἀγάπῃ γοῦν τὸ μὴ μοιχεῦσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐπιθυμῆσαι τῆς τοῦ πλησίον τελειοῦται, φόβῳ πρότερον κεκωλυμένον. τὸ αὐτὸ γοῦν ἔργον διαφορὰν ἴσχει ἢ διὰ φόβον γενόμενον ἢ δἰ ἀγάπην τελεσθὲν καὶ ἤτοι διὰ πίστεως ἢ καὶ γνωστικῶς ἐνεργούμενον. εἰκότως γοῦν καὶ τὰ τούτων ἀθλα διάφορα· τῷ μὲν γνωστικῷ ἡτοίμασται ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν οὐδὲ οὖς ἤκουσεν οὐδὲ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου ἀνέβη. τῷ δὲ ἁπλῶς πεπιστευκότι μαρτυρεῖ ἑκατονταπλασίονα ὧν ἀπολέλοιπεν, ἣν ἐπαγγελίαν εἰς σύνεσιν ἀνθρώπων πίπτειν συμβέβηκεν. Ἐνταῦθα γενόμενος ἀνεμνήσθην τινὸς φάσκοντος ἑαυτὸν γνωστικόν. ἐξηγούμενος γὰρ τὸ ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω, ὁ ἐμβλέψας τῇ γυναικὶ πρὸς ἐπιθυμίαν ἤδη μεμοίχευκεν οὐ ψιλὴν τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἠξίου κρίνεσθαι, ἀλλὰ ἐὰν τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τὸ κατ’ αὐτὴν ἔργον περαιτέρω τῆς ἐπιθυμίας χωροῦν ἐν αὐτῇ ἐκτελῆται· εἰ γὰρ ὄναρ τῇ φαντασίᾳ, συγκαταχρῆται ἤδη καὶ τῷ σώματι. λέγουσιν οὖν οἱ τὰς ἱστορίας συνταξάμενοι Βοκχόριδος τοῦ δικαίου κρίσιν τοιάνδε. ἐρῶν ἑταίρας νεανίας πείθει μισθῷ τινι ὡρισμένῳ τὴν παῖδα ἀφικέσθαι τῇ ὑστεραίᾳ πρὸς αὐτόν. προλαβούσης ὄναρ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τὴν παῖδα παρ’ ἐλπίδα κορεσθεὶς ἥκουσαν τὴν ἐρωμένην κατὰ τὸ τεταγμένον εἴργει τῆς εἰσόδου, ἣ δὲ ἐκμαθοῦσα τὸ γεγονὸς ἀπῄτει τὸν μισθόν, καὶ τῇδέ πως αὐτὴ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τῷ ἐραστῇ πεπληρωκέναι λέγουσα. ἧκον οὖν ἐπὶ τὸν κριτήν. τὸ βαλλάντιον οὗτος τοῦ μισθώματος τὸν νεανίσκον προτείνειν κελεύσας, ἐν ἡλίῳ δέ, τὴν ἑταίραν λαβέσθαι προσέταξεν τῆς σκιᾶς, χαριέντως εἴδωλον μισθώματος ἀποδιδόναι κελεύσας εἰδώλου συμπλοκῆς. Ὀνειρώττει μὲν οὖν τις συγκαταθεμένης τῇ φαντασίᾳ τῆς ψυχῆς, ὕπαρ δὲ ὀνειρώττει ὁ πρὸς ἐπιθυμίαν βλέπων, οὐ μόνον ὡς ἐκεῖνος ἔλεγεν ὁ δῆθεν γνωστικός, ἐὰν ἅμα τῇ ὄψει τῆς γυναικὸς συλλάβῃ κατ’ ἔννοιαν τὴν ὁμιλίαν (τοῦτο γὰρ ἤδη ἔργον ἐστὶν ἐπιθυμίας ὡς ἐπιθυμίας), ἀλλ’ ἐὰν εἰς κάλλος σώματος βλέψῃ τις, ὁ λόγος φησί, καὶ αὐτῷ ἡ σὰρξ εἶναι κατ’ ἐπιθυμίαν δόξῃ καλή, σαρκικῶς ἰδὼν καὶ ἁμαρτητικῶς δἰ οὗ τεθαύμακεν κρίνεται· ἔμπαλιν γὰρ ὁ δἰ ἀγάπην τὴν ἁγνὴν προσβλέπων τὸ κάλλος οὐ τὴν σάρκα ἡγεῖται, ἀλλὰ τὴν ψυχὴν καλήν, τὸ σῶμα, οἶμαι, ὡς ἀνδριάντα θαυμάσας, δἰ οὗ κάλλους ἐπὶ τὸν τεχνίτην καὶ τὸ ὄντως καλὸν αὐτὸς αὑτὸν παραπέμπει, σύμβολον ἅγιον τὸν χαρακτῆρα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τὸν φωτεινὸν ἐπιδεικνύμενος τοῖς ἐφεστῶσι τῇ ἀνόδῳ ἀγγέλοις, τὸ χρῖσμα τῆς εὐαρεστήσεως λέγω, τὴν ποιότητα τῆς διαθέσεως τὴν ἐπικειμένην τῇ ψυχῇ κατ’ ἐπιχώρησιν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος γεγανωμένῃ. ταύτην τὴν δόξαν τὴν ἐκλάμψασαν ἐπὶ τοῦ προσώπου Μωυσέως ὁ λαὸς οὐχ οἷός τε ἦν προσβλέπειν, διὸ καὶ κάλυμμα ἐλάμβανε τῆς δόξης πρὸς τοὺς σαρκικῶς θεωμένους. τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ἐπαγομένους τινὰ τῶν κοσμικῶν κατέχουσιν οἱ τὸ τέλος ἀπαιτοῦντες τοῖς σφετέροις βαρουμένους πάθεσι, τὸν δὲ γυμνὸν μὲν τῶν ὑποπιπτόντων τῷ τέλει, πλήρη δὲ γνώσεως καὶ τῆς ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοσύνης συνευχόμενοι παραπέμπουσι, τὸν ἄνδρα σὺν καὶ τῷ ἔργῳ μακαρίσαντες· καὶ τὸ φύλλον αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἀπορρυήσεται, τοῦ ζωτικοῦ ξύλου, τοῦ κατὰ τὰς διεξόδους τῶν ὑδάτων τεθραμμένου· καρποφόροις δὲ ὁ δίκαιος ἀπεικάζεται δένδροις, οὐ μόνον τοῖς κατὰ τὴν τῶν μεταρσίων θυσίαν· ἦσαν δὲ κἀν ταῖς τῶν θυσιῶν προσαγωγαῖς παρὰ τῷ νόμῳ οἱ τῶν ἱερείων μωμοσκόποι. ὄρεξιν οὖν ἐπιθυμίας διακρίνουσιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοί, καὶ τὴν μὲν ἐπὶ ἡδοναῖς καὶ ἀκολασίᾳ τάττουσιν ἄλογον οὖσαν, τὴν δὲ ὄρεξιν ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἀναγκαίων λογικὴν ὑπάρχουσαν κίνησιν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Many people have a disposition like the stubbornness of winter, uncontrolled and irrational. Unbelief has accomplished many good things, and faith has accomplished bad ones. Remember Epicharmus's saying: 'Disbelieve, for these are the joints of the mind.' Disbelieving the truth brings death just as believing brings life; conversely, believing a lie and disbelieving the truth drags one down to destruction. The same reasoning applies to self-control and self-indulgence. Self-control produces good works, and abstaining from injustice is the beginning of salvation. It seems to me that the Sabbath, through abstinence from evil, signifies self-control and poses the question of what distinguishes human beings from beasts. In this respect the angels of God are wiser; Scripture says, 'You have made him a little lower than the angels' (Psalm 8:5). They do not await the Scripture's fulfillment in the Lord, even though He bore flesh, but in the perfect Gnostic who in time and clothing is made lower than the angels. I therefore affirm that wisdom is something other than mere knowledge, since life itself does not differ; mortal nature — that is, humanity — shares the common lot, yet has been deemed worthy of immortality by living with the habit of contemplation and self-control, which sets it apart. It seems to me that Pythagoras, too, says that God alone is wise (since the apostle writes in Romans of the mystery made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, 'to the only wise God through Jesus Christ,' Romans 16:26), while he calls himself a philosopher through friendship toward God. 'God spoke to Moses as a friend speaks to a friend' (Exodus 33:11). The truth is clear to God; truth begets, and the Gnostic loves truth. Solomon says, 'Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider its ways and be wise' (Proverbs 6:6), and become a disciple of the bee. If each creature has its single proper work — ox, horse, and dog alike — what shall we say is humanity's proper work? Humanity appears to me to resemble a centaur, a Thessalian composite of rational and irrational parts, soul and body. The body works the earth and hastens back to earth, but the soul stretches toward God; educated by true philosophy, it hastens toward its kindred above, turning away from the body's desires and toward the pains and fears that accompany them — though we have shown that endurance and fear can serve the good. If knowledge of sin comes through the law, as those who run after the law say, and 'sin was in the world until the law' (Romans 5:13), yet 'sin is dead apart from the law' (Romans 7:8), we answer them: when you remove the cause of fear — sin — you remove fear, and far more so punishment, when the natural desire is gone. 'The law is not laid down for the just,' Scripture says (1 Timothy 1:9). Heraclitus rightly says the name of justice would never have been known if these things did not exist; Socrates says law would not have been enacted for the sake of good things. Yet the accusers did not grasp this, as the apostle declares: 'The one who loves his neighbor does no evil' (Romans 13:10). For the commandments — 'You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,' and any other commandment — are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Galatians 5:14; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). This is how you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37-40). If the one who loves his neighbor works no evil, and every commandment is summed up in loving the neighbor, then the commandments that implant fear produce love, not hatred. Fear is not a passion of which the law is the generator. Therefore the law is holy, and truly spiritual, according to the apostle (Romans 7:12, 14). It is necessary, as it seems, to investigate the body's nature and the soul's substance, to grasp the end of each, and not to regard death as an evil. 'When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness,' the apostle says (Romans 6:20). What fruit did you have then? Things you are now ashamed of, for the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life (Romans 6:22). For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). It follows that death is the soul's communion with the body while the soul is sinful, and life is separation from sin. Many have trenches and ditches of desire, and pits of anger and rage, which one must leap over and avoid every contrivance of plots, no longer beholding the knowledge of God through a mirror. 'Half of a man's virtue does wide-seeing Zeus take away when the day of slavery seizes him' (Homer, Odyssey 17.322-323). Scripture knows those who are under sin and sold into sins as lovers of pleasure and lovers of body, more beasts than men, likened to cattle — wanton horses neighing after their neighbors' possessions. The self-indulgent man is an insolent donkey, the covetous a wild wolf, the deceiver a snake. The soul's separation from the body, practiced throughout life by the philosopher, builds a readiness to bear natural death easily — the dissolution of the bonds between soul and body. 'The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world,' he says (Galatians 6:14), 'and I live, though in the flesh, as one who lives in heaven, conducting my life as a citizen of heaven' (Philippians 3:20).

greek: οἱ πολλοὶ δὲ τῇ τῶν χειμώνων καταστάσει ὁμοίαν ἔχουσι τὴν διάθεσιν ἀνέδραστόν τε καὶ ἀλόγιστον. Πολλὰ ἀπιστία δέδρακεν ἀγαθὰ καὶ πίστις κακά. ὅ τε Ἐπίχαρμος μέμνασο ἀπιστεῖν φησίν· ἄρθρα ταῦτα τῶν φρενῶν. αὐτίκα τὸ μὲν ἀπιστεῖν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ θάνατον φέρει ὡς τὸ πιστεύειν ζωήν, ἔμπαλιν δὲ τὸ πιστεύειν τῷ ψεύδει, ἀπιστεῖν δὲ τῇ ἀληθείᾳ εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑποσύρει. ὁ αὐτὸς λόγος ἐπί τε ἐγκρατείας καὶ ἀκρασίας. ἐγκρατεύεσθαι μὲν γὰρ ἀγαθοεργίας κακίας ἔργον, ἀπέχεσθαι δὲ ἀδικίας σωτηρίας ἀρχή. ᾗ μοι δοκεῖ τὸ σάββατον δἰ ἀποχῆς κακῶν ἐγκράτειαν αἰνίσσεσθαι καὶ τί ποτ’ ἐστὶν ᾧ διαφέρει θηρίων ἄνθρωπος. τούτου τε αὖ οἱ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄγγελοι σοφώτεροι· ἠλάττωσας αὐτόν, φησί, βραχύ τι παρ’ ἀγγέλους· οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ κυρίου ἐκδέχονται τὴν γραφήν *καίτοι κἀκεῖνος σάρκα ἔφερεν), ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ τελείου καὶ γνωστικοῦ τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τῷ ἐνδύματι ἐλαττουμένου παρὰ τοὺς ἀγγέλους. οὐκοῦν ἄλλο τι σοφίαν παρὰ τὴν ἐπιστήμην λέγω, ἐπεὶ μὴ διαφέρει ζωή· κοινὸν γὰρ τῇ φύσει τῇ θνητῇ, τουτέστι τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, πρὸς τὸ ἀθανασίας κατηξιωμένον τὸ ζῆν, ἕξιν θεωρίας τε καὶ ἐγκρατείας θατέρου διαφέροντος. ᾗ μοι δοκεῖ καὶ Πυθαγόρας σοφὸν μὲν εἶναι τὸν θεὸν λέγειν μόνον (ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐπιστολῇ γράφει· εἰς ὑπακοὴν πίστεως εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη γνωρισθέντος, μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), ἑαυτὸν δὲ διὰ φιλίαν τὴν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν φιλόσοφον. διελέγετο γοῦν Μωυσεῖ, φησίν, ὁ θεὸς ὡς φίλος φίλῳ. τὸ μὲν οὖν ἀληθὲς τῷ θεῷ σαφές. αὐτίκα τὴν ἀλήθειαν γεννᾷ, ὁ γνωστικὸς δὲ ἀληθείας ἐρᾷ. ἴσθι, φησί, πρὸς τὸν μύρμηκα, ὦ ὀκνηρέ, καὶ μελίττης γενοῦ μαθητής, ὁ Σολομὼν λέγει· εἰ γὰρ ἑκάστου τῆς οἰκείας φύσεως ἔργον ἓν καὶ βοὸς ὁμοίως καὶ ἵππου καὶ κυνός, τί ἂν φήσαιμεν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ ἔργον τὸ οἰκεῖον; ἔοικεν δ’ οἶμαι, κενταύρῳ, Θετταλικῷ πλάσματι, ἐκ λογικοῦ καὶ ἀλόγου συγκείμενος, ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν σῶμα γῆν τε ἐργάζεται καὶ σπεύδει εἰς γῆν, τέταται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ πρὸς τὸν θεόν, ἥ γε διὰ φιλοσοφίας τῆς ἀληθοῦς παιδευομένη, πρός τε τοὺς ἄνω σπεύδει συγγενεῖς, ἀποστραφεῖσα τῶν τοῦ σώματος ἐπιθυμιῶν πρός τε ταύταις πόνου τε καὶ φόβου· καίτοι πρὸς ἀγαθοῦ καὶ τὴν ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὸν φόβον ἐδείξαμεν. εἰ γὰρ διὰ νόμου ἐπίγνωσις ἁμαρτίας, ὡς οἱ κατατρέχοντες τοῦ νόμου φασί, καὶ ›ἄχρι νόμου ἁμαρτία ἦν ἐν κόσμῳ,‹ ἀλλὰ ›χωρὶς νόμου ἁμαρτία νεκρὰ‹ ἀντᾴδομεν αὐτοῖς. ὅταν γὰρ ἀφέλῃς τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ φόβου, τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, ἀφεῖλες τὸν φόβον, πολὺ δὲ ἔτι μᾶλλον τὴν κόλασιν, ὅταν ἀπῇ τὸ πεφυκὸς ἐπιθυμεῖν· δικαίῳ γὰρ οὐ κεῖται νόμος, ἡ γραφή φησιν. καλῶς οὖν Ἡράκλειτος δίκης ὄνομα φησὶν οὐκ ἂν ᾔδεσαν, εἰ ταῦτα μὴ ἦν, Σωκράτης δὲ νόμον ἕνεκα ἀγαθῶν οὐκ ἂν γενέσθαι. ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τοῦτο ἔγνωσαν οἱ κατήγοροι, ὡς ὁ ἀπόστολός φησιν ὅτι ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται· τὸ γὰρ οὐ φονεύσεις, οὐ μοιχεύσεις, οὐ κλέψεις, καὶ εἴ τις ἑτέρα ἐντολή, ἐν τούτῳ μόνῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται τῷ λόγῳ, τῷ· ›ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν.‹ ταύτῃ που ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φησὶν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας σου, καὶ ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν. εἰ δὴ ὁ τὸν πλησίον ἀγαπῶν κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται καὶ πᾶσα ἐντολὴ ἐν τούτῳ ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται, τῷ ἀγαπᾶν τὸν πλησίον, αἱ τὸν φόβον ἐπαρτῶσαι ἐντολαὶ ἀγάπην, οὐ μῖσος κατασκευάζουσιν. οὔκουν πάθος ὁ φόβος οὗ γεννητικὸς ὁ νόμος. ὥστε ὁ νόμος ἅγιος καὶ τῷ ὄντι πνευματικός ἐστι κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον. δεῖ δή, ὡς ἔοικε, τήν γε τοῦ σώματος φύσιν καὶ τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσίαν πολυπραγμονήσαντας τὸ ἑκατέρου τέλος καταλαβέσθαι καὶ μὴ τὸν θάνατον ἡγεῖσθαι κακόν· ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ. τίνα οὖν καρπὸν εἴχετε τότε; ἐφ’ οἷς νῦν ἐπαισχύνεσθε· τὸ γὰρ τέλος ἐκείνων θάνατος. νῦν δὲ ἐλευθερωθέντες ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, δουλωθέντες δὲ τῷ θεῷ, ἔχετε τὸν καρπὸν ὑμῶν εἰς ἁγιασμόν, τὸ δὲ τέλος ζωὴν αἰώνιον. τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν. Κινδυνεύει τοίνυν δεδεῖχθαι θάνατος μὲν εἶναι ἡ ἐν σώματι κοινωνία τῆς ψυχῆς ἁμαρτητικῆς οὔσης, ζωὴ δὲ ὁ χωρισμὸς τῆς ἁμαρτίας. πολλοὶ δὲ οἱ ἐν ποσὶ χάρακες καὶ τάφροι τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τά τε ὀργῆς καὶ θυμοῦ βάραθρα, ἃ διαπηδᾶν ἀνάγκη καὶ πᾶσαν ἀποφεύγειν τὴν τῶν ἐπιβουλῶν ἀνασκευὴν τὸν μηκέτι δἰ ἐσόπτρου τὴν γνῶσιν τοῦ θεοῦ κατοψόμενον· ἥμισυ γάρ τ’ ἀρετῆς ἀποαίνυται εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς ἀνέρος, εὖτ’ ἄν μιν κατὰ δούλιον ἦμαρ ἕλῃσι. δούλους δὲ τοὺς ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις πεπραμένους, τοὺς φιληδόνους καὶ φιλοσωμάτους οἶδεν ἡ γραφή, καὶ θηρία μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώπους, τοὺς παρομοιωθέντας τοῖς κτήνεσι, θηλυμανεῖς ἵππους ἐπὶ τὰς τῶν πλησίον χρεμετίζοντας· ὄνος ὑβριστὴς ὁ ἀκόλαστος, λύκος ἄγριος ὁ πλεονεκτικὸς καὶ ὄφις ὁ ἀπατεών. ὁ τοίνυν ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ψυχῆς χωρισμὸς ὁ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον μελετώμενος τῷ φιλοσόφῳ προθυμίαν κατασκευάζει γνωστικὴν εὐκόλως δύνασθαι φέρειν τὸν τῆς φύσεως θάνατον, διάλυσιν ὄντα τῶν πρὸς τὸ σῶμα τῆς ψυχῆς δεσμῶν· ἐμοὶ γὰρ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται κἀγὼ τῷ κόσμῳ λέγει, βιῶ δὲ ἤδη ἐν σαρκὶ ὢν ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ πολιτευόμενος.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — An Answer to the Jews 2
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let us move forward and lay out the core question clearly. Why would anyone claim that God—the founder of the universe, governor of the whole world, shaper of man, sower of all nations—gave the Law through Moses to a single people instead of to all nations? If He had not given it to all, He would never have allowed proselytes from the nations access to it. But, consistent with the goodness and equity of the shaper of the human race, He gave the same Law to every nation, commanding it to be kept at set times, when He willed, through whom He willed, and as He willed. In the beginning of the world He gave Adam and Eve themselves a law: not to eat from the fruit of the tree planted in the middle of paradise, on pain of death (Gen 2:16–17); that law would have sufficed had it been kept. In this law given to Adam we recognize every commandment that later sprouted through Moses: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul," "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness," "Honor your father and your mother," "You shall not covet what belongs to another." This primordial law, given in paradise, is the matrix of all God's commandments. If they had loved the Lord their God, they would not have broken His command; if they had loved their neighbor—that is, themselves—they would not have believed the serpent, and so would not have committed suicide by cutting themselves off from immortality through disobedience; they would have abstained from theft, since they would not have secretly tasted the fruit; they would not have hidden from the sight of the Lord their God under the tree; they would not have become accomplices in the devil's lie by believing they would become like God; they would not have offended God as Father, who formed them from the clay of the earth as from a mother's womb; if they had not coveted what belonged to another, they would not have tasted the forbidden fruit. Therefore, in this general and primordial law of God, sanctioned to be observed in the fruit of the tree, we recognize that all the commandments of the later Law were specially implanted and published in their own times. It is the same God who later teaches the Law who previously sent forth the commandment, since it belongs to Him to instruct later those He previously formed as just. What is surprising if He who instituted increases discipline, if He who began perfects? I contend that before the written Law of Moses on stone tablets there existed an unwritten law, naturally understood and kept by the fathers. Whence was Noah found just, if not preceded by the justice of natural law? Whence was Abraham called the friend of God, if not from the equity and justice of natural law? Whence was Melchizedek named priest of the Most High God, if not before the Levitical priesthood and Levi's sacrifices? The Law was given to Moses after they left Egypt, after an interval of many times and spaces—finally, after four hundred and thirty years from Abraham. From this we understand that God's Law existed also before Moses, not only at Horeb, Sinai, or the desert, but earlier: first in paradise, then to the patriarchs, and thus also to the Jews, reformed at certain times. So we must not treat Moses' Law as the primary Law, but as a subsequent one, which God exhibited to the nations at a set time, reformed for the better through the prophets, and foretold would be observed temporarily—just as the Law was given through Moses at a certain time, so it is believed to have been kept temporarily. We must not strip God of this power to reform the Law's commandments according to the condition of the times for man's salvation. Finally, anyone who insists that the Sabbath must still be kept as a remedy for salvation, and circumcision on the eighth day because of the death threat (Gen 17:10–14), let him prove that the just of the past kept the Sabbath or were circumcised and so became friends of God. If circumcision purifies man, why did God not circumcise Adam when He made him, or later after he sinned? In paradise God established uncircumcised Adam as steward of paradise. Since God did not institute Adam as circumcised or Sabbath-keeping, He likewise praised Abel—uncircumcised, not keeping the Sabbath—accepting his sacrifice offered in simplicity of heart, while rejecting Cain's, who did not offer rightly. God also freed Noah from the flood, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath. He also translated Enoch, the most just, uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, from this world before he tasted death, to show us that we too can please God without the burden of Moses' Law. Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, was also uncircumcised and not keeping the Sabbath, yet called to God's priesthood. And Lot, Abraham's brother, proves he was rescued from the burning of Sodom by the merits of his justice, without observing the Law.

latin: Igitur gradum conferamus, et summam quaestionis ipsius certis lineis determinemus. Cur etenim Deus, universitatis conditor, mundi totius gubernator, hominis plasmator, universarum gentium sator, legem per Moysen uni populo dedisse credatur, et non omnibus gentibus attribuisse dicatur? Nisi enim omnibus eam dedisset, nullo pacto ad eam etiam proselytos ex gentibus accessum habere permitteret: sed, ut congruit bonitati Dei et aequitati ipsius, utpote plasmatoris generis humani, omnibus gentibus eamdem legem dedit: quam certis et statutis temporibus observari praecepit, quando voluit, et per quos voluit, et sicut voluit. Namque in principio mundi, ipsi Adae et Evae legem dedit, ne de fructu arboris plantatae in medio paradisi ederent; quod si contra fecissent, morte morerentur: quae lex eis sufficeret, si esset custodita. In hac enim lege Adae data, omnia praecepta condita recognoscimus quae postea pullulaverunt data per Moysen, id est, Diliges Dominum Deum tuum de toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua; et, Diliges proximum tibi tanquam te; et, Non occides, non moechaberis, non furaberis, falsum testimonium non dices. Honora patrem tuum et matrem: et, Alienum non concupisces. Primordialis lex est enim data Adae et Evae in paradiso, quasi matrix omnium praeceptorum Dei. Denique, si Dominum Deum suum dilexissent, contra praeceptum ejus non fecissent: si proximum diligerent, id est semetipsos, persuasioni serpentis non credidissent; atque ita in semetipsos homicidium non commisissent, excidendo de immortalitate, faciendo contra Dei praeceptum; a furto quoque abstinuissent, si de fructu arboris clam non degustassent, nec a conspectu Domini Dei sui sub arbore delitescere gestissent: nec falsum asseveranti diabolo participes efficerentur, credendo ei quod similes Dei essent futuri: atque ita nec Deum offendissent, ut patrem, qui eos de limo terrae quasi ex utero matris figuraverat: si alienum non concupissent, de fructu illicito non gustassent. Igitur in hac generali et primordiali Dei lege, quam in arboris fructu observari Deus sanxerat, omnia praecepta legis posterioris specialiter indita fuisse cognoscimus, quae suis temporibus edita germinaverunt Ejusdem est enim postea subdocere legem, qui ante praemiserat praeceptum, quoniam et ipsius est erudire postea qui ante justos formare instituerat. Quid enim mirum, si is auget disciplinam qui instituit? si is perfecit qui coepit? Denique ante legem Moysi scriptam in tabulis lapideis legem fuisse contendo non scriptam, quae naturaliter intelligebatur, et a patribus custodiebatur. Nam unde Noe justus inventus, si non illum naturalis legis justitia praecedebat? unde Abraham amicus Dei deputatus, si non de aequitate et justitiae legis naturalis? unde Melchisedech sacerdos Dei summi nuncupatus, si non ante Leviticae legis sacerdotium Levitae fuerunt, qui sacrificia Deo offerebant? Sic enim post supra scriptos patriarchas data lex est Moysi eo tempore posteaquam ab Aegypto excesserunt, post intervallum multorum temporum et spatia Denique, post quadringentos et triginta annos Abrahae data est lex. Unde intelligimus Dei legem etiam ante Moysen, nec in Horeb tantum, aut in Sina et in cremo, sed antiquiorem primum in paradiso, post patriarchis, atque ita et Judaeis certis temporibus reformatam; ut non jam ad Moysi legem ita attendamus, quasi ad principalem legem, sed ad subsequentem, quam certo tempore Deus et gentibus exhibuit, et repromissam per prophetas in melius reformavit, et praemonuit futurum ut, sicuti certo tempore data est lex per Moysen, ita temporaliter observata et custodita credatur: nec adimamus hanc Dei potestatem, pro temporum conditione legis praecepta reformantem in hominis salutem. Denique, qui contendit et sabbatum adhuc observandum quasi salutis medelam, circumcisionem octavi diei propter mortis comminationem, doceat in praeteritum justos sabbatizasse aut circumcidisse, et sic amicos Dei effectos. Nam, si circumcisio purgat hominem, Deus Adam incircumcisum cum faceret, cur eum non circumcidit, vel posteaquam deliquit, si purgat circumcisio? Certe in paradiso constituens eum incircumcisum, colonum paradisi praefecit. Igitur, cum neque circumcisum neque sabbatizantem Deus Adam instituerit, consequenter quoque sobolem ejus Abel offerentem sibi sacrificia, incircumcisum nec sabbatizantem laudavit, accepto ferens quae offerebat in simplicitate cordis, et reprobans sacrificium fratris ejus Cain, qui non offerebat, non recte dividebat. Noe quoque incircumcisum Deus, sed et non sabbatizantem, de diluvio liberavit. Nam et Enoch justissimum non circumcisum, nec sabbatizantem, de hoc mundo transtulit; qui necdum mortem gustavit, ut aeternitatis candidatus, jam nobis ostenderet nos quoque sine legis onere Moysi, Deo posse placere. Melchisedech quoque summi Dei sacerdos incircumcisus, et non sabbatizans, ad sacerdotium Dei allectus est. Probat et Loth frater Abrahae, quod pro meritis justitiae suae sine legis observatione de Sodomitarum incendio sit liberatus.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It is patience itself that both follows faith and precedes it. Take Abraham: he believed God, and God reckoned it to him as justice; yet patience proved his faith when he was ordered to sacrifice his son—not, I should say, as a test of faith, but as a symbolic witness. God, who had reckoned him just, knew the heart of the matter. Abraham heard so grave a command—one that not even the Lord was willing to carry out—patiently, and he would have fulfilled it had God so willed. Deservedly, then, is he called blessed, because he was faithful; deservedly faithful, because he was patient. Thus faith, illuminated by patience, when it was being sown among the nations through the seed of Abraham, which is Christ, and was bringing grace to supersede the law, appointed patience as its helper for amplifying and fulfilling the law, because patience alone had previously been lacking for the doctrine of justice. In former times they used to demand an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and to return evil for evil, because patience was not yet on earth—nor was faith—and so impatience enjoyed the occasions the law provided. It was easy enough when the lord and teacher of patience was absent. But after he arrived and joined patience to the grace of faith, it is no longer permitted even to provoke with a word, nor even to say 'Fool' without danger of judgment. Anger is prohibited, spirits are restrained, the petulance of hands is curbed, the venom of the tongue is removed, and the law finds more than it lost, Christ saying: 'Love your enemies, and bless those who curse you, and pray for your persecutors, so that you may be sons of your heavenly Father' (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27-28). You see what Father patience acquires for us? By this principal command the whole discipline of patience is summed up, when not even to return evil is allowed.

latin: Ipsa adeo est, quae fidem, et subsequitur, et antecedit. Denique Abraham Deo credidit, et justitiae deputatus ab illo est: sed fidem ejus patientia probavit, cum filium immolare jussus est, ad fidei non tentationem dixerim, sed typicam contestationem. Caeterum Deus, quem justitiae deputasset, sciebat. Tam grave praeceptum, quod nec Domino perfici placebat, patienter et audivit, et si Deus voluisset, implesset. Merito ergo benedictus, quia et fidelis; merito fidelis, quia et patiens. Ita fides patientia illuminata, cum in nationes seminaretur per semen Abrahae, quod est Christus, et gratiam legi superduceret, ampliandae adimplendaeque legi adjutricem suam patientiam praefecit, quod ea sola ad justitiae doctrinam retro defuisset. Nam olim et oculum pro oculo, et dentem pro dente repetebant, et malum malo foenerabant: nondum enim patientia in terris, quia nec fides: scilicet interim impatientia occasionibus legis fruebatur. Facile erat, absente domino patientiae et magistro. Qui postquam supervenit, et gratiam fidei patientia composuit, jam nec verbo quidem lacessere, nec Fatue quidem dicere sine judicii periculo licet. Prohibita ira, restricti animi, compressa petulantia manus, exemptum linguae venenum, plus lex quam amisit invenit, dicente Christo: Diligite inimicos vestros, et maledicentibus benedicite: et orate pro persecutoribus vestris, ut filii sitis Patris vestri coelestis. Vides quem nobis patrem patientia acquirat? Hoc principali praecepto universa patientiae disciplina succincta est, quando ne digne quidem malefacere concessum est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Servants of the living God, my fellow servants and sisters, by what right am I placed over you? I am, in fact, the least among you by right of our shared servitude and brotherhood, yet I dare to address you—not from affectation, but from affection for your salvation. That salvation belongs not only to women but also to men, and it is grounded especially in the display of purity. Since we are all the temple of God, the Holy Spirit having been brought in and consecrated in us, purity is the caretaker and priest of this temple; it allows nothing impure or profane to enter, lest the God who inhabits it, offended, abandon the defiled seat. But now I speak not of purity itself—divine precepts everywhere are sufficient to command and exact that—but of the things that pertain to it: how you ought to conduct yourselves. Many women—and I reprove them; may God permit me to reprove them—either ignorantly or boldly feigning ignorance, act as if purity consisted only in bodily integrity and the avoidance of sexual sin, as though nothing internal were required regarding dress and adornment. Yet they persist in their old pursuits of beauty and brilliance, parading the same appearance as women of the nations who lack the consciousness of true purity, because there is nothing true in those who do not know God as the guardian and master of truth. Even if some purity can be believed to exist among the pagans, it is nonetheless imperfect and unformed; although it may hold on somewhat in the mind, it dissolves in the license of habits, chasing the perversity of the pagans while avoiding its effect. How many women do not even desire to please outsiders? Who does not want to paint herself in order to deny desire? Yet this too is characteristic of pagan purity: not to sin, yet to will it; or even not to will it, yet not to deny it. What is surprising? All things not from God are perverse. Let them see, then, what they easily obtain and what they obtain mixed with evil. You, however, must turn away from them—as in other things, so also in your walk—because you ought to be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect (Matthew 5:48). And you who are perfect—that is, Christian and pure women—must know that desire for yourselves is not only not to be desired but to be execrated: first, because the effort to please through beauty does not spring from a clean conscience, and we know beauty naturally invites lust. So what evil are you stirring up in yourself? What are you inviting, when you profess to be a stranger to it? Then, because we must not open the way to temptations, which sometimes, even when God drives them off, still accomplish their purpose by insisting, and certainly stir the spirit to scandal. We must walk so holily and with the whole substance of faith that we are confessed and secure in our conscience, wishing to persevere in this, yet not presuming. For whoever presumes fears less, guards less, and endangers himself more. Fear is the foundation of salvation; presumption blocks fear. It is more useful, therefore, to hope that we cannot sin than to presume we cannot; for by hoping we fear, by fearing we guard, by guarding we are saved; but if we presume, neither fearing nor guarding, we will hardly be saved. Whoever acts securely is not watchful and does not possess true, firm security; but whoever is watchful can truly be secure. And the Lord, out of his mercy, will care for his servants so that they may even presume upon their good happily. But what danger do we bring to another? What desire do we import into another? If the Lord, expanding the law, does not distinguish the act of sexual sin in punishment, I do not know whether the woman who caused someone's perdition goes unpunished. For he perishes in your appearance at the same moment—if he desires, he has already admitted in his mind what he desired, and you have become a sword to him. So that you may be free from guilt, you will not escape envy; just as when a robbery is committed in someone's field, the crime does not touch the owner, yet his estate is stained with shame and he himself is sprinkled with infamy. Shall we adorn ourselves so that another may perish? Where then is the command: Love your neighbor as yourself; do not care only for your own, but also for another's? (Matthew 22:39). No utterance of the Holy Spirit ought to be directed and received only for the present matter and not for every occasion of utility. Since, therefore, both our own cause and another's are at stake in the pursuit of the most dangerous beauty, you must know that not only the suggestion of artificial and elaborate beauty is to be rejected, but even natural beauty is to be obliterated by concealment and neglect, so that it may not be troublesome to the eyes that invade it. For even if beauty is not to be blamed—as the felicity of the body, as the addition of divine craftsmanship, as some urban garment of the soul—yet it is to be feared because of the injury and violence of spectators; even Abraham, the father of faith, feared for his wife's appearance, and by lying that she was his sister, redeemed his safety with contempt. Now the dignity of beauty ought not to be feared, so that it is not burdensome to those who possess it, nor destructive to those who desire it, nor perilous to those joined in marriage; it ought not to be considered exposed to temptations nor surrounded by scandals: it is enough that it is not necessary for the angels of God. For where purity is, there beauty is empty, because the proper use and fruit of beauty is luxury, unless someone thinks there is another harvest of bodily beauty. Let those women extend the beauty given them and seek what is not given, who think they can provide for themselves what another demands when they provide it for another. Someone will say: What then? With luxury excluded and chastity admitted, is it not allowed to enjoy the praise of beauty alone and glory in the good of the body? Let him see to it who delights to glory in the flesh. But for us, first, there is no pursuit of glory, because glory is the spirit of exaltation. Further, exaltation does not suit those who profess humility by God's precepts. Next, if all glory is vain and foolish, how much more that which is only in the flesh! For even if we ought to glory, we ought to wish to please in the good things of the spirit, not in the flesh, because we are followers of spiritual things; in these we work, in these we rejoice; from these we gather glory, from which we hope for salvation. Certainly the Christian will also glory in the flesh—but when it has been lacerated for Christ's sake and endured, so that the spirit may be crowned in it, not so that it draws the eyes and sighs of young people after it. So whatever is empty in you, you ought to despise with merit, both having it and not having it. Let the holy woman be naturally beautiful, but not so as to be an occasion; certainly, if she is, she ought not to be ignorant, but also to hinder herself. As if I were speaking to pagans, addressing you with a pagan and common precept of all: you ought to please only your husbands. And you will please them to the extent that you do not care to please others. Be secure, blessed women; no wife is ugly to her husband; it is enough that she pleased him when she was chosen, either by character or by commended beauty. Let none of you think that if she moderates her adornment, she will be pursued by the hatred and aversion of her husband. Every husband is an exactor of chastity; the faithful husband does not demand beauty, because we are not taken by the same goods pagans think; the unfaithful husband, on the contrary, even suspects it, on account of that wicked opinion of pagans against us. To whom, then, do you nourish your beauty? If to the faithful, he does not demand it; if to the pagan, he does not believe it. What are you doing trying to please either the suspect or the undesiring?

latin: Ancillae Dei vivi, conservae et sorores meae, quo jure deputor vobiscum, postremissimus equidem meo jure conservitii et fraternitatis, audeo ad vos facere sermonem, non utique affectationis, sed affectioni procurans in caussa vestrae salutis. Ea salus nec foeminarum modo, sed etiam virorum, in exhibitione praecipue pudicitiae statuta est. Nam cum omnes templum Dei simus, illato in nos et consecrato Spiritu Sancto, ejus templi aedituus et antistes pudicitia est, quae nihil immundum nec profanum inferri sinat, ne Deus ille, qui inhabitat, inquinatam sedem offensus derelinquat. Sed modo nos non de pudicitia, cui indicendae et exigendae sufficiunt instantia ubique divina praecepta, verum de pertinentibus ad eam, id est qualiter vos incedere oporteat. Pleraeque enim, quod ipsum mihi utique [reprehendendo in omnibus] reprehendere Deus permittat, aut ignorantes simpliciter aut dissimulantes audacter ita ingrediuntur, quasi pudicitia in sola carnis integritate et stupri aversione consistat, nec quicquam intrinsecus opus sit, de cultus et ornatus dispositione. Sed enim perseverant in pristinis studiis formae et nitoris, eamdem sui speciem circumferentes, quam foeminae nationum, a quibus abest conscientia verae pudicitiae, quia nihil verum in his, qui Deum nesciunt praesidem et magistrum veritatis. Nam etsi qua in gentilibus pudicitia credi potest, usque adeo eam imperfectam et inconditam constat, ut licet in animo aliquatenus tenax sui agat, in habitus tamen licentia sese dissolvat, pro perversitate gentilium appetendo, cujus rei devitat effectum. Quota denique est, quae nec placere quidem extraneis concupiscat? quae non velit idcirco se expingere, ut neget appetitum? Quanquam et hoc gentili pudicitiae familiare sit, non delinquere, attamen velle; vel etiam nolle, attamen non denegare. Quid mirum? perversa sunt omnia, quae a Deo non sunt. Videant igitur, quae non totum bonum obtinendo facile et quod obtinent malo commiscent. Vos ab illis, ut in caeteris, incessu quoque devertere necessarium est, quoniam perfectae esse debetis, sicut Pater vester qui est in coelis. Perfectae autem, id est, christianae pudicae, appetitionem sui, non tantum non appetendam, sed etiam exsecrandam vobis sciatis: primo quod non de integra conscientia venit studium placendi per decorem, quem naturaliter invitatorem libidinis scimus; quid igitur in te excitas malum istud? Quid invitas, cujus te profiteris extraneam? Tum quod tentationibus viam aperire non debemus, quae nonnunquam quod Deus a suis abigat instando perficiunt, certe vel spiritum scandalo permovent. Debemus quidem ita sancte et tota fidei substantia incedere, ut confessae et securae simus de conscientia nostra optantes perseverare id in nobis, non tamen praesumentes. Nam qui praesumit, minus veretur, minus praecavet, plus periclitatur. Timor fundamentum salutis est, praesumptio impedimentum timoris Utilius ergo, si speremus non posse delinquere, quam si praesumamus non posse; sperando enim timebimus, timendo cavebimus, cavendo salvi erimus; contra si praesumamus neque timendo neque cavendo, difficile salvi erimus. Qui securus agit, non est sollicitus, non possidet tutam et firmam securitatem. At qui sollicitus est, is vere poterit esse securus. Et de suis quidem servis Dominus pro misericordia sua curet, ut etiam praesumere illis de bono suo feliciter liceat. Quid autem alteri periculo sumus? quid alteri concupiscentiam importamus? quam si Dominus ampliando legem a facto stupri non discernit in poena, nescio an impune habeat, quae alicui fuerit caussa perditionis. Perit enim ille simul in tua forma, si concupierit, et admisit jam in animo, quod concupivit, et facta es tu gladius illi. Ut a culpa vaces, ab invidia non liberaberis; ut cum in alicujus agro latrocinium gestum est, crimen quidem dominum non contingit; dum rus tamen ejus ignominia notatur, ipse quoque infamia aspergitur. Expingamus nos, ut alteri pereant? Ubi est ergo: Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum; nolite vestra tantum curare, sed alterius? Nulla enuntiatio Spiritus Sancti ad praesentem tantum materiam et non ad omnem utilitatis occasionem dirigi et suscipi debet. Cum igitur et nostra et aliorum caussa versetur in studio periculosissimi decoris, jam non tantum confictae et elaboratae pulchritudinis suggestum recusandum a vobis sciatis, sed etiam naturalis speciositatis obliterandum dissimulatione et incuria, ut proinde oculorum incursibus molestum. Nam etsi accusandus decor non est, ut felicitas corporis, ut divinae plasticae accessio, ut animae aliqua vestis urbana; timendum tamen est vel propter injuriam et violentiam spectatorum, quae etiam pater fidei Abraham in uxoris suae specie pertimuit, et sororem mentitus Saram, salutem contumelia redemit. Nunc non sit timenda dignitas formae, ut nec possidentibus gravis, nec appetentibus exitiosa, nec conjunctis periculosa; non exposita tentationibus, non circumdata scandalis existimetur: sufficit, quod angelis Dei non est necessaria. Nam ubi pudicitia, ibi vacua pulchritudo, quia proprie usus et fructus pulchritudinis luxuria, nisi si quis aliam messem decori corporis arbitratur. Illae sibi formositatem et datam extendant et non datam conquirant, quae quod ab illa flagitatur, sibi quoque praestare se putant, cum alteri praestant. Dicet aliquis: Quid ergo non, et exclusa luxuria, et admissa castitate, laude formae sola frui et de bono corporis gloriari licet? Viderit, quem juvat de carne gloriari. Nobis autem primo quidem nullum gloriae studium, quia gloria exaltationis ingenium est. Porro exaltatio non congruit professoribus humilitatis ex praescriptis Dei. Deinde si omnis gloria vana et stuporata, quanto magis quae in carne nobis duntaxat! Nam etsi gloriandum est, in spiritus bonis, non in carne placere velle debemus, quia spiritualium sectatores sumus; in quibus operamur, illis et gaudeamus; de his gloriam carpamus, de quibus salutem speramus. Plane gloriabitur Christianus etiam in carne, sed cum propter Christum lacerata duraverit, ut et spiritus in ea coronetur, non ut oculos et suspiria adolescentium post se trahat. Ita quod ex omni parte in vobis vacat, merito et non habentes fastidiatis et habentes negligatis. Sancta foemina sit naturaliter speciosa, non adeo sit occasioni; certe si fuerit, non ignorare, sed etiam impedire se debet. Quasi gentilibus dicam, gentili et communi omnium praecepto alloquens vos, solis maritis vestris placere debetis. In tantum autem placebitis eis, in quantum alteris placere non curaveritis. Securae estote, benedictae; uxor nulla deformis est marito suo; satis placuit, cum electa est, seu moribus, seu forma commendata. Ne qua vestrum putet, si temperaverit a compositione sui, se odium et aversionem maritorum prosecuturam. Omnis maritus castitatis exactor est; formam vero fidelis non expostulat, quia non iisdem bonis, quae gentiles putant, capimur; infidelis contra etiam suspectam habet, vel propter illam sceleratam in nos opinionem gentilium. Cui ergo pulchritudinem tuam nutris? Si fidelis, non exigit; si gentilis, non credit. Quid gestis aut suspecto aut non desideranti placere?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If the Father sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, then the flesh visible in him will not be called a phantom on that account. He had assigned sin to the flesh in the first place and turned it into a law of sin dwelling in its members and opposing the law of the mind. That is why the Son was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh: to redeem sin's flesh with a matching substance—that is, with flesh resembling sinful flesh while itself not being sinful. This will be God's power: to accomplish salvation in a substance that is the counterpart. It is no great thing if the Spirit of God were to heal flesh; the wonder is if flesh, akin to sinful flesh, while still being flesh, is not of sin. So the likeness attaches to the label 'sin', not to a falsity of substance. He would not have added 'of sin' if he had wanted the likeness of substance to be understood so as to deny the truth; he would have said only 'flesh', not also 'of sin'. But when he framed it as 'flesh of sin', he confirmed the substance—that is, the flesh—and referred the likeness to the vice of the substance, that is, to sin. Suppose the likeness of substance is what is spoken of: the truth of the substance is not thereby denied. Why then is it similar if it is true? Because it is indeed true, but not from seed; it is similar and true in condition, but not similar in origin. Besides, there is no likeness between opposites. The Spirit would not be called the likeness of flesh—since flesh would not take on the likeness of Spirit—but it would be called a phantom if what does not exist were seen. Likeness is spoken of when there is something actually seen, because it exists while matching another. A phantom, merely by being that, is not a likeness. Here too he himself, explaining how he does not want us to be in the flesh while we are in the flesh, so that we may not be in the works of the flesh, shows that he wrote for this reason: 'flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God' (1 Corinthians 15:50), not condemning the substance but its works; which, because they can be rejected by us while we remain in the flesh, belong not to the guilt of the substance but to our conduct.

latin: Hunc si pater misit in similitudinem carnis peccati, non ideo phantasma dicetur caro, quae in illo uidebatur. peccatum enim carni supra adscripsit et illam fecit legem peccati habitantem in membris suis et aduersantem legi sensus. ob hoc igitur missum filium in similitudinem carnis peccati, ut peccati carnem simili substantia redimeret, id est carne, quae peccatrici carni similis esset, cum peccatrix ipsa non esset. nam et haec erit dei uirtus in substantia pari perficere salutem. non enim magnum, si spiritus dei carnem remediaret, sed si caro, consimilis peccatrici, dum caro est, sed non peccati. ita similitudo ad titulum peccati pertinebit, non ad substantiae mendacium. nam nec addidisset \'peccati\', si substantiae similitudinem uellet intellegi, ut negaret ueritatem; tantum enim (carnis) posuisset, non et (peccat ? . cum uero tunc sic struxit: \'carnis peccati\', et substantiam confirmauit, id est carnem, et similitudinem ad uitium substantiae retulit, id est ad peccatum. puta nunc similitudinem substantiae dictam: non ideo negabitur substantiae ueritas. (cur ergo similis, (si) uera\'? quia uera quidem, sed non ex semine: de statu similis et uera, de censu non uero dissimilis. ceterum similitudo in contrariis nulla est. spiritus non diceretur carnis similitudo, — quia nec caro similitudinem spiritus caperet — sed phantasma diceretur, si id quod non erat uidebatur. similitudo autem dicitur, cum est quod uidetur. est enim, dum alterius par est. phantasma autem, qua hoc tantum est, non est similitudo. Et hic autem ipse edisserens, quomodo nolit nos esse in carne, cum simus in carne, ut scilicet non simus in operibus carnis, ostendit hac ratione scripsisse: caro et sanguis regnum dei non consequentur, non substantiam damnans, sed opera eius; quae, (quia) possunt non admitti a nobis in carne adhuc positis, non ad reatum substantiae, sed ad conuersationispertinebunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I say this to you who are listening — pointing out that the Creator gave this command long ago: 'Speak to the ears of those who hear' — love your enemies, bless those who hate you, and pray for those who slander you (Isaiah). The Creator wrapped all this into a single statement through Isaiah: say to those who hate you, 'You are our brothers.' If people who are enemies, who hate, curse, and slander are to be called brothers, then the One who ordered them to be called brothers certainly also ordered that those who hate be blessed and that prayer be made for slanderers. 'Christ teaches a brand-new patience, even restraining the revenge the Creator permitted — an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth — while commanding that the other cheek also be offered and that the cloak be given up along with the tunic.' True enough. If Christ added these as supplements that fit the Creator's teaching, we must immediately ask: is the discipline of patience preached by the Creator? Through Zechariah He commanded: let no one remember the evil of his brother — nor that of his neighbor; for He says again: let no one recall the evil of his neighbor, so He taught patience toward injury who taught forgetfulness of it (Zechariah). And when He says, 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' He teaches patience as the posture that awaits vengeance (Deuteronomy). To the degree that faith cannot accept that the same God who forbids not only revenge but even the memory and recollection of injury would demand an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth in return for injury, to that degree it becomes clear how He judged 'an eye for an eye': not to permit a second injury as retaliation — which He had already prohibited by banning vengeance — but to restrain the first injury by the threat of retaliation, so that each person, looking ahead to the license a second injury would bring, would hold himself back from the first. He knew violence is more easily checked by the representation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance. Both had to be established for human nature and faith: so the one who believes in God expects vengeance from God, and the one with less faith fears the law's retaliation. The Lord Christ revealed and fulfilled the will of this law — a will straining to be understood, the Lord of Sabbath, Law, and every paternal disposition — by commanding the offer of the other cheek, so that He might extinguish revenge far more thoroughly than the Law and its retaliation ever aimed to, and than prophecy clearly restrained, since prophecy banned the memory of injury and referred vengeance to God (Isaiah; Ezekiel). So if Christ introduced anything, He did it not as an adversary to the command but as its helper; He did not destroy the Creator's disciplines. Finally, if we examine the very reason for teaching patience — and such full, perfect patience — it cannot hold together unless it comes from the Creator, who promises vengeance and provides a Judge. Otherwise, if patience carries this much weight — not only refusing to strike back but offering the other cheek, not only refusing to curse but blessing, not only keeping your tunic but handing over your cloak as well — the One imposing this on me is the One who will not defend me. He commands patience in vain, without showing me the reward of the command, the fruit of patience, which is vengeance. He ought to have permitted me that vengeance if He does not provide it Himself, or, if He forbade it to me, He ought to provide it Himself, since it is in the interest of discipline that injury be avenged. Fear of vengeance restrains all wickedness; but given free rein, wickedness will dominate, gouging out both eyes and knocking out every tooth, secure in its impunity. Yet this — avenging injury, opening the door to violence, failing to defend the righteous, failing to restrain the wicked — is said to be the mark of a supremely good God, a God who is only good. Give to everyone who asks, certainly to the needy, or even more so to the needy, even if also to the one who has abundance. So that no one might lack a giver, you have the form of the Creator's command in Deuteronomy: 'There will be no one in need among you,' says the Lord your God, 'blessing you' — that is, the giver who makes it so there is no one in need (Deuteronomy). And this goes further. He does not command that something be given to the one who asks; He says, 'Let there be no one in need among you,' that is, 'See to it beforehand, lest there be.' All the more, therefore, does He prejudge the case in favor of giving to the one who asks, and also in what follows: if anyone among your brothers is in need, do not harden your heart or close your hand against your needy brother. You will open your hand wide to him; you will lend to him, as much as he desires. For a loan is not usually given except to the one who asks. But we will return to loans later. Now, if someone wants to argue that the Creator commanded giving to brothers, but Christ commanded giving to all who ask, so that this is something new and different — it is actually one and the same, through which the Creator's Law will be in Christ. For Christ commanded nothing different for all people than what the Creator commanded for brothers. Although the goodness shown to outsiders is greater, it is not prior to the goodness owed to neighbors. Who can love outsiders if he has not first loved his neighbor? And if the second degree of goodness is toward outsiders, while the first is toward neighbors, the second degree will belong to the same One to whom the first belongs, more easily than it would belong to the One to whom the first does not belong. Thus the Creator first taught kindness to neighbors according to the natural order, intending to extend it later to outsiders; and according to the plan of His disposition, first to the Jews, then to all humankind. So as long as the sacrament was within Israel, He rightly commanded mercy only for brothers. But when Christ gave the Gentiles their inheritance and possession — the boundaries of the earth — and the word spoken through Hosea began to be fulfilled: 'Not My people — My people,' and 'No mercy — mercy obtained,' that is, for the nation — from then on Christ extended the law of paternal kindness to all, excluding no one from mercy, just as from the call (Hosea). So even if He taught something more, He received this too as part of the Gentiles' inheritance. 'And as you want people to treat you, so you must treat them.' In this command the other half is certainly implied: 'As you do not want people to treat you, so you must not treat them.' If a new and unknown God, not yet fully revealed, commanded this — a God who had not previously formed me through any institution by which I might know beforehand what I ought to will or not will, and so do to others what I want done to me and not do what I do not want — He permitted the passivity of my judgment and did not bind me to the agreement of will and deed, so that I might do to others what I will, and not do to others what I do not will. For He did not define what I ought to will or not will for myself and others, so that my deed might conform to the law of will. And I can now fail to give another what I want another to give me — love, obedience, comfort, protection, and such goods — and likewise do to another what I do not want done to me — violence, injury, insult, fraud, and such evils. Finally, Gentiles not yet instructed by God act with this inconsistency of will and deed. Although nature knows good and evil, it is not yet the discipline of God, which, once known, is then acted upon in the agreement of will and deed through faith, under the fear of God. So the God of Marcion, even if He were revealed — which He is not — could not have issued such a strict and obscure command, still blind and more easily interpreted by my own whim, for which He had established no distinction. But my Creator long ago and everywhere commanded that the needy, the poor, orphans, and widows be protected, helped, and comforted, just as through Isaiah: 'Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, cover him' (Isaiah). Likewise through Ezekiel concerning the just man: 'He gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked' (Ezekiel). So He already taught me to do to others what I want done to me. Thus, proclaiming: 'Do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness,' He taught me not to do to others what I do not want done to me. And therefore the command in the Gospel will be His, who previously established and distinguished it, and arranged it according to the judgment of His discipline, and rightly subjected it to a summary, since the Lord Christ was going to make a concise statement on earth — that is, to preach.

latin: Sed uobis dico, inquit, qui auditis — ostendens hoc olim mandatum a creatore: loquere in aures audientium —-.diligiteinimicosuestrosetbenediciteeos, qui uos oderunt, et orate pro eis, qui uos calumniantur. haec creator una pronuntiatione clusit per Esaiam: dicite \'fratres nostri estis\' eis, qui uos oderunt. si enim qui inimici sunt et oderunt et maledicunt et calumniantur fratres appellandi sunt, utique et benedici odientes et orari pro calumniatoribus iussit qui eos fratres deputari praecepit. \'Nouam plane patientiam docet Christus, etiam uicem iniuriae cohibens permissam a creatore, oculum exigente pro oculo et dentem pro dente, contra ipse alteram amplius maxillam offerri iubens et super tunicam pallio quoque cedi.\' plane. (ni) haec Christus adiecerit ut supplementa consentanea disciplinae creatoris. atque adeo hoc statim renuntiandum est: an disciplina patientiae praedicatur penes creatorem? si per Zachariam praecepit: ne unusquisque malitiae fratris sui meminerit, — sed nec proximi; nam et rursus: malitiam, inquit, proximi sui unusquisque ne recogitet multo magis patientiam indixit iniuriae qui indixit obliuionem. sed et cum dicit: mihi uindictam, et ego uindicabo, proinde patientiam docet, uindictae expectatricem. in quantum ergo fidem non capit, ut idem uideatur oculum pro oculo et dentem pro dente in uicem iniuriae exigere, qui non modo uicem sed etiam ultionem, etiam recordationem et recogitationem iniuriae prohibet, in tantum aperitur nobis, quomodo oculum pro oculo et dentem pro dente censuerit: non ad secundam iniuriam talionis permittendam, quam prohibuerat interdicta ultione, sed ad primam coercendam [quam prohibuerat] opposito talione, ut unusquisque respiciens licentiam secundae iniuriae a prima semetipsum contineret. facilius enim uim comprimi sciit repraesentatione talionis quam repromissione ultionis. utrumque autem constituendum fuit pro natura et fide hominum, ut qui deo crederet, ultionem a deo expectaret, qui minus fideret, legis taliones timeret. hanc legis uoluntatem de intellectu laborantem dominus et sabbati et legis et omnium paternarum dispositionum, Christus, et reuelauit et compotem fecit, mandans alterius quoque maxillae oblationem, ut tanto magis uicem iniuriae extingueret, quam et lex et per talionem uoluerat impedisse, certe quam prophetia manifeste coercuerat, et memoriam iniuriae prohibens et ultionem ad deum redigens. ita si quid Christus intulit, non aduersario sed adiutore praecepto, non destruxit disciplinas creatoris. denique si in ipsam rationem patientiae praecipiendae, et quidem tam plenae atque perfectae, consideremus, non consistet, si non est creatoris, qui uindictam repromittit, qui iudicem praestat. alioquin si tantum patientiae pondus non modo non repercutiendi sed et aliam maxillam praebendi, et non modo non remaledicendi sed etiam benedicendi, et non modo non retinendi tunicam sed et amplius et pallium concedendi, is mihi imponit, qui non sit me defensurus, in uacuum patientiam praecipit, non exhibens mihi mercedem praecepti, patientiae dico fructum, quod est ultio, quam mihi permisisse debuerat, si ipse non praestat, aut, si mihi non permittebat. ipse praestare, quoniam et disciplinae interest iniuriam uindicari. metu enim ultionis omnis iniquitas refrenatur, ceterum passim emissa libertate dominabitur, utrumque oculum effossura et omnem dentem excitatura prae impunitatis securitate. sed hoc est dei optimi et tantum boni, patientiae iniuriam facere, uiolentiae ianuam pandere, probos non defendere, improbos non coercere. Omni petentitedato, utique indigenti, uel tanto magis indigenti, si etiam et abundanti. ne quis ergo indigeat datorem, imperatam habes in Deuteronomio formam creatoris: non erit, inquit, in te indigens, uti benedicens benedicat te dominus deus tuus, datorem scilicet, qui fecerit non esse indigentem. et plus hic. non enim petenti iubet dari, sed non sit, inquit, indigens in te, id est \'cura ultro, ne sit\'. quo magis petenti praeiudicat dandum, etiam in sequentibus: si autem fuerit indigens ex fratribus tuis, non auertes cor tuum nec constringes manum tuam a fratre tuo indigente. aperiens aperies illi manum, fenus fenerabis illi, quantum desiderarit. fenus enim nisi petenti dari non solet. sed de fenore postmodum. nunc, si qui uoluerit argumentari creatorem quidem fratribus dari iussisse, Christum uero omnibus petentibus, ut hoc sit nouum atque diuersum, immo unum erit ex his, per quae lex creatoris erit * in Christo. non enim aliud Christus in omnes praecepit quam quod creator in fratres. nam etsi maior est bonitas, quae operatur in extraneos, sed non prior ea, quae ante debetur in proximos. quis enim poterit diligere extraneos, ***? quodsi secundus gradus bonitatis est in extraneos, qui in proximos primus est, eiusdem erit secundus gradus, cuius et primus, facilius quam ut eius sit secundus, cuius non extitit primus. ita creator et secundum naturae ordinem primum in proximos docuit benignitatem, emissurus eam postea et in extraneos, et secundum rationem dispositionis suae primo in Iudaeos, postea et in omne hominum genus. ideoque quamdiu intra Israhelem erat sacramentum, merito in solos fratres misericordiam mandabat, at ubi Christo dedit gentes hereditatem et possessionem terminos terrae et coepit expungi quod dictum est per Osee: non populus meus populus meus, et non misericordiam consecuta misericordiam consecuta, natio scilicet, exinde Christus in omnes legem paternae benignitatis extendit, neminem excipiens in miseratione, sicut in uocatione. ita et si quid amplius docuit, hoc quoque in hereditatem gentium accepit. Et sicut uobis fieri uultis ab hominibus, ita et uos facite illis. in isto praecepto utique alia pars eius subauditur: et sicut uobis fieri non uultis ab hominibus, ita et uos ne faciatis illis. hoc si nouus deus et ignotus retro et nondum plane editus praecepit, qui me nulla antehac institutione formauerit, qua prius scirem, quid deberem mihi uelle uel nolle atque ita et aliis facere quae et mihi uellem, non facere quae et mihi nollem, passiuitatem sententiae meae permisit nec adstrinxit me ad conuenientiam uoluntatis et facti, ut id aliis faciam, quod mihi uelim, et id nec aliis faciam, quod mihi nolim. non enim definiit, quid mihi atque aliis debeam uelle uel nolle, ut ad legem uoluntatis parem factum. et possum (iam) alii non praestare quod ab alio mihi uelim praestitum, amorem obsequium solatium praesidium et eiusmodi bona, proinde et alii facere quod ab alio fieri mihi nolim, uim iniuriam contumeliam fraudem et eiusmodi mala. denique hac inconuenientia uoluntatis et facti agunt ethnici nondum a deo instructi. nam etsi natura bonum et malum a notum est, non tamen dei disciplina, qua cognita tunc demum conuenientia uoluntatis et facti ex fide, ut sub metu dei, agitur. itaque deus Marcionis cum maxime reuelatus, si tamen reuelatus, non potuit huius praecepti, de quo agitur, tam strictum et obscurum et caecum adhuc et facilius pro meo s potius arbitrio interpretandum compendium emittere, cuius nullam praestruxerat distinctionem. at enim creator meus olim et ubique praecepit indigentes pauperes et pupillos et uiduas protegi iuuari refrigerari, sicut et per Esaiam: infringito panem tuum mendicis, et qui sine tecto sunt in domum tuam inducito, et nudum si uideris, tegito; item per Ezechielem de uiro iusto: panem suum dabit esurienti et nudum conteget. satis ergo iam tunc me docuit ea facere aliis, quae mihi uelim fieri. proinde denuntians: non occides, non adulterabis, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, docuit, ne faciam aliis quae fieri mihi nolim. et ideo ipsius erit praeceptum in euangelio, qui illud retro et praestruxit et distinxit et ad arbitrium disciplinae suae disposuit et merito iam compendio substrinxit, quoniam et alias recisum sermonem facturus in terris dominus, id est Christus, praedicabatur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Consider the evidence and you see the whole order of God the Judge laid bare—or, to put it more precisely, the defender of that catholic and supreme goodness which the Marcionites refuse to acknowledge in the same God who sends rain on the good and the evil alike and makes his sun rise on the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), a generosity no other god even attempts. Marcion had the audacity to cut this very testimony of Christ about the Creator out of his gospel, but the world itself is written large and every conscience reads it. That same patience of the Creator will stand as evidence against Marcion on judgment day: the patience that waits for a sinner's repentance rather than his death, that prefers mercy to sacrifice. It turned aside the doom decreed for Nineveh, granted Hezekiah an extension on life in answer to his tears, and restored the Babylonian tyrant's kingdom after he repented. This is the mercy that spared Saul's son at the people's pleading, that pardoned David when he confessed his crime against Uriah's house, that restored Israel every time it judged her and recalled her every time it rebuked her. So do not merely stare at the Judge; turn and conform to his supreme example. Mark when he avenges, weigh when he spares; set his gentleness against his severity. When you have taken the measure of both in the Creator, you will find in him the very quality that drove you to invent a second god. Come now, finally, to a close inspection of his teachings, disciplines, precepts, and counsels. You may object that these are merely the stuff of human law codes. But Moses and God preceded every Lycurgus and Solon; no later generation fails to receive from the origins. Still, my Creator did not learn his legislation from your god: 'You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor's goods; honor your father and your mother; and love your neighbor as yourself' (Deut. 5:6–21). To these chief counsels of innocence and chastity, justice and piety, are added precepts of sheer humanity: every seventh year servitudes are dissolved into freedom; at that same time the field is left fallow to give the needy a place; even the ox treading the grain has its muzzle loosened so it may eat of the fruit of its present labor—so that humanity, rehearsed on beasts, might be more easily taught for the relief of human beings.
