latin: Haec ita dispecta totum ordinem dei iudicis operarium et, ut dignius dixerim, protectorem catholicae et summae illius bonitatis ostendunt, quam (ut) semotam a iudiciariis sensibus et in suo statu puram nolunt Marcionitae in eodem deo agnoscere, pluente super bonos et malos et solem suum oriri faciente super iustos et iniustos, quod alius deus omnino non praestat. nam etsi hoc quoque testimonium Christi in creatorem Marcion. de euangelio eradere ausus est, sed ipse mundus inscriptus est et omni a conscientia legitur. et erit haec ipsa patientia creatoris in iudicium Marcionis, illa patientia, quae expectat paenitentiam potius peccatoris quam mortem et mauult misericordiam quam sacrificium, auertens destinatum iam exitium Niniuitis et largiens spatium uitae Ezechiae lacrimis et restituens statum regni Babylonis tyranno paenitentia functo: illam dico misericordiam, quae et filium Saulis moriturum ex deuotione populo concessit et Dauid delicta in domum Uriae confessum uenia liberauit et ipsum Israhel totiens restituit quotiens iudicauit, totiens refouit quotiens et increpuit. non solum igitur iudicem aspiciens conuertere et ad optimi exempla: notans cum ulciscitur considera cum indulget; repende austeritati lenitatem. cum utrumque conueneris in creatore, inuenies in eo et illud, propter quod alterum deum credis. ueni denique ad inspectationem doctrinarum disciplinarum praeceptorum consiliorumque eius. dices forsitan haec etiam humanis legibus determinari. sed ante Lycurgos et Solonas omnes Moyses et deus. nulla posteritas non a primordiis accipit. tamen non a tuo deo didicit creator meus praescribere : non occides, non adulterabis, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, alienum non concupisces, honora patrem et matrem, et diliges proximum tuum ut temetipsum. ad haec innocentiae et pudicitiae, iustitiae et pietatis principalia consulta accedunt etiam humanitatis praescripta, cum septimo quoque anno seruitia libertate soluuntur, cum eodem tempore agro parcitur egenis cedendo locum, (cum) boui etiam terenti uincula oris remittuntur ad fructum praesentis laboris, quo facilius in pecudibus praemeditata humanitas in hominum refrigeria erudiretur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I set another rule before him: just as natural things are, so rational things ought to be in God. I demand a rational basis for goodness, because nothing else can count as good unless it is rationally good—much less can goodness itself be found irrational. It would be easier for evil, once some reason attaches to it, to pass as good than for good, deserted by reason, to escape being judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God, first of all because he proceeded to the salvation of a foreign man. I know they will say this is the principal and perfect goodness, since it is poured out voluntarily and freely on strangers without any debt of kinship—precisely the standard by which we are commanded to love our enemies, who are already strangers to us by that very name. Why then did he not regard man from the beginning, from the beginning a stranger? By holding back, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the stranger. Moreover, the discipline of loving a stranger or enemy preceded the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Even though that command comes from the Creator's law, you must accept it too, since Christ did not destroy it but built upon it. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and the stranger. Exacting what is owed is an exaggeration of due goodness. But due goodness precedes undue goodness—as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, undue goodness, which comes first. Therefore, when the first reason for goodness is to show it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to show it to a foreigner out of the overflow of justice beyond the scribes and Pharisees, what kind of second reason can be assigned to one who lacks the first, who does not have his own man, and is therefore deficient? Furthermore, how did what is deficient, which never had its own, overflow into a foreigner? Produce the principal reason, and then vindicate the subsequent one. Nothing can be vindicated without rational order; so far is it from reason itself losing order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second grade, namely toward the foreigner: nor will that second grade hold together rationally for him, since it has been destroyed another way. For only then will the second goodness toward a foreigner count as rational if it operates without injury to the one whose property it is. Whatever goodness justice first establishes is rational. Just as in the principal grade, when it is shown to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also toward a foreigner it can appear rational if it is not unjust. But what sort of goodness consists through injustice, and that for a foreigner? Perhaps injurious goodness might be considered rational to some extent for a household servant. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended as rational? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, more wicked than to benefit a foreign servant in such a way that he is stolen from his master, claimed for another, and suborned against his master's head—and, what is more shameful, while still living in the master's house, eating from the master's stores, trembling under the master's blows? Such an advocate would be condemned even in the world, let alone the plagiarist. In no other way does Marcion's God, bursting into a foreign world, snatch man from God, son from father, pupil from teacher, servant from master, so that he makes him impious toward God, irreligious toward father, ungrateful toward teacher, wicked toward master. I ask you: if rational goodness produces such a man, what would irrational goodness produce? I cannot think of anyone more shameless than the one who is baptized in another's water for another god, ascends to another god's heaven, is laid out on another god's earth, offers thanksgiving over another's bread to another god, and operates with another's goods in the name of charity and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil from him, so favorable that he makes another god—indeed his own master—angry?

latin: aliam illi regulam praetendo: sicut naturalia, ita rationalia esse debere in deo omnia. exigo rationem bonitatis, quia nec aliud quid bonum haberi liceat, quod non rationaliter bonum sit, nedum ut ipsa bonitas inrationalis deprehendatur. facilius malum, cui rationis aliquid adfuerit, pro bono habebitur quam ut bonum ratone desertum non pro malo iudicetur. nego rationalem bonitatem\', dei Marcionis iam hoc primo, quod in salutem processerit; hominis alieni. scio dicturos atquin hanc esse principalem \' et perfectam bonitatem, cum sine ullo debito familiaritatis iri extraneos uoluntaria et libera effundatur, secundum quam inimicos quoque nostros et hoc nomine iam extraneos diligere iubeamur. cur ergo non a primordio hominem respexit. a primordio extraneum? cessando praeiudicauit cum extraneo nihil sibi esse. ceterum disciplinam diligendi extraneum uel inimicum antecessit praeceptum diligendi proximum tamquam te ipsum. quod etsi ex lege creatoris, et tu quoque illud excipere debebis, ut a Christo non destructum, sed potius exstructum. nam quo magis proximum diligas, diligere iuberis inimicum et extraneum. exaggeratio est debitae bonitatis exactio indebitae. antecedit autem debita indebitam, ut principalis, ut dignior, ut ministra et comite sua [id est indebita] prior. igitur cum prima bonitatis ratio sit in rem suam exhiberi ex iustitia, secunda autem in alienam ex redundantia iustitiae super scribarum et Pharisaeorum, quale est secundam ei rationem referri, cui deficit prima, non habenti proprium hominem ac per hoc quoque exiguae? porro exigua, quae suum non habuit, quomodo in alienum redundauit? exhibe principalem rationem, et tunc uindica sequentem. nulla res sine ordine rationalis potest uindicari; tanto abest, ut ratio ipsa in aliquo ordinem amittat. sit nunc et a secundo gradu incipiens ratio bonitatis, in extraneum scilicet: nec secundus illi gradus ratione constabit, alio modo destructus. tunc enim rationalis habebitur uel secunda in extraneum bonitas, si sine iniuria eius operetur, cuius est res. quamcumque bonitatem iustitia prima efficit rationalem. sicut in principali gradu, cum in rem suam exhibetur, rationalis erit si iusta sit, sic et in extraneum rationalis uideri poterit, si non sit iniusta. ceterum qualis bonitas quae per iniuriam constat, et quidem pro extraneo? fortasse enim pro domestico aliquatenus rationalis habeatur bonitas iniuriosa. pro extraneo uero, cui nec proba legitime deberetur, qua ratione tam iniusta rationalis defendetur? quid enim iniustius, quid iniquius et improbius quam ita alieno benefacere seruo, ut domino eripiatur, ut alii uindicetur, ut aduersus caput domini subornetur, et quidem, quod indignius, in ipsa adhuc domo domini, de ipsius adhuc horreis uiuens, sub ipsius adhuc plagis tremens? talis adsertor etiam damnaretur in saeculo, nedum plagiator. non aliter ** deus Marcionis, inrumpens in alienum mundum, eripiens deo hominem, patri filium, educatori aluminum, domino famulum, ut eum efficiat deo impium, patri inreligiosum, educatori ingratum, domino nequam. oro te, si rationalis bonitas talem facit, qualem faceret inrationalis? non putem impudentiorem quam qui in aliena aqua alii deo tingitur, ad alienum caelum alii deo expanditur, in aliena terra alii deo sternitur, super alienum panem alii deo gratiarum actionibus fungitur, de alienis bonis ob alium deum nomine elemosynae et dilectionis operatur. quis iste deus tam bonus, ut homo ab illo malus fiat, tam propitius, ut alium illi deum, et dominum quidem ipsius, faciat iratum?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The apostle adds that he is still speaking in human terms: while we were mere children, we were placed under the elemental spirits of the world to serve them. Yet this is no mere human illustration; it is the truth itself. For what child — certainly in understanding, since the nations are such children — is not subject to the world's elemental spirits, which they worship as gods? That statement was made 'according to man' at that time; even so, no one sets aside or adds to a human will. By appealing to the binding force of a human will, he safeguards the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say 'seeds', as if referring to many, but 'seed', as if one — and that one is Christ (Gal 3:16). Let Marcion's erasing sponge be ashamed! Unless I am simply drawing out what he deleted, since it is even more damning to convict him from the very texts he preserved.

When the fullness of time arrived, God sent his Son — the very one who is also God of those times that constitute the age, who ordained the signs of the times, sun and moon and stars, who both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the end of the ages: 'In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest' (Isa 2:2-3), and 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,' according to Joel (Joel 2:28-29). It belonged to him to sustain the fullness of time, since the end of time was his no less than its beginning. What, then, did that idle god accomplish — a god with no operation, no prediction, and therefore no time of his own — to bring about the fullness of time and sustain it now that it is being fulfilled? If nothing, it is utterly vain that he, serving the Creator, merely sustained the Creator's times.

To what end did he send his Son? To redeem those who were under the law — that is, to make the crooked straight and the rough places smooth, according to Isaiah (Isa 40:3-4), so that the old order might pass away and the new arise: 'A new law from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem' — and so that we might receive adoption as sons, we nations who were not sons. For he himself will be the light of the nations, and the nations will hope in his name (Isa 42:6; 49:6). Therefore, to make it certain that we are God's children, he sent his Spirit into our hearts crying, 'Abba, Father' (Gal 4:6). 'For in the last days,' he says, 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28-29). Whose grace is this, if not his, whose is also the promise of grace?

si nihil, satis uanum est, ut creatoris tempora sustinuerit seruiens creatori. cui autem rei misit filium suum? ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret - hoc est ut efficeret tortuosa in uiam rectam et aspera in uias leues secundum Esaiam, ut uetera transirent et noua orirentur: lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem — et ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus, utique nationes, quae filii non eramus. et ipse enim erit lux nationum et in nomine eius nationes sperabunt. itaque ut certum esset nos filios dei esse, misit spiritum suum in corda nostra clamantem: abba, pater. in nouissimis enim, inquit, diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem. cuius gratia, nisi cuius et promissio gratiae?

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Resurrection of the Flesh IX
excerpts.author: Tertullian
excerpts.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
english: So let me reexamine what God built with His own hands in the image of God, what He animated with His own breath to the likeness of His own vivacity, what He placed in charge of dwelling, fruit, dominion, and all His work, what He clothed with His own sacraments and disciplines — whose purity He loves, whose chastisements He approves, whose passions He esteems for Himself. Will this not rise again, so often God's? God forbid, God forbid, that He should abandon to eternal destruction the work of His hands, the care of His intellect, the sheath of His breath, the queen of His molding, the heir of His liberality, the priest of His religion, the soldier of His testimony, the sister of His Christ! We know God is good; we learn from Christ that He is the only Best. Christ, who commanded love — after His own — for the neighbor, will Himself do what He commanded: He will love the flesh, so many ways near to Him, even if weak; but virtue is perfected in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). Even if feeble; but those who are well do not need a physician (Matt 9:12-13). Even if dishonorable; but we surround the more dishonorable with greater honor (1 Cor 12:23-24). Even if lost; but I came to save what was lost, He says (Luke 19:10). Even if sinful; but I desire the sinner's salvation, not death, He says (Ezek 33:11). Even if condemned; but I will strike and I will heal, He says (Hos 6:1). What do you reproach this flesh for, which awaits God, which hopes in God, which is honored by Him, to which He brings help? I dare say: if these things had not happened to the flesh, the kindness, the grace, the mercy, all the beneficial power of God would have been empty.

latin: Igitur, ut retexam quam Deus manibus suis ad imaginem Dei struxit, quam de suo adflatu ad similitudinem suae vivacitatis animavit, quam incolatui, fructui, dominatui, totius suae operationis praeposuit, quam sacramentis suis disciplinisque vestivit: cujus munditias amat, cujus castigationes probat, cujus passiones sibi adpretiat; haeccine non resurget totiens Dei? Absit, absit, ut Deus manuum suarum operam ingenii sui curam, adflatus sui vaginam, molitionis suae reginam, liberalitatis suae haeredem, religionis suae sacerdotem, testimonii sui militem, Christi sui sororem, in aeternum destituat interitum! Bonum Deum novimus; solum optimum a Christo ejus addiscimus; qui dilectionem mandans, post suam, in proximum, faciet et ipse quod praecepit: diliget carnem, tot modis sibi proximam, etsi infirmam; sed virtus in infirmitate perficitur; etsi imbecillam; sed medicum non desiderant, nisi male habentes; etsi inhonestam; sed inhonestioribus majorem circumdamus honorem; etsi perditam; sed ego, inquit, veni ut quod periit salvum faciam; etsi peccatricem; sed malo mihi, inquit, salutem peccatoris, quam mortem; etsi damnatam; sed ego, inquit, percutiam, et sanabo. Quid ea exprobras carni, quae Deum exspectant, quae in Deum sperant, quae honorantur ab illo, quibus subvenit? Ausim dicere, si haec carni non accidissent, benignitas, gratia, misericordia, omnis vis Dei benefica, vacuisset.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We are not frightened, nor do we fear what we suffer at the hands of ignorant people. We entered this movement with eyes open, accepting its terms, so that we might commit our very lives to these battles—hoping to gain what God promises and dreading what a different life threatens. Indeed, we meet your every cruelty head-on, even stepping forward of our own accord, and we rejoice more when we are condemned than when we are acquitted. That is why we sent this pamphlet: not because we fear for ourselves, but for your sake and for the sake of all our enemies, not merely our friends. Our discipline commands us to love enemies, too, and to pray for those who persecute us, so that our goodness may be perfect and distinctive, not commonplace. After all, anyone can love friends; only Christians love enemies. Since we grieve over your ignorance, pity human error, watch the future, and see the signs of these things being prepared daily, we are compelled to speak out in this way and lay before you the truths you refuse to hear openly.

latin: Nos quidem neque expavescimus, neque pertimescimus ea, quae ab ignorantibus patimur: cum ad hanc sectam, utique suscepta conditione ejus, pacti venerimus, ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus, ea quae Deus repromittit consequi optantes, et ea quae diversae vitae comminatur pati timentes. Denique cum omni saevitia vestra concertamus, etiam ultro erumpentes, magisque damnati quam absoluti gaudemus. Itaque hunc libellum non nobis timentes misimus, sed vobis et omnibus inimicis nostris, nedum amicis: ita enim disciplina jubemur diligere inimicos quoque, et orare pro eis qui nos persequuntur: ut haec sit perfecta et propria bonitas nostra, non communis. Amicos enim diligere omnium est, inimicos autem solorum christianorum. Qui ergo dolemus de ignorantia vestra, et miseremur erroris humani, et futura prospicimus, et signa eorum quotidie intentari videmus, necesse est vel hoc modo erumpere ad proponenda vobis ea, quae palam non vultis audire.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I would be astonished if the Psychics were driven only by luxury — the vice that makes them marry so often — and not also torn apart by gluttony, the vice that makes them hate fasting. For lust without gluttony would be a monstrosity, since these two are so tightly fused that if they could be completely separated, the genitals would never have stuck to the belly in the first place. Look at the body: it is one continuous region. And just as the members are arranged, so the vices line up: the belly comes first, and immediately the rest are built up by lust. Gluttony is the gateway to lechery. I therefore recognize their animal faith for what it is — a life powered entirely by fleshly appetite, prone to both massive eating and serial marrying. Spiritual discipline, the rival of that substance, rightly indicts it on this front of self-control too, putting a bridle on gluttony by sometimes prescribing even dry or meager rations, just as it curbs lust by limiting marriage to a single union. I am fed up with engaging such people; I am ashamed even to argue with them, since their defense has no shame. How else can I defend chastity and sobriety without calling out their opponents? Let me name them once for all: the external and internal parasites of the Psychics.

They pick a fight with the Paraclete; that is why the new prophecies are rejected — not because Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla preach another God, or dissolve Jesus Christ, or overturn any rule of faith or hope, but because they plainly teach people to fast more often than to marry. We have already published a defense of monogamy on the manner of marrying. Now, regarding the discipline of diet, there is a second — or rather the first — battle of self-control. They accuse us because we keep our own fasts; because we often extend our fast-days until evening; because we also observe xerophagies, drying our food of all meat, all juice, and every moist fruit, so that we neither eat nor drink anything with a wine-like quality; and because we abstain from bathing, which suits a dry diet. So they reject the novelty, prescribing its illegitimacy, or they judge it a heresy if it is human presumption, or they denounce it as a false prophecy if it is a spiritual indictment — while we hear anathema from every side, simply because we proclaim it differently.

latin: Mirarer Psychicos si sola luxuria tenderentur, qua saepius nubunt; et non etiam ingluvie lacerarentur, qua jejunia oderunt, monstrum scilicet haberetur libido sine gula, cum duo haec tam unita atque concreta sint, ut si disjungi omnino potuissent, ipsi prius ventri pudenda non adhaererent. Specta corpus, et una regio est. Denique pro dispositione membrorum, ordo vitiorum; prior venter, et statim caetera saginae substructa lascivia est. Per edacitatem salacitas transit. Agnosco igitur animalem fidem studio carnis qua tota constat, tam multivorantiae quam multinubentiae pronam; ut merito spiritalem disciplinam pro substantia aemulam, in hac quoque specie continentiae accuset, proinde gulae frenos induentem per nullas interdum vel seras vel aridas escas, quemadmodum et libidini per unicas nuptias. Piget jam cum talibus congredi, pudet et jam de eis altercari, quorum nec defensio verecunda est. Quomodo enim protegam castitatem et sobrietatem sine taxatione adversariorum? Quinam isti sint semel nominabo exteriores et interiores botuli Psychicorum. Hi Paracleto controversiam faciunt; propter hoc novae prophetiae recusantur: non quod alium Deum praedicent Montanus et Priscilla et Maximilla, nec quod Jesum Christum solvant, nec quod aliquam fidei aut spei regulam evertant; sed quod plane doceant saepius jejunare, quam nubere. De modo quidem nubendi jam edidimus monogamiae defensionem. Nunc de castigatione victus, secunda, vel magis prima continentiae pugna est. Arguunt nos, quod jejunia propria custodiamus; quod stationes plerumque in vesperam producamus; quod etiam xerophagias observemus, siccantes cibum ab omni carne, et omni jurulentia, et uvidioribus quibusque pomis, ne quid vinositatis vel edamus vel potemus; lavacri quoque abstinentiam, congruentem arido victui. Novitatem igitur abjectant, de cujus inlicito praescribant, aut haeresim judicandam, si humana praesumptio est, aut pseudoprophetiam pronuntiandam, si spiritalis indictio est, dum quaqua ex parte anathema audiamus, qui aliter adnuntiamus.

excerpts.citation: Origen — On First Principles Translation from the Greek
excerpts.author: Origen
english: In the church's preaching one will hear the word concerning the just anointing of God, which — since it is believed to be true — also urges us to live well and to flee sin in every way, so that we may take up privately the most necessary problem: understanding what the self-moved is. We must unfold the notion of it so that, once it has been clearly explained, what is being sought may be precisely presented.

Of things that are moved, some have the cause of movement in themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried — such as wood, stones, and all matter held together only by habit — are moved only from outside. Let the notion that speaks of the movement of bodies be set aside for now, since it is not needed for what is proposed. But animals, plants, and in general all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of movement in themselves; from these they say metals also arise, and fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among things that have the cause of movement in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves. The inanimate are moved from outside themselves; the animate are moved from themselves. And animate things are moved from themselves when a fantasy arises and provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals fantasies arise that provoke impulse, as their imaginative nature moves the impulse in an orderly way — as in the spider, where the fantasy of weaving arises and an impulse follows to weave, its imaginative nature prompting it in an orderly way to that very thing, and the animal believes nothing else beyond its imaginative nature; and in the bee, toward making honeycomb.

But the rational animal also possesses reason alongside its imaginative nature, a reason that judges fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others so that the animal may be led according to them. Therefore, since in the nature of reason there are starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following which we contemplate the good and the bad, we choose the good and turn away from the bad. We are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. One must not be ignorant, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered to all things exists in animals, and for the most part or for the lesser part, so that it is near, so to speak, the work of the rational in tracking dogs and in war horses. That this or that external thing happens to us, provoking a fantasy in us, is admittedly not in our power; but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or another is the work of the reason within us — either by working in us according to the starting points that urge us toward the good and toward what is fitting, or by turning us away from the opposite.

If someone says that what is from outside is of such a kind that it is impossible to resist when it occurs in this way, let him examine his own passions and movements to see whether consent and sympathy and an inclination of the ruling part do not arise toward this or that thing through these persuasions. For it is not the case — to give an example — that the woman who appears and provokes and summons one to do something contrary to intention becomes the self-sufficient cause of abandoning intention; rather, having consented to the tickling and the smoothness of pleasure, and not having willed to resist or to confirm what had been anointed, one does the intemperate thing. But another person, to whom the same things have happened yet who has received more lessons and has been exercised — the ticklings and irritations happen to him as well, but reason, having been strengthened and nourished by practice and confirmed by doctrines toward the good, or having come near to being confirmed, has become steadfast.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On Jealousy and Envy On Jealousy and Envy
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: It seems like a light, minor offense to some of you, dear brothers, to be zealous for what is good and to envy those who are better. Because it is regarded as slight, no one fears it; because no one fears it, it is despised; and because it is despised, it is not easily avoided. It becomes a hidden, secret ruin that, precisely because it is barely noticed, escapes the prudent and secretly afflicts the careless. The Lord, however, commanded us to be prudent and to keep watch with careful concern, so that the adversary—always watching, always lying in wait—might not creep into our hearts and kindle fires from sparks, magnify great evils from small ones, and, while he flatters the lax and incautious with a gentle breeze and a softer breath, stir up storms and whirlwinds that threaten shipwreck of faith, salvation, and life. (1 Peter 5:8) Therefore, dear brothers, we must keep watch and strive with all our strength, so that with anxious, full vigilance we may resist the savage enemy who aims his darts at every part of the body by which we can be struck and wounded, just as the apostle Peter warns and teaches in his letter: 'Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' He circles each one of us, and like a hostile besieger he probes the walls, testing whether any section is less stable or less trustworthy, so that through that breach he may penetrate to the interior. He offers enticing forms and easy pleasures to the eyes, to destroy chastity by sight. He tempts the ears with melodious music, so that the hearing of a sweeter sound may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue with abuse; he incites the hand to violent murder through provoking injuries. To make a deceiver, he sets out unjust gains; to capture the soul with money, he brings in destructive shortcuts. He promises earthly honors, so that he may take away heavenly ones; he displays false things, so that he may steal the true. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens openly and plainly, brandishing the terror of turbulent persecution—always restless, always hostile toward God's servants, cunning in peace, violent in persecution. Consequently, dear brothers, a mind that is instructed and armed must stand against all the devil's deceitful snares and open threats, as prepared to resist as the enemy is always prepared to attack. Since his darts that creep in secretly are more frequent, and the more hidden and clandestine the assault, the less it is perceived and the more seriously and often it ravages our wounds, we must also be watchful to recognize and repel these attacks, which spring from the evil of zeal and envy. If anyone examines the matter thoroughly, he will find nothing a Christian must avoid more carefully, nothing he must guard against more cautiously, than being seized by envy and malice—lest someone, caught in the blind snares of the deceiving enemy, while brotherly zeal turns into hatred of a brother, perish unknowingly by his own sword. So that we may grasp this more fully and see it more clearly, let us go back to its head and origin. Let us see where zeal comes from, and when and how it began. For we will avoid this most pernicious evil more easily if we know both its origin and its magnitude. From the very beginning of the world, the devil perished first and was lost. He, supported by angelic majesty, he, accepted and dear to God, after he saw man made in God's image, broke out into malicious zeal and envious malice. He did not cast down another by the impulse of zeal before he himself was cast down by zeal; he was a captive before he took captive, lost before he caused loss. Goaded by envy, he tore away from man the gift of immortality, and he himself lost what he had been before. What an evil this is, dear brothers, by which an angel fell, by which that high and noble sublimity could be deceived and overthrown, by which the deceiver himself was deceived! From that time envy has raged on earth, while the one doomed to perish by envy serves the master of perdition, while he imitates the devil who envies, as it is written: 'But by the envy of the devil, death entered the world.' Therefore those who belong to his party imitate him.

latin: ZELARE quod bonum videas et invidere melioribus leve apud quosdam et modicum crimen videtur, fratres dilectissimi; dumque existimatur leve esse et modicum, non timetur; dum non timetur, contemnitur; dum contemnitur, non facile vitatur, et fit caeca et occulta pernicies: quae, dum minus perspicitur ut caveri a providentibus possit, improvidas mentes latenter affligit. Porro autem Dominus prudentes esse nos jussit, et cauta sollicitudine vigilare praecepit, ne adversarius vigilans semper et semper insidians, ubi in pectus obrepserit, de scintillis conflet incendia, de parvis maxima exaggeret, et, dum remissis et incautis leniore aura et flatu molliore blanditur, procellis ac turbinibus excitatis, ruinas fidei et salutis ac vitae naufragia moliatur. Excubandum est itaque, fratres dilectissimi, atque omnibus viribus elaborandum ut inimico saevienti et jacula sua in omnes corporis partes quibus percuti et vulnerari possumus, dirigenti sollicita et plena vigilantia repugnemus, secundum quod Petrus apostolus in Epistola sua praemonet et docet dicens: Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tamquam leo rugiens circuit, aliquem devorare quaerens. Circuit ille nos singulos, et tamquam hostis clausos obsidens, muros explorat, et tentat an sit pars aliqua murorum minus stabilis et minus fida, cujus aditu ad interiora penetretur. Offert oculis formas illices et faciles voluptates, ut visu destruat castitatem. Aures per canora musica tentat, ut soni dulcioris auditu solvat et molliat christianum vigorem. Linguam convicio provocat, manum injuriis lacessentibus ad petulantiam caedis instigat; ut fraudatorem faciat, lucra opponit injusta; ut animam pecunia capiat, ingerit perniciosa compendia; honores terrenos promittit, ut coelestes adimat; ostentat falsa, ut vera subripiat: et cum latenter non potest fallere, exerte atque aperte minatur, terrorem turbidae persecutionis intentans, ad debellandos Dei servos inquietus semper et semper infestus, in pace subdolus, in persecutione violentus. Quamobrem, fratres dilectissimi, contra omnes diaboli fallaces insidias vel apertas minas stare debet instructus animus et armatus, tam paratus semper ad repugnandum quam est ad impugnandum semper paratus inimicus. Et, quoniam frequentiora sunt tela ejus quae latenter obrepunt, magisque occulta et clandestina jaculatio quo minus perspicitur, hoc et gravius et crebrius in vulnera nostra grassatur, ad haec quoque intelligenda et depellenda vigilemus ex quibus est zeli et livoris malum. Quod si quis penitus inspiciat, inveniet nihil magis Christiano cavendum, nihil cautius providendum quam ne quis invidia et livore capiatur; ne quis fallentis inimici caecis laqueis implicatus, dum zelo frater in fratris odia convertitur, gladio suo nescius ipse perimatur. Quod ut colligere plenius et manifestius perspicere possimus, ad caput ejus atque originem recurramus. Videamus unde zelus, et quando et quomodo coeperit. Facilius enim a nobis malum tam perniciosum vitabitur, si ejusdem mali et origo et magnitudo noscatur. Hinc diabolus inter initia statim mundi et periit primus et perdidit. Ille angelica majestate subnixus, ille Deo acceptus et charus, postquam hominem ad imaginem Dei factum conspexit, in zelum malivolo livore prorupit, non prius alterum dejiciens instinctu zeli quam ipse zelo ante dejectus, captivus antequam capiens, perditus antequam perdens, dum, stimulante livore, homini gratiam datae immortalitatis eripit, ipse quoque id quod prius fuerat amisit. Quale malum est, fratres dilectissimi, quo angelus cecidit, quo circumveniri et subverti alta illa et praeclara sublimitas potuit, quo deceptus est ipse qui decepit! Exinde invidia grassatur in terris, dum livore periturus magistro perditionis obsequitur, dum diabolum qui zelat imitatur, sicut scriptum est: Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Imitantur ergo illum qui sunt ex parte ejus.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On the Advantage of Patience On the Advantage of Patience
excerpts.author: Cyprian
excerpts.work: Treatises — On the Advantage of Patience
english: I am about to speak on patience, dearest brothers, and to proclaim its advantages and benefits. Where better to begin than with the very patience that I see is necessary for your hearing right now, so that you may not even be able to do this thing that you hear and learn without patience? For only then is a sermon and a saving discourse effectively learned, if what is said is patiently heard. Nor do I find, dearest brothers, among the other ways of heavenly discipline by which our sect is directed toward the attainment of divinely bestowed rewards of hope and faith, anything more useful for life or greater for glory than that we, who lean on the Lord's precepts with the obedience of fear and devotion, should especially guard patience with all observance. Philosophers also profess to follow this virtue. But the patience there is just as false as the wisdom there is false. For how can anyone be wise or patient who knows neither the wisdom nor the patience of God? Since He Himself warns and says concerning those who seem to be wise in the world: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject" (1 Corinthians 1:19; Job 5:13). Also the blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form the Gentiles, testifies and instructs, saying: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ, for in Him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:8–9). And in another place: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, 'He catches the wise in their craftiness,' and again, 'The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile'" (1 Corinthians 3:18–20; Psalm 94:11). Therefore, if wisdom is not true there, true patience cannot exist there either. For if the wise man is he who is humble and gentle, we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but are pleased with themselves, and by this very fact that they please themselves they displease God. It is apparent that true patience is not there where there is the audacity of an affected freedom and the shameless boasting of an exerted and semi-nude breast. But we, dearest brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, and who prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting, who do not speak great things but live them, as servants and worshippers of God, let us offer the patience that we learn from heavenly teachings through spiritual obediences. For this virtue is common to us with God. From there patience begins; from there its clarity and dignity take their start. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as author. A thing is to be loved by man which is dear to God; the good that divine majesty loves, it commends. If the Lord is our master and God our Father, let us follow the patience of the Lord and of the Father alike: because it is fitting for servants to be obedient, and for sons not to be degenerate. But what kind and how great is the patience in God? He most patiently endures profane temples and earthly figments and sacrilegious rites instituted by men in contempt of His majesty and honor. Over the good and the evil alike He makes the day rise and the light of the sun shine, and with rains He waters the earth; no one is excluded from His benefits, so that He bestows indiscriminate rains on the just and on the unjust alike (Matthew 5:45)! We see, with an inseparable equality of patience, the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, those giving thanks and the ungrateful, all obeying God's nod as the times serve, the elements serving, the winds blowing, the fountains flowing, the crops of harvests growing, the fruits of vineyards ripening, the trees abounding with fruit, the groves leafing, the meadows flowering. And although God is provoked by frequent, indeed continuous, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently awaits the predetermined day of retribution. And although He has vengeance in His power, He prefers to hold patience for a long time, sustaining and deferring, so that, if it can be, prolonged wickedness may sometime be changed, and man, having been rolled in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late, God Himself warning and saying: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11). And again: "Return to me, says the Lord." And again: "Return to the Lord your God, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and relents over disaster" (Joel 2:13). The blessed apostle Paul also commemorates this, recalling the sinner to repentance, and proposes and says: "Or do you presume on the riches of His kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works" (Romans 2:4–6). He said that the judgment of God is just because it is late, because it is deferred for a long time, so that by the long patience of God man may be provided for a long life. Then punishment is represented to the impious and the sinner when repentance can no longer benefit the sin.

latin: DE patientia locuturus, fratres dilectissimi, et utilitates ejus et commoda praedicaturus, unde potius incipiam quam quod nunc quoque ad audientiam vestram patientiam video esse necessariam, ut nec hoc ipsum quod auditis et discitis, sine patientia facere possitis. Tunc enim demum sermo et ratio salutaris efficaciter discitur, si patienter quod dicitur audiatur. Nec invenio, fratres dilectissimi, inter caeteras coelestis disciplinae vias quibus ad consequenda divinitus praemia spei ac fidei nostrae secta dirigitur, quid magis sit vel utilius ad vitam vel majus ad gloriam, quam ut qui praeceptis dominicis obsequio timoris ac devotionis innitimur, patientiam maxime tota observatione tueamur. Hanc se sectari philosophi quoque profitentur. Sed tam illic patientia falsa est, quam et falsa sapientia est. Unde enim vel sapiens esse vel patiens possit qui nec sapientiam nec patientiam Dei novit? quando ipse de his qui sibi sapere in mundo videntur moneat et dicat: Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Item beatus apostolus Paulus, plenus Spiritu sancto et vocandis formandisque Gentibus missus, contestetur et instruat dicens: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, et non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Et alio loco: Nemo se, inquit, decipiat. Si quis se putat sapientem esse in vobis, mundo huic stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi hujus stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Reprehendam sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et iterum: Cognovit Dominus cogitationes sapientium, quia sunt stultae. Quare, si sapientia illic vera non est, esse non potest et vera patientia. Nam si sapiens ille est qui est humilis et mitis, philosophos autem nec humiles videmus esse nec mites, sed sibi multum placentes, et hoc ipso quod sibi placeant Deo displicentes, apparet illic veram non esse patientiam ubi sit insolens affectatae libertatis audacia et exerti ac seminudi pectoris inverecunda jactantia. Nos autem, fratres dilectissimi, qui philosophi non verbis sed factis sumus, nec vestitu sapientiam, sed veritate praeferimus, qui virtutum conscientiam magis quam jactantiam novimus, qui non loquimur magna sed vivimus, quasi servi et cultores Dei, patientiam quam magisteriis coelestibus discimus obsequiis spiritalibus praebeamus. Est enim nobis cum Deo virtus ista communis. Inde patientia incipit, inde claritas ejus et dignitas caput sumit. Origo et magnitudo patientiae Deo auctore procedit. Diligenda res homini quae Deo chara est: bonum quod amat majestas divina commendat. Si dominus nobis et pater Deus est, sectemur patientiam domini pariter et patris: quia et servos oportet esse obsequentes, et filios non decet esse degeneres. Qualis vero in Deo et quanta patientia, quod, in contumeliam suae majestatis et honoris instituta ab hominibus profana templa et terrena figmenta et sacra sacrilega patientissime sustinens, super bonos et malos aequaliter facit diem nasci et lumen solis oboriri, et cum imbribus terras rigat, nemo a beneficiis ejus excluditur quominus justis similiter et injustis indiscretas pluvias largiatur! Videmus inseparabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus et innoxiis, religiosis et impiis, gratias agentibus et ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, fructus maturescere vinearum, exuberare pomis arbusta, nemora frondescere, prata florere. Et cum crebris immo continuis exacerbetur offensis Deus, indignationem suam temperat, et praestitutum semel retributionis diem patienter exspectat. Cumque habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens scilicet clementer et differens, ut, si fieri potest, multum malitia protracta aliquando mutetur, et homo in errorum et scelerum contagione volutatus vel sero ad Deum convertatur, ipso monente et dicente: Nolo mortem morientis, quantum ut revertatur et vivat. Et iterum: Revertimini ad me, dicit Dominus. Et iterum: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quoniam misericors et pius et patiens et multae miserationis, et qui sententiam flectat adversus malitias irrogatas. Quod item beatus apostolus Paulus commemorans et peccatorem ad poenitentiam revocans, proponit et dicit: An numquid opulentiam bonitatis ejus et sustinentiam et patientiam contemnis, ignorans quoniam patientia et bonitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem, secundum duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. Justum judicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multumque differtur, ut homini ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Tunc repraesentatur poena impio et peccatori, quando jam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccati.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On the Lord's Prayer On the Lord's Prayer
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: The commands of the Gospel, my dearest brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings: foundations on which to build hope, reinforcements that strengthen faith, nourishment that fosters the heart, guides that direct our journey, and defenses that secure salvation. By instructing the minds of believers here on earth, they lead us to the heavenly kingdom.

God chose to speak and be heard many times through his servants the Prophets, but the words of the Son are far greater. The Word of God, who was present in the Prophets, now testifies with his own voice. He no longer commands that a way be prepared for the one who is coming; he himself comes, opening and showing us the way. We once wandered in the darkness of death, ignorant and blind, but now, illuminated by the light of grace, we hold to the path of life with the Lord as our guide and director.

Among his other salutary admonitions and divine precepts given for the salvation of his people, he also gave us the very form of prayer himself, instructing us what to ask for. The One who gave us life taught us to pray, out of the same kindness by which he deigned to give us everything else, so that when we speak to the Father with the prayer the Son taught us, we may be heard more easily.

He had already foretold that the hour was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and in truth, and he fulfilled that promise. We who have received the Spirit and the truth from his sanctification can now worship him truly and spiritually, following his own tradition. What prayer could be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What prayer could be more true before the Father than the one spoken from the mouth of the Son, who is the Truth? Therefore, to pray in any other way than he taught is not merely ignorance; it is guilt. As he himself said: "You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition."

So let us pray, my dearest brothers, just as God our Master taught us. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what belongs to him, letting Christ's prayer carry our words to the Father's ears. When we pray, may the Father recognize the words of his Son. May the One who dwells within our breast also dwell in our voice. Since we have him as our Advocate with the Father for our sins, let us sinners, when we ask forgiveness for our offenses, speak the very words of our Advocate. He said that whatever we ask the Father in his name he will give us; how much more effectively, then, do we obtain what we seek in Christ's name if we ask using his own prayer?

Yet our speech and prayer must be marked by discipline, characterized by quiet and modesty. Let us remember that we stand before the eyes of God. We must please his divine gaze with both our bodily posture and the manner of our voice. Just as it is shameless to cry out with loud shouts, so it is fitting for the reverent to pray with modest prayers.

Finally, the Lord commanded us to pray in secret—in hidden and remote places, in our own rooms—because this best suits our faith. It teaches us that God is present everywhere, hears everything, and sees everything, and that the fullness of his majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places. As Scripture says: "I am a God who is near, and not a God who is far away. If a man hides in hidden places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" And again: "The eyes of the Lord watch over both the good and the evil in every place."

When we gather together with our brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we must remain mindful of modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers with uncontrolled voices, nor commend our petitions to God with tumultuous, loquacious speech, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. He does not need to be reminded by loud cries, for he sees the thoughts of men. The Lord himself proves this when he says: "Why do you think evil in your hearts?" And elsewhere: "All the churches will know that I am the one who searches the kidneys and the heart."

latin: EVANGELICA praecepta, fratres dilectissimi, nihil aliud sunt quam magisteria divina, fundamenta aedificandae spei, firmamenta corroborandae fidei, nutrimenta fovendi cordis, gubernacula dirigendi itineris, praesidia obtinendae salutis; quae, dum dociles credentium mentes in terris instruunt, ad coelestia regna perducunt. Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione? Sit autem orantibus sermo et precatio cum disciplina, quietem continens et pudorem. Cogitemus nos sub conspectu Dei stare. Placendum est divinis oculis et habitu corporis et modo vocis. Nam, ut impudentis est clamoribus strepere, ita contra congruit verecundo modestis precibus orare. Denique magisterio suo Dominus secreto orare nos praecepit, in abditis et semotis locis, in cubiculis ipsis, quod magis convenit fidei; ut sciamus Deum ubique esse praesentem, audire omnes et videre, et majestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quoque et occulta penetrare, sicut scriptum est: Ego Deus approximans, et non Deus de longinquo. Si absconditus fuerit homo in absconditis, ego ergo non videbo eum? Nonne coelum et terram ego impleo? Et iterum: In omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos. Et quando in unum cum fratribus convenimus, et sacrificia divina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus, verecundiae et disciplinae memores esse debemus, non passim ventilare preces nostras inconditis vocibus, nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosa loquacitate jactare, quia Deus non vocis sed cordis auditor est. Nec admonendus est clamoribus qui cogitationes hominum videt, probante Domino et dicente: Quid cogitatis nequam in cordibus vestris? Et alio loco: Et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis.

excerpts.locus: On the Unity of the Church
english:
When the Lord warns us, "You are the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13), and commands us to be innocent as doves yet wise as serpents, what else should we do, beloved brothers, than watch with anxious hearts — understanding and guarding against the cunning enemy's plots — so that we who have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, do not appear less wise in guarding our salvation? We must fear not only open persecution that attacks God's servants to overthrow them; caution is easy when danger is plain, and the mind readies for battle when the adversary shows himself. The enemy is far more dangerous when he creeps in stealthily, disguising himself as peace and slipping in by hidden approaches — which is why he is called the serpent. This has always been his cunning: the blind, hidden deceit of circumventing humanity. From the world's beginning he deceived, flattering with lies and trapping unsuspecting souls. He even tried to tempt the Lord Himself, approaching stealthily as if to deceive again; but he was recognized, repulsed, and cast down. From this we have an example: flee the way of the old man, follow in the footsteps of the living Christ, lest we incautiously fall again into death's snare, but rather, foreseeing danger, lay hold of immortality. And how can we possess immortality unless we keep Christ's commandments, by which death is overcome and conquered — He Himself warning, "If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments" (Matt 19:17), and again, "If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends" (John 15:14)? These He calls strong and stable, founded on solid rock, made firm with immovable strength against every storm and whirlwind of the world. "Everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock" (Matt 7:24–25). Therefore we must stand firm on His words, learning and doing all He taught and commanded. How can anyone believe he is in Christ if he does not do what Christ commanded? How will he reach the reward of faith who refuses to keep the faith of the commandment? He must waver and wander, seized by the spirit of error, blown like dust before the wind; he will not advance toward salvation who does not hold the truth of the way of life. 

Beloved brothers, we must beware not only of open and manifest dangers, but also of the subtle deceit of cunning fraud. What could be more cunning or subtle than this: the enemy, detected and cast down by Christ's advent, after light came to the Gentiles and the saving light shone so that the deaf might hear spiritual grace, the blind open their eyes to God, the weak recover by eternal health, the lame run to the Church, the mute pray with clear voices — seeing idols abandoned and his own seats and temples deserted by the multitude of believers — he devises a new fraud, to deceive the incautious under the very title of the Christian name? He invents heresies and schisms to subvert faith, corrupt truth, and divide unity. Those he cannot hold in the blindness of the old way, he encircles and deceives by the error of a new way. He snatches men from the Church itself; and while they think they have approached the light and escaped the world's night, he pours fresh darkness over them, unknown to them, so that — not standing with Christ's Gospel, His observance, and His law — they call themselves Christians, and walking in darkness think they have the light. The adversary flatters and deceives, transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14) and his ministers into ministers of righteousness, calling night day, destruction salvation, despair hope, perfidy faith, antichrist Christ — so that by speaking plausibly they frustrate the truth through subtlety. This happens, beloved brothers, because we do not return to the origin of truth, nor seek the Head, nor preserve the heavenly Master's doctrine. If anyone considers and examines this, no long discussion or argument is needed; the proof is easy for faith by the compendium of truth. 

The Lord speaks to Peter: "I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matt 16:18–19). And again after His resurrection He says to him: "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17). He builds His Church on him alone, and entrusts His sheep to him. Although He gives equal power to all the Apostles after His resurrection — "As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained" (John 20:21–23) — yet, to manifest unity, He establishes one chair, and by His authority disposes the origin of unity to proceed from one. The other Apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with equal partnership in honor and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, and primacy is given to Peter, so that one Church of Christ and one chair may be shown. All are shepherds, and one flock is shown, fed by all the Apostles with unanimous consent, that the one Church of Christ may be shown. The Holy Spirit also designates this one Church in the Song of Songs, saying in the person of the Lord: "One is my dove, my perfect one, the only one of her mother, chosen of her who bore her" (Song 6:9). Who does not hold this unity of the Church, yet believes he holds the faith? Who resists and opposes the Church, who deserts the chair of Peter on which the Church is founded — does he trust that he is in the Church? The blessed Apostle Paul teaches this same thing and shows the sacrament of unity, saying: "One body and one Spirit, one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God" (Eph 4:4–6).

latin: CUM moneat Dominus et dicat: Vos estis sal terrae, cumque esse nos jubeat ad innocentiam simplices, et tamen cum simplicitate prudentes, quid aliud, fratres dilectissimi, quam providere nos convenit, et sollicito corde vigilantes, subdoli hostis insidias intelligere pariter et cavere ne qui Christum sapientiam Dei Patris induimus, minus sapere in tuenda salute videamur? Neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est et ea quae subruendis ac dejiciendis Dei servis aperta impugnatione grassantur. Facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est, et ad certamen animus ante praestruitur quando se adversarius confitetur. Plus metuendus est et cavendus inimicus cum latenter obrepit, cum, per pacis imaginem fallens, occultis accessibus serpit; unde et nomen serpentis accepit. Ea est ejus semper astutia, ea est circumveniendi hominis caeca et latebrosa fallacia. Sic ab initio statim mundi fefellit, et, verbis mendacibus blandiens, rudes animas incauta credulitate decepit. Dominum ipsum tentare conatus, quasi obreperet rursus et falleret, latenter accessit. Intellectus tamen est et retusus; et ideo prostratus, quia agnitus atque detectus. Unde nobis exemplum datum est veteris hominis viam fugere, vestigiis Christi viventis insistere; ne denuo incauti in mortis laqueum revolvamur, sed, ad periculum providi, accepta immortalitate potiamur. Immortalitate autem potiri quomodo possumus, nisi ea quibus mors expugnatur et vincitur, Christi mandata servemus, ipso monente et dicente: Si vis ad vitam venire, serva mandata. Et iterum: Si feceritis quae mando vobis, jam non dico vos servos, sed amicos. Hos denique fortes dicit et stabiles, hos super petram robusta mole fundatos, hos contra omnes tempestates et turbines saeculi immobili et inconcussa firmitate solidatos. Qui audit, inquit, verba mea et facit ea, similabo eum viro sapienti qui aedificavit domum suam supra petram. Descendit pluvia, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti et impegerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit; fundata enim fuit super petram. Verbis igitur ejus insistere, quaecumque et docuit et fecit discere et facere debemus. Caeterum credere se in Christum, quomodo dicit qui non facit quod Christus facere praecepit? Aut unde perveniet ad praemium fidei, qui fidem non vult servare mandati? Nutet necesse est et vagetur, et, spiritu erroris abreptus, velut pulvis quem ventus excutit ventiletur; nec ambulando proficiet ad salutem, qui salutaris viae non tenet veritatem. Cavenda sunt autem, fratres dilectissimi, non solum quae sunt aperta atque manifesta, sed et astutae fraudis subtilitate fallentia. Quid vero astutius, quidve subtilius, quam ut Christi adventu detectus ac prostratus inimicus, postquam lux Gentibus venit et sospitandis hominibus salutare lumen effulsit, ut surdi auditum gratiae spiritalis admitterent, aperirent ad Deum oculos suos caeci, infirmi aeterna sanitate revalescerent, claudi ad Ecclesiam currerent, muti claris vocibus et precibus orarent, videns ille idola derelicta et per nimium credentium populum sedes suas ac templa deserta, excogitaverit novam fraudem, ut sub ipso christiani nominis titulo fallat incautos? Haereses invenit et schismata, quibus subverteret fidem, veritatem corrumperet, scinderet unitatem. Quos detinere non potest in viae veteris caecitate, circumscribit et decipit novi itineris errore. Rapit de ipsa Ecclesia homines; et, dum sibi appropinquasse jam lumini atque evasisse saeculi noctem videntur, alias nescientibus tenebras rursus infundit, ut cum Evangelio Christi et cum observatione ejus et lege non stantes, Christianos se vocent, et ambulantes in tenebris habere se lumen existiment, blandiente adversario atque fallente, qui, secundum Apostoli vocem, transfigurat se velut angelum lucis, et ministros suos subornat velut ministros justitiae, asserentes noctem pro die, interitum pro salute, desperationem sub obtentu spei, perfidiam sub praetextu fidei, antichristum sub vocabulo Christi; ut, dum verisimilia mentiuntur, veritatem subtilitate frustrentur. Hoc eo fit, fratres dilectissimi, dum ad veritatis originem non reditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri coelestis doctrina servatur. Quae si quis consideret et examinet, tractatu longo atque argumentis opus non est. Probatio est ad fidem facilis compendio veritatis. Loquitur Dominus ad Petrum: Ego tibi dico, inquit, quia tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portae inferorum non vincent eam. Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum: et quae ligaveris super terram, erunt ligata et in coelis; et quaecumque solveris super terram, erunt soluta et in coelis. Et iterum eidem post resurrectionem suam dicit: Pasce oves meas. Super illum unum aedificat Ecclesiam suam, et illi pascendas mandat oves suas. Et quamvis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuat et dicat, Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos: accipite Spiritum sanctum; si cujus remiseritis peccata, remittentur illi, si cujus tenueritis, tenebuntur, tamen, ut unitatem manifestaret, unam cathedram constituit, unitatis ejusdem originem ab uno incipientem sua auctoritate disposuit. Hoc erant utique et caeteri Apostoli quod fuit Petrus, pari consortio praediti et honoris et potestatis, sed exordium ab unitate proficiscitur, et primatus Petro datur, ut una Christi Ecclesia et cathedra una monstretur. Et pastores sunt omnes, et grex unus ostenditur, qui ab Apostolis omnibus unanimi consensione pascatur, ut Ecclesia Christi una monstretur. Quam unam Ecclesiam etiam in Cantico canticorum Spiritus sanctus ex persona Domini designat et dicit: Una est columba mea, perfecta mea, una est matri suae, electa genitrici suae. Hanc Ecclesiae unitiatem qui non tenet, tenere se fidem credit? Qui Ecclesiae renititur et resistit, qui cathedram Petri, super quem fundata est Ecclesia, deserit, in Ecclesia se esse confidit? quando et beatus apostolus Paulus hoc idem doceat et sacramentum unitatis ostendat dicens: Unum corpus et unus spiritus, una spes vocationis vestrae, unus Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma, unus Deus.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Humanity must be preserved if we wish to be called human beings in the true sense. And what is preserving humanity but loving a human being because he is a human being, the same as we are? Discord and division, therefore, are not in keeping with human reason; the saying of Cicero stands true: a person who obeys nature cannot harm another person. Since harming a human being is contrary to nature, benefiting a human being must necessarily accord with nature. Anyone who fails to do so strips himself of the very name 'human,' for the duty of humanity is to come to the aid of a person in need and danger. I put this question to those who claim that being moved to pity is not the mark of the wise: if a man seized by a wild beast begs an armed man for help, do they think he ought to be rescued, or not? They are not so shameless as to deny that what humanity demands and requires must be done. Likewise, if someone is encircled by fire, crushed by a collapsing building, drowning in the sea, or swept away by a river, do they imagine it is not a man's duty to help? Let them not call themselves human if they think so — for no one can escape such dangers — but rather they will acknowledge it is the part of a human being, and of a brave man, to save one who is perishing. Since they concede that in such cases, because they threaten human life, it is humanity's duty to come to the rescue, what reason can there be for refusing to help when a man is hungry, thirsty, or cold? These conditions are equal in nature to those sudden disasters and call for the same single humanity; yet they make a distinction between them, because they measure everything not by the truth of the matter itself but by present utility. They hope that those they snatch from danger will repay them with gratitude, but they reckon that the needy — since they hold out no hope of return — will simply perish, and they consider whatever they give to such people as lost.

latin: Conseruanda est igitur humanitas, si homines recte dici uelimus. id autem ipsum, conseruare humanitatem, quid aliut est quam diligere hominem, quia homo sit et idem quod nos sumus? -discordia igitur ac dissensio non est secundum hominis rationem uerumque illut est Ciceronis, quod ait hominem naturae oboedientem homini nocere non posse. ergo si nocere homini contra naturam est, prodesse igitur homini secundum naturam sit necesse est. quod qui non facit, hominis se appellatione despoliat, quia humanitatis officium est necessitati hominis ac periculo subuenire. quaero igitur ab iis qui flecti et misereri non putant esse sapientis, si homo ab aliqua bestia conprehensus auxilium sibi armati hominis inploret, utrumne succurrendum putent an minime. non sunt tam inpudentes, ut negent fieri oportere quod flagitat, quod exposcit humanitas. item, si aliquis circumueniatur igni, ruina opprimatur, mergatur mari, flumine rapiatur, num putent hominis esse non auxiliari. non sint ipsi homines, si putent — nemo enim potest eiusmodi periculis non esse subiectus —, immo uero et hominis et fortis uiri esse dicent seruare periturum. si ergo in eiusmodi casibus, quia periculum uitae homini adferunt, succurrere humanitatis esse concedunt, quid causae est cur, si homo esuriat sitiat algeat, succurrendum esse non putent? quae cum sint paria natura cum illis casibus fortuitis et unam eandemque humanitatem desiderent, tamen illa discernunt, quia non re ipsa uera, sed utilitate praesenti omnia metiuntur. illos enim quos periculo subripiunt sperant sibi gratiam relaturos, egentes autem quia non sperant, perire arbitrantur quidquid eiusmodi hominibus inpertiant.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Two paths lie before us in human life, one that carries us to heaven, another that presses us down to the lower world, and both poets in their songs and philosophers in their treatises have set them forth.

The philosophers, for their part, designated one path for virtue and the other for vice, assigning the steep and rugged first approach to virtue; if someone overcomes that initial difficulty and gains the summit, the way thereafter becomes level, a bright and pleasant field where he reaps rich and delightful fruits from all his labors, but those whom the first steepness deters slip aside into the path of vice, which at its entrance appears pleasant and well‑trodden, yet once they have gone a little farther the pleasantness is suddenly withdrawn and a precipitous way arises, now rough with rocks, now blocked with thorns, now cut off by whirlpools or rapid torrents, so that to toil, to stick, to slip, and to fall becomes inevitable.

All this is set forth to show that the pursuit of virtue entails the greatest labors, but once virtue is attained it yields the greatest fruits and solid, uncorrupted pleasures, while vice allures men's minds with natural enticements and leads those captured by the show of empty pleasures into bitter hardships and miseries.

It would be a wise discussion if the philosophers had known the true forms and boundaries of the virtues themselves, for they had not learned what the virtues are or what reward from God awaits them, and that is what we shall teach in these two books.

Because they were ignorant or doubted that human souls are immortal, they measured virtues and vices by earthly honors or punishments, and so their whole discourse on the two paths looks only to frugality and luxury.

They liken the course of human life to the letter Y: each person, upon reaching the threshold of early youth and arriving at the place where the way divides in two, stands hesitant, not knowing which branch to take; if he finds a guide who directs his stumbling steps toward better things — that is, if he learns philosophy or eloquence or some honorable art by which he may escape to good fruit, which cannot happen without the greatest labor — they say he will lead an honorable and abundant life; but if he lacks a teacher of frugality, he falls into the left‑hand path that pretends to be better, surrendering himself to idleness, inertia, and luxury, which seem sweet for a time to one ignorant of true goods, yet after he has lost all dignity and property he will live in every misery and ignominy.

Thus they referred the boundaries of those paths to the body and to this earthly life; the poets perhaps did better by placing the fork in the lower world, yet they erred in proposing those paths to the dead.
Both, therefore, are true in a sense, yet both are not correct, because the paths themselves ought to be referred to life, their boundaries to death.

We, therefore, speak better and more truly when we say that those two paths are the paths of heaven and the lower world, because immortality is set before the just and eternal punishment before the unjust.

How these paths either raise to heaven or precipitate to the lower world I will explain, and I will reveal the virtues which the philosophers did not know; then I will show the rewards of those virtues, and at the same time the vices and their punishments.

Perhaps someone expects me to treat vices and virtues separately, but when we discuss good or evil the contrary can also be understood: without virtues vices depart of their own accord, or if you remove vices virtues come of their own accord; the nature of good and evil is so constituted that they always fight against each other and always expel each other, so that vices cannot be removed without virtues nor virtues introduced without the removal of vices.

We therefore introduce these paths in a far different way than the philosophers do: first, we say that a leader is set over each, both immortal, but one honored, who presides over virtues and goods, the other condemned, who presides over vices and evils; the philosophers place a leader only on the right‑hand path, and not a single or perpetual one, since they bring in any teacher of a good art who recalls men from laziness and teaches them frugality, and they admit no one to that path except boys and young men, evidently because arts are learned at those ages.
We, however, lead into this heavenly path all people of every sex, kind, and age, because God, who is the leader of that path, denies immortality to no human being born.

The very form of the paths is not as they imagined: what need is there of the letter Y in things that are contrary and diverse? Rather, the better path turns toward the sunrise, the worse toward the sunset, because he who follows truth and justice, having received the reward of immortality, will possess eternal light, while he who, allured by that evil leader, prefers vices to virtues and falsehood to truth, must be carried away to the setting and to darkness eternal.
I will therefore describe each path and show their properties and habits.
