excerpts.citation: Tertullian — To His Wife Book II
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Dearest fellow servant in the Lord, I have already laid out as best I could what a holy woman must pursue when marriage has been taken from her, no matter the circumstances. Now we must turn to a second line of counsel, prompted by human weakness and the warning example of certain women. They were given the chance for continence through divorce or a husband's death, yet they not only threw away that great good but also refused to remember the discipline even when remarrying, so that they would marry in the Lord above all (1 Corinthians 7:8). My mind is in turmoil: I who recently urged you to persevere as a one-man woman and a widow may now, by merely mentioning marriage, make it easier for you to slip from higher things. But if you are truly wise, you know you must hold to what is more useful for you. What is difficult, and not without necessities, is also this greatest proposal for the supreme safeguard of life. I would not have brought this up again unless I grasped the gravity of my concern. For as great as the continence of the flesh that serves widowhood is, its failure can seem excusable; difficult things win easy pardon. But to the extent that marrying in the Lord lies within our power, it is all the more culpable not to observe what you can. Add to this that the Apostle advises widows and the unmarried to remain as they are, saying: "I wish all to persevere according to my example" (1 Corinthians 7:8).

latin: Proxime tibi, dilectissima in domino conserva, quid foeminae sanctae, matrimonio quacunque sorte adempto, sectandum sit, ut potui prosecutus sum. Nunc ad secunda consilia convertamur, respectu humanae infirmitatis, quarumdam exemplis admonentibus, quae divortio vel mariti excessu, oblata continentiae occasione, non modo abjecerunt opportunitatem tanti boni, sed ne in nubendo quidem rursum disciplinae meminisse voluerunt, ut in Domino potissimum nuberent. Itaque mihi confusus est animus, ne qui nuper te ad univiratus et viduitatis perseverantiam hortatus sum, nunc mentione nuptiarum, proclivium tibi labendi ab altioribus faciam. Quod si integre sapis, certe scis id servandum tibi esse, quod sit utilius. Quod vero difficile est, et non sine necessitatibus et hoc maximum propositum vitae supremi praesidii. Nec mihi de isto quoque referendi ad te caussae fuissent, nisi graviorem meam sollicitudinem comprehendissem. Nam quanto grandis est continentia carnis, quae viduitatem ministrat, tanto, si non sustineatur, ignoscibilis videri potest; difficilium enim facilis est venia. Quanto autem nubere in Domino perpetrabile est, uti nostrae potestatis, tanto culpabilius est non observare quod possis. Eo accedit quod Apostolus de viduis quidem et innuptis, ut ita permaneant, suadet, cum dicit: Cupio autem omnes meo exemplo perseverare.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Apparel of Women Book I
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If the faith on earth matched the reward expected in heaven, not one of you, beloved sisters, would have wanted a more joyful — let alone glorious — appearance after knowing the living God and learning your own condition as women. You would rather have chosen filth and squalor, dragging around a mourning, repentant Eve, so as to fully atone for what you inherited from her: the ignominy of the first sin and the envy of human perdition. "In pain and anxiety you will bear children, woman, and your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" (Genesis 3:16). Do you not know you are Eve? God's sentence still stands over this sex in this age, and the guilt must remain. You are the devil's gateway, the one who unsealed that tree, the first deserter of divine law, the one who persuaded the man the devil could not attack. You so easily destroyed God's image, man; because of your merit — death — even the Son of God had to die. And you still think to adorn yourself beyond your woolen tunics? Come now: even if from the beginning the Milesians sheared sheep, the Seres wove silk, the Tyrians dyed, the Phrygians sewed, the Babylonians embroidered, pearls gleamed and corals sparkled, gold itself came up from the earth with desire, and mirrors were allowed to lie — Eve, expelled from paradise and already dead, would have craved these things, I think. So she should neither desire nor know them now, if she wants to live again, since she neither had nor knew them when she was alive. All these things are the impediments of a condemned, dead woman, set up like funeral pomp. Those who invented them are likewise sentenced to death: the angels who plunged from heaven to the daughters of men, adding this disgrace to women. They revealed hidden materials and obscure arts to an ignorant world — metalworking, herbal lore, incantations, even astrology — and specifically gave women the tools of female vanity: gemstones for necklaces, gold bands for arms, dyes for wool, black powder to outline the eyes. The quality of these things is already declared by the character of their teachers: they offered nothing for integrity, nothing for chastity, nothing for the fear of God — only for sinners, lovers, deserters of the Spirit. If these are teachings, evil teachers taught evil. If they are rewards for lust, no shameful reward is honorable. What was the point of displaying these things as gifts? Could women not please men without splendor and artifice — the same crude, unrefined women who moved angels? Or would the angels have seemed sordid, insulting lovers, if they gave nothing to the women they seduced into marriage? But that calculation fails: they could desire nothing more, since they possessed angels and had married in high style. Indeed, those angels who sometimes remembered their fall and sighed for heaven after their fleeting lust rewarded women's natural beauty — the very cause of evil — so that their own happiness would not benefit them, but they would be dragged down from simplicity and sincerity into offense against God. They knew full well that all glory, ambition, and affectation of pleasing God through the flesh displeases God. These are the angels we will judge; these are the angels we renounce in baptism; these are the things by which they deserved to be judged by men. What will their gifts do before their judges? What commerce can the damned have with the damned? I say it is like Christ and Belial. With what consistency do we ascend that tribunal to condemn those whose gifts we crave? The same angelic substance is promised to you, the same sex as men, the same dignity of judging — unless we have already prejudged the matter here by condemning their things, which we will later damn in them; then they will judge and condemn us. I know the Book of Enoch, which assigned this order to angels, is rejected by some because it is not in the Jewish canon. They think it could not have survived the flood, the destroyer of all things. If so, let them remember Noah, Enoch's great-grandson, survived the flood and heard by family tradition of his ancestor's favor with God and all his prophecies; Enoch charged his son Methuselah to pass this knowledge down. Noah could certainly have succeeded in his preaching mission, since he spoke of God who preserved him and of his own house's glory. Even if that record was lost, the flood's violence could not destroy what the Spirit can reform — just as Ezra restored all Jewish literature after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem. Since Enoch also prophesied the Lord in that same scripture, we reject nothing that pertains to us. We read that all Scripture is divinely inspired for edification. The Jews reject it for the same reason they reject nearly everything that speaks of Christ — no surprise, since they would not receive him speaking in person. Moreover, Enoch has the testimony of the apostle Jude. Let no mark of condemnation stain female pomp because of its authors' fate. Charge those angels only with rejecting heaven and marrying flesh. Let us examine the things themselves, to uncover the desires behind them. A woman's appearance has two forms: cultivation and ornament. Cultivation is what they call the worldly woman — gold, silver, gems, clothing. Ornament is what befits the impure woman — care of hair, skin, and those body parts that draw the eye. We charge the first with ambition, the second with prostitution. So look ahead, handmaid of God, and see which of these suits your discipline, you who are judged by a different standard: humility and chastity.

latin: Si tanta in terris moraretur fides, quanta merces ejus exspectatur in coelis, nulla omnino vestrum, sorores dilectissimae, ex quo Deum vivum cognovisset, et de sua, id est de foeminae conditione didicisset, laetiorem habitum, ne dicam gloriosiorem appetiisset, ut non magis in sordibus ageret, et squalorem potius affectaret, ipsam se circumferens Evam lugentem et poenitentem; quo plenius id quod de Eva trahit (ignominiam dico primi delicti, et invidiam perditionis humanae) omni satisfactionis habitu expiaret. In doloribus et anxietatibus paries, mulier, et ad virum tuum conversio tua; et ille dominabitur tui; et Evam te esse nescis? Vivit sententia Dei super sexum istum, in hoc saeculo: vivat et reatus necesse est. Tu es diaboli janua, tu es arboris illius resignatrix, tu es divinae legis prima desertrix, tu es quae eum persuasisti, quem diabolus aggredi non valuit. Tu imaginem Dei, hominem, tam facile elisisti: propter tuum meritum, id est mortem, etiam Filius Dei mori habuit; et adornari tibi in mente est super pelliceas tuas tunicas? Age nunc, si ab initio rerum et Milesii oves tonderent, et Seres arbores nerent, et Tyrii tinguerent, et Phryges insuerent, et Babylonii intexerent, et margaritae canderent et ceraunia coruscarent, si ipsum quoque aurum jam de terra cum cupiditate prodisset; si jam et speculo tantum mentiri liceret: et haec Eva concupisset de paradiso expulsa, jam mortua, opinor. Ergo nec nunc appetere debet, aut nosse, si cupit reviviscere, quae nec habuerat, nec noverat, quando vivebat. Ideo omnia ista damnatae et mortuae mulieris impedimenta sunt, quasi ad pompam funeris constituta. Nam et illi qui ea constituerunt, damnati in poenam mortis deputantur: illi scilicet angeli, qui ad filias hominum de coelo ruerunt, ut haec quoque ignominia foeminae accedat. Nam cum et materias quasdam bene occultas, et artes plerasque non bene revelatas, saeculo multo magis imperito prodidissent (siquidem et metallorum opera nudaverant, et herbarum ingenia traduxerant, et incantationum vires provulgaverant, et omnem curiositatem, usque ad stellarum interpretationem, designaverant) proprie et quasi peculiariter foeminis instrumentum istud muliebris gloriae contulerunt: lumina lapillorum quibus monilia variantur: et circulos ex auro, quibus brachia arctantur: et medicamenta ex fuco, quibus lanae colorantur: et illum ipsum nigrum pulverem, quo oculorum exordia producuntur. Haec qualia sint, interim jam ex doctorum suorum qualitate et conditione pronuntiari potest, quod nihil ad integritatem peccatores, nihil ad castitatem adamatores, nihil ad timorem Dei desertores spiritus, aut monstrare potuerunt aut praestare. Si doctrinae dicendae sunt, mali magistri male docuerint necesse est. Si mercedes pro libidine, nullius rei turpis merces decora est. Quid autem tanti fuit ista monstrare sicut conferre? utrumne mulieres, sine materiis splendoris, et sine ingeniis decoris, placere non possent hominibus, quae adhuc incultae et incompositae et (ut ita dixerim) crudae ac rudes, angelos moverant? Anne sordidi, et per gratuitum usum contumeliosi amatores viderentur, si nihil foeminis in connubium allectis contulissent? Sed haec non capit aestimare, nihil plus desiderare poterant, quae angelos possidebant, magno scilicet nupserant. Enimvero, qui utique interdum cogitabant unde cecidissent, et post libidinum vaporata momenta coelum suspirabant, illud ipsum bonum foeminarum naturalis decoris, ut caussam mali, sic remuneraverunt, ne eis profuisset felicitas sua, sed ut devectum de simplicitate et sinceritate una cum ipsis in offensam Dei pervenirent. Certi erant omnem, et gloriam, et ambitionem, et affectationem per carnem placendi Deo displicere. Hi sunt nempe angeli quos judicaturi sumus, hi sunt angeli quibus in lavacro renuntiamus; haec sunt utique, per quae ab homine judicari meruerunt. Quid ergo facient apud judices suos res eorum? quod est commercium damnaturis cum damnandis? Opinor, quod Christo et Beliae. Qua constantia tribunal illud ascendimus, decreturi adversus eos, quorum munera appetimus? Nam et vobis eadem tunc substantia angelica repromissa, idem sexus qui et viris, eamdem judicandi dignationem pollicetur: nisi ergo hic jam praejudicaverimus, res eorum praedamnando, quas in illis tunc damnaturi sumus, illi potius nos judicabunt atque damnabunt. Scio scripturam Enoch, quae hunc ordinem angelis dedit, non recipi a quibusdam, quia nec in armarium judaicum admittitur. Opinor, non putaverunt illam ante cataclysmum editam, post eum casum orbis, omnium rerum abolitorem, salvam esse potuisse. Si ista ratio est, recordentur pronepotem ipsius Enoch fuisse superstitem cataclysmi Noë, qui utique domestico nomine et haereditaria traditione audierat et meminerat, de proavi sui penes Deum gratia, et de omnibus praedicatis ejus; cum Enoch filio suo Mathusalae nihil aliud mandaverit, quam ut notitiam eorum posteris suis traderet. Igitur sine dubio potuit Noë, in praedicationis delegatione successisse, vel quia et alias non tacuisset tam de Dei conservatoris sui dispositione, quam de ipsa domus suae gloria. Hoc si non tam expedite haberet, illud quoque assertionem scripturae illius tueretur. Perinde potuit abolefactam eam violentia cataclysmi, in spiritu rursus reformare: quemadmodum et Hierosolymis Babylonia expugnatione deletis, omne instrumentum judaicae litteraturae per Esdram constat restauratum. Sed cum Enoch eadem scriptura etiam de Domino praedicarit, a nobis quidem nihil omnino rejiciendum est, quod pertinet ad nos. Et legimus, omnem Scripturam aedificationi habilem divinitus inspirari. A Judaeis potest jam videri propterea rejecta, sicut et caetera fere quae Christum sonant. Nec utique mirum hoc, si scripturas aliquas non receperunt de eo locutas, quem et ipsum coram loquentem non erant recepturi. Eo accedit, quod Enoch apud Judam Apostolum testimonium possidet. Nulla nunc muliebri pompae nota inusta sit praedamnationis, de exitu auctorum. Nihil angelis illis imputetur, praeter repudium coeli, et matrimonium carnis. Rerum ipsarum qualitates examinemus, ut consilia quoque concupiscentiae earum deprehendamus. Habitus foeminae duplicem speciem circumfert, cultum, ornatum. Cultum dicimus, quem mundum muliebrem vocant; ornatum, quem immundum muliebrem convenit dici. Ille in auro, et argento, et gemmis, et vestibus deputatur: ista in cura capilli, et cutis, et earum partium corporis, quae oculos trahunt. Alteri ambitionis crimen intendimus, alteri prostitutionis: ut jam hinc prospicias, Dei ancilla, quid ex his disciplinae tuae conveniat, quae de diversis institutis censearis, scilicet humilitatis et castitatis.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Apparel of Women Book II
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I address you as servants of the living God, my fellow servants and sisters, though I claim no higher right among you than my own lowly standing in servitude and brotherhood; I dare this appeal not from vanity, but from genuine care for your salvation. That salvation, established for men no less than women, rests especially on the display of chastity. Since we all are the temple of God, with the Holy Spirit brought in and consecrated within us, chastity stands as the guardian and priest of this temple, refusing admission to anything unclean or profane, lest the God who dwells there, offended, abandon his defiled seat. My present subject is not chastity itself — divine precepts everywhere suffice to urge and demand that — but the things that belong to it: how you ought to conduct yourselves. Most women, whom God permits me to rebuke in every respect, either through simple ignorance or bold pretense behave as if chastity consisted only in bodily integrity and the avoidance of sexual violation, as though nothing internal were required concerning the arrangement of dress and adornment. Yet they persist in their old pursuit of beauty and splendor, parading the same appearance as the women of the nations, who lack the consciousness of true chastity because nothing true exists in those who do not know God as the guardian and master of truth. Even if some chastity can be credited among the gentiles, it remains imperfect and unformed, so that however tenacious it may be in the mind, it dissolves in the license of habits, chasing the perversity of the gentiles whose very effect it shuns. How many women, finally, do not even desire to please outsiders? Who does not wish to adorn herself in order to deny desire? Although this, too, is characteristic of gentile chastity — not to sin, yet to will it; or even not to will it, yet not to refuse it. What is surprising? All things are perverse that are not from God. Let them see, then, how they fail to obtain the whole good easily, and whatever they do obtain they mix with evil. You must turn away from them, as in all other matters, so also in your gait, because you ought to be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven.

Ea salus nec foeminarum modo, sed etiam virorum, in exhibitione praecipue pudicitiae statuta est. Nam cum omnes templum Dei simus, illato in nos et consecrato Spiritu Sancto, ejus templi aedituus et antistes pudicitia est, quae nihil immundum nec profanum inferri sinat, ne Deus ille, qui inhabitat, inquinatam sedem offensus derelinquat. Sed modo nos non de pudicitia, cui indicendae et exigendae sufficiunt instantia ubique divina praecepta, verum de pertinentibus ad eam, id est qualiter vos incedere oporteat. Pleraeque enim, quod ipsum mihi utique [reprehendendo in omnibus] reprehendere Deus permittat, aut ignorantes simpliciter aut dissimulantes audacter ita ingrediuntur, quasi pudicitia in sola carnis integritate et stupri aversione consistat, nec quicquam intrinsecus opus sit, de cultus et ornatus dispositione. Sed enim perseverant in pristinis studiis formae et nitoris, eamdem sui speciem circumferentes, quam foeminae nationum, a quibus abest conscientia verae pudicitiae, quia nihil verum in his, qui Deum nesciunt praesidem et magistrum veritatis. Nam etsi qua in gentilibus pudicitia credi potest, usque adeo eam imperfectam et inconditam constat, ut licet in animo aliquatenus tenax sui agat, in habitus tamen licentia sese dissolvat, pro perversitate gentilium appetendo, cujus rei devitat effectum. Quota denique est, quae nec placere quidem extraneis concupiscat? quae non velit idcirco se expingere, ut neget appetitum? Quanquam et hoc gentili pudicitiae familiare sit, non delinquere, attamen velle; vel etiam nolle, attamen non denegare. Quid mirum? perversa sunt omnia, quae a Deo non sunt. Videant igitur, quae non totum bonum obtinendo facile et quod obtinent malo commiscent. Vos ab illis, ut in caeteris, incessu quoque devertere necessarium est, quoniam perfectae esse debetis, sicut Pater vester qui est in coelis.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 10
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let’s be clear: this isn't about a few badges. It is flatly inhumane that women, subjected to men in every respect, get to flaunt an honorific badge of their virginity—a badge that makes them suspects, spectacles, and celebrities among the brothers—while men, so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs, march on in their private virtue carrying nothing that would also make them illustrious. The men ought to defend some insignia for themselves too: Garamantian feathers, Barbarian strophiums, Athenian cicadas, German braids, British tattoos—or, failing that, let them veil their heads and hide in church. We are certain the Holy Spirit could have more readily authorized such a distinction for men, if he had authorized it for women; besides the authority of sex, the very name of continence ought to have been more honored in men, since their sex burns hotter and hungers more fiercely for women, their continence labors with greater ardor, and is therefore more worthy of all display—if display is virginity’s dignity. After all, continence does not outrank virginity, whether of widows or those who by mutual consent have already refused the common shame. Virginity consists in grace; continence consists in virtue. Not desiring, when you have grown accustomed to desiring, is a mighty struggle. But if you have never tasted the fruit of desire, you will not easily desire it, having no adversary—the desire for the fruit. How, then, did God not authorize such a distinction more for men, whether because they are more familiar to him—namely, his image—or because they labor more? But if nothing for the male, then much more for the female.

Certi sumus Spiritum Sanctum magis masculis tale aliquid subscribere potuisse, si foeminis subscripsisset, cum praeter sexus auctoritatem, etiam ipsius continentiae nomine masculos potius honorari oportuisset; quorum quanto sexus avidior et calidior in foeminas, tanto continentia majoris ardoris laboratior, ideoque dignior omni ostentatione: si ostentatio, virginitatis est dignitas. Non enim et continentia virginitati antistat, sive viduorum, sive qui ex consensu contumeliam communem jam recusaverunt? Nam virginitas gratia constat, continentia vero virtute. Non concupiscendi, cui concupiscendo inoleveris, grande certamen est. Cujus autem concupiscendi ignoraveris fructum, facile non concupisces, adversarium non habens, concupiscentiam fructus. Quomodo ergo non magis viris aliquid tale Deus in honorem subscripsisset, vel quia familiariori, scilicet imagini suae, vel quia plus laboranti? Si autem nihil masculo, multo magis foeminae.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 11
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We left something out earlier, a chunk of the follow‑up argument, so as not to shatter its coherence; now we clear it up in reply. We pinned our case on the Apostle's flat statement that 'every woman' means exactly that — women of every age. The pushback, then, had to run the other way: if the rule applies to all women, a female must be veiled from birth, from the very moment she gets the label 'virgin.' That does not follow. The obligation kicks in when she begins to understand herself, when she enters the census of her own nature, walks out of the category 'virgin,' and undergoes the new thing that belongs to the next stage of life. Adam and Eve, the first of the race, went about naked as long as they lacked understanding. The moment they tasted the tree of knowledge, the very first thing they sensed was that they ought to be ashamed (Gen 2–3). So each sex marked its new awareness with a covering. Even if the stated reason for veiling is 'because of the angels,' the law of the veil unmistakably takes effect at the age when daughters of men can stir concupiscence in themselves and become eligible for marriage (Gen 6:2). From that point a virgin ceases to be a virgin — from the moment she can no longer be one. That is why in Israel it was illegal to hand a girl over to a man until her maturity had been attested by blood; before that sign the thing is unripe. Therefore, if she is a virgin only while she is unripe, she stops being a virgin once she is recognized as mature, and she becomes subject to the law just as she becomes subject to marriage. Betrothed women have the precedent of Rebecca: when she was being led to a husband she had not yet met, the instant she recognized him — the one she had spotted from afar — she did not put up with a hand‑clasp, or a kiss, or an exchange of greetings. She confessed what she had perceived, that she was already married in spirit, and she denied she was still a virgin by unveiling right there (Gen 24). O woman already schooled by Christ! She proves that marriage happens through sight and mind, just as adultery does. Unless, of course, some people still keep Rebecca veiled. As for the rest — those not betrothed — let the parents' foot‑dragging, born of stinginess or scrupulosity, answer for itself, and let the vow of continence answer for itself. Neither has anything to do with the age that is running its own course and paying its own debts to maturity. Another mother, nature, working in secret, and another father, time, lurking in the dark, have married off their daughter by their own laws. Look: your 'virgin' is already married — her soul in expectation, her flesh in transfiguration — and you are busy lining up a flesh‑and‑blood husband for her. Her voice has already deepened, her limbs are fully formed, modesty clothes her everywhere, the monthly cycles pay their tribute: and you deny she is a woman, even while you admit she suffers womanly things! If intercourse with a man makes a woman, then let them not be veiled until after the very consummation of marriage. Yet even among the gentiles veiled women are led to their husbands. If they are veiled at betrothal because they have been mingled with a male in both body and spirit through a kiss and joined right hands — the acts by which they first surrendered the shame of the spirit, through the common pledge of conscience by which they contracted the whole confusion — how much more will time itself veil them, since without time they cannot be betrothed, and when time presses, virgins cease to be virgins! The gentiles, too, watch the clock, so that from the law of nature they render to each age its due. They send girls to work at twelve, boys at fourteen, fixing puberty by years, not by betrothals or weddings. A virgin is called a matron, and an unmarried man a patron. Among us, however, natural realities go unobserved, as if the God of nature were someone other than our own.

latin: Sed quod supra intermisimus, ex parte subsecutae disputationis, ne cohaerentiam ejus dispergeremus, nunc responso expungemus. Ubi enim gradum fiximus de Apostoli absoluta definitione, omnem mulierem etiam omnis aetatis intelligendam, responderi ex diverso habebat, ergo a nativitate et a primo nomine aetatis virginem operiri oportere. Non ita est autem, sed ex quo se intelligere coeperit, et censum naturae suae intrare, et de virginis exire, et pati novum illud quod alterius aetatis est. Nam et principes generis Adam et Eva, quamdiu intellectu carebant, nudi agebant. At ubi de arbore agnitionis gustaverunt, nihil primum senserunt quam erubescendum. Itaque sui quique sexus intellectum tegmine notaverunt. Sed et si propter angelos velanda est, sine dubio ab ea aetate lex velaminis operabitur, a qua potuerunt filiae hominum concupiscentiam sui adducere, et nuptias pati. Ex illo enim virgo desinit, ex quo potest non esse. Et ideo penes Israel illicitum est ad virum tradere, nisi post contestatam sanguine maturitatem: ita ante hunc indicem acerba res est. Igitur si tamdiu virgo, quamdiu acerba est, desinit virginem cum matura cognoscitur, et ut non virgo jam legi applicatur, sicut et nuptiis. Et desponsatae quidem habent exemplum Rebeccae, quae cum ad sponsum ignotum adhuc ignota perduceretur, simul ipsum cognovit esse, quem de longinquo prospexerat, non sustinuit dexterae colluctationem, nec osculi congressionem, nec salutationis communicationem, sed confessa quod senserat, id est spiritu nuptam, negavit virginem velata ibidem. O mulierem jam de Christi disciplina! Ostendit enim etiam nuptias de aspectu et animo fieri, quemadmodum stuprum. Nisi quod etiam Rebeccam quidam adhuc velant. De caeteris vero, id est, quae desponsatae non sunt, viderit parentum procrastinatio ex angustiis vel scrupulositate descendens, viderit et ipsum continentiae votum. Nihil pertinet ad aetatem sua spatia currentem, suaque debita maturitati luentem. Alia in occulto mater, natura, et alius in latenti pater, tempus, filiam suam legibus suis maritarunt. Aspice nuptam jam illam tuam virginem, et animam expectatione, et carnem transfiguratione, cui tu secundum paras maritum. Jam et vox obsolefacta est, et membra completa sunt, et pudor ubique vestitur, et menses tributa dependunt: ac tu mulierem negas, quam muliebria pati dicis! Si congressio viri mulierem facit, non tegantur, nisi post ipsam nuptiarum passionem. Atquin etiam apud ethnicos velatae ad virum ducuntur. Si autem ad desponsationem velantur, quia et corpore et spiritu masculo mixtae sunt per osculum et dexteras, per quae primum resignarunt pudorem spiritus, per commune conscientiae pignus, quo totam condixerunt confusionem, quanto magis tempus illas velabit, sine quo sponsari non possunt, et quo urgente sine sponsalibus virgines desinunt esse! Tempus etiam ethnici observant, ut ex lege naturae jura sua aetatibus reddant. Nam foeminas quidem a duodecim annis, masculum vero a duobus amplius ad negotia mittunt, pubertatem in annis, non sponsalibus aut nuptiis decernentes. Materfamiliae vocatur licet virgo, et paterfamiliae licet investis. A nobis nec naturalia observantur, quasi alius sit Deus naturae quam noster.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 12
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Recognize the woman, recognize the married woman too, from the testimony of both body and spirit, which she endures in conscience and in flesh. These are the original documents of natural betrothals and marriages. Impose a veil from the outside on one who already has a covering within. Let the upper parts be covered as well, whose lower parts are not naked. Do you want to know what authority age carries? Set both side by side: the immature girl compressed into a woman's habit, and the one who has matured yet remains a virgin in her own habit. That woman will be denied more easily than this virgin will be believed. Such is the credibility of age that not even a habit can obscure it. What is more, our own women confess the change of age by their very habit, and at the same time, once they have understood themselves to be women, they are led out from virginity, laying aside from their head what they were; they twist their hair, and with a more wanton needle they fasten it, parting their locks from the forehead to profess their womanhood openly. Already they seek the counsel of their appearance from a mirror, and they soften their face with lavish washing, perhaps even doctoring it with some cosmetic; they throw a cloak over the outside, they lace on a multiform shoe, they carry more equipment to the baths. Why should I pursue individual points? Their preparations alone, manifest as they are, parade their entire womanhood in public. Yet they want to pass for virgins solely by the nakedness of their head, denying with one habit what they proclaim with their whole demeanor.

latin: Agnosce et mulierem, agnosce et nuptam, de testimoniis et corporis et spiritus, quae patitur et in conscientia et in carne. Hae sunt tabellae priores naturalium sponsalium et nuptiarum. Impone velamen extrinsecus, habenti tegumen intrinsecus. Tegantur etiam superiora, cujus inferiora nuda non sunt. Vis scire quae sit aetatis auctoritas? Propone utramque, immature compressam in habitu mulieris, et quae maturitate progressa in virginitate duret cum suo habitu, facilius illa mulier negabitur, quam ista virgo credetur. Tanta est adeo fides aetatis, ut nec habitu obstrui possit. Quid quod etiam hae nostrae etiam habitu mutationem aetatis confitentur, simulque se mulieres intellexerunt, de virginibus educantur, a capite quidem ipso deponentes quod fuerunt: vertunt capillum, et acu lasciviore comam sibi inserunt, crinibus a fronte divisis apertam professae mulieritatem. Jam et consilium formae a speculo petunt, et faciem morosiorem lavacro macerant, forsitan et aliquo eam medicamine interpolant, pallium extrinsecus jactant, calceum stipant multiformem, plus instrumenti ad balneas deferunt. Quid singula persequar? Solae autem manifestae paraturae totam circumferunt mulieritatem. Sed virginari volunt sola capitis nuditate, uno habitu negantes quod toto suggestu profitentur.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 13
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If you misuse the habit to impress people, then live up to it in this way too: veil your head among the Gentiles. In church you hide your virginity, which you conceal outside of church. You fear strangers; reverence your brothers as well. Or be consistent: dare to be seen as virgins in the streets just as you dare in the churches. I'll praise your mettle if you also peddle your virginity among the Gentiles. The same nature exists outside as inside; the same institution stands among men and before the Lord with the same freedom. So why do you hide your good outside, but broadcast it in church? I demand an answer: is it to please your brothers, or to please God Himself? If it's to please God: He is just as able to see what is done in secret as He is just to reward what is done for Him alone. Finally, He commands us not to broadcast the deeds that will earn a reward from Him, nor to settle for human praise instead. If we're forbidden to perform even a single act of charity with a guilty conscience, how much more must we shroud ourselves in darkness when we offer God so great an oblation—our own body and our own spirit—when we consecrate that very nature? Therefore, what cannot be seen as done for God, because God does not will it to be done that way, follows as done for the sake of men: certainly first it is unlawful, as it is lustful for glory. For glory is unlawful to those whose proof consists in all humility. And if the virtue of continence is conferred by God, why do you boast as if you had not received it? If you haven't received it, what do you have that was not given to you? But this very fact proves it was not given to you by God, because you do not present it to God alone. Let us see, then, what is human, whether it is firm and true.

latin: Si propter homines habitu abutuntur, impleant illum etiam in hoc, ut et apud ethnicos caput velent. Certe in ecclesia virginitatem suam abscondant, quam extra ecclesiam celant. Timent extraneos, revereantur et fratres: aut constanter audeant, et in vicis virgines videri sicut audent in ecclesiis. Laudabo vigorem, si aliquid et apud ethnicos virginitatis nundinarent. Eadem natura foris quae et intus, eadem institutio apud homines et apud Dominum eadem libertate constat. Quo ergo foris quidem bonum suum abstrudunt, in ecclesia vero provulgant? Exposco rationem; utrumne ut fratribus suis placeant, an ut ipsi Deo? Si ut ipsi Deo: tam idoneus est ad conspicienda quae in occulto fiunt, quam justus ad remuneranda quae soli sibi fiunt. Denique praecipit, nihil debuccinemus eorum quae apud illum mercedem merebuntur, nec ea ab hominibus compensemus. Quod si unius victoriati, vel quamcunque eleemosynae operationem, sinistra conscia facere prohibemur, quantum tenebrarum circumfundere debemus, cum tantam oblationem Deo offerimus, ipsius corporis et ipsius spiritus nostri, cum illam ipsam naturam consecramus. Ergo quod non potest videri propter Deum fieri, quia sic fieri Deus non vult, sequitur ut hominum gratia fiat: utique primo illicitum, ut gloriae libidinosum. Gloria enim illicitum est eis, quorum probatio in omni humiliatione constat. Et si a Deo confertur continentiae virtus; Quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? Si vero non accepisti, quid habes quod datum tibi non est? Hoc ipso autem constat a Deo datam tibi non esse, quod illam non soli Deo praestas. Videamus ergo quod humanum est, an firmum sit et verum.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 14
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: People still repeat what a certain woman said when this question was first raised: "And how will we get the others to sign on for this kind of work?" They will make us happy, if there are more of them, and not by the grace of God or the merits of each one. Do virgins adorn the church for God, or does the church commend the virgins? So it is admitted that the whole enterprise is about glory. And where there is glory, there is recruitment; where there is recruitment, there is coercion; where there is coercion, there is necessity; where there is necessity, there is weakness. So while they leave their heads uncovered in order to be recruited for the sake of glory, they end up forced to cover their bellies because weakness has ruined them. Rivalry produces these women, not religion: sometimes even their own belly is their god, because the sisterhood of virgins easily accepts it. And they do not just rush into it; they also drag a long rope of sins behind them. For when they are put on public display and their virtue is proclaimed, and the brothers heap every honor and work of charity on them, while they cannot hide where something has been admitted, they feel as much shame as they once had honor. If an uncovered head is the badge of virginity, and a virgin falls from the grace of virginity, she keeps her head uncovered so she will not be exposed — and at that point she is already walking in a habit that belongs to someone else, the one that virginity claims for itself. She stays in the habit anyway, or at least in a borrowed one, so that a change of clothing does not betray her. Conscious of a womanhood that is now undeniable, they dare to approach God with uncovered heads. But God and the Lord is a rival who said: "Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed" (Luke 8:17), and he drags many of them into the open. They will not confess unless the cries of their own infants betray them. The more of them there are, the more you must suspect them of greater crimes. I will say it, though I do not want to: it is hard for a woman to become someone who does not fear becoming pregnant, and who, once she has, can lie about being a virgin under God. How far will she go to hide what happens in her own womb, so that even the mother stays concealed? God knows that infants have already been brought to birth intact, after being fought off for a time by their mothers. These virgins always conceive very easily and give birth very happily, and the children look just like their fathers. This forced, unwilling virginity admits to shameful acts. The very desire not to stay hidden is not modest; it endures something unworthy of a virgin — the desire to please, certainly even men. However much she tries with a good mind, she must risk herself by being put on display, while she is struck by uncertain and countless eyes, while she is titillated by pointing fingers, while she is loved too much, while she grows warm among constant embraces and kisses. Thus the forehead is hardened, thus modesty is worn away, thus it is dissolved, thus she learns to desire to please in a different way.

latin: Referunt aliquando dictum a quadam, cum primum quaestio ista tentata est: Et quomodo caeteras sollicitabimus ad hujusmodi opus. Scilicet felices nos facient, si plures erunt, et non Dei gratia vel merita cujusque. Virgines ecclesiam, an ecclesia virgines ornat Deo, sive commendat? Confessa est igitur gloriam esse in caussa. Porro ubi gloria, illic sollicitatio; ubi sollicitatio, illic coactio; ubi coactio, illic necessitas; ubi necessitas, illic infirmitas. Merito itaque dum caput non tegunt ut sollicitentur gloriae caussa, ventres tegere coguntur infirmitatis ruina. Aemulatio enim illas, non religio producit: aliquando et ipse venter Deus earum, quia facile virginis fraternitas suscipit. Nec tantum autem ruunt, sed et funem longum delictorum sibi adtrabunt. Prolatae enim in medium, et publicato bono suo elatae, et a fratribus omni honore et caritatis operatione cumulatae, dum non latent ubi quid admissum est, tantum dedecoris cogitant, quantum honoris habuerunt. Si intectum caput virginitati adscribitur, si qua virgo exciderit de gratia virginitatis, ne prodatur, intecto permanet capite: et tunc jam alieno ambulat habitu, id est quem sibi vindicat virginitas: permanet nihilominus in habitu, vel tunc saltem alieno, ne scilicet mutatione prodatur. Consciae mulieritatis jam indubitatae, audent nudo capite ad Deum adire. Sed aemulator Deus et Dominus, qui dixit: Nihil occultum quod non revelabitur, plerasque etiam in conspectum deducit. Non enim confitebuntur, nisi ipsorum infantium suorum vagitibus proditae. Quantum autem plures, non etiam de pluribus sceleribus suspectas habebis? Dicam, licet nolim, difficile mulier semel fit, quae non timet fieri, quaeque jam facta potest virginem mentiri sub Deo. Quanta item circa uterum suum audebit, ne etiam mater detegatur! Scit Deus quod jam infantes et perfici et perduci ad partum integros duxerit, debellatos aliquandiu a matribus. Facillime semper concipiunt, et felicissime pariunt hujusmodi virgines, et quidem simillimos patribus. Haec admittit flagitia coacta et invita virginitas. Ipsa concupiscentia non latendi non est pudica, patitur aliquid quod virginis non sit, studium placendi, utique et viris. Quantum velis bona mente conetur, necesse est publicatione sui periclitetur, dum percutitur oculis incertis et multis, dum digitis demonstrantium titillatur, dum nimium amatur, dum inter amplexus et oscula assidua concalescit. Sic frons duratur, sic pudor teritur, sic solvitur, sic discitur aliter jam placere desiderare.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — On the Veiling of Virgins 15
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: True, whole, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. It refuses to endure even the eyes of other women; it keeps its own eyes for itself. It takes refuge in a head-veil as if it were a helmet, a shield to protect its good against the blows of temptation, the darts of scandal, against suspicions, whispers, envy, and sheer malice. There is even something to fear among the pagans — what they call the *fascinum*, the wretched fallout of praise and outsized glory. We sometimes read this as the devil's work, for he is the hatred of the good; sometimes we ascribe it to God, for he is the judgment on pride, exalting the humble and humbling the proud. The holier virgin will therefore fear, whether you call it *fascinum* or not, both the adversary on one side and God on the other: the one's envious nature, the other's censorial light. She will rejoice in being known to herself alone and to God. Yet even if she becomes known to someone, she acts wisely if she has blocked the path to temptation. Who would dare press his eyes upon a closed face, a face that feels nothing, a face — to put it bluntly — that looks sad? Any evil thought will be shattered by her very severity. She even ceases to count as a woman, the one who hides her virginity.

Sed et si cui innotuerit, sapit si tentationibus gradum obstruxerit. Quis enim audebit oculis suis premere faciem clausam, faciem non sentientem, faciem, ut dixerim, tristem? Quicunque malus cogitatus ipsa severitate frangetur. Jam se etiam mulierem negat, quae virginem celat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I do not doubt, brother, that after your wife went ahead of you in peace you have turned your mind to composing yourself and are now weighing what it means to stay single — and you certainly need counsel. True, everyone ought to hash this out with his own faith and test its strength; but because the flesh's necessity keeps prodding the thought, and that necessity almost always resists the very conscience of faith, you need faith's counsel from outside, like an advocate against the flesh's demands. That necessity is easily overcome if you weigh God's will instead of indulgence. No one earns anything by claiming indulgence; you earn by obeying the will. And God's will is our sanctification. He wants us to become his image and likeness so that we may be holy as he is holy. That good — sanctification, I mean — he parcels out into several forms so that we might be caught in one of them. The first form is virginity from birth. The second virginity comes from the second birth, that is, from baptism: it either keeps itself pure within marriage by mutual agreement, or it perseveres in widowhood by choice. The third step left is monogamy: after one marriage ends, you renounce sex altogether. The first virginity is happiness — never knowing at all the thing you will later long to be free of. The second is virtue — despising the power you know all too well. The remaining form, marrying again after death has dissolved a marriage, wins praise not only for virtue but also for modesty. For modesty means not craving what has been taken away, and taken away by the Lord God, without whose will not a leaf falls from a tree nor a sparrow drops to the ground for a single coin.

latin: Non dubito, frater, te post uxorem in pace praemissam, ad compositionem animi conversum, de exitu singularitatis cogitare, et utique consilii indigere. Quamquam in hujusmodi cum fide sua conloqui debet unusquisque, ejusque vires consulere; tamen quoniam, in ista specie, carnis necessitas cogitatum movet, quae fere apud eamdem conscientiam fidei resistit, opus est fidei extrinsecus consilio, tanquam advocato adversus carnis necessitates. Quae quidem necessitas facillime circumscribi potest, si voluntas potuis Dei, quam indulgentia consideratur. Nemo indulgentia utendo promeretur, sed voluntati obsequendo. Voluntas Dei est sanctificatio nostra. Vult enim imaginem suam nos etiam similitudinem fieri, ut simus sancti, sicuti ipse sanctus est. Id bonum, sanctificationem dico, in species distribuit complures, ut in aliqua earum deprehendamur. Prima species, virginitas a nativitate. Secunda virginitas, a secunda nativitate, id est a lavacro, quae aut in matrimonio purificat ex compacto, aut in viduitate perseverat ex arbitrio. Tertius gradus superest monogamia, cum post matrimonium unum interceptum exinde sexui renuntiatur. Prima virginitas felicitatis est, non nosse in totum a quo postea optabis liberari. Secunda virtutis est, contemnere cujus vim optime noris. Reliqua species hactenus nubendi post matrimonium morte disjunctum, praeter virtutis, etiam modestiae laus est. Modestia est enim, ablatum non desiderare, et ablatum a Domino Deo; sine cujus voluntate nec folium de arbore delabitur, nec passer assis unius ad terram cadit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english:
We must renounce carnal things so that at some point we may reconsider spiritual ones. Seize the opportunity, even if it is not the one you most desire, for it is still opportune: you no longer have anyone to whom you owe a debt, nor anyone from whom you might be freed; you have ceased to be a debtor. How fortunate you are! You have dismissed the debtor; now endure the loss. But what if what we call loss you experience as gain? For through continence you will indeed secure a great wealth of sanctity; by sparing the flesh, you acquire the spirit.

Let us re-examine our own conscience, which a person perceives as different from himself: when he happens to abstain from his own wife, he gains spiritual understanding. If he prays to the Lord, he is near heaven. If he devotes himself to the Scriptures, he is entirely there. If he sings a psalm, it pleases him. If he adjures a demon, he trusts in himself. Therefore the Apostle added a temporary purification for the sake of commendable prayers, so that we may know that what profits for a time must always be exercised by us, so that it may always profit. Prayer is necessary for human beings every day, indeed at every moment, and continence likewise, since prayer is necessary. Prayer proceeds from conscience. If conscience is ashamed, prayer is ashamed. The Spirit leads prayer to God. If the spirit stands guilty before itself because of a conscience that is ashamed, how will it dare to lead prayer from that very source, when even the holy minister is stained by its shame?

Indeed, there is a prophetic voice of the Old Testament: "You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy" (Leviticus 11:44); and again: "With the holy you show yourself holy, and with the innocent man you show yourself innocent, and with the elect you show yourself elect" (Psalm 18:26). For we ought to enter the discipline of the Lord in a manner worthy of him, not according to the hot desires of the flesh. For thus the Apostle also says that to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:6). If this obscuration, even when the fleshly act is exercised within a single marriage, drives away the Holy Spirit, how much more when a second marriage is undertaken?

latin: Renuntiemus carnalibus, ut aliquando spiritalia retractemus. Rape occasionem, etsi non exoptatissimam, attamen opportunam, non habere cui debitum solveres, et a quo exsolvereris: desiisti esse debitor. O te felicem! dimisisti debitorem; sustine damnum. Quid si, quod diximus damnum, lucrum sentias? Per continentiam enim negotiaberis magnam substantiam sanctitatis; parcimonia carnis, spiritum adquires. Recogitemus enim ipsam conscientiam nostram, quam alium se homo sentiat: cum forte a sua foemina cessat, spiritaliter sapit. Si orationem facit ad Dominum, prope est coelo. Si scripturis incumbit, totus illic est. Si psalmum canit, placet sibi. Si daemonem adjurat, confidit sibi. Ideo Apostolus temporalem purificationem orationum commendandarum caussa adjecit; ut sciremus, quod ad tempus prodest semper nobis exercendum esse, ut semper prosit. Quotidie, imo omni momento oratio hominibus necessaria est, utique et continentia, postquam oratio necessaria est. Oratio de conscientia procedit. Si conscientia erubescat, erubescit oratio. Spiritus deducit orationem ad Deum. Si spiritus reus apud se sit conscientiae erubescentis, quomodo audebit orationem ducere ab illa, de qua erubescente et ipse suffunditur sanctus minister? Etenim est prophetica vox veteris Testamenti: Sancti eritis, quia Deus sanctus; et rursus: Cum sancto sanctificaberis, et cum viro innocente innocens eris, et cum electo electus. Debemus enim ita ingredi in disciplina Domini, ut dignum est, non secundum carnis calentes concupiscentias. Ita enim et Apostolus dicit, quod sapere secundum carnem mors sit; secundum spiritum vero sapere vita aeterna sit in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Si haec obfusio, etiam cum in unis nuptiis res carnis exercetur, Spiritum Sanctum avertit, quanto magis cum in secundo matrimonio agitur?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: There's a double shame in it: in a second marriage two wives close in on the same husband — one in spirit, the other in flesh. You cannot hate the first, not when you reserve a more religious affection for her, now that she's been received by the Lord; you pray for her spirit, you make annual offerings for her. So will you stand before the Lord with as many wives as you name in prayer? Will you offer for two? Will you commend those two through a priest ordained from monogamy, or even consecrated from virginity, surrounded by virgins and men of one wife, and will your sacrifice go up with a free forehead? And among the other desires of a good mind, will you ask for chastity for yourself and your wife?

latin: Duplex enim rubor est; quia in secundo matrimonio duae uxores eumdem circumstant maritum; una spiritu, alia in carne: neque enim pristinam poteris odisse, cui etiam religiosiorem reservas affectionem, ut jam receptae apud Dominum, pro cujus spiritu postulas, pro qua oblationes annuas reddis. Stabis ergo ad Dominum cum tot uxoribus, quot in oratione commemoras? et offeres pro duabus? et commendabis illas duas per sacerdotem de monogamia ordinatum, aut etiam de virginitate sancitum, circumdatum virginibus ac univiris, et ascendet sacrificium tuum libera fronte? et inter caeteras voluntates bonae mentis, postulabis tibi et uxori castitatem?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If we press the logic to its core, a second marriage turns out to be nothing but a species of fornication. Scripture says husbands are anxious about how to please themselves (1 Cor 7:33) — not about character, since the text would never disparage a good anxiety; it means they fuss over grooming, adornment, and every effort to enhance their looks in order to arouse desire. But pleasing through appearance and polish is the very signature of carnal lust, which is also the engine of fornication. So does a second marriage strike you as kin to fornication? I catch in it the very marks of fornication. The Lord himself says: "Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matt 5:28). The man who looks at her intending to marry her — has he done less, or more? What if he actually marries her? He would never have done so unless he had first lusted after her and looked with that intent. Unless, of course, a man can marry a woman he has never seen or desired. There is a vast difference between a married man and a celibate lusting after another woman. To a celibate, every woman is 'another woman' as long as she belongs to someone else; yet she becomes a wife only through the very act that would also make her an adulteress. The law tries to separate marriage from fornication by labeling one licit and the other illicit, not by any difference in the thing itself. Otherwise, what single reality is common to both marriage and fornication for men and women alike? The mingling of flesh — and the Lord has equated the lust for that mingling with fornication. "So you're wiping out first marriages too," you object. Not undeservedly, since they are built from the same stuff as fornication. That is why "it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman" (1 Cor 7:1), and why the virgin's preeminent holiness consists precisely in lacking any kinship with fornication. If these arguments hold even for a first and only marriage as a motive for continence, how much more do they condemn a second! Be grateful if God indulged you once to marry; you will be grateful if you never learn that he indulged you a second time. You abuse the indulgence when you use it without measure; modesty is defined by measure. It wasn't enough for you to fall from the summit of spotless virginity into a second marriage; you roll on to a third, a fourth, perhaps more — because you failed continence at the second stage, and the One who refused to legislate second marriages did not want to forbid multiple ones either. So let us marry every day, and be caught on the Last Day like Sodom and Gomorrah — the day when "Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants" (Matt 24:19; Luke 21:23) will be fulfilled, that is, over husbands and the incontinent: for marriage means wombs, breasts, and babies. When does the marrying stop? I suspect only when life itself ends.

latin: Si penitus sensus ejus interpretemur, non aliud dicendum erit secundum matrimonium, quam species stupri. Cum enim dicat, maritos hoc in sollicitudine habere, quemadmodum sibi placeant; non utique de moribus (nam bonam sollicitudinem non sugillaret); et de cultu, et ornatu, et omni studio formae, ad illecebras movendas sollicitos intelligi velit; de forma autem et cultu placere carnalis concupiscentiae ingenium sit, quae etiam stupri caussa est: ecquid videtur tibi stupri adfine esse secundum matrimonium, quoniam ea in illo deprehendo quae stupro competunt? Ipse Dominus: Qui viderit, inquit, mulierem ad concupiscendum, jam stupravit eam in corde suo. Qui autem eam ad ducendum viderit, minus an plus fecit? Quid, si etiam duxerit? quod non faceret. nisi et ad ducendum concupisset, et ad concupiscendum vidisset. Nisi si potest duci uxor, quam non videris nec concupieris. Multum sane interest, maritus an caelebs aliam concupiscat. Omnis mulier etiam caelibi alia est, quamdiu aliena; nec per aliud tamen fit marita, nisi per quod et adultera. Leges videntur matrimonii et stupri differentiam facere per diversitatem illiciti, non per conditionem rei ipsius. Alioquin quae res et viris et foeminis omnibus adest ad matrimonium et stuprum? commixtio carnis scilicet, cujus concupiscentiam Dominus stupro adaequavit. Ergo, inquis. jam et primas, id est, unas nuptias destruis. Nec immerito, quoniam et ipsae ex eo constant, quo et stuprum. Ideo optimum est homini mulierem non attingere, et ideo virginis principalis sanctitas, quia caret stupri adfinitate. Et cum haec etiam de primis et unis nuptiis praetendi ad caussam continentiae possint, quanto magis secundo matrimonio recusando praejudicabunt! Gratus esto, si semel tibi indulsit Deus nubere; gratus autem eris, si iterum indulsisse illum tibi nescias. Caeterum, abuteris indulgentia, cum sine modestia uteris. Modestia a modo intelligitur. Non tibi sufficit de summo illo immaculatae virginitatis gradu in secundum recidisse nubendo; sed in tertium adhuc devolveris, et in quartum, et fortassis in plures, postquam in secunda statione continens non fuisti: quia nec prohibere plures nuptias voluit, qui de secundis provocandis retractavit. Nubamus igitur quotidie, et nubentes ab ultimo die deprehendamur tanquam Sodoma et Gomorra: quo die, Vae illud super praegnantes \[adimplebitur\], id est, super maritos et incontinentes: de nuptiis enim uteri, et ubera, et infantes. Et quando finis nubendi? Credo post finem vivendi.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ forbids divorce: "Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and the man who marries a divorced woman is equally an adulterer." He makes remarriage after divorce unlawful, thereby forbidding divorce itself. Moses, however, permits divorce in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife, lives with her, then finds no favor in her because he discovers something indecent, he writes a certificate of divorce, hands it to her, and sends her away (Deut 24:1–4). You see the clash between the Law and the Gospel, between Moses and Christ? Of course you do. You haven't accepted that Gospel—the same truth, the same Christ—in which, while forbidding divorce, he settles his own question: "Moses, because of your hard hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. The Creator made them male and female, and said, ‘The two shall become one flesh.’ So what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Matt 19:8–6; Gen 2:24). By that answer he both shields Moses' statute as his own and upholds the Creator's institution as Christ's own.

Now, to convict you on the grounds you actually accept, I'll meet you on your own turf—as if my Christ were yours. Doesn't he, while forbidding divorce, still share the mind of the One who joined male and female, and therefore *excuse* Moses' law rather than destroy it? But look: if your Christ teaches the opposite of Moses and the Creator, then he's mine—unless I can prove the opposite. I say he imposed the ban *conditionally*: "If a man divorces his wife *in order to marry another*, he commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman divorced *on that ground* is likewise an adulterer, because the original marriage was never lawfully dissolved. As long as that marriage stands, remarrying is adultery." So if the prohibition is conditional, it's not total; and what isn't totally forbidden is permitted in cases where the reason for the ban disappears.

latin: (Sed Christus diuortium inhibet dicens: qui dimiserit uxorem suam et aliam duxerit, adulterium committet, (et) qui dimissam a uiro duxerit, aeque adulter est, - ut sic quoque prohibeat diuortium, inlicitum facit repudiatae matrimonium — Moyses uero permittit repudium in Deuteronomio: si sumserit quis uxorem et habitauerit cum ea, et euenerit non inuenire eam apud eum gratiam, eo quod inuentum sit in illa impudicum negotium, scribet libellum repudii et dabit in manu eius et dimittet illam de domo sua. uides diuersitatem legis et euangelii, Moysi et Christi\'? plane. non enim recepisti illud quoque euangelium eiusdem ueritatis et eiusdem Christi, in quo prohibens diuortium propriam quaestionem eius absoluit: Moyses propter duritiam cordis uestri praecepit libellum repudii dare; a primordio autem non fuit sic; quia scilicet qui marem et feminam fecerat, erunt duo, dixerat, in carne una; quod deus itaque iunxit, homo (non) disiunxerit. hoc enim responso et Moysi constitutionem protexit, ut sui, et creatoris institutionem direxit, ut Christus ipsius. sed quatenus ex his reuincendus es, quae recepisti, sic tibi occurram, ac si meus Christus (tuus:) nonne et ipse prohibens diuortium et parem tamen gestans eius, qui marem et feminam iunxit, excusauerit potius quam destruxerit Moysi constitutionem? sed ecce sic tuus sit iste Christus contrarium docens Moysi et creatori, ut, si non contrarium ostendero, meus sit. dico enim illum condicionaliter nunc fecisse diuortii prohibitionem, si ideo quis dimittat uxoiem, ut aliam ducat: qui dimiserit, inquit, uxorem et aliam duxerit, adulterium commisit, et qui a marito dimissam duxerit aeque adulter est, ex eadem utique causa dimissam, qua non licet dimitti, ut alia ducatur; inlicite enim dimissam pro indimissa ducens adulter est. manet enim matrimonium quod non rite diremptum est; manente (autem) matrimonio nubere adulterium est. ita si condicionaliter prohibuit dimittere uxorem, non in totum prohibuit, et quod non prohibuit in totum, permisit alias, ubi causa cessat, ob quam prohibuit;

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Heretics abolish marriage; Psychics multiply it. The former refuse to marry even once, the latter refuse to stop at once. What are you doing, law of the Creator? You complain about domestic obedience just as much as foreign contempt, so both those who abuse marriage and those who refuse it wound you alike. Truly, such continence deserves no praise because it is heretical, and such license deserves no defense because it is psychic. The one blasphemes; the other wallows in lust. The one destroys the God of marriage; the other confuses him. But among us—who are rightly called spiritual because we acknowledge spiritual gifts—continence is as devout as license is modest, since both stand with the Creator. Continence honors the law of marriage; license moderates it. The former is not forced; the latter is governed. The former exercises judgment; the latter observes measure. We know one marriage, just as we know one God. The law of marriage gains greater honor where it also has shame. Yet Psychics, because they do not receive the Spirit, find no pleasure in the things of the Spirit. So while the things of the Spirit displease them, the things of the flesh will please them, as contrary to the Spirit. "The flesh," it says, "desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh" (Gal 5:17). What, then, will the flesh desire except what is more fleshly? Because of this, the flesh was also made alien to the Spirit from the beginning: "My Spirit," it says, "will not remain in these men forever, because they are flesh" (Gen 6:3).

latin: Haeretici nuptias auferunt, Psychici ingerunt. Illi nec semel, isti non semel nubunt. Quid agis, lex Creatoris? Inter alienos spadones et aurigas tuos tantumdem quereris de domestico obsequio, quantum de fastidio extraneo; proinde et te laedunt qui abutuntur, quemadmodum qui non utuntur. Verum neque continentia ejusmodi laudanda, quia haeretica est; neque licentia defendenda, quia psychica est. Illa blasphemat, ista luxuriat. Illa destruit nuptiarum Deum, ista confundit. Penes nos autem, quos spirituales merito dici facit agnitio spiritalium charismatum, continentia tam religiosa est, quam licentia verecunda, quandoquidem ambae cum Creatore sunt. Continentia legem nuptiarum honorat, licentia temperat. Illa non cogitur; ista regitur. Illa arbitrium habet, haec modum. Unum matrimonium novimus, sicut unum Deum. Magis honorem refert lex nuptiarum, ubi habet et pudorem. Sed Psychicis non recipientibus spiritum, ea quae sunt spiritus non placent. Ita, dum quae sunt spiritus non placent, ea quae sunt carnis placebunt, ut contraria spiritui. Caro, inquit, adversus spiritum concupiscit, et spiritus adversus carnem. Quid autem concupiscet caro, quam quae magis carnis sunt? Propter quod et in primordio extranea spiritus facta est: Non, inquit, permanebit spiritus meus in istis hominibus in aevum, eo quod caro sint.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I see we are now being summoned to the Apostle. To make his mind more easily understood, it must be driven home all the more urgently that a woman is bound to her dead husband and cannot take another. Consider: divorce arises from discord, or discord causes it; but death comes by the law of God, not by a man's offense. And death is a debt owed by all, even the unmarried. So if a woman divorced because of discord, anger, hatred, and their causes — injury, insult, or any grievance — is separated in soul and body, she remains bound to her enemy, I will not say her husband; how much more, then, is the woman bound who, neither by her own fault nor her husband's, but by the outcome of the Lord's law, was not severed from marriage but left behind? She will belong to him even in death, the very man to whom she owes concord even now that he is dead. She never heard a repudiation from him; she was never turned away. No certificate of divorce was written for her; she remains with him. She did not want to lose him; she keeps him. She holds the freedom of her mind, which presents to a man everything he lacks as an imaginary fruit. (1 Corinthians 7)

I put the question to the woman herself: Tell me, sister, did you send your husband ahead in peace? What will she answer? Or in discord? Then she is bound to him all the more, because she has a case with him before God. The one who is held back does not depart — but in peace. Therefore she must persevere in that bond with him, since she cannot repudiate him now — not even if she were to marry, had she been able to repudiate him. For indeed she prays for his soul, asks refreshment for him in the meantime, and a share in the first resurrection, and she makes offerings on the annual anniversaries of his death. If she does not do these things, she has truly repudiated him, as far as it lies in her power; and this is all the more unjust, because she could not do it, precisely because she could not; and all the more unworthy, because it is now more unworthy, if she did not deserve it. Or do we suppose we become nothing after death, following some Epicurean rather than Christ? But if we believe the resurrection of the dead, we will surely be held to account, together with those with whom we will rise, to render an account of each other. (1 Corinthians 7)

Even if in that age they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels, that does not mean we will not be held to our deceased spouses, simply because marriage will not be restored. On the contrary, we will be held all the more, because we are destined for a better state: to rise into a spiritual fellowship, recognizing both ourselves and our own. How else will we sing thanks to God for eternity, if the sense and memory of this debt do not remain in us? If we are reformed in substance, not in conscience? Therefore, when we are with God, we will be together — while all of us, with God, are one (though rewards vary, though there are many dwellings with the same Father), having worked for the same wage, namely eternal life, in which God will no more separate those He has joined than He forbids separation in this lesser life. (1 Corinthians 7)

Since this is so, how will she be free for another man, when she is occupied with her own even in the future? We address both sexes, though the speech is directed to one; for a single discipline governs both. Will she have one man in spirit and another in flesh? That would be adultery — the conscience of one woman divided between two men. If the first is separated from the flesh but remains in the heart, there — where even a thought without bodily union perfects adultery from desire, and marriage from will — he is still a husband, possessing that by which he was made, namely the mind. If another dwells in that mind, it is a crime. Yet he is not excluded, if he has departed from the lower commerce of the flesh. The husband is more honored when he has been made purer. (1 Corinthians 7)

latin: Video jam hinc ad Apostolum nos provocari. Ad cujus sensum facilius perspiciendum, tanto instantius praeculcandum est mulierum magis defuncto marito teneri, quominus alium virum admittat. Recogitemus enim repudium, aut discordia fieri, aut discordiam facere; mortem vero ex lege Dei, non ex hominis offensa evenire. Idque omnium esse debitum, etiam non maritorum. Igitur si repudiata quae per discordiam, et iram, et odium, et caussas eorum, injuriam vel contumeliam, vel quamlibet querelam, et anima et corpore separata est, tenetur inimico, ne dicam marito; quanto magis, illa, quae neque suo, neque mariti vitio, sed dominicae legis eventu, a matrimonio non separata, sed relicta, ejus erit etiam defuncti, cui etiam defuncto concordiam debet! A quo repudium non audiit, non divertit; cui repudium nn scripsit, cum ipso est; quem amisisse noluit, retinet. Habet secum animi licentiam, qui omnia homini quae non habet, imaginario fructu repraesentat. Ipsam denique interrogo foeminam: Dic mihi, soror, in pace praemisisti virum tuum? Quid respondebit? An in discordia? Ergo hoc magis ei vincta est, cum quo habet apud Deum caussam. Non discessit, quae tenetur. Sed in pace. Ergo perseveret in ea cum illo necesse est, quem jam repudiare non poterit, ne sic quidem nuptura si repudiare potuisset. Enim vero et pro anima ejus orat, et refrigerium interim adpostulat ei, et in prima resurrectione consortium, et offert annuis diebus dormitionis ejus. Nam haec nisi fecerit, vere repudiavit, quantum in ipsa est; et quidem hoc iniquius, quanto quo modo potuit, quia non potuit; et hoc indignius, quanto jam indignius, si quia non meruit. Aut numquid nihil crimus post mortem? Secundum aliquem Epicurum, et non secundum Christum. Quod si credimus mortuorum resurrectionem, utique tenebimur, cum quibus resurrecturi sumus, rationem de alterutro reddituri. Si autem in illo aevo neque nubent neque nubentur, sed erunt aequales angelis; non ideo non tenebitur conjugibus defunctis, quia non erit restitutio conjugii. Atquin eo magis tenebimur, quia in meliorem statum destinamur, resurrecturi in spiritale consortium, agnituri tam nosmetipsos, quam et nostros. Caeterum, quomodo gratias Deo in aeternum canemus, si non manebit in nobis sensus et memoria debiti hujus? si substantia, non conscientia reformabimur? Ergo qui cum Deo erimus, simul erimus, dum omnes apud Deum unum (licet merces varia, licet. multae mansiones penes patrem eumdem) uno denario ejusdem mercedis operati, id est vitae aeternae, in qua magis non separabit quos conjunxit Deus, quam in ista minore vita separari vetat. Cum haec ita sint, quomodo alii viro vacabit, quae suo etiam in futurum occupata est? Utrique autem sexui loquimur, etsi ad alterum sermo est; quia una disciplina praeest. Alium habebit in spiritu, alium in carne? Hoc erit adulterium, unius foeminae in duos viros conscientia. Si alter a carne disjunctus est, sed in corde remanet; illic (ubi etiam cogitatus sine carnis congressu, et adulterium ante perficit ex concupiscentia, et matrimonium ex voluntate) usque adhuc maritus est, ipsum illud possidens, per quod et factus est, id est animum: in quo si et alius habitabit, hoc erit crimen. Caeterum, non est exclusus, si a viliore commercio carnis decessit. Honoratior maritus est, quando mundior factus est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If you really want to marry "in the Lord" according to the Law and the Apostle, what kind of marriage are you after, when the very people you petition—a monogamous bishop, presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament, widows whose sect you rejected in yourself—are forbidden to have it? They will hand out husbands and wives as casually as morsels of bread, for their rule is: "Give to everyone who asks you" (Luke 6:30). They will join you in the Church, that virgin, the unique bride of the one Christ, and then you will pray for your husbands—new and old alike. Choose which one you will offer yourself to as an adulteress; I suspect it will be both. But if you have any sense, you will keep silent about the deceased one. Let your silence serve as your repudiation of him, already inscribed in another woman's marriage contract. That is how you will produce a new husband: by forgetting the old. You ought to please this new man more, since you chose not to please God for his sake. (1 Corinthians 7:39)

The Psychics want to prove that the Apostle approved this arrangement—or simply never considered it—when he wrote: "A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, only in the Lord." From this passage they defend the license for a second marriage, indeed for as many as you like once you allow a second; for what has ceased to be once is subject to every number. But the sense in which the Apostle wrote will become clear only if we first establish that he did not write it in the sense the Psychics exploit. That will be established if anyone recalls the things that clash with this chapter—in doctrine, in will, and in Paul's own proper discipline. If he permits second marriages, which did not exist from the beginning, how can he affirm that all things are gathered up again in Christ from the beginning (Ephesians 1:10)? If he wants us to repeat marriages, how does he defend our lineage in Isaac, authored by one husband? How does he constitute the entire order of the Church from monogamists, if that discipline does not precede among the laity, from whom the Church's order arises? How does he call those still in marriage away from its fruit, saying "the appointed time has grown short" (1 Corinthians 7:29), if through death he recalls them back into marriage after they have lapsed from it? If these things contradict the chapter in question, it will stand proved, as we said, that he did not write it in the sense the Psychics use. For it is easier for that one chapter to have some rationale that harmonizes with the others than for the Apostle to appear to teach contradictory things. We can discern that rationale in the subject matter itself. (1 Corinthians 7:39)

What was the occasion for the Apostle to write such things? It was the training of the new and especially the rising Church, which he was still feeding with milk, not yet with the solid food of stronger doctrine—so much so that, in that infancy of faith, they did not yet know what to do about the necessity of flesh and sex. We can see the very shape of these issues from his replies. When he says: "Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife" (1 Corinthians 7:1-2), he shows there were those who, caught in marriage by faith, feared it was no longer permitted for them to use their marriage, because they had believed in the holy flesh of Christ. Yet he concedes this by permission, not by command—that is, indulging them, not prescribing it. Moreover, he preferred that all be as he himself was. So also, writing back concerning divorce, he shows that some were thinking along those lines as well—especially because they did not think they should persevere in pagan marriages after faith. They sought counsel about virgins (for there was no command of the Lord), that it is good for a man to remain as he is; certainly, just as he was found by faith. "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned" (1 Corinthians 7:27-28): because, having been freed from a wife before faith, a second wife after faith will not be counted as a second, since she is the first after faith. For from faith onward, even our life itself is reckoned. But here he says he is sparing them: otherwise the pressure of the flesh would follow, and those who refuse the burdens of marriage because of the distress of the present time would be hindered—rather, one should have solicitude for the Lord, to secure it, than for a husband. And thus he revokes what he permitted. (1 Corinthians 7:25-28)

So then, in the very chapter where he defines that each one ought to remain in the calling in which he was called, adding: "A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord"—from this he also demonstrates that the woman to be understood here is one who has been found free from her husband just as a man is free from his wife: certainly through death, not through repudiation, the divorce having been made; because he would not permit the divorced to marry, against the former command. Therefore, if a woman marries, she does not sin, because neither will a second husband be reckoned to her, who is the first after faith; and it is so precisely that he added: "Only in the Lord"—because he was dealing with a woman who had a pagan husband and, having lost him, believed; lest she also presume that she can marry a pagan after faith—though the Psychics do not care about this. Let us know plainly that the authentic Greek does not read as it has come into use through the clever or simple reversal of two syllables: "If her husband dies," as if it sounds like the future, and thus seems to pertain to her who has already lost her husband in the faith. For if it were so, the license would extend infinitely—as many times as a husband is lost, she could marry without any shame, even to pagans. But even if it were so, as if about the future: "If a woman's husband has died," it would pertain equally to her whose husband will die before faith. Take whatever reading you will, as long as you do not overturn the rest. For when even those sentences yield—"Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it. Were you called uncircumcised? Do not become circumcised. Were you called circumcised? Do not become uncircumcised" (1 Corinthians 7:21, 18)—to which is added: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife" (1 Corinthians 7:27)—it is sufficiently clear that these pertain to those who, established in a new and recent calling, were seeking counsel about the very things in which they had been caught by faith. This will be the interpretation of that chapter to be examined—whether it fits the time, the cause, both the preceding examples and arguments, and the subsequent sentences and senses; and first, whether it agrees with the Apostle's own counsel and institution: for nothing is more to be guarded against than that someone be found to be at odds with himself. (1 Corinthians 7:39, 1 Corinthians 7:25-28)
