greek: Ἡ οὖν ὁδὸς τοῦ φωτός ἐστιν αὕτη: ἐάν τις θέλων ὁδὸν ὁδεύειν ἐπὶ τὸν ὡρισμένον τόπον, σπεύσῃ τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ. ἔστιν οὖν ἡ δοθεῖσα ἡμῖν γνῶσις τοῦ περιπατεῖν ἐν αὐτῇ τοιαύτη. ἀγαπήσεις τὸν ποιήσαντά σε, φοβηθήσῃ τόν σε πλάσαντα, δοξάσεις τόν σε λυτρωσάμενον ἐκ θανάτου: ἔσῃ ἁπλοῦς τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ πλούσιος τῷ πνεύματι: οὐ κολληθήσῃ μετὰ τῶν πορευομένων ἐν ὁδῷ θανάτου, μισήσεις πᾶν, ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρεστὸν τῷ θεῷ, μισήσεις πᾶσαν ὑπόκρισιν: οὐ μὴ ἐγκαταλίπῃς ἐντολὰς κυρίου. οὐχ ὑψώσεις σεαυτόν, ἔσῃ δὲ ταπεινόφρων κατὰ πάντα: οὐκ ἀρεῖς ἐπὶ σεαυτὸν δόξαν. οὐ λήμψῃ βουλὴν πονηρὰν κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου, οὐ δώσεις τῇ ψυχῇ σου θράσος. οὐ πορνεύσεις, οὐ μοιχεύσεις, οὐ παιδοφθορήσεις. οὐ μή σου ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐξέλθῃ ἐν ἀκαθαρσίᾳ τινῶν. οὐ λήμψῃ πρόσωπον ἐλέγξαι τινὰ ἐπὶ παραπτώματι. ἔσῃ πραΰς, ἔσῃ ἡσύχιος, ἔσῃ τρέμων τοὺς λόγους οὓς ἤκουσας. οὐ μνησικακήσεις τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου. οὐ μὴ διψυχήσῃς, πότερον ἔσται ἢ οὔ. οὐ μὴ λάβῃς ἐπὶ ματαίῳ τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου. ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὑπὲρ τὴν ψυχήν σου. οὐ φονεύσεις τέκνον ἐν φθορᾷ, οὐδὲ πάλιν γεννηθὲν ἀποκτενεῖς. οὐ μὴ ἄρῃς τὴν χεῖρά σου ἀπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ σου ἡ ἀπὸ τῆς θυγατρός σου, ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ νεότητος διδάξεις φόβου θεοῦ. οὐ μὴ γένῃ ἐπιθυμῶν τὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου, οὐ μὴ γένῃ πλεονέκτης. οὐδὲ κολληθήσῃ ἐκ ψυχῆς σου μετὰ ὑψηλῶν, ἀλλὰ μετὰ ταπεινῶν καὶ δικαίων ἀναστραφήσῃ. τὰ συμβαίνοντά σοι ἐνεργήματα ὡς ἀγαθὰ προσδέξῃ, εἰδώς, ὅτι ἄνευ θεοῦ οὐδὲν γίνεται. οὐκ ἔσῃ διγνώμων οὐδὲ γλωσσώδης, ὑποταγήσῃ κυρίοις ὡς τύπῳ θεοῦ ἐν αἰσχύνῃ καὶ φόβῳ: οὐ μὴ ἐπιτάξῃς δούλῳ σου ἡ παιδίσκῃ ἐν πικρίᾳ, τοῖς ἐπὶ τὸν αὐτὸν θεὸν ἐλπίζουσιν, μή ποτε οὐ μὴ φοβηθήσονται τὸν ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροις θεόν: ὅτι οὐκ ἦλθεν κατὰ πρόσωπον καλέσαι, ἀλλ’ ἐφ̓ οὓς τὸ πνεῦμα ἡτοίμασεν. κοινωνήσεις ἐν πᾶσιν τῷ πλησίον σου καὶ οὐκ ἐρεῖς ἴδια εἶναι: εἰ γὰρ ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ κοινωνοί ἐστε, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς φθαρτοῖς; οὐκ ἔσῃ πρόγλωσσος: παγὶς γὰρ τὸ στόμα θανάτου. ὅσον δύνασαι, ὑπὲρ τῆς ψυχῆς σου ἁγνεύσεις. μὴ γίνου πρὸς μὲν τὸ λαβεῖν ἐκτείνων τὰς χεῖρας, πρὸς δὲ τὸ δοῦναι συσπῶν. ἀγαπήσεις ὡς κόρην τοῦ ὀφθαλμοῦ σου πάντα τὸν λαλοῦντά σοι τὸν λόγον κυρίου. μνησθήσῃ ἡμέραν κρίσεως νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας, καὶ ἐκζητήσεις καθ̓ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν τὰ πρόσωπα τῶν ἁγίων, ἢ διὰ λόγου κοπιῶν καὶ πορευόμενος εἰς τὸ παρακαλέσαι καὶ μελετῶν εἰς τὸ σῶσαι ψυχὴν τῷ λόγῳ, ἢ διὰ τῶν χειρῶν σου ἐργάσῃ εἰς λύτρωσιν ἁμαρτιῶν σου. οὐ διστάσεις δοῦναι οὐδὲ διδοὺς γογγύσεις: γνώσῃ δέ, τίς ὁ τοῦ μισθοῦ καλὸς ἀνταποδότης. φυλάξεις ἃ παρέλαβες, μήτε προστιθεὶς μήτε ἀφαιρῶν. εἰς τέλος μισήσεις τὸ πονηρόν. κρινεῖς δικαίως. οὐ ποιήσεις σχίσμα, εἰρηνεύσεις δὲ μαχομένους συναγαγών. ἐξομολογήσῃ ἐπὶ ἁμαρτίαις σου. οὐ προσήξεις ἐπὶ προσευχὴν ἐν συνειδήσει πονηρᾷ. αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ὁδὸς, τοῦ φωτός.

excerpts.author: Hermas
english: He tells me, "You know that you are living here as foreigners, you servants of God, because your true city is far from this one. Since you know the city where you are going to live, why are you preparing fields, expensive arrays, buildings, and useless houses here? The one who prepares such things for this city cannot return to his own."

"You foolish, double-minded, wretched man! Do you not understand that all these things are alien and under another's power? The Lord of this city will say, 'I do not want you to dwell in my city; go out, because you do not follow my laws.' So you, having fields, houses, and many other possessions — when he casts you out, what will you do with your field, your house, and everything else you prepared for yourself?

For the Lord of this land says to you justly: 'Either follow my laws or leave my land.' So what will you do, since you have a law in your own city? On account of your fields and your other possessions, will you certainly deny your law and follow the law of this city? Watch out — it is unprofitable to deny your law. If you wish to return to your city, you will not be received, because you denied the law of your city, and you will be shut out.

Therefore, while you dwell as a foreigner, do not prepare anything more for yourself except what is sufficient, and be ready. Then when the Master of this city wants to cast you out for opposing his law, you can leave his city, go to your own, and use your law freely and joyfully.

So then, you who serve the Lord and have him in your heart: do the works of God, remembering his commands and the promises he made. Trust him that he will fulfill them, if his commands are kept. Instead of fields, buy afflicted souls, as each of you is able. Visit widows and orphans and do not overlook them. Spend your wealth and all your arrays on such fields and houses — the ones you received from God.

For the Master enriched you for this very purpose: to carry out these services for him. It is far better to buy such fields, possessions, and houses, which you will find in your city when you sojourn there. This luxury is good and holy; it has no grief or fear, but joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations — it is unprofitable for you, servants of God. Practice your own luxury, the kind in which you can rejoice. Do not go beyond it, do not touch what belongs to another, and do not desire it — for it is evil to desire what is another's. Do your own work, and you will be saved.

greek: Λέγει μοι: Οἴδατε, φησίν, ὅτι ἐπὶ ξένης κατοικεῖτε ὑμεῖς οἱ δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ: ἡ γὰρ πόλις ὑμῶν μακράν ἐστιν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης: εἰ οὖν οἴδατε, φησί, τὴν πόλιν ὑμῶν, ἐν ᾗ μέλλετε κατοικεῖν, τί ὧδε ὑμεῖς ἑτοιμάζετε ἀγροὺς καὶ παρατάξεις πολυτελεῖς καὶ οἰκοδομὰς καὶ οἰκήματα μάταια; ταῦτα οὖν ὁ ἑτοιμάζων εἰς ταύτην τὴν πόλιν οὐ δύναται ἐπανακάμψαι εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν. ἄφρον καὶ δίψυχε καὶ ταλαίπωρε ἄνθρωπε, οὐ νοεῖς, ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα ἀλλότριά εἰσι καὶ ὑπ’ ἐξουσίαν ἑτέρου εἰσίν; ἐρεῖ γὰρ ὁ κύριος τῆς πόλεως ταύτης: Οὐ θέλω σε κατοικεῖν εἰς τὴν πόλιν μου, ἀλλ’ ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης, ὅτι τοῖς νόμοις μου οὐ χρᾶσαι. σὺ οὖν ἔχων ἀγροὺς καὶ οἰκήσεις καὶ ἑτέρας ὑπάρξεις πολλάς, ἐκβαλλόμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τί ποιήσεις σου τὸν ἀγρὸν καὶ τὴν οἰκίαν καὶ τὰ λοιπά, ὅσα ἡτοίμασας σεαυτῷ; λέγει γάρ σοι δικαίως ὁ κύριος τῆς χώρας ταύτης: Ἢ τοῖς νόμοις μου χρῶ ἢ ἐκχώρει ἐκ τῆς χώρας μου. σὺ οὖν τί μέλλεις ποιεῖν, ἔχων νόμον ἐν τῇ σῇ πόλει; ἕνεκεν τῶν ἀγρῶν σου καὶ τῆς λοιπῆς ὑπάρξεως τὸν νόμον σου πάντως ἀπαρνήσῃ καὶ πορεύσῃ τῷ νόμῳ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης; βλέπε, μὴ ἀσύμφορόν ἐστιν ἀπαρνῆσαι τὸν νόμον σου: ἐὰν γὰρ ἐπανακάμψαι θελήσῃς εἰς τὴν πόλιν σου, οὐ μὴ παραδεχθήσῃ, ὅτι ἀπηρνήσω τὸν νόμον τῆς πόλεώς σου, καὶ ἐκκλεισθήσῃ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς. βλέπε οὖν σύ: ὡς ἐπὶ ξένης κατοικῶν μηδὲν πλέον ἑτοίμαζε σεαυτῷ εἰ μὴ τὴν αὐτάρκειαν τὴν ἀρκετήν σοι, καὶ ἕτοιμος γίνου, ἵνα, ὅταν θέλῃ ὁ δεσπότης τῆς πόλεως ταύτης ἐκβαλεῖν σε ἀντιταξάμενον τῷ νόμῳ αὐτοῦ, ἐξέλθῃς ἐκ τῆς πόλεως αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπέλθῃς ἐν τῇ πόλει σου καὶ τῷ σῷ νόμῳ χρήσῃ ἀνυβρίστως ἀγαλλιώμενος. βλέπετε οὖν ὑμεῖς οἱ δουλεύοντες τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ ἔχοντες αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν καρδίαν: ἐργάζεσθε τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ μνημονεύοντες τῶν ἐντολῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν ὧν ἐπηγγείλατο, καὶ πιστεύσατε αὐτῷ, ὅτι ποιήσει αὐτάς, ἐὰν αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὐτοῦ φυλαχθῶσιν. ἀντὶ ἀγρῶν οὖν ἀγοράζετε ψυχὰς θλιβομένας, καθά τις δυνατός ἐστι, καὶ χήρας καὶ ὀρφανοὺς ἐπισκέπτεσθε καὶ μὴ παραβλέπετε αὐτούς, καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον ὑμῶν καὶ τὰς παρατάξεις πάσας εἰς τοιούτους ἀγροὺς καὶ οἰκίας δαπανᾶτε, ἃς ἐλάβετε παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπλούτισεν ὑμᾶς ὁ δεσπότης, ἵνα ταύτας τὰς διακονίας τελέσητε αὐτῷ: πολὺ βέλτιόν ἐστι τοιούτους ἀγροὺς ἀγοράζειν καὶ κτήματα καὶ οἴκους, οὓς εὑρήσεις ἐν τῇ πόλει σου, ὅταν ἐπιδημήσῃς εἰς αὐτήν. αὕτη ἡ πολυτέλεια καλὴ καὶ ἱερά, λύπην μὴ ἔχουσα μηδὲ φόβον, ἔχουσα δὲ χαράν. τὴν οὖν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἐθνῶν μὴ πράσσετε: ἀσύμφορον γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῖν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ. τὴν δὲ ἰδίαν πολυτέλειαν πράσσετε, ἐν ᾗ δύνασθε χαρῆναι, καὶ μὴ παραχαράσσετε μηδὲ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου ἅψησθε μηδὲ ἐπιθυμεῖτε αὐτοῦ: πονηρὸν γάρ ἐστιν ἀλλοτρίων ἐπιθυμεῖν. τὸ δὲ σὸν ἔργον ἐργάζου, καὶ σωθήσῃ.

excerpts.author: Hermas
english: After I finished writing this book, the messenger who had handed me over to the shepherd arrived at the house where I was staying. He sat down on the couch and took his place at the shepherd’s right hand. Then he called me over and said: “I have entrusted you and your household to this shepherd so that he may protect you.” “Very well, Lord,” I replied. “If you want to be shielded from every affliction and every cruelty,” he continued, “and to succeed in every good work and word and to possess all the virtue of righteousness, then follow the commands I gave you. You will then be able to master all wickedness. For if you keep his commands, every desire and pleasure of this world will become subject to you, and success in every good endeavor will follow you. Take his maturity and modesty into yourself. Tell everyone that he holds great honor and dignity with the Lord, that he is a mighty and powerful guardian in his office. To him alone throughout the whole world has the authority of repentance been given. Does he not seem powerful to you? Yet you despise the maturity and modesty he shows toward you.”

I said to the messenger, “Ask him, Lord, since he has been in my house, whether I have done anything out of order or have offended him in any way.” The messenger answered, “I know that you have done nothing out of order, nor will you do so. That is why I am speaking with you now—so that you may persevere. He holds a good opinion of you before me. Now, you must tell these words to the others, so that those who have repented or will repent may share your conviction, and so that he may speak well of them before me and I before the Lord.”

I said, “Lord, I will proclaim the Lord’s mighty deeds to everyone. I hope that all who have sinned before, upon hearing this, will gladly repent and recover life.” The messenger replied, “Remain in this ministry and fulfill it. Whoever carries out these commands will have life and great honor with the Lord. Whoever fails to keep them flees from life itself and sets himself against the shepherd; they do not follow his commands but hand themselves over to death, and each becomes guilty of his own blood. But I tell you this so that you may serve these commands and find a remedy for your sins.”

He went on: “I have sent you these virgins to live with you, because I saw they are well-disposed toward you. They are your helpers, enabling you to keep these commands more fully; these commands cannot be kept without them. I see they are glad to be with you, but I will command them never to leave your house. You must simply keep your house pure, for they gladly dwell in a clean house—they are pure, chaste, diligent, and possess all grace with the Lord. If your house remains pure, they will stay with you. But if even a small defilement occurs, they will leave immediately, for these virgins do not tolerate any defilement at all.”

I said to the messenger, “Lord, I hope to please them so that they will gladly live in my house forever. Just as the shepherd to whom you entrusted me does not blame me, so these virgins will not blame me either.” The messenger said to the shepherd, “I know that the servant of God wants to live and will keep these commands and will establish the virgins in purity.” After saying this, he handed me back to the shepherd and called the virgins. He told them, “I see that you gladly live in this man’s house. I commend him and his house to you, so that you never depart from it.” The virgins received these words gladly.

Then the messenger said to me: “Conduct yourself courageously in this ministry. Proclaim the Lord’s mighty deeds to everyone, and you will find grace in this ministry. Whoever walks in these commands will live and be happy; whoever neglects them will not live and will be miserable. Tell everyone not to stop—whoever can do what is right should do it, for practicing good works benefits them. I also say that every person must be rescued from trouble. The one who is in need and suffers daily hardship endures great torment and necessity. Whoever rescues such a soul from necessity gains great joy. The one afflicted by such trouble suffers torment equal to a prisoner in chains. Many, unable to bear such calamities, bring death upon themselves. Therefore, whoever knows of such a person’s calamity and does not rescue him commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood. So do good works, all of you who have received them from the Lord, lest the tower’s structure be consumed while you delay. The building work has been halted because of you. Unless you hurry to do what is right, the tower will be consumed and you will be excluded.”
After he had spoken with me, he rose from the couch, took the shepherd and the virgins, and departed, telling me that he would send the shepherd and the virgins back to my house.

latin: postquam perscripseram librum hunc, venit nuntius ille, qui me tradiderat huic pastori, in domum, in qua eram, et consedit supra lectum, et adstitit ad dexteram hic pastor. deinde vocavit me et haec mihi dixit: tradidi te, inquit, et domum tuam huic pastori, ut ab eo protegi possis. ita, inquam, domine. si vis ergo protegi, inquit, ab omni vexatione et ab omni saevitia, successum autem habere in omni opere bono atque verbo et omnem virtutem aequitatis, in mandatis huius ingredere, quae dedi tibi, et poteris dominari omni nequitiae. custodienti enim tibi mandata huius subiecta erit omnis cupiditas et dulcedo saeculi huius, successus vero in omni bono negotio te sequetur. maturitatem huius et modestiam suscipe in te et die omnibus, in magno honore esse eum et dignitate apud dominum et magnae potestatis eum praesidem esse et potentem in officio suo. huic soli per totum orbem paenitentiae potestas tributa est. potensne tibi videtur esse? sed vos maturitatem huius et verecundiam, quam in vos habet, despicitis. dico ei : interroga ipsum, doniine, ex quo in domo mea est, an aliquid extra ordinem fecerim, ex quo eum offenderim. et ego, inquit, scio nihil extra ordinem fecisse te neque esse facturum. et ideo haec loquor tecum, ut perseveres. bene enim de te hic apud me existimavit. tu autem ceteris haec verba dices, ut et illi, qui egerunt aut acturi sunt paenitentiam, eadem quae tu sentiant et hic apud me de his bene interpretetur et ego apud dominum. et ego, inquam, domine, omni homini indico magnalia domini; spero autem, quia omnes, qui antea peccaverunt, si haec audiant, libenter acturi sunt paenitentiam vitam recuperantes. permane ergo, inquit, in hoc ministerio et consuinma illud. quicumque autem mandata huius efficiunt, habebunt vitam, et hic apud dominum magnum honorem. quicumque vero huius mandata non ser­vant, fugiunt a sua vita et ilium adversus ; nec mandata eius sequuntur, sed morti se tradunt et unusquisque eorum reus fit sanguinis sui. tibi autem dico, ut servias mandatis his, et remedium peccatorum habebis. misi autem tibi has virgines, ut habitent tecum; vidi enim eas affabiles tibi esse. habes ergo eas adiutrices, quo magis possis huius mandata servare; non potest enim fieri, ut sine his virginibus haec mandata serventur. Video autem eas libenter esse tecum; sed ego praecipiam eis, ut omnino a domo tua non discedant. tu tantum communda domum tuam; in munda enim domo libenter habitabunt; mundae enim sunt atque castae et industriae et omnes habentes gratiam apud dominum. igitur si habuerint domum tuam puram, tecum permanebunt. sin autem pusillum aliquid inquinationis acciderit, protinus a domo tua recedent; hae enim virgines nullum omnino diligunt inquinationem. dico ei: spero me, domine, placiturum eis, ita ut in domo mea libenter habitent σεμπερ. καὶ ὥσπερ οὗτος, ᾧ παρέδωκάς με, οὐ μέμφεταί με, οὐδὲ αὗται μέμψονταί me. λέγει τῷ ποιμένι: Οἶδα, ὅτι ὁ δοῦλος τοῦ θεοῦ θέλει ζῆν καὶ τηρήσει τὰς ἐντολὰς ταύτας καὶ τὰς παρθένους ἐν καθαρότητι καταστήσει. ταῦτα εἰπὼν τῷ ποιμένι πάλιν παρέδωκέν με καὶ τὰς παρθένους καλέσας... λέγει αὐταῖς: θυονιαμ video vos libenter in domo huius habitare, commendo eum vobis et domum eius, ut a domo eius non recedatis omnino. illae vero haec verba libenter audierunt. ait deinde mihi: Viriliter in ministerio hoc conversare, omni homini indica magnalia domini, et habebis gratiam in hoc ministerio. quicumque ergo in his mandatis ambulaverit, vivet et felix erit in vita sua; quicumque vero neglexerit, non vivet et erit infelix in vita sua. dic omnibus, ut non cessent, quicumque recte facere possunt; bona opera exercere utile est illis. dico autem, omnem hominem de incommodis eripi oportere. et is enim̆, qui eget et in cotidiana vita patitur incommoda, in magno tormento est ac necessitate. qui igitur huiusmodi animam eripit de necessitate, magnum gaudium sibi adquirit. is enim, qui huiusmodi vexatur incommodo, pari tormento cruciatur atque torquet se qui in vincula est. multi enim propter huiusmodi calamitates, cum eas sufferre non possunt, mortem sibi adducunt. qui novit igitur calamitatem huiusmodi hominis et non eripit eum, magnum peccatum admittit et reus fit sanguinis eius. facite igitur opera bona, quicumque accepistis a domino, ne, dum tardatis facere, consummetur structura turris. propter vos enim intermissum est opus aedificationis eius. nisi festinetis igitur facere recte, consummabitur turris, et excludemini. postquam vero locutus est mecum, surrexit de lecto et apprehenso pastore et virginibus abiit, dicens autem mihi, remissurum se pastorem ilium et virgines in domum meam.

excerpts.author: Hermas
english: I was walking through the field, looking at an elm and a vine and thinking about them and their fruit, when the Shepherd appeared to me. He asked, "What are you debating within yourself about the elm and the vine?" I replied, "Lord, I am discussing it because they are remarkably suited to each other." He said, "These two trees are set as a pattern for the servants of God." I told him, "Lord, I want to understand the pattern of these trees you speak of." He asked, "Do you see the elm and the vine?" I answered, "Yes, Lord, I see them." He explained, "This vine bears fruit, but the elm is a barren tree. However, if this vine does not climb up onto the elm, it cannot bear much fruit lying thrown on the ground, and whatever fruit it does produce is rotten because it is not suspended on the elm. But when the vine is thrown upon the elm, it bears fruit both from itself and from the elm. So do you see that the elm also yields a great deal of fruit, not less than the vine, but actually more?" I asked, "How can it be more, Lord?" He said, "Because the vine hanging on the elm produces abundant good fruit, but thrown on the ground it yields only a little rotten fruit."

He continued, "This parable is set for the servants of God, for the poor and the rich." I said, "Lord, make it known to me." He said, "Listen. The rich man has money, but he is poor toward the Lord, distracted by his own wealth. He has very little prayer and confession to the Lord, and what he does have is feeble, small, and lacks power. But when the rich man approaches the poor man and supplies what he needs, he believes that by working for the poor man he will find his reward from God. For the poor man is rich in prayer and confession, and his prayer has great power with God. The rich man therefore supplies the poor man with everything without hesitation. The poor man, being supplied by the rich man, prays to God, giving thanks on behalf of the one who gave to him. And the rich man keeps caring for the poor man so that his life may continue uninterrupted, because he knows that the poor man's prayer is acceptable and rich toward the Lord. Both, then, complete the work. The poor man works by means of the prayer in which he is rich, which he received from the Lord; he gives this back to the Lord who supplies him. And the rich man, in the same way, provides the wealth he received from the Lord to the poor man without hesitation. This is a great and acceptable work before God, because he made good use of his wealth and labored for the poor man from the Lord's gifts and carried out the ministry correctly."

He added, "Among people, the elm appears not to bear fruit, and they do not know or understand that when drought comes, the elm, having water, sustains the vine, and the vine, having uninterrupted water, yields double fruit — both for itself and for the elm. So also the poor, interceding for the rich before the Lord, fill up their wealth, and again the rich, supplying the poor with what they need, fill up their prayers. They become, then, both partners in the work of righteousness. The one who does these things will not be abandoned by God, but will be written in the books of the living. Blessed are those who possess and understand, because they are enriched by the Lord; for the one who understands this will be able to serve something good."

greek: Περιπατοῦντός μου εἰς τὸν ἀγρὸν καὶ κατανοοῦντος πτελέαν καὶ ἄμπελον καὶ διακρίνοντος περὶ αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν καρπῶν αὐτῶν, φανεροῦταί μοι ὁ ποιμὴν καὶ λέγει: Τί σὺ ἐν ἑαυτῷ ζητεῖς περὶ τῆς πτελέας καὶ τῆς ἀμπέλου; Συζητῶ, φημί, κύριε, ὅτι εὐπρεπέσταταί εἰσιν ἀλλήλαις. Ταῦτα τὰ δύο δένδρα, φησίν, εἰς τύπον κεῖνται τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ. Ἤθελον, φημί, γνῶναι τὸν τύπον τῶν δένδρων τούτων ὧν λέγεις. Βλέπεις, φησί, τὴν πτελέαν καὶ τὴν ἄμπελον; Βλέπω, φημί, κύριε. Ἡ ἄμπελος, φησίν, αὕτη καρπὸν φέρει, ἡ δὲ πτελέα ξύλον ἄκαρπόν ἐστιν: ἀλλ’ ἡ ἄμπελος αὕτη ἐὰν μὴ ἀναβῇ ἐπὶ τὴν πτελέαν, οὐ δύναται καρποφορῆσαι πολὺ ἐρριμμένη χαμαί, καὶ ὃν φέρει καρπόν, σεσηπότα φέρει μὴ κρεμαμένη ἐπὶ τῆς πτελέας, ὅταν οὖν ἐπιρριφῇ ἡ ἄμπελος ἐπὶ τὴν πτελέαν, καὶ παῤ ἑαυτῆς φέρει καρπὸν καὶ παρὰ τῆς πτελέας. βλέπεις οὖν, ὅτι καὶ ἡ πτελέα πολὺν καρπὸν δίδωσιν, οὐκ ἐλάσσονα τῆς ἀμπέλου, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ πλείονα. Πῶς, φημί, κύριε, πλείονα; Ὅτι, φησίν, ἡ ἄμπελος κρεμαμένη ἐπὶ τὴν πτελέαν τὸν καρπὸν πολὺν καὶ καλὸν δίδωσιν, ἐρριμμένη δὲ χαμαὶ ὀλίγον καὶ σαπρὸν φέρει. αὕτη οὖν ἡ παραβολὴ εἰς τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ κεῖται, εἰς πτωχὸν καὶ πλούσιον. Πῶς, φημί, κύριε, γνώρισον μοι. Ἄκουε, φησίν: ὁ μὲν πλούσιος ἔχει χρήματα, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὸν κύριον πτωχεύει, περισπώμενος περὶ τὸν πλοῦτον ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ λίαν μικρὰν ἔχει τὴν ἔντευξιν καὶ τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν πρὸς τὸν κύριον, καὶ ἣν ἔχει, βληχρὰν καὶ μικρὰν καὶ ἄλλην μὴ ἔχουσαν δύναμιν. ὅταν οὖν ἐπαναπάῃ ἐπὶ τὸν πένητα ὁ πλούσιος καὶ χορηγήσῃ αὐτῷ τὰ δέοντα, πιστεύει, ὅτι ἐὰν ἐργάσηται εἰς τὸν πένητα δυνηθήσεται τὸν μισθὸν εὑρεῖν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ: ὅτι ὁ πένης πλούσιός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἐντεύξει καὶ ἐν τῇ ἐξομολογήσει καὶ δύναμιν μεγάλην ἔχει παρὰ τῷ θεῷ ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτοῦ. ἐπιχορηγεῖ οὖν ὁ πλούσιος τῷ πένητι πάντα ἀδιστάκτως. ὁ πένης δὲ ἐπιχορηγούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ πλουσίου ἐντυγχάνει τῷ θεῷ εὐχαριστῶν αὐτῷ, ὑπὲρ τοῦ διδόντος αὐτῷ: κἀκεῖνος ἔτι ἐπισπουδάζει περὶ τοῦ πένητος, ἵνα ἀδιάλειπτος γένηται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ: οἶδε γάρ, ὅτι ἡ τοῦ πένητος ἔντευξις προσδεκτή ἐστι καὶ πλουσία πρὸς κύριον. ἀμφότεροι οὖν τὸ ἔργον τελοῦσιν: ὁ μὲν πένης ἐργάζεται τῇ ἐντεύξει, ἐν ᾗ πλουτεῖ, ἣν ἔλαβεν παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου: ταύτην ἀποδίδωσι τῷ κυρίῳ τῷ ἐπιχορηγοῦντι αὐτῷ. καὶ ὁ πλούσιος ὡσαύτως τὸ πλοῦτος, ὃ ἔλαβεν παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου, ἀδιστάκτως παρέχεται τῷ πένητι. καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον μέγα ἐστὶ καὶ δεκτὸν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ, ὅτι συνῆκεν ἐπὶ τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰργάσατο εἰς τὸν πένητα ἐκ τῶν δωρημάτων τοῦ κυρίου καὶ ἐτέλεσε τὴν διακονίαν ὀρθῶς. παρὰ τοῖς οὖν ἀνθρώποις ἡ πτελέα δοκεῖ καρπὸν μὴ φέρειν, καὶ οὐκ οἴδασιν οὐδὲ νοοῦσιν, ὅτι, ὅταν ἀβροχία γένηται, ἡ πτελέα ἔχουσα ὕδωρ τρέφει τὴν ἄμπελον καὶ ἡ ἄμπελος ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχουσα τὸ ὕδωρ διπλοῦν τὸν καρπὸν ἀποδίδωσι, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς πτελέας. οὕτως καὶ οἱ πένητες ὑπὲρ τῶν πλουσίων ἐντυγχάνοντες πρὸς τὸν κύριον πληροφοροῦσι τὸ πλοῦτος αὐτῶν, καὶ πάλιν οἱ πλούσιοι χορηγοῦντες τοῖς πένησι τὰ δέοντα πληροφοροῦσι τὰς εὐχὰς αὐτῶν. γίνονται οὖν ἀμφότεροι κοινωνοὶ τοῦ ἔργου τοῦ δικαίου. ταῦτα οὖν ὁ ποιῶν οὐκ ἐγκαταλειφθήσεται ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ’ ἔσται γεγραμμένος εἰς τὰς βίβλους τῶν ζώντων. μακάριοι οἱ ἔχοντες καὶ συνιέντες, ὅτι παρὰ τοῦ κυρίου πλουτίζονται, ὁ γὰρ συνίων τοῦτο δυνήσεται καὶ διακονῆσαί τι ἀγαθόν.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I will now take up the affairs of the Christian sect, so that after refuting the charges against us I may display what is good. We are a body knit together by conscience, religion, divine discipline, and the covenant of our hope. We assemble as a congregation to address God in prayer with united voices, as though with a single voice. This power is pleasing to God. We pray also for the emperors, for their ministers and authorities, for the condition of the world, for peace, and for a delay of the end. We are driven to revisit the divine writings, whether the quality of the present times demands warning or recognition. Surely we feed our faith with holy words, lift up our hope, fix our confidence, and tighten the discipline of the precepts even under compulsion; there we also have exhortations, castigations, and divine censure. For judgment is carried out with great weight, as before the very gaze of God, and it serves as a prejudgment of the final judgment, if anyone has so offended that he is excluded from the communion of prayer, assembly, and all holy intercourse. Approved elders preside, having won this honor not by payment but by testimony; for nothing that belongs to God is purchased with a price. Even if there is a kind of treasury, it is not collected from an honorary sum as though religion were being redeemed; rather each person contributes a small monthly amount on a fixed day, or whenever he wishes, and only if he wishes and is able, for no one is compelled but all give freely. These are, as it were, deposits of piety. For from them nothing is spent on banquets or drinking bouts or useless waste, but on feeding and burying the needy, on orphan boys and girls destitute of property and parents, on aged members of our household, on shipwreck victims, on those in mines, on those exiled to islands, or in custody — provided they have become disciples of the confession of God's sect for that very reason. Yet this very practice of love earns us a bad reputation with some people. 'Look,' they say, 'how they love one another' — while they themselves hate one another; 'and how they are ready to die for one another' — while they themselves are more ready to kill one another. Moreover, they slander us precisely because we are called brothers; I suspect for no other reason than that among them every claim of blood kinship is feigned out of mere affectation. We are your brothers too, by the law of nature from a single mother, even though you are hardly human because you are evil brothers. But how much more worthily are those called and regarded brothers who have acknowledged one God as Father, who have drunk one Spirit of holiness, who have been born from one womb of ignorance into one light of truth. Perhaps we are thought less legitimate because no tragedy cries out over our brotherhood, or because we are brothers by a family substance that among you almost destroys brotherhood. Therefore those who are mingled in soul and spirit entertain no doubt about sharing possessions. All things are common among us except wives. In that one point we dissolve the partnership, which is the only partnership other people practice — people who not only usurp the marriages of friends but even obligingly lend their own wives to friends, following, I suppose, the discipline of the greatest and wisest men, the Greek Socrates and the Roman Cato, who shared with friends the wives they had married for the sake of children and for begetting them elsewhere, I do not know whether the wives were willing; for why would they care about chastity when husbands gave it away so easily? O example of Attic wisdom, O Roman gravity! The philosopher acts as a pimp and a censor. What wonder, then, that such great love is practiced among us? Even our dinners — apart from those infamous for crime — you brand as prodigal. Of us it was said, surely, that we feast as if we would die tomorrow, yet build as if we would never die. But who sees a straw in another's eye more easily than a beam in his own? The air grows sour with the belching of so many tribes, curiae, and decuriae. A necessary creditor will be required for the expenses of the Salian feasts. The accountants calculate the costs of the Herculanean tables and pollucta. The choice of cooks is announced for the Apaturia, the Dionysia, and the Attic mysteries. Spartan broths are stirred up by the smoke of the Serapian dinner. Yet only the Christian dining-room comes under scrutiny. Our dinner, by its very name, shows its rationale: it is called by the Greek word for love. Whatever the cost, it is gain to spend in the name of piety, because we relieve every needy person with this refreshment — not as parasites who fawn for the glory of serving liberty under the belly's authority amid insults and fattening, but as those for whom the contemplation of the moderate is greater before God. If the cause of the dinner is honorable, judge the rest of the order of discipline, which belongs to the office of religion: it admits nothing base, nothing immodest; we do not recline before prayer to God has been tasted; we eat only as much as the hungry can take; we drink only as much as is useful for the chaste. Thus they are satisfied in such a way that they remember they must worship God even through the night; thus they converse as those who know the Lord is listening. After the hand-washing and the lights, each is invited to sing to God from the holy scriptures or from his own gift; and so it is proved how he has drunk. Prayer brings the dinner to an end. From there they depart not into crowds of the lewd, nor into classes of dissolute talk, nor into outbreaks of lasciviousness, but to the same care for modesty and chastity, as those who have not so much dined as disciplined themselves. This gathering of Christians is rightly deemed illicit only if it is to be condemned on the same grounds as illicit gatherings; if anyone complains of it under the same title as a complaint against factions. For whose destruction do we ever assemble? We are gathered for this — which we are also when dispersed; we are a whole — which we are also as individuals; we harm no one, we grieve no one. When the upright, the good, the pious, and the chaste come together, it is not to be called a faction, but a curia.

latin: Edam jam nunc ego ipsa negotia christianae factionis, ut qui mala refutaverim, bona ostendam. Corpus sumus de conscientia religionis et disciplinae divinitate et spei foedere. Coimus in coetum et congregationem, ut ad Deum, quasi manu facta, precationibus ambiamus. Haec vis Deo grata est. Oramus etiam pro imperatoribus, pro ministeriis eorum ac potestatibus, pro statu seculi, pro rerum quiete, pro mora finis. Cogimur ad litterarum divinarum commemorationem, si quid praesentium temporum qualitas aut praemonere cogit aut recognoscere. Certe fidem sanctis vocibus pascimus, spem erigimus, fiduciam figimus, disciplinam praeceptorum nihilominus in compulsationibus densamus; ibidem etiam exhortationnes, castigationnes et censura divina. Nam et judicatur magno cum pondere, ut apud certos de Dei conspectu, summumque futuri judicii praejudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit, ut a communicatione orationis et conventus et omnis sancti commercii relegetur, Praesident probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio sed testimonio adepti; neque enim pretio ulla res Dei constat. Etiam si quod arcae genus est, non de honoraria summa, quasi redemptae religionis congregatur; modicam unusquisque stipem menstrua die, vel quum velit, et si modo velit et si modo possit, apponit: nam nemo compellitur, sed sponte confert. Haec quasi deposita pietatis sunt. Nam inde non epulis nec potaculis, nec ingratis voratrinis dispensatur, sed egenis alendis humandisque, et pueris ac puellis re ac parentibus destitutis, jamque domesticis senibus, item naufragis, et si qui in metallis, et si qui in insulis, vel in custodiis, duntaxat ex caussa Dei sectae alumni confessionis suae fiunt. Sed ejusmodi vel maxime dilectionis operatio notam nobis inurit penes quosdam. Vide, inquiunt, ut invicem se diligant: ipsi enim invicem oderunt; et ut pro alterutro mori sint parati: ipsi enim ad occidendum alterutrum paratiores erunt. Sed et quod fratrum appellatione censemur, non alias, opinor, infamant, quam quod apud ipsos omne sanguinis nomen de affectatione simulatum est. Fratres autem etiam vestri sumus, jure naturae matris unius, etsi vos parum homines, quia mali fratres. At quanto dignius fratres et dicuntur et habentur, qui unum patrem Deum agnoverunt, qui unum Spiritum biberunt sanctitatis, qui de uno utero ignorantiae ejusdem ad unam lucem expaverunt veritatis. Sed eo fortasse minus legitimi existimamur, quia nulla de nostra fraternitate tragoedia exclamat, vel quia ex substantia familiari fratres sumus, quae penes vos fere dirimit fraternitatem. Itaque qui animo animaque miscemur, nihil de rei communicatione dubitamus. Omnia indiscreta sunt apud nos, praeter uxores: in isto loco consortium solvimus, in quo solo caeteri homines consortium exercent, qui non amicorum solummodo matrimonia usurpant, sed et sua amicis patientissime subministrant, ex illa, credo, majorum et sapientissimorum disciplina, Graeci Socratis et Romani Catonis, qui uxores suas amicis communicaverunt, quas in matrimonium duxerant liberorum caussa et alibi creandorum, nescio quidem an invitas; quid enim de castitate curarent, quam mariti tam facile donaverant? O sapientiae Atticae, o Romanae gravitatis exemplum! Leno est philosophus et censor. Quid ergo mirum, si tanta caritas convivatur? Nam et coenulas nostras, praeterquam sceleris infames, ut prodigas quoque suggillatis. De nobis scilicet Diogenis dictum est: Megarenses obsonant quasi crastina die morituri, aedificant vero quasi nunquam morituri. Sed stipulam quis in alieno oculo facilius perspicit, quam in suo trabem. Tot tribubus et curiis et decuriis ructantibus acescit aër. Saliis coenaturis creditor erit necessarius. Herculanarum decimarum et polluctorum sumptus tabularii supputabant. Apaturiis, Dionysiis, mysteriis Atticis coquorum delectus indicentur. Ad fumum coenae Serapiacae sparteoli excitabuntur. De solo triclinio Christianorum retractatur, Coena nostra de nomine rationem sui ostendit; id vocatur, quod dilectio penes Graecos est. Quantiscumque sumptibus constet, lucrum est pietatis nomine facere sumptum, siquidem inopes quosque refrigerio isto juvamus, non qua penes vos parasiti affectant ad gloriam famulandae libertatis sub auctoramento ventris inter contumelias saginandi, sed qua penes Deum major est contemplatio mediocrium. Si honesta caussa est convivii, reliquum ordinem disciplinae aestimate, qui sit de religionnis officio: nihil vilitatis, nihil immodestiae admittit; non prius discumbitur, quam oratio ad Deum praegustetur; editur quantum esurientes capiunt; bibitur quantum pudicis est utile. Ita saturantur, ut qui meminerint etiam per noctem adorandum Deum sibi esse; ita fabulantur, ut qui sciant dominum audire. Post aquam manualem et lumina, ut quisque de scripturis sanctis vel de proprio ingenio potest provocatur in medium Deo canere hinc probatur quomodo biberit. Oeque oratio convivium dirimit. Inde disceditur non in catervas caesionum neque n classes discursationum, nec in eruptiones lasciviarum, sed ad eamdem curam modestiae et pudicitiae ut qui non tam coenam coenaverint, quam disciplinam. Haec coitio christianorum merito sane illicita, si illicitis pari merito damnanda, [si non dissimilis damnandis,] si quis de ea queritur eo titulo, quo de factionibus querela est. In cujus perniciem aliquando convenimus? Hoc sumus congregati, quod et dispersi; hoc universi, quod et singuli; neminem laedentes, neminem contristantes. Quum probi, quum boni coeunt, quum pii, quum casti congregantur, non est factio dicenda, sed curia.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Since we have shown that the arrangement for converting humanity — an arrangement that is good and salvific — is necessarily received from the Word for repentance and for preventing sins, the next thing to consider is the Word's gentleness. The Word has been shown to be just, and he sets forth his own counsels, which are persuasive toward salvation; through these he wants us to know what is good and profitable by the Father's will (Proverbs 8:4-6). Consider these matters: the good belongs to the encomiastic mode, the profitable to the advisory mode. The advisory mode relates both to urging on and to turning away, while the encomiastic mode becomes both praising and blaming. How does the advisory mind become urging, and how does it become turning away? Likewise, how does the encomiastic become blaming, and how does it become praising? The righteous Paedagogus, who has aimed at our profit, is concerned with these very things. But the blaming and turning-away kind has already been shown to us earlier; now we must employ the urging and praising kind, and, as on a balance, weigh the equal weights of the just scales.

The Paedagogus therefore uses the urging toward what is profitable through Solomon, saying: "I call to you, O men, and I lift my voice to the children of men. Hear me, for I will speak noble things" (Proverbs 8:4-6) and what follows. He advises the things that save, because advice serves for choosing and fleeing, just as he does through David: "Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psalm 1:1-3). Advice has three parts: one takes its examples from past times — for instance, what the Hebrews suffered when they worshipped the golden calf, and what they suffered when they committed fornication, and similar things; a second is understood from present times — that is, what is perceived by the senses, as was said to those asking the Lord, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" — "Go and tell John: the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear, the lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, and blessed is the one who is not offended by me" (Matthew 11:4-6). This, then, is what David prophesied: "As we have heard, so have we seen." The third part of advice is constituted from future things, which commands us to guard against what will happen; as it is also said: "Those who fall into sins will be thrown into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matthew 8:12) and similar passages. It is clear from these that the Lord, through every therapy, calls humanity to salvation. With consolation he comforts sins, lessening desire and at the same time giving hope for salvation.

greek: Εἰ τοίνυν τὴν περὶ τὸ ἐπιστύφειν τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα οἰκονομίαν, ἀγαθὴν οὖσαν καὶ σωτήριον, ἀναγκαίως ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου παραλαμβανομένην ἐπεδείξαμεν πρός τε μετάνοιαν καὶ πρὸς τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὴν κώλυσιν εὔθετον γενομένην, ἑξῆς ἂν εἴη σκοπεῖν τὸ ἤπιον τοῦ λόγου· δίκαιος γὰρ οὗτος ἀποδέδεικται καὶ τὰς ἰδίας παρατίθεται γνώμας τὰς πρὸς σωτηρίαν παρακλητικάς, δι᾿ ὧν καὶ τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ συμφέρον πατρικῷ θελήματι γνωρίζειν ἡμῖν βούλεται. σκόπει δὲ ταῦτα· τὸ μὲν καλὸν τοῦ ἐγκωμιαστικοῦ, τὸ δὲ συμφέρον τοῦ συμβουλευτικοῦ· καὶ γὰρ οὖν τοῦ μὲν συμβουλευτικοῦ σχέσις τὸ προτρεπτικὸν καὶ ἀποτρεπτικόν, τοῦ δὲ ἐγκωμιαστικοῦ τὸ ἐπαινετικόν τε καὶ ψεκτικὸν γίνεται. πῶς γὰρ ἔχουσα ἡ διάνοια ἡ συμβουλευτικὴ προτρεπτικὴ γίνεται καὶ πῶς ἔχουσα ἀποτρεπτική. ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐγκωμιαστικὸν πῶς μὲν ἔχον ψεκτικὸν γίνεται, πῶς δὲ ἔχον ἐπαινετικόν· περὶ ἃ καταγίνεται μάλιστα ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ὁ δίκαιος ὁ τοῦ ἡμετέρου συμφέροντος ἐστοχασμένος. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τὸ μὲν ψεκτικὸν καὶ ἀποτρεπτικὸν εἶδος ὑποδέδεικται ἡμῖν ἤδη πρότερον, νῦν δὲ αὖ τὸ προτρεπτικὸν καὶ ἐπαινετικὸν μεταχειριστέον καὶ καθάπερ ἐπὶ ζυγοῦ τὰς ἰσοστασίους ἀντισηκώσωμεν τοῦ δικαίου πλάστιγγας. Τῇ μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τὰ συμφέροντα προτροπῇ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς διὰ Σολομῶντος ὧδέ πως χρῆται· »ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς, ἄνθρωποι, παρακαλῶ καὶ προΐεμαι ἐμὴν φωνὴν υἱοῖς ἀνθρώπων· ἐπακούσατέ μου, σεμνὰ γὰρ ἐρῶ« καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. συμβουλεύει δὲ τὰ σωτήρια, ὅτι ἡ συμβουλὴ πρὸς αἵρεσίν ἐστι καὶ φυγὴν ἐπιτήδειος, καθάπερ ποιεῖ διὰ τοῦ Δαβὶδ λέγων »μακάριος ἀνὴρ ὃς οὐκ ἐπορεύθη ἐν βουλῇ ἀσεβῶν καὶ ἐν ὁδῷ ἁμαρτωλῶν οὐκ ἔστη καὶ ἐπὶ καθέδραν λοιμῶν οὐκ ἐκάθισεν· ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ κυρίου τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ.« τῆς δὲ συμβουλίας μέρη τρία, τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῶν παρεληλυθότων χρόνων λαμβάνον τὰ παραδείγματα, οἷον τί ἔπαθον οἱ Ἑβραῖοι τῷ χρυσῷ εἰδωλολατρήσαντες ἐν μόσχῳ, καὶ τί ἔπαθον ἐκπορνεύσαντες καὶ τὰ ὅμοια, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῶν παρόντων χρόνων κατανοούμενον, οἷον αἰσθητικῶς καταλαμβανόμενον, ὡς ἐκεῖνο εἴρηται πρὸς τοὺς ἐρομένους τὸν κύριον »εἰ αὐτὸς εἶ ὁ Χριστός, ἢ ἄλλον περιμένομεν«· »ἀπέλθετε. καὶ εἴπατε Ἰωάννῃ· τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέπουσιν, κωφοὶ ἀκούουσιν, λεπροὶ καθαρίζονται, ἀνίστανται νεκροί, καὶ μακάριός ἐστιν ὃς ἐὰν μὴ σκανδαλισθῇ ἐν ἐμοί.« τοῦτ᾿ ἄρα ἦν ὃ προφητεύων εἴρηκεν Δαβὶδ »καθὼς ἠκούσαμεν, οὕτως καὶ εἴδομεν«. ἐκ δὲ τῶν μελλόντων τὸ τρίτον συνίσταται μέρος τῆς συμβουλίας, ᾧ τὰ ἀποβησόμενα κελεύει φυλάττεσθαι· καθὸ κἀκεῖνο εἴρηται· »οἱ δὲ ἁμαρτίαις περιπεσόντες βληθήσονται εἰς τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον· ἐκεῖ ἔσται ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων« καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια· ὡς ἐκ τούτων εἶναι συμφανὲς διὰ πάσης θεραπείας χωροῦντα τὸν κύριον εἰς σωτηρίαν ἐκκαλεῖσθαι τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα. τῇ δὲ παραμυθίᾳ παρηγορεῖ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, μειῶν μὲν τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν, ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἐλπίδα ἐνδιδοὺς εἰς σωτηρίαν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: I would also advise married men to love their wives at home, not face to face as if they were servants. Aristotle, after all, never even allows one to laugh with slaves; how much more necessary is it that a wife appear devoted to her husband in their presence. It is better for those who begin from marriage to display dignity at home. For the greatest union of self-control breathes out pure pleasure. The tragedy puts it wonderfully: 'Alas, alas, women, for neither gold, nor tyranny, nor the ornament of wealth holds so many varied pleasures as the judgment of a good man and a pious woman—thinking justly and bravely.' These are the commands of justice, and they must not be rejected even though they have been uttered by those who possess worldly wisdom.

Knowing therefore each person's work, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourning, knowing that you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your ancestors, not with perishable things like silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without defect or blemish (1 Peter 1:17–19). Peter says, 'The time that is past is enough for doing what the Gentiles desire, living in licentiousness, passions, drunkenness, revelries, carousing, and lawless idolatry' (1 Peter 4:3). Let us make the cross of the Lord our boundary, by which we are crucified and put to death to our former sins. Having been born again, therefore, let us cling to the truth, and let us be sobered and sanctified, 'for the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil' (1 Peter 3:12). And who will harm you if you become zealous for what is good?

The best way of life is orderliness, which is complete propriety and established strength, the successive elements well-disposed toward each other in action, unsurpassable in virtue. If I have spoken these things somewhat roughly, administering the salvation of correction, I have spoken, says the Pedagogue, since 'whoever reproves with frankness makes peace.' You, if you listen to me, will be saved; but if you do not pay attention to what has been said, I do not care—and yet I do care: 'for the Lord chooses the repentance of the sinner rather than his death.' 'If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good things of the land,' the Pedagogue says again, calling human goods good—beauty, wealth, health, strength, food. For the truly good things are 'what no ear has heard, nor has entered the human heart,' concerning the truly existing King; the truly existing good things exist and await us, for He is both giver and guardian of good things. But the things named good here are so only by a transfer of meaning, the Word pedagogically guiding human weakness from sensible things to the intellect.

greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ τοῖς γεγαμηκόσι παραινέσαιμι ἂν οἴκοι τὰς γυναῖκας τὰς σφῶν μήποτε κατὰ πρόσωπον οἰκετῶν φιλεῖν. οὐδὲ γὰρ προσγελᾶν δούλοις Ἀριστοτέλης εἴα ποτέ, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ κατ᾿ ὄψιν αὐτῶν φιλοφρονούμενον φαίνεσθαι τὴν γυναῖκα. ἄμεινον δὲ οἴκοθεν ἀρξαμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ γάμου τὴν σεμνότητα ἐπιδείκνυσθαι. μεγίστη γὰρ ἡ σωφροσύνης συζυγία καθαρᾶς ἡδονῆς ἀποπνέουσα. πάνυ γοῦν θαυμασίως ἡ τραγῳδία. φεῦ φεῦ, γυναῖκες, (φησίν) ὡς ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἄρα οὐ χρυσός, οὐ τυραννίς, οὐ πλούτου χλιδὴ τοσοῦτον εἶχε διαφόρους τὰς ἡδονὰς ὡς ἀνδρὸς ἐσθλοῦ καὶ γυναικὸς εὐσεβοῦς γνώμη δικαία καὶ φρονοῦσα τἄνδικα. ταῦτα τῆς δικαιοσύνης τὰ παραγγέλματα καὶ παρὰ τοῖς τὴν κοσμικὴν μετιοῦσι σοφίαν ἐκφωνηθέντα οὐ παραιτητέον. ἐγνωκότες οὖν »τὸ ἑκάστου ἔργον, ἐν φόβῳ τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον ἀναστράφητε, εἰδότες ὅτι οὐ φθαρτοῖς, ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ, ἐλυτρώθημεν ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ἡμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου, ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι ὡς ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου Χριστοῦ.« »ἀρκετὸς οὖν ὁ παρεληλυθὼς χρόνος,« ὁ Πέτρος φησί, »τὸ βούλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατειργάσθαι, πεπορευμένους ἐν ἀσελγείαις, ἐπιθυμίαις, οἰνοφλυγίαις, κώμοις, πότοις καὶ ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις.« ὅρον ἔχωμεν τὸν σταυρὸν τοῦ κυρίου, ᾧ περισταυρούμεθα καὶ περιθριγκούμεθα τῶν προτέρων ἁμαρτιῶν. ἀναγεννηθέντες τοίνυν προσηλωθῶμεν [ἐν] τῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀνανήψωμέν τε καὶ ἁγιασθῶμεν, »ὅτι οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους καὶ ὦτα αὐτοῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν, πρόσωπον δὲ κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιοῦντας κακά. καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ἡμᾶς, ἐὰν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ζηλωταὶ γενώμεθα;« ἡ δὲ ἀρίστη ἀγωγὴ εὐταξία ἐστίν, παντελὴς οὖσα εὐσχημοσύνη καὶ δύναμις τεταγμένη βεβαία, τῶν ἑξῆς ἀλλήλοις κειμένων ἐν ἔργῳ καλῶς ἀποδοτική, κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν ἀνυπέρβλητος. Ταῦτα, εἰ καὶ τραχύτερον προηνέχθην οἰκονομούμενος τῆς ἐπανορθώσεως τὴν σωτηρίαν, ἐμοὶ μὲν λελέχθων, φησὶν ὁ παιδαγωγός, ἐπειδὴ »ὁ ἐλέγχων μετὰ παρρησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ,« ὑμεῖς δὲ εἰ μὲν ἀκούσεσθέ μου, σωθήσεσθε, εἰ δ᾿ οὐ προσέξετε τοῖς εἰρημένοις, οὔ μοι μέλει· μέλει δὲ ὅμως καὶ οὕτως· »τὴν γὰρ μετάνοιαν τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ μᾶλλον ἢ τὸν θάνατον αἱρεῖται.« »ἢν δὲ εἰσακούσητέ μου, τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῆς γῆς φάγεσθε«, ὁ παιδαγωγὸς πάλιν λέγει, γῆς ἀγαθὰ τὰ ἀνθρώπεια ὀνομάζων καλά, τὸ κάλλος, τὸν πλοῦτον, τὴν ὑγίειαν καὶ τὴν ἰσχύν, τὴν τροφήν· ἀγαθὰ μὲν γὰρ ὄντως »ἃ οὔτε οὖς ἤκουσεν οὔτε ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνέβη ποτέ«, περὶ τὸν ὄντως ὄντα βασιλέα τὰ ὄντως ὄντα ἀγαθὰ ὄντα καὶ ἀναμένοντα ἡμᾶς· ἀγαθῶν γάρ ἐστι καὶ δοτὴρ καὶ φύλαξ· κατὰ μετουσίαν δὲ ἐκείνων τὰ τῇδε συνωνυμεῖ, παιδαγωγοῦντος ἐνθέως τοῦ λόγου τὴν ἀνθρώπων ἀσθένειαν ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἐπὶ τὴν νόησιν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: So matters stand. Thus the gnostic relates to body and soul, and to those near him—even if he is a servant, even if he has become an enemy by law, or whatever his condition—finding himself equal and similar to them. He does not overlook the brother who shares the divine law, being of the same Father and the same Mother; on the contrary, he lightens the burden of the oppressed with consolations and exhortations, helping with life's necessities and giving to all who are in need, yet not uniformly, but justly and according to worth. He extends this even to the one who persecutes and hates him, if that one has need. He pays little heed to what people say out of fear—unless it is fear that motivates him—and he acts out of helpfulness. For those who are generous and forbearing toward enemies, how much more so toward their own loved ones? From this the gnostic advances to know precisely to whom, how much, when, and how to give.

And who could reasonably become an enemy of a man who gives no cause whatsoever for hatred? Just as we say that God opposes no one and is no one's enemy—for He is the Creator of all, and nothing that exists fails to be willed by Him—yet we say that those who disobey and do not walk according to His commands are enemies to Him, namely those who hate His covenant. In the same way we would find it with the gnostic. He himself would never be an enemy to anyone, at any time, in any way. But those who turn onto the opposite path would be regarded as enemies to him. And this is not all: the habit of giving that we share, which is called justice, and the discerning distribution according to worth—more to some, less to others—upon which it is fitting to act according to knowledge. This is a form of the highest justice.

greek: Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ταύτῃ. οὕτω δὲ ἔχων ὁ γνωστικὸς πρὸς τὸ σῶμα καὶ τὴν ψυχήν, πρὸς [τε] τοὺς πέλας, κἂν οἰκέτης ᾖ κἂν πολέμιος νόμῳ γενόμενος κἂν ὁστισοῦν, ἴσος καὶ ὅμοιος εὑρίσκεται. οὐ γὰρ ὑπερορᾷ τὸν ἀδελφὸν κατὰ τὸν θεῖον νόμον ὁμοπάτριον ὄντα καὶ ὁμομήτριον· ἀμέλει θλιβόμενον ἐπικουφίζει παραμυθίαις, παρορμήσεσι, ταῖς βιωτικαῖς χρείαις ἐπικουρῶν, διδοὺς τοῖς δεομένοις πᾶσιν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ ὁμοίως, δικαίως δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἀξίαν, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τῷ καταδιώκοντι καὶ μισοῦντι, εἰ τούτου δέοιτο. ὀλίγα φροντίζων τῶν λεγόντων διὰ φόβον αὐτῷ δεδωκέναι, εἰ μὴ διὰ φόβον. δι᾿ ἐπικουρίαν δὲ τοῦτο ποιοίη. οἱ γὰρ πρὸς ἐχθροὺς ἀφιλάργυροι καὶ ἀμνησιπόνηροι πόσῳ μᾶλλον πρὸς τοὺς οἰκείους ἀγαπητικοί; ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐκ τούτου πρόεισιν ἐπὶ τὸ ἀκριβῶς εἰδέναι καὶ ὅτῳ ἄν τις μάλιστα καὶ ὁπόσον καὶ ὁπότε καὶ ὅπως ἐπιδῴη. τίς δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἐχθρὸς εὐλόγως γένοιτο ἀνδρὸς οὐδεμίαν οὐδαμῶς παρέχοντος αἰτίαν ἔχθρας: καὶ μή τι. καθάπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐδενὶ μὲν ἀντικεῖσθαι λέγομεν τὸν θεὸν οὐδὲ ἐχθρὸν εἶναί τινος (πάντων γὰρ κτίστης. καὶ οὐδέν ἐστι τῶν ὑποστάντων ὃ μὴ θέλει). φαμὲν δ᾿ αὐτῷ ἐχθροὺς εἶναι τοὺς ἀπειθεῖς καὶ μὴ κατὰ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ πορευομένους. οἷον τοὺς διεχθρεύοντας αὐτοῦ τῇ διαθήκῃ. τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ γνωστικοῦ εὕροιμεν ἄν. αὐτὸς μὲν γὰρ οὐδενὶ οὐδέποτε κατ᾿ οὐδένα τρόπον ἐχθρὸς ἂν γένοιτο. ἐχθροὶ δὲ εῖναι νοοῖντο αὐτῷ οἱ τὴν ἐναντίαν ὁδὸν τρεπόμενοι ἄλλως τε κἂν ἡ ἕξις ἡ μεταδοτικὴ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν δικαιοσύνη λέγηται· ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν διακριτικὴ πρὸς τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον. ἐφ᾿ ὧν καθήκει κατ᾿ ἐπιστήμην γενέσθαι. ἀκροτάτης δικαιοσύνης εἶδος τυγχάνει.

english: It is then clear also that all the other virtues , delineated in Moses , supplied the Greeks with the rudiments of the whole department of morals. I mean valour, and temperance , and wisdom, and justice , and endurance, and patience, and decorum, and self-restraint; and in addition to these, piety . But it is clear to every one that piety , which teaches to worship and honour , is the highest and oldest cause ; and the law itself exhibits justice , and teaches wisdom, by abstinence from sensible images, and by inviting to the Maker and Father of the universe . And from this sentiment, as from a fountain, all intelligence increases. For the sacrifices of the wicked are abomination to the Lord; but the prayers of the upright are acceptable before Him, Proverbs 15:8 since righteousness is more acceptable before God than sacrifice .

Such also as the following we find in Isaiah: To what purpose to me is the multitude of your sacrifices ? Says the Lord; and the whole section. Break every bond of wickedness ; for this is the sacrifice that is acceptable to the Lord, a contrite heart that seeks its Maker. Isaiah 58:6 Deceitful balances are abomination before God ; but a just balance is acceptable to Him. Proverbs 11:1 Thence Pythagoras exhorts not to step over the balance; and the profession of heresies is called deceitful righteousness; and the tongue of the unjust shall be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous drops wisdom. Proverbs 10:31 For they call the wise and prudent worthless. But it were tedious to adduce testimonies respecting these virtues , since the whole Scripture celebrates them.

Since, then, they define manliness to be knowledge of things formidable, and not formidable, and what is intermediate; and temperance to be a state of mind which by choosing and avoiding preserves the judgments of wisdom; and conjoined with manliness is patience, which is called endurance, the knowledge of what is bearable and what is unbearable; and magnanimity is the knowledge which rises superior to circumstances. With temperance also is conjoined caution, which is avoidance in accordance with reason. And observance of the commandments, which is the innoxious keeping of them, is the attainment of a secure life. And there is no endurance without manliness, nor the exercise of self-restraint without temperance .

And these virtues follow one another; and with whom are the sequences of the virtues , with him is also salvation , which is the keeping of the state of well-being. Rightly, therefore, in treating of these virtues , we shall inquire into them all; for he that has one virtue gnostically, by reason of their accompanying each other, has them all. Self-restraint is that quality which does not overstep what appears in accordance with right reason. He exercises self-restraint, who curbs the impulses that are contrary to right reason, or curbs himself so as not to indulge in desires contrary to right reason.

english: Before I undertake the proposed task, I must, in the form of a preface, supply what was left unfinished at the end of the fifth Stromata. For since I have demonstrated that the symbolic mode is ancient and was employed not only by our prophets but also by most of the ancient Greeks and by no few of the other barbarian nations, it was also necessary to examine the mysteries of the initiations; I shall defer that explanation until we come to the things the Greeks have said about first principles, for I will show that they hold both this theory and the mysteries. After demonstrating how the Greek mind's insight was illuminated by the truth given to us through the Scriptures, and after indicating that they received the stolen truth from us—if one may say so without offense—I have proved the point. Bring forward the Greeks themselves as witnesses against themselves: for they so openly steal from one another that they confirm they are thieves, yet even unwillingly they secretly demonstrate our truth to their own countrymen. They will not even refrain from stealing what belongs to their own, let alone what belongs to us. I will say nothing about philosophical dogmas, since the very men who propagate the sects admit in writing that they received the most important of their doctrines from Socrates, lest they be proved ungrateful. Using the testimonies of a few men esteemed among the Greeks, I will examine their thieving character, disregarding chronological order, and then proceed to what follows. Orpheus, then, in his poetry, says: 'So nothing was more dog‑like and cold than another woman'; Homer states openly:

greek: Πρὸ δὲ τῆς εἰς τὸ προκείμενον ἐγχειρήσεως ἐν προοιμίου εἴδει προσαποδοτέον τῷ πέρατι τοῦ πέμπτου Στρωματέως τὰ ἐνδέοντα. Ἐπεὶ γὰρ παρεστήσαμεν τὸ συμβολικὸν εἶδος ἀρχαῖον εἶναι, κεχρῆσθαι δὲ αὐτῷ οὐ μόνον τοὺς προφήτας τοὺς παρ’ ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων τῶν παλαιῶν τοὺς πλείονας καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη βαρβάρων οὐκ ὀλίγους, ἐχρῆν δὲ καὶ τὰ μυστήρια ἐπελθεῖν τῶν τελουμένων· ταῦτα μὲν ὑπερτίθεμαι διασαφήσων, ὁπηνίκα ἂν τὰ περὶ ἀρχῶν τοῖς Ἕλλησιν εἰρημένα ἐπιόντες διελέγχωμεν· τῆσδε γὰρ ἔχεσθαι τῆς θεωρίας ἐπιδείξομεν καὶ τὰ μυστήρια· παραστήσαντες δὲ τὴν ἔμφασιν τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς διανοίας ἐκ τῆς διὰ τῶν γραφῶν εἰς ἡμᾶς δεδομένης ἀληθείας περιαυγασθεῖσαν, καθ’ ὃ σημαινόμενον διήκειν εἰς αὐτοὺς τὴν κλοπὴν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκδεχόμενοι, εἰ μὴ ἐπαχθὲς εἰπεῖν, ἀπεδείξαμεν, φέρε μάρτυρας τῆς κλοπῆς αὐτοὺς καθ’ ἑαυτῶν παραστήσωμεν τοὺς Ἕλληνας· οἱ γὰρ τὰ οἰκεῖα οὕτως ἄντικρυς παρ’ ἀλλήλων ὑφαιρούμενοι βεβαιοῦσι μὲν τὸ κλέπται εἶναι, σφετερίζεσθαι δ’ ὅμως καὶ ἄκοντες τὴν παρ’ ἡμῶν ἀλήθειαν εἰς τοὺς ὁμοφύλους λάθρᾳ διαδείκνυνται. οἱ γὰρ μηδὲ ἑαυτῶν, σχολῇ γε τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀφέξονται. καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν σιωπήσομαι δόγματα, αὐτῶν ὁμολογούντων ἐγγράφως τῶν τὰς αἱρέσεις διανεμομένων, ὡς μὴ ἀχάριστοι ἐλεγχθεῖεν, παρὰ Σωκράτους εἰληφέναι τὰ κυριώτατα τῶν δογμάτων. ὀλίγοις δὲ τῶν καθωμιλημένων καὶ παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν εὐδοκίμων ἀνδρῶν χρησάμενος μαρτυρίοις, τὸ κλεπτικὸν διελέγξας εἶδος αὐτῶν, ἀδιαφόρως τοῖς χρόνοις καταχρώμενος, ἐπὶ τὰ ἑξῆς τρέψομαι. Ὀρφέως τοίνυν ποιήσαντος· ὣς οὐ κύντερον ἦν καὶ ῥίγιον ἄλλο γυναικός, Ὅμηρος ἄντικρυς λέγει·

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: It is not the outward appearance of the body that must be adorned, but the soul, with the ornament of goodness and beauty; one might even say that the body should be adorned with the ornament of self-control. But women who beautify the surface while neglecting the depths have forgotten themselves, just as the Egyptians adorn their temples. Those temples have gateways and porticoes, groves and orchards, and their courts are crowned with countless wreaths. Their walls shine with exotic stones and artistic inscriptions that lack nothing; the shrines gleam with gold, silver, and ivory, and sparkle with variegated stones from India and Ethiopia, while their innermost sanctuaries are shaded by golden canopies. Yet if you press into the depths of the precinct, eager to see the greater thing, you will look for the indwelling statue. A priest or some other temple servant, looking solemn, will draw back a corner of the curtain as if to reveal the god, and will show you the ridiculous object of worship. For the god you sought will not be found within — the one you hurried to see — but a cat, or a crocodile, or a native snake, or some such creature, unworthy of the temple yet fit for a dung-heap, a den, or a sewer. The god of the Egyptians appears as a rolling beast on a purple couch.

In the same way, it seems to me, the gold-wearing women — anointing their elaborate hairstyles, painting their faces, dyeing their eyebrows, coloring their hair, and devising every other foolishness — adorn the fleshly enclosure, and by so doing they truly Egyptianize, striving to attract superstitious lovers. But if someone should pull back the veil of the shrine, that is, the hairstyle, the dye, the clothing, the gold, the purple, the ornaments — in short, the whole fabric woven from these things — expecting to find the true beauty within, he will be disgusted, I know well. For he will not find the honorable image of God dwelling inside, but a prostitute and adulteress of the soul has occupied the inner sanctuary. The true beast will be exposed as a monkey smeared with cosmetics, and that treacherous snake, slipping through the human mind by way of ambition, has made the soul its dung-heap. Having filled everything with deadly poisons and poured out the venom of his own deceit, this dragon, the promoter of corruption, has turned the women into harlots — for the love of adornment belongs not to a wife but to a courtesan. These women care little for the household duties that belong to wives, yet they loosen their husbands' purses and divert the household resources toward their own desires, as if they needed many witnesses to attest their beauty. They spend the whole day seated at their toilette, idle, attended by hired servants.

Just as bad food corrupts the flesh, so they devote the entire day to cosmetics, cloistered in their chambers lest they be caught looking sallow. But at evening, like something creeping from a hole, this counterfeit beauty steals toward the lamplight; for drunkenness and the dimness of the light both cooperate in their assault.

greek: Οὐκ ἄρα ἡ πρόσοψις τοῦ ἐκτὸς ἀνθρώπου, ἀλλὰ ἡ ψυχὴ καλλωπιστέα τῷ τῆς καλοκἀγαθίας κοσμήματι· εἴη δ᾿ ἂν καὶ τὴν σάρκα εἰπεῖν τῷ τῆς ἐγκρατείας κόσμῳ. αἳ δέ, τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν καλλωπιζόμεναι καὶ τὰ βάθη χερσούμεναι, λελήθασι σφᾶς αὐτὰς κατὰ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίων κοσμοῦσαι ναούς· προπύλαια παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καὶ προτεμενίσματα ἐξήσκηται, ἄλση τε καὶ ὀργάδες, κίοσίν τε παμπόλλοις ἐστεφάνωνται αἱ αὐλαί· τοῖχοι δὲ ἀποστίλβουσι ξενικοῖς λίθοις καὶ γραφῆς ἐντέχνου [οἷς] ἐνδεῖ οὐδὲ ἕν· χρυσῷ δὲ καὶ ἀργύρῳ καὶ ἠλέκτρῳ παραστίλβουσιν οἱ ναοί, καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ Ἰνδίας καὶ Αἰθιοπίας πεποικιλμένοι μαρμαίρουσι λιθιδίοις, τὰ δὲ ἄδυτα χρυσοπάστοις ἐπισκιάζεται πέπλοις· ἀλλ᾿ ἢν παρεισέλθῃς εἰς τὸ βάθος τοῦ περιβόλου σπεύδων ἐπὶ τὴν θέαν τοῦ κρείττονος, ζητήσεις τὸ ἄγαλμα τὸ ἔνοικον τοῦ νεώ, παστοφόρος δὲ ἤ τις ἄλλος τῶν ἱεροποιούντων περὶ τὸ τέμενος σεμνὸν δεδορκώς, παιᾶνα τῇ Αἰγυπτίων ᾄδων γλώττῃ, ὀλίγον ἐπαναστείλας τοῦ καταπετάσματος, ὡς δείξων τὸν θεόν, πλατὺν ἡμῖν ἐνδίδωσι γέλωτα τοῦ σεβάσματος. οὐ γὰρ θεὸς ὁ ζητούμενος ἔνδον εὑρεθήσεται, ἐφ᾿ ὃν ἐσπεύσαμεν, αἴλουρος δὲ ἢ κροκόδειλος ἢ αὐτόχθων ὄφις ἤ τι τοιοῦτον θηρίον ἀνάξιον μὲν τοῦ νεώ, χηραμοῦ δὲ ἢ φωλεοῦ ἢ βορβόρου ἀντάξιον· ὁ θεὸς Αἰγυπτίων ἐπὶ στρωμνῆς ἁλουργῆς καταφαίνεται κυλιόμενον θηρίον. ταύτῃ μοι δοκοῦσιν αἱ χρυσοφοροῦσαι γυναῖκες, τῶν πλοκάμων τοὺς ἐνουλισμοὺς ἀσκοῦσαι χρίσματά τε παρειῶν καὶ ὑπογραφὰς ὀφθαλμῶν καὶ βαφὰς μετιοῦσαι τριχῶν καὶ τὴν ἄλλην βλακείαν κακομηχανώμεναι, κοσμοῦσαι τὸν περίβολον τὸν σαρκικόν, αἰγυπτιάζουσαι ὡς ἀληθῶς, ἐπισπᾶσθαι τοὺς δεισιδαίμονας ἐραστάς. ἀλλ᾿ ἢν ἀποκαλύψῃ τις τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ νεώ, τὸν κεκρύφαλον λέγω, τὴν βαφήν, τὴν ἐσθῆτα, τὸ χρυσίον, τὸ φῦκος, τὰ ἐντρίμματα, τουτέστι τὸ ἐκ τούτων συγκείμενον ὕφος, [τὸ καταπέτασμα,] ὡς ἔνδον εὑρήσων τὸ κάλλος τὸ ἀληθινόν, μυσάξεται, εὖ οἶδ᾿ ἐγώ. οὐ γὰρ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ θεοῦ κατοικοῦσαν ἔνδον εὑρήσει τὴν ἀξιόλογον, πόρνη δὲ ἀντ᾿ αὐτῆς καὶ μοιχαλὶς τῆς ψυχῆς κατείληφε τὸ ἄδυτον, τό τε ἀληθινὸν θηρίον ἐλεγχθήσεται ψιμυθίῳ πίθηκος ἐντετριμμμένος, καὶ ὁ παλίμβολος ὄφις ἐκεῖνος διαβιβρώσκων τὸ νοερὸν τῆς ἀνθρώπου διὰ τῆς φιλοδοξίας χηραμὸν ἔχει τὴν ψυχήν· πάντα φαρμάκων ὀλεθρίων ἐμπλήσας καὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ τῆς πλάνης ἐνερευξάμενος ἰὸν μετεσκεύασεν τὰς γυναῖκας εἰς πόρνας ὁ προαγωγὸς οὗτος δράκων (οὐ γὰρ γυναικός, ἀλλ᾿ ἑταίρας τὸ φιλόκοσμον)· αἳ τῆς παρὰ μὲν τοῖς ἀνδράσιν οἰκουρίας ὀλίγα φροντίζουσιν, λύσασαι δὲ τἀνδρὸς τὸ βαλλάντιον ἐκτρέπουσι τὰς χορηγίας εἰς ἐπιθυμίας, ὡς πολλοὺς ἔχοιεν τοῦ καλαὶ δοκεῖν εἶναι μάρτυρας, καὶ τὴν πᾶσαν ἡμέραν κομμωτικῇ προσκαθεζόμεναι ἀργυρωνήτοις σχολάζουσιν ἀνδραπόδοις. καθάπερ οὖν ὄψον πονηρὸν ἡδύνουσι τὴν σάρκα καὶ τὴν μὲν ἡμέραν κομμωτικῇ προστετήκασι θαλαμευόμεναι, μὴ ἐλεγχθῶσιν ξανθιζόμεναι, ἑσπέρας δὲ καθάπερ ἐκ φωλεοῦ πρὸς τὸν λύχνον τὸ νόθον τοῦτο προσέρπει κάλλος· συνεργεῖ γὰρ καὶ ἡ μέθη καὶ τὸ ἀμυδρὸν τοῦ φωτὸς πρὸς τὴν ἐπίθεσιν αὐτῶν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Because they have sailed past the Spirit's proper order, we must turn back and censure the extravagance of their households. They flee from laboring for themselves and serving their own needs, taking refuge instead in an army of servants. They surround themselves with cooks, table-setters, and carvers who skillfully portion the meat, keeping company with a vast retinue. The labor of this household is divided in countless ways. Some slaves toil over their masters' gluttony as stewards, carvers, makers of delicacies, honey-cakes, and sauces. Others occupy themselves with excessive clothing. Some hoard gold like griffins; others guard silver, polish the ornaments, and prepare the feast arrangements. Still others groom the horses. A whole company of cupbearers is trained for them, along with troops of beautiful youths, tended like cattle, from whom they milk beauty. Male and female hairdressers attend the women—some holding mirrors, some headbands, others arranging their hair. Many eunuchs are on hand, and these act as pimps, serving without shame those who wish to indulge in pleasure. For a true eunuch is not one who cannot, but one who does not want to indulge in pleasure. The word of God testifies through the prophet Samuel to those Jews who transgressed by demanding a king. He did not promise them a benevolent Lord, but threatened them with a self-willed, luxurious tyrant who would take their daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers, ruling by the law of war rather than seeking a peaceful administration (1 Samuel 8:11-18). Many Celts are employed to lift the women's litters high and carry them in procession. There are no carders, spinners, seamstresses, or honest women's work among them. Instead, those who counterfeit womanhood spend their days with them, telling erotic tales and corrupting both their bodies and souls with falsehood and deceit. Scripture warns, 'You shall not be with many in wickedness, nor shall you join with the multitude,' because wisdom is found among the few, but disorder is revealed in the multitude (Proverbs 22:24-25). These women do not avoid riding in litters because they wish to be modest and unseen; if that were their disposition, the covering would be welcome. Rather, in their shamelessness, they tag along behind the servants, enjoying the spectacle. When the litter curtain is drawn back, they gaze boldly at those looking at them and often draw reproach, shaming their own superficial modesty with their excessive curiosity. Scripture says, 'Do not look around in the streets of the city, nor wander in its deserts,' for a desert is truly any place where no sober person is found, even if a crowd of the licentious is present. They frequent the temples, sacrificing and seeking oracles, escorting fortune-tellers, priestesses, and old women who destroy households. Daily they endure the whispers of old men at the doors, learning love-potions and incantations from sorcerers to the ruin of marriages. Some men they already have; others they desire; and the prophets promise still more to them. They do not realize they are being deceived. They offer themselves as vessels of pleasure to those who lust, and they count the destruction of their own chastity as gain—a shameful transaction. Many are the servants of licentiousness who sneak in from every side; for the licentious are as easily led to wantonness as pigs to the trough. Therefore Scripture strongly advises: 'Do not bring every person into your house, for the snares of the deceitful are many'; and elsewhere: 'Let righteous men be your dinner guests, and your glory will abide in the fear of the Lord.' Fornication is like a crow; the apostle says, 'Be sure of this: every fornicator or covetous person (who is an idolater) has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God' (Ephesians 5:5). Women who enjoy effeminate men admit crowds of them indoors—men unclean in body and speech, corrupted for shameful service, agents of adultery. They lisp and whisper, using effeminate gestures and tones to please the licentious and provoke laughter, a precursor to fornication. Sometimes they are inflamed by sudden passion—whether as fornicators themselves or as those who have stirred up a mob of effeminates to destruction—they snap their fingers like frogs, as if bile were resident in their nostrils. But the more refined among these women raise Indian parrots and Median peacocks, and recline at table playing with foxes and monkeys. They hear Thersites and laugh, yet they themselves are bought as expensive Thersites—not for worthy husbands, but for men who are a burden on the earth. They ignore a chaste widow, who is far better than a lapdog, and overlook a venerable old man, more decent, I think, than a silver-plated monster. They will not even approach an orphan child, these women who rear parrots and magpies. They expose their own human infants at home, while adopting the fledglings of birds. They have preferred the irrational to the rational, when they ought to support elders who profess sobriety—even apes and nightingales, which can utter something better. The Lord says, 'As much as you have done to one of the least of these, you have done to me' (Matthew 25:40). Yet they have preferred ignorance to sobriety, turning their estates into pearls and Indian emeralds. Yes, they even squander and scatter their wealth on worthless dyes and gilded statues, like sated birds fouling the means of life with their droppings. Scripture says, 'Poverty humbles a man' (Proverbs 21:17); it means the poverty of stinginess, by which the rich become poor in giving, as though they had nothing.

greek: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐλελήθειν παραπλεύσας τῷ πνεύματι τὴν ἀκολουθίαν, ἐφ᾿ ἣν αὖθις παλινδρομητέον καὶ τῶν οἰκετῶν τὴν πολυκτημοσύνην ὀνειδιστέον. φεύγοντες γὰρ αὐτουργίαν καὶ αὐτοδιακονίαν ἐπὶ τοὺς θεράποντας καταφεύγουσιν, ὀψοποιῶν καὶ τραπεζοποιῶν καὶ τῶν ἐντέχνως εἰς μοίρας κατατεμνόντων τὰ κρέα τὸν πολὺν συνωνούμενοι ὄχλον. μεμέρισται δὲ αὐτοῖς ἡ θητεία πολυσχιδῶς· καὶ οἳ μὲν περὶ τὴν γαστριμαργίαν αὐτῶν πονοῦσι δαιτροί τε καὶ καρυκευταὶ καὶ οἱ τῶν πεμμάτων καὶ οἱ τῶν μελιπήκτων καὶ οἱ τῶν ῥοφημάτων συσκευασταί τε καὶ δημιουργοί, οἳ δὲ περὶ τὰς ἐσθῆτας ἀσχολοῦνται τὰς περιττάς, οἳ δὲ χρυσοφυλακοῦσιν ὡς γρῦπες, οἳ δὲ τὸν ἄργυρον φυλάττουσι καὶ σμήχουσιν τὰ ἐκπώματα καὶ τὰς περὶ τὰς ἑστιάσεις παρασκευὰς εὐτρεπίζουσιν, ἄλλοι καταψήχουσι τὰ ὑποζύγια, οἰνοχόων τε ὅμιλος ἀσκεῖται παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς καὶ μειρακίων ὡραίων ἀγέλαι καθάπερ θρεμμάτων, παρ᾿ ὧν ἀμέλγονται τὸ κάλλος. κομμωταὶ δὲ καὶ κομμώτριαι περὶ τὰς γυναῖκας ἀμφιπολεύουσιν αἳ μὲν τὰ κάτοπτρα, αἳ δὲ τοὺς κεκρυφάλους, ἄλλαι τοὺς κτένας * *, εὐνοῦχοι πολλοὶ καὶ οὗτοι μαστροποί, τῷ ἀξιοπίστῳ τοῦ μὴ δύνασθαι φιληδεῖν τοῖς εἰς ἡδονὰς ἐθέλουσιν ῥᾳθυμεῖν ἀνυπόπτως διακονούμενοι. εὐνοῦχος δὲ ἀληθὴς οὐχ ὁ μὴ δυνάμενος, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὴ βουλόμενος φιληδεῖν. διαμαρτυρόμενος γοῦν ὁ λόγος διὰ τοῦ προφήτου Σαμουὴλ πρὸς τοὺς παραβεβηκότας τῶν Ἰουδαίων αἰτοῦντι τῷ λαῷ βασιλέα οὐ τὸν φιλάνθρωπον ὑπισχνεῖται κύριον, ἀλλά τινα αὐτοῖς αὐθάδη τύραννον ἀπειλεῖ τρυφητικόν, »ὃς λήψεται«, φησί, »τὰς θυγατέρας ὑμῶν εἰς μυρεψοὺς καὶ εἰς μαγειρίσσας καὶ εἰς πεσσούσας«, νόμῳ πολέμου κρατήσας, οὐκ εἰρηνικὴν οἰκονομίαν ζηλώσας. οἳ δὲ τὰ φορεῖα εἰς ὕψος αἴροντες τῶν γυναικῶν καὶ φοράδην βαστάζοντες Κελτοὶ πολλοί· ἔριθοι δὲ καὶ ταλασίαι καὶ ἱστοπονίαι καὶ ἡ γυναικωνῖτις ἐργάνη καὶ ἡ οἰκουρία οὐδαμοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ οἱ ψευδοποιοῦντες τὰς γυναῖκας διημερεύουσι μετ᾿ αὐτῶν μύθους ἐρωτικοὺς ἀδολεσχοῦντες καὶ τὸ σῶμα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν διακναίοντες ψευδεργίᾳ καὶ ψευδολογίᾳ. »οὐκ ἔσῃ δὲ μετὰ πολλῶν«, φησίν, »ἐπὶ κακίᾳ, οὐδὲ προσθήσῃ μετὰ πλήθους«, ὅτι ἡ σοφία ἐν ὀλίγοις, ἀταξία δὲ ἐν πλήθει καταφαίνεται. αἳ δὲ οὐ διὰ σεμνότητα τοῦ κατασκοπεῖσθαι μὴ βούλεσθαι συνωνοῦνται τοὺς φορεῖς (ἀγαπητὸν γὰρ ἦν ἄν, εἰ τῇ διαθέσει ταύτῃ προσεβάλλοντο τὴν σκέπην), ἀλλὰ θρυπτόμεναι ἐποχοῦνται τοῖς οἰκέταις ἐμπομπεύειν γλιχόμεναι. ἀναπεπταμένης γοῦν τῆς αὐλαίας περιβλέπουσαι δριμύτερον τοὺς εἰς αὐτὰς ἀφορῶντας διελέγχονται τὸν τρόπον, πολλάκις δὲ καὶ προκύπτουσιν ἔνδοθεν τὴν ἐπιπόλαιον σεμνότητα καταισχύνουσαι τῇ ὀλισθαινούσῃ περιεργίᾳ. »μὴ περιβλέπου δέ«, φησί, »ἐν ῥύμαις πόλεως, μηδὲ πλανῶ ἐν ταῖς ἐρημίαις αὐτῆς«, ἐρημία γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς, κἂν ὄχλος ἀκολάστων ᾖ, ἔνθα μὴ πάρεστιν ἄνθρωπος σωφρονῶν. περιφέρονται δὲ αὗται ἀνὰ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐκθυόμεναι καὶ μαντευόμεναι, ἀγύρταις καὶ μητραγύρταις καὶ γραίαις βωμολόχοις οἰκοφθορούσαις ὁσημέραι συμπομπεύουσαι καὶ τοὺς παρὰ ταῖς κύλιξι ψιθυρισμοὺς γραϊκοὺς ἀνεχόμεναι, φίλτρα ἄττα καὶ ἐπῳδὰς παρὰ τῶν γοήτων ἐπ᾿ ὀλέθρῳ γάμων ἐκμανθάνουσαι. καὶ τοὺς μὲν ἔχουσι τῶν ἀνδρῶν, τοὺς δὲ εὔχονται, ἄλλους δὲ αὐταῖς οἱ μάντεις ὑπισχνοῦνται. οὐκ ἴσασι δὲ ἀπατώμεναι καὶ αὑτὰς μὲν ὡς σκεῦος ἐκδιδοῦσαι ἡδονῆς τοῖς λαγνεύειν ἐθέλουσι, τὴν δὲ ἁγνείαν τὴν σφῶν τῆς αἰσχίστης ἀντικαταλλαττόμεναι ὕβρεως ἔργον ἡγοῦνται χρηματισμοῦ τὴν ἐπονείδιστον φθοράν. πολλοὶ δὲ οἱ τῆς ἑταιρικῆς διάκονοι ἀκολασίας ἄλλος ἄλλοθεν παρεισδύοντες· εὐεπίφοροι γὰρ οἱ ἀκόλαστοι πρὸς τὴν ἀσέλγειαν καθάπερ οἱ χοῖροι πρὸς τὸ καταδυόμενον τοῦ σκάφους ἐπιφερόμενοι. ὅθεν ἐρρωμενέστατα ἡ γραφὴ παραινεῖ· »μὴ πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἴσαγε εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου, πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ ἔνεδρα τοῦ δολίου·« ἀλλαχοῦ δὲ »ἄνδρες δίκαιοι« φησὶν »ἔστωσαν σύνδειπνοί σου, καὶ ἐν φόβῳ κυρίου τὸ καύχημά σου διαμενεῖ.« ἐς κόρακας ἡ πορνεία· »εὖ γὰρ τοῦτο ἴστε«, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, »ὅτι πᾶς πόρνος ἢ πλεονέκτης, ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης, οὐκ ἔχει κληρονομίαν ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θεοῦ.« αἳ δὲ ἀνδρογύνων συνουσίαις ἥδονται, παρεισρέουσι δὲ ἔνδον κιναίδων ὄχλοι ἀθυρόγλωσσοι, μιαροὶ μὲν τὰ σώματα, μιαροὶ δὲ τὰ φθέγματα, εἰς ὑπουργίας ἀκολάστους ἠνδρωμένοι, μοιχείας διάκονοι, κιχλίζοντες καὶ ψιθυρίζοντες καὶ τὸ πορνικὸν ἀνέδην εἰς ἀσέλγειαν διὰ ῥινῶν ἐπιψοφοῦντες ἐπικιναίδισμα, ἀκολάστοις ῥήμασι καὶ σχήμασι τέρπειν πειρώμενοι καὶ εἰς γέλωτα ἐκκαλούμενοι πορνείας πρόδρομον· ἔστι δ᾿ ὅτε καὶ ὑπεκκαιόμενοι διὰ τὴν τυχοῦσαν ὀργήν, ἤτοι πόρνοι αὐτοὶ ἢ καὶ κιναίδων ὄχλον εἰς ὄλεθρον ἐζηλωκότες, ἐπικροτοῦσι τῇ ῥινὶ βατράχων δίκην, καθάπερ ἔνοικον τοῖς μυκτῆρσι τὴν χολὴν κεκτημένοι. ἀλλ᾿ αἵ γε ἀστειότεραι τούτων ὄρνεις Ἰνδικοὺς καὶ ταῶνας Μηδικοὺς ἐκτρέφουσιν καὶ συνανακλίνονται τοῖς φοξοῖς παίζουσαι, σικίννοις τέρασι γανύμεναι· καὶ τὸν μὲν Θερσίτην ἀκούουσαι γελῶσιν, αὐταὶ δὲ πολυτιμήτους ὠνούμεναι Θερσίτας οὐκ ἐπ᾿ ἀνδράσιν ὁμοζύγοις, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνοις αὐχοῦσιν, ἃ δὴ ἄχθος ἐστὶ γῆς· καὶ χήραν μὲν παρορῶσι σωφρονοῦσαν Μελιταίου πολλῷ διαφέρουσαν κυνιδίου, καὶ πρεσβύτην παραβλέπουσι δίκαιον, εὐπρεπέστερον, οἶμαι, τέρατος ἀργυρωνήτου· παιδίον δὲ οὐδὲ προσίενται ὀρφανὸν αἱ τοὺς ψιττακοὺς καὶ τοὺς χαραδριοὺς ἐκτρέφουσαι, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν οἴκοι κυϊσκόμενα ἐκτιθέασι παιδία, τοὺς δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων ὑπολαμβάνουσι νεοττούς· καὶ τὰ ἄλογα τῶν λογικῶν προκεκρίκασιν, δέον ὑποτρέφειν τοὺς σωφροσύνην ἐπαγγελλομένους γέροντας, καὶ πιθήκων, οἶμαι, εὐπροσωποτέρους καὶ ἀηδόνων φθέγξασθαί τι βέλτιον δυναμένους. »ἐφ᾿ ὅσον δέ«, φησίν, »ἑνὶ τούτων ἐποιήσατε τῶν ἐλαχίστων, ἐμοὶ ἐποιήσατε.« αἳ δὲ ἔμπαλιν ἀπαιδευσίαν προτετιμήκασι σωφροσύνης, τὰς ἑαυτῶν οὐσίας ἀπολιθοῦσαι εἰς τοὺς μαργαρίτας καὶ τὰς σμαράγδους τὰς Ἰνδικάς· ναὶ μὴν καὶ εἰς τὰς ἐξιτήλους βαφὰς καὶ εἰς τὰ ἀργυρώνητα ἀνδράποδα σπαθῶσι καὶ διαρρίπτουσι τὰ χρήματα, δίκην ὀρνίθων κεκορεσμένων τὰ τοῦ βίου σκαλεύουσαι κόπρια. »πενία δέ«, φησίν, »ἄνδρα ταπεινοῖ·« τὴν φειδωλίαν πενίαν λέγει, καθ᾿ ἣν οἱ πλούσιοι πένονται μεταδόσεως, ὡς οὐκ ἔχοντες.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: All the points made so far appear to have been handed down by the great Moses to the Greeks as doctrines. Through these texts he teaches that everything belongs to the wise man, and because God had mercy on me, all things are mine. He also indicates that Moses was a friend of God by quoting, "God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob." For a person who is explicitly called a friend is found face to face with God, whereas the one who sees God is shown to be renamed. He allegorized Isaac as a consecrated sacrifice, choosing him as a type of the economy of salvation for us. Among the Greeks, Minos is sung of as a nine-year king and a friend of Zeus, since they had heard that God once spoke with Moses as a man speaks to his own friend. Moses was indeed wise, a king, and a lawgiver, but our Savior surpasses all human nature. He is beautiful as the only one worthy to be loved by us who long for the true reality, for he is the true light. He was proclaimed king even by infants and by the Jews—who were unbelieving and ignorant—and he is announced by the prophets. He is rich to such a degree that he despises all the gold on and under the earth, together with every glory given him by the opposing power. What need is there to add that he is the only high priest, the sole knower of the service of God, the king of peace, Melchizedek, who is most fit to recount the race of humankind? He is also a lawgiver, giving the law through the mouth of the prophets, commanding and teaching most clearly what must be done and what must not. Who is more noble than the one whose only Father is God?

Let us also bring forward Plato, who propounds the same doctrines. In the Phaedrus he declares that the wise man is rich, praying, "Oh dear Pan and all you other gods, grant that I may become beautiful within; and whatever I have outside, let it be at peace with what is within, for I consider the wise man rich." The Athenian stranger criticizes those who think wealth consists in many possessions: "It is impossible for those whom the many call rich to be both rich and good. They call rich the few who possess property worth the most money, and even a wicked man may possess it." Solomon says, "The whole world of wealth belongs to the faithful, but the unbeliever does not even have an obol." We must therefore believe the Scripture that says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to philosophize (Matt. 19:24). On the contrary, it blesses the poor, as Plato says: "Poverty should be considered not as the reduction of one's substance, but as the increase of greed." For it is not scarcity of wealth but greed that is the problem, by which even a good and rich person would be defrauded. In the Alcibiades he calls wickedness 'slave-like' and virtue 'free-like.' Scripture says, "Take away the heavy yoke from you and take the light one," just as the poets also call a yoke 'slavery.' And the statement "You were sold to your sins" agrees with what was said before. Everyone who commits sin is a slave. But the slave does not remain in the house forever. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed, and the truth will set you free (John 8:34–36). The Athenian also says it is good to be wise: "If someone were to insist that the righteous are beautiful in the most righteous character, even if their bodies happen to be ugly, almost no one would think that a faulty statement." And the prophecy foretold that his appearance was lacking compared to all the sons of men. Plato calls the wise man a king in the Statesman, and the passage is there. Having demonstrated these things, let us return once more to the discourse on faith.

Indeed, with full demonstration Plato shows that faith is needed everywhere, at the same time praising peace: "For it is not possible to be faithful and sound in civil strife without complete virtue." Many mercenaries are willing to die in war, but most of them become reckless, unjust, insolent, and foolish—except for a very few. If these things are rightly said, every lawgiver, however small the benefit, will establish laws looking chiefly to the greatest virtue. And this is faithfulness, which we need at all times—in peace, in every war, and in all of life. For it seems to contain all the other virtues. The best thing is neither war nor strife, for it is to be avoided to have need of them; peace and friendliness toward one another are the strongest. It is clear, then, that the greatest prayer is to have peace, according to Plato, and the mother of the greatest virtues is faith. It is reasonable, therefore, that Solomon says, "Wisdom is in the mouth of the faithful," since Xenocrates also says in On Prudence that wisdom is the knowledge of the first causes and of intelligible substance, regarding prudence as twofold—practical and theoretical, which is human wisdom. Therefore wisdom is prudence, but not all prudence is wisdom. It has been shown that faith is knowledge of the principle of all things, not demonstration. For it would be absurd for the followers of Pythagoras of Samos to refuse demonstrations for the things they seek, yet to treat the teacher's mere statement as faith and be satisfied with that alone as confirmation of what they have heard, while those who love to contemplate the truth try to demand proofs from a trustworthy teacher, the only Savior God. "Let the one who has ears to hear, hear" (Matt. 11:15). And who is this? Epicharmus says: "The mind sees and the mind hears; the rest are deaf and blind." Heraclitus says that some are unbelievers, not knowing how to hear or speak, having perhaps been helped by Solomon, who says: "If you love to hear, you will receive, and if you incline your ear, you will be wise" (Prov. 2:2–6).
