latin: EVANGELICA praecepta, fratres dilectissimi, nihil aliud sunt quam magisteria divina, fundamenta aedificandae spei, firmamenta corroborandae fidei, nutrimenta fovendi cordis, gubernacula dirigendi itineris, praesidia obtinendae salutis; quae, dum dociles credentium mentes in terris instruunt, ad coelestia regna perducunt. Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione? Sit autem orantibus sermo et precatio cum disciplina, quietem continens et pudorem. Cogitemus nos sub conspectu Dei stare. Placendum est divinis oculis et habitu corporis et modo vocis. Nam, ut impudentis est clamoribus strepere, ita contra congruit verecundo modestis precibus orare. Denique magisterio suo Dominus secreto orare nos praecepit, in abditis et semotis locis, in cubiculis ipsis, quod magis convenit fidei; ut sciamus Deum ubique esse praesentem, audire omnes et videre, et majestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quoque et occulta penetrare, sicut scriptum est: Ego Deus approximans, et non Deus de longinquo. Si absconditus fuerit homo in absconditis, ego ergo non videbo eum? Nonne coelum et terram ego impleo? Et iterum: In omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos. Et quando in unum cum fratribus convenimus, et sacrificia divina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus, verecundiae et disciplinae memores esse debemus, non passim ventilare preces nostras inconditis vocibus, nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosa loquacitate jactare, quia Deus non vocis sed cordis auditor est. Nec admonendus est clamoribus qui cogitationes hominum videt, probante Domino et dicente: Quid cogitatis nequam in cordibus vestris? Et alio loco: Et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: We must preserve our humanity if we wish to be called human beings in the true sense. And what is preserving humanity but loving a person simply because he is a person, the same as we are? Discord and dissension are therefore contrary to human reason, while the truth lies in Cicero's statement: a man who obeys nature cannot harm another man. Since harming a man is against nature, benefiting him must necessarily be according to nature. Anyone who fails to do this strips himself of the name of man, for the duty of humanity is to come to the aid of human need and danger. I therefore ask those who claim it is not wise to be moved or to show pity: if a man seized by a wild beast begs an armed man for help, do they think he ought to be helped or not? They are not so shameless as to deny that what humanity demands must be done. Likewise, if someone is surrounded by fire, crushed by a collapsing building, drowning in the sea, or swept away by a river, do they think it is not a man's duty to help? Let them not call themselves men if they think so — for no one is immune to such dangers — but rather they will admit it is the duty of a man, and of a strong man, to save one who is perishing. If they concede that in such cases, because they bring danger to life, it is humanity's duty to help, what reason can they give for refusing to help when a man is hungry, thirsty, or cold? These conditions are equal in nature to those chance events and call for the same humanity, yet they draw a distinction between them, because they measure everything not by the truth of the matter itself but by present utility. They hope that those they rescue from danger will return gratitude, but since they expect no return from the needy, they consider whatever they give to such people lost. From this comes that detestable saying of Plautus: "He deserves ill who gives a beggar food to eat, for both the gift perishes and he prolongs the beggar's life in misery." But perhaps the poet was speaking in character.

latin: Conseruanda est igitur humanitas, si homines recte dici uelimus. id autem ipsum, conseruare humanitatem, quid aliut est quam diligere hominem, quia homo sit et idem quod nos sumus? -discordia igitur ac dissensio non est secundum hominis rationem uerumque illut est Ciceronis, quod ait hominem naturae oboedientem homini nocere non posse. ergo si nocere homini contra naturam est, prodesse igitur homini secundum naturam sit necesse est. quod qui non facit, hominis se appellatione despoliat, quia humanitatis officium est necessitati hominis ac periculo subuenire. quaero igitur ab iis qui flecti et misereri non putant esse sapientis, si homo ab aliqua bestia conprehensus auxilium sibi armati hominis inploret, utrumne succurrendum putent an minime. non sunt tam inpudentes, ut negent fieri oportere quod flagitat, quod exposcit humanitas. item, si aliquis circumueniatur igni, ruina opprimatur, mergatur mari, flumine rapiatur, num putent hominis esse non auxiliari. non sint ipsi homines, si putent — nemo enim potest eiusmodi periculis non esse subiectus —, immo uero et hominis et fortis uiri esse dicent seruare periturum. si ergo in eiusmodi casibus, quia periculum uitae homini adferunt, succurrere humanitatis esse concedunt, quid causae est cur, si homo esuriat sitiat algeat, succurrendum esse non putent? quae cum sint paria natura cum illis casibus fortuitis et unam eandemque humanitatem desiderent, tamen illa discernunt, quia non re ipsa uera, sed utilitate praesenti omnia metiuntur. illos enim quos periculo subripiunt sperant sibi gratiam relaturos, egentes autem quia non sperant, perire arbitrantur quidquid eiusmodi hominibus inpertiant. hinc est illa Plauti detestanda sententia: male meretur qui mendico dat quod edat: nam et illut quod dat perit et illi producit uitam ad miseriam. at enim poeta fortasse pro persona locutus est.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: This perfect justice safeguards the human society the philosophers discuss; it is the greatest and truest fruit of wealth. Wealth must not be spent on one’s own pleasure but on the salvation of many, not on present personal gain but on justice, which alone does not perish. Therefore we must hold firmly that the duty of mercy excludes every hope of reward from people; its wage is to be expected from God alone. If you look for repayment from human beings, the act ceases to be humanity and becomes benefit-usury, and no one can be said to have deserved well who acts for himself rather than for another. Yet the matter circles back to the same point: whoever provides for another while hoping for nothing in return truly provides for himself, because he will receive the reward from God. Likewise God commands that when we prepare a dinner we invite those who cannot reciprocate or repay, so that no act of our life may lack the gift of mercy. No one should think, however, that he is forbidden either communion with friends or charity with neighbors; God has made known to us what the true and just work is, so that we ought to live with our neighbors while knowing that the one pertains to man, the other to God.

Hospitality is the chief virtue, as the philosophers also say, but they twist it away from true justice toward utility. Cicero rightly reports Theophrastus’ praise of hospitality, calling it very becoming to open the houses of illustrious men to illustrious guests. He erred in the same way, though, when he said generosity should be directed to the worthy. The house of a just and wise man ought not to be open to the illustrious but to the humble and cast out; the illustrious and powerful lack nothing, since their own wealth and honor defend and honor them. A just man must do nothing except what is beneficial, yet a benefit that is returned perishes and ends, for we cannot keep something whole whose price has been paid to us. The logic of justice therefore turns on those benefits that remain safe and uncorrupted, and they remain only when given to people who can in no way be of use. Cicero, when receiving illustrious guests, looked to nothing but utility and did not hide the advantage he hoped to gain; he says the man who does this will become powerful among foreigners through the favor of princes whom he has bound to himself by the rights of hospitality and friendship. Oh, how many arguments could convict Cicero’s inconsistency if I pursued them — and not so much with my words as with his own! He declares that whoever refers everything to his own utility is in no way a good man, and he also denies that it belongs to a simple and open person to scheme, feign, pretend, seem to do one thing while doing another, or offer himself to another while actually serving himself; such conduct belongs rather to the malicious, cunning, deceitful, and sly. How then could he defend that ambitious hospitality against the charge of malice? You circle every gate, inviting the leaders of peoples and cities into your house so that through them you may gain power among their citizens, yet you wish to appear just, humane, and hospitable while you strive for your own advantage. He did this not so much from inadvertence — what fits Cicero less? — but, ignorant of the true law, he knowingly and wisely fell into these snares. So that he might be forgiven, he testified that he gave precepts not for true justice, which he does not hold, but for the shadow and image of justice. Therefore the shadowy, imaginary teacher deserves pardon, and truth must not be demanded of one who confesses he does not know it.

The redemption of captives is a great and noble work of justice, which Cicero himself approved. He says this kindness is also useful to the republic: captives are redeemed from servitude, the poor are enriched. I prefer this practice of kindness to the giving of gifts; it is the work of serious and great men. It is therefore the proper work of just men to feed the poor and redeem captives, since among the unjust, if anyone does these things, they are called serious and great; those who were not expected to do good earn the highest praise for doing it. Whoever does good for a relative, neighbor, or friend deserves either no praise or certainly not great praise, because he ought to do it, and it is impious and detestable not to do what nature and kinship demand; if he does it, he acts not so much for glory as to avoid reproach. But the one who does good for a stranger and an unknown person is truly worthy of praise, because he is moved by humanity alone. Justice exists where no bond of necessity compels the doing of good. This duty of kindness should not be ranked even below the giving of gifts, which is the act of one who compares and chooses the better of two goods. That lavish giving by men who throw away their patrimony in gifts is empty, slight, and furthest from all justice; such things should not even be called gifts, since no one receives them except those who do not deserve to receive. Protecting and defending destitute orphans and widows who need aid is no less a work of justice; divine law prescribes it to all, because all good judges consider it their duty to favor those who lack natural protection and to strive to benefit them. These works, however, are properly ours, who have received the law and the very words of God commanding. The philosophers feel by nature that it is just to protect those who lack protection, but they do not perceive why. God, whose clemency is perpetual, commands that widows and orphans be defended and nurtured so that no one may be held back by respect and pity for his own children from undergoing death for justice and faith, but may face it without hesitation and with courage, knowing he leaves his dear ones to God and that they will never lack protection. It is also a work of the highest humanity and great importance to take in and care for the sick who have no one to attend them; whoever does this acquires a living sacrifice for God, and what he gives to another for a time he will receive from God for eternity. The last and greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor, which those teachers of virtue and justice did not even touch. They could not see it because they measured all duties by utility. In the other matters mentioned above, although they did not hold the true limit, they perceived some utility and were held by a kind of scent of truth, erring less; but this duty, because they could see no utility in it, they abandoned. Indeed there were not lacking those who called burial superfluous and said there is no evil in lying unburied and cast out.

latin: Haec est illa perfecta iustitia quae custodit humanam de qua philosophi locuntur societatem, hic diuitiarum maximus ac uerissimus fructus est, non uti opibus ad propriam unius uoluptatem, sed ad multorum salutem, non ad praesentem suum fructum, sed ad iustitiam, quae sola non interit. tenendum est igitur omni modo ut ab officio misericordiae spes recipiendi absit omnino: huius enim operis et officii merces a deo est expectanda solo. nam si ab homine expectes, iam non humanitas erit illa, sed beneficii faeneratio, nec potest uideri bene meruisse qui quod facit non alteri, sed sibi praestat. et tamen res eodem redit, ut quod alteri quisque praestiterit nihil ab eo commodi sperans, uere sibi praestet, quia mercedem capiet a deo. item deus praecipit ut si quando cenam parauerimus, eos in conuictum adhibeamus qui reuocare non possint et uicem reddere, ut omnis actus uitae nostrae non careat misericordiae munere. nec tamen quisquam interdictum sibi putet aut communione cum amicis aut caritate cum proximis, sed notum nobis deus fecit quod sit uerum et iustum opus: ita nos oportet cum proximis uiuere, dummodo sciamus illut ad hominem, hoc ad deum pertinere. praecipua igitur uirtus hospitalitas, quod philosophi quoque aiunt, sed eam detorquent a uera iustitia et ad commodum rapiunt. recte inquit Cicero a Theophrasto est laudata hospitalitas. est enim, ut mihi quidem uidetur, ualde decorum patere domus hominum inlustrium hospitibus inlustribus. eodem modo rursus errauit quo tum, cum idoneis esse diceret largiendum. non enim iusti et sapientis uiri domus inlustribus debet patere, sed humilibus et abiectis: nam inlustres illi ac potentes nulla re possunt indigere, quos opulentia sua et munit et honorat. nihil autem a iusto uiro faciendum est nisi quod sit beneficum. beneficium autem si refertur, interit atque finitur: nec enim possumus id habere integrum cuius pretium nobis persolutum est. in iis itaque beneficiis iustitiae ratio uersatur quae salua et incorrupta permanserint, permanent autem non aliter quam si praestentur iis hominibus qui prodesse nullo modo possunt. at ille m recipiendis lnlustribus nihil spectauit aliut nisi utilitatem nec dissimulauit homo ingeniosus quid ex eo commodi speraret. ait enim, qui id faciat, potentem aput exteros futurum per gratiam principum, quos sibi hospitii et amicitiae iure constrinxerit. o quam multis argumentis (Ciceronis inconstantia, si id agerem, coargui posset! nec tam nostris quam suis uerbis refelleretur. idem quippe ait, ut quisque maxime ad suum commodum referat quaecumque agit, ita minime esse uirum bonum. idem etiam negat simplicis et aperti hominis esse ambire, simulare aliquid et praetendere, aliut agere uideri, cum aliut agat, praestare se alteri fingere quod sibi praestet, sed malitiosi potius et astuti et fallacis et subdoli. quomodo ergo defenderet quominus ambitiosa illa hospitalitas malitia esset? tu mihi per omnes portas circumcurses, ut aduenientes populorum atque urbium principes domum tuam inuites, ut per eos aput ciues eorum potentiam consequare, uelisque te iustum et humanum et hospitalem uideri, cum studeas utilitati tuae ? uerum hoc ille non potius incaute, — quid enim minus in Ciceronem conuenit? — sed ignorantia ueri iuris prudens ac sciens in hos se laqueos induit. quod ut ei possit ignosci, testificatus est non ad ueram iustitiam, quam non teneat, praecepta se dare, sed ad umbram imaginemque iustitiae. ignoscendum est igitur umbratico et imaginario praeceptori uec ab eo ueritas exigenda est qui se nescire fateatur. — captiuorum redemptio magnum atque praeclarum iustitiae munus est, quod idem ipse Tullius adprobauit. atque haec benignitas inquit etiam rei publicae est utilis, redimi e seruitute captos, locupletari tenuiores. hanc ego consuetudinem benignitatis largitioni munerum longe antepono, haec est grauium hominum atque magnorum. proprium igitur iustorum opus est alere pauperes ac redimere captiuos, cum aput iniustos, si qui haec faciant, graues et magni appellentur: iis enim maxime laudis est bene facere quibus nemo sperauit esse facturos. nam qui bonum facit uel consanguineo uel proximo uel amico, aut nullam aut certe non magnam laudem meretur, quia facere debet sitque impius ac detestabilis, nisi fecerit id quod ab eo et natura ipsa et necessitudo exigit, et si facit, non tam gloriae adsequendae quam reprehensionis uitandae gratia facit. qui autem facit alieno et ignoto, is uero dignus est laude, quoniam ut faceret sola ductus est humanitate. ibi ergo iustitia est ubi ad bene faciendum necessitatis uinculum nullum est. hoc igitur officium benignitatis ne anteponere quidem largitioni munerum debuit: quod est conparantis et e duobus bonis id quod sit melius eligentis. illa enim largitio hominum patrimonia sua in munera abicientium inanis et leuis et ab omni iustitia remotissima est. itaque ne dici quidem munera oportet in quibus nemo accipit nisi qui accipere non meretur. non minus magnum iustitiae opus est pupillos et uiduas destitutos et auxilio indigentes tueri atque defendere: quod adeo uniuersis diuina lex illa praescribit, quandoquidem boni quique iudices ad officium suum iudicant pertinere ut iis naturali humanitate faueant ac prodesse nitantur. uerum haec opera proprie nostra sunt, qui legem, qui uerba ipsius dei praecipientis accepimus. nam illi sentiunt quidem natura esse iustum tueri eos qui tutela carent, sed cur ita sit non perspiciunt. deus enim, cuius perpetua clementia est, idcirco uiduas pupillosque defendi ac foueri iubet, ne quis respectu ac miseratione pignorum suorum retardetur quominus mortem pro iustitia fideque suscipiat, sed incunctanter ac fortiter subeat, cum sciat se caros suos deo relinquere nec iis umquam praesidium defuturum. aegros quoque quibus defuerit qui adsistat, curandos fouendosque suscipere summae humanitatis et magnae operationis est: quod qui fecerit, hic uiuam hostiam deo adquiret et quod alteri dederit ad tempus, ipse a deo accipiet in aeternum. ultimum illud et maximum pietatis officium est peregrinorum et pauperum sepultura: quod illi uirtutis iustitiaeque doctores prorsus non attigerunt. nec enim poterant id uidere qui utilitate omnia officia metiebantur. in ceteris enim quae supra dicta sunt quamuis uerum limitem non tenuerint, tamen quoniam commodi aliquid in iis deprehenderunt, quasi odore quodam ueritatis retenti propius aberrarunt, hoc autem, quia nihil uidere in eo commodi poterant, reliquerunt. quin etiam non defuerunt qui superuacaneam facerent sepulturam nihilque esse dicerent mali iacere inhumatum et abiectum.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: The Stoics try to tear the emotions out of a person as if they were diseases, but the Peripatetics oppose them, not only retaining the emotions but also defending them, insisting that nothing in a human being is innate without great reason and providence. That claim would be correct if they knew the true boundaries of each thing. Consequently they call anger the whetstone of virtue, as though no one could fight bravely against an enemy unless stirred by anger, and in doing so they reveal that they understand neither what virtue is nor why God gave anger to humanity.

If anger were given to us so that we might use it to kill people, what could be more inhuman, what more like wild beasts, than the creature God made for communion and innocence? There are three emotions that drive people into every kind of crime: anger, greed, and lust. For this reason the poets spoke of three Furies that agitate human minds: anger craves vengeance, greed craves wealth, lust craves pleasure.

God has set definite limits for all these emotions; if they are crossed and become excessive, they inevitably corrupt their own nature and turn into diseases and vices. The limits are not hard to show: greed is given to acquire the necessities of life, lust to propagate offspring, and the emotion of anger to restrain the sins of those under our authority — that is, so that the younger generation may be shaped to virtue and justice by stricter discipline; without the restraint of fear, licentiousness arises and leads to every shameful act and crime. Thus it is just and necessary to use anger against inferiors, but against equals it is both pernicious and impious: impious because it violates our common humanity, pernicious because resistance forces either the destruction of the other or one's own ruin.

The reason I have given for why the emotion of anger was granted to humanity can be seen from God's own precepts, which command us not to become angry with those who curse and harm us, yet to keep our hands over those who are inferior, correcting sinners with frequent punishments lest useless love and excessive indulgence rear them in evil and vice. Those who are ignorant of reality and of reason have eradicated the emotions given for good use and have let them run beyond what reason demands; from this comes unjust and impious living. They wield anger against equals, producing discord, expulsions, and wars contrary to justice. They wield greed to amass wealth, producing fraud, robbery, and every kind of crime. They wield lust to seize pleasure alone, producing adultery, corruption, and every form of debauchery.
Therefore, whoever restrains those emotions within their proper bounds — a feat impossible for those who do not know God — is patient, is strong, and is just.

latin: Stoici cum adfectus ei homine tamquam morbos conantur euellere, Peripatetici se opponunt eosque non modo retinent, sed etiam defendunt nihilque in homine esse dicunt quod non magna ratione ac prouidentia sit innatum. recte id quidem, si singularum rerum ueros terminos scirent. itaque hanc ipsam iram cotem dicunt esse uirtutis, tamquam nemo possit aduersus hostem fortiter dimicare, nisi fuerit ira concitatus. quo plane ostendunt nec quid sit uirtus scire se nec cur homini tribuerit iram deus. quae si nobis ideo data est, ut ea utamur ad occidendos homines, quid inmanius homine, quid similius feris beluis existimandum est quam id animal quod ad communionem atque innocentiam deus fecit? tres sunt igitur adfectus qui homines in omnia facinora praecipites agant, ira cupiditas libido. propterea poetae tres Furias esse dixerunt, quae mentes hominum exagitent: ira ultionem desiderat, cupiditas opes, libido uoluptates. sed his omnibus deus certos limites statuit: quos si transcenderint maioresque esse coeperint, necesse est naturam suam deprauent et in morbos ac uitia uertantur. qui autem sint isti limites, non est magni laboris ostendere. cupiditas ad ea conparanda nobis data est quae sunt ad uitam necessaria, libido ad subolem propagandam, irae adfectus ad coercenda peccata eorum qui sunt in nostra potestate, id est ut artiore disciplina minor aetas ad probitatem iustitiamque formetur: quae nisi metu cohibeatur, licentia pariet audaciam, quae ad omne flagitium et facinus euadet. itaque ut ira uti aduersus minores et iustum est et necessarium, sic aduersus pares et perniciosum est et impium: impium, quod uiolatur humanitas, perniciosum, quod illis repugnantibus aut perdere necesse est aut perire. hanc autem quam dixi esse rationem cur homini sit irae adfectus datus, ex ipsius dei praeceptis intellegi potest, qui iubet uti maledicis et laedentibus non irascamur, manus autem nostras supra minores semper habeamus, hoc est ut peccantes eos adsiduis uerberibus corrigamus, ne amore inutili et indulgentia nimia educentur ad malum et ad uitia nutriantur. sed rerum imperiti et rationis ignari eos adfectus qui sunt homini ad usus bonos dati exterminauerunt et latius quam ratio postulat euagantur. inde iniuste atque impie uiuitur. utuntur ira. contra pares: hinc discidia, hinc expulsiones, hinc bella contra iustitiam nata sunt. utuntur cupiditate ad congerendas opes: hinc fraudes, hinc latrocinia, hinc omnia scelerum genera exorta sunt. utuntur libidine ad capiendas tantum uoluptates: hinc stupra, hinc adulteria, hinc corruptelae omnes extiterunt. quicumque igitur illos -adfectus intra fines suos redegerit, quod ignorantes deum facere non possunt, hic patiens, hic fortis, hic iustus est.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: First I argued that knowing what is good is not the same as virtue; then I defined virtue and showed where it resides. It follows that I must now briefly demonstrate that the philosophers were ignorant of what good and evil truly are, since this was nearly proven in the third book when I discussed the highest good. Those who did not know the highest good necessarily erred concerning all other goods and evils, which are not the highest; no one can rightly judge these things who does not grasp the very source from which they flow. The source of all good is God; the source of evil is the one who is the constant enemy of the divine name, whom I have often mentioned. From these two principles all good and evil originate. Whatever comes from God has this purpose: it brings immortality, which is the highest good. Whatever comes from that other source has this function: it kills and destroys those who have been drawn away from heavenly things and plunged into earthly things, consigning them to eternal punishment, which is the highest evil. Is it doubtful, then, that all those philosophers were ignorant of good and evil, since they knew neither God nor God's adversary? Consequently they limited the end of all goods to the body and to this brief life, which must inevitably dissolve and die; they advanced no further. All their precepts and all the goods they propose cling to the earth and lie in the dust, because they perish together with the body, which is earth. These things do not pertain to the true life of man, but to the pursuit or increase of wealth, honors, glory, and power — all of which are mortal, just like the person who toiled to obtain them. Hence the saying: virtue consists in knowing the end and measure of a thing. For they teach the means and arts by which family wealth is to be sought, because they see it is usually sought badly. But such virtue is not set before the wise; virtue is not the quest for wealth, whose discovery and possession are not in our power. Thus both the seeking and the obtaining of wealth are easier for the wicked than for the good. Therefore virtue cannot reside in those things which are sought, since it is in despising them that virtue's power and reason appear; nor will virtue turn to those very things which a great and lofty soul strives to trample and spurn. Nor is it right that a soul intent on heavenly goods should be diverted from its immortal possessions to acquire these fragile things. Rather, the reason of virtue consists in securing those goods which neither any human being nor death itself can take from us.

latin: Dixi, quod erat primum, scientiam boni non esse uirtutem, deinde, quid sit uirtus et in quo sit: sequitur ut id quoque ipsum, quid sit bonum et malum, nescisse philosophos breuiter ostendam, quia paene declaratum est in libro tertio, cum de summo bono disputarem. qui autem quid esset summum nescierunt, et in ceteris bonis malisue, quae summa non sunt, errauerint necesse est: quae non potest uero iudicio examinare qui fontem ipsum non tenet unde illa descendunt. fons autem bonorum deus est, malorum uero ille scilicet diuini nominis semper inimicus, de quo saepe diximus: ab his duobus principiis bona malaque oriuntur. quae ueniunt a deo, hanc habent rationem, ut inmortalitatem parent, quod est summum bonum: quae autem ab illo altero, id habent officium, ut a caelestibus auocatum terrenisque demersum ad poenam interficiant sempiternam, quod est summum malum. num igitur dubium est quin illi omnes quid esset bonum et malum ignoraueriut, qui nec deum nec aduersarium dei scierunt? itaque finem bonorum ad corpus et ad hanc uitam breuem retulerunt, quam scilicet solui et occidere necesse est, non sunt progressi ulterius, sed omnia eorum praecepta et omnia quae inducunt bona, terrae inhaerent et humi iacent, quoniam simul cum corpore, quod est terra, moriuntur. pertinent enim non ad uitam homini conparandam, sed ad quaerendas uel augendas opes honores gloriam potentiam: quae sunt uniuersa mortalia, tam scilicet quam ille qui ut ea sibi contingerent laborauit. hinc est illud: uirtus, quaerendae finem rei scire modumque. praecipiunt enim quibus modis et quibus artibus res familiaris quaerenda sit, quia uident male quaeri solere. sed huiusmodi uirtus non est proposita sapienti: nec enim uirtus est opes quaerere, quarum neque inuentio neque possessio in nostra potestate est. itaque et quaesitu et obtentu faciliores sunt malis quam bonis. non potest ergo uirtus esse in iis rebus quaerendis in quarum contemptu uis ac ratio uirtutis apparet, nec ad ea ipsa transfugiet quae magno et excelso animo calcare ac proterere gestit, neque fas est animam caelestibus intentam bonis, ut haec fragilia sibi conparet, ab inmortalibus suis opibus auocari, sed potissimum in iis rebus conparandis uirtutis ratio consistit quas nobis nec homo ullus nec mors ipsa possit auferre.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Among the physical rations supplied to you, blessed martyrs-designate — rations sent by our Lady Mother Church from her own breasts and by individual brothers from their own resources — let us also contribute something to nourish the spirit. Fattening the flesh while starving the spirit helps nothing. Indeed, if something weak is being cured, the weaker thing must not be neglected. I am not great enough to address you, yet even the most perfect gladiators are exhorted not only by their own trainers and superiors but also by private citizens and idle onlookers from a distance; often the shouted suggestions of the crowd itself have proved useful. First of all, then, blessed ones, do not grieve the Holy Spirit who entered prison with you. If he had not entered with you now, you would not be there today. So take care that he perseveres with you there, so that he may lead you through to the Lord. The prison is indeed the devil's house, where he keeps his family. But you have arrived in prison precisely to trample him in his own house, since you have already trampled him outside. Let him not say: 'They are in my domain; I will test them with vile temptations, lusts, or dissensions among themselves.' Let him flee your sight and hide his lowest parts, contracted and numb, like a snake that has been charmed or smoked out. Nor let him be so comfortable in his kingdom that he can hand you over; let him find you fortified and armed with harmony, because your peace is war to him. Some who lack this peace in the Church are accustomed to beg it from martyrs in prison. And therefore you ought to have, nurture, and guard this peace, so that if perhaps you may be able to provide it to others as well.

latin: Inter carnis alimenta, benedicti martyres designati, quae vobis et domina mater Ecclesia de uberibus suis, et singuli fratres de opibus suis propriis in carcerem subministrant, capite aliquid et a nobis quod faciat ad spiritum quoque educandum. Carnem enim saginari, et spiritum esurire non prodest. Imo, si quod infirmum est, curatur; aeque, quod infirmius est, negligi non debet. Nec tantus ego sum, ut vos alloquar; verumtamen et gladiatores perfectissimos non tantum magistri et praepositi sui, sed etiam idiotae et supervacui quique adhortantur de longinquo, ut saepe de ipso populo dictata suggesta profuerint. In primis ergo, benedicti, nolite contristare Spiritum sanctum, qui vobiscum introiit carcerem. Si enim non vobiscum nunc introisset, nec vos illic hodie fuissetis. Et ideo date operam, ut illic vobiscum perseveret: ita vos inde perducat ad Dominum. Domus quidem diaboli est et carcer, in qua familiam suam continet. Sed vos ideo in carcerem pervenistis, ut illum etiam in domo sua conculcetis. Jam enim foris congressi conculcaveratis. Non ergo dicat: In meo sunt, tentabo illos vilibus scidiis, affectionibus, aut inter se dissensionibus. Fugiat conspectum vestrum, et ima sua delitescat contractus et torpens, tanquam coluber excantatus aut effumigatus. Nec illi tam bene sit in suo regno, ut vos committat sed inveniat munitos, et concordia armatos: quia pax vestra bellum est illi. Quam pacem quidam in Ecclesia non habentes, a martyribus in carcere exorare consueverunt. Et ideo eam etiam propterea in vobis habere et fovere et custodire debetis, ut si forte et aliis praestare possitis.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Other hindrances of the mind have led you right up to the prison threshold, just as they led your parents. From that point on, he is cut off from the world itself — how much more from the age and all that belongs to it? And this should not shake you: you have been separated from the world. If we stop to consider that the world itself is the greater prison, we will see that you have actually left prison, not entered it. The world holds a deeper darkness, the kind that blinds men's hearts. It clamps heavier chains, the kind that bind men's very souls. It exhales fouler impurities — men's lusts. In the end, it holds more prisoners: the whole human race. And it awaits judgment not from a proconsul, but from God. So why, you blessed ones, would you think you've been transferred from prison to a mere guardhouse? The place has darkness, but you are the light; it has chains, but you have been set free for God. It breathes misery, but you are the fragrance of sweetness. A judge is expected there, but you are the ones who will sit among the judges themselves. Let the man who sighs for the world's rewards be the one who is saddened. A Christian has already renounced the world even outside prison; inside prison, he renounces the prison itself. It makes no difference where you are in the world, you who stand outside it. And if you have lost some of life's joys, think of it as a transaction: you lose something to gain far more. I am not even touching yet on the reward to which God calls martyrs. Let us simply compare, for now, the daily reality of the world against that of prison. Does the spirit not gain more in prison than the flesh loses? Indeed, the flesh does not even lose what is rightfully its own, thanks to the Church's care and the brothers' love. On top of that, the spirit acquires everything that faith finds useful. You do not see foreign gods; you do not stumble over their images; you do not take part in the nations' holy days by mere presence; you are not battered by filthy stenches; you are not struck by the roars of spectacles — their cruelty, their fury, their shamelessness. Your eyes do not fall on public brothels. You are free from scandals, from temptations, from evil memories, and now even from persecution. This is what prison gives a Christian — what the desert gave the prophets. The Lord himself withdrew into solitude more often, so he could pray more freely, so he could yield to the age. Finally, he revealed his glory to his disciples in solitude. So let us drop the name 'prison' and call it solitude. Even if the body is shut in, even if the flesh is detained, everything stands open to the spirit. Wander in the spirit, walk in the spirit — not preferring dark stadiums or long porticoes, but choosing that way which leads to God. As often as you walk it in spirit, that often you are not in prison. The leg feels no pain in the nerve when the mind is in heaven. The mind carries the whole man wherever it wishes. Where your heart is, there your treasure will be also. So let our heart be where we want our treasure to be.

latin: Caetera aeque animi impedimenta usque ad limen carceris deduxerint vos, quousque et parentes vestri. Exinde segragati est is ab ipso mundo, quanto magis a saeculo, rebusque ejus? Nec hoc vos consternet, quod segregati estis a mundo. Si enim recogitemus ipsum magis mundum carcerem esse, exisse vos e carcere, quam in carcerem introisse, intelligemus. Majores tenebras habet mundus, quae hominum praecordia excaecant. Graviores catenas induit mundus, quae ipsas animas hominum constringunt. Pejores immunditias exspirat mundus, libidines hominum. Plures postremo mundus reos continet, scilicet universum hominum genus. Judicia denique non proconsulis, sed Dei sustinet. Quo vos, benedicti, de carcere in custodiarium si forte translatos existimetis. Habet tenebras, sed lumen estis ipsi: habet vincula, sed vos soluti Deo estis. Triste illic exspirat, sed vos odor estis suavitatis; Judex exspectatur, sed vos estis de judicibus ipsis judicaturi. Contristetur illic, qui fructum saeculi suspirat. Christianus etiam extra carcerem saeculo renuntiavit, in carcere autem etiam carceri. Nihil interest, ubi sitis in saeculo, qui extra saeculum estis; et si aliqua amisistis vitae gaudia, negotiatio est aliquid amittere, ut majora lucreris. Nihil adhuc dico de praemio, ad quod Deus martyres invitat. Ipsam interim conversationem saeculi et carceris comparemus, si non plus in carcere spiritus acquirit quam caro amittit, imo et quae justa sunt caro non amittit per curam Ecclesiae, agapen fratrum: et insuper quae semper utilia fidei, spiritus adipiscitur. Non vides alienos deos, non imaginibus eorum incurris, non solemnes nationum dies ipsa commixtione participas, non nidoribus spurcis verberaris, non clamoribus spectaculorum, atrocitate, vel furore, vel impudicitia celebrantium caederis: non in loca libidinum publicarum oculi tui impingunt: vacas a scandalis, a tentationibus, a recordationibus malis, jam et a persecutione. Hoc praestat carcer christiano, quod eremus prophetis. Ipse Dominus in secessu frequentius agebat, ut liberius oraret, ut saeculo cederet. Gloriam denique suam discipulis in solitudine demonstravit. Auferamus carceris nomen, secessum vocemus. Etsi corpus includitur, etsi caro detinetur, omnia spiritui patent. Vagare spiritu, spatiare spiritu, et non stadia opaca aut porticus longas praeponens tibi, sed illam viam, quae ad Deum ducit. Quotiens eam spiritu deambulaveris, totiens in carcere non eris. Nihil crus sentit in nervo cum animus in coelo est. Totum hominem animus circumfert, et quo velit transfert: Ubi autem erit cor tuum, illic erit et thesaurus tuus. Ibi ergo sit cor nostrum, ubi volumus habere thesaurum.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Is prison now, blessed ones, even a bother to Christians? We were called to the military service of the living God at the very moment we answered the words of the sacrament. No soldier goes to war dragging luxuries; he does not march to the line from a bedroom, but from stripped‑down, packed‑up tents where every harshness, unpleasantness, and disagreeableness lives. Even in peacetime they already learn to endure the hardships and troubles of war — marching under arms, running the field, digging trenches, locking shields in a testudo. They push through everything with sweat so their bodies and minds will not flinch: from shade into sun, from sun into heaven, from tunic into armor, from silence into shouting, from quiet into tumult. Therefore, you blessed ones, treat whatever is hard in this as training for the virtues of soul and body. You are about to enter a noble contest whose judge is the living God, whose master of the games is the Holy Spirit, and whose prize is the substance of angels, citizenship in heaven, glory for ages of ages (2 Timothy 4:8). And so your Master, Christ Jesus, who anointed you with the Spirit and brought you to this arena, chose to pull you from a freer condition into harsher treatment before the day of the contest, so that your strength might be confirmed in you. For even athletes are set apart for stricter discipline so they can devote themselves to building power: they are denied luxury, richer food, more pleasant drink. They are forced, tormented, wearied: the more they labor in training, the more they hope for victory. And those, says the Apostle, do it to win a perishable crown; we, to win an imperishable one. Let us treat prison as our gymnasium, so that, well‑exercised by every hardship, we may be led into the stadium of the tribunal: because virtue is built by harshness and destroyed by softness.

latin: Sit nunc, benedicti, carcer etiam christianis molestus? Vocati sumus ad militiam Dei vivi jam tunc, cum in sacramenti verba respondimus. Nemo miles ad bellum cum deliciis venit; nec de cubiculo ad aciem procedit, sed de papilionibus expeditis et substrictis, ubi omnis duritia et imbonitas et insuavitas constitit. Etiam in pace, labore et incommodis bellum pati jam ediscunt, in armis deambulando, campum decurrendo, fossam moliendo, testudinem densando. Sudore omnia constant, ne corpora atque animi expavescant: de umbra ad solem, de sole ad coelum de tunica ad loricam, de silentio ad clamorem, de quiete ad tumultum. Proinde vos, benedicti, quodcumque hoc durum est, ad exercitationem virtutum animi et corporis deputate. Bonum agonem subituri estis in quo agonothetes, Deus vivus est; xystarches, Spiritus sanctus corona, aeternitatis; brabium, angelicae substantiae, politia in coelis, gloria in saecula saeculorum. Itaque Epistates vester Christus Jesus, qui vos spiritu unxit, et ad hoc scamma produxit, voluit vos ante diem agonis ad duriorem tractationem a liberiore conditione seponere, ut vires corroborarentur in vobis. Nempe enim et athletae segregantur ad strictiorem disciplinam, ut robori aedificando vacent: continentur a luxuria, a cibis laetioribus, a potu jucundiore. Coguntur, cruciantur, fatigantur: quanto plus in exercitationibus laboraverint, tanto plus de victoria sperant. Et illi, inquit Apostolus, ut coronam corruptibilem consequantur; nos aeternam consecuturi. Carcerem nobis pro palaestra interpretemur, ut ad stadium tribunalis bene exercitati incommodis omnibus producamur: quia virtus duritia extruitur, mollitia vero destruitur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We know from the Lord's own teaching that the flesh is weak while the spirit is willing. So let's not coddle ourselves just because the Lord has admitted the flesh's frailty. He highlighted the spirit's eagerness precisely to show what the flesh owes its superior: the weaker must serve the stronger, drawing strength from that service. The spirit needs to talk to the flesh about their shared salvation—not about the discomforts of prison anymore, but about the actual contest and battle ahead. The flesh may well flinch at the heavy sword, the high cross, the savagery of beasts, the ultimate penalty of fire, and every diabolical device the executioner can invent. But the spirit must confront both itself and the flesh with a different ledger: bitter as these torments are, countless people have endured them with equanimity, even sought them out voluntarily, all for the sake of fame and glory—and not just men, but women too, so that you, blessed ones, can answer the call of your own sex.

It would take too long to list every individual who fell on their own sword at their mind's prompting. Among women, Lucretia stands ready: raped, she drove a dagger into herself before her kinsmen's eyes to win glory for her chastity. Mucius Scaevola burned his right hand on the altar so his deed would win renown. The philosophers did less: Heraclitus smeared himself with cow dung and burned himself alive; Empedocles threw himself into the fires of Mount Etna; and Peregrinus, not long ago, leaped onto a pyre. Women have despised fire as well: Dido, rather than be forced to remarry after her beloved husband's death; and the wife of Hasdrubal, watching her husband beg Scipio for mercy as Carthage burned, hurled herself and her children into the flames of her homeland. Regulus, a Roman general captured by the Carthaginians, refused to be exchanged for many Carthaginian prisoners; he chose to be handed back to the enemy, shut in a kind of chest, and pierced all over with nails from the outside—suffering, in effect, countless crosses. A woman eagerly courted the beasts, and specifically asps—serpents more dreadful than bull or bear—which Cleopatra applied to herself rather than fall into enemy hands. Yet the fear of death is nothing compared to the fear of torture. So did an Athenian prostitute break under the executioner? She knew of a conspiracy; when the tyrant tortured her for it, she never betrayed the conspirators, and at the end she chewed off her own tongue and spat it in the tyrant's face, proving that torments could do nothing to her even if they continued. We all know the Lacedaemonians' greatest solemnity today, the διαμαστίγωσις—that is, flagellation. In this sacred rite, noble youths are whipped before the altar while their parents and relatives watch and urge them to endure. It counts as a higher honor and glory if the soul yields to the blows before the body does. Therefore, if mere earthly glory can draw such strength from body and soul that they despise sword, fire, cross, beasts, and torture for the reward of human praise, I can say these sufferings are moderate indeed for gaining heavenly glory and a divine reward. If people pay so much for glass, what will they pay for a pearl? Who, then, would not gladly spend as much for the truth as others spend for a lie?

latin: Scimus ex dominico praecepto, quod caro infirma sit, spiritus promptus. Non ergo nobis blandiamur, quia Dominus consensit carnem infirmam esse. Propterea enim praedixit spiritum promptum, ut ostenderet, quid cui debeat esse subjectum, scilicet, ut caro serviat spiritui, infirmior fortiori, ut ab eo etiam ipsam fortitudinem assumat. Colloquatur spiritus cum carne de communi salute, nec jam de incommodis carceris, sed ipso agone et praelio cogitans. Timebit forsitan caro gladium gravem, et crucem excelsam, et rabiem bestiarum, et summam ignium poenam, et omne carnificis ingenium in tormentis. Sed spiritus contra ponat sibi et carni, acerba licet ista, a multis tamen aequo animo excepta, imo et ultro appetita, famae et gloriae caussa; nec a viris tantum, sed etiam a foeminis, ut vos quoque, benedictae, sexui vestro respondeatis. Longum est, si enumerem singulos, qui se gladio confecerint, animo suo ducti. De foeminis ad manum est Lucretia, quae vim stupri passa, cultrum sibi adegit in conspectu propinquorum, ut gloriam castitati suae pareret, Mutius, manum suam dexteram in ara cremavit, ut hoc factum ejus fama haberet. Minus fecerunt philosophi: Heraclitus, qui se bubulo stercore oblitum exussit; item Empedocles, qui in ignes Aetnaei montis dissilivit; et Peregrinus, qui non olim se rogo immisit: cum foeminae quoque contempserint ignes: Dido, ne post virum dilectissimum nubere cogeretur; item quum Asdrubalis uxor, quae jam ardente Carthagine maritum suum supplicem Scipionis videret, cum filiis suis in incendium patriae devolavit. Regulus, dux Romanorum, captus a Carthaginiensibus, cum se unum pro multis captivis Carthaginiensibus compensari noluisset, maluit hostibus reddi et in arcae genus stipatus undique extrinsecus clavis transfixus, tot cruces sensit. Bestias foemina libens appetiit, et utique aspides, serpentes tauro vel urso horridiores, quas Cleopatra immisit sibi, ne in manus inimici perveniret. Sed mortis metus non tantus est, quantus tormentorum. Itaque, cessit carnifici meretrix atheniensis? quae conscia conjurationis, cum propterea torqueretur a tyranno, et non prodidit conjuratos, et novissime linguam suam comestam in faciem tyranni exspuit, ut nihil agere se scirent tormenta, etsi ultra perseverarent. Nam quod hodie apud Lacedaemonas solemnitas maxima est, διαμαστίγωσις, id est, flagellatio, non latet. In quo sacro, ante aram nobiles quique adolescentes, flagellis affliguntur, astantibus parentibus et propinquis, et uti perseverent adhortantibus. Ornamentum enim et gloria deputabitur majore quidem titulo, si anima potius cesserit plagis, quam corpus. Igitur, si tantum terrenae gloriae licet de corporis et animi vigore, ut gladium, ignem, crucem bestias, tormenta contemnant, sub praemio laudis humanae, possum dicere, modicae sunt istae passiones ad consecutionem gloriae coelestis et divinae mercedis. Si tanti vitrum? quanti margaritum? Quis ergo non libentissime tantum pro vero habeat erogare, quantum alii pro falso?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So you ask why we complain of your persecution when you yourselves are willing to suffer, since you ought to love those through whom you suffer exactly what you want. We do want to suffer, but the way a soldier faces war — nobody embraces battle gladly, because trembling and danger are unavoidable; yet he still fights with everything he has, and the man who complained about the fight ends up rejoicing in victory because he wins both glory and spoils. Our battle is the courtroom: you drag us before tribunals so that we must contend for the truth with our lives on the line. Victory means gaining what you fought for, and this victory carries a double prize — the glory of pleasing God and the spoil of eternal life. We are "covered over" only when we have won; therefore we conquer precisely when we are killed, and we escape precisely when we are covered. You mock us now as worthless kindling and half-axe men, because we are burned alive, bound to a stake and ringed with brushwood. That is what our victory looks like; that is our triumphal robe; in such a chariot we ride in triumph. Naturally we do not please the defeated; that is why we are written off as desperate and lost. But this very desperation and loss, in the cause of glory and fame, raises the banner of virtue. Mucius willingly left his right hand on the altar — oh, the loftiness of his soul! Empedocles threw himself entire into the fires of Aetna — oh, the strength of his mind! A founder of Carthage gave herself to the pyre as a second marriage — oh, the praise of her chastity! Regulus, rather than live while many enemies lived, endured the cross with his whole body — oh, the strong man, the victor even in captivity! Anaxarchus, pounded like a pestle, cried, "Pound, pound the shell of Anaxarchus; you are not pounding Anaxarchus" — oh, the philosopher's magnanimity, joking at his own death! I pass over those who bought praise with their own sword or a milder death. You yourselves crown the contests of torture. The Attic courtesan, after the executioner grew tired, finally spat her chewed-off tongue into the face of the raging tyrant so that she might spit out her voice as well and never betray the conspirators, even if she had wanted to when broken. Zeno of Elea, asked by Dionysius what philosophy offers, answered "contempt of death," and under the tyrant's whips he sealed that sentence with his life. The Spartan lash, made more bitter under the very eyes of cheering relatives, brings a house as much honor of endurance as it sheds blood. Oh, the glory that is permitted because it is human — to which neither lost presumption nor desperate persuasion is ascribed in its contempt for death and every kind of cruelty, for which it is permitted to suffer as much for fatherland, for land, for empire, for friendship as it is not permitted for God! And yet you cast statues, inscribe images, engrave titles for all these into eternity; as far as monuments can, you yourselves give the dead a kind of resurrection. The man who hopes for true resurrection from God if he suffers for God — he is insane. But go ahead, good Governors, you will look far better to the people if you slaughter Christians. Crucify, torture, condemn, grind us down: the proof of our innocence is your injustice. That is why God lets us suffer these things. For recently, by sentencing a Christian woman to a brothel instead of the lions, you confessed that a stain on purity counts as worse among us than any punishment and any death. Nor does your cruelty, however refined, gain anything: it is an enticement to the sect. We multiply every time you mow us down: the blood of Christians is seed. Many among you urge endurance of pain and death — Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations, Seneca in On Providence, Diogenes, Pyrrho, Callinicus. Yet their words do not find as many disciples as Christians gain by teaching through deeds. That very obstinacy you reproach is the teacher. For who is not shaken by contemplating it into asking what lies inside the matter? Who, having asked, does not draw near, and having drawn near, does not long to suffer, so that he may redeem the whole grace of God, so that he may obtain all forgiveness from Him in exchange for his own blood? For in this work all sins are forgiven. That is why we give thanks for your sentences; it is an emulation of the divine and the human: when we are condemned by you, we are absolved by God.

latin: Ergo, inquitis, cur querimini quod vos insequamur, si pati vultis, cum diligere debeatis per quos patimini quod vultis? Plane volumus pati, verum eo more, quo et bellum nemo quidem libens patitur, cum et trepidare et periclitari sit necesse; tamen et proeliatur omnibus viribus, et vincens in proelio gaudet, qui de proelio querebatur, quia et gloriam consequitur et praedam. Proelium est nobis, quod provocamur ad tribunalia, ut illic sub discrimine capitis pro veritate certemus. Victoria est autem, pro quo certaveris, obtinere. Ea victoria habet, et gloriam placendi Deo, et praedam vivendi in aeternum. Sed obducimur, certe cum obtinuimus: ergo vicimus, cum occidimur; denique evadimus, cum obducimur: licet nunc sarmenticios et semaxios appelletis, quia ad stipitem dimidii axis revincti sarmentorum ambitu exurimur. Hic est habitus victoriae nostrae; haec palmata vestis; tali curru triumphamus. Merito itaque victis non placemus; propterea enim desperati et perditi existimamur. Sed haec desperatio et perditio penes vos, in caussa gloriae et famae, vexillum virtutis extollunt. Mucius dextram suam libens in ara reliquit: o sublimitas animi! Empedocles totum sese Catanensium Aetnaeis incendiis donavit: o vigor mentis! Aliqua Carthaginis conditrix rogo secundum matrimonium dedit: o praeconium castitatis! Regulus, ne unus pro multis hostibus viveret, toto corpore cruces patitur: o virum fortem et in captivitate victorem! Anaxarchus, cum in exemplum ptisanae pilo contunderetur: Tunde, tunde, aiebat, Anaxarchi follem, Anaxarchum enim non tundis: o philosophi magnanimitatem, qui de tali suo exitu etiam jocabatur! Omitto eos qui cum gladio proprio aliove genere mortis mitiore de laude pepigerunt. Ecce enim et tormentorum certamina coronantur a vobis. Attica meretrix, carnifice jam fatigato, postremo linguam suam comestam in faciem tyranni saevientis exspuit, ut exspueret et vocem, ne conjuratos confiteri posset, si etiam victa voluisset. Zeno Eleates, consultus a Dionysio quidnam philosophia praestaret, quum respondisset, contemptum mortis, flagellis tyranni subjectus sententiam suam ad mortem usque signabat. Certe Laconum flagella, sub oculis etiam hortantium propinquorum acerbata, tantum honorem tolerantiae domui conferunt, quantum sanguinis fuderint. O gloriam licitam, quia humanam, cui nec praesumptio perdita, nec persuasio desperata deputatur in contemptu mortis et atrocitatis omnimodae, cui tantum pro patria, pro agro, pro imperio, pro amicitia pati permissum est, quantum pro Deo non licet! Et tamen illis omnibus et statuas defunditis, et imagines inscribitis, et titulos inciditis in aeternitatem; quantum de monumentis potestis scilicet, praestatis et ipsi quodammodo mortuis resurrectionem. Hanc qui veram a Deo sperat, si pro Deo patiatur, insanus est. Sed hoc agite, boni Praesides, meliores multo apud populum, si illis Christianos immolaveritis. Cruciate, torquete, damnate, atterite nos: probatio est enim innocentiae nostrae iniquitas vestra. Ideo nos haec pati Deus patitur. Nam et proxime, ad lenonem damnando christianam potius quam ad leonem, confessi estis labem pudicitiae apud nos atrociorem omni poena et omni morte reputari. Nec quicquam tamen proficit exquisitior quaeque crudelitas vestra: illecebra est magis sectae. Plures efficimur, quoties metimur a vobis: semen est sanguis Christianorum. Multi apud vos ad tolerantiam doloris et mortis hortantur, ut Cicero in Tusculanis, ut Seneca in Fortuitis, ut Diogenes, ut Pyrrhon, ut Callinicus. Nec tamen tantos inveniunt verba discipulos, quantos Christiani factis docendo. Illa ipsa obstinatio, quam exprobratis, magistra est. Quis enim non contemplatione ejus concutitur ad requirendum, quid intus in re sit? Quis non, ubi requisivit, accedit, ubi accessit, pati exoptat, ut totam Dei gratiam redimat, ut omnem veniam ab eo compensatione sanguinis sui expediat? Omnia enim huic operi delicta donantur. Inde est, quod ibidem sententiis vestris gratias agimus; ut est aemulatio divinae rei et humanae, cum damnamur a vobis, a Deo absolvimur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We should skip these examples of constancy born of showmanship about what is coming. Let us turn instead to the very contemplation of the human condition so that these things, too, may instruct us, if there are any things that must be faced steadfastly—things that are accustomed to happen even to the unwilling. How many times have fires burned people alive! How many times have wild beasts, both in their own woods and after escaping from cages in the middle of cities, devoured men! How many have been killed by robbers with a chain, by enemies even with a cross—tortured first, indeed even afflicted with every insult! No one is unable to suffer even for the sake of a mere human being what he hesitates to suffer for the sake of God. Indeed, the present times themselves serve as lessons for us: how many and what kind of persons bring about unexpected outcomes, for the sake of a man—either by him, if they have acted against him, or by his adversaries, if they have stood for him—regardless of their own births, dignities, bodies, and ages.

Convertamur ad ipsam conditionis humanae contemplationem, ut et illa nos instruant, si qua constanter adeunda sint, quae et invitis evenire consueverunt. Quotiens enim incendia vivos cremaverunt! quotiens ferae et in silvis suis et in mediis civitatibus elapsae caveis, homines devoraverunt! quot a latronibus fetro, ab hostibus etiam cruce extincti sunt, torti prius, imo et omni contumelia expuncti! Nemo non etiam hominis caussa pati potest, quod in caussa Dei pati dubitat. Ad hoc quidem vel praesentia nobis tempora documenta sint, quantae qualesque personae inopinatos, natalibus, et dignitatibus, et corporibus, et aetatibus suis, exitus referunt, hominis caussa: aut ab ipso, si contra eum fecerint: aut ab adversariis ejus, si pro eo steterint.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: In the twenty-third book of his *Exegetics*, Basilides comments on the words that punish people 'according to the testimony.' He says: 'I tell you this: as many as fall under these so-called afflictions, either they have sinned in other hidden faults and are led to this good by the kindness of the One who guides all things, being truly accused of different sins than the ones they are punished for, so that they may not suffer as condemned for admitted evils, nor be reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they have been made Christians— which will comfort them so that they do not even seem to suffer; or even if someone has not sinned at all and comes to suffer (rare though that is), yet this one will not suffer by the force of any power, but will suffer as the infant who seems not to have sinned.'

Then, returning to the point, he adds: 'So the infant, not having sinned beforehand, or at least not having sinned in action, yet having within itself the capacity to sin, when subjected to suffering is benefited, gaining much that is hard to win. Thus even the perfect person who has not sinned in deed, if he suffers, has suffered in a way exactly resembling the infant. For he has within himself the sinful tendency, but because he did not take the opportunity to sin, he did not sin. Therefore the fact that he did not sin is not to be reckoned to his credit. For just as the one who wants to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not accomplish the act, and the one who wants to commit murder is a murderer, even if he cannot kill, so also the sinless one of whom I speak, if I see him suffering, even if he has done no evil, I will say the evil lies in his willingness to sin. For I will say all things rather than say that evil lies in God’s forethought.'

Then, pressing further, he speaks plainly about the Lord as if about a man: ‘If, leaving aside all these arguments, you come to calumniate me through certain persons, saying, “So-and-so sinned, for so-and-so suffered,” then if you permit, I will say: he did not sin, but was like the suffering infant. But if you force the argument more strongly, I will say: whoever you name as a man is a man, and God is just. For no one is pure from filth, as someone has said. But Basilides’ hypothesis says that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, endures its punishment here: the elect one enduring it through martyrdom, the other being purified by its own punishment.'

μαρτυρίου, τὴν ἄλλην δὲ καθαιρομένην οἰκείᾳ κολάσει.

excerpts.author: Minucius Felix
english: What a magnificent spectacle a Christian offers God when he faces suffering head-on, steeling himself against threats, punishments, and tortures. He snatches away death's terror and the executioner's horror and tramples them underfoot. He asserts his freedom against kings and princes, yet yields to God alone, to whom that freedom belongs. As a conqueror and victor, he mocks the very judge who sentenced him, for the true victor is the one who gains what he strives for.

What soldier would not court danger more boldly under the emperor's gaze? No one receives a reward without being tested, yet the emperor cannot give what he does not possess: he cannot prolong life, only honor military service. But God's soldier is never abandoned in suffering, nor does death finish him. A Christian may look wretched, but he cannot be found wretched.

You yourselves exalt tragic figures to the heavens—Mucius Scaevola, who would have perished at enemy hands after failing to assassinate a king, had he not thrust his own right hand into the fire. And how many of ours have endured not just a hand, but their entire bodies being burned and consumed, without a single cry, even though release was in their power? Do I compare our people with Mucius, or with Aquilius or Regulus? Our boys and young women, strengthened by the patience that suffering inspires, laugh at crosses, torments, wild beasts, and every terror of punishment.

You do not understand, you wretched ones, that no one willingly undergoes punishment without reason, and no one can endure torture without God. Perhaps you are deceived because, in your ignorance of God, you overflow with riches, flourish in honors, and wield great power. Miserable creatures! You are lifted higher only to fall deeper. Like victims fattened for slaughter, like sacrificial beasts crowned for the altar, you are prepared for punishment. Some are raised to empire and dominion so that their genius may freely traffic in the licentiousness of a lost mind's power. Without knowledge of God, what solid happiness can exist when death is like a dream—slipping away before it can be grasped?

Are you a king? You fear as much as you are feared, and despite your vast retinue, you face danger alone. Are you rich? Fortune is a poor credit risk; a massive fortune does not provision life's brief journey—it burdens it. Do you glory in fasces and purple? That is a vain human error and an empty cult of dignity: to shine in purple while the mind grows sordid. Are you noble by birth? Do you praise your parents? We are all born to the same lot; only virtue distinguishes us.

Therefore we, who are judged by our character and our sense of shame, rightly abstain from your wicked pleasures, pomp, and spectacles. We know their sacred origins, and we condemn their harmful allurements. In the curule games, who does not shudder at the insanity of a populace rioting against itself? In the gladiatorial games, you witness the discipline of homicide. In the scenic games, turpitude is no less, only prolonged by fury: now the mime exposes or enacts adulteries; now the effeminate actor, while feigning love, inflicts it. The same performer dishonors your gods by portraying rapes, sighs, and hatreds. With simulated pains, he provokes your tears through empty gestures and nods. Thus you commit homicide in truth, but weep in falsehood.

latin: Quam pulchrum spectaculum Deo, quum Christianus cum dolore congreditur, quum adversum minas et supplicia et tormenta componitur; quum strepitum mortis55 et horrorem carnificis irripiens inculcat; quum, libertatem suam adversus reges et principes erigit, soli Deo, cujus est, cedit; quum triumphator et victor, ipsi qui adversum se sententia dixit, stultat ! Vicit enim qui quod contendit obtinuit. Quis non miles sub oculis imperatoris audacius periculum provocet? nemo enim praemium percipit ante experimentum: et imperator tamen, quod non habet, non dat; non potest propagare vitam, potest honestare militiam. At enim Dei miles nec in dolore deseritur, nec morte finitur. Sic Christianus miser videri potest, non potest inveniri. Vos ipsi calamitosos viros fertis ad coelum, Mucium Scaevolam, qui, quum errasset in regem, periisset in hostibus, nisi dexteram perdidisset. Et quot ex nostris non dextram solum, sed totum corpus uri, cremari, sine ullis ejulatibus, pertulerunt, quum dimitti praesertim haberent in sua potestate? Viros cum Mucio, vel cum Aquilio aut Regulo comparo? Pueri et mulierculae nostrae cruces et tormenta, feras et omnes suppliciorum terriculas, inspirata patientia doloris, illudunt. Nec intelligilis, o miseri, neminem esse qui, aut sine ratione velit poenam subire, aut tormenta sine Deo posse sustinere. Nisi forte vos decipit, quod, Deum nescientes, divitiis affluant, honoribus floreant, polleant potestatibus. Miseri! in hoc altius tolluntur, ut decidant altius. Hi enim, ut victimae, ad supplicium saginantur; ut hostiae ad poenam, coronantur. In hoc adeo quidam imperiis ac dominationibus eriguntur, ut ingenium eorum perditae mentis licentiae potestatis libere nundinentur: absque enim notitia Dei, quae potest esse solida felicitas, quum mors sit somnio similis? antequam tenetur, elabitur. Rex es? et tam times quam timeris: et, quamlibet sis multo comitatu stipatus, ad periculum tamen solus es. Dives es? sed fortunae male creditur, et magno viatico breve vitae iter non instruitur, sed oneratur. Fascibus et purpuris gloriaris? vanus error hominis et inanis cultus dignitatis, fulgere purpura, mente sordescere. Nobilitate generosus es? parentes tuos laudas? Omnes tamen pari sorte nascimur; sola virtute distinguimur. Nos igitur qui moribus et pudore censemur, merito malis voluptatibus et pompis vestris et spectaculis abstinemus: quorum et de sacris originem novimus, et noxia blandimenta damnamus. Nam in ludis curulibus, quis non horreat populi in se rixantis insaniam? In gladiatoriis, homicidii disciplinam? In scenicis etiam non minor furore turpitudo prolixior: nunc enim mimus vel exponit adulteria, vel monstrat; nunc enervis histrio amorem dum fingit, infligit. Idem deos vestros, induendo stupra, suspiria, odia, dedecorat. Idem, simulatis doloribus, lacrymas vestras vanis gestibus et nutibus provocat. Sic homicidium in vero flagitatis, in mendacio fletis.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: Since you wanted to learn the precise details of the topics you proposed to us, my beloved brother Theophilus, I thought it right to draw abundantly from the divine Scriptures themselves as from a holy spring and set before your eyes the things you seek. I do this so that you may not only be delighted by hearing these things with your ears, but also, having been instructed by the power of the matters themselves, you may be able to glorify God in every way. May this serve as a safe provision for you in the present life, so that, bringing forward from prepared words the things that are unknown and hard for many to grasp, you may sow them in the breadth of your heart as in fertile and pure soil, and despise those who contradict and speak against the saving word.

excerpts.citation: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity — Passion of Perpetua and Felicity 1
excerpts.author: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity
english: The authorities seized the young catechumens — Revocatus, Felicity his fellow servant, Saturninus, and Secundulus. Among them was also Vivia Perpetua, well-born, liberally educated, respectably married, with a father and mother and two brothers, one of whom was also a catechumen, and an infant son at her breast. She herself was about twenty-two years old. She will now narrate the whole order of her martyrdom, exactly as she left it written in her own hand and from her own understanding.

"While we were still with the persecutors," she says, "my father kept trying to turn me away and cast me down out of his affection. 'Father,' I said, 'do you see, for example, this vessel lying here, a little jug or something else?' He said, 'I see.' I said to him, 'Can it be called by any other name than what it is?' He said, 'No.' 'So I also cannot say that I am anything other than what I am, a Christian.'" Then her father, moved by this word, threw himself at her to gouge out her eyes; but he only harassed her and went away defeated, overcome by the devil's arguments. After a few days, when she had been without her father, she gave thanks to the Lord, and his absence was a relief to her. In that same space of a few days they were baptized, and the Spirit dictated to her that she should ask for nothing else in the water except the endurance of the flesh. After a few days they were taken back to prison, and she was terrified because she had never experienced such darkness. O harsh day! With strong heat and turmoil from the soldiers' rough handling; finally she was worn out with worry about her infant. There Tertius and Pomponius, blessed deacons who were ministering to them, arranged by a bribe that, once released for a few hours, they might refresh themselves in a better part of the prison. Then, going out of prison, everyone was free to attend to their own needs. She was nursing her infant, who was already failing from lack of food. Anxious about him, she spoke to her mother and comforted her brother, entrusting her son to him. She was wasting away because she saw them wasting away on her account. She endured such worries for many days, and she managed that her infant might remain with her in prison; and immediately she recovered, and was relieved of the labor and worry of her infant, and the prison suddenly became like a palace to her, so that she preferred to be there rather than anywhere else.

Then her brother said to her, 'Lady sister, you are now in great dignity, and so great that you can ask for a vision, and it will be shown to you whether you will undergo passion or reprieve.' And she, knowing that she was speaking with the Lord, whose great benefits she had experienced, confidently promised him, saying, 'Tomorrow I will tell you.' And she asked, and it was shown to her: She sees a golden ladder of amazing size reaching up to heaven, narrow, so that only one person can ascend at a time; and on the sides of the ladder every kind of iron tool is fixed — swords, lances, hooks, daggers — so that if anyone ascends carelessly or without looking upward, he will be torn and his flesh will cling to the iron tools. And under the ladder a dragon of amazing size lies in wait, preparing ambushes for those ascending and frightening them so they will not ascend. But Saturus ascended first, who later handed himself over voluntarily on their behalf, and at that time, when they were led away, he was not present; he reached the top of the ladder, turned to her, and said, 'Perpetua, I am waiting for you. But see that the dragon does not bite you.' She said, 'It will not harm me in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.' And from under the ladder, as if fearing her, it slowly lifted its head; and when she had stepped on the first rung, she stepped on its head. She ascended and saw an immense garden, and in the middle of the garden a man of dog-like appearance, seated, dressed as a shepherd, large, milking sheep; and around him many thousands of white-robed candidates stood. He lifted his head and looked at her and said, 'You have come well, child.' He called her and gave her some of the cheese he was milking, like a little morsel; she took it with joined hands and ate, and all those standing around said, 'Amen.' At the sound of the voice she awoke, still chewing something sweet she did not know. She told her brother at once, and they understood that a passion would follow; and they began to have no more hope in the world.

latin: I. Apprehensi sunt adolescentes catechumini, Revocatus et Felicitas conserva ejus, Saturninus et Secundulus. Inter quos et Vivia Perpetua, honeste nata, liberaliter instituta, matronaliter nupta, habens patrem et matrem et fratres duos, alterum aeque catechuminum, et filium infantem ad ubera. Erat autem ipsa annorum circiter viginti duorum. Haec ordinem totum martyrii sui jam hinc ipsa narrabit, sicut conscriptum manu sua et suo sensu reliquit. II. « Cum adhuc, inquit, cum persecutoribus essemus, et me pater avertere et dejicere pro sua affectione perseveraret: Pater, inquio, vides, verbi gratia, vas hoc jacens, urceolum, sive aliud? » Et « dixit: Video. » Et ego dixi ei: « Numquid alio nomine vocari potest quam quod est? » Et ait: « Non. » « Sic et ego aliud me dicere non possum, nisi quod sum Christiana. » Tunc pater motus in hoc verbo, misit « se in me ut oculos mihi erueret: sed vexavit tantum, et profectus est victus cum argumentis diaboli, Tunc paucis diebus quod caruissem patre, Domino gratias egi, et refrigeravit absentia illius. In ipso spatio paucorum dierum baptizati sumus; mihi autem Spiritus dictavit nihil aliud petendum in aqua, nisi sufferentiam carnis. Post paucos dies recipimur in carcerem, et expavi, quia numquam experta eram tales tenebras. O diem asperum! aestus validos turbarum beneficio concussurae militum: novissime macerabar sollicitudine infantis. Ibi tunc Tertius et Pomponius, benedicti diacones, qui nobis ministrabant, constituerunt praemio ut, paucis horis emissi, in meliorem locum carceris refrigeraremus. Tunc exeuntes de carcere universi sibi vacabant. Ego infantem lactabam jam inedia defectum. Sollicita pro eo adloquebar matrem, et confortabam fratrem, commendabam filium. Tabescebam ideo quod illos tabescere videram mei beneficio. Tales sollicitudines multis diebus passa sum, et usurpavi ut mecum infans in carcere maneret; et statim convalui, et relevata sum a labore et sollicitudine infantis: et factus est mihi carcer subito quasi praetorium, ut ibi mallem esse quam alibi. « III. Tunc dixit mihi frater meus: Domina soror, jam in magna dignitate es; et tanta ut postules visionem, et ostendatur tibi an passio sit, an commeatus. Et ego, quae me sciebam fabulari cum Domino, cujus beneficia tanta experta eram, fidenter repromisi ei dicens: « Crastina die tibi renuntiabo. » Et postulavi, et ostensum est mihi hoc: Video scalam auream mirae magnitudinis pertingentem usque ad coelum et angustam, per quam non nisi singuli ascendere possent: et in lateribus scalae omne genus ferramentorum infixum. Erant ibi gladii, lanceae, hami, machaerae; ut si quis negligenter, aut non sursum adtendens ascenderet, laniaretur et carnes ejus inhaererent ferramentis. Et erat sub ipsa scala draco cubans mirae magnitudinis, qui ascendentibus insidias parabat, et exterrebat ne ascenderent. Ascendit autem Saturus prior, qui postea se propter nos ultro tradiderat, et tunc cum adducti sumus, praesens non fuerat: et pervenit in caput scalae, et convertit se ad me, et dixit mihi: « Perpetua, sustineo te. Sed vide ne te mordeat draco ille. » Et dixi ego: « Non me nocebit in nomine Domini Jesu Christi. » Et de sub ipsa scala quasi timens me, lente elevavit caput: et cum primum gradum calcassem, calcavi illius caput. Et ascendi et vidi spatium horti immensum, et in medio horti sedentem hominem canum, in habitu pastoris, grandem, oves mulgentem; et circumstantes candidati millia multa. Et levavit caput et adspexit me, et dixit mihi: « Bene venisti, tecnon. » Et clamavit me, et de caseo quod mulgebat dedit mihi quasi buccellam, et ego accepi junctis manibus, et manducavi: et universi circumstantes dixerunt, Amen. Et ad sonum vocis experrecta sum, commanducans adhuc dulcis nescio quid. Et retuli statim fratri meo, et intelleximus passionem esse futuram: et coepimus nullam jam spem in saeculo habere.
