english: A few days later word spread that we would be brought to trial. My father arrived from the city, worn out with anxiety, and came to me trying to break my resolve. "Have pity on my grey hairs, daughter," he said. "Have pity on your father, if I deserve to be called father by you. I brought you to this prime of life; I favored you above all your brothers. Do not hand me over to public disgrace. Look at your brothers. Look at your mother and aunt. Look at your son, who cannot survive you. Give up this stubbornness, or you will destroy us all. None of us will be able to speak freely if you suffer anything." He spoke out of paternal love, kissing my hands and throwing himself at my feet. With tears he called me not daughter but lady. I ached for his grey hairs, because he alone of my whole family would find no joy in my suffering. I comforted him: "What happens on that platform will be as God wills. Know that we are not in our own power, but in God's." He left me in sorrow.

Another day, while we were eating, we were suddenly seized for the hearing and taken to the forum. The news raced through the surrounding streets, and an immense crowd gathered. We mounted the tribunal. The others were questioned and confessed. When my turn came, my father appeared at once with my son, pulled me down from the step, and pleaded: "Have pity on the infant." Hilarianus the procurator — who held the power of the sword in place of the deceased proconsul Minucius Timinianus — said: "Spare your father's grey hairs; spare the boy's childhood. Offer sacrifice for the emperors' safety." I answered: "I will not." Hilarianus asked: "Are you a Christian?" I answered: "I am a Christian." When my father tried to drag me down, Hilarianus ordered him thrown aside and struck with a rod. I felt his fall as if I had been struck myself; I grieved for his miserable old age. Then he pronounced sentence on us all and condemned us to the beasts. We went down to prison joyful. Because my infant was used to nursing from me and staying with me in prison, I immediately sent Pomponius the deacon to my father asking for the child. My father refused to give him up. But as God willed, the child no longer craved milk, and I did not develop fever, so that I would not be worn out by anxiety for the infant and the pain of my breasts.

After a few days, while we were all praying, a voice came to me in the middle of the prayer and I named Dinocrates. I was astonished that he had never entered my mind until that moment, and I grieved at the memory of his death. I knew at once that I was worthy, and that I ought to pray for him. I began to pray earnestly for him and to groan to the Lord. That same night a vision was shown to me: I saw Dinocrates coming out of a dark place where many others were, panting and very thirsty, his face dirty and pale, with a wound on his face from his death. This Dinocrates was my flesh-and-blood brother, seven years old, who had died horribly of a cancerous face, so that his death was repulsive to everyone. I had prayed for him, and between us there was a great gulf, so that neither could reach the other. In that same place where Dinocrates was, there was a pool full of water, its rim higher than the boy's height. He stretched himself out as if to drink. I grieved that the pool held water, yet because of the height of the rim he could not drink. I awoke, and I knew my brother was suffering. But I trusted my prayer would help his suffering, and I prayed for him every day until we were transferred to the military prison, for we were to fight in the garrison games. It was then the birthday of Caesar Geta, and I prayed for him day and night, groaning and weeping, that he might be granted to me.

On the day we were in the stocks, a vision was shown to me: I saw that same place I had seen before as dark, now bright. Dinocrates had a clean body, was well dressed, and was refreshed. Where the wound had been, I saw a scar. The pool I had seen before now had its rim lowered to the boy's navel. He drew water from it without ceasing, and on the rim stood a cup full of water. Dinocrates came and began to drink from it, and the cup did not fail. When he had drunk his fill, he left the water to play, rejoicing like a child. I awoke. Then I understood that he had been delivered from his punishment.

latin: « I. Post paucos dies rumor cucurrit ut audiremur. Supervenit autem et de civitate pater meus, consumptus taedio, ascendit ad me ut me dejiceret, dicens: « Miserere, filia, canis meis; miserere patri, si dignus sum a te pater vocari. Si his te manibus ad hunc florem aetatis provexi; si te praeposui omnibus fratribus tuis, ne me dederis in dedecus hominum. Aspice ad fratres tuos, aspice ad matrem tuam et materteram, aspice ad filium tuum qui post te vivere non poterit. Depone animos, ne universos nos extermines. Nemo enim nostrum libere loquetur, si tu aliquid fueris passa. » Haec dicebat pater pro sua pietate basians mihi manus; et se ad pedes meos jactans, et lacrymis non filiam sed dominam me vocabat. Et ego dolebam canos patris mei, quod solus de passione mea gavisurus non esset de toto genere meo; et confortavi eum, dicens: « Hoc fiet in illa catasta quod Deus voluerit. Scito enim nos non in nostra potestate esse constitutos, sed in Dei. » Et recessit a me contristatus. « II. Alio die cum pranderemus, subito rapti sumus ut audiremur: et pervenimus ad forum. Rumor statim per vicinas fori partes cucurrit, et factus est populus immensus. Ascendimus in catasta. Interrogati caeteri confessi sunt. Ventum est et ad me, et apparuit pater illico cum filio meo, et extraxit me de gradu, et dixit supplicans: « Miserere infanti. » Et Hilarianus procurator, qui tunc, loco proconsulis Minucii Timiniani defuncti, jus gladii acceperat: « Parce, inquit, canis patris tui: parce infantiae pueri. Fac sacrum pro salute imperatorum. » Et ego respondi: « Non facio. » Hilarianus, « Christiana es? » « inquit. Et ego respondi: « Christiani sum. » Et cum staret pater ad me dejiciendam, jussus est ab Hilariano dejici, et virga percussus est. Et doluit mihi casus patris mei, quasi ego fuissem percussa: sic dolui pro senecta ejus misera. Tunc nos universos pronuntiat, et damnat ad bestias: et hilares descendimus ad carcerem. Tunc, quia consueverat a me infans mammas accipere et mecum in carcere manere, statim mitto ad patrem Pomponium diaconum, postulans infantem: sed pater dare noluit: et quomodo Deus voluit, neque ille amplius mammas desideravit; neque mihi fervorem fecerunt, ne sollicitudine infantis et dolore mammarum macerarer. « III. Post dies paucos, dum universi oramus, subito media oratione profecta est mihi vox, et nominavi Dinocratem: et obstupui quod numquam mihi in mentem venisset nisi tunc, et dolui commemorata casus ejus. Et cognovi me statim dignam esse, et pro eo petere debere. Et coepi pro ipso orationem facere multum, et ingemiscere ad Dominum. Continuo ipsa nocte ostensum est mihi hoc in oromate: video Dinocratem exeuntem de loco tenebroso, ubi et complures erant, aestuantem et sitientem valde, sordido vultu et colore pallido, et vulnus in facie ejus quod cum moreretur habuit. Hic Dinocrates fuerat frater meus carnalis, annorum septem, qui per infirmitatem, facie cancerata, male obiit, ita ut mors ejus odio fuerit omnibus hominibus. Pro hoc ego orationem feceram: et inter me et illum grande erat diadema, ita ut uterque ad invicem accedere non possemus. Erat deinde in ipso loco ubi Dinocrates erat, piscina plena aqua, altiorem marginem habens quam erat statura pueri, et extendebat se Dinocrates quasi bibiturus. Ego dolebam quod et piscina illa aquam habebat, et tamen propter altitudinem marginis bibiturus non esset. Et experrecta sum, et cognovi fratrem meum laborare. Sed confidebam profuturam orationem meam labori ejus, et orabam pro eo omnibus diebus quousque transivimus in carcerem castrensem; munere enim castrensi eramus pugnaturi. Natale tunc Getae Caesaris: et feci pro illo orationem die et nocte gemens et lacrymans ut mihi donaretur. « IV. Die autem quo in nervo mansimus, ostensum est mihi hoc: Video locum illum quem retro videram tenebrosum, esse lucidum; et Dinocratem mundo corpore, bene vestitum, refrigerantem. Et ubi erat vulnus, video cicatricem; et piscinam illam quam retro videram, summisso margine usque ad umbilicum pueri; et aquam de ea trahebat sine cessatione, et super margine phiala erat, plena aqua; et accessit Dinocrates, et de ea bibere coepit, quae phiala non deficiebat. Et satiatus abscessit de aqua ludere more infantium gaudens: et experrecta sum. Tunc intellexi translatum eum esse de poena.

english: The blessed Saturus published this vision, which he himself wrote down.

He said: We were suffering, and we left the body behind; four angels began carrying us toward the east without touching us. We were not lying on our backs as we rose, but moving as if we were climbing a gentle slope. Once freed, we immediately saw the first immense light, and I said, ‘Perpetua — for she was at my side — this is what the Lord promised us; we have received the promise.’

While those same four angels were still carrying us, a great space opened before us, like a park filled with rose trees and every kind of flower. The trees stood as tall as cypresses, and their leaves fell without ceasing. In that park four other angels, brighter than the rest, saw us, honored us, and told the other angels, ‘Here they are, here they are,’ with admiration. The four angels who had been carrying us trembled and set us down, and we walked across a broad avenue on foot.

There we found Jocundus, Saturninus, and Artaxius, who had endured the same persecution and were burning alive; we also found Quintus, who had left prison as a martyr. We asked them where the others were, but the angels said to us, ‘Come first, enter, and greet the Lord.’

We approached a place whose walls seemed to be built of light. Four angels stood before its door and clothed those entering in white robes. Once clothed, we entered and saw immense light; we heard a united voice crying, ‘Holy, holy, holy,’ without ceasing. In the center of that place sat one who looked like a man with white hair and a youthful face, whose feet we could not see. Twenty-four elders sat on his right and left, and behind them many others stood. We entered with great awe, stood before the throne, and the four angels lifted us up so we could kiss him; he passed his hand over our faces in blessing. The other elders said, ‘Let us stand.’ We stood and exchanged peace. Then the elders said, ‘Go, and enjoy yourselves.’ I said, ‘Perpetua, you have what you want.’ She replied, ‘Thanks be to God; just as I was cheerful in the flesh, I am even more cheerful here.’

We went out and saw Optatus the bishop on the right and Aspasius the presbyter and teacher on the left, standing before the doors, separated and sad. They threw themselves at our feet and said, ‘Reconcile us, because you have separated from us and left us like this.’ We answered, ‘Are you our father, and are you our presbyter, that you should throw yourselves at our feet?’ We threw ourselves down and embraced them. Perpetua began speaking with them, and we set them apart in the park under a rose tree.

While we were speaking with them, the angels told them, ‘Let them be; let them refresh themselves. If you have any disputes among yourselves, forgive one another,’ and the angels troubled them. They said to Optatus, ‘Correct your people, for they come to you as if returning from the circus and contending in factions.’ It seemed to us as if they wanted to shut the gates. We began to recognize many brothers there, and martyrs as well. All were nourished by an indescribable fragrance that satisfied us. Then, rejoicing, I awoke.

latin: I. Sed et Saturus benedictus hanc visionem suam edidit, quam ipse conscripsit. « Passi, inquit, eramus, et exivimus de carne, et coepimus ferri a quatuor Angelis in orientem, quorum manus nos non tangebant. Ibamus autem non supini sursum versi, sed quasi mollem clivum ascendentes. Et liberati primam jam vidimus lucem immensam; et dixi: Perpetua (erat enim haec in latere meo), hoc est quod nobis Dominus promittebat: percepimus promissionem. Et dum gestamur ab ipsis quatuor Angelis, factum est nobis spatium grande, quod tale fuit quasi viridarium arbores habens rosae, et omne genus floris. Altitudo autem arborum erat in modum cypressi, quarum folia cadebant sine cessatione. Ibi autem in viridario, alii quatuor Angeli fuerunt clariores caeteris, qui ubi viderunt nos, honorem nobis dederunt, et dixerunt caeteris Angelis: Ecce sunt, ecce sunt; cum admiratione. Et expavescentes quatuor illi Angeli qui gestabant nos, deposuerunt nos: et pedibus nostris transivimus stadium via lata. Ibi invenimus Jocundum et Saturninum et Artaxium qui, eamdem persecutionem passi, vivi arserunt; et Quintum, qui et ipse martyr in carcere exierat; et quaerebamus ab illis ubi essent caeteri. Dixerunt autem nobis Angeli: Venite prius, introite, et salutate Dominum. II. Et venimus prope locum, cujus loci parietes tales erant quasi de luce aedificati; et ante ostium loci illius quatuor Angeli stabant, qui introeuntes vestierunt stolas candidas. Et nos vestiti introivimus, et vidimus lucem immensam, et audivimus vocem unitam dicentium: Agios, agios, agios; sine cessatione. Et vidimus in medio loci illius sedentem quasi hominem canum, niveos habentem capillos et vultu juvenili, cujus pedes non vidimus. Et in dextra et in sinistra seniores viginti quatuor, et post illos caeteri complures stabant. Introivimus cum magna admiratione, et stetimus ante thronum; et quatuor Angeli sublevaverunt nos, et osculati sumus illum, et de manu sua trajecit nobis in facie. Et caeteri seniores dixerunt nobis: Stemus. Et stetimus, et pacem fecimus. Et dixerunt nobis seniores: Ite, et ludite. Et dixi: Perpetua, habes quod vis. Et dixit mihi: Deo gratias, ut, quomodo in carne hilaris fui, hilarior sum et heic modo. III. Et exivimus, et vidimus ante fores Optatum episcopum ad dexteram, et Aspasium presbyterum doctorem ad sinistram, separatos et tristes, et miserunt se ad pedes nobis, et dixerunt nobis: Componite inter nos quia existis, et sic nos reliquistis. Et diximus illis: Non tu es papa noster, et tu presbyter, ut vos ad pedes nostros mittatis? et misimus nos, et complexi illos sumus. Et coepit Perpetua cum illis loqui, et segregavimus eos in viridario sub arbore rosae. Et dum loquimur cum eis, dixerunt illis Angeli: Sinite illos, refrigerent; et si quas habetis inter vos dissensiones, dimittite vobis invicem; et conturbaverunt eos. Et dixerunt Optato: Corrige plebem tuam; quia sic ad te conveniunt quasi de circo redeuntes, et de factionibus certantes. Et sic nobis visum est, quasi vellent claudere portas. Et coepimus illic multos fratres cognoscere, sed et martyres. Universi odore inenarrabili alebamur, qui nos satiabat. Tunc gaudens experrectus sum. »

english: These are the more remarkable visions of the most blessed martyrs Saturus and Perpetua, which they themselves wrote down. God called Secundulus out of this world with a more mature exit while he was still in prison — not without grace — so that he might gain the beasts. His flesh, if not his soul, certainly acknowledged the joy.

As for Felicity, the Lord's grace of this kind had also come upon her. She was already eight months pregnant when the day of the spectacle drew near, for she had been arrested while with child. She was in great grief, fearing that her pregnancy would cause a delay, since pregnant women are not permitted to face punishment, and dreading that she would have to shed her holy and innocent blood later among wicked people apart from her companions. Her fellow martyrs were also deeply saddened, lest they leave so good a companion, like a fellow traveler, alone on the road of the same hope. So they joined together in a united groan and poured out a prayer to the Lord three days before the games. Immediately after the prayer, labor pains seized her. As she suffered in childbirth from the natural difficulty of the eighth month, one of the prison attendants said to her, "If you groan like this now, what will you do when you are thrown to the beasts — you who despised them by refusing to sacrifice?" She answered, "Right now I am suffering what I suffer, but then another will be in me who will suffer for me, because I too am going to suffer for him." So she gave birth to a girl, and a certain sister of hers raised her as a daughter.

Since the Holy Spirit permitted it, and by permitting willed that the account of the spectacle itself be recorded — though we are unworthy to describe such great glory — we nevertheless carry it out as if by a mandate of the most holy Perpetua, or rather as a trust committed by her faith, adding one further testimony to her constancy and loftiness of spirit. When the tribune treated them more harshly because he feared, from the warnings of utterly worthless men, that they might be spirited out of prison by magical incantations, Perpetua looked him in the face and replied, "Why do you not allow the most noble Caesar's prisoners to be refreshed and to prepare for his birthday, the day on which they will fight? Or is it not to your credit if we are produced fatter for it?" The tribune shuddered and blushed, and so he ordered that they be treated more humanely, granting her brothers and the others permission to enter and refresh themselves with them — even the warden himself having come to believe.

On the day before, when they shared that last meal which they call a free supper, they made it not a free supper but a love feast, as far as lay in them. With the same constancy they spoke these words to the crowd, threatening the Lord's judgment, testifying to the joy of their passion, and mocking the curiosity of the onlookers. Saturus said, "The day after tomorrow will not be enough for you — you who gladly watch what you hate. Today friends, tomorrow enemies. But take careful note of our faces, so that you may recognize us on that day of judgment." And so all departed from there astonished, and among them many believed.

latin: I. Hae visiones insigniores ipsorum martyrum beatissimorum Saturi et Perpetuae, quas ipsi conscripserunt. Secundulum vero Deus maturiore exitu de saeculo, adhuc in carcere evocavit, non sine gratia, ut bestias lucraretur. Gaudium tamen etsi non anima, certe caro ejus agnovit. II. Circa Felicitatem vero (nam et illi gratia Domini ejusmodi contigit), cum octo jam mensium suum ventrem haberet (nam praegnans fuerat apprehensa), instante spectaculi die, in magno erat luctu, ne propter ventrem differretur, quia non licet praegnantes poenae repraesentari: et ne inter aliquos postea sceleratos, sanctum et innocentem sanguinem funderet. Sed et commartyres ejus graviter contristabantur, ne tam bonam sociam, quasi comitem, solam in via ejusdem spei relinquerent. Conjuncto itaque unito gemitu, ad Dominum orationem fuderunt ante tertium diem muneris. Statim post orationem dolores eam invaserunt. Et cum, pro naturali difficultate octavi mensis, in partu laborans doleret, ait illi quidam ex ministris Cataractariorum: Quae sic modo doles, quid facies objecta bestiis, quas contempsisti cum sacrificare noluisti? Et illa respondit: « Modo ego patior quod patior, illic autem alius erit in me qui patietur pro me, quia et ego pro illo passura sum. » Ita enixa est puellam, quam sibi quaedam soror in filiam educavit. III. Quoniam ergo permisit, et permittendo voluit Spiritus sanctus ordinem ipsius muneris conscribi, etsi indigni ad supplementum tantae gloriae describendum; tamen, quasi mandatum sanctissimae Perpetuae, immo fidei commissum ejus exsequimur, unum adjicientes documentum de ipsius constantia et animi sublimitate. Cum a tribuno castigatius eo tractarentur, quia ex admonitionibus hominum vanissimorum verebatur ne subtraherentur de carcere incantationibus aliquibus magicis; in faciem respondit Perpetua, et dixit: « Quid utique non permittis refrigerare noxiis nobilissimi Caesaris scilicet, et natali ejusdem pugnaturis? Aut non tua gloria est, si pinguiores illo producamur? » Horruit et erubuit tribunus; et ita jussit illos humanius haberi, ut fratribus ejus et caeteris facultas fieret introeundi et refrigerandi cum eis; jam et ipso optione carceris credente. IV. Pridie quoque, cum illa coena ultima quam liberam vocant, quantum in ipsis erat, non coenam liberam, sed agapen coenarent; eadem constantia ad populum verba ista jactabant, comminantes judicium Domini, contestantes passioni suae felicitatem, irridentes concurrentium curiositatem, dicente Saturo: « Crastinus dies satis vobis non est, quod libenter videtis, quod odistis. Hodie amici, cras inimici. Notate tamen nobis facies nostras diligenter, ut recognoscatis nos in die illo judicii. » Ita omnes inde attoniti discedebant: ex quibus multi crediderunt.

english: The day of their victory dawned, and they walked from the prison into the amphitheater as if entering heaven, cheerful and composed; if they trembled, it was with joy, not fear. Perpetua followed with a calm face and steady step, like a noblewoman of Christ, beloved of God, lowering her eyes from the gaze of the crowd. Felicity rejoiced that she had given birth safely, so that she might fight the beasts; from blood and the midwife to the net-fighter, she was about to be washed after childbirth with a second baptism. When they were brought to the gate and forced to put on the robes of the priests of Saturn for the men and the vestments of the consecrated of Ceres for the women, that noble constancy resisted to the end. She said: "We came here of our own free will so that our freedom would not be obscured. We pledged our souls so that we would not do such a thing; this was our agreement with you." Injustice recognized justice, and the tribune conceded that they be led in just as they were, simply dressed. Perpetua sang psalms, now treading on the head of the Egyptian. Revocatus, Saturninus, and Saturus threatened the watching crowd about this. When they came into Hilarianus's sight, they gestured and nodded to him: "You will judge us, but God will judge you." The people, enraged, demanded they be scourged according to the order of the hunters. And indeed they rejoiced that they had attained a share in the Lord's sufferings.

But he who said, "Ask and you will receive" (Matt 7:7; Luke 11:9), gave to those who asked the exit each one desired. When they discussed the vow of their martyrdom, Saturninus professed he wanted to be thrown to all the beasts, so that he might win a more glorious crown. In the contest of the spectacle, he and Revocatus faced the leopard and were also torn by the bear on the platform. Saturus, however, dreaded nothing more than the bear; he expected to be finished by a single bite of the leopard. When a boar was provided, the hunter who had brought it was gored by the same beast and died after some days of the games. Saturus alone was dragged out. When he was bound to the bear on the bridge, the bear refused to leave its cage. So Saturus was recalled a second time, unharmed.

For the women, the devil prepared a most ferocious cow, procured contrary to custom, even emulating their sex in the beast. Stripped and dressed in nets, they were led out. The people shuddered at the sight of one young woman, delicate, and the other with breasts dripping from recent childbirth. So they were recalled and allowed to dress again. Perpetua was led in first; she was thrown and fell on her loins. Seeing her tunic torn at the side, she drew it over her thighs, mindful of modesty rather than pain. Then, asked to do so, she pinned up her disheveled hair, for it was not fitting for a martyr to suffer with hair unbound, lest she appear to be lamenting in her glory. She rose, and seeing Felicity bruised, she went to her, gave her hand, and lifted her up. Both stood together, and when the people's hostility was overcome, they were recalled to the Gate of Life. There Perpetua was received by a catechumen named Rusticus, who clung to her. As if awakened from sleep — so deeply was she in spirit and ecstasy — she looked around and said to everyone's amazement: "When are we led out to that cow? I do not know." When she heard it had already happened, she would not believe until she recognized the marks of torment on her body and clothing, and saw the catechumen. Then she summoned her brother and spoke to the catechumen: "Stand firm in faith, love one another, and do not be scandalized by our sufferings."

At another gate, Saturus encouraged the soldier Pudens: "I am here, just as I promised and predicted; I have not yet felt any beast. Now believe with all your heart. See, I go to that one and will be consumed by a single bite of the leopard." Immediately at the end of the spectacle, he was thrown to the leopard and so drenched in blood from one bite that the crowd, as he returned, cried out as a testimony to a second baptism: "Washed and saved, washed and saved." Truly he was saved, who had been glorified in this spectacle. Then to Pudens he said: "Farewell, and remember my faith; let these things not disturb you but confirm you." At the same time he asked for a ring from Pudens's finger, dipped it in his wound, and returned it, leaving a pledge of his guarantee and a memory of his blood. Then, lifeless, he fell with the others to the slaughter in the usual place. When the people demanded they be brought into the middle so that, with the sword piercing their bodies, their eyes might join the spectators as companions of the homicide, they rose of their own accord and went where the people wanted. They had already kissed one another, so as to consummate their martyrdom through the solemnities of peace. The others received the sword immobile and in silence; even more so Saturus, who had also ascended the ladder first, gave up his spirit first, for he was also supporting Perpetua. Perpetua, however, so that she might taste some pain, cried out when pierced between the ribs, and herself placed the trembling right hand of the young gladiator on her throat. Perhaps such a woman could not have been killed otherwise, because she was feared by the unclean spirit, unless she herself had willed it.

latin: I. Illuxit dies victoriae illorum, et processerunt de carcere in amphitheatrum, quasi in coelum, hilares, vultu decori; si forte, gaudio paventes, non timore. Sequebatur Perpetua placido vultu et pedum incessu, ut matrona Christi Dei dilecta: vigorem oculorum suorum dejiciens ab omnium conspectu. Item Felicitas salvam se peperisse gaudens, ut ad bestias pugnaret, a sanguine, ab obstetrice ad retiarium, lotura post partum baptismo secundo. Et cum delati essent in portam, et cogerentur habitum induere i viri quidem sacerdotum Saturni, feminae vero sacratarum Cereri: generosa illa in finem usque constantia repugnavit. Dicebat enim: « Ideo ad hoc sponte pervenimus; ne libertas nostra obduceretur. Ideo animas nostras addiximus, ne tale aliquid faceremus: hoc vobiscum pacti sumus. » Agnovit injustitia justitiam: concessit tribunus, ut quomodo erant, simpliciter inducerentur. Perpetua psallebat, caput jam Aegyptii calcans. Revocatus, et Saturninus, et Saturus populo spectanti comminabantur de hoc. Ut sub conspectu Hilariani pervenerunt, gestu et nutu coeperunt Hilariano dicere: « Tu nos, inquiunt, te autem Deus judicabit. » Ad hoc populus exasperatus, flagellis eos vexari pro ordine venatorum postulavit. Et utique illi gratulati sunt, quod aliquid et de Dominicis passionibus essent consecuti. II. Sed qui dixerat: Petite et accipietis , petentibus dedit eum exitum quem quisque desideraverat. Nam, si quando inter se de martyrii sui voto sermocinabantur, Saturninus quidem omnibus bestiis velle se objici profitebatur, ut scilicet gloriosiorem gestaret coronam. Itaque in commissione spectaculi, ipse et Revocatus leopardum experti, etiam super pulpitum ab urso vexati sunt. Saturus autem nihil magis quam ursum abominabatur: sed uno morsu leopardi confici se jam praesumebat. Itaque, cum aper subministraretur, venator potius qui illum aprum subministraverat, subfossus ab eadem bestia, post dies muneris obiit. Saturus solummodo tractus est. Et cum ad ursum substrictus esset in ponte, ursus de cavea prodire noluit. Itaque secundo Saturus illaesus revocatur. III. Puellis autem ferocissimam vaccam, ideoque praeter consuetudinem comparatam, diabolus praeparavit: sexui earum etiam de bestia aemulatus. Itaque despoliatae et reticulis indutae producebantur. Horruit populus, alteram respiciens puellam delicatam, alteram a partu recenti stillantibus mammis. Ita revocatae discinguntur. Inducitur prior Perpetua; jactata est, et concidit in lumbos: et ut conspexit tunicam a latere discissam, ad velamentum femorum adduxit, pudoris potius memor, quam doloris. Dehinc requisita, et dispersos capillos infibulavit: non enim decebat martyrem dispersis capillis pati, ne in sua gloria plangere videretur. Ita surrexit; et elisam Felicitatem cum vidisset, accessit, et manum ei tradidit, et sublevavit illam. Et ambae pariter steterunt, et, populi duritia devicta, revocatae sunt in portam Sanavivariam. Illic Perpetua a quodam tunc catechumino, Rustico nomine, qui ei adhaerebat, suscepta, et quasi a somno expergita, adeo in spiritu et in ecstasi fuerat, circumspicere coepit, et stupentibus omnibus ait: « Quando, inquit, producimur ad vaccam illam nescio. » Et cum audisset quod jam evenerat, non prius credidit, nisi quasdam notas vexationis in corpore et habitu suo recognovisset, et illum catechuminum. Exinde accersitum fratrem suum, et illum catechuminum allocuta est eos, dicens: « In fide state, et invicem omnes diligites; et passionibus nostris ne scandalizemini. » IV. Idem Saturus in alia porta militem Pudentem exhortabatur dicens: « Adsum certe, sicut promisi et praedixi; nullam usque adhuc bestiam sensi. Et nunc de toto corde credas. Ecce prodeo illo, et ab uno morsu leopardi consumar. » Et statim in fine spectaculi, leopardo objectus, de uno morsu ejus tanto perfusus est sanguine, ut populus revertenti illi secundi baptismatis testimonium reclamaverit: « Salvum lotum, salvum lotum. » Plane utique salvus erat, qui hoc spectaculo claruerat. Tunc Pudenti militi: « Vale, inquit, et memor esto fidei meae; et haec te non conturbent, sed confirment. » Simulque ansulam de digito ejus petiit, et vulneri suo mersam reddidit ei, haereditatem pignoris relinquens illi, et memoriam sanguinis. Exinde jam exanimis prosternitur cum caeteris ad jugulationem solito loco. Et cum populus illos in medium postularet, ut, gladio penetrante in eorum corpore, oculos suos comites homicidii adjungeret, ultro surrexerunt et se quo volebat populus transtulerunt: ante jam osculati invicem, ut martyrium per solemnia pacis consummarent. Caeteri quidem immobiles et cum silentio ferrum receperunt: multo magis Saturus, qui et prior scalam ascenderat, prior reddidit spiritum; nam et Perpetuam sustinebat. Perpetua autem, ut aliquid doloris gustaret, inter costas puncta exululavit; et errantem dexteram tirunculi gladiatoris ipsa in jugulum suum posuit. Fortasse tanta femina aliter non potuisset occidi, quia ab immundo spiritu timebatur, nisi ipsa voluisset.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — De Fuga in Persecutione De Fuga in Persecutione (Tertullian)
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Brother Fabius, you recently asked whether a Christian should flee when persecution threatens, prompted by rumors of some unspecified trouble. I touched on the question at the time, as the occasion and the insistence of certain people allowed, but I carried the half-treated subject away to write it out fully now, since your request and the urgency of the times demanded it. The more frequent persecutions become, the more carefully faith must examine how to receive them. That examination falls to you especially, because if you have not received the Paraclete, the guide into all truth, you remain answerable for other questions as well (John 16:13). So let us bring order to your inquiry: first we must decide the nature of persecution itself—whether it comes from God or from the devil—so that we can know how to respond. Every investigation is clearer when the author is known. It is true enough to say that nothing happens without God's will, but we cannot simply stop there, or we would be dragged off the point by the objection: "Then evil comes from God, and sin from God; the devil has no role, and neither do we." The question is specifically about persecution. For now, I say that nothing happens without God's will, because persecution is especially worthy of God and, I might even say, necessary—for the testing of his servants or their rejection. What else is the outcome of persecution but the testing and rejection of faith, by which the Lord examines his own? Persecution is that whole judgment through which someone is judged either approved or rejected, and judgment belongs to God alone. It is the winnowing fan that even now purifies the Lord's threshing floor, the Church, sifting the confused heap of the faithful into the wheat of martyrs and the chaff of deniers. Like the ladder Jacob saw in his dream, it shows some ascending to higher things, others descending to lower (Genesis 28:12). Persecution can also be understood as a contest. Who announces the contest if not the one who offers the crown and the rewards? The rules of this contest are written in the Apocalypse, listing the rewards that invite to victory—especially for those who have truly conquered in persecution, struggling and winning, not against flesh and blood but against spiritual wickedness (Ephesians 6:12). So you will recognize that the judgment of the contest belongs to the same judge who invites to the reward. Everything that happens in persecution is the glory of God who tests and rejects, who appoints and deposes. And what pertains to God's glory certainly happens by his will. But when is God more believed than when he is more feared? And when is that truer than in a time of persecution? Then the Church stands in awe; then faith becomes more earnest and disciplined in fasts, vigils, prayers, humility, diligence, love, holiness, and self-control. Nothing is done except in fear and hope. From this alone it is shown that persecution cannot be credited to the devil, since it makes God's servants better. If wickedness comes not from God but from the devil, and persecution consists of wickedness—for what is more wicked than treating the priests of the true God, all followers of truth, like the worst criminals?—then it seems persecution comes from the devil, from whom wickedness proceeds and from which persecution is constituted. Yet we must understand: persecution is not without the devil's wickedness, nor is the testing of faith without persecution. Because the testing of faith requires wickedness, the devil's wickedness serves not as patronage for persecution but as its instrument. God's will precedes, ordaining the testing of faith, which is the reason for persecution; the devil's wickedness follows as the instrument of persecution, which is the reason for the testing. Even elsewhere, insofar as wickedness rivals justice, it becomes material for the testimonies of him whose rival it is, so that justice is perfected in wickedness, just as virtue is perfected in weakness. God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and the foolish things to shame the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27). So wickedness is used to prove justice, confounding wickedness. Therefore, since the devil's role is not judgment but service—the Lord's judgment is persecution for the testing of faith, while the devil's wickedness is the ministry for the conduct of persecution—we believe persecution happens through the devil, if you will, but not from the devil. Nothing is permitted to Satan against the living servants of God except what the Lord allows, either so that he may destroy them through the victorious faith of the elect in temptation, or so that he may hand over to him those who have defected to him. You have the example of Job: the devil could bring no temptation against him except what he received from God, nor even against his possessions, until the Lord said, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand; only do not lay a hand on him" (Job 1:12). And he did not lay a hand on him until the Lord, to the one asking, said, "Behold, I deliver him to you; only spare his life" (Job 2:6). So also with the apostles: he asked for the power of temptation, not possessing it except by permission. The Lord said to Peter in the Gospel, "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail" (Luke 22:31–32)—that is, it would not be permitted to the devil to the point that faith was endangered. This shows that both the shaking of faith and its protection are with God, since both are asked of him: the shaking by the devil, the protection by the Son. And when the Son of God holds the protection of faith in his power, which he asks from the Father, from whom he receives all authority in heaven and on earth, how could the devil hold the shaking of faith in his own hand? In the Lord's Prayer we say to the Father, "Lead us not into temptation"—and what greater temptation is there than persecution? We confess that it comes from him from whom we beg deliverance: "But deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). That is, "Do not lead us into temptation by handing us over to the evil one." For we are snatched from the devil's hands precisely when we are not handed over to him in temptation. Even the legion of demons had no power over the herd of swine except what they obtained from God, let alone over the sheep of God (Mark 5:12–13). I could say that even the bristles of the swine were numbered before God at that moment; how much more the hairs of the saints (Matthew 10:30). The devil appears to have his own power only over those who do not belong to God—once given over to him, like chaff on the threshing floor, like the spittle of nations appointed by God and thus exposed to the devil in a kind of empty possession. But among God's household, nothing is permitted to him by his own right; the examples marked in Scripture show when and why it is permitted. Either the right of temptation is granted to him for the sake of testing, whether provoked or provoking, as in the cases above; or the sinner is handed over to him as to an executioner for punishment, as with Saul: "The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the Lord tormented him" (1 Samuel 16:14). Or for the sake of discipline, as the apostle reports: a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me; and this is not permitted to the devil among the saints to humble them through the affliction of the flesh, except so that the virtue of endurance may be perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The apostle himself handed Hymenaeus and Alexander over to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). You see now that the devil receives power more readily from the servants of God, so far is he from possessing it by his own right. Since these examples occur especially in persecutions—when we are more tested or rejected, more humbled or corrected—it is necessary that these things be permitted or commanded by God, from whom both the shaking and the protection of faith proceed. If persecution comes from God, then it must not be fled, because it is good. For everything God has seen to be good is necessarily good. Is it not written in Genesis: "And God saw that it was good"—not because he did not know it was good unless he saw it, but to signal by this very statement that what God sees is good (Genesis 1)? Many things happen by God's will that turn out evil for some; yet they are good because they happen by God's will, as divine and rational. What is divine that is not rational and good? What is good that is not divine? If something seems evil to someone's perception, human perception does not prejudge the reality; reality prejudges perception. The reality of a thing is fixed and gives perception its law, so that perception matches the reality as it is. If the reality is good—what comes from God (for nothing from God is not good, because it is divine and rational)—but it seems evil to perception, then the reality stands secure and the perception is at fault. Chastity, truth, and justice are optimal realities, yet they displease the perception of many. Does reality therefore become subject to perception? So persecution is good in reality, because it is a divine and rational arrangement; it displeases only the perception of those to whom it comes for evil. You see also that evil has its reason with God, when someone loses salvation in persecution, just as good happens by reason when someone gains salvation from it. Unless someone perishes or is saved irrationally before the Lord, he cannot call persecution evil, which is good even in its evil aspect, because it is administered by reason. So if persecution is good in any way, because it is established by reality, we rightly conclude that what is good must not be avoided: to refuse the good is a fault; all the more so because God has seen it so. And indeed it cannot be avoided, because it happens by God's will, which cannot be evaded.

latin: Quaesisti proxime, Fabi frater, fugiendum necne sit in persecutione, quod nescio quid annuntiaretur. Ibidem ego oblocutus aliquid pro loco ac tempore, et quarumdam personarum importunitate, semitractatam materiam abstuli mecum, plenius eam de stylo nunc renuntiaturus, utpote quam mihi et tua consultatio commendarat, et conditio temporum suo jam nomine injunxerat. Quanto enim frequentiores imminent persecutiones, tanto examinatio procuranda est, quomodo eas excipere fides debeat. Procuranda autem examinatio penes vos, qui, si forte, Paracletum non recipiendo deductorem omnis veritatis, merito adhuc etiam aliis quaestionibus obnoxii estis. Igitur consultationi tuae ordinem quoque induimus, animadvertentes ante determinari oportere de statu ipsius persecutionis, utrum a Deo obveniat, an a diabolo, quo facilius de obitu ejus constare possit. Omnis enim rei inspectio, auctore cognito, planior. Satis est quidem praescribere nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate. Sed non statim hac sententia caeteris retractatibus locum dabimus, ne a praesenti articulo avocemur, si quis responderit: Ergo et malum a Deo, et delictum a Deo; nihil jam in diabolo, nihil etiam in nobis ipsis. De persecutione nunc quaeritur. Circa hanc interim dixerim nihil fieri sine Dei voluntate, respiciens eam in primis dignam Deo esse, et, ut ita dixerim, necessariam, ad probationem scilicet servorum ejus sive reprobationem. Quis est enim exitus persecutionis, quis effectus alius, nisi probatio et reprobatio fidei, qua suos utique Dominus examinavit? Hoc omne judicium est persecutio per quam quis aut probatus aut reprobatus judicatur. Porro judicium soli Deo competit. Haec pala illa, quae et nunc Dominicam aream purgat, Ecclesiam scilicet, confusum acervum fidelium eventilans, frumentum martyrum et paleas negatorum. Haec enim, scalae quas somniat Jacob, aliis ascensum in superiora, aliis descensum ad inferiora demonstrantes. Sic et agonem intelligi capit persecutionem. A quo certamen edicitur, nisi a quo corona et praemia proponuntur? Legis edictum agonis istius in Apocalypsi, quibus praemiis ad victoriam invitet, vel maxime illos qui proprie vicerint in persecutione, vincendo luctati, revera non adversus carnem et sanguinem, sed adversus spiritalia nequitiae. Ita agnosces ad eumdem agonothetam pertinere certaminis arbitrium, qui invitat ad praemium. Totum quod agitur in persecutione, gloria Dei est probantis et reprobantis, imponentis et deponentis. Quod autem ad gloriam Dei pertinet, utique ex voluntate illius eveniet. Sed quando Deus magis creditur, nisi cum magis timetur, nisi in tempore persecutionis? Tunc Ecclesia in attonito est; tunc et fides in expeditione sollicitior et disciplinatior in jejuniis et stationibus, et orationibus, et humilitate, in alterutra diligentia et dilectione, in sanctitate et sobrietate. Non enim vacatur nisi timori et spei. Adeo et ex hoc ipso ostenditur nobis non posse diabolo deputari eam, quae meliores efficit Dei servos. Si quod iniquitas a Deo non est, sed a diabolo, persecutio autem ex iniquitate consistit (quid enim iniquius quam veri Dei antistites, omnis sectatores veritatis, nocentissimorum more tractari?), ideo videtur persecutio a diabolo evenire, a quo iniquitas agitur, ex qua constat persecutio: seire debemus, quatenus nec persecutio est sine iniquitate diaboli, nec probatio fidei sine persecutione, propter probationem fidei necessariam iniquitatem, non patrocinium praestare persecutioni, sed ministerium; praecedere enim Dei voluntatem circa fidei probationem, quae est ratio persecutionis, sequi autem diaboli iniquitatem ad instrumentum persecutionis, quae ratio est probationis. Nam et alias, in quantum justitiae iniquitas aemula est, in tantum materia est ad testimonia ejus, cujus est aemula; ut sic justitia in iniquitate perficiatur, quomodo virtus in infirmitate perficitur. Nam infirma mundi electa sunt a Deo, ut confundantur fortia; et stulta ejus, ut confundantur sapientia. Ita et iniquitas adhibetur ut justitia probetur, confundens iniquitatem. Igitur quod ministerium non est arbitrii, sed servitii (arbitrium enim Domini, persecutio, propter fidei probationem, ministerium autem iniquitas diaboli, propter persecutionis instructionem); ita eam per diabolum, si forte, non a diabolo evenire credimus. Nihil Satanae in servos Dei vivi licebit, nisi permiserit Dominus, ut aut ipsum destruat per fidem electorum in tentatione victricem: aut homines ejus fuisse traducat, qui defecerint ad illum. Habes exemplum Job, cui diabolus nullam potuit incutere tentationem, nisi a Deo accepisset potestatem, nec in substantiam quidem ejus, nisi Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, omnia quae sunt ei, in manu tua do, in ipsum autem ne extenderis manum. Denique nec extendit, nisi posteaquam et hoc postulanti Dominus, Ecce, dixisset, trado tibi illum, tantum animam ejus custodi. Sic et in Apostolos facultatem tentationis postulavit, non habens eam nisi ex permissu. Siquidem Dominus in Evangelio ad Petrum: Ecce, inquit, postulavit Satanas uti cerneret vos velut frumentum: verum ego rogavi pro te, ne deficeret fides tua: id est, ne tantum diabolo permitteretur, ut fides periclitaretur. Quo ostenditur, utrumque apud Deum esse, et concussionem fidei, et protectionem, cum utrumque ab eo petitur, concussio a diabolo, protectio a Filio. Et utique cum Filius Dei protectionem fidei habet in sua potestate quam a Patre postulat, a quo omnem accipit potestatem in coelis et in terris, quale est ut concussionem fidei diabolus in manu sua habeat? Sed in legitima Oratione cum dicimus ad Patrem: Ne nos inducas in tentationem (quae aut major tentatio quam persecutio?); ab eo illam profitemur accidere, a quo veniam ejus deprecamur: hoc est enim quod sequitur: Sed erue nos a maligno; id est, ne nos induxeris in tentationem, permittendo nos maligno. Tunc enim eruimur diaboli manibus, cum illi non tradimur in tentationem. Nec in porcorum gregem diaboli legio habuit potestatem, nisi eam de Deo impetrasset, tantum abest ut in oves Dei habeat. Possum dicere, porcorum quoque setas tunc numeratas apud Deum fuisse; nedum capillos sanctorum. Habere videtur diabolus propriam jam potestatem, si forte in eos qui ad Deum non pertinent, semel in stillam situtae, et in pulverem areae, et in salivam nationibus deputatis a Deo, ac per hoc diabolo expositis in vacuam quodammodo possessionem. Caeterum, in domesticos Dei nihil illi licet ex propria potestate; quia quando liceat, id est, ex quibus caussis, exempla in Scripturis signata demonstrant. Aut enim ex caussa probationis conceditur ei jus tentationis provocato vel provocanti, ut in superioribus: aut ex caussa reprobationis traditur ei peccator quasi carnifici in poenam, ut Saul: Et abscessit, inquit, spiritus Domini a Saule, et concutiebat eum spiritus nequam a Domino, et suffocabat. Aut ex caussa cohibitionis, ut Apostolus refert datum sibi sudem angelum Satanae ut colaphizetur: nec hanc speciem permitti diabolo in sanctos humiliandos per carnis vexationem, nisi simul ut et virtus tolerantiae scilicet in infirmitate perfici possit; nam et ipse Apostolus Phigellum et Hermogenem tradidit Satanae, uti emendentur, ne blasphement. Vides jam et a servis Dei facilius diabolum accipere potestatem, tanto abest ut eam ex proprietate possideat. Cum ergo et haec exempla magis in persecutionibus eveniant, siquidem magis tunc probamur vel reprobamur, et magis tunc humiliamur vel emendamur, ab eo permittatur vel imperetur necesse est catholice fieri haec, a quo et ex parte, scilicet ab illo qui dicit: Ego sum qui facio pacem, et condo mala, id est bellum. Hoc est enim contrarium paci. Nostrae autem paci quid est bellum, quam persecutio? Si persecutionis vel maxime exitus aut vitam afferunt aut mortem, aut plagam aut sanationem, habes auctorem ejusdem: Ego percutiam, et sanabo; ego vivificabo, et mortificabo. Uram, inquit, illos, sicut uritur argentum; et probabo, inpuid, illos, sicut probatur aurum. Cum enim exurimur persecutionis ardore, tunc probamur de fidei tenore. Haec erunt ignea jacula diaboli, per quae fidei ustio et conflatio administratur; ex Dei tamen voluntate. De isto quis dubitare possit ignoro, nisi plane frivola et frigida fides, deprehendens eos qui timide conveniunt in Ecclesiam. Dicitis enim, Quoniam incondite convenimus, simul convenimus, et complures concurrimus in Ecclesiam, quaerimur a nationibus, et timemus ne turbentur nationes. Annon scitis quod Deus omnium sit Dominus? Et si velit Deus, tunc persecutionem patieris; si vero noluerit, silebunt nationes. Credas utique; si tamen in eum Deum credis, sine cujus voluntate nec passer unius assis cadit in terram. Nos autem, puto, multis passeribus antistamus. Igitur si constat a quo persecutio eveniat, possumus jam consultationem tuam inducere, et determinare ex hoc ipso praetractatu, fugiendum in persecutione non esse. Si enim persecutio a Deo evenit, nullo modo fugiendum erit quod a Deo evenit. Sicut duplex ratio defendit, quia neque debeat devitari, neque evadi possit quod a Deo evenit. Non debet devitari, quia bonum. Necesse est enim bonum esse omne quod Deo visum est. Et numquid ideo in Genesi sic positum est: Et vidit Deus quia bonum est; non quod ignoraret bonum esse, nisi vidisset; sed ut hoc sono portenderet bonum esse, quod Deo visum est? Multa quidem sunt, quae a Deo eveniant, et alicujus malo eveniant. Imo bonum est ideo, quia a Deo evenit, ut divinum et rationale. Quid enim divinum non rationale, non bonum? Quid bonum non divinum? Si autem sensui cujusque videtur, non sensus hominis praejudicat statui, sed status sensui. Status enim uniuscujusque certum quid est, et dat sensui legem, ita sentiendi statum, sicuti est. Si autem statu quidem bonum quod a Deo venit (nihil enim a Deo non bonum, quia divinum, quia rationale), sensui vero malum videtur, erit status in tuto, sensus in vitio. Statu optima res pudicitia, et veritas, et justitia, quae a multorum sensu displicent. Nunquid ideo status sensui addicitur? Ita et persecutio statu bona est, quia divina et rationalis dispositio; sensui eorum vero quorum malo venit, displicet. Vides etiam illud malum rationem apud Deum habere, cum quis in persecutione evertitur de salute, sicut et illud bonum ratione contingere, cum quis ex persecutione proficit in salute? Nisi si irrationaliter quis aut perit apud Dominum, aut salvus est: is non poterit persecutionem malum dicere, quae etiam in mali parte bonum est, dum ratione administratur. Ita si bonum persecutio quoquo modo, quia de statu constat, merito definimus, quod bonum est, vitari non oportere: quia delictum sit, quod bonum est recusare; eo amplius, quod Deo visum est: jam vero nec posse vitari, quia a Deo evenit, cujus voluntas non poterit evadi.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The most excellent emperors had just staged a largesse; crowned soldiers were being discharged from camp. A certain soldier of God stood there, more steadfast than the rest of the brothers, men who had presumed they could serve two masters — he alone, bareheaded, with a laurel wreath idle in his hand. By now the Christians' discipline was notorious. Soon individuals began singling him out, mocking him from a distance, sneering up close. A murmur reached the tribune, and the man had already stepped forward in ranks. The tribune demanded at once, "Why do you look so different?" He denied that what the others did was permitted to him; pressed for a reason, he answered, "I am a Christian." O glorious soldier in God! From then on votes were cast, the case escalated, and the defendant was hauled before the prefects. There he accepted the harshest penalties, seeking discharge; he cast off the sluggish watch from his feet, planted himself on holy ground, refused to treat the sword as necessary for the Lord's defense, and the laurel fell from his hand as well. And now, spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the Gospel's preparation, girded with the sharper word of God, fully armed with the Apostle and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits Christ's gift in prison. Afterward came the verdicts on him — I do not know whether from Christians, for certainly not from the gentiles — as if from a sheer precipice, steep and death-desiring, that a man questioned about his uniform should make an issue of the Name: alone, truly strong, among so many brother comrades-in-arms, alone a Christian. It follows, of course, that those who have spat on the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit now intend to refuse martyrdom as well. They whisper at the end that such a good and long peace is being endangered for them. And I do not doubt some will migrate, pack their bags, prepare flight from city to city; for they care for no other memory of the Gospel. I know their shepherds too: lions in peace, deer in battle. But we will teach on the questions of confessions elsewhere. Now, however, as far as they also object: "Where are we forbidden to be crowned?" I will tackle this concrete core of the present case, so that both those who ask from anxious ignorance may be instructed and those who strive to defend the offense may be confuted — especially the Christian laureates themselves, for whom this is the only question; as if there could be no offense, or at least an uncertain one, that would admit debate. It is neither non-existent nor uncertain, and I will show that, at least for now.

latin: Proxime facta est liberalitas praestantissimorum imperatorum; expungebantur in castris milites laureati. Adhibetur quidam illic magis Dei miles, caeteris constantior fratribus, qui se duobus dominis servire posse praesumpserant, solus libero eapite, coronamento in manu otioso. Vulgata jam et ista disciplina Christianorum relucebat. Denique singuli designare, et eludere eminus, infrendere cominus. Murmur tribuno defertur, et persona jam ex ordine accesserat. Statim tribunus: Cur, inquit, tam diversus habitu? Negavit ille cum caeteris sibi licere; caussas expostulatus, Christianus sum, respondit. O militem in Deo gloriosum! Suffragia exinde, et res ampliata, et reus ad praefectos. Ibidem gravissimas penulas posuit, relevari auspicatus, speculatoriam morosissimam de pedibus absolvit, terrae sanctae insistere incipiens, gladium nec dominicae defensioni necessarium reddidit: laurea et de manu corruit. Et nunc russatus sanguinis sui spe, calceatus de Evangelii paratura, succinctus acutiore verbo Dei, totus de Apostolo armatus et de martyrii candida melius coronandus, donativum Christi in carcere exspectat. Exinde sententiae super illo, nescio an Christianorum, non enim aliae ethnicorum, ut de abrupto, et praecipiti, et mori cupido, qui de habitu interrogatus nomini negotium fecerit: solus scilicet fortis, inter tot fratres commilitones solus Christianus. Plane superest ut etiam martyria recusare meditentur, qui prophetias ejusdem Spiritus sancti respuerunt. Mussitant denique, tam bonam et longam sibi pacem periclitari. Nec dubito quosdam Scripturas emigrare, sarcinas expedire, fugae accingi de civitate in civitatem; nullam enim aliam Evangelii memoriam curant. Novi et pastores corum, in pace leones, in praelio cervos. Sed de quaestionibus confessionum alibi docebimus. At nunc quatenus et illud opponunt: Ubi autem prohibemur coronari? Hanc magis localem substantiam caussae praesentis aggrediar, ut et qui ex sollicitudine ignorantiae quaerunt, instruantur; et qui in defensionem delicti contendunt, revincantur; ipsi vel maxime Christiani laureati, quibus id solum quaestio est; quasi aut nullum aut incertum saltem haberi possit delictum quod patiatur quaestionem. Nec nullum autem nec incertum, hinc interim ostendam.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You argue that the ornaments of secular gods turn up even in God's house, so that the crown on the head must be defended as common property. By that logic, you yourself have already ruled that anything not found in God's things has no place in the communion of use. What could be more unworthy of God than what counts as worthy of an idol? And what suits an idol better than what suits the dead? The dead, after all, are crowned the same way: they instantly become idols by their dress and the cult of their consecration, which is a second idolatry for us (Psalm 115:4-8). So the senseless will use that thing exactly as the senseless would, and as if they wanted to abuse it, if they weren't senseless. There is no difference between use and abuse when the truth of use ceases, because the very capacity to perceive has ceased; how can anyone abuse what they lack the faculty to use? For us, however, abuse is not permitted, since the apostle teaches that it is easier not to use a thing at all — unless it is that those who feel nothing do not abuse (1 Corinthians 10:19-21). But the whole thing is void; it is a dead work so far as idols go, yet positively alive with demons, to whom superstition belongs. David says the idols of the nations are silver and gold: they have eyes but do not see, noses but do not smell, hands but do not touch. Through such things one 'enjoys flowers.' If the makers of idols will become like that, those who use anything according to the ornament of idols already are like that. All things are pure to the pure, and all things impure to the impure; but nothing is more impure than idols. Pure substances, as God's things, are common to use by their very nature; what differs is the administration of that use. I myself sacrifice a chicken for my own dinner, no less than Socrates did for Asclepius; if a place smells bad, I burn Arabian incense; but not with the same rite, dress, or equipment used at idols. If the mere word 'idol-offering' pollutes the thing, as the apostle teaches — 'If anyone says, "This is idol food," do not eat it' — how much more when you have gone through the dress, rite, and equipment of idol-offerings? Thus the crown itself becomes idol food. With that rite, dress, and equipment it is sacrificed to the idol by its authors, whose use is especially proper to it, so that it cannot be admitted into communion because it is not found in God's things. Therefore the apostle cries: 'Flee from idolatry' — entirely and completely. Recognize the forest, and how many hidden thorns lie in it. Nothing is to be given to an idol, so nothing is to be taken from an idol. If reclining in an idol's temple is alien to faith, what is it to be seen in an idol's dress? What communion has Christ with Belial? That is why we must flee. A long divorce from idolatry is commanded; we must not approach it closely in anything. Even the earthly dragon sucks the spirit of people from afar. John goes deeper: 'Little children, keep yourselves from idols' — not merely from idolatry as if from an office, but from the very image of them. For it is unworthy that the image of the living God should become the image of an idol and of the dead (1 John 5:21). We have claimed the property of this dress for idols both from its origin and from its superstitious use; and also because, while it is not referred to in God's things, it is more and more assigned as the image of those in whose antiquities, solemnities, and offices it is found. Even their doors, victims, altars, ministers, and priests are crowned. You have the crowns of all the priestly colleges under Claudius. But we have also woven in the distinction between rational and irrational, which meets those who defend communion in all things on the strength of certain examples. It remains, then, to examine the coronation causes themselves, so that while we show they are foreign — indeed contrary to discipline — we may prove that none of them is backed by reason enough to defend such dress and its use for communion, even though some people throw examples at us.

latin: Ita cum idcirco proponis deorum saecularium ornamenta etiam apud Deum deprehendi, ut inter haec coronam quoque capitis communi usui vindices; ipse tibi jam praescribis non habendum in communionem usus, quod non inveniatur in Dei rebus. Quid enim tam indignum Deo, quam quod dignum idolo? quid autem tam dignum idolo, quam quod et mortuo? Nam et mortuorum est ita coronari: quoniam et ipsi idola statim fiunt et habitu et cultu consecrationis, quae apud nos secunda idololatria est. Igitur qui sensu careant, illorum erit perinde uti ea re cujus careant sensu, atque si abuti ea vellent, si sensu non carerent. Nulla vero distantia est abutendi, cum veritas cessat utendi, cessante natura sentiendi; qua vult quis abutatur, cum non habeat qua utatur? Nobis autem abuti apud apostolum non licet, facilius non uti docentem, nisi quod nec abutuntur qui nihil sentiunt. Sed vacat totum, et est ipsum quoque opus mortuum, quantum in idolis; vivum plane quantum in daemoniis, ad quae pertinet superstitio. Idola nationum, inquit David, argentum et aurum: oculos habent, nec vident, nares, nec odorantur, manus, nec contrectant. Per haec enim floribus frui est. Quod si tales edicit futuros qui idola fabricantur, tales jam sunt qui secundum idolorum ornatum quid utuntur. Omnia munda mundis, ita et immunda omnia immundis: nihil autem immundius idolis. Caeterum substantiae mundae, ut Dei res, et hac sua conditione communes usui: sed ipsius usus administratio interest. Nam et ego mihi gallinaceum macto, non minus quam Aesculapio Socrates: et si me odor alicujus loci offenderit, Arabiae aliquid incendo; sed non eodem ritu, nec eodem habitu, nec eodem apparatu, quo agitur apud idola. Si enim verbo nudo conditio polluitur, ut apostolus docet: Si quis autem dixerit: Hoc idolothytum est, ne contigeris; multo magis cum saltitaveris habitu, et ritu et apparatu idolothytorum, contaminatur. Ita et corona idolothytum efficitur. Hoc enim ritu, et habitu, et apparatu idolo immolatur auctoribus suis: quorum eo vel maxime proprius est usus, ne in communionem possit admitti, quod in Dei rebus non invenitur. Propterea apostolus inclamat: Fugite idololatriam; omnem utique et totam. Recognita silvam, et quantae latitant spinae. Nihil dandum idolo, sic nec sumendum ab idolo. Si in idolio recumbere alienum est a fide, quid in idoli habitu videri? quae communio Christo et Beliae? et ideo fugite. Longum enim divortium mandat ab idololatria; in nullo proxime agendum. Draco etiam terrenus de longinquo homines spiritu absorbet. Altius Joannes: Filioli, inquit, custodite vos ab idolis; non jam ab idololatria quasi ab officio, sed ab ipsa effigie eorum. Indignum enim ut imago Dei vivi, imago idoli et mortui fias. Usque adhuc proprietatem istius habitus et ex originis censu, et ex superstitionis usu idolis vindicamus, ex eo praeterea quod, dum in rebus Dei non refertur, magis magisque imago illorum deputatur, in quorum et antiquitatibus, et solemnitatibus, et officiis convenitur. Ipsae denique fores, et ipsae hostiae et arae, ipsi ministri et sacerdotes eorum coronantur. Habes omnium collegiorum sacerdotalium coronas apud Claudium. Sed et illam interstruximus distinctionem differentiae rationalium et irrationalium, eis occurrentem qui communionem in omnibus de quorumdam exemplorum occasione defendunt. Ad hanc itaque partem caussas jam ipsas coronarias inspici superest, ut dum ostendimus extraneas, imo et contrarias disciplinae, nullam earum rationis patrocinio fultam probemus, quo possit habitus hujusmodi, usus quoque communioni vindicari: etsi sunt quidam quorum exempla nobis objectantur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I start with the whole question because I want to get at the real issue: is military service even compatible with being a Christian? It makes no sense to debate the details when the root is rotten. Do we really think a human oath can override a divine one, or that we can pledge allegiance to another lord after Christ? Do we abandon father, mother, and every neighbor the Law commands us to honor and love after God—people the Gospel also honored, without putting them above Christ alone? Can we live by the sword when the Lord says whoever uses the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52)? Can a son of peace take part in battle when it does not even become him to quarrel? Will he inflict chains, prison, torture, and execution without avenging his own wrongs? Will he pull guard duty, or do more than Christ did? Will he do it on the Lord's Day when not even Christ did? Will he stand watch over temples he has renounced? Will he eat where the apostle says not to? Will he defend at night the very spirits he exorcised by day, leaning on the spear that pierced Christ's side? Will he carry a standard that rivals Christ's? Will he demand a sign from a commander when he has already received one from God? Even dead, will a bugler's trumpet disturb him when he waits for the angel's trumpet? Will a Christian be burned by military discipline when burning was forbidden him and Christ granted him the merit of fire? How many other violations of military duty must be counted as sins? Simply moving your name from the camp of light to the camp of darkness is itself a sin.

If faith finds a man already in the ranks, his case is different—like the centurions John baptized, whom Christ approved and Peter instructed. But once they have accepted the faith and been sealed, they must either desert immediately, as many did, or find every possible way to avoid anything that opposes God, since military service does not allow it; or, finally, they must endure everything for God, which even pagan faith permits. Military service promises neither impunity for sins nor immunity from martyrdom. A Christian is a Christian everywhere. There is one Gospel, one Jesus, who denies every denier and confesses every confessor of God, who saves the soul lost for his name and destroys the one who gained the world against his name. In his eyes a faithful pagan soldier is no different from an unfaithful pagan soldier. The demands of faith admit no exemptions based on rank. There is no necessity to sin when the only necessity is not to sin. Even when someone is forced by torture or punishment to sacrifice or deny directly, discipline does not yield to that pressure, because the necessity of refusing to deny and accepting martyrdom outweighs the necessity of avoiding suffering and doing one's duty. Moreover, this kind of justification guts the whole substance of the sacrament, loosening the bond even for voluntary sins. Will can masquerade as necessity when it has something to gain. I have already established this for the other official crowns where the plea of necessity is commonplace: either the offices must be avoided so we do not fall into sin, or martyrdoms must be endured so we can break with those offices. I will not press the first part of the question—the illegitimacy of military service itself—any further, so the second part can be addressed; otherwise, if I drive out military service entirely, I will have raised the issue of the military crown in vain.

latin: Etenim, ut ipsam caussam coronae militaris aggrediar, puto prius conquirendum an in totum Christianis militia conveniat. Quale est alioquin de accidentibus retractare, cum a praecedentibus culpa sit? Credimusne humanum sacramentum divino superduci licere, et in alium dominum respondere post Christum? et ejerare patrem ac matrem, et omnem proximum, quos et lex honorari et post Deum diligi praecipit, quos et Evangelium solo Christo pluris non faciens, sic quoque honoravit? Licebit in gladio conversari, Domino pronuntiante, gladio periturum qui gladio fuerit usus? Et praelio operabitur filius pacis, cui nec litigare conveniet? Et vincula et carcerem et tormenta et supplicia administrabit, nec suarum ultor injuriarum? Jam stationes, aut alii magis faciet quam Christo? aut et Dominico die, quando nec Christo? et excubabit pro templis, quibus renuntiavit? et coenabit illic ubi apostolo non placet? et quos interdiu exorcismis fugavit, noctibus defensabit, incumbens et requiescens super pilum quo perfossum est latus Christi? vexillum quoque portabit aemulum Christi? et signum postulabit a principe, qui jam a Deo accepit? mortuus etiam tuba inquietabitur aeneatoris, qui excitari a tuba angeli exspectat? et cremabitur ex disciplina castrensi Christianus, cui cremare non licuit, cui Christus merita ignis indulsit? Quanta alia in delictis circumspici possunt castrensium munium, transgression interpretanda? Ipsum de castris lucis in castra tenebrarum nomen deferre, transgressio est. Plane, si quos militia praeventos fides posterior invenit, alia conditio est, ut illorum quos Joannes admittebat ad lavacrum, ut centurionum fidelissimorum, quem Christus probat, et quem Petrus catechizat: dum tamen, suscepta fide atque signata, aut deserendum statim sit, ut a multis actum, aut omnibus modis cavillandum, ne quid adversus Deum committatur, quae nec ex militia permittuntur; aut novissime perpetiendum pro Deo, quod aeque fides pagana condixit. Nec enim delictorum impunitatem, aut martyriorum immunitatem militia promittet. Nusquam Christianus aliud est. Unum Evangelium, et idem Jesus, negaturus omnem negatorem, et confessurus omnem confessorem Dei, et salvam facturus animam pro nomine ejus amissam, perditurus autem de contrario adversus nomen ejus lucri habitam. Apud hunc tam miles est paganus fidelis, quam paganus est miles infidelis. Non admittit status fidei necessitates. Nulla est necessitas delinquendi, quibus una est necessitas non delinquendi. Nam et ad sacrificandum et directo negandum necessitate quis premitur tormentorum sive poenarum: tamen nec illi necessitati disciplina connivet, quia potior est necessitas timendae negationis et obeundi martyrii, quam evadendae passionis et implendi officii. Caeterum subvertit totam substantiam sacramenti causatio ejusmodi, ut etiam voluntariis delictis fibulam laxet. Nam et voluntas poterit necessitas contendi, habens scilicet unde cogatur. Vel ipsam praestruxerim et ad caeteras officialium coronarum caussas, quibus familiarissima est advocatio necessitatis: cum idcirco aut officia fugienda sint, ne in delictis incidamus; aut et martyria toleranda sint, ut officia rumpamus. De prima specie quaestionis etiam militiae ipsius illicitae, plura non faciam, ut secunda reddatur, ne si omni ope expulero militiam, frustra jam de corona militari provocarim.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let us assume that military service is permitted up to the point of the crown. But first, let us speak about the crown. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Liber: to Apollo, as the god of projectiles; to Liber, as the god of triumphs. Claudius confirms this when he says that soldiers are customarily wreathed with myrtle. Myrtle belongs to Venus, the mother of Aeneas, not laurel; it also belongs to the loved ones of Mars, through Ilium and Romulus, to the Romans. But I do not believe Venus sides with the Romans alongside Mars in a context where there is the pain of skin. When the olive, too, is used to crown military service, it becomes idolatry directed at Minerva, goddess of arms equally, but also of peace—once peace was established with Neptune, she was crowned from this tree. In these things, the superstition of the military garland is both polluted and polluting, and now all things will be polluted, causes included. Look at the annual declaration of vows—what does it look like? The first part occurs at the *principia*, the second at the *capitolia*. Now take the setting and the words: "Then to you, Jupiter, with a horned ox decorated with gold, we vow to be." Whose voice is that sentence? Unquestionably, the voice of negation. Even if the Christian keeps his mouth silent there, his crowned head answers. That same laurel is openly proclaimed in the distribution of donatives—plainly, not a gratuitous idolatry, but one selling Christ to some for gold, just as Judas did for silver. This will amount to: "You cannot serve God and mammon" (Luke 16:13)—to hand yourself over to mammon and stand apart from God? This will amount to: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matthew 22:21)—not to render a man to God, and to withhold a denarius from Caesar? Is the triumphal laurel constructed from leaves or from corpses? Is it adorned with blades or with busts? Is it anointed with perfumes or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps even of some Christians: for Christ is also among the barbarians. He who bears this cause on his head—has he not also fought against it? There is also another kind of military service: that of royal households. For the camp largesses are called *munificentiae*, and they themselves belong to the Caesarean solemnities. But you, too, are a soldier and a servant of another; and if you serve two—God and Caesar—then certainly not Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common matters, I believe, to the more important one.

latin: Puta denique licere militiam usque ad caussam coronae. Sed et de corona prius dicamus. Laurea ista Apollini vel Libero sacra est: illi, ut deo telorum; huic, ut deo triumphorum. Sic docet Claudius cum et myrto ait milites redimiri solere. Veneris enim myrtum, matris Aeneae, non laurum, etiam amiculae Martis, per Iliam et Romulos Romani. Sed ego Venerem non credo ex hac parte cum Marte Romanam, qua pellicis dolor est. Quum et olea militia coronatur, ad Minervam est idololatria, armorum aeque deam, sed et paci cum Neptuno initae ex hac arbore coronatam. In his erit serti militaris superstitio polluta et polluens, omniaque jam polluentur et caussis. Ecce annua votorum nuncupatio quid videtur? prima in principiis, secunda in capitoliis. Accipe post loca et verba: Tunc Tibi, Jupiter, Bove Cornibus Auro Decoratis Vovimus Esse Futurum. Cujus sententiae vox est? utique negationis. Etiamsi tacet illic Christianus ore, coronatus capite respondit. Eadem laurea in donativi dispensatione denuntiatur plane non gratuita idololatria, aliquibus aureis venditans Christum, ut argenteis Judas. Hoc erit, Non potestis Deo servire et mammonae: mammonae manum tradere, et a Deo absistere? Hoc erit, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae Dei Deo: nec hominem Deo reddere, et denarium Caesari auferre? Triumphi laurea foliis struitur, an cadaveribus? lamnis ornatur, an bustis? unguentis delibuitur an lacrymis conjugum et matrum? Fortasse quorumdam et Christianorum: et apud barbaros enim Christus. Qui hanc portaverit in capite caussam, nonne et ipse oppugnavit? Est et alia militia regiarum familiarum. Nam et castrenses appellantur munificiae, et ipsae solemnium Caesareanorum. Sed et tu proinde miles ac servus alterius es: et si duorum, Dei et Caesaris, certe tunc non Caesaris, cum te Deo debes, etiam in communibus, credo, potiori.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Public orders are crowned with laurels for public causes, magistrates with gold; Etruscan insignia are laid on top of them. The word means crowns set with gems and gold oak leaves, marked for Jupiter, worn when officials in palm-embroidered togas lead out the sacred processions. Provincial gold crowns also exist, now seeking larger heads for statues rather than men. But your orders, your magistrates, and the very name of the senate is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of his life. There your purple is the Lord's blood and the spear-wound in his cross; there the axe lies at the tree's trunk, there the rods from Jesse. Let them look at the public horses wearing their own crowns. When your Lord wished to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture, he did not even have a donkey of his own (Matthew 21:5). Those men ride in chariots and on horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God. We have been removed from the very dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John, let alone the tribunal (Revelation 18:4). The crowd is crowned now from the exultation of imperial victories, now from the splendor of municipal festivals — every luxury of public joy is a trap. But you are a stranger in this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. "Our municipality," he says, "is in the heavens." You have your own senses, your own calendar; you have nothing to do with the age's joys — indeed you owe the opposite: the age will rejoice, but you will mourn. And I think he calls blessed those who mourn, not those who are crowned. Weddings crown the betrothed, which is why we do not marry pagans, lest they drag us into idolatry — since their weddings begin with it. You have the law from the Patriarchs, you have the apostle commanding marriage in the Lord. Secular freedom also crowns. But you have already been redeemed by Christ, and at a great price. How can the world free a slave who belongs to another? Even if freedom appears, slavery also once appeared. Everything in the age is imaginary, nothing true. For even then you were a free man redeemed by Christ; now you are Christ's slave, though freed by a man. If you think the world's freedom is true, so that you also ratify the crown, you have returned to the slavery of man, which you mistake for freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you mistake for slavery. Will agonistic causes also be debated — causes their own titles condemn at once? Sacred and funeral ones too, of course, since all that remains is for Olympian Jupiter, Nemean Hercules, wretched Archemorus, and unhappy Antinous to be crowned on a Christian, so that he becomes the spectacle he ought to be watching. I think we have enumerated every cause. None belongs to us; all are foreign, profane, illicit, rejected once for all in the testimony of the sacrament. These were the pomp of the devil and the offices of his angels: the age's honors, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human services, empty praises, shameful glories — and in all of them idolatry, in the very sense of the crowns with which all these things are adorned. Claudius indeed crowns heaven with stars in Homer's songs; certainly by God, certainly by man — therefore man himself is also to be crowned by God. Meanwhile the age crowns brothels, latrines, bakeries, prison, the game, the amphitheaters, the spoliariums, and funeral processions. How sacred, how holy and clean this habit is — do not judge it from one poetic heaven, but from the commerce of the whole world. But a Christian will not defile his door with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has fixed on doorways: Janus on the door, Limentinus on the threshold, Forculus and Cardus on the doors and hinges, and among the Greeks, Thyreus Apollo and Antelios demons.
