latin: Coronant et publicos ordines laureis publicae caussae, magistratus vero insuper aureis. Superferuntur etiam illis Hetruscae. Hoc vocabulum est coronarum, quas gemmis et foliis ex auro quercinis ob Jovem insignis ad deducendas thensas cum palmatis togis sumunt. Sunt et provinciales aureae, imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes. Sed tui ordines et tui magistratus, et ipsum curiae nomen Ecclesia est Christi. Illius es conscriptus in libris vitae. Illic purpurae tuae sanguis Domini et clavus latus in cruce ipsius; illic securis ad caudicem arboris posita, illic virgae ex Jesse. Viderint et publici equi cum coronis suis. Dominus tuus, ubi secundum Scripturam Jerusalem ingredi voluit, nec asinum habuit privatum. Isti in curribus et isti in equis, nos autem in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocabimus. Ab ipso incolatu Babylonis illius in Apocalypsi Joannis submovemur, nedum a suggestu. Coronatur et vulgus nunc ex principalium prosperitatum exultatione, nunc ex municipalium solemnitatum proprietate: et est omnis publicae laetitiae luxuria captatrix. Sed tu peregrinus mundi hujus, civis supernae Jerusalem. Noster, inquit, municipatus in coelis. Habes tuos sensus, tuos fastos: nihil tibi cum gaudiis saeculi; imo contrarium debes: Saeculum enim gaudebit, vos vero lugebitis. Et puto, felices ait lugentes, non coronatos. Coronant et nuptiae sponsos, ideo non nubamus ethnicis, ne nos ad idolatriam usque deducant, a qua apud illos nuptiae incipiunt: habes legem a Patriarchis quidem, habes apostolum in Domino nubere jubentem. Coronat et libertas saecularis. Sed tu jam redemptus es a Christo, et quidem magno. Servum alienum quomodo saeculum manumittet? Etsi libertas videtur, sed et servitus videbatur. Omnia imaginaria in saeculo, et nihil veri. Nam et tunc liber hominis eras redemptus a Christo: et nunc servus es Christi, licet manumissus ab homine. Si veram putes saeculi libertatem, ut et corona consignes, rediisti in servitutem hominis, quam putes libertatem; amisisti libertatem Christi, quam putas servitutem. Numquid et agonisticae caussae disputabuntur, quas statim tituli sui damnant? et sacras et funebres scilicet, hoc enim superest ut Olympius Jupiter, et Nemaeus Hercules, et misellus Archemorus, et Antinous infelix in Christiano coronentur, ut ipse spectaculum fiat, quod spectare debet. Universas, ut arbitror, caussas enumeravimus. Nec ulla nobiscum est: omnes alienae, profanae, illicitae, semel jam in sacramenti testatione ejeratae. Haec enim erant pompae diaboli et angelorum ejus officia, saeculi honores, solemnitates, popularitates, falsa vota, humana servitia, laudes vanae, gloriae turpes: et in omnibus istis idololatria, in solo quoque sensu coronarum quibus omnia ista redimita sunt. Praefabitur quidem Claudius etiam coelum sideribus apud Homeri carmina coronatum; certe a Deo, certe homini, igitur et homo ipse a Deo coronandus est. Caeterum a saeculo coronantur et lupanaria, et latrinae, et pistrina, et carcer, et ludus, et ipsa amphitheatra, et ipsa spoliaria, ipsaeque libitinae. Quam sacer sanctus, quamque honestus ac mundus sit habitus iste, noli de uno poetico coelo, sed de totius mundi commerciis aestimare. At enim Christianus nec januam suam laureis infamabit, si norit quantos deos etiam ostiis diabolus affinxerit, Janum a janua, Limentinum a limine, Forculum et Cardam a foribus et cardinibus et apud Graecos Thyreum Apollinem et Antelios daemonas.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Idolatry is so far from honoring its own head that it does the opposite; I've already made this point to Christ, since Christ is the head of man, and man stands as free as Christ himself — not even subject to a veil, let alone a binding obligation. A woman's head, by contrast, is already subject to the veil; that very fact occupies it, leaving no room for an additional obligation, because it already carries the burden of its own humility. Since a woman ought not appear with her head uncovered on account of the angels, a crown would scandalize those angels far more. What is a crown on a woman's head but a panderer to beauty, the hallmark of sheer wantonness, the final repudiation of modesty, a convergence of enticement? Consequently, the Apostle's perspective forbids a woman to adorn herself more elaborately, so that she not be crowned with hair arranged as artifice. Yet Christ Jesus is both the head of the man and the face of the woman, the man of the Church; tell me, what garland did he endure for both sexes? I think it was woven of thorns and tribulations, figuring the sins that the earth of our flesh produced for us, though the power of the cross removed them, blunting every sting of death in the Lord's own endurance. Apart from the figure, there is outright contempt, shame, and disgrace, intertwined with the savagery that defiled and lacerated the Lord's temples at that time. And yet you now crown yourself with laurel, myrtle, olive, some splendid leaf, and — most conveniently — with roses by the hundred plucked from Midas' garden, with both kinds of lilies, with every violet, perhaps even with gems and gold, all to emulate the crown that came to Christ afterward, because he tasted honey after gall; nor was the King of Glory welcomed by the heavenly host until the King of the Jews was condemned to the cross, first lowered a little by the Father to a rank beneath the angels, and so crowned with glory and honor. If you owe your head to him on these grounds, repay him in kind, if you can, with the sort he offered for yours: either do not crown yourself with flowers, if you cannot with thorns, because you are not able to with flowers.

latin: Tanto abest ut capiti suo munus inferat idololatriae, imo jam dixerim Christo, siquidem caput viri Christus est, tam liberum quam et Christus: ne velamento quidem obnoxium, nedum obligamento. Porro et quod obnoxium est velamento, caput foeminae, hoc ipso jam occupatum, non vacat etiam obligamento; habet humilitatis suae sarcinam. Si nudo capite videri non debet propter angelos, multo magis coronatos fortasse tunc illos coronatos scandalizaverit. Quid enim est incapite foeminae corona, quam formae lena, quam summa lasciviae nota, extrema negatio verecundiae, conflatio illecebrae? Propterea nec ornabitur operosius mulier ex Apostoli prospectu, ut nec crinium artificio coronetur. Qui tamen et viri caput est, et foeminae facies, vir Ecclesiae Christus Jesus, quale oro te, sertum pro utroque sexu subiit? Ex spinis opinor et tribulis, in figuram delictorum quae nobis protulit terra carnis, abstulit autem virtus crucis, omnem aculeum mortis in Dominici capitis tolerantia obtundens. Certe praeter figuram, contumelia in promptu est, et turpitudo et dedecoratio, et his implexa saevitia, quae tunc Domini tempora et foedaverunt et lancinaverunt; uti tu nunc laurea, et myrtho, et olea, et illustri aliqua fronde, et quod magis usui est, centenariis quoque rosis de horto Midae lectis, et utrisque liliis, et omnibus violis coroneris, etiam gemmis forsitan et auro, ut et illam Christi coronam aemuleris, quae postea ei obvenit, quia et favos post fella gustavit; nec ante rex gloriae a coelestibus salutatus est, quam rex Judaeorum proscriptus cruci; minoratus primo a patre modicum quid citra angelos, et ita gloria et honore coronatus. Si ob haec caput ei tuum debes, tale si potes ei repende, quale suum pro tuo obtulit: aut nec floribus coroneris, si spinis non potes, quia non floribus potes.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Keep what belongs to God intact. He will crown it if He wishes—and He does wish it; in fact, He extends the invitation: "To the one who conquers I will give the crown of life" (Rev 2:10). Be faithful to death yourself. Fight the good contest, the very one whose crown the Apostle confidently trusted had been laid up for him. The angel also receives the crown of victory, riding out on a white horse so that he may conquer. Another is adorned with a rainbow's circle, a heavenly meadow. The presbyters sit crowned, and with that same gold the Son of Man shines above the cloud. If such images appear in a vision, what truths must exist in the reality? Look at them, inhale them. Why do you condemn a head destined for a diadem with a mere wreath or a snake-like band? Christ Jesus has made us kings to God and His Father. What do you want with a flower that dies? You have the flower from the rod of Jesse, the one on whom the full grace of the divine Spirit rested—the incorrupt, unwithering, eternal flower. By choosing it, the good soldier advanced in dignity within the heavenly order. Be ashamed, His fellow-soldiers: you are now being judged not by Him but by some soldier of Mithras. When that initiate enters the cave—in the camps of true darkness—a crown is offered to him with a sword interposed, a mockery of martyrdom, then fitted to his head. He is warned by an outstretched hand to push it from his head and transfer it to his shoulder, if he can, declaring that Mithras is his crown. From then on he is never crowned again; he keeps this as a sign for his testing, so that wherever he is questioned about the sacrament he can prove himself. The Mithraic soldier is believed the moment he throws away the crown and says it belongs to his god. Recognize the devil's cunning: he mimics certain divine realities precisely to confuse us and pass judgment on us through the faith of his own followers.

latin: Serva Deo rem suam intaminatam. Ille eam, si volet, coronabit; imo et vult; denique invitat: Qui vicerit, inquit, dabo ei coronam vitae. Esto et tu fidelis ad mortem. Decerta et tu bonum agonem, cujus coronam et Apostolus repositam sibi merito confidit. Accipit et angelus victoriae coronam procedens in candido equo, ut vinceret. Et alius iridis ambitu ornatur, coelesti prato. Sedent et presbyteri coronati: eodemque auro et ipse Filius hominis supra nubem micat. Si tales imagines in visione, quales veritates in repraesentatione? illas aspice, illas odora. Quid caput strophiolo aut dracontario damnas, diademati destinatum? Nam et reges nos Deo et Patri suo fecit Christus Jesus. Quid tibi cum flore morituro? Habes florem ex virga Jesse, super quem tota divini spiritus gratia requievit, florem incorruptum, immarcescibilem, sempiternum: quem et bonus miles eligendo, in coelesti ordinatione, dignatione profecit. Erubescite, commilitones ejus, jam non ab ipso judicandi, sed ab aliquo Mithrae milite, qui cum initiatur in spelaeo, in castris vere tenebrarum, coronam interposito gladio sibi oblatam, quasi mimum martyrii, dehinc capiti suo accommodatam, monetur obvia manu a capite pellere, et in humerum, si forte, transferre, dicens Mithram esse coronam suam, atque exinde numquam coronatur, idque in signum habet ad probationem sui, sicubi tentatus fuerit de sacramento: statimque creditur Mithrae miles, si dejecerit coronam, si eam in Deo suo esse dixerit. Agnoscamus ingenia diaboli, idcirco quaedam de divinis affectantis, ut nos de suorum fide confundat et judicet.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We are not frightened, nor do we fear what we suffer at the hands of ignorant people. We embraced this sect precisely on its terms, pledging our souls so we could enter these battles—hoping to gain what God promises and dreading what a different life threatens. We meet your every cruelty head-on, even volunteering for the fight, and we rejoice more when condemned than when acquitted. That is why we sent this pamphlet: not because we fear for ourselves, but for you and all our enemies—not to mention our friends. Our discipline commands us to love even enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that our goodness may be perfect and distinctive, not ordinary. Everyone loves their friends; only Christians love their enemies. Since we grieve over your ignorance, pity human error, watch the future, and see the signs of these things being prepared daily, we must break out in this way to lay before you what you refuse to hear openly.

latin: Nos quidem neque expavescimus, neque pertimescimus ea, quae ab ignorantibus patimur: cum ad hanc sectam, utique suscepta conditione ejus, pacti venerimus, ut etiam animas nostras auctorati in has pugnas accedamus, ea quae Deus repromittit consequi optantes, et ea quae diversae vitae comminatur pati timentes. Denique cum omni saevitia vestra concertamus, etiam ultro erumpentes, magisque damnati quam absoluti gaudemus. Itaque hunc libellum non nobis timentes misimus, sed vobis et omnibus inimicis nostris, nedum amicis: ita enim disciplina jubemur diligere inimicos quoque, et orare pro eis qui nos persequuntur: ut haec sit perfecta et propria bonitas nostra, non communis. Amicos enim diligere omnium est, inimicos autem solorum christianorum. Qui ergo dolemus de ignorantia vestra, et miseremur erroris humani, et futura prospicimus, et signa eorum quotidie intentari videmus, necesse est vel hoc modo erumpere ad proponenda vobis ea, quae palam non vultis audire.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Still, we have to grieve, because no state will escape punishment for shedding our blood—just as under the governor Hilarian, when they shouted from our burial grounds, 'No more burial grounds!' their own burial grounds vanished; they did not reap their own harvests. Meanwhile, what last year's rain brought the human race is plain: the flood, and the fact that it once came because of human unbelief and injustice. And the fires that recently hung over Carthage's walls at night—those who saw them know what they threatened. The former thunderclaps—those who hardened themselves know what they proclaimed. All these are signs of God's impending wrath, which we must, however we can, announce and preach and pray stays local for now; the universal and supreme wrath will come in its own time for those who interpret his signs otherwise. Even the sun at the assembly of Utica, its light nearly extinguished, was such a portent that it could not be an ordinary eclipse, fixed as it was in its own height and dwelling. You have your astrologers. We can just as well cite the ends of certain governors who, at the end of their lives, remembered they had sinned by persecuting Christians. Vigellius Saturninus, who first drew the sword against us here, lost his eyes. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, resenting that his wife had converted to this sect and treating Christians cruelly, was alone laid waste by pestilence in his own palace, boiling alive with worms. 'Let no one know,' he said, 'or the Christians will rejoice.' Later, recognizing his error in having forced some from their faith through torture, he died almost a Christian. Caecilius Capella, in that Byzantine crisis, cried out, 'Christians, rejoice!' But even those who think they have escaped unpunished will face the day of divine judgment. We also wish for you that the warning alone was enough: when you condemned Adrian and Mavilus to the beasts, this affliction followed immediately, and now the bloodshed has stopped for the same reason. But remember, for the future.

latin: Tamen (sicut supra diximus) doleamus necesse est, quod nulla civitas impune latura sit sanguinis nostri effusionem, sicut et sub Hilariano praeside, cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum acclamassent: Areae non sint; areae ipsorum non fuerunt. Messes enim suas non egerunt. Caeterum et imbre anni praeteriti quid commeruerit genus humanum apparuit, cataclysmum scilicet et retro fuisse propter incredulitates et iniquitates hominum; et ignes qui super moenia Carthaginis proxime pependerunt per noctem, quid minati sint, sciunt qui viderunt; et pristina tonitrua quid sonaverunt, sciunt qui obduruerunt. Omnia haec signa sunt imminentis irae Dei, quam necesse est, quoquo modo possumus, ut et annuntiemus, et praedicemus, et deprecemur interim localem esse: universalem enim et supremam suo tempore sentient, qui exempla ejus aliter interpretantur. Nam et sol ille in conventu Uticensi, extincto pene lumine, adeo portentum fuit, ut non potuerit ex ordinario deliquio hoc pati, positus in suo hypsomate et domicilio. Habetis astrologos. Possumus aeque et exitus quorumdam praesidum tibi proponere, qui in fine vitae suae recordati sunt deliquisse, quod vexassent chritianos. Vigellius Saturninus qui primus hic gladiumin nos egit, lumina amisit. Claudius Lucius Herminianus in Cappadocia, cum indigne ferens uxorem suam ad hanc sectam transisse, christianos crudeliter tractasset, solusque in praetorio suo vastatus peste, cum vivus vermibus ebullisset: Nemo sciat, aiebat, ne gaudeant christiani. Postea cognito errore suo, quod tormentis quosdam a proposito suo excidere fecisset, pene christianus decessit. Caecilius Capella in illo exitu bysantino: Christiani gaudete, exclamavit. Sed et qui videntur sibi impune tulisse, venient in diem divini judicii. Tibi quoque optamus admonitionem solam fuisse, quod cum Adrimeticum Mavilum ad bestias damnasses, et statim haec vexatio subsecuta est, et nunc ex eadem caussa interpellatio sanguinis. Sed memento de caetero.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We aren't trying to frighten you; you don't scare anyway. My aim is to keep everyone safe by warning you not to fight against God. You can do your job as governor and still remember basic humanity — especially since you, too, live under the sword. What exactly does your commission order? To condemn confessed criminals, and to send those who deny the charge to the rack. So look at what you're doing: you force the very people who have confessed to recant, which means you're acting against your own orders. You all but admit we're innocent when you refuse to condemn us on the spot after a confession. And if you press on to destroy us, you're not punishing guilt — you're attacking innocence.

Plenty of governors — tougher and more brutal than you — have quietly let this kind of case drop. Cincius Severus coached the Thystrians on how Christians would answer so he could release them. Vespronius Candidus dismissed a Christian as a mere disturber of the peace to calm his own citizens. Asper roughed a man up lightly, then let him go without demanding a sacrifice, after telling his legal advisers and assessors he regretted ever getting mixed up in the case. Pudens sent a Christian away after realizing his statement was incoherent; with the speech falling apart and no accuser present, he refused to hear the man, citing his orders. All this can be cited to you as a matter of duty — and your own legal advisers know it, since they've benefited from Christians themselves, no matter what they shout in court.

Even a notary, thrown down by a demon, was set free. Relatives and little children of prominent men — not to mention the men themselves, honest and high-ranking, not commoners — have been healed of demons or sickness. The emperor Severus, Antoninus' father, kept Christians in mind. He tracked down Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, procurator of Euhodea, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until the man died; Antoninus knew him well, having been raised on a Christian woman's milk. Severus also knew that the most distinguished women and men belonged to this sect — and he not only refused to harm them, he honored them publicly and stood up to a mob raging against us. Marcus Aurelius, on campaign in Germany, got rain for his parched army through the prayers of Christian soldiers. When have our kneeling and fasting ever failed to break a drought? The crowd itself shouted to the God of gods, the only Power, invoking Jupiter's name while bearing witness to our God.

On top of that: we don't embezzle deposits, we don't violate anyone's marriage, we raise orphans with care, we relieve the poor, we return no evil for evil. Let the people who slander our sect look at the lives they themselves reject. Who accuses us under any other name? What crime does a Christian commit except belonging to this sect? And for all this time, no one has proved it incestuous or cruel. For such innocence, such integrity, for justice, chastity, faith, truth, and the living God — we are burned alive. Not even sacrilegious criminals, not even public enemies, not even those guilty of the worst treason, usually suffer this. Even now the name is harassed by the legion's commander and the governor of Mauretania — but only with the sword, as ordered from the start. Greater struggles lie ahead; greater rewards follow.

latin: Non te terremus, qui nec timemus: sed velim, ut omnes salvos facere possimus, monendo μὴ θεομαχεῖν. Potes et officio jurisdictionis tuae fungi, et humanitatis meminisse, vel quia et vos sub gladio estis. Quid enim amplius tibi mandatur, quam nocentes confessos damnare, negantes autem ad tormenta revocare? Videtis ergo quomodo ipsi vos contra mandata faciatis, ut confessos negare cogatis. Adeo confitemini innocentes esse nos, quos damnare statim ex confessione non vultis. Si autem contenditis ad elidendos nos, jam ergo innocentiam expugnatis. Quanti autem praesides, et constantiores et crudeliores, dissimulaverunt ab hujusmodi caussis! ut Cincius Severus, qui Thystri ipse dedit remedium, quomodo responderent christiani, ut dimitti possent; ut Vespronius Candidus, qui christianum quasi tumultuosum civibus suis satisfacere dimisit; ut Asper, qui modice vexatum hominem, et statim dejectum, nec sacrificium compulit facere, ante professus inter advocatos et adsessores, dolere se incidisse in hanc caussam. Pudens etiam missum ad se christianum in elogio concussione ejus intellecta dimisit, scisso eodem elogio, sine accusatore negans se auditurum hominem secundum mandatum. Haec omnia tibi et de officio suggeri possunt, et ab eisdem advocatis, qui ipsi beneficia habent Christianorum, licet acclament, quae volunt. Nam et cujusdam notarius cum a daemone praecipitaretur, liberatus est: et quorumdam propinquus et puerulus, et quanti honesti viri (de vulgaribus enim non dicimus) aut a daemoniis aut valetudinibus remediati sunt! Ipse etiam Severus pater Antonini, Christianorum memor fuit. Nam et Proculum christianum qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodeae procuratorem, qui eum per oleum aliquando curaverat, requisivit, et in palatio suo habuit usque ad mortem ejus: quem et Antoninus optime noverat lacte christiano educatus. Sed et clarissimas foeminas et clarissimos viros Severus sciens hujus sectae esse, non modo non laesit, verum et testimonio exornavit, et populo furenti in nos palam restitit. Marcus quoque Aurelius in Germanica expeditione christianorum militum orationibus ad Deum factis, imbres in siti illa impetravit. Quando non geniculationibus et jejunationibus nostris etiam siccitates sunt depulsae? Tunc et populus acclamans Deo deorum, qui solus potens, in Jovis nomine Deo nostro testimonium reddidit. Praeter haec depositum non abnegamus, matrimonium nullius adulteramus, pupillos pie tractamus, indigentibus refrigeramus, nulli malum pro malo reddimus. Viderint, qui sectam mentiuntur, quos et ipsi recusamus. Quis denique de nobis alio nomine queritur? quod aliud negotium patitur christianus, nisi suae sectae? quam incestam, quam crudelem, tanto tempore nemo probavit. Pro tanta innocentia, pro tanta probitate, pro justitia, pro pudicitia, pro fide, pro veritate, pro Deo vivo, cremamur; quod nec sacrilegi, nec hostes publici, verum nec tot majestatis rei pati solent. Nam et nunc a praeside legionis, et a praeside Mauritaniae vexatur hoc nomen, sed gladio tenus, sicut et a primordio mandatum est animadverti in hujusmodi. Sed majora certamina, majora sequuntur praemia.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Your cruelty is our glory. Make sure it does not look as if we endure these torments only to prove a point—that we do not fear them, but actually invite them. When Arrius Antoninus was persecuting Christians hard in Asia, every Christian in that city presented themselves at his tribunal. He ordered a few of them led away, then told the rest, "You wretches, if you want to die, you have cliffs or nooses." If you want that same scene here, what will you do with thousands upon thousands of men and women, of every sex, age, and rank, offering themselves to you? How many fires, how many swords will it take? What will become of Carthage itself, decimated by you, when each person recognizes their own relatives and comrades there—perhaps even men of your own rank, noblewomen, leading citizens, and the friends or kin of your own friends? So spare yourself, if not us; spare Carthage, if not yourself; spare the province, which your policy has already handed over to extortion by soldiers and by every man's enemies alike. We have no master but God alone. He stands before you; He cannot be hidden, yet you can do nothing to Him. As for those you take for masters, they are mere men who will die someday. Still this sect will not fail—you can see it grows stronger precisely when it seems to be cut down. For anyone who witnesses such endurance feels a stab of doubt, begins to ask what drives it, and once they grasp the truth, they follow it at once.

latin: Crudelitas vestra gloria est nostra. Vide tantum ne hoc ipso, quod talia sustinemus, ad hoc solum videamur erumpere, ut hoc ipsum probemus, nos haec non timere, sed ultro vocare. Arrius Antoninus in Asia cum persequeretur instanter, omnes illius civitatis christiani ante tribunalia ejus se manu facta obtulerunt, cum ille, paucis duci jussis, reliquis ait, ὧ δεῖλοι, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνήσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε. Hoc si placuerit et hic fieri, quid facies de tantis millibus hominum, tot viris ac foeminis, omnis sexus, omnis aetatis, omnis dignitatis, offerentibus se tibi? Quantis ignibus, quantis gladiis opus erit! quid ipsa Carthago passura est, decimanda a te, cum propinquos, cum contubernales suos illic unusquisque cognoverit, cum viderit illic fortasse et tui ordinis viros et matronas, et principales quasque personas, et amicorum tuorum vel propinquos vel amicos? Parce ergo tibi, si non nobis, parce Carthagini, si non tibi, parce provinciae, quae visa intentione tua obnoxia facta est concussionibus et militum et inimicorum suorum cujusque. Magistrum neminem habemus, nisi Deum solum. Hic ante te est, nec abscondi potest, sed cui nihil facere possis. Caeterum quos putas tibi magistros, homines sunt et ipsi morituri quandoque. Nec tamen deficiet haec secta, quam tunc magis aedificari scias, cum caedi videtur. Quisque enim tantam tolerantiam spectans, ut aliquo scrupulo percussus, et inquirere accenditur, quid sit in causa, et ubi cognoverit veritatem, et ipse statim sequitur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The earth breeds a massive evil from a tiny thing: the scorpion. Nicander writes and paints it— as many poisons as kinds, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors. Yet for all that variety, a single gesture of violence does the harm: the strike of the tail. That tail is whatever extends from the body's rear, and it lashes out. So the scorpion's segmented tail, a poisonous vein inside, rises on a curved impulse and locks a hooked barb at the summit of its torment mechanism; hence a siege engine, its projectile springing from a drawn-back position, takes its name from the scorpion. That barb is also a duct, its open fineness channeling wound and venom; with it the creature strikes and injects. Summer is the familiar season of danger; the south wind and the African wind hoist its savagery. Remedies abound in nature; magic also binds something, and medicine meets the crisis with iron and cup. Some even drink beforehand, rushing protection; but intercourse exhausts the antidote, and they thirst again.

For us, faith is the shield— if it is not itself struck by the hesitation to sign, to adjure, to drive the beast's heel at once. In this way, finally, we often come to the aid of gentiles as well, endowed by God with the power the Apostle consecrated when he despised a viper's bite. So what does this pen promise, if faith is safe on its own account? That it may be safe on its own account in other matters too, when it endures its own scorpions. A bitter mediocrity belongs to these as well: varied kind, armed in one way, deployed at a set time, and driven by nothing but ardor. This, among Christians, is persecution.

When faith boils and the Church burns from the figure of the ruby, then the Gnostics burst out, the Valentinians break forth, and all the refusers of martyrdom boil over, hot themselves to offend, to stab, to kill. They know well that many are simple and unskilled, then weak, most indeed in the wind, and if it pleases, Christians— never do they perceive them more approachable than when fear of the soul has loosened the approach; especially when some atrocity has crowned the martyrs' faith. So at first, still drawing the tail from the affections, they apply it, or lash out as into a vacuum. Are innocent men to suffer this? So that you might take him for a brother, or one of the better gentiles? Is a sect that harms no one to be treated thus? Then they drive men to perish without cause. For to perish, and without cause, is the first piercing. From then on they kill.

But simple souls do not know what, how, where, when, or before whom it is written that confession must be made— unless it is not that simplicity, but vanity, indeed madness, to die for God. And: Who will save me, if the one who ought to save me kills? Christ died once for us, was killed once so that we might not be killed. If he demands a turn, does he now expect salvation from my death? Or does God demand the blood of the world's men, especially since he refuses that of bulls and goats? Certainly he prefers a sinner's repentance to death. And how does he not desire the death of sins? These poisons of the heretics, and any others— what do they not fix, whether in a scruple or in destruction? Or in bile, if not in death?

But you, if faith keeps watch, there strike the scorpion with a sandal, anathema applied, and leave the dying thing in its own sleep. Yet if the wound has had its fill, the venom announces itself and rushes to the vitals; at once all former senses grow numb, the soul's blood chills, the flesh's spirit goes cold, nausea at the Name swells. Even the mind now seeks something to vomit. And so, once struck, the weakness expires— wounded faith breathing its last either into heresy or into the world.

And now the present reality is the midday heat, the very dog-star of persecution: from the dog-headed one himself. Fire has tested some Christians, sword others, beasts others. Others in prison, having tasted martyrdom with rods and nails, hunger for it still. We ourselves, like hares marked for the hunt, are besieged from afar, and heretics prowl as is their custom. So the time has warned us to prepare a remedy against our little beasts: to compound a therapeutic writing with the pen; you who read, will drink. The draught is not bitter. If the Lord's words are sweeter than honey and comb, the seasonings come from there; if God's promise flows with milk and honey, these words taste the way that leads there. Woe to those who turn sweet to bitter and light to darkness. For just as those who resist martyrdom, interpreting salvation as perdition, turn sweet to bitter and light to darkness, so they pervert this most wretched life by preferring the most blessed one— substituting bitter for sweet, darkness for light.

latin: Magnum de modico malum scorpios terra suppurat: tot venena, quot genera; tot pernicies, quot et species; tot dolores, quot et colores, Nicander scribit et pingit: et tamen unus omnium violentiae gestus nocere de cauda; quae cauda erit, quodcumque de postumo corporis propagatur, et verberat. Proinde scorpii series illa nodorum, venenata intrinsecus venula subtilis, arcuato impetu surgens, hamatile spiculum in summo tormenti ratione stringit; unde et bellicam machinam, retractu tela vegetantem, de scorpio nominant. Id spiculum, et fistula est, patula tenuitate in vulnus et virus, qua figit effundit. Familiare periculi tempus aestas; Austro et Africo saevitia velificat. In remediis naturalia plurima; aliquid et magia circumligat, medicina cum ferro et poculo occurrit. Nam et praebibunt quidam, festinando tutelam; sed concubitus exhaurit, et denuo sitiunt. Nobis fides praesidium, si non et ipsa percutitur diffidentia signandi statim et adjurandi, et urgendi bestiae calcem: hoc denique modo etiam ethnicis saepe subvenimus; donati a Deo ea potestate, quam Apostolus dedicavit, cum morsum viperae sprevit. Quid ergo promittit stylus iste, si fides de suo tuta est? Ut et alias de suo tuta sit, cum suos scorpios patitur. Acerba mediocritas et istis, et genus varium, et uno modo armantur, et certo tempore subornantur, nec alio quam ardoris. Hoc apud Christianos persecutio est. Cum igitur fides aestuat, et Ecclesia exuritur de figura rubi, tunc Gnostici erumpunt, tunc Valentiniani proserpunt, tunc omnes martyriorum refragatores ebulliunt, calentes et ipsi offendere, figere, occidere. Nam quod sciant multos simplices ac rudes, tum infirmos, plerosque vero in ventum, et si placuerit, christianos, nunquam magis adeundos sapiunt, quam cum aditus animae formido laxavit; praesertim cum aliqua atrocitas fidem martyrum coronavit. Itaque primo trahentes adhuc caudam de affectibus applicant, aut quasi in vacuum flagellant. Haeccine pati homines innocentes? ut putes fratrem, aut de melioribus ethnicum? Siccine tractari sectam nemini molestam? Dehinc adigunt, perire homines sine caussa. Perire enim, et sine caussa, prima fixura. Exinde jam caedunt. Sed nesciunt simplices animae, quid, quomodo scriptum sit, ubi, et quando, et coram quibus confitendum, nisi quod nec simplicitas ista, sed vanitas, imo dementia, pro Deo mori. Et: Quis me salvum faciat, si is occidet, qui salvum facere debebit? Semel Christus pro nobis obiit, semel occisus est ne occideremur. Si vicem repetit, nunc et ille salutem de mea nece exspectat? An Deus hominum mundi sanguinem flagitat, maxime si taurorum et hircorum recusat? Certe peccatoris poenitentiam mavult quam mortem. Et quomodo non peccatorum desiderat mortem? Haec, et si qua alia admenta haereticorum venenorum, quem non vel in scrupulum figant, si non in exitium? vel in bilem, si non in mortem? At tu, fides si vigilat, ibidem scorpio pro solea anathema illidito, et relinquito in suo sopore morientem. Caeterum, si plagam satiaverit, intimat virus, et properat in viscera; statim omnes pristini sensus retorpescunt, sanguis animi gelascit, carne spiritus exolescit, nausea nominis inaccrescit. Jam et ipsa mens sibi quo vomat quaerit. Atque ita semel infirmitas quae percussa est, sauciatam fidem vel in haeresim, vel in saeculum exspirat. Et nunc praesentia rerum est medius ardor ipsa canicula persecutionis: ab ipso scilicet cynocephalo. Alios ignis, alios gladius, alios bestiae Christianos probaverunt. Alii fustibus interim et ungulis insuper degustata martyria in carcere esuriunt. Nos ipsi ut lepores, destinata venatio, de longinquo obsidemur, et haeretici ex more grassantur. Itaque tempus admonuit adversus nostrates bestiolas (promptam) mederi theriacam stylo temperare; qui legeris, biberis. Non amarum potio. Si eloquia Domini dulcia super mella et favos, inde pigmenta sunt; si lacte et melle promissio Dei manat, hoc sapiunt quae illuc faciunt. Vae autem qui dulce in amarum, et lumen in tenebras convertunt. Perinde enim et qui martyriis refragantur, salutem perditionem interpretantes, tam dulce in amarum, quam lucem in tenebras reformant, atque ita miserrimam hanc vitam illi beatissimae praevertendo, tam amarum pro dulci, quam tenebras pro luce supponunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: But as to those who think that not here, that is, not within this environment of earth, nor during this period of existence , nor before men possessing this nature shared by us all, has confession been appointed to be made, what a supposition is theirs, being at variance with the whole order of things of which we have experience in these lands, and in this life, and under human authorities! Doubtless, when the souls have departed from their bodies, and begun to be put upon trial in the several stories of the heavens, with reference to the engagement (under which they have come to Jesus), and to be questioned about those hidden mysteries of the heretics , they must then confess before the real powers and the real men, — the Teleti, to wit, and the Abascanti, and the Acineti of Valentinus !

For, say they , even the Demiurge himself did not uniformly approve of the men of our world, whom he counted as a drop of a bucket, Isaiah 40:15 and the dust of the threshing-floor, and spittle and locusts, and put on a level even with brute beasts. Clearly, it is so written. Yet not therefore must we understand that there is, besides us, another kind of man , which — for it is evidently thus (in the case proposed)— has been able to assume without invalidating a comparison between the two kinds , both the characteristics of the race and a unique property. For even if the life was tainted, so that condemned to contempt it might be likened to objects held in contempt, the nature was not immediately taken away, so that there might be supposed to be another under its name.

Rather is the nature preserved, though the life blushes; nor does Christ know other men than those with reference to whom He says, Whom do men say that I am? Matthew 16:13 And, As you would that men should do to you, do likewise so to them. Consider whether He may not have preserved a race such that He is looking for a testimony to Himself from them, as well as consisting of those on whom He enjoins the interchange of righteous dealing. But if I should urgently demand that those heavenly men be described to me, Aratus will sketch more easily Perseus and Cepheus, and Erigone, and Ariadne, among the constellations.

But who prevented the Lord from clearly prescribing that confession by men likewise has to be made where He plainly announced that His own would be; so that the statement might have run thus: Whosoever shall confess in me before men in heaven, I also will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven? He ought to have saved me from this mistake about confession on earth, which He would not have wished me to take part in, if He had commanded one in heaven; for I knew no other men but the inhabitants of the earth, man himself even not having up to that time been observed in heaven.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We defend the same pattern in everything else that belongs to martyrdom. "Whoever does more," he says, "and makes his own soul count for more than me, is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:39). That is, whoever prefers to live by denying me rather than to die by confessing me. "Whoever finds his life will lose it; whoever loses it for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25; Luke 17:33). So the one who denies Christ to gain his life actually finds it — but only to lose it in Gehenna. The one who thinks he gains it by denying Christ loses it there. But the one who is killed after confessing loses his life now, yet will find it in eternal life.

Even the judges themselves, when they urge denial, say, 'Save your soul, and do not lose your soul.' How else would Christ speak than in the way a Christian is treated? When he forbids rehearsing a defense before the tribunal, he instructs his servants and promises the Holy Spirit will speak for them. When he wants a brother visited in prison, he commands care for the confessor. When he affirms that God will avenge his elect, he consoles their sufferings. Even in the parable of the seed after the thorns wither, he depicts the heat of persecutions (Matthew 13:6).

If these words are not taken exactly as they are spoken, they certainly sound different from what they mean; one thing will be in the words, another in the senses — like allegories, like parables, like riddles. Whatever scorpion has conceived a wind of argument for them, whatever sharpness they thrust themselves with, there is now a single line: they will be driven to the things themselves, to see whether they are carried out according to the Scriptures.

For if something else is signified in the Scriptures, but the same thing is not found in the events, then what is written will not happen. What is written must happen. And it will happen what is written — if nothing else happens instead. Look: we are hated by all people for the name's sake, just as it is written (Matthew 10:22). We are betrayed even by those closest to us, just as it is written (Matthew 24:9). We are hauled before authorities, interrogated, tortured, we confess, and we are slaughtered — just as it is written. So the Lord decreed.

If he decreed these things differently, why do they not happen differently than he decreed — that is, exactly as he decreed? But they do not happen differently than he decreed. Therefore, as they happen, so he decreed; so they happen. It was not permitted for them to happen otherwise than he decreed; nor would he have decreed otherwise than he wanted them to happen. Thus the Scriptures will not signify anything other than what we recognize in the events.

Or if the things predicted are not yet done, how are these things done which were not predicted? For the things that are happening are not predicted if other things are predicted and not these things that are happening. But now, because the same things are in the events as in the words, people believe things spoken otherwise. What would happen if the events themselves turned out differently? But this is the perversity of faith: not to believe proven things, to presume unproven things.

To that perversity I also oppose this: if these things that are happening exactly as written are not the very things predicted, then those things that ought not to happen exactly as written — lest they also be endangered by the example of these — must be excluded. For one thing is in the words, another in the events. And it remains that predicted things are not recognized when they happen, if they are predicted otherwise than they come to pass. And how will those things be believed which are not predicted, because they are not predicted in the way they happen? So heretics believe the things predicted not as they have been proven by believing, but the things that are not predicted at all.

latin: Eadem igitur forma, caetera quoque ad martyrii pertinere defendimus. Qui pluris, inquit, fecerit etiam animam suam quam me, non est me dignus; id est, qui maluerit vivere me negando, quam mori confitendo. Qui animam suam invenerit, perdet illam; qui vero perdiderit mei caussa, inveniet illam. Proinde enim invenit eam, qui negarit lucrifaciendo vitam; sed perdet in gehennam, qui se putat negando lucrifacere eam. Perdet autem eam ad praesens, qui confessus occiditur; sed inventurus eam in vitam aeternam. Ipsi denique praesides, cum hortantur negationi, serva animam tuam, dicunt, et noli animam tuam perdere. Quo modo loqueretur Christus, nisi quo modo tractaretur christianus? Sed cum prohibet meditari responsionem ad tribunal, famulos suos instruit, Spiritum Sanctum responsurum repromittit; et cum in carcere fratrem vult visitari, confessoris imperat curam; et cum Deum vindictam facturum electorum suorum affirmat, passiones consolatur illorum: etiam in parabola seminis post cespitem arefacti, persecutionum figurat ardorem. Haec si non ita accipiuntur quemadmodum pronuntiantur, sine dubio praeterquam sonant sapiunt; et aliud in vocibus erit, aliud in sensibus; ut allegoriae, ut parabolae, ut aenigmata. Quemcumque igitur conceperint ventum argumentationis scorpii isti, quocumque se acumine impegerint, una jam linea est: ad ipsas res provocabuntur, an secundum Scripturas transigantur. Siquidem tunc aliud significabitur in Scripturis, si non idipsum reperiatur in rebus. Quod enim scriptum est, hoc evenire oportebit. Porro, tunc eveniet quod est scriptum, si non aliud eveniet. Ecce autem et odio habemur ab omnibus hominibus, nominis caussa, quomodo et scriptum est; et tradimur etiam a proximis, quomodo et scriptum est; et perducimur ad potestates, et interrogamur, et torquemur, et confitemur, et trucidamur, quomodo et scriptum est. Sic Dominus edixit. Si aliter edixit haec, cur non aliter eveniunt, quam edixit, id est, quemadmodum edixit? Atquin non aliter eveniunt quam edixit: ergo sicut eveniunt, ita edixit, ita eveniunt. Nam nec licuisset aliter evenire, quam edixit; nec ipse aliter edixisset, quam evenire voluisset. Ita, non aliud significabunt Scripturae, quam in rebus recognoscimus. Aut si nondum aguntur illa quae praedicantur, quomodo haec aguntur quae praedicata non sunt? Non sunt enim haec praedicata quae aguntur, si alia sunt quae praedicantur, et non haec quae aguntur. At nunc, quia ipsa sunt in rebus, quae in vocibus, aliter dicta creduntur; quid fieret si aliter facta invenirentur? Sed haec est perversitas fidei, probata non credere, non probata praesumere. Cui perversitati illud quoque opponam, ut si haec quae sic aguntur quemadmodum scripta sunt, non erunt ipsa quae praedicantur, illa quae non debeant sic agi quemadmodum scripta sunt, ne et ipsa horum exemplo periclitentur, excludi siquidem aliud in vocibus, aliud in rebus est; et relinquitur nec praedicata videri cum evenerint, si aliter praedicantur quam evenire habent. Et quomodo credentur quae non erunt praedicata, quia non ita erunt praedicata quomodo eveniunt? Ita haeretici quae praedicantur non ut probata sunt credendo, ea quae nec praedicata sunt, credunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Who today knows the innermost depths of Scripture better than Christ's own school? The Lord adopted the apostles as his own disciples so they would be taught everything, and he appointed them as our teachers so they would teach everything. To whom would he have disclosed the sound of his voice rather than to those to whom he revealed the image of his glory — Peter, James, John, and later Paul, whom he made a partaker of paradise before his martyrdom? Or do they write something other than what they think, as masters of deceit instead of truth? Peter tells the Pontics: 'What glory is it if you are not punished as evildoers but endure?' (1 Peter 2:20). 'This is grace; for this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his steps.' And again: 'Beloved, do not be terrified by the fiery ordeal taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice to the extent that you share in Christ's sufferings, so that you may also rejoice exulting when his glory is revealed' (1 Peter 3:14). 'If you are reviled in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the glory and Spirit of God rest upon you — provided none of you suffers as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or meddler. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; let him glorify the Lord in that name.' John exhorts us to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters, denying that fear exists in love: 'Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfected in love' (1 John 4:18). What fear is understood except the fear of denial? What perfect love does he affirm except the love that drives out fear and inspires confession? What punishment does fear inflict except the punishment the denier will suffer — to be killed in Gehenna, body and soul? And if one must die for one's brothers, how much more must one die for the Lord, as he teaches, sufficiently instructed from his own Apocalypse! The Spirit commanded the angel of the church in Smyrna: 'Behold, the devil will throw some of you into prison so that you may be tested for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life' (Revelation 2:10). Likewise to the Pergamenes concerning Antipas, the faithful martyr slain where Satan dwells. Likewise to the Philadelphians, that they would be kept from the final trial because they did not deny the Lord's name. From then on he promises each conqueror: the tree of life and exemption from the second death; hidden manna with a white stone and a new name; authority of an iron rod and the brightness of the morning star; to be clothed in white, never blotted from the book of life, and made a pillar in God's temple bearing the name of God and the Lord and the new Jerusalem; to sit with the Lord on his throne — a privilege once denied to the sons of Zebedee. Who are these supremely blessed conquerors if not the martyrs themselves? Theirs are the victories, theirs the battles, theirs the blood. Meanwhile, under the altar, the souls of the martyrs rest in peace; confident of vengeance, they feed their patience, and clothed in white robes they wear the brightness of purity until others complete the fellowship of their glory. Again, a countless multitude robed in white and bearing victory palms appears — those who have conquered the Antichrist, as one of the elders says: 'These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb' (Revelation 7:14). For the garment of the soul is the flesh. Filth is washed away by baptism, but stains are whitened by martyrdom. Isaiah promises that from crimson and scarlet shall come white as wool. Great Babylon is described as drunk on the blood of the saints; without doubt, her drunkenness is supplied by the cups of the martyrs, whose fear reveals what it will bring — equally. Among all the reprobates; indeed, before all of them. 'But to the timid,' he says, 'and the rest, a portion in the lake of fire and sulfur.' Thus the fear that love casts out carries its own punishment, as shown in his Epistle.

latin: Quis nunc medullas Scripturarum magis nosset, quam ipsa Christi schola? quos et sibi discipulos Dominus adoptavit, omnia utique edocendos; et nobis magistros adornavit, omnia utique docturos. Cui potius figuram vocis suae declarasset, quam cui effigiem gloriae suae revelavit, Petro, Jacobo, Joanni, et postea Paulo, quem paradisi quoque compotem fecit ante martyrium? An et illi aliter quam sentiunt scribunt, fallaciae magistri, non veritatis? Petrus quidem ad Ponticos: Quanta enim, inquit, gloria, si non ut delinquentes puniamini, sustinetis! Haec enim gratia est, in hoc et vocati estis, quoniam et Christus passus est pro nobis, relinquens vobis exemplum semetipsum, ut assequamini vestigia ipsius. Et rursus: Dilecti, ne expavescatis ustionem, quae agitur in vobis in tentationem, quasi novum accidat vobis: etenim secundum quod communicatis passionibus Christi, gaudete, uti et in revelatione gloriae ejus gaudeatis exultantes. Si dedecoramini in nomine Christi, beati estis, quoniam gloria et Dei spiritus requiescit in vobis, dum ne quis vestrum patiatur, ut homicida, aut fur, aut maleficus, aut alieni speculator. Si autem ut christianus, ne erubescat; glorificet autem Dominum in nomine isto. Joannes vero, ut etiam pro fratribus nostris animas ponamus, hortatur, negans timorem esse in dilectione: Perfecta enim dilectio foras abjicit timorem: quoniam timor poenam habet; et qui timet, non est perfectus in dilectione. Quem timorem intelligi praestat, nisi negationis auctorem? Quam dilectionem perfectam affirmat, nisi fugatricem timoris, et animatricem confessionis? Quam poenam timore puniat, nisi quam negator relaturus est, cum corpore et anima occidendus in gehenna? Quod si pro fratribus, quanto magis pro Domino moriendum docet, satis de Apocalypsi quoque sua instructus haec suadere! Mandaverat etenim spiritus ad angelum ecclesiae Smyrnaeorum: Ecce diabolus ex numero tuo conjiciet in carcerem, ut tentemini diebus decem. Esto fidelis ad mortem usque, et dabo tibi vitae coronam. Item ad Pergamenorum de Antipa fidelissimo martyre interfecto in habitatione Satanae. Item ad Philadelphenorum, quod a tentatione ultima liberaretur, qui Domini nomen non negarat. Exinde victori cuique promittit nunc arborem vitae, et mortis veniam secundae: nunc latens manna cum calculo candido, et nomine ignoto: nunc ferreae virgae potestatem, et stellae matutinae claritatem: nunc albam vestiri, nec deleri de libro vitae, et columnam fieri in Dei templo, in nomine Dei et Domini, et Jerusalem coelestis inscripta, nunc residere cum Domino in throno ejus, quod aliquando Zebedaei filiis negabatur. Quinam isti tam beati victores, nisi proprie martyres? Illorum etenim victoriae, quorum et pugnae; eorum vero pugnae, quorum et sanguis. Sed et interim sub altari martyrum animae placidum quiescunt, et fiducia ultionis patientiam pascunt, et indutae stolis, candidam claritatis usurpant, donec et alii consortium illarum gloriae impleant. Nam et rursus innumera multitudo albati et palmis victoriae insignes revelantur; scilicet de Antichristo triumphantes, sicut unus ex presbyteris; Hi sunt, ait, qui veniunt ex illa pressura magna, et laverunt vestimentum suum, et candidaverunt ipsum in sanguine agni: vestitus enim animae, caro. Sordes quidem baptismate abluuntur, maculae vero martyrio candidantur. Quia et Esaias ex russeo et coccino niveum et laneum repromittit. Magna etiam Babylon cum describitur ebria sanctorum cruore, sine dubio ebrietas ejus martyriorum poculis ministratur, quorum formido quid relatura sit, aeque ostenditur. Inter omnes enim reprobos; imo ante omnes. Timidis autem, inquit, dehinc caeteris, particula in stagno ignis et sulphuris. Sic timor ejus in Epistola ejus, quem dilectio foras abjicit, habet poenam.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: But how Paul , an apostle , from being a persecutor, who first of all shed the blood of the church, though afterwards he exchanged the sword for the pen, and turned the dagger into a plough, being first a ravening wolf of Benjamin, then himself supplying food as did Jacob, — how he, (I say,) speaks in favour of martyrdoms , now to be chosen by himself also, when, rejoicing over the Thessalonians, he says, So that we glory in you in the churches of God , for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations, in which you endure a manifestation of the righteous judgment of God , that you may be accounted worthy of His kingdom, for which you also suffer!

2 Thessalonians 1:4 As also in his Epistle to the Romans: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also, being sure that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope; and hope makes not ashamed. Romans 5:3 And again: And if children, then heirs, heirs indeed of God , and joint-heirs with Christ: if so be that we suffer with Him, that we may be also glorified together. For I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. Romans 8:17 And therefore he afterward says: Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?

(As it is written: For Your sake we are killed all the day long; we have been counted as sheep for the slaughter.) Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors, through Him who loved us. For we are persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God , which is in Christ Jesus our Lord . Romans 8:35 But further, in recounting his own sufferings to the Corinthians, he certainly decided that suffering must be borne: In labours, (he says,) more abundant, in prisons very frequent, in deaths oft. Of the Jews five times received I forty stripes, save one; thrice was I beaten with rods; once was I stoned , 2 Corinthians 11:23 and the rest.

And if these severities will seem to be more grievous than martyrdoms , yet once more he says: Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions , in distresses for Christ's sake. 2 Corinthians 12:10 He also says, in verses occurring in a previous part of the epistle: Our condition is such, that we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; and are in need, but not in utter want; since we are harassed by persecutions , but not forsaken; it is such that we are cast down, but not destroyed; always bearing about in our body the dying of Christ . 2 Corinthians 4:8 But though, says he, our outward man perishes — the flesh doubtless, by the violence of persecutions — yet the inward man is renewed day by day — the soul , doubtless, by hope in the promises.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: He bluntly warns the Romans to submit to every authority, because no authority exists except from God, because the ruler does not carry the sword for nothing, and because it is a ministry of God—but also an avenger, he says, bringing wrath on the one who does evil (Romans 13:1-7). Scripture had already laid the groundwork: rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. You want to stop fearing authority? Do good, and you will win its praise. So it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. Therefore, the command to submit is not given to sabotage martyrdom, but to provoke good living even under their gaze, as if they were assistants of justice, ministers of divine judgment, here already passing preliminary sentence on wrongdoers. He then spells out what that submission looks like: pay what you owe—tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax is due; that is, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21); the human person belongs to God alone. Peter had agreed that a king deserves honor, yet a king is honored only when he stays in his lane, keeping his distance from divine honors; a father and mother are loved precisely because they are not equated with God. Beyond that, loving anything more than God is not permitted—not even your own soul.

latin: Plane monet Romanos omnibus potestatibus subjici, quia non sit potestas nisi a Deo, quia non sine caussa gladium gestet, et quia ministerium sit Dei; sed et ultrix, inquit, in iram ei qui malum fecerit. Nam et praemiserat: Principes enim non sunt timori bono operi, sed malo. Vis autem non timere potestatem? fac bonum, et laudem ab ea referes. Dei ergo ministra est tibi in bonum. Si vero malum facias, time. Ita, non in occasione frustrandi martyrii jubet te subjici potestatibus, sed in provocatione bene vivendi, etiam sub illarum respectu, quasi adjutricum justitiae, quasi ministrarum divini judicii, hic etiam de nocentibus praejudicantis. Dehinc et exequitur quomodo velit te subjici potestatibus, reddere jubens, cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal; id est quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, et quae Dei, Deo; solius autem Dei homo. Condixerat scilicet Petrus, regem quidem honorandum; ut tamen tunc rex honoretur, cum suis rebus insistit, cum a divinis honoribus longe est; quia et pater et mater diligentur, cum Deo non comparabuntur. Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Are the Apostles’ writings also changeable? And are we merely simple souls everywhere, nothing but doves, willingly wandering astray? I put it down to a desire to stay alive. Very well, then: let the meanings depart from their letters. What the Apostles suffered is plain doctrine; I grasp it simply by reading through Acts. I need nothing else. Prisons, chains, whips, stones, swords, attacks by Jews, riots of the nations, speeches before tribunes, audiences with kings, tribunals of proconsuls, the very name of Caesar — none of these requires an interpreter. That Peter was struck down, that Stephen was overwhelmed, that James was slaughtered, that Paul was torn apart — these things were written in their own blood. And if a heretic wants to test the faith of the Commentaries, the instruments of empire will speak, like the stones of Jerusalem. We read the Lives of the Caesars; Nero first bloodied the rising faith at Rome. Then Peter was girded by another when he was bound to the cross. Then Paul obtained the birthright of Roman citizenship when he was reborn there through the nobility of martyrdom. Wherever I read these things now, I learn to suffer; it does not matter which teachers of martyrdom I follow, whether the meanings or the outcomes of the Apostles — except that I also recognize the meanings in the outcomes. For they would not have suffered anything they had not first recognized as something that had to be suffered. When Agabus prophesied Paul’s chains even by a gesture, the disciples wept and prayed that he not go up to Jerusalem; they prayed in vain. For he, driven by what he had always taught, said: ‘Why do you weep and break my heart? I not only wish to suffer chains in Jerusalem, but also to die for the name of my Lord Jesus Christ.’ And so they yielded, saying: ‘Let the will of the Lord be done’ — trusting, of course, that sufferings belong to God’s will. They had tried to restrain him not with the counsel of dissuasion, but with the bond of love, wanting to keep the Apostle because they desired him, not because they were dissuading him from martyrdom. But if Prodicus or Valentinus had been there then, suggesting that one should not confess on earth among men; much less that God thirsts for human blood, nor that Christ, as if he himself were going to obtain salvation from it, demands the substitute of passion — he would have heard at once from the servant of God what the devil heard from the Lord: ‘Depart, Satan, you are a scandal to me; it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him only’ (Matt. 4:10). And he ought to hear it now as well, since he poured out those poisons so much later; none of the weak will easily drink them unless they have already drunk — or even overdosed on — this potion of our faith.

latin: Num ergo et Apostolorum litterae mobiles? et nos usquequaque simplices animae, et solummodo columbae, libenter errantes? credo vivendi cupiditate. Ita vero sit, ut recedant a litteris suis sensus. Quae tamen passos Apostolos scimus, manifesta doctrina est; hanc intelligo solam Acta decurrens; nihil quaero; carceres illic, et vincula, et flagella, et saxa, et gladii, et impetus Judaeorum, et coetus nationum, et tribunorum elogia, et regum auditoria, et proconsulum tribunalia, et Caesaris nomen interpretem non habent. Quod Petrus caeditur, quod Stephanus opprimitur, quod Jacobus immolatur, quod Paulus distrahitur, ipsorum sanguine scripta sunt. Et si fidem Commentarii voluerit haereticus, instrumenta imperii loquentur, ut lapides Jerusalem. Vitas Caesarum legimus; orientem fidem Romae primus Nero cruentavit. Tunc Petrus ab altero cingitur, cum cruci adstringitur. Tunc Paulus civitatis romanae consequitur nativitatem, cum illic martyrii renascitur generositate. Haec ubicumque jam legero, pati disco; nec mea interest quos sequar martyrii magistros, sensusne an exitus Apostolorum; nisi quod et sensus in exitibus recognosco. Nihil enim passi fuissent, quod non prius patiendum esse sensissent. Cum vincula Paulo Agabus gestu quoque prophetasset, discipuli flentes et orantes ne se Jerosolyma committeret, frustra oraverunt. Ille enim, quod semper docuerat animatus: Quid fletis, inquit, et contristatis cor meum? At ego non modo vincula Jerosolymis pati optaverim, verum etiam mori pro nomine Domini mei Jesu Christi. Atque ita cesserunt, dicendo: Fiat voluntas Domini; fidentes scilicet, passiones ad voluntatem Dei pertinere. Non enim dehortationis consilio, sed dilectionis retinere tantaverant, ut Apostolum desiderantes, non ut martyrium dissuadentes. Quod si jam tunc Prodicus aut Valentinus assisteret, suggerens, non in terris esse confitendum apud homines; minus vero, ne Deus humanum sanguinem sitiat, nec Christus vicem passionis, quasi et ipse de ea salutem consecuturus exposcat; statim audisset a servo Dei, quod audierat a Domino diabolus: Recede, Satana, scandalum mihi es; scriptum est: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, et illi soli servies. Sed et nunc audire debebit, quatenus multo post, venena ista suffudit; nulli infirmorum facile nisi nocitura, si qui non hanc nostram ex fide praebiberit, vel etiam superbiberit potionem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If this offense was established as forbidden from the very beginning—backed by so many and such great precepts, never committed with impunity, and confirmed by so many and such great examples—and if no crime counts as more arrogant before God than a transgression of this kind, then we ought to grasp of our own accord the intention behind divine warnings and punishments. That intention was already supported by martyrdoms back then, martyrdoms that were not only not to be doubted but also to be endured, since idolatry was prohibited precisely so that martyrdoms could occur; otherwise martyrdoms would not have happened. And God certainly established His own authority, wishing to bring about the very things for which He had made room.

Now we are pricked by the will of God, and the scorpion doubles the blow by denying this will and accusing it—so that it may insinuate another God whose will this is not; or else destroy our God, whose will is of this kind; or altogether deny the will of God, if it cannot deny God Himself. But we, who fight about God elsewhere and about the rest of the body of each heretical doctrine, now lead forth certain lines of a single kind of contest. We defend not the will of some other God, but the will of the God of Israel—the will that made room for martyrdoms, both through precepts that always prohibited idolatry and through judgments that punished it.

For if an observed precept suffers violence, this will be in a certain way observing the precept: I suffer that very violence so that I can keep the precept, namely whatever violence threatens me as I avoid idolatry. And certainly the One who imposes the precept exacts obedience. Therefore He could not have failed to wish those things to happen through which obedience would be established.

It is prescribed to me not to speak of any other God; not even by speaking to form a God with my tongue, no less than with my hand; not to adore any other, or to venerate in any way, except the one and only God who so commands. He is the One I am also commanded to fear, lest I be deserted by Him, and to love with all my substance, so that I may die for Him. Fighting for this sacrament, I am provoked by enemies; I am their equal if I give in. Defending this, I fight in battle, I am wounded, I am struck down, I am killed. Who wished this outcome for His soldier, if not the One who sealed him with such a sacrament?

latin: Hanc igitur si a primordio constat et prohibitam de tot tantisque praeceptis, et nunquam impune commissam, de tot tantisque documentis, nec ullum tam superbum crimen apud Deum deputari, quam hujusmodi transgressionem, ultro intelligere debemus divinarum et denuntiationum et executionum intentionem, jam tunc martyriis patrocinatam, non modo non dubitandis, verum etiam sustinendis, quibus scilicet locum fecerat prohibendo idololatriam: aliter enim martyria non evenirent; et utique auctoritatem suam praestruxerat, volens ea evenire quibus locum fecerat. Nunc enim de Dei voluntate compungimur, et ingeminat scorpius plagam, hanc negans, hanc accusans voluntatem, ut aut alium Deum insinuet, cujus haec non sit voluntas; aut nostrum nihilominus destruat, cujus talis sit voluntas; aut omnino neget voluntatem Dei, si ipsum negare non poterit. Nos autem de Deo alibi dimicantes, et de reliquo corpore haereticae cujusque doctrinae, nunc in unam speciem congressionis certas praeducimus lineas, non alterius Dei, quam Israelis, eam defendentes voluntatem, quae martyriis locum fecerit, tam ex praeceptis prohibitae semper, quam ex judiciis punitae idololatriae. Si enim praeceptum observatum vim patitur, hoc erit quodammodo observandi praeceptum, ut id patiar per quod potero observare praeceptum: vim scilicet quaecumque mihi imminet caventi ab idololatria. Et utique qui imponit praeceptum, extorquet obsequium. Non potuit ergo noluisse ea evenire, per quae constabit obsequium. Praescribitur mihi ne quem alium Deum dicam; ne, vel dicendo, non minus lingua quam manu Deum fingam; ne quem alium adorem, aut quoque modo venerer, praeter unicum illum qui ita mandat; quem et jubeor timere, ne ab eo deserar; et de omni substantia diligere, ut pro eo moriar. Huic sacramento militans ab hostibus provocor, par sum illis si manus dedero; hoc defendendo depugno in acie, vulneror, concidor, occidor. Quis hunc militi suo exitum voluit, nisi qui tali eum sacramento consignavit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It remains to recount the newness of Christianity, because antiquity also had its own sacrament, as if there were another God and therefore a rival discipline whose wisdom does not know how to slaughter its own sons. Clearly in Christ there is another divinity, another will, another school, which has commanded either no martyrdoms at all or martyrdoms understood differently, since it urges no one into such danger, promises nothing to those who suffer for it, because it does not want them to suffer. And so, drawing out the principles of his teachings, he says: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:10-12). This statement applies absolutely to everyone; then specifically to the Apostles themselves: Blessed will you be when they insult you, persecute you, and speak every kind of evil against you on my account; rejoice and be glad, because your reward is very great in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were your fathers (Matthew 5:11-12). This was so that he might also prophesy that they themselves would have to be killed, following the example of the prophets. Although even if he had destined this entire conditional persecution only for the Apostles at that time, he would certainly have looked through them—along with the whole sacrament, the propagation of the name, and the tradition of the Holy Spirit to us—to the discipline of undergoing persecution as well, treating us as heirs of the disciples and fruits of apostolic seed. For again he directs his words to the Apostles: Look, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; and: Beware of men, for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues, and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations (Matthew 10:16-18). But when he adds: A brother will hand over a brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death, he clearly pronounced this wickedness against others, a wickedness we do not find among the Apostles. For none of them suffered a brother or a father as a betrayer, which many of ours have already suffered.

latin: Superest, ne antiquitas suum quoque habuerit sacramentum, novitatem christianam recensere, quasi et de Deo aliam, ac proinde disciplina quoque aemulam, cujus sophia filios suos jugulare non norit. Plane alia in Christo et divinitas et voluntas et schola, martyria aut nulla in totum, aut aliter intelligenda mandarit, qui neminem ad hujusmodi discrimen hortetur, qui pro eo passis nihil repromittat, quia pati eos nolit. Et ideo praeceptorum principia deducens: Beati, inquit, qui persecutionem patiuntur ob justitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Hoc quidem absolute ad omnes, dehinc proprie ad Apostolos ipsos: Beati eritis cum vos dedecoraverint, et persecuti fuerint, et dixerint adversus vos omnia mala propter me; gaudete et exultate, quoniam merces vestra plurima in coelo: sic enim faciebant et prophetis patres eorum. Ut etiam prophetaret quod et ipsi occidi haberent ad exemplum prophetarum. Quanquam et si omnem hanc persecutionem conditionalem in solos tunc Apostolos destinasset, utique per illos cum toto sacramento, cum propagine nominis, cum traduce Spiritus Sancti in nos quoque spectasset etiam persecutionis obeundae disciplina, ut in haereditarios discipulos, et apostolici seminis frutices. Nam et rursus ad Apostolos dirigit: Ecce ego mitto vos tanquam oves in medio luporum; et: Cavete ab hominibus; tradent enim vos in consessus, et in synagogis suis flagellabunt vos, et ad praesides et reges perducemini, mei caussa, in testimonium illis et nationibus, etc. Cum autem subjicit: Tradet autem frater fratrem, et pater filium in mortem, et insurgent filii in parentes, et mortificabunt eos; manifeste iniquitatem istam in caeteros pronuntiavit, quam in Apostolis non invenimus. Nemo enim eorum aut fratrem aut patrem passus est traditorem, quod plerique jam nostri.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — An Address to Demetrianus An Address to Demetrianus
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: I have often held you in contempt, Demetrianus, because you blaspheme the one true God with a sacrilegious mouth and impious words. I judged it more decent and better to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. I did not do this on my own authority, but on that of divine teaching, for it is written: "Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words" (Proverbs 9:7-8), and again: "Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself" (Proverbs 26:4). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, as the Lord says: "Do not give what is holy to dogs; do not throw your pearls to pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces" (Matthew 7:6). You came to me often, more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud voices you insisted on imposing your own views impudently rather than listening to ours patiently. Engaging with you seemed pointless, since it would be easier to calm a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussion. Offering light to the blind, speech to the deaf, or wisdom to a brute is labor in vain and without effect; a brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear. Weighing this, I often kept silent and overcame your impatience with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious by religion, nor calm the raging with gentleness.

But now you claim that many complain of wars breaking out more frequently, of plagues and famines raging, and of long droughts withholding rain — and you blame us because your gods are no longer worshiped. I can no longer stay silent, lest my silence look not like modesty but like diffidence, and lest my refusal to refute false charges seem like an admission of guilt. So I answer you, Demetrianus, and the others you have stirred up with your slanderous voices, sowing hatred against us and gathering a crowd from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reason of our words, for whoever is driven to evil by deceit will be driven even more powerfully to good by compelling truth.

You say these disasters happen through us and should be imputed to us because we do not worship your gods. Since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you must first understand this: the world has grown old. It no longer stands with the strength it once had, nor does it thrive with its former vigor. Even without our testimony from Scripture or divine preaching, the world itself testifies to its own decline. Winter rains no longer nourish the seed abundantly; summer sun no longer ripens the crops with such heat; spring sowings are no longer so joyful; autumn harvests are no longer so rich in fruit. Less marble is quarried from exhausted mountains; less silver and gold are mined, for the veins are spent and dwindle daily. The farmer fails in the field, the sailor at sea, the soldier in camp; innocence fails in the forum, justice in the courts, concord among friends, skill in the arts, discipline in morals. Do you think a thing grown old can retain the substance it had when it was new and flourishing? Whatever nears its end and declines into extreme old age must diminish. The setting sun casts its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; the waning moon shrinks with worn horns; a tree once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed in old age, its branches withering; a spring that once flowed abundantly now barely trickles as its veins fail. This is the sentence given to the world, this is the law of God: all that has arisen will decline, all that has grown will age, the strong will be weakened, the great diminished, and when weakened and diminished, they will end.

You blame Christians for the diminishing of individual things in an aging world. What if the old blamed Christians for their own failing strength — for hearing, running, eyesight, vigor, moisture, and mass not holding as they once did? Human life once exceeded eight or nine hundred years; now it scarcely reaches a hundred. We see gray hair on children; hair falls out before it grows. Age does not end in old age — it begins with it. From its very birth, nativity hastens to its end; whatever is born now degenerates because the world itself is old. No one should wonder that individual things in the world begin to fail when the whole world is already in decline and at its end.
