latin: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.

english: God is so offended by idolatry that He has even commanded the death of anyone who persuades others to sacrifice to and serve idols. Deuteronomy says that if your brother, your son, your daughter, the wife who lies in your bosom, or your friend who is as your own soul secretly urges you, "Let us go and serve other gods, the gods of the nations," you must not consent, you must not listen, your eye must not spare him, and you must not conceal him; instead you shall denounce him. Your hand shall be the first to strike him down, and the hand of all the people shall follow; they shall stone him and he shall die, because he sought to turn you away from the Lord your God (Deuteronomy 13:6-10). The Lord speaks again and declares that no city is to be spared even if the whole city has agreed to idolatry. If you hear in one of the cities the Lord your God gives you to inhabit that its people say, "Let us go and serve other gods" whom you have not known, you shall kill all who are in that city by the sword, burn the city with fire, and leave it a desolation forever; it shall never be rebuilt, so that the Lord may turn from the fierceness of His anger. Then He will grant you mercy, show compassion, and multiply you, provided you obey the voice of the Lord your God and keep His commandments (Deuteronomy 13:12-16). Remembering the force of this command, Mattathias killed the man who approached the altar to sacrifice. If these commandments concerning the worship of God and the rejection of idols were kept before Christ's coming, how much more must they be kept after His coming. For when He came He not only exhorted us by words but also by deeds: after enduring every injury and insult He suffered and was crucified, so that by His example He might teach us to suffer and die, leaving no one an excuse for refusing to suffer, since He suffered for us; and since He suffered for the sins of others, how much more ought each person to suffer for his own sins. Therefore in the Gospel He warns and says: "Whoever confesses Me before men, I also will confess before My Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies Me before men, I also will deny before My Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 10:32-33). Likewise the Apostle Paul declares: "If we endure, we shall also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He also will deny us" (1 Corinthians 15:57-58). Likewise John says: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son has the Son and the Father also" (1 John 2:23). From this the Lord urges and strengthens us to despise death, saying: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). And again: "Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."

In Deuteronomio: Quod si rogaverit te frater tuus, aut filius tuus, aut filia tua, aut uxor tua quae est in sinu tuo, aut amicus tuus, qui aequalis est animae tuae, latenter dicens: « Eamus et serviamus diis aliis, diis gentium; » non consenties ei, et non exaudies eum, et non parcet oculus tuus super eum, et non celabis eum, annuntians annuntiabis de illo. Manus tua erit super eum, in primis interficere eum, et manus omnis populi postremo; et lapidabunt eum et morietur, quoniam quaesivit avertere te a Domino Deo tuo. Et iterum loquitur Dominus et dicit nec civitati parcendum, etiamsi universa consenserit ad idololatriam: Aut si audieris in una ex civitatibus quas Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi inhabitare te illic, dicentes: « Eamus et serviamus diis aliis, » quos non nosti, interficiens necabis omnes qui sunt in civitate caede gladii, et incendes civitatem igni, et erit sine habitaculo in aeternum. Non reaedificabitur etiam nunc, ut avertatur Dominus ab indignatione irae suae. Et dabit tibi misericordiam et miserebitur tui, et multiplicabit te, si exaudieris vocem Domini Dei tui, et observaveris praecepta ejus. Cujus praecepti et vigoris memor Mattathias interfecit eum qui ad aram sacrificaturus accesserat. Quod si ante adventum Christi circa Deum colendum et idola spernenda haec praecepta servata sunt, quanto magis post adventum Christi servanda sunt; quando ille veniens non verbis tantum nos hortatus sit, sed et factis, post omnes injurias et contumelias passus quoque et crucifixus, ut nos pati et mori exemplo suo doceret, ut nulla sit homini excusatio pro se non patienti, cum passus sit ille pro nobis; et cum ille passus sit pro alienis peccatis, multo magis pro peccatis suis pati unumquemque debere? Et ideo in Evangelio comminatur et dicit: Quicumque confessus fuerit me coram hominibus, et ego confitebor eum coram Patre meo, qui in caelis est; qui autem negaverit me coram hominibus, et ego negabo eum coram Patre meo, qui in caelis est. Item Apostolus Paulus: Si enim commorimur, inquit, et convivemus: si toleramus, et conregnabimus: si negabimus, et ipse negabit nos. Item Joannes: Qui negat Filium, neque Patrem habet: qui confitetur Filium, et Filium et Patrem habet. Unde nos ad contemptum mortis hortatur Dominus et corroborat dicens: Nolite timere eos qui occidunt corpus, animam autem non possunt occidere. Magis autem metuite eum qui potest animam et corpus occidere in gehennam. Et iterum: Qui amat animam suam, perdet eam: et qui odit animam suam in isto saeculo, in vitam aeternam conservabit illam.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — On the Advantage of Patience On the Advantage of Patience
excerpts.author: Cyprian
excerpts.work: Treatises — On the Advantage of Patience
english: I am about to speak on patience, most beloved brothers, and to proclaim its benefits. Where better to begin than with the patience you need right now simply to hear me, so that you cannot even receive and learn what you hear without it? A saving message and sound reasoning are truly grasped only when what is said is heard patiently. Among all the paths of heavenly discipline that lead our company toward the divine rewards of hope and faith, I find nothing more useful for life or greater for glory than this: we who rest on the Lord's commands with the obedience of fear and devotion must above all guard patience with complete observance. Philosophers also claim to follow it, but their patience is as false as their wisdom. How can anyone be wise or patient who does not know the wisdom or patience of God? He Himself warns of those who seem wise in the world: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject" (1 Cor 1:19). The blessed apostle Paul, full of the Holy Spirit and sent to call and shape the Gentiles, also testifies and teaches: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Col 2:8–9). And again: "Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God" (1 Cor 3:18–19). For it is written: "He catches the wise in their craftiness" (1 Cor 3:19), and again: "The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile" (1 Cor 3:20). Therefore, if wisdom is not true there, true patience cannot exist either. True wisdom is humility and gentleness; philosophers, however, are neither humble nor gentle. They please themselves, and by pleasing themselves they displease God. Thus true patience cannot be found where there is the audacity of pretended freedom and the shameless boasting of a bared and outstretched chest. But we, most beloved brothers, are philosophers not in words but in deeds. We prefer wisdom not in clothing but in truth. We know the conscience of virtues rather than boasting. We do not speak great things; we live them, as servants and worshipers of God. So let us offer the patience we have learned from heavenly teachings through spiritual obedience. For this virtue is common to us with God. From God patience begins; from God its clarity and dignity take their rise. The origin and greatness of patience proceed from God as its author. What is dear to God must be loved by man; the good that divine majesty loves, it commends. If the Lord is our master and God our Father, let us follow the patience of both Lord and Father alike: for servants must be obedient, and sons must not be degenerate. Consider what kind and how great is the patience of God. He patiently endures the profane temples, earthly idols, and sacrilegious rites that men have set up in contempt of His majesty and honor. Yet He makes the sun rise and the rain fall on the good and the evil alike (Matt 5:45). No one is excluded from His benefits; He lavishes indiscriminate rain on the just and the unjust. We see the inseparable equality of His patience toward the harmful and the innocent, the religious and the impious, the grateful and the ungrateful. At His command the elements serve: winds blow, springs flow, harvests grow, vineyards ripen, trees abound with fruit, groves leaf out, meadows flower. Though God is provoked by frequent, indeed continual, offenses, He tempers His indignation and patiently awaits the appointed day of retribution. Though He holds vengeance in His power, He prefers to prolong patience, bearing and deferring, so that—if it can be—prolonged malice may sometime be changed, and man, wallowing in the contagion of errors and crimes, may turn to God, even if late. He Himself warns and says: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezek 18:23; 33:11). And again: "Return to me, says the Lord" (Jer 3:12; Zech 1:3). And again: "Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and relents over disaster" (Joel 2:13). The blessed apostle Paul also recalls this, calling the sinner to repentance: "Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works" (Rom 2:4–6). He calls God's judgment just because it is late, because it is long deferred, so that God's long patience may serve for man's life. Punishment comes to the impious and the sinner only when repentance can no longer benefit the sin.

latin: DE patientia locuturus, fratres dilectissimi, et utilitates ejus et commoda praedicaturus, unde potius incipiam quam quod nunc quoque ad audientiam vestram patientiam video esse necessariam, ut nec hoc ipsum quod auditis et discitis, sine patientia facere possitis. Tunc enim demum sermo et ratio salutaris efficaciter discitur, si patienter quod dicitur audiatur. Nec invenio, fratres dilectissimi, inter caeteras coelestis disciplinae vias quibus ad consequenda divinitus praemia spei ac fidei nostrae secta dirigitur, quid magis sit vel utilius ad vitam vel majus ad gloriam, quam ut qui praeceptis dominicis obsequio timoris ac devotionis innitimur, patientiam maxime tota observatione tueamur. Hanc se sectari philosophi quoque profitentur. Sed tam illic patientia falsa est, quam et falsa sapientia est. Unde enim vel sapiens esse vel patiens possit qui nec sapientiam nec patientiam Dei novit? quando ipse de his qui sibi sapere in mundo videntur moneat et dicat: Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Item beatus apostolus Paulus, plenus Spiritu sancto et vocandis formandisque Gentibus missus, contestetur et instruat dicens: Videte ne quis vos depraedetur per philosophiam et inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, et non secundum Christum, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo divinitatis. Et alio loco: Nemo se, inquit, decipiat. Si quis se putat sapientem esse in vobis, mundo huic stultus fiat, ut fiat sapiens. Sapientia enim mundi hujus stultitia est apud Deum. Scriptum est enim: Reprehendam sapientes in astutia ipsorum. Et iterum: Cognovit Dominus cogitationes sapientium, quia sunt stultae. Quare, si sapientia illic vera non est, esse non potest et vera patientia. Nam si sapiens ille est qui est humilis et mitis, philosophos autem nec humiles videmus esse nec mites, sed sibi multum placentes, et hoc ipso quod sibi placeant Deo displicentes, apparet illic veram non esse patientiam ubi sit insolens affectatae libertatis audacia et exerti ac seminudi pectoris inverecunda jactantia. Nos autem, fratres dilectissimi, qui philosophi non verbis sed factis sumus, nec vestitu sapientiam, sed veritate praeferimus, qui virtutum conscientiam magis quam jactantiam novimus, qui non loquimur magna sed vivimus, quasi servi et cultores Dei, patientiam quam magisteriis coelestibus discimus obsequiis spiritalibus praebeamus. Est enim nobis cum Deo virtus ista communis. Inde patientia incipit, inde claritas ejus et dignitas caput sumit. Origo et magnitudo patientiae Deo auctore procedit. Diligenda res homini quae Deo chara est: bonum quod amat majestas divina commendat. Si dominus nobis et pater Deus est, sectemur patientiam domini pariter et patris: quia et servos oportet esse obsequentes, et filios non decet esse degeneres. Qualis vero in Deo et quanta patientia, quod, in contumeliam suae majestatis et honoris instituta ab hominibus profana templa et terrena figmenta et sacra sacrilega patientissime sustinens, super bonos et malos aequaliter facit diem nasci et lumen solis oboriri, et cum imbribus terras rigat, nemo a beneficiis ejus excluditur quominus justis similiter et injustis indiscretas pluvias largiatur! Videmus inseparabili aequalitate patientiae nocentibus et innoxiis, religiosis et impiis, gratias agentibus et ingratis, Dei nutu tempora obsequi, elementa famulari, spirare ventos, fontes fluere, grandescere copias messium, fructus maturescere vinearum, exuberare pomis arbusta, nemora frondescere, prata florere. Et cum crebris immo continuis exacerbetur offensis Deus, indignationem suam temperat, et praestitutum semel retributionis diem patienter exspectat. Cumque habeat in potestate vindictam, mavult diu tenere patientiam, sustinens scilicet clementer et differens, ut, si fieri potest, multum malitia protracta aliquando mutetur, et homo in errorum et scelerum contagione volutatus vel sero ad Deum convertatur, ipso monente et dicente: Nolo mortem morientis, quantum ut revertatur et vivat. Et iterum: Revertimini ad me, dicit Dominus. Et iterum: Revertimini ad Dominum Deum vestrum, quoniam misericors et pius et patiens et multae miserationis, et qui sententiam flectat adversus malitias irrogatas. Quod item beatus apostolus Paulus commemorans et peccatorem ad poenitentiam revocans, proponit et dicit: An numquid opulentiam bonitatis ejus et sustinentiam et patientiam contemnis, ignorans quoniam patientia et bonitas Dei ad poenitentiam te adducit? Tu autem, secundum duritiam tuam et cor impoenitens, thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae et revelationis justi judicii Dei, qui reddet unicuique secundum opera sua. Justum judicium Dei dixit esse, quia serum est, quia diu multumque differtur, ut homini ad vitam longa Dei patientia consulatur. Tunc repraesentatur poena impio et peccatori, quando jam non potest poenitentia prodesse peccati.

english: Behold, dearest brothers, peace has returned to the Church, and by God's own aid and vengeance our security has been restored—something that recently seemed impossible to the unbelieving and the faithless. Minds turn back to joy, and now that the storm of oppression has blown over and the cloud has been dispersed, tranquility and serenity shine forth once more. We must give praise to God and celebrate his benefits and gifts with thanksgiving, even though our voice never stopped giving thanks even during the persecution. For the enemy cannot be given so much power that we—who love the Lord with our whole heart and soul and strength—fail to proclaim his blessings and praises always and everywhere with glory. The day that everyone longed for has come, and after the horrible, gloomy darkness of the long night, the world has shone out radiant with the Lord's light. We look upon the confessors with joyful eyes—men renowned for their good name and glorious in the praise of virtue and faith—clinging to them with holy kisses and embracing those we have longed for with an insatiable desire. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers stands here, those who broke the ferocious turbulence of the persecution by their steadfast stand, ready for the endurance of prison, armed for the endurance of death. You resisted the world mightily; you offered a glorious spectacle to God; you became an example for the brothers who follow. A religious voice confessed Christ, in whom it declared it had once believed. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, refused to take part in sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your heads remained free from the impious and wicked veil with which the heads of the captive sacrificers were covered. Your foreheads, marked pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil's crown; they reserved themselves for the Lord's crown. How joyfully mother Church welcomes you, returning from battle! How blessed and rejoicing she opens her gates so that you may enter with gathered ranks, carrying back trophies from the prostrate enemy! Women come alongside the triumphant men—women who, fighting against the world, also conquered their own sex. The virgins come too, bearing the double glory of their warfare, and boys who have spent their years in virtues. The rest of the multitude of the standing follows your glory as well, their insignia of praise so closely joined to yours that they walk in your footsteps. They share the same sincerity of heart, the same integrity of tenacious faith. Rooted in the unshaken roots of the heavenly precepts and strengthened by the evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, the loss of their family property, or the punishments of their bodies. The days were predetermined for the testing of faith. But whoever remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world; nor does he calculate earthly times, since he hopes for eternity from God. No one, dearest brothers, must mutilate this glory; no one must weaken the incorrupt steadfastness of the standing with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those who denied had passed, whoever had not professed within that day confessed that he is a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to be reserved for the Lord by a cautious withdrawal. The former is a public confession, the latter a private one. The former conquers the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, guards a pure conscience with integrity of heart. In the former, fortitude is more prompt; in the latter, solicitude is more secure. The one was found mature when his hour approached; the other was perhaps delayed—he who, having abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he would not deny; he would certainly have confessed if he had also been detained. One sorrow afflicts these heavenly crowns of the martyrs, these spiritual glories of the confessors, these greatest and most excellent virtues of the standing brothers: the violent enemy has thrown down a torn part of our own bowels through the slaughter of his people. What shall I do in this place, dearest brothers? My mind tossed by a varied storm, what shall I say, or how? Tears are needed more than words to express the grief with which the wound of our body must be lamented, and the manifold loss of a once numerous people must be mourned. For who is so hard or iron-hearted, who so forgetful of fraternal charity, that standing amid the manifold ruins and the mournful, squalid remnants of his own people he can keep his eyes dry, and not—immediately bursting into weeping—pour out his groans in tears rather than in voice? I grieve, brothers, I grieve with you; my own integrity and private health do not flatter me into easing my grief, when the shepherd is wounded all the more in the wound of his flock. My heart is joined to each of you; I share the mournful weights of sorrow and funeral. I lament with those who lament, I weep with those who weep, I feel that I lie down with those who lie down. The darts of the raging enemy have struck my members at the same time; the raging swords have passed through my own bowels. The mind could not be immune and free from the onslaught of persecution. In my prostrate brothers, affection has prostrated me as well.

latin: PAX ecce, dilectissimi fratres, Ecclesiae reddita est et, quod difficile nuper incredulis ac perfidis impossibile videbatur, ope atque ultione divina securitas nostra reparata est. In laetitiam mentes redeunt, et, tempestate pressurae ac nube discussa, tranquillitas ac serenitas refulserunt. Dandae laudes Deo, et beneficia ejus ac munera cum gratiarum actione celebranda, quamvis agere gratias nostra vox nec in persecutione cessaverit. Neque enim tantum inimico licere potest ut non, qui Dominum toto corde et anima et virtute diligimus, benedictiones ejus et laudes semper et ubique cum gloria praedicemus. Exoptatus votis omnium dies venit, et, post longae noctis horribilem tetramque caliginem, Domini luce radiatus mundus eluxit. Confessores, praeconio boni nominis claros et virtutis ac fidei laudibus gloriosos, laetis conspectibus intuemur, sanctis osculis adhaerentes, desideratos diu inexplebili cupiditate complectimur. Adest militum Christi cohors candida, qui persecutionis urgentus ferociam turbulentam stabili congressione fregerunt, parati ad patientiam carceris, armati ad tolerantiam mortis. Repugnastis fortiter saeculo, spectaculum gloriosum praebuistis Deo, secuturis fratribus fuistis exemplo. Religiosa vox Christum locuta est, in quem se semel credidisse confessa est. Illustres manus, quae non nisi divinis operibus assueverant, sacrificiis sacrilegis restiterunt. Sanctificata ora coelestibus cibis, post corpus et sanguinem Domini, profana contagia et idolorum reliquias respuerunt. Ab impio sceleratoque velamine, quo illic velabantur sacrificantium capita captiva, caput vestrum liberum mansit. Frons cum signo Dei pura, diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reservavit. Quam vos laete sinu suo excipit mater Ecclesia de praelio revertentes! quam beata, quam gaudens portas suas aperit, ut adunatis agminibus intretis, de hoste prostrato trophaea referentes! Cum triumphantibus viris et feminae veniunt, quae cum saeculo dimicantes, sexum quoque vicerunt. Veniunt et geminata militiae suae gloria virgines, et pueri annos suos virtutibus transeuntes. Necnon et caetera stantium multitudo vestram gloriam sequitur, proximis et pene conjunctis laudis insignibus vestigia vestra comitatur. Eadem et in illis sinceritas cordis, eadem fidei tenacis integritas. Inconcussis praeceptorum coelestium radicibus nixos et evangelicis traditionibus roboratos, non praescripta exilia, non destinata tormenta, non rei familiaris damna, non corporis supplicia terruerunt. Explorandae fidei praefiniebantur dies. Sed qui saeculo renuntiasse se meminit, nullum saeculi diem novit; nec tempora terrena jam computat qui aeternitatem de Deo sperat. Nemo, fratres dilectissimi, nemo hanc gloriam mutilet, nemo incorruptam stantium firmitatem maligna obtrectatione debilitet. Cum dies negantibus praestitutus excessit, quisquis professus intra diem non est, Christianum se esse confessus est. Primus est victoriae titulus, gentilium manibus apprehensum Dominum confiteri: secundus ad gloriam gradus est cauta secessione subtractum Domino reservari. Illa publica, haec privata confessio est. Ille judicem saeculi vincit, hic contentus Deo suo judice conscientiam puram cordis integritate custodit. Illic, fortitudo promptior, hic sollicitudo securior. Ille appropinquante hora sua, jam maturus inventus est; hic fortasse dilatus est qui, patrimonio derelicto, idcirco secessit quia non erat negaturus: confiteretur utique si fuisset et ipse detentus. Has martyrum coelestes coronas, has confessorum glorias spiritales, has stantium fratrum maximas eximiasque virtutes moestitia una contristat, quod avulsam nostrorum viscerum partem violentus inimicus populationis suae strage dejecit. Quid hoc loco faciam, dilectissimi fratres? fluctuans vario mentis aestu, quid aut quomodo dicam? Lacrymis magis quam verbis opus est ad exprimendum dolorem quo corporis nostri plaga deflenda est, quo populi aliquando numerosi multiplex lamentanda jactura est. Quis enim sic durus aut ferreus, quis sic fraternae charitatis oblitus, qui inter suorum multiformes ruinas et lugubres ac multo squalore deformes reliquias constitutus siccos oculos tenere praevaleat, nec, erumpente statim fletu, prius gemitus suos lacrymis quam voce depromat? Doleo, fratres, doleo vobiscum, nec mihi ad leniendos dolores meos integritas propria et sanitas privata blanditur, quando plus pastor in gregis sui vulnere vulneretur. Cum singulis pectus meum copulo, moeroris et funeris pondera luctuosa participo. Cum plangentibus plango, cum deflentibus defleo, cum jacentibus jacere me credo. Jaculis illis grassantis inimici mea simul membra percussa sunt, saevientes gladii per mea viscera transierunt. Immunis et liber a persecutionis incursu fuisse non potest animus. In prostratis fratribus et me prostravit affectus.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Although many of you, beloved brothers, have a steadfast mind, a firm faith, and a devoted soul—one that the present onslaught of mortality does not shake, but rather, like a strong and stable rock, breaks the world's turbulent assaults and the age's violent waves without being broken itself, and is not conquered by temptations but proven by them—nevertheless, I see among the common people some who stand less firmly, whether from weakness of mind, smallness of faith, the sweetness of worldly life, softness of sex, or, what is worse, error about the truth, and who do not exercise the divine and invincible strength of their hearts. This matter could not be concealed or passed over in silence, so that, as far as my mediocrity allows, with full vigor and a sermon drawn from the Lord's reading, the laziness of a delicate mind may be suppressed, and whoever has begun to be a man of God and of Christ may be deemed worthy of God and of Christ. For he must recognize, beloved brothers, that the one who serves God, who is stationed in the heavenly camp and already hopes for divine things, should feel no trepidation, no disturbance, when the Lord, with the exhortation of a provident voice—instructing, teaching, preparing, and strengthening his Church's people for all endurance of future things—foretold and declared that wars, fires, earthquakes, and pestilences would arise in various places (Luke 21:31). And lest an unexpected and new fear of threatening things disturb us, he warned beforehand that adversities would increase more and more in the last times. Behold, the things that were said are happening; and when the things predicted beforehand come to pass, the things promised will also follow, the Lord himself promising and saying: "When you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near." The kingdom of God, beloved brothers, has begun to draw near. The reward of life and the joy of eternal salvation, and perpetual security, and the possession of paradise, recently lost, are now coming as the world passes away; now heavenly things and great things succeed earthly and small and transitory things. What room is there here for anxiety and worry? Who is disturbed and sad amid these things, except the one who lacks hope and faith? For it belongs to the one who fears death to be unwilling to go to Christ. It belongs to the one unwilling to go to Christ to not believe that he will begin to reign with Christ. For it is written: "The just shall live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). If you are just and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why do you not, secure in the Lord's promise, embrace the future with Christ, and rejoice that you are called to Christ and freed from the devil? Finally, Simeon, that just man, who was truly just, who kept God's commandments with full faith—when he had received a divine answer that he would not die before seeing Christ, and Christ came to the temple as an infant with his mother, he recognized in the Spirit that Christ had already been born, the one foretold to him beforehand; and when he saw him, he knew he would soon die. So, rejoicing in his approaching death and secure in his near summons, he took the child in his hands, and blessing the Lord, exclaimed and said: "Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation"; proving and testifying that peace belongs to God's servants, then freedom, then tranquil rest, when, extracted from the world's turbulences, we seek the harbor of eternal security, when, having finished this death, we come to immortality. For that is the true peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable and firm and perpetual security. But what else is there in the world except a daily battle against the devil, a constant conflict against his darts and arrows? We face confrontation with avarice, impudicity, anger, ambition; we wage a constant and troublesome struggle with carnal vices and worldly allurements. The human mind, besieged and hemmed in on all sides by the devil's infestation, can hardly meet or resist individual attacks. If avarice is prostrated, lust rises up; if lust is compressed, ambition succeeds; if ambition is despised, anger exasperates, pride inflates, drunkenness invites, envy breaks concord, and zeal cuts off friendship. You will be forced to curse what divine law prohibits, compelled to swear what is not allowed.

latin: Etsi apud plurimos vestrum, fratres dilectissimi, mens solida est et fides firma et anima devota, quae ad praesentis mortalitatis copiam non movetur, sed tamquam petra fortis et stabilis turbidos impetus mundi et violentos saeculi fluctus frangit potius ipsa nec frangitur, et tentationibus non vincitur, sed probatur, tamen quia animadverto in plebe quosdam vel imbecillitate animi, vel fidei parvitate, vel dulcedine saecularis vitae, vel sexus mollitie, vel, quod majus est, veritatis errore minus stare fortiter nec pectoris sui divinum atque invictum robur exercere, dissimulanda res non fuit nec tacenda quo minus quantum nostra mediocritas sufficit, vigore pleno et sermone de dominica lectione concepto delicatae mentis ignavia comprimatur, et qui homo Dei et Christi esse jam coepit, Deo et Christo dignus habeatur. Agnoscere enim se debet, fratres dilectissimi, qui Deo militat, qui positus in coelestibus castris divinam jam sperat, ut ad procellas et turbines mundi trepidatio nulla sit in nobis, nulla turbatio, quando haec ventura praedixerit Dominus providae vocis hortatu instruens et docens et praeparans atque corroborans Ecclesiae suae populum ad omnem tolerantiam futurorum, bella et fumes et terrae motus et pestilentias per loca singula exsurgere praenuntiavit et cecinit. Et ne inopinatus nos et novus rerum infestantium metus quateret, magis ac magis in novissimis temporibus adversa crebrescere ante praemonuit. Fiunt ecce quae dicta sunt; et quando fiunt quae ante praedicta sunt, sequentur et quaecumque promissa sunt, Domino ipso pollicente et dicente: Cum autem videritis haec omnia fieri, scitote quoniam in proximo est regnum Dei.. Regnum Dei, fratres dilectissimi, esse coepit in proximo. Praemium vitae et gaudium salutis aeternae, et perpetua securitas, et possessio paradisi nuper amissa, mundo transeunte jam veniunt; jam terrenis coelestia et magna parvis et caducis aeterna succedunt. Quis hic anxietatis et sollicitudinis locus est? Quis inter haec trepidus et moestus est, nisi cui spes et fides deest? Ejus est enim mortem timere qui ad Christum nolit ire. Ejus est ad Christum nolle ire qui se non credat cum Christo incipere regnare. Scriptum est enim justum fide vivere. Si justus es, et fide vivis, si vere in Christum credis, cur non cum Christo futurus et de Domini pollicitatione securus quod ad Christum voceris amplecteris, et quod diabolo careas gratularis. Simeon denique ille justus, qui vere justus fuit, qui fide plena Dei praecepta servavit, dum ei divinitus responsum fuisset quod non ante moreretur quam Christum vidisset, et Christus infans in templum cum matre venisset, agnovit in Spiritu natum esse jam Christum, de quo sibi fuerat ante praedictum; quo viso, scivit se cito esse moriturum. Laetus itaque de morte jam proxima, et de vicina accersitione securus, accepit in manus puerum, et benedicens Dominum exclamavit et dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secuudum verbum tuum in pace, quoniam viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum; probans scilicet atque contestans tunc esse servis Dei pacem, tunc liberam, tunc tranquillam quietem, quando, de istis mundi turbinibus extracti, sedis et securitatis aeternae portum petimus, quando expuncta hac morte ad immortalitatem venimus. Illa est enim vera pax, illa fida tranquillitas, illa stabilis et firma et perpetua securitas. Caeterum, quid aliud in mundo, quam pugna adversus diabolum, quotidie geritur, quam adversus jacula ejus et tela conflictationibus assiduis dimicatur? Cum avaritia nobis, cum impudicitia, cum ira, cum ambitione congressio est, cum carnalibus vitiis, cum illecebris saecularibus assidua et molesta luctatio est. Obsessa mens hominis et undique diaboli infestatatione vallata vix occurrit singulis, vix resistit. Si avaritia prostrata est, exsurgit libido: si libido compressa est, succedit ambitio: si ambitio contempta est, ira exasperat, inflat superbia, vinolentia invitat, invidia concordiam rumpit, amicitiam zelus abscindit. Cogeris maledicere quod divina lex prohibet, compelleris jurare quod non licet.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
excerpts.work: Treatises — On the Unity of the Church
excerpts.locus: On the Unity of the Church
english: When the Lord warns us and says, "You are the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13), and commands us to be simple in innocence yet prudent with that simplicity, what else should we do, beloved brothers, but take care? With watchful, anxious hearts we must discern and guard against the cunning enemy's hidden plots, lest we who have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, appear less wise in protecting our own salvation. It is not only open persecution we must fear, the kind that attacks and overthrows God's servants openly. Caution comes easily when danger is plain, and the mind readies itself for battle when the adversary shows himself. The enemy is far more dangerous and to be avoided when he creeps in secretly, deceiving under the guise of peace and slipping in by hidden approaches; that is why he is called the serpent. This has always been his cunning, his blind and concealed deceit in circumventing humanity. From the very beginning of the world he deceived, flattering with lying words and trapping simple souls through their unsuspecting credulity. He even attempted to tempt the Lord Himself, approaching secretly as if to creep in and deceive again. But he was recognized and repelled, and so he fell prostrate because he was detected. From this we are given an example: we must flee the way of the old man and walk in the footsteps of the living Christ, so that we do not fall unawares once more into the snare of death, but, foreseeing the danger, may take hold of immortality. And how can we possess immortality unless we keep the commandments of Christ, by which death is overcome and conquered? He Himself warns and says: "If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments" (Matt 19:17). And again: "If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends" (John 15:14). These He calls strong and stable, founded on a massive rock, solidified with immovable and unshakable firmness against all the tempests and whirlwinds of the age. "Whoever hears my words and does them," He says, "I will compare him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock" (Matt 7:24-25). Therefore we must stand firm on His words, and learn to do everything He taught and commanded. But how can someone believe he is in Christ if he does not do what Christ commanded? Or how will he reach the reward of faith if he refuses to keep the faith of the commandment? Such a person must waver and wander, seized by a spirit of error and blown about like dust before the wind; he will make no progress toward salvation, because he does not hold to the truth of the saving way. Yet, beloved brothers, we must beware not only of what is open and manifest, but also of what deceives through the subtle cunning of fraud. What could be more cunning or subtle than this: the enemy, detected and prostrated by the advent of Christ, after the light came to the Gentiles and the saving light shone for humanity so that the deaf might receive the hearing of spiritual grace, the blind open their eyes to God, the weak recover through eternal health, the lame run to the Church, and the mute pray with clear voices, seeing that idols were abandoned and his seats and temples deserted by the multitude of believers, he devises a new deceit to trap the unwary under the very title of the Christian name? He invents heresies and schisms to subvert the faith, corrupt the truth, and divide the unity. Those he cannot hold in the blindness of the old way, he ensnares through the error of a new way. He snatches men from the very Church; and while they think they have approached the light and escaped the night of the world, he pours in another darkness, unknown to them, so that, not standing with the Gospel of Christ and His observance and law, they call themselves Christians, and walking in darkness, imagine they have the light. The adversary flatters and deceives, transforming himself, as the Apostle says, into an angel of light, and his ministers into ministers of righteousness (2 Cor 11:14-15), calling night day, destruction salvation, despair under the pretext of hope, perfidy under the pretext of faith, antichrist under the name of Christ, so that by speaking plausible things they may frustrate the truth through subtlety. This happens, beloved brothers, when we do not return to the origin of truth, nor seek the head, nor keep the doctrine of the heavenly Master. If anyone considers and examines this, there is no need for lengthy discussion or arguments. The proof is easy, a compendium of truth. The Lord speaks to Peter: "I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matt 16:18-19). And again, after His resurrection, He says to him: "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17). He builds His Church on him alone, and commands him to feed His sheep. And although He grants equal power to all the Apostles after His resurrection, saying, "As the Father has sent me, even so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained" (John 20:21-23), yet, to manifest unity, He establishes one chair, and by His authority arranges the origin of that unity to proceed from one. The other Apostles were indeed what Peter was, endowed with equal partnership of honor and power, but the beginning proceeds from unity, and primacy is given to Peter, so that one Church of Christ and one chair may be shown. And all are shepherds, and one flock is shown, which is fed by all the Apostles with unanimous consent, so that the one Church of Christ may be shown. The Holy Spirit also designates this one Church in the Song of Songs, speaking in the person of the Lord: "My dove is one, my perfect one, she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her" (Song 6:9). Who does not hold this unity of the Church believes he holds the faith? Who resists and opposes the Church, who deserts the chair of Peter on which the Church is founded, trusts that he is in the Church? Especially when the blessed Apostle Paul teaches this same thing and displays the sacrament of unity, saying: "One body and one Spirit, one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God" (Eph 4:4-6).

latin: CUM moneat Dominus et dicat: Vos estis sal terrae, cumque esse nos jubeat ad innocentiam simplices, et tamen cum simplicitate prudentes, quid aliud, fratres dilectissimi, quam providere nos convenit, et sollicito corde vigilantes, subdoli hostis insidias intelligere pariter et cavere ne qui Christum sapientiam Dei Patris induimus, minus sapere in tuenda salute videamur? Neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est et ea quae subruendis ac dejiciendis Dei servis aperta impugnatione grassantur. Facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est, et ad certamen animus ante praestruitur quando se adversarius confitetur. Plus metuendus est et cavendus inimicus cum latenter obrepit, cum, per pacis imaginem fallens, occultis accessibus serpit; unde et nomen serpentis accepit. Ea est ejus semper astutia, ea est circumveniendi hominis caeca et latebrosa fallacia. Sic ab initio statim mundi fefellit, et, verbis mendacibus blandiens, rudes animas incauta credulitate decepit. Dominum ipsum tentare conatus, quasi obreperet rursus et falleret, latenter accessit. Intellectus tamen est et retusus; et ideo prostratus, quia agnitus atque detectus. Unde nobis exemplum datum est veteris hominis viam fugere, vestigiis Christi viventis insistere; ne denuo incauti in mortis laqueum revolvamur, sed, ad periculum providi, accepta immortalitate potiamur. Immortalitate autem potiri quomodo possumus, nisi ea quibus mors expugnatur et vincitur, Christi mandata servemus, ipso monente et dicente: Si vis ad vitam venire, serva mandata. Et iterum: Si feceritis quae mando vobis, jam non dico vos servos, sed amicos. Hos denique fortes dicit et stabiles, hos super petram robusta mole fundatos, hos contra omnes tempestates et turbines saeculi immobili et inconcussa firmitate solidatos. Qui audit, inquit, verba mea et facit ea, similabo eum viro sapienti qui aedificavit domum suam supra petram. Descendit pluvia, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti et impegerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit; fundata enim fuit super petram. Verbis igitur ejus insistere, quaecumque et docuit et fecit discere et facere debemus. Caeterum credere se in Christum, quomodo dicit qui non facit quod Christus facere praecepit? Aut unde perveniet ad praemium fidei, qui fidem non vult servare mandati? Nutet necesse est et vagetur, et, spiritu erroris abreptus, velut pulvis quem ventus excutit ventiletur; nec ambulando proficiet ad salutem, qui salutaris viae non tenet veritatem. Cavenda sunt autem, fratres dilectissimi, non solum quae sunt aperta atque manifesta, sed et astutae fraudis subtilitate fallentia. Quid vero astutius, quidve subtilius, quam ut Christi adventu detectus ac prostratus inimicus, postquam lux Gentibus venit et sospitandis hominibus salutare lumen effulsit, ut surdi auditum gratiae spiritalis admitterent, aperirent ad Deum oculos suos caeci, infirmi aeterna sanitate revalescerent, claudi ad Ecclesiam currerent, muti claris vocibus et precibus orarent, videns ille idola derelicta et per nimium credentium populum sedes suas ac templa deserta, excogitaverit novam fraudem, ut sub ipso christiani nominis titulo fallat incautos? Haereses invenit et schismata, quibus subverteret fidem, veritatem corrumperet, scinderet unitatem. Quos detinere non potest in viae veteris caecitate, circumscribit et decipit novi itineris errore. Rapit de ipsa Ecclesia homines; et, dum sibi appropinquasse jam lumini atque evasisse saeculi noctem videntur, alias nescientibus tenebras rursus infundit, ut cum Evangelio Christi et cum observatione ejus et lege non stantes, Christianos se vocent, et ambulantes in tenebris habere se lumen existiment, blandiente adversario atque fallente, qui, secundum Apostoli vocem, transfigurat se velut angelum lucis, et ministros suos subornat velut ministros justitiae, asserentes noctem pro die, interitum pro salute, desperationem sub obtentu spei, perfidiam sub praetextu fidei, antichristum sub vocabulo Christi; ut, dum verisimilia mentiuntur, veritatem subtilitate frustrentur. Hoc eo fit, fratres dilectissimi, dum ad veritatis originem non reditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri coelestis doctrina servatur. Quae si quis consideret et examinet, tractatu longo atque argumentis opus non est. Probatio est ad fidem facilis compendio veritatis. Loquitur Dominus ad Petrum: Ego tibi dico, inquit, quia tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, et portae inferorum non vincent eam. Et tibi dabo claves regni coelorum: et quae ligaveris super terram, erunt ligata et in coelis; et quaecumque solveris super terram, erunt soluta et in coelis. Et iterum eidem post resurrectionem suam dicit: Pasce oves meas. Super illum unum aedificat Ecclesiam suam, et illi pascendas mandat oves suas. Et quamvis Apostolis omnibus post resurrectionem suam parem potestatem tribuat et dicat, Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos: accipite Spiritum sanctum; si cujus remiseritis peccata, remittentur illi, si cujus tenueritis, tenebuntur, tamen, ut unitatem manifestaret, unam cathedram constituit, unitatis ejusdem originem ab uno incipientem sua auctoritate disposuit. Hoc erant utique et caeteri Apostoli quod fuit Petrus, pari consortio praediti et honoris et potestatis, sed exordium ab unitate proficiscitur, et primatus Petro datur, ut una Christi Ecclesia et cathedra una monstretur. Et pastores sunt omnes, et grex unus ostenditur, qui ab Apostolis omnibus unanimi consensione pascatur, ut Ecclesia Christi una monstretur. Quam unam Ecclesiam etiam in Cantico canticorum Spiritus sanctus ex persona Domini designat et dicit: Una est columba mea, perfecta mea, una est matri suae, electa genitrici suae. Hanc Ecclesiae unitiatem qui non tenet, tenere se fidem credit? Qui Ecclesiae renititur et resistit, qui cathedram Petri, super quem fundata est Ecclesia, deserit, in Ecclesia se esse confidit? quando et beatus apostolus Paulus hoc idem doceat et sacramentum unitatis ostendat dicens: Unum corpus et unus spiritus, una spes vocationis vestrae, unus Dominus, una fides, unum Baptisma, unus Deus.

english: In this period, Polycarp met his end through martyrdom when the fiercest persecutions yet erupted throughout Asia, and I consider it essential to record his most necessary death in writing, preserving it within the memory of this history. The document comes from the church he himself led, addressed to the neighboring congregations to inform them of what happened to him. It reads: "The church of God dwelling in Smyrna sends greetings to the church of God dwelling in Philomelium and to all the churches in every place of the holy catholic church: may mercy, peace, and love from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be multiplied to you. We have written to you, brothers, about those who were martyred and about the blessed Polycarp, who by his martyrdom, as if sealing it with a seal, brought the persecution to an end." Before launching into the narrative about Polycarp, the account first describes the other martyrs and the endurance they displayed amid their sufferings. The writer says that onlookers stood amazed as they watched the martyrs being scourged until even their innermost veins and arteries were laid bare, so that the very organs and limbs hidden deep within their bodies were exposed. At times the victims were forced onto sharp stakes and pointed rods, and they were subjected to every kind of punishment and torture before finally being thrown to the beasts for food. The narrative especially highlights the noble Germanicus, who, strengthened by divine grace, overcame the natural fear of death that belongs to the body.

greek: ἐν τούτῳ δὲ ὁ Πολύκαρπος μεγίστων τὴν Ἀσίαν ἀναθορυβησάντων διωγμῶν μαρτυρίῳ τελειοῦται, ἄναγκαιότατον δ᾿ αὐτοῦ τὸ τέλος ἐγγράφως ἔτι φερόφερόμενον ἡγοῦμαι δεῖν μνήμῃ τῆσδε τῆς ἱστορίας καταθέσθαι. ἔστιν δὲ ἡ γραφὴ ἐκ προσώπου ἦς αὐτὸς ἐκκλησίας ἡγεῖτο, ταῖς κατὰ τόπον παροικίαις τὰ κατ’ αὐτὸν ἀποσημαίνουσα διὰ τούτων· “ ῾Η ἐκκλησία τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ παροικοῦσα Σμύρναν τῆ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ τῆ παροικούσῃ ἐν Φιλομηλίῳ καὶ πάσαις ταῖς κατὰ πάντα τόπον τῆς ἁγίας καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας παροικίαις ἔλεος εἰρήνη καὶ ἀγάπη θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ κυρίου ἡμῶν ’Ιησοῦ Χριστοῦ πληθυνθείη. ἐγράψαμεν ὑμῖν, ἀδελφοί, τὰ κατὰ τοὺς μαρτυρήσαντας καὶ τὸν μακάριον Πολύκαρπον, ὅστις ὥσπερ ἐπισφραγίσας διὰ τῆς μαρτυρίας αὐτοῦ κατέπαυσε τὸν διωγμόν.’’ Τούτοις τούτοις ἑξῆς πρὸ τῆς ἀμφὶ τοῦ Πολυκάρπου διηγήσεως τὰ κατὰ τοὺς λοιποὺς ἀνιστοροῦσι μάρτυρας, οἵας ἐνστάσεις πρὸς τὰς ἀλγηδόνας ἐνεδείξαντο, διαγράφοντες. καταπλῆξαι γάρ φασι τοὺς ἐν κύκλῳ περιεστῶτας , θεωμένους τοτὲ μὲν μάστιξι μέχρι καὶ τῶν ἐνδοτάτω φλεβῶν καὶ ἀρτηριῶν καταξαινομένους, ὡς ἤδη καὶ τὰ ἐν μυχοῖς ἀπόρρητα τοῦ σώματος σπλάγχνα τε αὐτῶν καὶ μέλη κατοπτεύεσθαι, τοτὲ δὲ τοὺς ἀπὸ θαλάττης κήρυκας καί τινας ὀξεῖς ὀβελίσκους ὑποστρωννυμένους, καὶ διὰ παντὸς εἴδους κολάσεων καὶ βασάνων προιόντας καὶ τέλος θηραὶν εἰς βορὰν παραδιδομένους . μάλιστα δὲ ἱστοροῦσιν διαπρέψαι τὸν γενναιότατον Γερμανικόν, ὑπορρωννύντα σὺν θείᾳ χάριτι τὴν ἔμφυτον περὶ τὸν θάνατον τοῦ σώματος δειλίαν.

english: A woman once lived with a licentious husband, and she herself had formerly been licentious as well. When she learned the teachings of Christ, she became self-controlled and tried to persuade her husband to practice the same self-control, citing those teachings and warning him of the eternal fire awaiting those who live without self-control and right reason. He, however, persisted in the same licentiousness and, through his actions, made his wife a stranger to him. Since she considered it impious to continue sharing a bed with a husband who, contrary to the law of nature and what is right, sought to make pleasure from every possible source, she wanted to separate from the marriage. When her own people urged her to wait longer, advising that her husband might yet change, she forced herself to endure. But when it was reported that her husband, after going to Alexandria, was committing even worse acts, she gave him the divorce paper — what you call a *repudium* — and separated, so that she would not become a partner in his injustices and impieties by remaining in the marriage and sharing bed and board.

Her excellent husband — who should have been glad that she had stopped the deeds she once easily committed with servants and hired workers, indulging in drunkenness and every evil, and that she wanted him to stop doing the same — brought a charge against her, saying she was a Christian. She presented a petition to you, Emperor, asking first to be allowed to manage her own affairs and then to make her defense concerning the charge after that management was complete; you granted this request. Her husband, no longer able to confront her directly, turned to a certain Ptolemy, whom Urbicus had summoned, and who had become her teacher in the Christian doctrines. He had a centurion throw Ptolemy, his own friend, into prison, then persuaded the centurion to take Ptolemy and ask him only this: whether he was a Christian. Ptolemy, a lover of truth but neither deceitful nor a liar, confessed that he was a Christian; the centurion put him in chains and punished him for a long time in prison. Finally, when Ptolemy was brought before Urbicus, he was examined on that one point alone: whether he was a Christian. Again, knowing the good things in himself through the teaching from Christ, he confessed the teaching of divine virtue. For anyone who denies or condemns anything becomes a renouncer, or considers himself unworthy and alien to the matter and flees from the confession — neither of which belongs to the true Christian.

When Urbicus ordered him to be led away, a certain Lucius, also a Christian, seeing the unreasonable judgment, said to Urbicus: "What is the reason that this man, who has been convicted of neither adultery nor prostitution nor murder nor theft nor robbery nor any injustice, but has only confessed to the name of Christian, has been punished? You are not judging, Urbicus, in a manner fitting for a pious emperor, or a philosophical son of Caesar, or a sacred council." Urbicus answered nothing else but said to Lucius: "You seem to me to be the same kind." Lucius replied: "Certainly." And again Urbicus ordered him to be led away. Lucius confessed with gratitude, knowing that he had escaped evil masters of that sort and was going to the Father and King of the heavens. And another, a third, came forward and was deemed worthy of punishment.

greek: Γυνή τις συνεβίου ἀνδρὶ ἀκολασταίνοντι, ἀκολασταίνουσα καὶ αὐτὴ πρότερον. Ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγματα ἔγνω, αὐτὴ ἐσωφρονίσθη καὶ τὸν ἄνδρα ὁμοίως σωφρονεῖν πείθειν ἐπειρᾶτο, τὰ διδάγματα ἀναφέρουσα, τήν τε μέλλουσαν τοῖς οὐ σωφρόνως καὶ μετὰ λόγου ὀρθοῦ βιοῦσιν ἔσεσθαι ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ κόλασιν ἀπαγγέλλουσα. Ὁ δὲ ταῖς αὐταῖς ἀσελγείαις ἐπιμένων ἀλλοτρίαν διὰ τῶν πράξεων ἐποιεῖτο τὴν γαμετήν. Ἀσεβὲς γὰρ ἡγουμένη τὸ λοιπὸν ἡ γυνὴ συγκατακλίνεσθαι ἀνδρί, παρὰ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον καὶ παρὰ τὸ δίκαιον πόρους ἡδονῆς ἐκ παντὸς πειρωμένῳ ποιεῖσθαι, τῆς συζυγίας χωρισθῆναι ἐβουλήθη. Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων, ὡς εῖς ἐλπίδα μεταβολῆς ἥξοντός ποτε τοῦ ἀνδρός, βιαζομένη ἑαυτὴν ἐπέμενεν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ ταύτης ἀνὴρ εἰς τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν πορευθεὶς χαλεπώτερα πράττειν ἀπηγγέλθη, ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδικημάτων καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται μένουσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁμοδίαιτος καὶ ὁμόκοιτος γινομένη, τὸ λεγόμενον παρ᾿ ὑμῖν ῥεπούδιον δοῦσα ἐχωρίσθη. Ὁ δὲ καλὸς κἀγαθὸς ταύτης ἀνήρ, δέον αὐτὸν χαίρειν, ὅτι, ἃ πάλαι μετὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν καὶ τῶν μισθοφόρων εὐχερῶς ἔπραττε, μέθαις χαίρουσα καὶ κακίᾳ πάσῃ, τούτων μὲν τῶν πράξεων πέπαυτο καὶ αὐτὸν τὰ αὐτὰ παύσασθαι πράττοντα ἐβούλετο, μὴ βουλομένου ἀπαλλαγείσης κατηγορίαν πεποίηται, λέγων αὐτὴν Χριστιανὴν εἶναι. Καὶ ἡ μὲν βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε, πρότερον συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῇ διοικήσασθαι τὰ ἑαυτῆς ἀξιοῦσα, ἔπειτα ἀπολογήσασθαι περὶ τοῦ κατηγορήματος μετὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῆς διοίκησιν, καὶ συνεχώρησας τοῦτο. Ὁ δὲ ταύτης ποτὲ ἀνήρ, πρὸς ἐκείνην μὲν μὴ δυνάμενος τανῦν ἔτι λέγειν, πρὸς Πτολεμαῖόν τινα, ὃν Οὔρβικος ἐκαλέσατο, διδάσκαλον ἐκείνης τῶν Χριστιανῶν μαθημάτων γενόμενον ἐτράπετο διὰ τοῦδε τοῦ τρόπου. Ἑκατόνταρχον εἰς δεσμὰ ἐμβαλόντα τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φίλον αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντα, ἔπεισε λαβέσθαι τοῦ Πτολεμαίου καὶ ἀνερωτῆσαι, εἰ, αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον, Χριστιανός ἐστι. Καὶ τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φιλαλήθη ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπατηλὸν οὐδὲ ψευδολόγον τὴν γνώμην ὄντα, ὁμολογήσαντα ἑαυτὸν εἶναι Χριστιανόν, ἐν δεσμοῖς γενέσθαι ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος πεποίηκε, καὶ ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ ἐκολάσατο. Τελευταῖον δέ, ὅτε ἐπὶ Οὔρβικον ἤχθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁμοίως αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον ἐξητάσθη, εἰ εἴη Χριστιανός. Καὶ πάλιν, τὰ καλὰ ἑαυτῷ συνεπιστάμενος διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδαχήν, τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν. Ὁ γὰρ ἀρνούμενος ὁτιοῦν ἢ κατεγνωκὼς τοῦ πράγματος ἔξαρνος γίνεται, ἢ ἑαυτὸν ἀνάξιον ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀλλότριον τοῦ πράγματος τὴν ὁμολογίαν φεύγει· ὦν οὐδὲν πρόσεστι τῷ ἀληθινῷ Χριστιανῷ. Καὶ τοῦ Οὐρβίκου κελεύσαντος αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι, Λούκιός τις, καὶ αὐτὸς ὢν Χριστιανός, ὁρῶν τὴν ἀλόγως οὕτω γενομένην κρίσιν, πρὸς τὸν Οὔρβικον ἔφη· Τίς ἡ αἰτία, τοῦ μήτε μοιχὸν μήτε πόρνον μήτε ἀνδροφόνον μήτε λωποδύτην μήτε ἅρπαγα μήτε ἁπλῶς ἀδίκημά τι πράξαντα ἐλεγχόμενον, ὀνόματος δὲ Χριστιανοῦ προσωνυμίαν ὁμολογοῦντα τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον ἐκολάσω; Οὐ πρέποντα Εὐσεβεῖ αὐτοκράτορι οὐδὲ φιλοσόφῳ Καίσαρος παιδὶ οὐδὲ τῇ ἱερᾷ συγκλήτῳ κρίνεις, ὦ Οὔρβικε. Καὶ ὃς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἀποκρινάμενος καὶ πρὸς τὸν Λούκιον ἔφη· Δοκεῖς μοι καὶ σὺ εἶναι τοιοῦτος. Καὶ τοῦ Λουκίου φήσαντος· Μάλιστα, πάλιν καὶ αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι ἐκέλευσεν. Ὁ δὲ καὶ χάριν εἰδέναι ὡμολόγει, πονηρῶν δεσποτῶν τῶν τοιούτων ἀπηλλάχθαι γινώσκων καὶ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα τῶν οὐρανῶν πορεύεσθαι. Καὶ ἄλλος δὲ τρίτος ἐπελθὼν κολασθῆναι προσετιμήθη.

excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: If you judge this to rest on reason and truth, honor it; but if it strikes you as nonsense, treat it as the worthless thing it is — despise it as such. Do not sentence to death people who have done no wrong, as though they were enemies. We warn you: you will not escape the coming judgment of God if you persist in injustice, and we will cry out against it — let what is dear to God be done! We also hold a letter from the greatest and most illustrious Caesar Hadrian, your father. We invoke it to demand that you order fair trials, just as we requested — not because we asked Hadrian to decree this, but because we know our petition and explanation are just. We have also submitted a copy of Hadrian's letter so that you may know we speak the truth in this matter as well. Here is that copy: To Minucius Fundanus. I received a letter written to me by Serenius Granianus, a most illustrious man, whom you succeeded. It does not seem right to me to leave the matter uninvestigated, lest people be disturbed and informers be given a handle for wickedness. If the provincials can clearly accuse the Christians, as if answering before a court, let them proceed only with that — not with mere cries or petitions. For it is far more proper, if someone wishes to accuse, for you to investigate the charge. If someone accuses and proves they are doing something contrary to the laws, judge accordingly, in proportion to the offense. But if someone brings the charge for the sake of calumny, take the gravity of it to heart and see to it that you avenge it.

greek: Καὶ εἰ μὲν δοκεῖ ὑμῖν λόγου καὶ ἀληθείας ἔχεσθαι, τιμήσατε αὐτά· εἰ δὲ λῆρος ὑμῖν δοκεῖ, ὡς ληρωδῶν πραγμάτων καταφρονήσατε, καὶ μὴ ὡς κατ᾿ ἐχθρῶν κατὰ τῶν μηδὲν ἀδικούντων θάνατον ὁρίζετε. Προλέγομεν γὰρ ὑμῖν, ὅτι οὐκ ἐκφεύξεσθε τὴν ἐσομένην τοῦ θεοῦ κρίσιν, ἐὰν ἐπιμένητε τῇ ἀδικίᾳ· καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐπιβοήσομεν· Ὃ φίλον τῷ θεῷ, τοῦτο γενέσθω! Καὶ ἐξ ἐπιστολῆς δὲ τοῦ μεγίστου καὶ ἐπιφανεστάτου Καίσαρος Ἀδριανοῦ, τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν, ἔχοντες ἀπαιτεῖν ὑμᾶς καθὰ ἠξιώσαμεν κελεῦσαι τὰς κρίσεις γενέσθαι, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ κεκρῖσθαι τοῦτο ὑπὸ Ἀδριανοῦ μᾶλλον ἠξιώσαμεν, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τοῦ ἐπίστασθαι δίκαια ἀξιοῦν τὴν προσφώνησιν καὶ ἐξήγησιν πεποιήμεθα. Ὑπετάξαμεν δὲ καὶ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς Ἀδριανοῦ τὸ ἀντίγραφον, ἵνα καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀληθεύειν ἡμᾶς γνωρίζητε. Καὶ ἔστι τὸ ἀντίγραφον τοῦτο. Μινουκίῳ Φουνδανῷ. Ἐπιστολὴν ἐδεξάμην γραφεῖσάν μοι ἀπὸ Σερηνίου Γρανιανοῦ, λαμπροτάτου ἀνδρός, ὅντινα σὺ διεδέξω. Οὐ δοκεῖ οὖν μοι τὸ πρᾶγμα ἀζήτητον καταλιπεῖν, ἵνα μήτε οἱ ἄνθρωποι ταράττωνται καὶ τοῖς συκοφάνταις χορηγία κακουργίας παρασχεθῇ. Ἄν οὖν σαφῶς εἰς ταύτην τὴν ἀξίωσιν οἱ ἐπαρχιῶται δύνωνται διϊσχυρίζεσθαι κατὰ τῶν Χριστιανῶν, ὡς καὶ πρὸ βήματος ἀποκρίνεσθαι, ἐπὶ τοῦτο μόνον τραπῶσιν, ἀλλ οὐκ ἀξιώσεσιν οὐδὲ μόναις βοαῖς. Πολλῷ γὰρ μᾶλλον προσῆκεν, εἴ τις κατηγορεῖν βούλοιτο, τοῦτό σε διαγινώσκειν. Εἴ τις οὖν κατηγορεῖ καὶ δείκνυσί τι παρὰ τοὺς νόμους πράττοντας, οὕτως διόριζε κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἁμαρτήματος· ὡς μὰ τὸν Ἡρακλέα, εἴ τις συκοφαντίας χάριν τοῦτο προτείνοι, διαλάμβανε ὑπὲρ τῆς δεινότητος καὶ φρόντιζε ὅπως ἂν ἐκδικήσειας.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You claim you have gods too. Fine — then explain how you get caught being impious, sacrilegious, and irreligious toward your own deities. You presume they exist, yet you neglect them. You fear them, yet you destroy them. You claim to avenge them, yet you mock them. Check the record if you think I'm lying.

Start with the obvious: when you worship some gods and ignore others, you inevitably offend the ones you snub. You can't elevate one without contempt for the other, because there is no election without rejection. So you despise the gods you reject, and you don't even fear offending them by that rejection.

As we noted earlier, every god's standing hung on the senate's vote. A deity wasn't a god unless a consulted senator wanted him; by refusing to want him, the senate condemned him. You treat your household gods — your Lares — like household property: you pawn them, sell them, melt them down into a chamber pot for Saturn or a ladle for Minerva, whichever one's worn out and battered after years of worship, whichever one's master has felt the pinch of domestic necessity.

You defile the public gods just as badly under public law. You put them up for auction as taxable assets. The Capitolium, the vegetable market — it's all the same: same auctioneer's voice, same spear, same quaestor's notation. Divinity is sold and leased like any other lot. Fields burdened with tribute go cheaper; human heads counted for the poll tax are more ignoble — those are the marks of captivity. But the gods? The more tribute they owe, the holier they are; or rather, the holier they are, the more tribute they owe. Majesty has become a revenue stream. Religion goes begging through the taverns. You charge admission to the temple floor, a fee for the sacred entrance; you can't know the gods for free — they're for sale.

What exactly do you do to honor them that you don't also do for your dead? Buildings, altars — same thing. The statues wear the same attire and insignia. Whatever the dead man's age, art, or trade was, that's what the god becomes. How does Jupiter's silicernium differ from a funeral feast, the obba from the simpulum, the pollinctor from the haruspex? Even the haruspex shows up for the dead.

So by all means, vote divine honors to dead emperors — you already attributed divinity to them while they were alive. Your gods will accept it; better yet, they'll congratulate themselves, since their masters have just been made their equals.

But when you worship Larentina, a public prostitute — or at least Lais or Phryne — among the Junos, Cereses, and Dianas; when you consecrate Simon Magus with a statue and an inscription as a holy god; when you promote some unknown palace tutor to a synod deity — the older gods may not be more noble, but they'll count it an insult from you that this privilege, which only antiquity conferred on them, has now been allowed to others.

latin: Sed nobis dii sunt, inquitis. Et quomodo vos e contrario impii et sacrilegi et irreligiosi erga deos vestros deprehendimini, qui quos praesumitis esse, negligatis, quos timetis, destruatis, quos etiam vindicatis, illudatis? Recognoscite, si mentiar. Primo quidem, cum alii alios colitis, utique quos non colitis offenditis. Praelatio alterius sine contumelia alterius non potest procedere, quia nec electio sine reprobatione. Jam ergo contemnitis quos reprobatis, quos reprobando offendere non timetis. Nam ut supra perstrinximus, status dei cujusque in senatus aestimatione pendebat. Deus non erat, quem homo consultus noluisset et nolendo damnasset. Domesticos deos, quos lares dicitis, domestica potestate tractatis pignerando, venditando, demutando aliquando in cacabulum de Saturno, aliquando in trullam de Minerva, ut quisque contritus atque contusus est, dum diu colitur, ut quisque dominus sanctiorem expertus est domesticam necessitatem. Publicos aeque publico jure foedatis, quos in hastario vectigales habetis. Sic Capitolium, sic olitorium forum petitur; sub eadem voce praeconis, sub eadem hasta, sub eadem annotatione quaestoris divinitas addicta conducitur. Sed enim agri tributo onusti viliores, hominum capita stipendio censa ignobiliora; nam hae sunt notae captivitatis. Dii vero qui magis tributarii, magis sancti; imo qui magis sancti, magis tributarii. Majestas quaestuaria efficitur. Circuit cauponas religio mendicans. Exigitis mercedem pro solo templi, pro aditu sacri; non licet deos nosse gratis, venales sunt. Quid omnino ad honorandos eos facitis, quod non etiam mortuis vestris conferatis? aedes proinde, aras proinde. Idem habitus et insignia in statuis. Ut aetas, ut ars, ut negotium mortui fuit, ita deus est. Quo differt ab epulo Jovis silicernium, a simpulo obba, ab haruspice pollinctor? nam et haruspex mortuis apparet. Sed digne imperatoribus defunctis honorem divinitatis dicatis, quibus et viventibus eum addicitis. Accepto ferent dii vestri, imo gratulabuntur, quod pares eis fiant domini sui. Sed quum Larentinam, publicum scortum, velim saltem Laidem aut Phrynen, inter Junones et Cereres ac Dianas adoratis; quum Simonem Magum statua et inscriptione sancti dei inauguratis; quum de paedagogiis aulicis nescio quem synodi deum facitis: licet non nobiliores dii veteres, tamen contumeliam a vobis deputabunt, hoc et aliis licuisse, quod solis antiquitas contulit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Suppose we really are the worst criminals. Why, then, do you treat us differently from our peers — that is, from every other guilty person — when identical offenses demand identical handling? Other defendants speak for themselves or hire advocates to proclaim their innocence; the right to answer and to argue stands open because no one may be condemned without a defense or a hearing. Yet Christians alone are forbidden to say anything that could clear their case, uphold the truth, or keep the judge from acting unjustly. You demand only what public hatred requires: confession of the name, not examination of the crime. If you investigate a homicide or sacrilege or incest or treason, you are not satisfied with the mere admission of the label; you insist on the details — quality, number, place, manner, time, accomplices, associates. With us, nothing of the sort, even though it should be extracted with equal force: whatever is falsely alleged, how many infanticides each has tasted, how many incests each has concealed, which cooks and which dogs were present. Oh, the governor's glory if he could uncover someone who had already eaten a hundred infants! Yet we find that investigation itself is barred in our case.

When Pliny Secundus governed the province, he executed some Christians and stripped others of rank, but the sheer multitude unsettled him. He consulted Emperor Trajan, reporting that beyond their obstinate refusal to sacrifice he had discovered nothing about their rites except that they met before dawn to sing to Christ as God and to bind themselves by discipline against homicide, adultery, fraud, perfidy, and other crimes. Trajan replied that such people must not be sought out, but if brought before the court they must be punished. A verdict tangled by necessity! He denies they should be investigated as innocent, yet orders them punished as guilty. He spares and rages, feigns ignorance and takes notice. What are you doing to yourselves with this judgment? If you condemn, why not also investigate? If you will not investigate, why not also absolve? Military posts scour the provinces for robbers; every citizen becomes a soldier against enemies of the state, and inquiry reaches accomplices and associates alike. Only the Christian may not be investigated — only presented — as if investigation would produce anything but the presentation itself. So the accused is presented, then condemned — a man no one wanted to find, who, I suspect, earned punishment not because he was guilty but because, unsearched, he was discovered.

Thus you do not follow the standard form of judging crimes: you torture others who deny in order to extract a confession, but you torture Christians alone to force a denial. If Christianity were truly a crime, we would deny it and you would compel confession by torture. You do not think crimes should go uninvestigated because you are certain they are admitted by the mere confession of the name — yet even today, when a confessed murderer admits what murder is, you still extort a formal admission. More perversely still, you presume our crimes from the confession of the name, then use torture to make us withdraw that confession, so that in denying the name we equally deny the crimes you presumed from it.

I suspect you do not actually want us to perish, you who consider us the worst. You typically tell murderers: "Deny, and I will have you torn apart if you persist in confessing." If you do not act that way toward the guilty, then you judge us most innocent — since you do not want us to persist in a confession you know is condemned by necessity, not justice. A man cries, "I am a Christian." He tells you what he is; you want to hear what he is not. Presidents of truth, you labor to hear a lie from us alone. "This is what I am," he says, "the very thing you asked about. Why twist me the wrong way? I confess, and you twist. What would you do if I denied?" You hardly trust others who deny; us, if we deny, you believe at once. Let that perversity alarm you, lest some hidden force serve you against the form and nature of judgment, against the laws themselves. Unless I am mistaken, the laws order the guilty to be punished, not concealed; they prescribe that the confessed be condemned, not absolved. Senatorial decrees, imperial mandates, the empire whose ministers you are — all define this. Your rule is civil, not tyrannical. Under tyrants torture serves as punishment; under you it is reserved for questioning. Keep your law for them up to the point of confession; if confession forestalls it, the charge collapses. A sentence is required; the guilty must be removed by right, not excused. No one strives to absolve him; that is not permitted; therefore no one is compelled to deny.

You regard the Christian — a man charged with every crime, enemy of gods, emperors, laws, morals, all nature — and you compel him to deny so you can absolve a man you cannot absolve unless he denies. You transgress the laws. You want him to deny his guilt so you can make him innocent, and unwillingly so, no longer guilty of the past. Where does this perversity come from? So that you do not even reflect that a spontaneous confession deserves more credence than a forced denial; or that, compelled to deny, he does not deny from conviction; and once absolved, he may laugh at your rivalry, again a Christian, after leaving the tribunal. Since in everything you treat us differently from other criminals, insisting on this one point — that we be excluded from that name (for we are excluded if we do what non-Christians do) — you can see that the case involves no crime, but the name, which a certain rival doctrine pursues, first ensuring that men do not want to know for certain what they know for certain they do not know. Therefore they believe about us what is unproven, and refuse to investigate lest they prove we are not what they prefer to believe, so that the name of that rival doctrine, on presumed rather than proven crimes, may be condemned from its own confession alone. Hence we are tortured for confessing, punished for persisting, absolved for denying — because it is a battle over the name. Finally, why do you read "Christian" from the tablet, but not "homicide"? If the Christian is a homicide, why not "incestuous"? Or whatever else you believe we are? In us alone is it shameful or distasteful to pronounce the names of crimes? If the Christian is guilty of no crime, the name is intensely hostile — if the crime consists only of the name.
