excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You are misreading repentance in God's case, as if He repented out of instability or improvidence, or simply because He remembers some sin — since He said, 'I repent that I made Saul king,' as though repentance always means confessing an evil deed or mistake. But it does not always work that way. Scripture itself shows repentance confessed even over good deeds, to the envy and reproach of the one who proved ungrateful for a benefit. Take Saul: the Creator, who had not sinned, announced His repentance about burdening Saul when He took him into the kingdom and increased him with the Holy Spirit — for he was still the best, as God said, 'There was not such a one among the sons of Israel,' and He had chosen him most worthily. Yet He was not ignorant of how it would turn out. No one will saddle God with improvidence, since you yourself confess Him to be God and provident; providence is the very property of His divinity. The evil deed of Saul, as I said, burdened God's repentance with a profession that — with no sin attaching to the choice of Saul — is to be understood as envious rather than criminal. (1 Samuel 15:35)

You object: 'But I see it as criminal in the case of the Ninevites, for Jonah says: "The Lord repented of the evil which He had said He would do to them, and He did not do it." And Jonah himself said to God: "Therefore I fled beforehand to Tarshish, because I knew you to be merciful and full of mercy, patient and very merciful, repenting of evils."' Well put — he led with the title of the best God, the most patient over the wicked and most abundant in mercy and pity toward those who acknowledge and lament their sins, like the Ninevites then. If that is what 'best' means, you should have stopped earlier: evil does not belong to such a one, that is, to the best. Even Marcion admits a good tree cannot produce evil fruit, yet he named an evil that the best cannot comprehend. Is there some interpretation of those evils that could also have occurred in the best? There is. We say that 'evil' here does not mean evil reduced to the Creator's nature, but evil assigned to His power as Judge — according to which He announced: 'I am He who creates evils,' and: 'Behold, I send evils upon you' — not sinful, but avenging. We have sufficiently cleared the infamy of such evils as befitting a Judge. Just as evils are spoken of a judge without reproach, nor do they make the judge evil by that name, so this 'evil' is to be understood as drawn from judicial evils and belonging to the Judge. Even among the Greeks, 'evils' sometimes means vexations and injuries, not malignities — just as in this passage. So if the Creator repented of His 'evil' as if it were a creature to be reproached and judged for sin, yet no admitted crime will be reckoned to the Creator, who justly and deservedly decreed the abolition of the most wicked city. What He justly destined, He destined not evilly but from justice, not from evil; He named the punishment itself 'evil' from the evil and merit of its suffering. (Jonah 3:10)

So you will say: if you excuse 'evil' as a name of justice because He justly destined destruction for the Ninevites, then He is also to be blamed for repenting of justice, which is not to be repented of. On the contrary, God does not repent of justice. It remains to acknowledge what God's repentance actually is. It is not that because a man repents from the memory of much sin, sometimes even from the ingratitude of some good work, God repents in the same way. Inasmuch as God neither admits evil nor condemns good, to that extent there is no place for repentance of good or evil with Him. The same Scripture determines this for you, when Samuel says to Saul: 'The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, who is better than you, and Israel will be split in two, and it will not turn back nor repent, because He is not a man to repent.' This definition establishes a different form of divine repentance in all things — not reckoned from improvidence or levity or any condemnation of good or evil work, like human repentance. What then is the manner of divine repentance? It is now clear, if you do not refer it to human conditions. Nothing else is understood than a simple conversion of the prior sentence, which can be admitted without reproach even in a man, much less in God, whose every sentence lacks fault. Even in the Greek, the word for repentance is composed not from confession of sin but from change of mind — which we show happens with God because of the occurrence of changing things.

non conuertetur neque paenitentiam aget, quia non sicut homo est ad paenitendum, haec itaque definitio in omnibus aliam formam diuinae paenitentiae statuit, quae neque ex improuidentia neque ex paenitentiae nomen non ex delicti confessione, sed ex animi demutatione compositum est, quam apud deum pro rerum uariantium sese occursu fieri ostendimus.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The whole debate centers on the number: whether two gods can be posited — perhaps by poetic and pictorial license, and now also by heretical license. But Christian truth has spoken distinctly: if God is not one, he is not God, because we believe it is more worthy for whatever is not as it ought to be not to exist at all. So that you may know God must be one, seek what God is, and you will find no other answer. As far as the human condition can define God, I define this, which every conscience will also acknowledge: God is the Highest, the Great, established in eternity — innate, unmade, without beginning, without end — for this state is what constitutes eternity, which makes God the Highest Great God while this state exists in God himself; and thus also the rest, so that God is the Highest Great One in form and reason and power. Since everyone agrees on this — for no one will deny that God is the Highest Great One, except someone who could pronounce the opposite, that God is the lowest small one, thereby denying God by taking away what belongs to God — what will be the condition of this Highest Great One? Namely, that nothing equals it; that is, that there is no other Highest Great One, because if there were, it would be equal, and if it were equal, it would no longer be the Highest Great One, with the condition overturned and, so to speak, the law that allows nothing to equal the Highest Great One. Therefore the Highest Great One must be unique — not having a peer — so that it may remain the Highest Great One. Therefore it cannot be otherwise than through what it has its being by, that is, unique altogether. Therefore, since God is the Highest Great One, our truth has pronounced rightly: God, if not one, is not God — not as if we doubt that God exists by saying 'if not one, he is not,' but because we define as God the very One we confess to be God, so that if that One is not, God is not. Furthermore, if the Highest Great One must be unique, then God will also be unique — not God in any other way except as the Highest Great One, and not the Highest Great One in any other way except by not having a peer, and not not having a peer in any other way except by being unique. Certainly, whatever other god you introduce, you will not be able to preserve him as God in any other form than by ascribing to him also the property of divinity, just as eternal, so also the Highest Great One. How, then, can two Highest Great Ones coexist, since to be the Highest Great One is not to have a peer, and not having a peer belongs to one alone, and in two it cannot exist in any way?

latin: Principalis itaque et exinde tota congressio de numero, an duos deos liceat induci, si forte, poetica et pictoria licentia, et tertia iam, haeretica. sed ueritas Christiana destricte pronuntiauit: deus si non unus est, non est, quia dignius credimus non esse quodcumque non ita fuerit, ut esse debebit. deum autem ut scias unum esse debere, quaere quid sit deus, et non aliter inuenies. quantum humana condicio de deo definire potest, id definio, quod et omnium conscientia agnoscet: deum summum esse magnum in aeternitate constitutum, [innatum, infectum, sine initio, sine-fine] — hunc enim statum aeternitati t censendum, quae summum magnum deum efficiat, dum hoc est in deo ipsa — atque ita et cetera, ut sit deus summum magnum et forma et ratione et ui et potestate. cum de isto conuenit apud omnes, — nemo enim negabit deum summum magnum quid esse, nisi qui potuerit deum imum modicum quid e contrario pronuntiare, ut deum neget auferendo quod dei est - quae erit iam condicio ipsius summi magni? nempe, ut nihil illi adaequetur, id est, ut non sit aliud summum magnum, quia, si fuerit, adaequabitur, et si adaequabitur, non erit iam summum magnum, euersa condicione et, ut ita dixerim, lege, quae summo magno nihil sinit adaequari. ergo unicum sit necesse est summum magnum, — quod fuerit par non habendo — ne non sit summum magnum. ergo non aliter erit quam per quod habet esse, id est unicum omnino. proinde deus cum summum magnum sit, recte ueritas nostra pronuntiauit: deus, si non. unus est, non est, non quasi dubitemus esse deum dicendo: si non unus, non est, sed quia quem confidimus esse, id eum definiamus esse, quod si non est, deus non est. [et summum scilicet magnum] porro (si) summum magnum unicum sit necesse est, ergo et deus unicus erit, non aliter deus, nisi summum magnum, nec aliter summum magnum, nisi parem non habens, nec aliter parem non habens, nisi unicus fuerit. certe quemcumque alium deum induxeris, non alia poteris eum forma tueri deum quam ut et illi proprium diuinitatis adscripseris, sicut aeternum ita et summum magnum. duo ergo summa magna quomodo consistent, cum hoc sit summum magnum, par non habere, par autem non habere uni competat, in duobus esse nullo modo possit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You'll try to shake the retracted point about the name of God, relying on the fact that Scripture permits it passively and to others too: "God stands in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he judges" (Psalm 82:1), and "I said, 'You are gods'" (Psalm 82:6). But that doesn't mean the title 'Highest Great One' belongs to them just because they're called gods; the same goes for the Creator. I'll answer the fool who hasn't thought this through, lest the same retort boomerang against Marcion's God: he may be called God, but that doesn't prove he's the Highest Great One — any more than the Creator's angels or men are. If sharing a name prejudges the nature, then how many wicked slaves insult the names of kings — Alexander, Darius, Holofernes? Yet that doesn't strip the kings of what they are. The idols of the nations are commonly called gods, but no one is God by the mere fact of being called God. So I don't defend the Highest Great One in the Creator because of the name, the sound, or the label, but because of the substance that bears the name. Finding that substance alone innate, uncorrupted, alone eternal, and the maker of the universe, I ascribe and vindicate the Highest Great One to the reality, not the label; to the condition, not the appellation. And because that substance already holds the name God, you think I'm defending the name — since I must use the name to show which substance I mean, the one by which God is called God. But the Highest Great One is reckoned from the substance, not the name. Even Marcion, vindicating his God, does it by the reality, not the word. So we insist that the Highest Great One — which we ascribe to God by the law of substance, not the lottery of the name — must be equal in the two who share that substance called God. Because insofar as they are called gods, that is, Highest Great Ones, of substances innate and eternal and therefore great and highest, to that extent one Highest Great One cannot be less or worse than another. If the happiness, sublimity, and integrity of the Highest Great One stand in Marcion's God, they stand equally in ours; if not in ours, then equally not in his. Therefore the two Highest Great Ones won't be equal, because the established rule of the Highest Great One won't tolerate comparison; nor unequal, because another rule of the Highest Great One appears, refusing diminution. You're stuck, Marcion, in the middle of your Pontic storm. The waves of truth close in on both sides. You can't present gods as equal or unequal. There aren't two. As for the retracted number — though the whole fight is about two gods — we've boxed him in within these lines, inside which we'll now engage on the individual properties.

nec tamen ideo regibus id quod sunt detrahetur. nam et ipsa idola gentium dei uulgo, sed deus nemo ea re, qua deus dicitur. ita ego non nomini dei nec sono nec notae nominis huius summum magnum in creatore defendo, sed ipsi substantiae, cui nomen hoc contigit. hanc inueniens solam innatam infectam, solam aeternam et uniuersitatis conditricem, non nomini, sed statui, nec appellationi, sed condicioni eius summum magnum et adscribo et uindico. et ideo. quia deus iam uocari obtinuit substantia cui adscribo, nomini me adscribere putas, quia necesse est per nomen ostendam cui adscribam substantiae, scilicet qua constat qui deus dicitur. at summum magnum ex substantia, non ex nomine, deputatur. denique hoc et Marcion suo deo uindicans, secundum statum, non secundum uocabulum uindicat. id ergo summum magnum, quod deo adscribimus ex substantiae lege, non ex nominis sorte, contendimus ex pari esse debere in duobus, qui ea substantia constant, quae deus dicitur, quia in quantum dii uocantur, id est summa magna, substantiae scilicet mento innatae et aeternae ac per hoc magnae et summae, in tantum non possit summum magnum minus et deterius alio summo magno haberi. si summi magni felicitas et sublimitas et integritas stabit in deo Marcionis, stabit aeque et in nostro, si non et in nostro, aeque nec in Marcionis. ergo nec paria erunt duo summa magna, quia prohibet disposita iam regula summi magni comparationem non sustinens, nec disparia, quia et alia summi magni regula occurrit, diminutionem non admittens. haesisti, Marcion, in medio Ponti tui aestu. utrimque te fluctus ueritatis inuoluunt. nec pares nec dispares deos sistere potes. duo enim non sunt. quod pertineat proprie ad numeri retractatum, quamquam tota materia de duobus deis dimicetur, his interim lineis eum clusimus, intra quas de singularibus iam proprietatibus congrediemur.

english: 1. My brother Fabius, you very lately asked, because some news or other were communicated, whether or not we ought to flee in persecution . For my part, having on the spot made some observations in the negative suited to the place and time, I also, owing to the rudeness of some persons , took away with me the subject but half treated, meaning to set it forth now more fully by my pen; for your inquiry had interested me in it, and the state of the times had already on its own account pressed it upon me. As persecutions in increasing number threaten us, so the more are we called on to give earnest thought to the question of how faith ought to receive them, and the duty of carefully considering it concerns you no less, who no doubt , by not accepting the Comforter, the guide to all truth , have, as was natural, opposed us hitherto in regard to other questions also. We have therefore applied a methodical treatment, too, to your inquiry, as we see that we must first come to a decision as to how the matter stands in regard to persecution itself, whether it comes on us from God or from the devil , that with the less difficulty we may get on firm ground as to our duty to meet it; for of everything one's knowledge is clearer when it is known from whom it has its origin. It is enough indeed to lay it down, (in bar of all besides,) that nothing happens without the will of God . But lest we be diverted from the point before us, we shall not by this deliverance at once give occasion to…

For in other respects, too, injustice in proportion to the enmity it displays against righteousness affords occasion for attestations of that to which it is opposed as an enemy, that so righteousness may be perfected in injustice , as strength is perfected in weakness. For the weak things of the world have been chosen by God to confound the strong, and the foolish things of the world to confound its wisdom. I will smite and heal, I will make alive and put to death . excerpts.citation: Tertullian — A Treatise on the Soul 24
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I will not concede that the soul is capable of oblivion. The divinity granted to it is so great that it makes the soul equal to God. That alone — its innateness — would have been enough to testify to its full divinity. On top of that, it is said to be immortal, incorruptible, incorporeal, invisible, ineffable, uniform, principal, rational, intellectual — attributes believed to belong to God. What more could you prescribe for the soul if you were to call it God outright? We, however, attribute nothing to God. Therefore, we estimate the soul to be far inferior to God, because we recognize it as born. Its divinity is therefore diluted, its happiness meager. It is like a breath, not a spirit. Even if it is immortal, that immortality serves its divinity; but it is passible, and that passibility serves its birth. Consequently, it was capable of error from the beginning, and from there also akin to oblivion. That is enough on this point with Hermogenes.

Moreover, whatever can be considered a god by the equality of all divine properties will not be subject to any passion. Thus, it will not be subject to oblivion either, since oblivion is as great an injury as the glory of the one whose injury it is — namely, memory. Plato himself proclaimed memory the salvation of the senses and intellect, and Cicero called it the treasure of all studies. The question now is not whether such a divine soul could have lost memory, but whether, once lost, it can recover it again. For what it should not have forgotten, if it has forgotten, I do not know if it can recall. So both oblivion and recovery fit my soul, not the Platonic one.

Second, I will oppose you on this: you claim the soul is capable of those ideas by nature, do you not? "Indeed, by nature," you say. Then no one will concede that natural knowledge of natural things can fall away. Knowledge of studies, doctrines, disciplines may fall away. Perhaps talents and affections fall away too. These seem natural but are not, because they consist of accidents — institutions, bodily conditions, health, dominant powers, freedoms of the will. But the knowledge of natural things does not even fail in beasts. A lion will forget its ferocity when prevented by training, and with all its pride intact it will become the delight of some queen Berenice, licking her cheeks with its tongue. It will leave behind its beastly ways, yet the knowledge of natural things will remain. That same lion will not forget its natural food, its natural remedies, its natural terrors. Even if offered fish or royal delicacies, it will desire flesh. Even if a remedy is composed for it when sick, it will seek a monkey. And if no hunting spear is presented, it will still fear a rooster. Similarly, in man — perhaps the most forgetful of all — the knowledge of natural things will remain unobliterated, as the only truly natural thing. He will always be mindful of eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, smelling with the nose, tasting with the mouth, touching with the hand. These are the senses that philosophy devalues in favor of intellectual things. Therefore, if natural knowledge of sensual things remains, how can intellectual knowledge — considered superior — fall away?

Where, then, does the power of oblivion preceding recollection come from? "From the multitude of time," it is said. That is not well considered. The quantity of time does not pertain to what is said to be innate, and therefore believed to be eternal. What is eternal, because it is innate, admits neither beginning nor end of time, and suffers no mode of time. To what has no mode of time, no change of time applies, and no power of time belongs. If time is the cause of oblivion, why does memory slip away from the moment the soul is introduced into the body — as if the soul, certainly prior to the body, did not exist without time? Once it enters the body, does it immediately forget, or after some time? If immediately, what multitude of time — not yet reckoned — would there be? Clearly, infancy. If after some time, then in that space before the times of oblivion the soul would still be mindful. What kind of thing is it, that it later forgets, and then later recalls again? Whenever oblivion may strike, what mode of time would be involved? I think the whole course of life will not be enough to overturn the memory of so much time before the body.

But again, Plato shifts the cause to the body. As if this too were worthy of faith — that a born substance extinguishes the power of an innate one. There are great and many differences among bodies — by nation, size, condition, age, health. Will the differences of oblivion therefore be estimated? But oblivion is uniform. Therefore, the multiformity of the body cannot be the cause of a uniform exit. Many proofs, with Plato himself as witness, have demonstrated the soul's divination, which we have already proposed to Hermogenes. Not a single human being fails to sometimes feel his own soul as a predictor of things to come — an omen, a warning of danger, a sign of joy. If the body does not hinder divination, I think it will not hinder memory either. In the same body, souls both forget and recall. If some reason of the body incites oblivion, how will it admit the contrary recollection? Recollection after oblivion is a renewed memory. What contradicts the first memory — why does it not also contradict the second? Finally, who would recall more than children — as more recent souls, not yet immersed in domestic and public cares, dedicated solely to studies whose learning becomes recollections? Why do we not all recall equally, since we all forget equally — but only the philosophers? Not even all of them. Clearly, Plato alone, in such a vast multitude of nations, in such a vast field of wise men, was both forgetful and mindful of the ideas. Therefore, if this principal argument does not hold in any way, the whole structure to which it was accommodated is equally overturned — the belief that souls are innate, conversant in heavenly things, conscious of divine things there, thence transferred, and here recalled — providing occasions plainly for heretics.

latin: Primo quidem oblivionis capacem animam non cedam, quia tantam illi concessit divinitatem, ut Deo adaequetur: innatam eam facit, quod et solum armare potuissem ad testimonium plenae divinitatis: adjicit immortalem, incorruptibilem, incorporalem, quia hoc et Deum credidit, invisibilem, ineffigiabilem, uniformem, principalem, rationalem, intellectualem. Quid amplius proscriberet animam, si eam Deum nuncuparet? Nos autem qui nihil Deo appendimus, hoc ipso animam longe infra Deum expendimus, quod natam eam agnoscimus, ac per hoc dilutioris divinitatis, et exilioris felicitatis; ut flatum, non ut spiritum; et si immortalem, ut hoc sit divinitatis, tamen passibilem, ut hoc sit nativitatis: ideoque et a primordio exorbitationis capacem, et inde etiam oblivionis affinem. Satis de isto cum Hermogene. Caeterum, quae, ut haberi merito possit ex peraequatione omnium proprietatum deus, nulli passioni subjacebit; ita nec oblivioni, cum tanta sit injuria oblivio, quanta est gloria ejus, cujus injuria est, memoria scilicet: quam et ipse Plato sensuum et intellectuum salutem, et Cicero thesaurum omnium studiorum praedicavit. Nec hoc jam in dubium deducetur, an tam divina anima memoriam potuerit amittere; sed an quam amiserit, recuperare denuo possit. Quae enim non debuit oblivisci, si oblita sit, nescio an valeat recordari. Ita utrumque meae animae, non platonicae congruet. Secundo gradu opponam: natura compotem animam facis idearum illarum, annon? Imo natura, inquis. Nemo ergo concedet naturalem scientiam naturalium excidere artium. Excidet studiorum, excidet doctrinarum, disciplinarum, excidet fortasse et ingeniorum, et affectuum: quae naturae videntur, non tamen sunt, quia, ut praemisimus et pro locis, et pro institutionibus, et pro corpulentiis, ac valetudinibus, et pro potestatibus dominatricibus, pro libertatibus arbitrii, ex accidentibus constant. Naturalium vero scientia ne in bestiis quidem deficit. Plane obliviscetur feritatis leo, mansuetudinis eruditione praeventus, et cum toto suggestu jubarum, delicium fiet Berenices alicujus reginae, lingua genas ejus emaculans; mores bestiam relinquent: scientia naturalium permanebit. Non obliviscetur idem naturalium pabulorum, naturalium remediorum, naturalium terrorum; etsi de piscibus, etsi de placentis regina ei obtulerit, carnem desiderabit; etsi languenti theriacam composuerit, simiam leo requiret: et si nullum illi venabulum obfirmabit, gallum tamen formidabit. Perinde et homini omnium forsitan obliviosissimo inobliterata perseverabit sola scientia naturalium, ut sola scilicet naturalis; memor semper manducandi in esurie, et bibendi in siti, et oculis videndum, et auribus audiendum, et naribus odorandum, et ore gustandum, et manu contrectandum. Hi sunt certe sensus, quos philosophia depretiat intellectualium praelatione. Igitur si naturalis scientia sensualium permanet, quomodo intellectualium, quae potior habetur, intercidit? Unde nunc ipsa vis oblivionis antecedentis recordationem? Ex multitudine, ait, temporis. Satis improspecte. Quantitas enim temporis non pertinebit ad eam rem quae innata dicatur, ac per hoc potissimum aeterna credatur. Quod enim aeternum est, eo quia et innatum est, neque initium, neque finem temporis admittendo, nullum modum temporis patitur; cui temporis modus nullus est, nec ulla demutatione tempori subest, nec ea de multitudine tempori vis est. Si tempus in caussa est oblivionis, cur, ex quo anima corpori inducitur, memoria delabitur, quasi exinde tempus anima sustineat, quae sine dubio prior corpore, non fuit utique sine tempore? Ingressa vero corpus, statimne obliviscitur, an aliquanto post? Si statim, et quae erit temporis nondum supputandi multitudo? infantia scilicet. Si aliquando post, ergo illo in spatio ante tempora oblivionis memor adhuc aget anima, et quale est, ut postea obliviscatur, et rursus postea recordetur? Quoquo autem tempore illam oblivio irruerit, quantus hic etiam habebitur modus temporis? tota opinor vitae decursio satis non erit ad evertendam memoriam tanti ante corpus aevi. Sed rursus Plato caussam demutat in corpus. Quasi et hoc fide dignum, ut nata substantia innatae vim exstinguat. Magnae autem et multae differentiae corporum, pro gentilitate, pro magnitudine, pro habitudine, pro aetate, pro valetudine. Num ergo et oblivionum differentiae aestimabuntur? Sed uniformis oblivio est; ergo non erit corporalitas multiformis in caussa exitus uniformis. Multa item documenta, teste ipso Platone, divinationem animae probaverunt, quae proposuimus jam Hermogeni. Sed nec quisquam hominum, non et ipse aliquando praesagam animam suam sentit, aut ominis, aut periculi, aut gaudii augurem. Si divinationi non obstrepit corpus, nec memoriae, opinor, officiet. In eodem certe corpore, et obliviscuntur animae, et recordantur. Si qua corporis ratio incutit oblivionem, quomodo contrariam ejus admittet recordationem? quia et ipsa post oblivionem recordatio, memoria recidiva est. Quod primae memoriae adversatur, cur non et secundae refragatur? Postremo, qui magis reminiscerentur quam pueruli, ut recentiores animae, ut nondum immersae domesticis ac publicis curis, ut ipsis solis deditae studiis, quorum discentiae reminiscentiae fiunt? Imo cur non ex aequo omnes recordamur, cum ex aequo omnes obliviscamur, sed tantummodo Philosophi? Ne hi quidem omnes. Plato scilicet solus in tanta gentium sylva, in tanto sapientium prato, idearum et oblitus et recordatus est. Igitur si nullo modo consistit argumentatio ista praecipua, totum illud pariter eversum est, cui accommodata est, ut animae et innatae, et in coelestibus conversatae, et consciae divinorum illic, et inde delatae, et hic recordatae crederentur, ad occasiones plane haereticis subministrandas.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The most excellent emperors have just shown their generosity: laureled veterans were being discharged from camp. Among them stood a soldier of God, steadier in his faith than the rest of the brothers—men who had presumed they could serve two masters. He alone stood bareheaded, the laurel wreath lying idle in his hand. By now the Christians' discipline was an open secret. The other soldiers began singling him out, jeering from a distance and sneering to his face. A murmur reached the tribune, and the man was summoned at once. The tribune demanded, "Why do you look so different?" He replied that he was not permitted to do as the others did. Pressed for a reason, he answered: "I am a Christian." What a glorious soldier of God! From that moment the votes were cast, the charge escalated, and the accused was hauled before the prefects. There he threw down the crushing packs, daring to be relieved of them; he shook the most wretched sentinel duty from his feet, stepping onto holy ground. He declared the sword unnecessary for the Lord's defense, and the laurel fell from his hand as well. Now, spattered with the hope of his own blood, shod with the Gospel's readiness, girded with the sharper Word of God, fully armed with the Apostle, and better crowned with the white of martyrdom, he awaits Christ's gift in prison.

Opinions flew fast after that—whether from Christians I cannot say, but certainly not from the pagans. They acted as if pushed from a cliff, steep and headlong, desperate to die, all because a man questioned about his uniform made it a matter of his Name. Alone he was brave; among so many brother-soldiers, he alone was a Christian. Clearly those who have spat on the prophecies of the same Holy Spirit now intend to refuse martyrdom too. They are muttering that their good, long peace is being endangered. I have no doubt some are already preparing to emigrate, packing bags, girding themselves for flight from city to city, since they care nothing for any other memory of the Gospel. I know their shepherds: lions in peace, deer in battle. We will settle the questions of confessions elsewhere. But right now I must meet their objection: "Where are we forbidden to be crowned?" I will tackle the concrete substance of this case so that both those who ask from anxious ignorance may be instructed and those who fight to defend the offense may be confounded—especially the crowned Christian soldiers, for whom this is the only question, as if the offense were either nonexistent or at least uncertain. It is neither; I will prove that much for now.

latin: Proxime facta est liberalitas praestantissimorum imperatorum; expungebantur in castris milites laureati. Adhibetur quidam illic magis Dei miles, caeteris constantior fratribus, qui se duobus dominis servire posse praesumpserant, solus libero eapite, coronamento in manu otioso. Vulgata jam et ista disciplina Christianorum relucebat. Denique singuli designare, et eludere eminus, infrendere cominus. Murmur tribuno defertur, et persona jam ex ordine accesserat. Statim tribunus: Cur, inquit, tam diversus habitu? Negavit ille cum caeteris sibi licere; caussas expostulatus, Christianus sum, respondit. O militem in Deo gloriosum! Suffragia exinde, et res ampliata, et reus ad praefectos. Ibidem gravissimas penulas posuit, relevari auspicatus, speculatoriam morosissimam de pedibus absolvit, terrae sanctae insistere incipiens, gladium nec dominicae defensioni necessarium reddidit: laurea et de manu corruit. Et nunc russatus sanguinis sui spe, calceatus de Evangelii paratura, succinctus acutiore verbo Dei, totus de Apostolo armatus et de martyrii candida melius coronandus, donativum Christi in carcere exspectat. Exinde sententiae super illo, nescio an Christianorum, non enim aliae ethnicorum, ut de abrupto, et praecipiti, et mori cupido, qui de habitu interrogatus nomini negotium fecerit: solus scilicet fortis, inter tot fratres commilitones solus Christianus. Plane superest ut etiam martyria recusare meditentur, qui prophetias ejusdem Spiritus sancti respuerunt. Mussitant denique, tam bonam et longam sibi pacem periclitari. Nec dubito quosdam Scripturas emigrare, sarcinas expedire, fugae accingi de civitate in civitatem; nullam enim aliam Evangelii memoriam curant. Novi et pastores corum, in pace leones, in praelio cervos. Sed de quaestionibus confessionum alibi docebimus. At nunc quatenus et illud opponunt: Ubi autem prohibemur coronari? Hanc magis localem substantiam caussae praesentis aggrediar, ut et qui ex sollicitudine ignorantiae quaerunt, instruantur; et qui in defensionem delicti contendunt, revincantur; ipsi vel maxime Christiani laureati, quibus id solum quaestio est; quasi aut nullum aut incertum saltem haberi possit delictum quod patiatur quaestionem. Nec nullum autem nec incertum, hinc interim ostendam.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Before I take up the question of the military crown itself, I first have to investigate whether military service is compatible with Christianity at all. What is the point of debating the incidental details when the fault lies in the very foundation? Do we really think a human oath can override a divine one, or that we can serve another lord after Christ? Are we allowed to forsake father, mother, and every neighbor—people the Law commands us to honor and love after God, people the Gospel also honored without ranking them above Christ alone? Is it permitted to live by the sword when the Lord declared that whoever lives by the sword dies by the sword (Matthew 26:52)? Will the son of peace engage in battle when quarreling is unfitting for him? Will he administer chains, prison, torture, and execution when he is not an avenger of his own wrongs? Will he pull guard duty—perhaps even more than Christ did—or serve on the Lord's day when not even Christ did? Will he stand watch over temples he has renounced? Will he dine where the apostle says not to? Will he defend at night the very demons he exorcised by day, leaning on the spear that pierced Christ's side? Will he carry a standard that rivals Christ's? Will he demand a sign from a commander when he has already received one from God? Even in death, will a bugler's trumpet disturb him when he awaits the angel's trumpet? Will a Christian be burned by military discipline when burning was forbidden him, when Christ granted him the rewards of fire? How many other transgressions of military duty must we count as transgressions? Simply transferring the name from the camps of light to the camps of darkness is itself a transgression.

Admittedly, if faith overtakes men already in the service, the case is different—like those John admitted to baptism, like the most faithful centurions whom Christ approved and Peter catechized. Yet once faith is received and the seal given, there are only three options: desert immediately, as many have done; evade every possible way so as to commit nothing against God that the military permits; or finally, endure for God's sake, a path even pagan faith has allowed. Military service promises neither impunity for sins nor immunity for martyrs. The Christian is never anything else anywhere. There is one Gospel, and the same Jesus, who denies every denier and confesses every confessor of God, who saves the soul lost for his name and destroys the one gained against his name. Before him, a faithful pagan is as much a soldier as an unbelieving pagan is a soldier. The status of faith admits no necessities. There is no necessity to sin for those whose single necessity is not to sin. Even when someone is forced by torture or punishment to sacrifice or deny directly, discipline does not yield to that necessity, because the necessity of fearing denial and undergoing martyrdom outweighs the necessity of avoiding suffering and fulfilling duty. Moreover, this kind of justification subverts the entire substance of the sacrament, loosening the bond even for voluntary sins. The will itself can claim necessity, since it always has something to compel it. I have already established this for the other official crowns as well, where the plea of necessity is most familiar: either the offices must be avoided so we do not fall into sins, or martyrdoms must be endured so we break the offices. I will not belabor the first part of the question—the illegitimacy of military service itself—so that the second part may be addressed, lest I demolish the military entirely and then argue about its crown in vain.

latin: Etenim, ut ipsam caussam coronae militaris aggrediar, puto prius conquirendum an in totum Christianis militia conveniat. Quale est alioquin de accidentibus retractare, cum a praecedentibus culpa sit? Credimusne humanum sacramentum divino superduci licere, et in alium dominum respondere post Christum? et ejerare patrem ac matrem, et omnem proximum, quos et lex honorari et post Deum diligi praecipit, quos et Evangelium solo Christo pluris non faciens, sic quoque honoravit? Licebit in gladio conversari, Domino pronuntiante, gladio periturum qui gladio fuerit usus? Et praelio operabitur filius pacis, cui nec litigare conveniet? Et vincula et carcerem et tormenta et supplicia administrabit, nec suarum ultor injuriarum? Jam stationes, aut alii magis faciet quam Christo? aut et Dominico die, quando nec Christo? et excubabit pro templis, quibus renuntiavit? et coenabit illic ubi apostolo non placet? et quos interdiu exorcismis fugavit, noctibus defensabit, incumbens et requiescens super pilum quo perfossum est latus Christi? vexillum quoque portabit aemulum Christi? et signum postulabit a principe, qui jam a Deo accepit? mortuus etiam tuba inquietabitur aeneatoris, qui excitari a tuba angeli exspectat? et cremabitur ex disciplina castrensi Christianus, cui cremare non licuit, cui Christus merita ignis indulsit? Quanta alia in delictis circumspici possunt castrensium munium, transgression interpretanda? Ipsum de castris lucis in castra tenebrarum nomen deferre, transgressio est. Plane, si quos militia praeventos fides posterior invenit, alia conditio est, ut illorum quos Joannes admittebat ad lavacrum, ut centurionum fidelissimorum, quem Christus probat, et quem Petrus catechizat: dum tamen, suscepta fide atque signata, aut deserendum statim sit, ut a multis actum, aut omnibus modis cavillandum, ne quid adversus Deum committatur, quae nec ex militia permittuntur; aut novissime perpetiendum pro Deo, quod aeque fides pagana condixit. Nec enim delictorum impunitatem, aut martyriorum immunitatem militia promittet. Nusquam Christianus aliud est. Unum Evangelium, et idem Jesus, negaturus omnem negatorem, et confessurus omnem confessorem Dei, et salvam facturus animam pro nomine ejus amissam, perditurus autem de contrario adversus nomen ejus lucri habitam. Apud hunc tam miles est paganus fidelis, quam paganus est miles infidelis. Non admittit status fidei necessitates. Nulla est necessitas delinquendi, quibus una est necessitas non delinquendi. Nam et ad sacrificandum et directo negandum necessitate quis premitur tormentorum sive poenarum: tamen nec illi necessitati disciplina connivet, quia potior est necessitas timendae negationis et obeundi martyrii, quam evadendae passionis et implendi officii. Caeterum subvertit totam substantiam sacramenti causatio ejusmodi, ut etiam voluntariis delictis fibulam laxet. Nam et voluntas poterit necessitas contendi, habens scilicet unde cogatur. Vel ipsam praestruxerim et ad caeteras officialium coronarum caussas, quibus familiarissima est advocatio necessitatis: cum idcirco aut officia fugienda sint, ne in delictis incidamus; aut et martyria toleranda sint, ut officia rumpamus. De prima specie quaestionis etiam militiae ipsius illicitae, plura non faciam, ut secunda reddatur, ne si omni ope expulero militiam, frustra jam de corona militari provocarim.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Suppose, finally, that military service is permitted up to the point of the crown. But let us speak first about the crown itself. That laurel is sacred to Apollo or to Bacchus: to the one, as god of missiles; to the other, as god of triumphs. So Claudius teaches when he says that soldiers are also accustomed to be crowned with myrtle. For myrtle belongs to Venus, mother of Aeneas, not laurel — and also to the lovers of Mars, through Ilium and the Romuli of the Romans. But I do not believe Venus stands on the Romans' side with Mars, where the pain of flaying lies. When the olive also crowns military service, it is idolatry to Minerva, equally goddess of arms, but also of peace, established with Neptune from this tree. In these things the superstition of the military garland is polluted and polluting, and now all things will be polluted — causes included. Look at the annual declaration of vows: what does it look like? First at the principia, second at the capitolia. Take the places and the words: 'Then to you, Jupiter, with a bull with gold-adorned horns, we vow to be future.' Whose voice is that sentence? Certainly the voice of negation. Even if the Christian is silent there with his mouth, the crowned head answers. The same laurel, in the distribution of donatives, is plainly declared not to be gratuitous idolatry, selling Christ to some for gold, just as Judas did for silver. This will be: 'You cannot serve God and mammon' (Luke 16:13) — to hand yourself over to mammon and withdraw from God? This will be: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21) — not to render a man to God, and to snatch the denarius away from Caesar? Is the laurel of triumphs constructed with leaves, or with corpses? Is it adorned with lamina, or with busts? Is it anointed with ointments, or with the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps even of some Christians: for Christ is also among the barbarians. Whoever has borne this cause on his head, has he not also fought against it? There is also another military service, that of royal households. For the castrenses are called munificences, and they themselves belong to the solemnities of the Caesareans. But you, accordingly, are a soldier and a servant of another: and if of two, God and Caesar, then certainly not of Caesar, when you owe yourself to God, even in common matters, I believe, to the more important one.

latin: Puta denique licere militiam usque ad caussam coronae. Sed et de corona prius dicamus. Laurea ista Apollini vel Libero sacra est: illi, ut deo telorum; huic, ut deo triumphorum. Sic docet Claudius cum et myrto ait milites redimiri solere. Veneris enim myrtum, matris Aeneae, non laurum, etiam amiculae Martis, per Iliam et Romulos Romani. Sed ego Venerem non credo ex hac parte cum Marte Romanam, qua pellicis dolor est. Quum et olea militia coronatur, ad Minervam est idololatria, armorum aeque deam, sed et paci cum Neptuno initae ex hac arbore coronatam. In his erit serti militaris superstitio polluta et polluens, omniaque jam polluentur et caussis. Ecce annua votorum nuncupatio quid videtur? prima in principiis, secunda in capitoliis. Accipe post loca et verba: Tunc Tibi, Jupiter, Bove Cornibus Auro Decoratis Vovimus Esse Futurum. Cujus sententiae vox est? utique negationis. Etiamsi tacet illic Christianus ore, coronatus capite respondit. Eadem laurea in donativi dispensatione denuntiatur plane non gratuita idololatria, aliquibus aureis venditans Christum, ut argenteis Judas. Hoc erit, Non potestis Deo servire et mammonae: mammonae manum tradere, et a Deo absistere? Hoc erit, Reddite quae sunt Caesaris Caesari, et quae Dei Deo: nec hominem Deo reddere, et denarium Caesari auferre? Triumphi laurea foliis struitur, an cadaveribus? lamnis ornatur, an bustis? unguentis delibuitur an lacrymis conjugum et matrum? Fortasse quorumdam et Christianorum: et apud barbaros enim Christus. Qui hanc portaverit in capite caussam, nonne et ipse oppugnavit? Est et alia militia regiarum familiarum. Nam et castrenses appellantur munificiae, et ipsae solemnium Caesareanorum. Sed et tu proinde miles ac servus alterius es: et si duorum, Dei et Caesaris, certe tunc non Caesaris, cum te Deo debes, etiam in communibus, credo, potiori.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They crown public officials with laurel for public service, and magistrates get gold crowns on top of that. Etruscan crowns are added, too—this is the technical term for crowns studded with gems and golden oak leaves, marked for Jupiter, worn when leading the sacred processions in palm-embroidered togas. There are also provincial gold crowns, now hunting bigger heads for statues, not for living men. But your ranks, your magistrates, the very name of your senate—all of it is the Church of Christ. You are enrolled in the books of life. There your purple is the blood of the Lord and the spear wound in his side on the cross; there the axe lies at the root of the tree, there the rods spring from Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). Let them look at the public horses wearing their crowns. Your Lord, when he chose to enter Jerusalem according to Scripture (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5), didn't even own a private donkey. They ride in chariots and on horseback; we invoke the name of the Lord our God (Psalm 20:7). We have been removed from the very dwelling of that Babylon in the Apocalypse of John (Revelation 17–18), let alone from the speaker's platform. The mob gets crowned now for the thrill of high-office victories, now for the privilege of municipal festivals—and every luxury of public joy is a trap. But you are a stranger to this world, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem. "Our citizenship is in heaven," he says (Philippians 3:20). You have your own senses, your own calendar: you have nothing to do with the joys of the age; on the contrary, you must do the opposite. The age will rejoice, but you will mourn (Luke 6:25). And I think: "Blessed are those who mourn," he says, "not those who are crowned" (Matthew 5:4). Weddings crown the bridegroom, too—which is why we don't marry pagans, lest they drag us into idolatry, since their weddings begin with it. You have the law from the Patriarchs (Genesis 24:3), and you have the apostle commanding you to marry only in the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:39). Secular freedom crowns as well. But you have already been redeemed by Christ, and at a tremendous price (1 Corinthians 6:20; 7:23). How can the world free a slave who belongs to another? Even if freedom appears real, slavery also once appeared real. Everything in the age is imaginary; nothing is true. Even then you were a free man, redeemed by Christ; and now you are Christ's slave, even if freed by a human master. If you think the world's freedom is true—so true you ratify it with a crown—you have gone back into the slavery of man, which you mistake for freedom; you have lost the freedom of Christ, which you mistake for slavery. Will the athletic contests be debated, too—contests whose very titles condemn them? Both sacred and funereal games, I mean; all that's left is for Olympian Jupiter, Nemean Hercules, wretched Archemorus, and unhappy Antinous to be crowned on a Christian, so that he becomes the spectacle he ought to be watching. I think we have listed every possible occasion. None of them belongs to us: all are alien, profane, illicit, already rejected once for all in the testimony of the sacrament. These were the pomps of the devil and the offices of his angels—honors of the age, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human slaveries, vain praises, shameful glories—and idolatry in all of them, down to the very meaning of the crowns that adorn them all. Claudius even claims heaven is crowned with stars in Homer's songs; granted, by God—granted, by man—therefore man himself must also be crowned by God. Meanwhile, the age crowns brothels, latrines, bakeries, prisons, the games, the amphitheaters themselves, the very spoliaria, the very funeral processions. Judge how sacred, how holy and clean this habit is—not from one poetic heaven, but from the commerce of the whole world. But a Christian will not defile his doorway with laurels, if he knows how many gods the devil has nailed to doors: Janus on the door, Limentinus on the threshold, Forculus and Cardus on the leaves and hinges, and among the Greeks, Thyreus Apollo and the Antelios demons.

latin: Coronant et publicos ordines laureis publicae caussae, magistratus vero insuper aureis. Superferuntur etiam illis Hetruscae. Hoc vocabulum est coronarum, quas gemmis et foliis ex auro quercinis ob Jovem insignis ad deducendas thensas cum palmatis togis sumunt. Sunt et provinciales aureae, imaginum jam, non virorum, capita majora quaerentes. Sed tui ordines et tui magistratus, et ipsum curiae nomen Ecclesia est Christi. Illius es conscriptus in libris vitae. Illic purpurae tuae sanguis Domini et clavus latus in cruce ipsius; illic securis ad caudicem arboris posita, illic virgae ex Jesse. Viderint et publici equi cum coronis suis. Dominus tuus, ubi secundum Scripturam Jerusalem ingredi voluit, nec asinum habuit privatum. Isti in curribus et isti in equis, nos autem in nomine Domini Dei nostri invocabimus. Ab ipso incolatu Babylonis illius in Apocalypsi Joannis submovemur, nedum a suggestu. Coronatur et vulgus nunc ex principalium prosperitatum exultatione, nunc ex municipalium solemnitatum proprietate: et est omnis publicae laetitiae luxuria captatrix. Sed tu peregrinus mundi hujus, civis supernae Jerusalem. Noster, inquit, municipatus in coelis. Habes tuos sensus, tuos fastos: nihil tibi cum gaudiis saeculi; imo contrarium debes: Saeculum enim gaudebit, vos vero lugebitis. Et puto, felices ait lugentes, non coronatos. Coronant et nuptiae sponsos, ideo non nubamus ethnicis, ne nos ad idolatriam usque deducant, a qua apud illos nuptiae incipiunt: habes legem a Patriarchis quidem, habes apostolum in Domino nubere jubentem. Coronat et libertas saecularis. Sed tu jam redemptus es a Christo, et quidem magno. Servum alienum quomodo saeculum manumittet? Etsi libertas videtur, sed et servitus videbatur. Omnia imaginaria in saeculo, et nihil veri. Nam et tunc liber hominis eras redemptus a Christo: et nunc servus es Christi, licet manumissus ab homine. Si veram putes saeculi libertatem, ut et corona consignes, rediisti in servitutem hominis, quam putes libertatem; amisisti libertatem Christi, quam putas servitutem. Numquid et agonisticae caussae disputabuntur, quas statim tituli sui damnant? et sacras et funebres scilicet, hoc enim superest ut Olympius Jupiter, et Nemaeus Hercules, et misellus Archemorus, et Antinous infelix in Christiano coronentur, ut ipse spectaculum fiat, quod spectare debet. Universas, ut arbitror, caussas enumeravimus. Nec ulla nobiscum est: omnes alienae, profanae, illicitae, semel jam in sacramenti testatione ejeratae. Haec enim erant pompae diaboli et angelorum ejus officia, saeculi honores, solemnitates, popularitates, falsa vota, humana servitia, laudes vanae, gloriae turpes: et in omnibus istis idololatria, in solo quoque sensu coronarum quibus omnia ista redimita sunt. Praefabitur quidem Claudius etiam coelum sideribus apud Homeri carmina coronatum; certe a Deo, certe homini, igitur et homo ipse a Deo coronandus est. Caeterum a saeculo coronantur et lupanaria, et latrinae, et pistrina, et carcer, et ludus, et ipsa amphitheatra, et ipsa spoliaria, ipsaeque libitinae. Quam sacer sanctus, quamque honestus ac mundus sit habitus iste, noli de uno poetico coelo, sed de totius mundi commerciis aestimare. At enim Christianus nec januam suam laureis infamabit, si norit quantos deos etiam ostiis diabolus affinxerit, Janum a janua, Limentinum a limine, Forculum et Cardam a foribus et cardinibus et apud Graecos Thyreum Apollinem et Antelios daemonas.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Keep your reward intact for God; He will crown it if He wishes — indeed, He does wish it, and finally He issues the invitation: 'Whoever conquers, I will give him the crown of life' (Revelation 2:10). You, too, be faithful to death. You, too, fight the good fight, whose crown the Apostle confidently trusts has been laid up for him by merit. The angel of victory also receives a crown, riding forth on a white horse so that he may conquer. Another is adorned with the rainbow's circle, set in a heavenly meadow. The presbyters sit crowned, and with that same gold the Son of Man shines above the cloud. If such are the images in a vision, what must the realities be in their fulfillment? Look at them; smell them. Why do you condemn a head destined for a diadem to a mere wreath or a snake-like band? For Christ Jesus has also made us kings for God and His Father. What do you have to do with a dying flower? You possess a flower from the rod of Jesse, upon whom the whole grace of the divine Spirit has rested — an incorrupt, unwithering, eternal flower — which the good soldier, by choosing it, has advanced in heavenly rank and dignity. Be ashamed, His fellow soldiers: you are now being judged not by Him, but by some soldier of Mithras. When that initiate is inducted in a cave — the camps of true darkness — a crown is offered to him with a sword interposed, a mockery of martyrdom, then fitted to his head. He is warned to shove it away with his hand and, if need be, transfer it to his shoulder, declaring that Mithras is his crown. From then on he is never crowned again, and that very refusal serves as his sign for testing, wherever he may be challenged about the sacrament: instantly the Mithraic soldier is believed if he has thrown away the crown and said it resides in his god. Let us recognize the devil's cunning: he apes certain divine things precisely so he may confuse and condemn us over the faith of his own followers.

latin: Serva Deo rem suam intaminatam. Ille eam, si volet, coronabit; imo et vult; denique invitat: Qui vicerit, inquit, dabo ei coronam vitae. Esto et tu fidelis ad mortem. Decerta et tu bonum agonem, cujus coronam et Apostolus repositam sibi merito confidit. Accipit et angelus victoriae coronam procedens in candido equo, ut vinceret. Et alius iridis ambitu ornatur, coelesti prato. Sedent et presbyteri coronati: eodemque auro et ipse Filius hominis supra nubem micat. Si tales imagines in visione, quales veritates in repraesentatione? illas aspice, illas odora. Quid caput strophiolo aut dracontario damnas, diademati destinatum? Nam et reges nos Deo et Patri suo fecit Christus Jesus. Quid tibi cum flore morituro? Habes florem ex virga Jesse, super quem tota divini spiritus gratia requievit, florem incorruptum, immarcescibilem, sempiternum: quem et bonus miles eligendo, in coelesti ordinatione, dignatione profecit. Erubescite, commilitones ejus, jam non ab ipso judicandi, sed ab aliquo Mithrae milite, qui cum initiatur in spelaeo, in castris vere tenebrarum, coronam interposito gladio sibi oblatam, quasi mimum martyrii, dehinc capiti suo accommodatam, monetur obvia manu a capite pellere, et in humerum, si forte, transferre, dicens Mithram esse coronam suam, atque exinde numquam coronatur, idque in signum habet ad probationem sui, sicubi tentatus fuerit de sacramento: statimque creditur Mithrae miles, si dejecerit coronam, si eam in Deo suo esse dixerit. Agnoscamus ingenia diaboli, idcirco quaedam de divinis affectantis, ut nos de suorum fide confundat et judicet.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We worship one God—the same God everyone knows by nature, whose lightning and thunder make you tremble, whose blessings make you rejoice. You call the others gods as well; we know them for demons. Still, it is a human right and a natural prerogative for each person to worship whatever he chooses; another's religion neither harms nor helps anyone else. But religion is not the business of coercion: true religion must be embraced freely, not forced, because sacrifice is demanded from a willing heart. So even if you compel us to offer sacrifices, you will accomplish nothing for your gods, since they do not accept offerings from unwilling people—unless they are quarrelsome, and God is not quarrelsome. In the end, the true God provides for all equally, both his own and the profane, and for that very reason he has established an eternal judgment to separate the grateful from the ungrateful.

Yet you label us sacrilegious, though you have never caught us in theft, let alone sacrilege. By contrast, every temple robber swears by your gods, worships them, is not a Christian—and yet gets caught in sacrilege. It would take too long to list all the ways your own worshipers ridicule and despise every one of your gods. Likewise we are slandered regarding the Emperor's majesty, but no Christian has ever been found among the Albiniani, the Nigeriani, or the Cassiani. Instead, the very men who swore by the Emperors' guardian spirits, who offered and vowed sacrifices for their safety, who had often condemned Christians—those men turned out to be the Emperors' enemies. A Christian is no one's enemy, much less the Emperor's: knowing that the Emperor was established by his God, a Christian must love, revere, honor him, and pray for his safety along with the whole Roman empire for as long as the world endures—and it will endure that long.

Therefore we honor the Emperor in the only way that is both lawful for us and profitable for him: as a man second only to God, and whatever he possesses as a gift from God, inferior to God alone. That is what the Emperor himself should want, because only by being less than the true God is he greater than all; only by having the so-called gods under his power is he greater than they. So we do offer sacrifice for the Emperor's safety, but to our God and his—and we do it as God commanded, with pure prayer. God, the Creator of the universe, does not need the smell or blood of anything; those are the food of demons. Demons we not only reject, we defeat, we lead away daily, we cast out of human beings, as many people know. That is why we pray all the more effectively for the Emperor's safety, asking it from the One who can actually grant it. And the fact that we act from the discipline of divine patience should be obvious to you: a vast multitude, nearly the majority in every city, lives in silence and modesty, known individually perhaps more than collectively, and recognized only by the reform of their former vices. It is utterly foreign to us to bear suffering unworthily—we desire this suffering—or to devise any vengeance of our own, because we expect justice from God.

latin: Nos unum deum colimus, quem omnes naturaliter nostis, ad cujus fulgura et tonitrua contremiscitis, ad cujus beneficia gaudetis. Caeteros et ipsi putatis deos esse, quos nos daemonas scimus. Tamen humani juris et naturalis potestatis est unicuique, quod putaverit, colere; nec alii obest aut prodest, alterius religio. Sed nec religionis est cogere religionem, quae sponte suscipi debeat, non vi: cum et hostiae ab animo libenti expostulentur. Ita etsi nos compuleritis ad sacrificandum, nihil praestabitis diis vestris: ab invitis enim sacrificia non desiderabunt; nisi si contentiosi sunt; contensiosus autem deus non est. Denique qui est verus, omnia sua ex aequo et profanis et suis praestat. Ideoque et judicium constituit aeternum de gratis et ingratis. Tamen nos, quos sacrilegos existimatis, nec in furto unquam deprehendistis, nedum in sacrilegio. Omnes autem qui templa despoliant, et per deos jurant, et eosdem colunt, et christiani non sunt, et sacrilegi tamen deprehenduntur. Longum est si retexamus, quibus aliis modis et derideantur et contemnantur omnes dii, ab ipsis cultoribus suis. Sic et circa majestatem Imperatoris infamamur, tamen nunquam albiniani, nec nigriani, vel cassani inveniri potuerunt christiani: sed idem ipsi qui per genios eorum in pridie usque juraverunt, qui pro salute eorum hostias et fecerant et voverant, qui christianos saepe damnaverant, hostes eorum sunt reperti. Christianus nullius est hostis, nedum Imperatoris: quem sciens a Deo suo constitui, necesse est ut et ipsum diligat, et revereatur, et honoret, et salvum velit, cum toto romano imperio, quousque saeculum stabit. Tamdiu enim stabit. Colimus ergo et Imperatorem sic, quomodo et nobis licet, et ipsi expedit, ut hominem a Deo secundum, et quicquid est a Deo consecutum, solo Deo minorem. Hoc et ipse volet. Sic enim omnibus major est, dum solo vero Deo minor est: sic et ipsis diis major est, dum et ipsi in potestate sunt ejus. Itaque et sacrificamus pro salute Imperatoris, sed Deo nostro et ipsius: sed quomodo praecepit Deus, pura prece. Non enim eget Deus, conditor universitatis, odoris aut sanguinis alicujus. Haec enim daemoniorum pabula sunt. Daemones autem non tantum respuimus, verum et revincimus, et quotidie traducimus, et de hominibus expellimus, sicut plurimis notum est. Ita nos magis oramus pro salute Imperatoris, ab eo eam postulantes, qui praestare potest. Et utique ex disciplina patientiae divinae agere nos, satis manifestum esse vobis potest, cum tanta hominum multitudo, pars pene major civitatis cujusque, in silentio et modestia agimus, singuli forte noti magis quam omnes: nec aliunde noscibiles quam de emendatione vitiorum pristinorum. Absit enim ut indigne feramus ea nos pati quae optamus, aut ultionem a nobis aliquam machinemur, quam a Deo exspectamus.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english:
We aren't trying to frighten you — you don't scare — but we do want to bring everyone to safety by warning you not to fight against God. You can fulfill the duties of your office and still remember your humanity; after all, you too live under the sword. What exactly does your commission order beyond this: condemn the guilty when they confess, but send those who deny it to the rack? So look at what you're doing: you're acting against your own orders, forcing confessors to recant. That amounts to an admission that we're innocent, since you refuse to condemn us the moment we confess. And if you press on to destroy us, you're attacking innocence itself.

Plenty of governors — sterner and more brutal than you — have quietly looked the other way in cases like this. Cincius Severus once coached the Thystrians on how Christians should answer so they could be released. Vespronius Candidus let a Christian go, telling his citizens the man was a public disturbance. Asper roughed a man up a little, then released him at once and refused to force a sacrifice, having already told his legal advisers and assessors how sick it made him to be handed a case like this. Pudens dismissed a Christian sent to him once he saw the power of the man's eloquence; he tore up the charge sheet and, with no accuser left, refused to hear the case on the governor's orders. All of this can be cited to you both as a matter of official duty and by the very advocates who owe their own careers to Christians, no matter what they shout in court.

Even a notary, thrown down by a demon, was set free; so were relatives, a little boy, and any number of respectable men — I'm not talking about commoners — healed either of demons or of diseases. The emperor Severus, father of Antoninus, honored Christians. He tracked down Proculus, a Christian surnamed Torpacion and procurator of Euhodea, who had once cured him with oil, and kept him in his palace until the man died — a man Antoninus knew well, since he was raised on Christian milk. Severus also knew that many high‑ranking women and men belonged to this sect; he not only refused to harm them but decorated them with honors and publicly shielded them from a mob raging against us. Marcus Aurelius, on his German campaign, got rain for his parched army after Christian soldiers prayed to God. When have our kneeling and fasting ever failed to break a drought? At that moment the crowds themselves, crying out to the God of gods who alone holds power, invoked Jupiter's name and bore witness to our God.

On top of all this, we don't embezzle deposits, we don't violate anyone's marriage, we raise orphans with care, we relieve the needy, we never return evil for evil. Let the liars who slander our sect look to themselves — we disown them. Who brings any other charge against us? What crime does a Christian commit except belonging to this sect? No one has ever proved it incestuous or cruel, not in all this time. For such innocence, such integrity, for justice, chastity, faith, truth, and the living God, we are burned alive — a fate that even sacrilegious criminals, public enemies, and traitors guilty of the worst high treason don't usually suffer. Right now the name is being hunted by the legion's commander and the governor of Mauritania, but only by the sword, just as it was ordered from the beginning that such people be punished. Yet greater struggles bring greater rewards.

latin: Non te terremus, qui nec timemus: sed velim, ut omnes salvos facere possimus, monendo μὴ θεομαχεῖν. Potes et officio jurisdictionis tuae fungi, et humanitatis meminisse, vel quia et vos sub gladio estis. Quid enim amplius tibi mandatur, quam nocentes confessos damnare, negantes autem ad tormenta revocare? Videtis ergo quomodo ipsi vos contra mandata faciatis, ut confessos negare cogatis. Adeo confitemini innocentes esse nos, quos damnare statim ex confessione non vultis. Si autem contenditis ad elidendos nos, jam ergo innocentiam expugnatis. Quanti autem praesides, et constantiores et crudeliores, dissimulaverunt ab hujusmodi caussis! ut Cincius Severus, qui Thystri ipse dedit remedium, quomodo responderent christiani, ut dimitti possent; ut Vespronius Candidus, qui christianum quasi tumultuosum civibus suis satisfacere dimisit; ut Asper, qui modice vexatum hominem, et statim dejectum, nec sacrificium compulit facere, ante professus inter advocatos et adsessores, dolere se incidisse in hanc caussam. Pudens etiam missum ad se christianum in elogio concussione ejus intellecta dimisit, scisso eodem elogio, sine accusatore negans se auditurum hominem secundum mandatum. Haec omnia tibi et de officio suggeri possunt, et ab eisdem advocatis, qui ipsi beneficia habent Christianorum, licet acclament, quae volunt. Nam et cujusdam notarius cum a daemone praecipitaretur, liberatus est: et quorumdam propinquus et puerulus, et quanti honesti viri (de vulgaribus enim non dicimus) aut a daemoniis aut valetudinibus remediati sunt! Ipse etiam Severus pater Antonini, Christianorum memor fuit. Nam et Proculum christianum qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodeae procuratorem, qui eum per oleum aliquando curaverat, requisivit, et in palatio suo habuit usque ad mortem ejus: quem et Antoninus optime noverat lacte christiano educatus. Sed et clarissimas foeminas et clarissimos viros Severus sciens hujus sectae esse, non modo non laesit, verum et testimonio exornavit, et populo furenti in nos palam restitit. Marcus quoque Aurelius in Germanica expeditione christianorum militum orationibus ad Deum factis, imbres in siti illa impetravit. Quando non geniculationibus et jejunationibus nostris etiam siccitates sunt depulsae? Tunc et populus acclamans Deo deorum, qui solus potens, in Jovis nomine Deo nostro testimonium reddidit. Praeter haec depositum non abnegamus, matrimonium nullius adulteramus, pupillos pie tractamus, indigentibus refrigeramus, nulli malum pro malo reddimus. Viderint, qui sectam mentiuntur, quos et ipsi recusamus. Quis denique de nobis alio nomine queritur? quod aliud negotium patitur christianus, nisi suae sectae? quam incestam, quam crudelem, tanto tempore nemo probavit. Pro tanta innocentia, pro tanta probitate, pro justitia, pro pudicitia, pro fide, pro veritate, pro Deo vivo, cremamur; quod nec sacrilegi, nec hostes publici, verum nec tot majestatis rei pati solent. Nam et nunc a praeside legionis, et a praeside Mauritaniae vexatur hoc nomen, sed gladio tenus, sicut et a primordio mandatum est animadverti in hujusmodi. Sed majora certamina, majora sequuntur praemia.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Your cruelty is our glory. Just make sure that by enduring this, we do not appear to be rushing forward simply to prove that we do not fear these things but actually invite them. When Arrius Antoninus was persecuting Christians in Asia, every Christian in that city presented themselves at his tribunal. After he ordered a few to be led away, he told the rest, "You wretches, if you want to die, you have cliffs and ropes." If you intend the same here, what will you do with so many thousands of men and women, of every sex, age, and rank, offering themselves to you? How many fires, how many swords will you need? What will become of Carthage itself, decimated by you, when each person recognizes their own relatives and comrades there, perhaps even men and women of your own order, leading citizens, and the friends or kin of your own friends? Spare yourself, if not us; spare Carthage, if not yourself; spare the province, which your policy has left exposed to extortion by soldiers and enemies alike. We have no master but God alone. He stands before you, and cannot be hidden, yet you can do nothing to Him. As for those you take for masters, they are mere mortals who will die someday. Yet this sect will not perish; you can see it grows precisely when it seems to be cut down. For anyone who witnesses such endurance is pricked by conscience, driven to investigate the cause, and upon finding the truth, immediately follows.

latin: Crudelitas vestra gloria est nostra. Vide tantum ne hoc ipso, quod talia sustinemus, ad hoc solum videamur erumpere, ut hoc ipsum probemus, nos haec non timere, sed ultro vocare. Arrius Antoninus in Asia cum persequeretur instanter, omnes illius civitatis christiani ante tribunalia ejus se manu facta obtulerunt, cum ille, paucis duci jussis, reliquis ait, ὧ δεῖλοι, εἰ θέλετε ἀποθνήσκειν, κρημνοὺς ἢ βρόχους ἔχετε. Hoc si placuerit et hic fieri, quid facies de tantis millibus hominum, tot viris ac foeminis, omnis sexus, omnis aetatis, omnis dignitatis, offerentibus se tibi? Quantis ignibus, quantis gladiis opus erit! quid ipsa Carthago passura est, decimanda a te, cum propinquos, cum contubernales suos illic unusquisque cognoverit, cum viderit illic fortasse et tui ordinis viros et matronas, et principales quasque personas, et amicorum tuorum vel propinquos vel amicos? Parce ergo tibi, si non nobis, parce Carthagini, si non tibi, parce provinciae, quae visa intentione tua obnoxia facta est concussionibus et militum et inimicorum suorum cujusque. Magistrum neminem habemus, nisi Deum solum. Hic ante te est, nec abscondi potest, sed cui nihil facere possis. Caeterum quos putas tibi magistros, homines sunt et ipsi morituri quandoque. Nec tamen deficiet haec secta, quam tunc magis aedificari scias, cum caedi videtur. Quisque enim tantam tolerantiam spectans, ut aliquo scrupulo percussus, et inquirere accenditur, quid sit in causa, et ubi cognoverit veritatem, et ipse statim sequitur.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: He will declare in the church's preaching that the message concerning God's righteous anointing is contained there, and this message, once believed true, urges people to live well and to flee sin in every way, precisely so that we may take up for ourselves the most necessary problem—that we possess it. In order to understand what the self-moved is, one must develop its concept, so that once it is clarified, the question at hand may be set forth precisely. Of things that move, some have the cause of their motion within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Objects that are carried—such as wood, stones, and all matter held together solely by habit—are moved only from outside. Let the discussion of bodily motion be set aside for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals and plants, and in general all things held together by nature or soul, have the cause of their motion within themselves; some say metals belong to this group, and in addition fire is self-moved, and perhaps springs as well. Among things that have the cause of motion in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves: the non-living from outside themselves, the living from themselves. The living are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs and provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with nature having arranged the fantasy so as to move the impulse in a fixed way, as in the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, its fantasy nature having arranged it for this very thing, with no other thing believed by the animal after its fantasy, and in the bee for shaping wax. The rational animal, however, also possesses reason alongside its fantasy nature, reason that evaluates fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since there are starting points in the nature of reason for contemplating the good and the bad, by following them we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good and turn away from the bad; we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to practicing the good, blameworthy when we do the opposite. It must not be overlooked, however, that the greater part of the nature ordered in all things exists quantitatively in animals, and for the most part or for the lesser part, so that it is near, one might say, the work of the rational in tracking dogs and war horses. Submitting to something external that moves a fantasy in us this way or that is admittedly not in our power; but to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us, whether it operates in us according to the starting points that urge us toward the good and toward duty, or turns us away toward the opposite.

english: An excellent thing has silence proved itself in many another person on many an occasion, and at present it befits myself, too, most especially, who with or without purpose may keep the door of my lips, and feel constrained to be silent. For I am unpractised and unskilled in those beautiful and elegant addresses which are spoken or composed in a regular and unbroken train, in select and well-chosen phrases and words; and it may be that I am less apt by nature to cultivate successfully this graceful and truly Grecian art.

Besides, it is now eight years since I chanced myself to utter or compose any speech, whether long or short; neither in that period have I heard any other compose or utter anything in private, or deliver in public any laudatory or controversial orations, with the exception of those admirable men who have embraced the noble study of philosophy , and who care less for beauty of language and elegance of expression. For, attaching only a secondary importance to the words, they aim, with all exactness, at investigating and making known the things themselves, precisely as they are severally constituted. Not indeed, in my opinion, that they: do not desire, but rather that they do greatly desire, to clothe the noble and accurate results of their thinking in noble and comely language.

Yet it may be that they are not able so lightly to put forth this sacred and godlike power (faculty) in the exercise of its own proper conceptions, and at the same time to practise a mode of discourse eloquent in its terms, and thus to comprehend in one and the same mind — and that, too, this little mind of man — two accomplishments, which are the gifts of two distinct persons , and which are, in truth , most contrary to each other. For silence is indeed the friend and helpmeet of thought and invention. But if one aims at readiness of speech and beauty of discourse, he will get at them by no other discipline than the study of words, and their constant practice.

Moreover, another branch of learning occupies my mind completely, and the mouth binds the tongue if I should desire to make any speech, however brief, with the voice of the Greeks; I refer to those admirable laws of our sages by which the affairs of all the subjects of the Roman Empire are now directed, and which are neither composed nor learned without difficulty. And these are wise and exact in themselves, and manifold and admirable, and, in a word, most thoroughly Grecian; and they are expressed and committed to us in the Roman tongue, which is a wonderful and magnificent sort of language, and one very aptly conformable to royal authority, but still difficult to me. Nor could it be otherwise with me, even though I might say that it was my desire that it should be.
