excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — An Address to Demetrianus An Address to Demetrianus
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: I had long held you in contempt, Demetrius, because with sacrilegious mouth and impious words you frequently railed against the one true God. I thought it more reverent and better to pass over the ignorance of a wanderer in silence than to provoke a madman’s insanity by speaking. And I did not act without divine authority, since it is written: “Do not speak in the ears of a fool, lest he despise the wisdom of your words” (Prov. 9:7–8). And again: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself” (Prov. 9:7–8). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our own conscience and not to throw pearls before swine and dogs, for the Lord said: “Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you” (Matt. 7:6). For you often came to me more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud clamor you chose to force your own views on me rather than listen patiently to mine. It seemed pointless to engage you, because it would be easier to calm the raging waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your fury with reason. To offer light to the blind, speech to the deaf, wisdom to a brute beast is labor in vain and without effect; a beast cannot perceive, a blind man cannot receive light, a deaf man cannot hear. Weighing this, I often kept silent and overcame your impatience with my patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious by religion, nor calm the raging by gentleness.

But now you claim that many complain that wars break out more frequently, that plagues and famines rage, and that the long fair weather has given way to rains and showers — and that all this is to be laid at our door because your gods are not worshiped by us. If I stayed silent any longer it would look not like reverence but like fear, and by refusing to refute false accusations we would seem to admit the charge. So I answer you, Demetrius, and equally the others you may have stirred up, who with your slanderous voices have sown hatred against us and gathered many companions from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reason of our words: whoever is driven to evil by the deceit of falsehood will be driven much more to good by the compulsion of truth.

You say these disasters happen through us and must be imputed to us because your gods are not worshiped by us. On this point, since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you must first understand that the world has grown old. It no longer stands with the powers it once had, nor does it prevail with the vigor and strength it formerly possessed. Even if we kept silent and produced no testimonies from the holy Scriptures or divine preaching, the world itself now speaks and testifies to its own decline by the evidence of failing things. The winter rains are no longer so abundant to nourish the seed; the summer sun no longer burns so fiercely to ripen the fruit; spring crops are no longer so joyful, autumn no longer so fruitful with the produce of the trees. Less and less marble is quarried from the excavated and exhausted mountains; less and less silver and gold is yielded by mines now drained; the poor veins shrink day by day and dwindle. The farmer fails in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp; innocence fails in the forum, justice in the courts, concord in friendships, skill in the arts, discipline in morals.

Do you think a thing that is aging can still possess the substance it had when it was new and in vigorous youth? Whatever is already near its end and declining into its final stages must necessarily diminish. Thus the sun at its setting casts rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus the moon, its course declining, wanes with worn-out horns; and a tree once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed by withered branches in sterile old age. A spring that once flowed abundantly from overflowing veins, failing with age, barely drips a thin trickle. This sentence has been passed on the world; this is the law of God: that all things that arise will decline, all that grow will grow old, the strong will be weakened, the great diminished, and when weakened and diminished they will come to an end.

You blame Christians because individual things decrease while the world grows old. What if the elderly also blamed Christians because they are less strong in old age — because they do not thrive as before in hearing, in running, in sharpness of sight, in robustness of strength, in the moisture of their viscera, in the mass of their limbs? Human life once lasted eight or nine hundred years; now it can hardly reach a hundred. We see gray hair in children; hair falls out before it grows. Age does not end in old age; it begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, nativity hastens toward its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates with the old age of the world itself. No one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

latin: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.

english: Most beloved brothers, peace has been restored to the Church, and what seemed impossible to unbelievers and the faithless only a short time ago—our security—has been rebuilt by God's help and judgment. Our minds return to joy; now that the storm of oppression has blown over and the cloud has scattered, tranquility and serenity shine forth once more. We must give praise to God and celebrate his benefits and gifts with thanksgiving, even though our voice never stopped giving thanks even during the persecution. After all, the enemy cannot prevent those who love the Lord with all their heart, soul, and strength from proclaiming his blessings and praises with glory always and everywhere. The day that everyone longed for has arrived, and after the horrible, dark gloom of a long night, the world has blazed forth, radiant with the Lord's light.

We look upon the confessors—renowned for their good name and glorious for their virtues and faith—with joyful eyes, clinging to them with holy kisses, embracing those we have longed for with an insatiable desire. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers stands here, men who broke the fierce, turbulent fury of persecution by standing their ground, ready for the endurance of prison, armed for the endurance of death. You resisted the world bravely; you offered a glorious spectacle to God; you became an example for the brothers who would follow. A religious voice spoke Christ, confessing that it had believed in him once and for all. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, refused to take part in sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, having received the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your heads remained free of the impious, wicked veil that covered the heads of the captive sacrificers. Your foreheads, marked pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil's crown; they reserved themselves for the Lord's crown. How joyfully Mother Church welcomes you as you return from battle! How blessed and rejoicing she is as she opens her gates so that you may enter with gathered ranks, bringing back trophies from the prostrate enemy!

Women come alongside the triumphant men, women who, fighting against the world, also overcame their sex. Virgins come too, bearing the double glory of their military service, and boys who surpassed their years through virtue. The rest of the great multitude of those who stood firm follows your glory as well; with signs of praise close to your own and almost joined to them, they walk in your footsteps. The same sincerity of heart and the same tenacious integrity of faith are in them. Rooted in the unshaken roots of heavenly precepts and strengthened by the traditions of the Gospel, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, loss of property, or bodily punishments. The days for testing faith had been set. But the one who remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world; nor does the one who hopes for eternity from God calculate earthly times any longer.

No one, most beloved brothers—no one must mutilate this glory; no one must weaken the incorrupt firmness of those who stood firm with malicious detraction. When the appointed day for those who denied had passed, whoever had not confessed within that day confessed himself to be a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to be kept safe for the Lord by a cautious withdrawal. The former is public confession, the latter private. The former conquers the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, guards a pure conscience with integrity of heart. There, fortitude is more prompt; here, caution is more secure. There, the man whose hour was approaching was already found mature; here, perhaps the one who was delayed, having abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he was not going to deny—he certainly would have confessed if he had also been detained.

A single sorrow afflicts these heavenly crowns of martyrs, these spiritual glories of confessors, these greatest and most excellent virtues of the brothers who stood firm: the violent enemy has cast down a torn part of our very bowels through the slaughter of his rampage. What am I to do here, most beloved brothers? My mind tossed by a varied storm, what can I say, or how can I say it? Tears are needed more than words to express the grief with which we must lament the wound of our body, and mourn the manifold loss of a once numerous people. For who is so hard or iron-hearted, who has so forgotten fraternal charity, that standing amid the multiform ruins and the mournful, squalid remnants of his own, he can keep his eyes dry, and not, with tears bursting forth at once, pour out his groans first in tears rather than in voice? I grieve, brothers; I grieve with you. My own integrity and private health do not comfort me in alleviating my griefs, when the shepherd is wounded more deeply in the wound of his flock. My heart is joined to each one of you; I share the mournful weights of sorrow and funeral. I mourn with those who mourn, I lament with those who lament, I feel that I lie down with those who lie down. The darts of the raging enemy have struck my limbs at the same time; savage swords have passed through my bowels. The mind cannot be immune and free from the onslaught of persecution. In my fallen brothers, affection has laid me low as well.

latin: PAX ecce, dilectissimi fratres, Ecclesiae reddita est et, quod difficile nuper incredulis ac perfidis impossibile videbatur, ope atque ultione divina securitas nostra reparata est. In laetitiam mentes redeunt, et, tempestate pressurae ac nube discussa, tranquillitas ac serenitas refulserunt. Dandae laudes Deo, et beneficia ejus ac munera cum gratiarum actione celebranda, quamvis agere gratias nostra vox nec in persecutione cessaverit. Neque enim tantum inimico licere potest ut non, qui Dominum toto corde et anima et virtute diligimus, benedictiones ejus et laudes semper et ubique cum gloria praedicemus. Exoptatus votis omnium dies venit, et, post longae noctis horribilem tetramque caliginem, Domini luce radiatus mundus eluxit. Confessores, praeconio boni nominis claros et virtutis ac fidei laudibus gloriosos, laetis conspectibus intuemur, sanctis osculis adhaerentes, desideratos diu inexplebili cupiditate complectimur. Adest militum Christi cohors candida, qui persecutionis urgentus ferociam turbulentam stabili congressione fregerunt, parati ad patientiam carceris, armati ad tolerantiam mortis. Repugnastis fortiter saeculo, spectaculum gloriosum praebuistis Deo, secuturis fratribus fuistis exemplo. Religiosa vox Christum locuta est, in quem se semel credidisse confessa est. Illustres manus, quae non nisi divinis operibus assueverant, sacrificiis sacrilegis restiterunt. Sanctificata ora coelestibus cibis, post corpus et sanguinem Domini, profana contagia et idolorum reliquias respuerunt. Ab impio sceleratoque velamine, quo illic velabantur sacrificantium capita captiva, caput vestrum liberum mansit. Frons cum signo Dei pura, diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reservavit. Quam vos laete sinu suo excipit mater Ecclesia de praelio revertentes! quam beata, quam gaudens portas suas aperit, ut adunatis agminibus intretis, de hoste prostrato trophaea referentes! Cum triumphantibus viris et feminae veniunt, quae cum saeculo dimicantes, sexum quoque vicerunt. Veniunt et geminata militiae suae gloria virgines, et pueri annos suos virtutibus transeuntes. Necnon et caetera stantium multitudo vestram gloriam sequitur, proximis et pene conjunctis laudis insignibus vestigia vestra comitatur. Eadem et in illis sinceritas cordis, eadem fidei tenacis integritas. Inconcussis praeceptorum coelestium radicibus nixos et evangelicis traditionibus roboratos, non praescripta exilia, non destinata tormenta, non rei familiaris damna, non corporis supplicia terruerunt. Explorandae fidei praefiniebantur dies. Sed qui saeculo renuntiasse se meminit, nullum saeculi diem novit; nec tempora terrena jam computat qui aeternitatem de Deo sperat. Nemo, fratres dilectissimi, nemo hanc gloriam mutilet, nemo incorruptam stantium firmitatem maligna obtrectatione debilitet. Cum dies negantibus praestitutus excessit, quisquis professus intra diem non est, Christianum se esse confessus est. Primus est victoriae titulus, gentilium manibus apprehensum Dominum confiteri: secundus ad gloriam gradus est cauta secessione subtractum Domino reservari. Illa publica, haec privata confessio est. Ille judicem saeculi vincit, hic contentus Deo suo judice conscientiam puram cordis integritate custodit. Illic, fortitudo promptior, hic sollicitudo securior. Ille appropinquante hora sua, jam maturus inventus est; hic fortasse dilatus est qui, patrimonio derelicto, idcirco secessit quia non erat negaturus: confiteretur utique si fuisset et ipse detentus. Has martyrum coelestes coronas, has confessorum glorias spiritales, has stantium fratrum maximas eximiasque virtutes moestitia una contristat, quod avulsam nostrorum viscerum partem violentus inimicus populationis suae strage dejecit. Quid hoc loco faciam, dilectissimi fratres? fluctuans vario mentis aestu, quid aut quomodo dicam? Lacrymis magis quam verbis opus est ad exprimendum dolorem quo corporis nostri plaga deflenda est, quo populi aliquando numerosi multiplex lamentanda jactura est. Quis enim sic durus aut ferreus, quis sic fraternae charitatis oblitus, qui inter suorum multiformes ruinas et lugubres ac multo squalore deformes reliquias constitutus siccos oculos tenere praevaleat, nec, erumpente statim fletu, prius gemitus suos lacrymis quam voce depromat? Doleo, fratres, doleo vobiscum, nec mihi ad leniendos dolores meos integritas propria et sanitas privata blanditur, quando plus pastor in gregis sui vulnere vulneretur. Cum singulis pectus meum copulo, moeroris et funeris pondera luctuosa participo. Cum plangentibus plango, cum deflentibus defleo, cum jacentibus jacere me credo. Jaculis illis grassantis inimici mea simul membra percussa sunt, saevientes gladii per mea viscera transierunt. Immunis et liber a persecutionis incursu fuisse non potest animus. In prostratis fratribus et me prostravit affectus.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Although among many of you, my dearest brothers, the mind is solid, faith firm, and the soul devoted—unmoved by the present onslaught of death, but like a strong, stable rock breaking the world’s turbulent assaults and the violent waves of the age without being broken itself, unconquered by temptations and instead proven by them—nevertheless, because I see among the common people some who, whether from weakness of mind, smallness of faith, the sweetness of secular life, softness of sex, or, what is worse, error of the truth, stand less firmly and do not exercise the divine, invincible strength of their heart, this matter could not be hidden nor left unspoken. So, as far as my mediocrity suffices, with full vigor and a sermon drawn from the Lord’s reading, the laziness of a delicate mind may be suppressed, and he who has already begun to be a man of God and of Christ may be held worthy of God and of Christ.

For he who fights for God ought to recognize himself, my dearest brothers—he who, placed in the heavenly camp, already hopes for the divine—so that there may be no trepidation in us, no disturbance, when the Lord, with the exhortation of a provident voice, instructing, teaching, preparing, and strengthening his Church’s people for all endurance of future things, foretold and declared that wars, fires, earthquakes, and pestilences would arise in various places (Luke 21:10–11). And lest the unexpected, new fear of surrounding evils disturb us, he forewarned that adversities would increase more and more in the last times (2 Timothy 3:1). Behold, the things that were said are happening; and when the things predicted beforehand come to pass, the things that were promised will also follow, the Lord himself promising and saying: ‘When you see all these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near’ (Luke 21:31). The kingdom of God, my dearest brothers, has begun to draw near. The reward of life and the joy of eternal salvation, perpetual security, and the possession of paradise, recently lost, are now coming as the world passes away; now heavenly things succeed earthly ones, great things small, eternal things transient.

What place is there here for anxiety and worry? Who is troubled and sad among these things, except the one who lacks hope and faith? For it belongs to the one who fears death to be unwilling to go to Christ. It belongs to the one unwilling to go to Christ not to believe that he will begin to reign with Christ. For it is written: ‘The just shall live by faith’ (Habakkuk 2:4). If you are just and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why do you not, as you are about to be with Christ, embrace the Lord’s promise with confidence, and rejoice that you will be free of the devil?

Consider Simeon, that just man who was truly just, who kept God’s commandments with full faith. When he had received a divine response that he would not die before he saw Christ, and Christ came to the temple as an infant with his mother, he recognized in the Spirit that the Christ had been born, the one foretold to him beforehand (Luke 2:25–32); and when he saw him, he knew he would soon die. Therefore, rejoicing at his approaching death and secure in his near summons, he took the child in his hands, blessed the Lord, and exclaimed: ‘Lord, now you let your servant depart in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation’ (Luke 2:29–30)—proving and testifying that peace belongs to the servants of God, then freedom, then tranquil rest, when, extracted from the world’s turmoils, we seek the harbor of eternal security, when, having finished this death, we come to immortality. For that is the true peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable, firm, and perpetual security.

Moreover, what else is the world but a daily battle against the devil, a constant conflict against his darts and arrows? We confront avarice, impurity, anger, ambition; we struggle incessantly and painfully with carnal vices and secular allurements. The human mind, besieged and hemmed in on all sides by the devil’s infestation, can hardly meet each attack, hardly resist. If avarice is prostrated, lust rises; if lust is suppressed, ambition succeeds; if ambition is despised, anger inflames, pride swells, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, jealousy severs friendship. You will be forced to curse what the divine law prohibits, compelled to swear what is not allowed.

latin: Etsi apud plurimos vestrum, fratres dilectissimi, mens solida est et fides firma et anima devota, quae ad praesentis mortalitatis copiam non movetur, sed tamquam petra fortis et stabilis turbidos impetus mundi et violentos saeculi fluctus frangit potius ipsa nec frangitur, et tentationibus non vincitur, sed probatur, tamen quia animadverto in plebe quosdam vel imbecillitate animi, vel fidei parvitate, vel dulcedine saecularis vitae, vel sexus mollitie, vel, quod majus est, veritatis errore minus stare fortiter nec pectoris sui divinum atque invictum robur exercere, dissimulanda res non fuit nec tacenda quo minus quantum nostra mediocritas sufficit, vigore pleno et sermone de dominica lectione concepto delicatae mentis ignavia comprimatur, et qui homo Dei et Christi esse jam coepit, Deo et Christo dignus habeatur. Agnoscere enim se debet, fratres dilectissimi, qui Deo militat, qui positus in coelestibus castris divinam jam sperat, ut ad procellas et turbines mundi trepidatio nulla sit in nobis, nulla turbatio, quando haec ventura praedixerit Dominus providae vocis hortatu instruens et docens et praeparans atque corroborans Ecclesiae suae populum ad omnem tolerantiam futurorum, bella et fumes et terrae motus et pestilentias per loca singula exsurgere praenuntiavit et cecinit. Et ne inopinatus nos et novus rerum infestantium metus quateret, magis ac magis in novissimis temporibus adversa crebrescere ante praemonuit. Fiunt ecce quae dicta sunt; et quando fiunt quae ante praedicta sunt, sequentur et quaecumque promissa sunt, Domino ipso pollicente et dicente: Cum autem videritis haec omnia fieri, scitote quoniam in proximo est regnum Dei.. Regnum Dei, fratres dilectissimi, esse coepit in proximo. Praemium vitae et gaudium salutis aeternae, et perpetua securitas, et possessio paradisi nuper amissa, mundo transeunte jam veniunt; jam terrenis coelestia et magna parvis et caducis aeterna succedunt. Quis hic anxietatis et sollicitudinis locus est? Quis inter haec trepidus et moestus est, nisi cui spes et fides deest? Ejus est enim mortem timere qui ad Christum nolit ire. Ejus est ad Christum nolle ire qui se non credat cum Christo incipere regnare. Scriptum est enim justum fide vivere. Si justus es, et fide vivis, si vere in Christum credis, cur non cum Christo futurus et de Domini pollicitatione securus quod ad Christum voceris amplecteris, et quod diabolo careas gratularis. Simeon denique ille justus, qui vere justus fuit, qui fide plena Dei praecepta servavit, dum ei divinitus responsum fuisset quod non ante moreretur quam Christum vidisset, et Christus infans in templum cum matre venisset, agnovit in Spiritu natum esse jam Christum, de quo sibi fuerat ante praedictum; quo viso, scivit se cito esse moriturum. Laetus itaque de morte jam proxima, et de vicina accersitione securus, accepit in manus puerum, et benedicens Dominum exclamavit et dixit: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secuudum verbum tuum in pace, quoniam viderunt oculi mei salutare tuum; probans scilicet atque contestans tunc esse servis Dei pacem, tunc liberam, tunc tranquillam quietem, quando, de istis mundi turbinibus extracti, sedis et securitatis aeternae portum petimus, quando expuncta hac morte ad immortalitatem venimus. Illa est enim vera pax, illa fida tranquillitas, illa stabilis et firma et perpetua securitas. Caeterum, quid aliud in mundo, quam pugna adversus diabolum, quotidie geritur, quam adversus jacula ejus et tela conflictationibus assiduis dimicatur? Cum avaritia nobis, cum impudicitia, cum ira, cum ambitione congressio est, cum carnalibus vitiis, cum illecebris saecularibus assidua et molesta luctatio est. Obsessa mens hominis et undique diaboli infestatatione vallata vix occurrit singulis, vix resistit. Si avaritia prostrata est, exsurgit libido: si libido compressa est, succedit ambitio: si ambitio contempta est, ira exasperat, inflat superbia, vinolentia invitat, invidia concordiam rumpit, amicitiam zelus abscindit. Cogeris maledicere quod divina lex prohibet, compelleris jurare quod non licet.

english: We can see from this that the gods the common people worship do not exist. There were once kings who, because their subjects wanted to preserve the royal memory, began to be worshiped even after death. That is how temples were founded for them, and how images were carved to keep the faces of the dead before the living. People offered sacrifices and celebrated festival days to honor them. In time, these practices became sacred rites for later generations, though they began as consolations for the first mourners. Let us test whether this same pattern holds true in individual cases.

Melicertes and Leucothea were thrown into the sea and afterward became sea deities. The Castors die on alternate days so that they may live. Aesculapius was struck by lightning so that he might rise to the rank of a god. Hercules was burned on the fires of Mount Oeta so that he might shed his mortal nature. Apollo herded cattle for Admetus. Neptune built walls for Laomedon, yet the unhappy builder never received his wages. People still visit the cave of Jupiter in Crete, and his tomb is shown there; it is also clear that Saturn fled from him. Latium took its name from that hiding place. Saturn was the first to introduce the practice of minting coins and stamping letters in Italy; that is why the treasury bears his name. He also cultivated the rustic life, which is why he is depicted as an old man carrying a sickle. Janus welcomed this fugitive with hospitality; the Janiculum hill is named after him, and the month of January was instituted in his honor. Janus is portrayed with two faces because, standing at the midpoint of the year, he appears to look at both the year beginning and the year ending.

The Moors openly worship kings, making no attempt to disguise the fact. Consequently, the religion of the gods varies from nation to nation and province to province, since no single god is worshiped by all; instead, each people preserves the ancestral cult of its own forebears. Alexander the Great attests to this in a remarkable letter to his mother. He writes that a priest, terrified of Alexander's power, betrayed a secret about the gods: the memory of ancestors and kings was preserved, and from that preservation the rites of worship and sacrifice arose.

But if the gods were ever born, why are they not still being born today? Unless, perhaps, Jupiter has grown old, or childbirth has failed in Juno. Why do you suppose the gods can help the Romans when you see they could do nothing to save their own people against enemy arms? We know the Roman gods are homegrown. Romulus became a god through the perjury of Proculus. So did Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, and Consus — whom Romulus wanted worshiped as the god of fraud, or else as the god of counsel, after his treachery in the abduction of the Sabine women was exposed. Tatius discovered and worshiped the goddess Cloacina. Hostilius worshiped Fear and Pallor. Later, Fever was dedicated by someone unknown, along with Acca and Flora, who were prostitutes. Sometimes the Romans even invent divine names: there is a god Viduus, who severs the soul from the body; considered funereal and mournful, he is not admitted within the walls. Yet because he is an outcast, Roman religion condemns him rather than worships him. There is also Scansus, named from ascents; Forculus, from doors; Limentinus, from thresholds; Cardea, from hinges; and Orbona, from childlessness. These are the Roman gods.

Beyond them, Mars is Thracian, Jupiter is Cretan, Juno is either Argive, Samian, or Carthaginian, Diana is Taurian, the Mother of the Gods is Idaean, and the Egyptian portents are not divine powers at all — if they had any power, they would have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their people. Clearly, the Romans also possess conquered household gods, which the fugitive Aeneas brought with him. And there is Venus, depicted as bald — far more shamefully bald here than when Homer merely shows her wounded.

latin: Deos non esse quos colit vulgus hinc notum est. Reges olim fuerunt, qui ob regalem memoriam coli apud suos postmodum etiam in morte coeperunt. Inde illis instituta templa, inde, ad defunctorum vultus per imaginem detinendos, expressa simulacra; et immolabant hostias, et dies festos dando honore celebrabant. Inde posteris facta sunt sacra, quae primis fuerant assumpta solatia. Et videamus an stet haec apud singulos veritas. Melicertes et Leucothea praecipitantur in maria, et fiunt postmodum maris numina. Castores alternis moriuntur ut vivant. Aesculapius ut in Deum surgat fulminatur. Hercules ut hominem exuat Oeteis ignibus concrematur. Apollo Admeti pecus pavit. Laomedonti muros Neptunus instituit, nec mercedem operis infelix structor accepit. Antrum Jovis in Creta visitur, et sepulchrum ejus ostenditur, et ab eo Saturnum fugatum esse manifestum est. Inde Latium de latebra ejus nomen accepit. Hic litteras imprimere, hic signare nummos in Italia primus instituit: inde aerarium Saturni vocatur. Et rusticitatis hic cultor fuit: inde falcem ferens senex pingitur. Hunc fugatum hospitio Janus exceperat; de cujus nomine Janiculum dictum est, et mensis Januarius institutus est. Ipse bifrons exprimitur, quod, in medio constitutus, annum incipientem pariter et recedentem spectare videatur. Mauri vero manifeste reges colunt, nec ullo velamento hoc nomen obtexunt. Inde per gentes et provincias singulas varia deorum religio mutatur, dum non unus ab omnibus deus colitur, sed propria cuique majorum suorum cultura servatur. Hoc ita Alexander Magnus insigni volumine ad matrem suam scribit metu suae potestatis proditum sibi de diis hominibus a sacerdote secretum, quod majorum et regum memoria servata sit, inde colendi et sacrificandi ritus inoleverit. Si autem aliquando dii nati sunt, cur non hodieque nascuntur? nisi si forte Jupiter senuit, aut partus in Junone defecit. Cur vero deos putas pro Romanis posse, quos videas nihil pro suis adversus eorum arma valuisse? Romanorum enim vernaculos deos novimus. Est Romulus pejerante Proculo deus factus, et Picus, et Tiberinus, et Pilumnus, et Consus, quem Deum fraudis vel ut consiliorum deum, coli Romulus voluit postquam in raptum Sabinarum perfidia provenit. Deam quoque Cloacinam Tatius et invenit et coluit, Pavorem Hostilius atque Pallorem. Mox a nescio quo Febris dedicata, et Acca et Flora meretrices. [Interdum vero deorum vocabula apud Romanos finguntur, ut sit apud illos et Viduus deus, qui anima corpus viduet, qui quasi feralis et funebris intra muros non habetur; et nihilominus, quia extorris factus, damnatur potius Romana religione, quam colitur. Est et Scansus ab ascensibus dictus, et Forculus a foribus, et a liminaribus Limentinus, et Cardea a cardinibus et ab orbitatibus Orbona]. Hi dii Romani. Caeterum Mars Thracius, et Jupiter Creticus, et Juno vel Argiva vel Samia vel Poena, et Diana Taurica, et deorum mater Idaea, et Aegyptia portenta, non numina: quae utique si quid potestatis habuissent, sua ac suorum regna servassent. Plane sunt apud Romanos et victi penates, quos Aeneas profugus advexit. Est et Venus calva, multo hic turpius calva quam apud Homerum vulnerata.

english: 1. In Opposition to Those of the School of Epicurus Who Deny the Existence of a Providence, and Refer the Constitution of the Universe to Atomic Bodies. Is the universe one coherent whole, as it seems to be in our own judgment, as well as in that of the wisest of the Greek philosophers , such as Plato and Pythagoras, and the Stoics and Heraclitus? Or is it a duality, as some may possibly have conjectured? Or is it indeed something manifold and infinite , as has been the opinion of certain others who, with a variety of mad speculations and fanciful usages of terms, have sought to divide and resolve the essential matter of the universe , and lay down the position that it is infinite and unoriginated, and without the sway of Providence? For there are those who, giving the name of atoms to certain imperishable and most minute bodies which are supposed to be infinite in number, and positing also the existence of a certain vacant space of an unlimited vastness, allege that these atoms, as they are borne along casually in the void, and clash all fortuitously against each other in an unregulated whirl, and become commingled one with another in a multitude of forms, enter into combination with each other, and thus gradually form this world and all objects in it; yea, more, that they construct infinite worlds. This was the opinion of Epicurus and Democritus; only they differed in one point, in so far as the former supposed these atoms to be all most minute and consequently…

2. A Refutation of This Dogma on the Ground of Familiar Human Analogies. How, shall we bear with these men who assert that all those wise, and consequently also noble, constructions (in the universe ) are only the works of common chance? Those objects, I mean, of which each taken by itself as it is made, and the whole system collectively, were seen to be good by Him by whose command they came into existence . For, as it is said, God saw everything that He had made, and, behold, it was very good. Genesis 1:31 But truly these men do not reflect on the analogies even of small familiar things which might come under their observation at any time, and from which they might learn that no object of any utility, and fitted to be serviceable, is made without design or by mere chance, but is wrought by skill of hand, and is contrived so as to meet its proper use. And when the object falls out of service and becomes useless, then it also begins to break up indeterminately, and to decompose and dissipate its materials in every casual and unregulated way, just as the wisdom by which it was skilfully constructed at first no longer controls and maintains it. For a cloak, for example, cannot be made without the weaver, as if the warp could be set aright and the woof could be entwined with it by their own spontaneous action; while, on the other hand, if it is once worn out, its tattered rags are flung aside. Again, when a house or a city is built, it does not take on its stones, as if some of…

3. A Refutation on the Ground of the Constitution of the Universe. Or who can bear to hear it maintained, that this mighty habitation, which is constituted of heaven and earth, and which is called Cosmos on account of the magnitude and the plenitude of the wisdom which has been brought to bear upon it, has been established in all its order and beauty by those atoms which hold their course devoid of order and beauty, and that that same state of disorder has grown into this true Cosmos, Order? Or who can believe that those regular movements and courses are the products of a certain unregulated impetus? Or who can allow that the perfect concord subsisting among the celestial bodies derives its harmony from instruments destitute both of concord and harmony? Or, again, if there is but one and the same substance in all things, and if there is the same incorruptible nature in all — the only elements of difference being, as they aver, size and figure — how comes it that there are some bodies divine and perfect, and eternal , as they would phrase it, or lasting, as some one may prefer to express it; and among these some that are visible and others that are invisible — the visible including such as sun, and moon, and stars, and earth, and water; and the invisible including gods, and demons , and spirits? For the existence of such they cannot possibly deny however desirous to do so. And again, there are other objects that are long-lived, both animals and plants. As to animals, there…

4. A Refutation of the Same on the Grounds of the Human Constitution. Further, those men understand neither themselves nor what is proper to themselves. For if any of the leaders in this impious doctrine only considered what manner of person he is himself, and whence he comes, he would surely be led to a wise decision, like one who has obtained understanding of himself, and would say, not to these atoms, but to his Father and Maker, Your hands have made me and fashioned me. And he would take up, too, this wonderful account of his formation as it has been given by one of old: Have You not poured me out as milk, and curdled me as choose? You have clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and favour, and Your visitation has preserved my spirit. For of what quantity and of what origin were the atoms which the father of Epicurus gave forth from himself when he begot Epicurus ? And how, when they were received within his mother's womb, did they coalesce, and take form and figure? And how were they put in motion and made to increase? And how did that little seed of generation draw together the many atoms that were to constitute Epicurus , and change some of them into skin and flesh for a covering, and make bone of others for erectness and strength, and form sinews of others for compact contexture? And how did it frame and adapt the many other members and parts — heart and bowels, and organs of sense, some within and some…

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: When you have given your name to the warfare, you are held by a bridle. Therefore begin to put away your former doings. Shun luxuries, since labour is threatening arms. With all your virtue you must obey the king's command, if you wish to attain the last times in gladness . He is a good soldier, always wait for things to be enjoyed. Be unwilling to flatter yourself; absolutely put away sloth, that you may daily be ready for what is set before you. Be careful beforehand; in the morning revisit the standards. When you see the war , take the nearest contest. This is the king's glory , to see the soldiery prepared. The king is present; desire that you may fight beyond his hope. He makes ready gifts. He gladly looks for the victory, and assigns you to be a fit follower.
Be unwilling to spare yourself besides for Belial ; be rather diligent, that he may give fame for your death.

excerpts.author: Arnobius
english: I have found that certain people, convinced of their own superior wisdom, are actually raving and frenzied, spouting pronouncements as if they came straight from an oracle. They claim that ever since the Christian people appeared in the world, the earth has perished and the human race has been afflicted by every kind of evil. They even assert that the heavenly beings have abandoned their solemn duty of watching over our affairs and have been driven from the regions of the earth. Accordingly, I have decided — within the limits of my ability and my modest rhetorical skill — to counter this malicious envy and refute these slanderous accusations. I do this so that these accusers cannot delude themselves into thinking they are saying something profound merely by uttering popular slogans, nor can they claim victory by default if we remain silent, as if our silence proved their case rather than their own fault.

I will not deny that their accusation carries great weight, nor that we would deserve hostile hatred — if it were established that we are the cause of the world straying from its laws, of the gods being exterminated, and of such vast misfortunes being imported into human history. Let us therefore examine the mindset behind this opinion and test the truth of what is said. Setting aside all contentious wrangling that only obscures reality, let us weigh the claim on a balance of equal evidence. The logical consequence will inevitably show that the guilty parties are not us, but those very people who profess to be worshipers of the divine and devotees of ancient religion.

First, I put this question to them in a calm and reasonable tone: since the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth, what has nature itself — the world we see and experience — either perceived or suffered that is unseen, unknown, or contrary to the fundamental laws established at the beginning? Have the primary elements, from which all things are composed, been altered into opposite qualities? Has any part of the cosmic machine that encloses and sustains us been loosened or dissolved? Has the rotation of the world, which governs the primordial motion, begun to run slower or faster, or has it been seized by a wild, precipitous volatility? Have the stars begun to rise in the west and set in the east, reversing their appointed courses? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, whose light clothes all things and whose heat animates them, flared up or grown cold, corrupting the temperate balance of its usual governance? Has the moon ceased to renew itself, failing to return to its old phases through the cycle of new moons? Have cold, heat, and the moderate temperatures of the seasons perished in confusion? Has winter begun to have long days, and has night begun to recall the late dawns of summer? Have the winds breathed their last? And, with the winds dead, has the sky not been forced into clouds, and have rain-soaked fields not followed? Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds entrusted to it, or do the trees refuse to sprout? Has the flavor of edible fruits and the juice of the vine been changed? Does the oil pressed from olives no longer feed the lamp when it is extinguished? Do land animals and sea creatures no longer suckle or conceive? Do fetuses in the womb no longer develop according to their natural law? Finally, do human beings — scattered by the earliest navigation to the remotest shores — no longer join in marriage with the solemn rites of just nuptials? Do they no longer produce the sweetest offspring of children, nor conduct public, private, and domestic affairs?

latin: Quoniam comperi nonnullos, qui se plurimum sapere suis persuasionibus credunt, insanire, bacchari, et velut quiddam promptum ex oraculo dicere: postquam esse in mundo christiana gens coepit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum; ipsos etiam coelites, derelictis curis solemnibus, quibus quondam solebant invisere res nostras, terrarum ab regionibus exterminatos: statui pro captu, ac mediocritate sermonis contraire invidiae, et calumniosas dissolvere criminationes, ne aut illi sibi videantur, popularia dum verba depromunt, magnum aliquid dicere; aut, si nos talibus continuerimus a litibus, obtinuisse se causam putent, victam sui vitio, non assertorum silentio destitutam. Neque enim negaverim validissimam esse accusationem istam, hostilibusque condignos odiis nos esse, si apud nos esse constiterit causas, per quas suis mundus aberravit ab legibus, exterminati sunt dii longe, examina tanta moerorum mortalium importata sunt saeculis. Inspiciamus igitur opinionis istius mentem, et hoc quod dicitur, quale sit: summotisque omnibus contentionum studiis, quibus obscurari et contegi contemplatio rerum solet, an sit istud quod dicitur verum, momentorum parium examinatione pendamus. Efficietur enim profecto rationum consequentium copulatu, ut non impii nos magis, sed illi ipsi reperiantur criminis istius rei, qui se numinum profitentur esse cultores, atque inveteratis religionibus deditos. Ac primum ab his illud familiari et placida oratione perquirimus: postquam esse nomen in terris christianae religionis occoepit, quidnam invisitatum, quid incognitum, quid contra leges principaliter institutas, aut sensit aut passa est rerum ipsa quae dicitur appellaturque natura? Numquid in contrarias qualitates prima illa elementa mutata sunt, ex quibus res omnes consensum est esse concretas? Numquid machinae hujus, et molis, qua universi tegimur, et continemur inclusi, parte est in aliqua relaxata, aut dissoluta constructio? Numquid vertigo haec mundi, primigenii motus moderaren excedens, aut tardius repere, aut praecipiti coepit volubilitate raptari? Numquid ab occiduis partibus attolere se astra, atque in ortus fieri signorum coepta est inclinatio? Numquid ipse siderum sol princeps, cujus omnia luce vestiuntur, atque animantur calore, exarsit, intepuit, atque in contrarios habitus moderaminis soliti temperamenta corrupit? Numquid luna desivit redintegrare se ipsam, atque in veteres formas novellarum semper restitutione traducere? Numquid frigora, numquid calores, numquid tepores medii inaequalium temporum confusionibus occiderunt? Numquid longos habere dies bruma, revocare tardissimas luces nox coepit aestatis? Numquid suas animas expiraverunt venti? emortiusque flaminibus neque coelum coactatur in nubila, nec madidata ex imbribus arva succedunt? Commendata semina tellus recusat accidere, aut frondescere arbores nolunt? sapor frugibus esculentis, et vitis liquoribus mutatus est? olearum ex bacculis cruor teter exprimitur, nec lumini subministratur extincto? Animalia terris sueta, atque in aquis degentia non suriunt, nec concipiunt? foetus non in uteris sumptos suis moribus, et sua lege custodiunt? Ipsi homines denique, quos per inhabitabiles oras terrae sparsit prima incipiensque navitas, non matrimonia copulant nuptiarum solennibus justis? non dulcissimas procreant liberorum stirpes, non negotia publica, non privata, et familiares res agunt?

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: God cannot be known by measuring his magnitude; indeed, it is impossible to measure the Father. But according to his love, we are led to God through his Word. As we obey him, we learn continually just how great God is. He is the one who, in relation to us, establishes, chooses, and adorns. Therefore, we have been formed together with all things that are contained by him. This is the one of whom Scripture says: "God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Consequently, angels did not make us, nor did they form us; angels could not fashion the image of God, nor could anyone else except the Word of the Lord—not a power standing far off from the Father. God had no need of such helpers to do what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. For the Word and Wisdom, the Son and Spirit, are always present with him. Through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things. He speaks to them, saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness" (Genesis 1:26), while drawing the substance of creatures, the pattern of his works, and the form of the world's ornaments from himself.

Scripture has rightly declared: "First of all, believe that there is one God, who established, consummated, and made all things out of what did not exist, so that they might be—capable of all things, yet grasped by no one." Malachi also says well in the prophets: "Is there not one God who created us? Is there not one Father of us all?" (Malachi 2:10). The Apostle likewise affirms: "There is one God, the Father, who is over all and in all" (Ephesians 4:6). And the Lord himself says: "All things have been handed over to me by my Father" (Matthew 11:27)—clearly by the One who made all things, for they are not alien but his own. Nothing has been subtracted from his dominion; therefore he is the Judge of the living and the dead, holding the key of David: "He will open, and no one will shut; he will shut, and no one will open" (Revelation 3:7). No one else in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could open the Father's book or look upon it, except the Lamb who was slain. He redeemed us by his blood from the One who made all things by the Word and adorned them with Wisdom. When the Word became flesh, he received all authority, so that just as the Word of God held dominion in heaven, he might also hold dominion on earth—because he is the righteous man who committed no sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found (Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:22)—and dominion over those under the earth, having become the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18). Thus all things might see their King, the paternal light might shine forth in the Lord's flesh, radiant light might come to us from his flesh, and humanity might become incorruptible, clothed in the Father's light.

We have shown through many proofs that the Word, that is, the Son, was always with the Father. That Wisdom is the Spirit, present with him before any creation, Solomon declares: "By wisdom the Lord founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens. By his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds dropped down dew" (Proverbs 3:19–20). And again: "The Lord created me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth. When there were no depths I was brought forth, before the springs of water, before the mountains were shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth" (Proverbs 8:22–25). And again: "When he established the heavens, I was there; when he made firm the fountains of the deep, when he established the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, like a master workman. I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man" (Proverbs 8:27–31).

Therefore there is one God, who by the Word and Wisdom made and ordered all things. He is the Artificer who gave this world to the human race. In his magnitude he is unknown to all who were made by him; no one has searched out his height—neither the ancients who have rested nor those who live now. But according to his love, he is known always through the One by whom he established all things: our Lord Jesus Christ. In these last times he became a man among men, to join the end to the beginning. For this reason the prophets, receiving the prophetic gift from the same Word, proclaimed his coming in the flesh, through whom the mingling and communion of God and man came about according to the Father's good pleasure. From the beginning the Word of God foretold that God would be seen by men, would dwell with them on earth, would speak with them, and would be present to his creation—saving it, making it capable of perceiving him, and freeing us from the hands of all who hate us, that is, from the whole spirit of transgression—so that we might serve him in holiness and righteousness all our days (Luke 1:74–75), and that humanity, embracing the Spirit of God, might pass into the glory of the Father. The prophets signified these things prophetically, but not as some claim: that because the Father of all is invisible, the one seen by the prophets was a different God.

Et nos igitur cum his que continentur ab eo, factisumus. Et hic est de quo Scriptura ait; Ht plasmavit Deus hominem, limum terre accipiens, et insufflavit in faciem ejus Jjlatum vite. Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis preter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre uniNec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quie ipse apud se preefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ipse a semetipso substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens. 2. Nemo enim alius poterat nec in ccelo, nec in terra, nec sub terra aperire paternum librum, nec videre eum, nisi agnus qui occisus est, et sanguine suo redemit nos, ab eodem, qui omnia Verbo fecit et Sapientia adornavit, accipiens omnium potestatem, quando Verbum caro factum est, ut quemadmodum in ccelis principatum habuit Verbum Dei, sic et in terra haberet principatum, quoniam homo justus, gui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus; principatum autem habeat eorum que sunt sub terra, ipse primogenitus mortuorum factus, et ut videant omnia, quemadmodum preediximus, suum Regem: et ut in carnem Domini occurrat paterna lux, et a carne ejus rutila veniat in nos, et sic homo deveniat in incorruptelam, circumdatus paterno lumine. 3. Et rursus autem: Dominus creavit me principium viarum suarum in opera sua, ante swcula fundavit me, initio antequam terram faceret, priusqguam abyssos constitueret, et priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, antequam montes confirmarentur: ante omnes autem colles genuit me. Eyo eram cui adgaudebat, quotidie autem letabar ante faciem ejus in omni tempore, cum letaretur orbe perfecto, et jocundaretur in filiis hominum. 4. Hee prophetice significabant prophetze, sed non quemadmodum quidam dicunt, invisibili Patre omnium exsistente, alterum esse eum, qui a prophetis videretur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We have shown that the earliest Jewish writings back this sect, even though most people know it only dates to Tiberius’ reign and we ourselves claim it. Perhaps that is why its legal standing is challenged—as if, sheltering under the shade of a famous and certainly permitted religion, it were concealing some presumption of its own, or because, apart from its youth, we share none of the Jewish food restrictions, holy days, bodily sign, or common name that would be required if we served the same God. The public already knows Christ as a man—exactly the kind the Jews condemned—so it is easy to assume we worship a mere human. Yet we are not ashamed of Christ, since it serves us to be identified and condemned under his name, and we make no other presumption about God. We must therefore say a few things about Christ as God.

The Jews once enjoyed such grace with God that their founding fathers’ remarkable justice and faith produced national greatness, royal splendor, and immense prosperity; God’s own voices warned them how to merit his favor and avoid offending him. But see how far they fell: puffed up by ancestral pride to the point of madness, they abandoned discipline for profanity, and even if they will not admit it, their present condition proves the charge. Scattered, homeless, exiled from both heaven and their native sun, they wander the world without a leader, without a divine King, not even granted a stranger’s right to set foot in their homeland. When holy voices foretold this fate, those same voices almost always added that God would gather far more faithful worshippers from every nation, people, and place, transfer his grace to them, and give it in fuller measure because their discipline would have greater capacity. So the One who was to come to reform and illuminate, foretold by God, arrived—Christ the Son of God. Therefore the Son of God was proclaimed arbiter and master of this grace and discipline, illuminator and guide of the human race, not born in a way that would make him ashamed of the name Son or of the Father’s seed.

latin: Sed quoniam edidimus, antiquissimis Judaeorum instrumentis sectam istam esse suffultam, quam aliquanto novellam, ut Tiberiani temporis, plerique sciunt, profitentibus nobis quoque; fortasse an hoc nomine de statu ejus retractetur, quasi sub umbraculo insignissimae religionis, certe licitae, aliquid propriae praesumptionis abscondat, vel quia praeter aetatem neque de victus exceptionibus, neque de solemnitatibus dierum, neque de ipso signaculo corporis, neque de consortio nominis cum Judaeis agimus, quod utique oporteret, si eidem Deo manciparemur? Sed et vulgus jam scit Christum, hominem utique aliquem, qualem Judaei judicaverunt, quo facilius quis nos hominis cultores existimaverit. Verum neque de Christo erubescimus, quum sub nomine ejus deputari et damnari juvat, neque de deo aliter praesumimus. Necesse est igitur pauca dicamus de Christo ut Deo. Tantum Judaeis erat apud Deum gratia, ubi et insignis justitia et fides originalium auctorum, unde illis et generis magnitudo et regni sublimitas floruit et tanta felicitas, ut Dei vocibus, quibus edocebantur, de promerendo Deo, et non offendendo, praemonerentur. Sed quanta deliquerint, fiducia patrum inflati [ad delirandum], derivantes a disciplina in profanum modum, etsi ipsi non confiterentur, probaret exitus hodiernus ipsorum. Dispersi, palabundi, et coeli et soli sui extorres, vagantur per orbem, sine homine, sine Deo rege, quibus nec advenarum jure terram patriam saltem vestigio salutare conceditur. Cum haec illis sanctae voces praeminarentur, eaedem fere semper omnes ingerebant fore, uti sub extimis curriculis saeculi ex omni jam gente, et populo, et loco cultores sibi allegeret Deus multo fideliores, in quos gratiam transferret, et pleniorem quidem ob disciplinae auctioris capacitatem. [Venit igitur, qui ad reformandam et illuminandam eam venturus a Deo praenuntiabatur, Christus ille Filius dei]. Hujus igitur gratiae disciplinaeque arbiter et magister, illuminator atque deductor generis humani, Filius Dei annuntiabatur, non quidem ita genitus, ut erubescat de filii nomine aut de patris semine;

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: What follows must now be taken up, and the Greek appropriation of barbarian philosophy must be demonstrated more clearly. The Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in essence, just as they say the soul is. You will find all these things stated plainly in the Scriptures. Do not suppose that I am now treating their allegories as the truth which the gnosis delivers, if they show one thing while indicating another, just as the wise wrestlers of old did. But while they claim that God pervades all of existence, we call Him only the Creator, the Creator by His Word. The statement in Wisdom led them astray: "He passes through and fills all things because of His purity" (Wisdom 7:24), because they did not understand that these things are said of the primal wisdom created by God. "Yes," they say, "but the philosophers posit matter in the beginnings—both the Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic—not a single principle." Let them know, then, that the so-called matter is said by them to be without quality and without shape, and more boldly still, Plato says it does not exist. And in the Timaeus, knowing the most mystical, truly existing principle, he speaks in the very same words. Now then, let our position be this: the question concerning all things—whether principle or principles, or whatever they think about them—is not to be spoken of now, for no other reason than that it is difficult to set forth the things that seem right in the present manner of exposition. Besides, the prophetic utterance, "The earth was invisible and unformed" (Genesis 1:2), has given them an opening for material existence. For Epicurus, the intrusion of chance did not follow from what was said, and so came "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). And for Aristotle, providence reached only as far as the moon, drawing from this psalm: "Lord, Your mercy is in the heavens, and Your truth reaches to the clouds" (Psalm 36:5). For the prophetic revelation of mysteries had not yet been disclosed before the coming of the Lord. The punishments after death and the punishment by fire—all the poetic Muses, and Greek philosophy as well—owed these to barbarian philosophy. For Plato, in the last book of the Republic, says in these very words: "Here indeed wild men, fiery to look upon, stood by, discerning the cry; taking some privately, they led them away, but Aridaeus and the others, binding their hands, feet, and heads, throwing them down and flaying them, dragged them along the road outside, tearing them on thorns." For the fiery men, he says, represent angels who take the unjust and punish them: "He who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire" (Psalm 104:4). It follows from this that the soul is immortal. For what is punished or disciplined, being in sensation, lives, even if it is said to suffer. What then? Does Plato not know of rivers of fire and the depth of the earth, calling the Gehenna of the barbarians 'Tartarus' poetically, and introducing Cocytus, Acheron, Pyriphlegethon, and such places as penal realms for the purpose of discipline and chastening?

Φασὶ γὰρ σῶμα εἶναι τὸν θεὸν οἱ Στωϊκοὶ καὶ πνεῦμα κατ’ οὐσίαν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὴν ψυχήν. πάντα ταῦτα ἄντικρυς εὑρήσεις ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς. μὴ γάρ μοι τὰς ἀλληγορίας αὐτῶν ἐννοήσῃς τὰ νῦν ὡς ἡ γνωστικὴ παραδίδωσιν ἀλήθεια, εἰ ἄλλο τι δεικνύουσαι, καθάπερ οἱ σοφοὶ παλαισταί, ἄλλο μηνύουσιν. ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν διήκειν διὰ πάσης τῆς οὐσίας τὸν θεόν φασιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ποιητὴν μόνον αὐτὸν καλοῦμεν καὶ λόγῳ ποιητήν. παρήγαγεν δὲ αὐτοὺς τὸ ἐν τῇ Σοφίᾳ εἰρημένον διήκει δὲ καὶ χωρεῖ διὰ πάντων διὰ τὴν καθαριότητα, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνῆκαν λέγεσθαι ταῦτα ἐπὶ τῆς σοφίας τῆς πρωτοκτίστου τῷ θεῷ. ναί, φασίν, ἀλλὰ ὕλην ὑποτίθενται οἱ φιλόσοφοι ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς, οἵ τε Στωϊκοὶ καὶ Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ὁ Περιπατητικός, οὐχὶ δὲ μίαν ἀρχήν. ἴστωσαν οὖν τὴν καλουμένην ὕλην ἄποιον καὶ ἀσχημάτιστον λεγομένην πρὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ τολμηρότερον ἤδη μὴ ὂν πρὸς τοῦ Πλάτωνος εἰρῆσθαι. καὶ μή τι μυστικώτατα μίαν τὴν ὄντως οὖσαν ἀρχὴν εἰδὼς ἐν τῷ Τιμαίῳ αὐταῖς φησι λέξεσιν· νῦν δ’ οὖν τὸ παρ’ ἡμῶν ὧδε ἐχέτω· τὴν μὲν περὶ πάντων εἴτε ἀρχὴν εἴτε ἀρχὰς εἴτε ὅπῃ δοκεῖ τούτων πέρι, τὸ νῦν οὐ ῥητέον, δἰ ἄλλο μὲν οὐδέν, διὰ δὲ τὸ χαλεπὸν εἶναι κατὰ τὸν παρόντα τρόπον τῆς διεξόδου δηλῶσαι τὰ δοκοῦντα. ἄλλως τε ἡ λέξις ἡ προφητικὴ ἐκείνη ἡ δὲ γῆ ἦν ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος ἀφορμὰς αὐτοῖς ὑλικῆς οὐσίας παρέσχηται. Ναὶ μὴν Ἐπικούρῳ μὲν ἡ τοῦ αὐτομάτου παρείσδυσις οὐ παρακολουθήσαντι τῷ ῥητῷ γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης. Ἀριστοτέλει δὲ μέχρι σελήνης ἐπῆλθε καταγαγεῖν τὴν πρόνοιαν ἐκ τοῦδε τοῦ ψαλμοῦ· κύριε, ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ τὸ ἔλεός σου καὶ ἡ ἀλήθειά σου ἕως τῶν νεφελῶν. οὐδέπω γὰρ ἀποκεκάλυπτο ἡ τῶν προφητικῶν δήλωσις μυστηρίων πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας. Τάς τε αὖ μετὰ θάνατον κολάσεις καὶ τὴν διὰ πυρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπὸ τῆς βαρβάρου φιλοσοφίας ἥ τε ποιητικὴ πᾶσα μοῦσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ Ἑλληνικὴ φιλοσοφία ὑφείλετο. Πλάτων γοῦν ἐν τῷ τελευταίῳ τῆς Πολιτείας αὐταῖς φησι ταῖς λέξεσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὴ ἄνδρες ἄγριοι, διάπυροι ἰδεῖν, παρεστῶτες, καταμανθάνοντες τὸ φθέγμα, τοὺς μὲν ἰδίᾳ παραλαβόντες ἦγον, τὸν δὲ Ἀριδαῖον καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους συμποδίσαντες χεῖράς τε καὶ πόδας καὶ κεφαλήν, καταβαλόντες καὶ ἐκδείραντες, εἷλκον παρὰ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐκτὸς ἐπ’ ἀσπαλάθων κνάπτοντες. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἄνδρες οἱ διάπυροι ἀγγέλους αὐτῷ βούλονται δηλοῦν, οἳ παραλαβόντες τοὺς ἀδίκους κολάζουσιν· ὁ ποιῶν, φησί, τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον. ἕπεται δὲ τούτοις τὴν ψυχὴν εἶναι ἀθάνατον. τὸ γὰρ κολαζόμενον ἢ παιδευόμενον ἐν αἰσθήσει ὂν ζῇ, κἂν πάσχειν λέγηται. τί δ’; οὐκ οἶδεν ὁ Πλάτων καὶ πυρὸς ποταμοὺς καὶ τῆς γῆς τὸ βάθος, τὴν πρὸς τῶν βαρβάρων Γέενναν καλουμένην Τάρταρον ποιητικῶς ὀνομάζων, Κωκυτόν τε καὶ Ἀχέροντα καὶ Πυριφλεγέθοντα καὶ τοιαῦτά τινα εἰς τὴν παίδευσιν σωφρονίζοντα παρεισάγων κολαστήρια;

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: These are the dates for the earliest Greek sages and philosophers. Yet since most of them were foreigners by birth and received their education among foreign peoples, there is little need to add more examples: Pythagoras is reported to have been Tyrrhenian or Tyrian, Antisthenes was Phrygian, and Orpheus was either Odrysian or Thracian. Most authorities even claim Homer was Egyptian. Thales, a Phoenician by birth, is said to have associated with the Egyptian prophets, just as Pythagoras did with those same men; through them he was circumcised so that he could enter the innermost sanctuaries and learn the Egyptians’ mystical philosophy. He also consorted with the foremost Chaldeans and Magi, and he alludes to the assembly now called the church, which served as his own gathering place. Plato does not deny that philosophy’s finest gifts were imported from foreign peoples, and he acknowledges his own journey to Egypt. In the Phaedo he writes that the philosopher can profit from every quarter: ‘Greece is wide, Cebes, and in it there are thoroughly good men; there are also many foreign nations.’ Thus Plato believes that some foreigners are philosophers, whereas Epicurus holds the opposite view—that only Greeks can philosophize. In the Symposium Plato praises the barbarians for their surpassing practice, saying they alone truly philosophize, and he notes that others, both among Greeks and barbarians, have already had many sacred rites performed for them because of such men. The barbarians plainly honored their own lawgivers and teachers by calling them gods. For they believed that good souls, leaving the heavenly realm, descended into this underworld, took on bodies, and shared in all the evils of mortal life out of concern for the human race—giving them laws and proclaiming philosophy, the greatest good that has ever come or will come from the gods to humanity. It seems to me that, sensing the magnitude of this benefit conferred through the wise, they revered those men and practiced philosophy publicly. The Brahmans, the Odrysians, the Getae, and the Egyptian people have all spoken precisely about these matters, as have the Chaldeans and the Arabs called happy, all who dwelt in Palestine, no small portion of the Persian people, and countless other nations besides. Plato is clearly found to honor the barbarians continually, recalling that he and Pythagoras learned their most numerous and noblest doctrines among them. For this reason he spoke of ‘barbarian races,’ knowing that there are races of barbarian men who are philosophers. In the Phaedrus he presents the Egyptian king as wiser than ourselves, identifying him as Hermes. And in the Charmides he shows knowledge of certain Thracians who are said to make the soul immortal.

greek: οἵδε μὲν οἱ χρόνοι τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησι πρεσβυτάτων σοφῶν τε καὶ φιλοσόφων. ὡς δὲ οἱ πλεῖστοι αὐτῶν βάρβαροι τὸ γένος καὶ παρὰ βαρβάροις παιδευθέντες, τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν, εἰ γε Τυρρηνὸς ἢ Τύριος ὁ Πυθαγόρας ἐδείκνυτο, Ἀντισθένης δὲ Φρὺξ ἦν καὶ Ὀρφεὺς Οδρύσης ἢ Θρᾷξ; Ὅμηρον γὰρ οἱ πλεῖστοι Αἰγύπτιον φαίνουσιν. Θαλῆς δὲ Φοῖνιξ ὢν τὸ γένος καὶ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίων προφήταις συμβεβληκέναι εἴρηται, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Πυθαγόρας αὐτοῖς γε τούτοις, δἰ οὓς καὶ περιετέμετο, ἵνα δὴ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄδυτα κατελθὼν τὴν μυστικὴν παρ’ Αἰγυπτίων ἐκμάθοι φιλοσοφίαν, Χαλδαίων τε καὶ Μάγων τοῖς ἀρίστοις συνεγένετο καὶ τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τὴν νῦν οὕτω καλουμένην τὸ παρ’ αὐτῷ ὁμακοεῖον αἰνίττεται. Πλάτων δὲ οὐκ ἀρνεῖται τὰ κάλλιστα εἰς φιλοσοφίαν παρὰ τῶν βαρβάρων ἐμπορεύεσθαι εἴς τε Αἴγυπτον ἀφικέσθαι ὁμολογεῖ. δύνασθαι γοῦν ἐν τῷ Φαίδωνί φησι πανταχόθεν τὸν φιλόσοφον ὠφελεῖσθαι γράφων· πολλὴ μὲν ἡ Ἑλλάς, ἔφη, ὦ Κέβης, ἦ δ’ ὅς, ἐν ᾗ εἰσι πάμπαν ἀγαθοὶ ἄνδρες, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τὰ τῶν βαρβάρων γένη. οὕτως οἴεται ὁ Πλάτων καὶ βαρβάρων φιλοσόφους τινὰς εἶναι, ὁ δὲ Ἐπίκουρος ἔμπαλιν ὑπολαμβάνει μόνους φιλοσοφῆσαι Ἕλληνας δύνασθαι. ἔν τε τῷ Συμποσίῳ ἐπαινῶν Πλάτων τοὺς βαρβάρους ὡς διαφερόντως ἀσκήσαντας † μόνους ἀληθῶς φησι καὶ ἄλλοι ἄλλοθι πολλαχοῦ καὶ ἐν Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις, ὧν καὶ ἱερὰ πολλὰ ἤδη γέγονε διὰ τοὺς τοιούτους παῖδας. δῆλοι δέ εἰσιν οἱ βάρβαροι διαφερόντως τιμήσαντες τοὺς αὐτῶν νομοθέτας τε καὶ διδασκάλους θεοὺς προσειπόντες. ψυχὰς γὰρ ἀγαθὰς κατὰ Πλάτωνα καταλιπούσας τὸν ὑπερουράνιον τόπον ὑπομεῖναι ἐλθεῖν εἰς τόνδε τὸν τάρταρον καὶ σῶμα ἀναλαβούσας τῶν ἐν γενέσει κακῶν ἁπάντων μετασχεῖν ὑπολαμβάνουσι, κηδομένας τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους, αἳ νόμους τε ἔθεσαν καὶ φιλοσοφίαν ἐκήρυξαν, οὗ μεῖζον ἀγαθὸν τῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένει οὔτ’ ἦλθέν ποτε ἐκ θεῶν οὔτ’ ἀφίξεται. καὶ μοι δοκοῦσιν αἰσθόμενοι τῆς μεγάλης εὐποιίας τῆς διὰ τῶν σοφῶν σεβασθῆναί τε τοὺς ἄνδρας καὶ δημοσίᾳ φιλοσοφῆσαι. Βραχμᾶνές τε σύμπαντες καὶ Ὀδρύσαι καὶ Γέται καὶ τὸ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων γένος ἐθεολόγησαν ἀκριβῶς τὰ ἐκείνων, Χαλδαῖοί τε καὶ Ἀράβιοι οἱ κληθέντες εὐδαίμονες καὶ ὅσοι γε τὴν Παλαιστίνην κατῴκησαν καὶ τοῦ Περσικοῦ γένους οὐ τὸ ἐλάχιστον μέρος καὶ ἄλλα πρὸς τούτοις γένη μυρία. ὁ δὲ Πλάτων δῆλον ὡς σεμνύνων αἰεὶ τοὺς βαρβάρους εὑρίσκεται, μεμνημένος αὐτοῦ τε καὶ Πυθαγόρου τὰ πλεῖστα καὶ γενναιότατα τῶν δογμάτων ἐν βαρβάροις μαθόντος. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ γένη βαρβάρων εἶπεν, γένη φιλοσόφων ἀνδρῶν βαρβάρων γινώσκων, ἔν τε τῷ Φαίδρῳ τὸν Αἰγύπτιον βασιλέα καὶ τοῦ Θωὺθ ἡμῖν σοφώτερον δείκνυσιν, ὅντινα Ἑρμῆν οἶδεν ὄντα. ἀλλὰ κἀν τῷ Χαρμίδῃ Θρᾷκάς τινας ἐπιστάμενος φαίνεται, οἳ λέγονται ἀθανατίζειν τὴν ψυχήν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: As it appears, the Greek philosophers call him God but do not truly know him, because they do not reverence God as God deserves. Their philosophical systems, as Empedocles describes them, have come down to us through many tongues in vain, having seen only a tiny fraction of the whole. Just as a craftsman can focus the sun's light through a water-filled glass vessel to produce fire, so philosophy takes a spark from divine Scripture and makes it visible in only a few things. In the same way that all living creatures breathe the same air, yet each does so differently and for a different purpose, most people engage with the truth—or rather, with the discourse about truth. They do not speak about God; instead, they project their own passions onto God and then explain them. They have made their lives a pursuit of what is plausible rather than what is true, yet truth is not taught by imitation but by learning.

We do not believe in Christ merely to appear good, just as we do not step into the sunlight only to be seen in it. Rather, we strive to become good and virtuous for the sake of being Christians, because the kingdom belongs especially to those who strive—through seeking, learning, and complete discipline—to become kings. The one who imitates mere appearance deceives himself and loses true foresight. But when someone takes a spark from reality and kindles it within the soul with longing and learning, that person sets everything in motion toward genuine knowledge. For whoever does not grasp a thing will neither long for it nor welcome the benefit that comes from it. Consequently, the Gnostic, at the culmination of their achievements, imitates the Lord as far as humanly possible, receiving a lordly quality for the sake of likeness to God. Those who lack this knowledge cannot regulate the truth. It is impossible to share in Gnostic insights unless we first empty ourselves of prior conceptions.

Truth is properly said of everything that is intelligible and sensible. One can immediately perceive the truth of painting beyond the commonplace, and the dignity of music beyond the intemperate. Likewise there is a truth of philosophy beyond the other philosophers, and a true beauty beyond the counterfeit. We must not, then, busy ourselves with partial truths—those by which truth is categorized—but with truth itself, not seeking merely to learn names. For the matter of God is not a single thing but many, and seeking God differs from seeking the things about God. In general, when speaking of the substance of each thing, one must distinguish its accidents. It is enough for me to say that God is the Lord of all. I speak of the Lord of all in a self-sufficient way, leaving nothing out by exception. Since there are two kinds of truth—names and things—those who speak of names, who devote themselves to the beauties of words, are the philosophers among the Greeks; but those who possess the things themselves are among us, the barbarians.
