greek: Ἀλλ’, ὡς ἔοικεν, οἱ φιλόσοφοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων θεὸν ὀνομάζοντες οὐ γιγνώσκουσιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ σέβουσι κατὰ θεὸν τὸν θεόν. τὰ φιλοσοφούμενα δὲ παρ’ αὐτοῖς κατὰ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα ὡς διὰ πολλῶν δὴ γλώσσης ἐλθόντα ματαίως ἐκκέχυται στομάτων, ὀλίγον τοῦ παντὸς ἰδόντων. ὡς γάρ που τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου φῶς δἰ ὑελοῦ σκεύους πλήρους ὕδατος μεθοδεύει ἡ τέχνη εἰς πῦρ, οὕτω καὶ ἡ φιλοσοφία ἐκ τῆς θείας γραφῆς τὸ ἐμπύρευμα λαβοῦσα ἐν ὀλίγοις φαντάζεται. ναὶ μὴν ὡς τὸν αὐτὸν ἀέρα ἀναπνεῖ τὰ ζῷα ἅπαντα, ἄλλα δὲ ἄλλως καὶ εἴς τι διάφορον, οὕτως δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν μετίασιν οἱ πλείους, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸν περὶ ἀληθείας λόγον. οὐ γὰρ περὶ θεοῦ τι λέγουσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἑαυτῶν πάθη ἐπὶ θεὸν ἀνάγοντες ἐξηγοῦνται. γέγονεν γὰρ αὐτοῖς ὁ βίος τὸ πιθανὸν ζητοῦσιν, οὐ τὸ ἀληθές· ἐκ μιμήσεως δὲ ἀλήθεια οὐ διδάσκεται, ἀλλ’ ἐκ μαθήσεως. οὐ γὰρ ἵνα δόξωμεν εἶναι χρηστοί, εἰς Χριστὸν πιστεύομεν, καθάπερ οὐδὲ εἰς τὸν ἥλιον ἕνεκά γε τοῦ φαίνεσθαι μόνον ἐν ἡλίῳ ὄντας παρερχόμεθα, ἀλλ’ ἐνταῦθα μὲν τοῦ ἀλεαίνεσθαι χάριν, ἐκεῖ δὲ τοῦ εἶναι καλοὶ καὶ ἀγαθοὶ ἕνεκα Χριστιανοὶ εἶναι βιαζόμεθα, ὅτι μάλιστα βιαστῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία, ἐκ ζητήσεως καὶ μαθήσεως καὶ συνασκήσεως τελείας τὸ γενέσθαι βασιλέα καρπουμένων. ὁ μιμούμενος ἄρα τὴν δόκησιν δολοῖ καὶ τὴν πρόληψιν. ὅταν δέ τις ἔναυσμα λαβών του πράγματος ἐξάψῃ τοῦτο ἔνδον ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ πόθῳ καὶ μαθήσει, πάντα ἐπὶ τούτοις κινεῖ πρὸς τὸ ἐπιγνῶναι. οὗ γάρ τις μὴ ἀντιλαμβάνεται, οὐδὲ ποθεῖ αὐτὸ οὐδὲ ἀσπάζεται τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὠφέλειαν. τὸ ὕστερον οὖν ὁ γνωστικὸς ἐπὶ τέλει τῶν κατορθωμάτων μιμεῖται τὸν κύριον, εἰς ὅσον ἐφικτὸν ἀνθρώποις, ποιότητά τινα κυριακὴν λαβὼν εἰς ἐξομοίωσιν θεοῦ. οἱ δὲ μὴ ἐπιστάμενοι τὴν γνῶσιν οὐδὲ κανονίζειν δύνανται τὴν ἀλήθειαν. μεταλαμβάνειν οὖν τῶν γνωστικῶν θεωρημάτων οὐχ οἷόν τε, ἐὰν μὴ τῶν προτέρων διανοημάτων κενώσωμεν ἑαυτούς. ἁπλῶς γὰρ οὕτως ἀλήθεια κοινῶς λέγεται παντὸς νοητοῦ τε καὶ αἰσθητοῦ. αὐτίκα ἔνεστι θεάσασθαι καὶ ζωγραφίας ἀλήθειαν παρὰ τὴν δημώδη καὶ μουσικῆς σεμνότητα παρὰ τὴν ἀκόλαστον. καὶ φιλοσοφίας οὖν ἐστιν ἀλήθειά τις παρὰ τοὺς ἄλλους φιλοσόφους καὶ κάλλος ἀληθινὸν παρὰ τὸ δεδολωμένον. οὔκουν ποτὲ τὰς ἐπὶ μέρους ἀληθείας, καθ’ ὧν ἡ ἀλήθεια κατηγορεῖται, αὐτὴν δὲ τὴν ἀλήθειαν πολυπραγμονητέον, οὐκ ὀνόματα ζητοῦντας μαθεῖν· τὸ γὰρ περὶ θεοῦ πρᾶγμα οὐκ ἔστιν ἕν, ἀλλὰ μυρία, διαφέρει δὲ τὸν θεὸν ζητεῖν ἢ τὰ περὶ θεοῦ. καθόλου δὲ εἰπεῖν περὶ ἑκάστου πράγματος τῆς οὐσίας τὰ συμβεβηκότα διακριτέον. Καί μοι ἀπόχρη φάναι θεὸν εἶναι τὸν κύριον πάντων. αὐτοτελῶς λῶς δὲ λέγω τὸν κύριον πάντων, οὐδενὸς ὑπολειπομένου κατὰ ἐξαίρεσιν. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν δύο εἰσὶν ἰδέαι τῆς ἀληθείας, τά τε ὀνόματα καὶ τὰ πράγματα, οἳ μὲν τὰ ὀνόματα λέγουσιν, οἱ περὶ τὰ κάλλη τῶν λόγων διατρίβοντες, οἱ παρ’ Ἕλλησι φιλόσοφοι, τὰ πράγματα δὲ παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐστι τοῖς βαρβάροις.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: As many men drawing down the ship, cannot be called many causes, but one cause consisting of many — for each individual by himself is not the cause of the ship being drawn, but along with the rest — so also philosophy , being the search for truth , contributes to the comprehension of truth ; not as being the cause of comprehension, but a cause along with other things, and co-operator; perhaps also a joint cause . And as the several virtues are causes of the happiness of one individual; and as both the sun, and the fire, and the bath, and clothing are of one getting warm: so while truth is one, many things contribute to its investigation. But its discovery is by the Son. If then we consider, virtue is, in power, one.

But it is the case, that when exhibited in some things, it is called prudence , in others temperance , and in others manliness or righteousness. By the same analogy, while truth is one, in geometry there is the truth of geometry; in music, that of music; and in the right philosophy , there will be Hellenic truth . But that is the only authentic truth , unassailable, in which we are instructed by the Son of God . In the same way we say, that the drachma being one and the same, when given to the shipmaster, is called the fare; to the tax-gatherer, tax; to the landlord, rent; to the teacher, fees; to the seller, an earnest. And each, whether it be virtue or truth , called by the same name, is the cause of its own peculiar effect alone; and from the blending of them arises a happy life.

For we are not made happy by names alone, when we say that a good life is happiness , and that the man who is adorned in his soul with virtue is happy . But if philosophy contributes remotely to the discovery of truth , by reaching, by diverse essays, after the knowledge which touches close on the truth , the knowledge possessed by us, it aids him who aims at grasping it, in accordance with the Word, to apprehend knowledge . But the Hellenic truth is distinct from that held by us (although it has got the same name), both in respect of extent of knowledge , certainly of demonstration, divine power, and the like. For we are taught of God , being instructed in the truly sacred letters by the Son of God . Whence those, to whom we refer, influence souls not in the way we do, but by different teaching.

And if, for the sake of those who are fond of fault-finding, we must draw a distinction, by saying that philosophy is a concurrent and cooperating cause of true apprehension, being the search for truth , then we shall avow it to be a preparatory training for the enlightened man ( τοῦ γνωστικοῦ ); not assigning as the cause that which is but the joint- cause ; nor as the upholding cause , what is merely co-operative; nor giving to philosophy the place of a sine quâ non . Since almost all of us, without training in arts and sciences, and the Hellenic philosophy , and some even without learning at all, through the influence of a philosophy divine and barbarous, and by power, have through faith received the word concerning God , trained by self-operating wisdom.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We will address a little later how the philosophers' doctrines were received among the Hebrews, but first, as proper order requires, we must speak of the times of Moses; through them it will be shown beyond dispute that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has treated these matters exactly in his work Against the Greeks, and Cassian has done so in the first of his Exegetical books; nevertheless our memorandum also demands that we run through the statements relevant to this place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories — though he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and produces Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. His words run thus: Amosis, who became king after the Argive Inachus, destroyed Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles. This Ptolemy was a priest who set out the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, and he says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their exodus from Egypt, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of Greek traditions are the Argolic ones, that is, those reckoned from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. These are forty generations older than the Attic traditions, which begin with Cecrops, whom Tatian quotes verbatim as a double-born and autochthonous man. The Arcadian traditions, which begin with Pelasgus, are nine generations older, and Pelasgus is also said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic traditions, which begin with Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. Concerning the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are counted from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the Assyrian traditions are, as Ctesias says, many years older than the Greek ones, it will appear that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the departure of Moses from Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Europs, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; hence the poet of the Phoronis calls him the father of mortal men. Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the Timaeus:

greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει·

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Now, as the Greeks represent the gods as possessing human forms, so also do they as possessing human passions . And as each of them depict their forms similar to themselves, as Xenophanes says, Ethiopians as black and apes, the Thracians ruddy and tawny; so also they assimilate their souls to those who form them: the Barbarians, for instance, who make them savage and wild; and the Greeks, who make them more civilized, yet subject to passion. Wherefore it stands to reason, that the ideas entertained of God by wicked men must be bad, and those by good men most excellent. And therefore he who is in soul truly kingly and gnostic, being likewise pious and free from superstition , is persuaded that He who alone is God is honourable , venerable, august, beneficent, the doer of good, the author of all good things, but not the cause of evil .

And respecting the Hellenic superstition we have, as I think, shown enough in the book entitled by us The Exhortation , availing ourselves abundantly of the history bearing on the point. There is no need, then, again to make a long story of what has already been clearly stated. But in as far as necessity requires to be pointed out on coming to the topic, suffice it to adduce a few out of many considerations in proof of the impiety of those who make the Divinity resemble the worst men. For either those Gods of theirs are injured by men , and are shown to be inferior to men on being injured by us; or, if not so, how is it that they are incensed at those by whom they are not injured, like a testy old wife roused to wrath ? As they say that Artemis was enraged at the Ætolians on account of Œneus.

For how, being a goddess, did she not consider that he had neglected to sacrifice , not through contempt, but out of inadvertence, or under the idea that he had sacrificed ? And Latona, arguing her case with Athene, on account of the latter being incensed at her for having brought forth in the temple, says:— Man-slaying spoils Torn from the dead you love to see. And these To you are not unclean. But you regard My parturition here a horrid thing, Though other creatures in the temple do No harm by bringing forth their young. It is natural, then, that having a superstitious dread of those irascible [gods], they imagine that all events are signs and causes of evils .

If a mouse bore through an altar built of clay, and for want of something else gnaw through an oil flask; if a cock that is being fattened crow in the evening, they determine this to be a sign of something. Of such a one Menander gives a comic description in The Superstitious Man: — A. Good luck be mine, you honoured gods! Tying my, right shoe's string, I broke it. B. Most likely, silly fool, For it was rotten, and you, niggard, you Would not buy new ones. It was a clever remark of Antiphon, who (when one regarded it as an ill omen that the sow had eaten her pigs), on seeing her emaciated through the niggardliness of the person that kept her, said, Congratulate yourself on the omen that, being so hungry, she did not eat your own children. And what wonder is it, says Bion, if the mouse, finding nothing to eat, gnaws the bag?

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Fear of this kind leads both to repentance and to hope. Hope is the expectation of good things — the expectation of a good that is absent but anticipated. Even gentleness is drawn into hope, which we have learned to guide toward love. Love is the harmony of those who live by the word, the life, and the manner; to put it concisely, it is a community of life, a longing of friendship and natural affection, governed by right reason about how we treat our friends. A friend is another self; therefore we call brothers those who have been reborn through the same word. Hospitality stands beside love, a kind of skill in caring for strangers. Strangers are those for whom worldly things are alien. Worldly people, the apostle says, are those who set their hope on the earth and obey fleshly desires; "do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God — what is good, pleasing, and perfect" (Romans 12:2). Thus hospitality turns toward what benefits strangers; strangers are foreigners, foreigners are friends, friends are brothers — "dear brother," as Homer says. Philanthropy also accompanies love, for through it natural affection arises, a friendly use of people; and natural affection, a skill in caring for friends or relatives, runs together with love. If the true human being within us is the spiritual one, then philanthropy becomes love of brothers toward those who share the same Spirit. Affection is the keeping of goodwill or love; love is complete acceptance; to love is to delight in the good, both leading and being led. We are led into unity through harmony, which is the knowledge of common goods; for like‑mindedness is harmony of minds. And love, the apostle says, "let it be without hypocrisy; let us know ourselves, hating the evil and clinging to the good with brotherly love and the virtues that follow, as far as possible, living at peace with all people" (cf. Romans 12:9–18). Then "do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (cf. Romans 12:21). The same apostle testifies to the Jews that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for being ignorant of God's righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. They did not know the will of the law, nor did they do it; they thought the law willed whatever they themselves willed. Nor did they believe the law as prophesying, but followed it with empty words and fear, not with disposition and faith. "For the end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes," the one prophesied under the law (Romans 10:4). Therefore it was said to them by Moses: "I will provoke you to jealousy by those who are not a nation; by a nation without understanding I will anger you" (Deuteronomy 32:21), plainly to obedience. And through Isaiah: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I revealed myself to those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1), before the coming of the Lord, after which those things prophesied to Israel are now said to belong to it fittingly: "I stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient and contrary people." Do you see the reason for the calling of the nations, clearly stated by the prophet, because of the people's disobedience and contradiction? Then the goodness of God is also shown to them; for the apostle says: "but through their transgression salvation has come to the nations, to provoke them to jealousy and to repentance" (cf. Romans 11:11). The Shepherd, placing the word on the righteous who have fallen asleep, knows that there are some righteous ones among the nations and among the Jews — not only before the coming of the Lord, but also before the law, according to what pleases God, like Abel, like Noah, and any other righteous person. He says that the apostles and teachers who preached the name of the Son of God and fell asleep in power and faith also preached to those who had fallen asleep before. Then he adds: "and they themselves gave them the seal of the preaching." They went down with them into the water and came up again. But these, being alive, went down and came up alive; those who had fallen asleep, having died, went down, but came up alive, and through this they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God. For this reason they also rose together with them and were joined to the building of the tower, fitted together unharmed; for they fell asleep in righteousness and great purity, yet they lacked this one seal alone. For when nations that do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, though they have no law, are a law to themselves, according to the apostle (cf. Romans 2:14). Since virtues follow one another, what need is there to say more, now that it has been shown that faith follows repentance and hope, reverence follows faith, and perseverance and practice in these, together with learning, lead together to love, which is perfected by knowledge? But it must be noted that only the divine is wise by nature; therefore wisdom is the power of God, which teaches the truth; and perhaps the perfection of knowledge is taken from there. The philosopher loves and cherishes the truth, becoming a true servant through love and counted a friend. The beginning of this is to marvel at things, as Plato says in the Theaetetus, and Matthias in the Traditions, urging us to marvel at what is present, treating this as the first step toward the knowledge that lies beyond. In which also in the Hebrew gospel it is written: "the one who marvels will reign, and the one who reigns will rest." It is impossible for the unlearned, as long as they remain unlearned, to philosophize — I mean the one who has not received the notion of wisdom, since philosophy is a desire for what truly exists and the lessons that lead to it. Even if doing good is practiced by some, the knowing how to use and do and cooperate, so that one becomes like God — I say God the Savior — serving the God of all things through the word of the high priest, through which the truly good and just things are seen (Hebrews 13:15). Piety is a practice that follows and accompanies God.

greek: Ἀνάγει γοῦν ὁ τοιοῦτος φόβος ἐπί τε τὴν μετάνοιαν ἐπί τε τὴν ἐλπίδα. ἐλπὶς δὲ προσδοκία ἀγαθῶν ἡ ἀπόντος ἀγαθοῦ εὔελπις. ἀμέλει καὶ ἡ εὐεμπτωσία λαμβάνεται εἰς ἐλπίδα, ἣν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀγάπην χειραγωγεῖν μεμαθήκαμεν. ἀγάπη δὲ ὁμόνοια ἂν εἴη τῶν κατὰ τὸν λόγον καὶ τὸν βίον καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἢ συνελόντι φάναι κοινωνία βίου ἢ ἐκτένεια φιλίας καὶ φιλοστοργίας μετὰ λόγου ὀρθοῦ περὶ χρῆσιν ἑταίρω. ὁ δὲ ἑταῖρος ἕτερος ἐγώ· ᾗ καὶ ἀδελφοὺς τοὺς τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ ἀναγεννηθέντας προσαγορεύομεν. παράκειται δὲ τῇ ἀγάπῃ ἥ τε φιλοξενία, φιλοτεχνία τις οὖσα περὶ χρῆσιν ξένων· ξένοι δὲ ὧν ξένα τὰ κοσμικά. κοσμικοὺς γὰρ τοὺς εἰς γῆν ἐλπίζοντας καὶ τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἐξακούομεν· μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε, φησὶν ὁ ἀπόστολος, τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός, εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ εὐάρεστον καὶ τέλειον. ἀναστρέφει τοίνυν ἡ φιλοξενία περὶ τὸ ὠφέλιμον τοῖς ξένοις, ξένοι δὲ οἱ ἐπίξενοι, ἐπίξενοι δὲ οἱ φίλοι, φίλοι δὲ οἱ ἀδελφοί· φίλε κασίγνητε φησὶν Ὅμηρος, ἥ τε φιλανθρωπία, δἰ ἣν καὶ ἡ φιλοστοργία, φιλικὴ χρῆσις ἀνθρώπων ὑπάρχουσα, ἥ τε φιλοστοργία, φιλοτεχνία τις οὖσα περὶ στέρξιν φίλων ἢ οἰκείων, συμπαρομαρτοῦσιν ἀγάπῃ. εἰ δ’ ὁ τῷ ὄντι ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἐν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ὁ πνευματικός, φιλαδελφία ἡ φιλανθρωπία τοῖς τοῦ αὐτοῦ πνεύματος κεκοινωνηκόσιν· στέρξις δ’ αὖ τήρησίς ἐστιν εὐνοίας ἢ ἀγαπήσεως, ἀγάπησις δὲ ἀπόδεξις παντελής, καὶ τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ἀρέσκεσθαι τῷ ἤδει, ἀγόμενόν τε καὶ ἀπαγόμενον· ἄγονται δὲ εἰς ταὐτότητα δἰ ὁμόνοιαν, ἐπιστήμην οὖσαν κοινῶν ἀγαθῶν· καὶ γὰρ ἡ ὁμογνωμοσύνη συμφωνία γνωμῶν. καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη φησὶν ἀνυπόκριτος ἔστω ἡμῖν, αὐτοί τε ἀποστυγοῦντες τὸ πονηρὸν γινώμεθα, κολλώμενοι τῷ ἀγαθῷ τῇ φιλαδελφίᾳ τε καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς ἕως εἰ δυνατόν, τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν, μετὰ πάντων ἀνθρώπων εἰρηνεύοντες. ἔπειτα μὴ νικῶ λέγει ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ, ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν. Ἰουδαίοις τε ὁ αὐτὸς ἀπόστολος μαρτυρεῖν ὁμολογεῖ ὅτι ζῆλον θεοῦ ἔχουσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν· ἀγνοοῦντες γὰρ τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην, καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ζητοῦντες στῆσαι, τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐχ ὑπετάγησαν· οὐ γὰρ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ νόμου ἔγνωσάν τε καὶ ἐποίησαν, ἀλλ’ ὃ ὑπέλαβον αὐτοί, τοῦτο καὶ βούλεσθαι τὸν νόμον ᾠήθησαν· οὐδ’ ὡς προφητεύοντι τῷ νόμῳ ἐπίστευσαν, λόγῳ δὲ ψιλῷ καὶ φόβῳ, ἀλλ’ οὐ διαθέσει καὶ πίστει ἠκολούθησαν· τέλος γὰρ νόμου Χριστὸς εἰς δικαιοσύνην, ὁ ὑπὸ νόμου προφητευθείς, παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι. ὅθεν εἴρηται τούτοις παρὰ Μωυσέως· ἐγὼ παραζηλώσω ὑμᾶς ἐπ’ οὐκ ἔθνει, ἐπ’ ἔθνει ἀσυνέτῳ παροργιῶ ὑμᾶς, τῷ εἰς ὑπακοὴν δηλονότι εὐτρεπεῖ γενομένῳ. καὶ διὰ Ἡσαΐου εὑρέθην λέγει τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ζητοῦσιν, ἐμφανὴς ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἐμὲ μὴ ἐπερωτῶσι, πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας δηλαδή, μεθ’ ἣν καὶ τῷ Ἰσραὴλ ἐκεῖνα τὰ προφητευθέντα οἰκείως λέγεται νῦν· ἐξεπέτασα τὰς χεῖράς μου ὅλην τὴν ἡμέραν ἐπὶ λαὸν ἀπειθοῦντα καὶ ἀντιλέγοντα. ὁρᾷς τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς ἐξ ἐθνῶν κλήσεως σαφῶς πρὸς τοῦ προφήτου ἀπείθειαν τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ ἀντιλογίαν εἰρημένην; εἶθ’ ἡ ἀγαθότης καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις δείκνυται τοῦ θεοῦ· φησὶ γὰρ ὁ ἀπόστολος· ἀλλὰ τῷ αὐτῶν παραπτώματι ἡ σωτηρία τοῖς ἔθνεσιν εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτοὺς καὶ μετανοῆσαι βουληθῆναι. ὁ Ποιμὴν δὲ ἁπλῶς ἐπὶ τῶν κεκοιμημένων θεὶς τὴν λέξιν δικαίους οἶδέ τινας ἐν ἔθνεσι καὶ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις οὐ μόνον πρὸ τῆς τοῦ κυρίου παρουσίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸ νόμου κατὰ τὴν πρὸς θεὸν εὐαρέστησιν, ὡς Ἄβελ, ὡς Νῶε, ὡς εἴ τις ἕτερος δίκαιος. φησὶ γοῦν τοὺς ἀποστόλους καὶ διδασκάλους τοὺς κηρύξαντας τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ κοιμηθέντας τῇ δυνάμει καὶ τῇ πίστει κηρῦξαι τοῖς προκεκοιμημένοις. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει· καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔδωκαν αὐτοῖς τὴν σφραγῖδα τοῦ κηρύγματος. κατέβησαν οὖν μετ’ αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ πάλιν ἀνέβησαν. ἀλλ’ οὗτοι ζῶντες κατέβησαν καὶ πάλιν ζῶντες ἀνέβησαν· ἐκεῖνοι δὲ οἱ προκεκοιμημένοι νεκροὶ κατέβησαν, ζῶντες δὲ ἀνέβησαν, διὰ τούτων οὖν ἐζωοποιήθησαν καὶ ἐπέγνωσαν τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ συνανέβησαν μετ’ αὐτῶν καὶ συνήρμοσαν εἰς τὴν οἰκοδομὴν τοῦ πύργου καὶ ἀλατόμητοι συνῳκοδομήθησαν· ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ γὰρ ἐκοιμήθησαν καὶ ἐν μεγάλῃ ἁγνείᾳ, μόνην δὲ τὴν σφραγῖδα ταύτην οὐκ ἔσχον. ὅταν γὰρ ἔθνη τὰ μὴ νόμον ἔχοντα φύσει τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιῶσιν, οὗτοι νόμον μὴ ἔχοντες ἑαυτοῖς εἰσι νόμος κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον. Ὡς μὲν οὖν ἀντακολουθοῦσιν ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, τί χρὴ λέγειν, ἐπιδεδειγμένου ἤδη ὡς πίστις μὲν ἐπὶ μετανοίᾳ ἐλπίδι τε, εὐλάβεια δὲ ἐπὶ πίστει, καὶ ἡ ἐν τούτοις ἐπιμονή τε καὶ ἄσκησις ἅμα μαθήσει συμπεραιοῦται εἰς ἀγάπην, ἣ δὲ τῇ γνώσει τελειοῦται; ἐκεῖνο δὲ ἐξ ἀνάγκης παρασημειωτέον ὡς μόνον τὸ θεῖον σοφὸν εἶναι φύσει νοεῖσθαι χρή· διὸ καὶ ἡ σοφία δύναμις θεοῦ ἡ διδάξασα τὴν ἀλήθειαν· κἀνταῦθά που εἴληπται ἡ τελείωσις τῆς γνώσεως. φιλεῖ δὲ καὶ ἀγαπᾷ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁ φιλόσοφος, ἐκ τοῦ θεράπων εἶναι γνήσιος δἰ ἀγάπην ἤδη φίλος νομισθείς. ταύτης δὲ ἀρχὴ τὸ θαυμάσαι τὰ πράγματα, ὡς Πλάτων ἐν Θεαιτήτῳ λέγει, καὶ Ματθίας ἐν ταῖς Παραδόσεσι παραινῶν θαύμασον τὰ παρόντα, βαθμὸν τοῦτον πρῶτον τῆς ἐπέκεινα γνώσεως ὑποτιθέμενος· ᾗ κἀν τῷ καθ’ Ἑβραίους εὐαγγελίῳ ὁ θαυμάσας βασιλεύσει γέγραπται καὶ ὁ βασιλεύσας ἀναπαήσεται. ἀδύνατον οὖν τὸν ἀμαθῆ, ἔστ’ ἂν μένῃ ἀμαθής, φιλοσοφεῖν δέ, τόν γε μὴ ἔννοιαν σοφίας εἰληφότα, φιλοσοφίας οὔσης ὀρέξεως τοῦ ὄντως ὄντος καὶ τῶν εἰς τοῦτο συντεινόντων μαθημάτων. κἂν τὸ ποιεῖν καλῶς ᾖ τισιν ἐξησκημένον, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἐπίστασθαι, ὡς χρηστέον καὶ ποιητέον, καὶ συνεκπονητέον, καθὸ καὶ ὁμοιοῦταί τις θεῷ, θεῷ λέγω τῷ σωτῆρι, θεραπεύων τὸν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν διὰ τοῦ ἀρχιερέως λόγου, δἰ οὗ καθορᾶται τὰ κατ’ ἀλήθειαν καλὰ καὶ δίκαια. εὐσέβεια ἔστι πρᾶξις ἑπομένη καὶ ἀκόλουθος θεῷ.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — An Answer to the Jews 10
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You are actually doubting how His passion turned out, denying that the cross's suffering was preached in Christ, and arguing further that God could not have handed His Son over to this kind of death, since He Himself declared: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree" (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). But the proof of the facts comes before the sense of that curse. Deuteronomy says: "If someone has committed a capital offense and is put to death, and you hang his body on a tree, you must not leave it there overnight; you must bury him that same day, because anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, and you must not defile the land the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance" (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). Therefore God did not curse Christ in this passion; He drew a distinction, so that whoever had a death sentence for some sin and died hanging on a tree — that person was cursed by God, because he was hung on a tree due to the merits of his own sins. Christ, however, spoke no deceit from His mouth and displayed all justice and humility; as we recalled above, He was foretold not to be handed over to this death because of His own merits, but so that the things the prophets predicted would happen to Him through you would be fulfilled — just as the Spirit of Christ Himself was already singing in the Psalms: "They repay me evil for good" (Psalms 35:12); "I am forced to restore what I did not steal"; "They pierce my hands and feet"; "They put gall in my food and give me vinegar for my thirst" (Psalms 69:21); "They cast lots for my garment" — just as the other things you were going to commit against Him were foretold. He suffered all these things, yet not because of any evil act of His own, but so that the Scriptures from the prophets' mouths might be fulfilled. And indeed, the mystery of His passion had to be prefigured in the prophecies; the more incredible it was, the more it would become a scandal if preached plainly; the more magnificent, the more it had to be veiled, so that the difficulty of understanding it would drive people to seek God's grace. Thus, first of all, when Isaac was led as a sacrifice by his father and carried the wood himself, he was already signifying Christ's outcome: a victim yielded by the Father, bearing the wood of His own passion.

latin: De exitu plane passionis ejus ambigitis, negantes passionem crucis in Christum praedicatam, et argumentantes insuper non esse credendum, ut ad id genus mortis exposuerit Deus filium suum, quod ipse dixit: Maledictus omnis homo qui pependit in ligno. Sed hujus maledictionis sensum antecedit rerum probatio. Dicit enim in Deuteronomio: Si autem fuerit in aliquo delictum, ita ut judicium mortis sit, et morietur, et suspendetis eum in ligno. Sed et sepultura sepelietis cum ipsa die: quoniam maledictus a Deo est omnis qui suspensus fuerit in ligno, et non inquinabitis terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi in sortem. Igitur non in hanc passionem Christum maledixit; sed distinctionem fecit, ut qui in aliquo delicto judicium mortis habuisset et moreretur suspensus in ligno, hic maledictus a Deo esset, quia propter merita delictorum suorum suspenderetur in ligno. Alioquin Christus, qui dolum de ore suo locutus non est, quique omnem justitiam et humilitatem exhibuit; et ut supra de eo praedictum memoravimus, non pro meritis suis in id genus mortis expositus est, sed ut ea quae praedicta sunt a prophetis, per vos ei obventura implerentur, sicut in Psalmis ipse Spiritus Christi jam canebat, dicens: Retribuebant mihi mala pro bonis, et: Quae non rapueram, tunc exsolvebam; Exterminaverunt manus meas et pedes; et: Miserunt in potum meum fel, et in siti mea potaverunt me aceto; et, Super vestem meam miserunt sortem; sicuti caetera quae in illum commissuri essetis, praedicta sunt. Quae quidem omnia ipso perpessus, non pro actu suo aliquo malo passus est, sed ut Scripturae implerentur de ore prophetarum. Et utique sacramentum passionis ipsius figurari in praedicationibus oportuerat; quantoque incredibile, tanto magis scandalum futurum, si nude praedicaretur; quantoque magnificum, tanto magis obumbrandum, ut difficultas intellectus gratiam Dei quaereret. Itaque in primis Isaac cum a patre hostia duceretur, et lignum ipsi sibi portaret, Christi exitum jam tunc denotabat, in victimam concessi a patre, lignum passionis suae bajulantis.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Fever, that final installment in the grim ledger of deadly and torturous exits allotted to humanity, does not shock us simply because it exists; it exists. Nor does it shock us because it kills; that is its job. Heresies, engineered to rot and destroy faith, operate on the same brutal logic: if we tremble at what they *can* do, we must first tremble at the fact that they *are*; for as long as they exist, they possess the power to act, and as long as they can act, they exist. Yet we treat fever as the evil it is—rotten in cause and in force—abhorring it rather than gawking at it, and we take whatever precautions we can, precisely because we lack the power to abolish it. Heresies, however, inflict eternal death and the fiercer heat of a greater fire, and yet certain people choose to marvel at their destructive reach rather than avoid it, even though the power to avoid them lies in their own hands.

They will prevail only as long as people marvel that they prevail at all. Either the spectacle of marveling becomes a stumbling block, or they marvel *because* they have already stumbled, imagining that such potency must spring from some kernel of truth. It is a marvel, certainly, that evil wields power; unless, of course, heresies only flex their muscle among those who have no strength in the faith. In the arena, a fighter often wins not because he is strong, nor because he is invincible, but because the man he beat had no strength at all; match that same victor against a truly strong opponent later, and he goes down defeated. Heresies work the same way: they draw their only power from the weaknesses of certain people, prevailing over nothing at all, provided they never run into a robust faith.

latin: Febrem denique, inter caeteros mortiferos et cruciarios exitus erogando homini deputatam, neque quia est miramur, est enim; neque quia erogat hominem, ad hoc enim est. Proinde haereses, ad languorem et interitum fidei productas, si expavescimus hoc eas posse, prius est, ut expavescamus hoc eas esse; quae, dum sunt, habent posse; et dum possunt, habent esse. Sed enim febrem, ut malum et de caussa et de potentia sua, ut notum est, abominamur potius quam miramur, et, quantum in nobis est, praecavemus, non habentes abolitionem ejus in nostra potestate; haereses vero, mortem aeternam et majoris ignis ardorem inferentes, malunt quidam mirari quod hoc possint, quam devitare ne possint, cum habeant devitandi potestatem. Caeterum nihil valebunt, si illas tantum valere non mirentur. Aut enim, dum mirantur, in scandalum subministrantur; aut, quia scandalizantur, ideo mirantur, quasi, quod tantum valeant, ex aliqua veniat veritate. Mirum scilicet, ut malum vires suas habeat; nisi quod haereses apud eos multum valeant, qui in fide non valent. In pugna pugilum et gladiatorum, plerumque non quia fortis est vincit quis, aut quia non potest vinci, sed quoniam ille, qui victus est, nullis viribus fuit; adeo idem ille victor bene valenti postea comparatus, etiam superatus recedit. Non aliter haereses de quorumdam infirmitatibus habent quod valent, nihil valentes, si in bene valentem fidem incurrant.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — An Answer to the Jews 8
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We must pin down the dates for Christ's predicted and future birth, his passion, and the extermination of Jerusalem — that is, its devastation. Daniel says the holy city and the Holy One are to be exterminated along with the coming leader, and the pinnacle destroyed to the point of ruin (Daniel 9:24-27). So we must investigate the times of the coming leader Christ in Daniel; once we calculate them, we will prove he came — from the prescribed times, the fitting signs, and his works. We prove this from the events announced to follow his advent, so that we may believe everything foretold has been fulfilled as well as foreseen. Thus Daniel prophesied about him to show both when and at what time he would liberate the nations, and that after Christ's passion this city would be exterminated.

He says: 'In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, who ruled the Chaldean kingdom, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years. While I was still praying, the man Gabriel — whom I had seen in the earlier vision — came flying, touched me about the time of the evening sacrifice, gave me understanding, and spoke: "Daniel, I have come now to give you insight. At the start of your plea the word went out, and I came to tell you, because you are a man of desires. Consider the word and understand the vision." (Daniel 9:24-27). Seventy weeks are decreed for your people and your holy city, until transgression is finished, sin sealed up, iniquity atoned for, everlasting righteousness brought in, vision and prophet sealed, and the Holy of Holies anointed (Daniel 9:24-27). You will know, discern, and understand from the issuing of the word: restoring and rebuilding Jerusalem until Christ the leader — seven and a half weeks, and seventy-two and a half weeks. It will be turned and rebuilt with joy and a trench, and the times renewed. After those seventy-two weeks the Anointed One will be cut off and cease to be; the city and the sanctuary will be exterminated with the coming leader, and they will be cut off like a flood until the end of the war, which is decreed to the point of destruction. And he will confirm the covenant with many (Daniel 9:24-27).

latin: Itaque requirenda tempora praedictae et futurae nativitatis Christi, et passionis ejus, et exterminii civitatis Hierusalem, id est, vastationis ejus. Dicit enim Daniel et civitatem sanctam et sanctum exterminari cum duce venturo, et destrui pinnaculum usque ad interitum. Venturi itaque Christi ducis sunt tempora requirenda, quae investigabimus in Daniele: quibus computatis, probabimus venisse cum, etiam ex temporibus praescriptis, et ex signis competentibus, et ex operationibus ejus: quae probamus ex consequentibus quae post adventum ejus futura adnuntiabantur, ut tam adimpleta omnia quam prospecta credamus. Sic igitur de eo Daniel praedicavit, ut et quando et quo in tempore gentes esset liberaturus, ostenderet, et quoniam post passionem Christi ista civitas exterminari haberet. Dicit enim sic: In primo anno sub Dario filio Assueri ex semine Medorum, qui regnavit super regnum Chaldaeorum, ego Daniel intellexi in libris numerum annorum. Et adhuc me loquente in oratione, ecce vir Gabriel, quem vidi in visione in principio, volans, et tetigit me, quasi hora sacrificii vespertini, et intelligere fecit me, et locutus est mecum, et dixit: «Daniel, nunc exivi imbuere te intelligentia, in principio obsecrationis tuae exivit sermo. Et ego veni ut annuntiem tibi, quia vir desideriorum tu es, et cogita in verbo, et intellige in visione.» Septuaginta hebdomadae breviatae sunt super plebem tuam, et super civitatem sanctam, quoadusque inveteretur delictum, et signentur peccata, et exorentur injustitiae, et inducatur justitia aeterna, ut et signetur visio et prophetes, et ut ungatur Sanctus sanctorum. Et scies, et perspicies et intelliges a profectione sermonis, integrando et reaedificando Hierusalem usque ad Christum ducem, hebdomadas septem et dimidiam, et septuaginta duas et dimidiam: et convertet, et aedificabitur in laetitiam, et convallationem, et innovabuntur tempora: et post hebdomadas has septuaginta duas, et exterminabitur unctio, et non erit: et civitatem et sanctum exterminabit cum duce adveniente, et concidentur quomodo in cataclysmo usque ad finem belli, quod concidetur usque ad interitum. Et confirmabit testamentum in multis.

excerpts.citation: Tertullian — An Answer to the Jews 9
excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let us start, then, by proving the prophets announced Christ's birth. Isaiah says: "Listen, house of David; this is no trivial dispute with mere mortals, because God himself guarantees the outcome. Therefore the Lord will give you a sign himself: Look — a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will name him Emmanuel, which means 'God with us'" (Isaiah 7:14). "He will eat butter and honey. For before the child knows enough to call for father or mother, he will receive the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria from the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 7:15).

The Jewish objection runs like this: Let us test Isaiah's prophecy; let us compare whether the very first name Isaiah foretold fits the Christ who has already come, along with the identifying marks attached to him. Isaiah declares he must be called Emmanuel, and afterward he will take Damascus's power and Samaria's spoils from the Assyrian king. But the one who came, they insist, was neither born under that name nor did any warrior deeds.

We, on the contrary, think they need warning so they will also grasp this chapter's coherence. The interpretation "God with us" is appended to Emmanuel precisely so you weigh not just the sound of the name but its sense. The Hebrew sound "Emmanuel" belongs to his own people; the sense "God with us," however, becomes common property through translation. So I ask: has the phrase "God with us" — which is what Emmanuel means — been operative in Christ from the moment he appeared? I think you will not deny it entirely. Jews who believe in Christ, from the moment they believe, whenever they utter "Emmanuel" signify that God is with us. Thus it stands proved that the one prophesied as Emmanuel has already come, because what Emmanuel signifies has come — namely, God with us.

They are likewise misled by the bare sound of the name when they treat the taking of Damascus's power and Samaria's spoils from the Assyrian king as a portrait of Christ the warrior, overlooking Scripture's premise: "Before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria from the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 7:15). One must first examine the age indicator: can this age even present Christ as a man, let alone an emperor? The infant would be summoned to arms by crying; the battle signal would be not a trumpet but a rattle; he would engage the enemy not from horseback or a wall but from the back or neck of his nurse or carrier; and thus Damascus and Samaria would be subdued like breasts.

latin: Incipiamus igitur probare nativitatem Christi a prophetis esse nuntiatam. Sic Esaias dicit: Audite, domus David, non pusillum vobis certamen cum hominibus, quoniam Deus praestat certamen: propter hoc ipse Deus dabit vobis signum: Ecce virgo concipiet in utero et pariet filium, et vocabitis nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod interpretatur: Nobiscum Deus. Butyrum et mel manducabit. Quoniam, priusquam cognoscat infans vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum.. Itaque dicunt Judaei: Provocemus istam praedicationem Esaiae, et faciamus comparationem, an Christo qui jam venit, competat illi primo nomen quod Esaias praedicavit, et insignia ejus quae de eo nuntiavit. Equidem Esaias praedicat eum Emmanuelem vocari oportere, dehinc virtutem sumpturum Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Porro, inquiunt, iste qui venit, neque sub ejusmodi nomine est editus, neque re bellica functus. At nos e contrario admonendos eos existimavimus, uti cohaerentia quoque hujus capituli recognoscant: subjuncta est enim et interpretatio Emmanuel, Nobiscum Deus, uti non solum sonum nominis spectes, sed et sensum. Sonus enim hebraicus, quod est Emmanuel, suae gentis est; sensus autem ejus, quod est Deus nobiscum, ex interpretatione communis est. Quaero ergo an ista vox, Nobiscum Deus, quod est Emmanuel, exinde quo Christus inluxit, agitetur in Christo? Et puto, ex toto non negabis. Nam qui ex Judaismo credunt Christo, ex quo in eum credunt, Emmanuel cum volent dicere, nobiscum Deum esse significant. Atque ita constat jam venisse illum qui praedicabatur Emmanuel, quia quod significat Emmanuel, venit, id est Nobiscum Deus. Aeque et sono nominis inducuntur, cum virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum, sic accipiunt, quasi bellatorem portendant Christum, non animadvertentes quid Scriptura praemittat: Quoniam priusquam cognoscat puer vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Ante est enim inspicias aetatis demonstrationem, an virum jam Christum exhibere ista aetas possit, nedum imperatorem; scilicet vagitu ad arma esset convocaturus infans; et signum belli, non tuba, sed crepitacillo daturus; nec ex equo vel de muro, sed de nutricis et gerulae suae dorso sive collo hostem destinaturus; atque ita Damascum et Samariam pro mammis subacturus.

excerpts.citation: Hippolytus — On Christ and Antichrist On Christ and Antichrist (Hippolytus)
excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: Since you, my beloved brother Theophilus, wished to learn the chapters I had already set out, I thought it right to draw abundantly from the divine Scriptures as from a holy spring and to place before your eyes what you sought, so that you might rejoice not merely in hearing the words but also, instructed by the power of the realities themselves, be able to glorify God in every way. This will be a safeguard for you in the present life, free from danger, if you bring forth from ready speech the things that are unknown and hard for many to grasp; you will sow them in the breadth of your heart as in fertile and pure soil, and through them you will despise those who contradict and speak against the saving word. But I fear lest these things be entrusted to unbelieving and blaspheming tongues, for the danger is not slight. Rather, let us entrust them to devout and faithful men who wish to live holily and righteously with fear. For the blessed apostle did not advise Timothy in vain when he wrote, "Guard the deposit, turning away from profane empty talk and the contradictions of falsely named knowledge, which some, by professing it, have missed the faith" (2 Timothy 1:13-14). And again, "You then, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you heard from me through many witnesses entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:1-2). So the blessed apostle handed these things over with caution, since they are not for everyone, foreseeing by the Spirit that the faith of all will be in danger; how much more shall we be in danger if we simply and randomly hand over the words of God to unholy and unworthy men? Because the blessed prophets became our eyes, foreseeing through faith the mysteries of the Word, which they also served to later generations — not only telling the past but also proclaiming the present and the future — so that not only a single prophet at a time would be shown to be a prophet, but all generations would foretell the future and the prophet would be recognized as a prophet. For all of them were equipped with the prophetic Spirit and deemed worthy by the Word itself; they became instruments, always having the word as a plectrum, not moving on their own but proclaiming what God willed. For the prophets did not speak from their own power, nor did they proclaim what they themselves wanted; rather, they were first instructed rightly through the Word, then taught beforehand through visions the future things well, and thus, being sent, they spoke what had been revealed to them alone by God. For according to what basis will a prophet be called a prophet, if not because he saw the future things through the Spirit? If a prophet spoke about something that had already happened, he would not be a prophet by saying things everyone had seen with their own eyes; but by proclaiming the future he was rightly called a prophet. Therefore it is fitting that the prophets were called "seers" from the beginning. From them we also receive the things spoken beforehand...

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The centurion's faith deserves the highest praise. It would be incredible if he, having declared such faith, had not found its equal in Israel — especially since the faith of Israel was not even his concern. Nor could it have become his concern at that point: it was still raw, awaiting proof or comparison — or shall I say, still non-existent? If it had existed, he would have claimed that such faith had never appeared in Israel at all. Yet by saying he ought to have found such faith in Israel, and that he came precisely to find it, he implies that God, specifically the Christ of Israel, would not have begrudged it — unless he was its exactor and follower, an emulator who would rather have discovered such faith in order to weaken and destroy it than to confirm it.

He raised the widow's dead son. This is no new credential; the prophets of the Creator had done the same, so how much more the Son? In that moment Christ introduced no other God, with the result that everyone there gave glory to the Creator, declaring, 'A great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people' (Luke 7:16). Which God? Obviously the one whose people they were and from whom the prophets came. If they glorified the Creator, and Christ heard and knew it yet did not correct them — indeed, in the face of such a stupendous proof, the resurrection of the dead, they were still praying to the Creator — then beyond doubt Christ either was not proclaiming any other God than the one he allowed to be honored in his own benefits and powers, or else what kind of savior would he be, letting them wander in error for so long when he came precisely to heal that error?

But John took offense at hearing of Christ's works, as if they belonged to another. I will first explain the reason for that offense, so that I can more easily demolish the heretic's exploitation of it. Since the Lord himself — by the word and Spirit of the Father — was working on earth and preaching, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit which had been operating in John in the form of a prophetic model should now withdraw from him, having been returned, as it were, to the Lord as its rightful master. Thus John, now just a common man, one of the crowd, took offense — but as a man, not as one who hoped for or understood another Christ, a Christ who had no ground for hope since he taught and did nothing new. No one hesitates over someone he knows does not exist and for whom he feels neither hope nor understanding; but John was certain that no God exists except the Creator, whether as a Jew or even as a prophet. It is easier to hesitate over someone you know exists but are unsure whether he is the one. That, then, was John's fear: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' He was simply asking whether the one he expected had arrived. For he hoped, as everyone thought, that judging by the similarity of the signs a prophet might have been sent in the interim, from whom another — greater — one would come, the expected one, namely the Lord himself. And so John's offense was this: he doubted that the one they expected had come, the one he ought to have recognized from the predicted works. Or did the Lord intend to announce himself to be recognized through those very works? Since those predicted works are consistent with the Christ of the Creator, as we demonstrate case by case, it is thoroughly perverse to claim that Christ is not the Creator's through the very things that compel recognition of him as the Creator's. It is even more perverse if Christ bears witness to John — confirming him as a prophet, indeed as more than a prophet, an angel — and cites the scripture about him: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' (Malachi 3:1), elegantly recalling the prophecy to settle the scruple of the offended John's question: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' For once the forerunner has fulfilled his office, the Lord's way is prepared, and the one to whom the forerunner ministered is the one to be recognized. He is indeed greater than all born of women, but not therefore subject to the one who will be lesser in the kingdom of God, as if that kingdom belonged to another — a kingdom in which a lesser one would be greater than John, while another John is greater than all born of women. Whether he says this of anyone or of himself in humility, because he was regarded as lesser than John — since everyone flocked to John in the wilderness rather than to Christ — 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see?' — it amounts to the same thing: it belongs to the Creator that John is his, greater than all born of women, and that Christ — or any lesser figure who will be greater than John in the kingdom of God, equally the Creator's — will be greater than such a prophet because he was not offended by Christ, which is what diminished John.

We have spoken of the forgiveness of sins. The episode of that sinful woman bears on this: when she kissed the Lord's feet, drenched them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, she handled the solid reality of his body, not an empty phantom; and the penitence of the sinful woman, according to the Creator, earned forgiveness, taking precedence over sacrifice. Even if the impulse to penitence sprang from faith, through penitence justified by faith she heard from him: 'Your faith has saved you' — from the one who had declared through Habakkuk: 'The righteous will live by his faith' (Habakkuk 2:4).

Diximus de remissa peccatorum. illius autem peccatricis feminae argumentum eo pertinebit, ut cum pedes domini osculis figeret, lacrimis inundaret, crinibus detergeret, unguento perduceret, solidi corporis ueritatem, non phantasma inane tractauerit, et ut peccatricis paenitentia secundum creatorem meruerit ueniam, praeponere solitum sacrificio. sed et si paenitentiae stimulus ex fide acciderat, per paenitentiam ex fide iustificata ab eo audiit: fides tua te saluam fecit, qui per Abacuc pronuntiarat: iustus ex fide sua uiuet.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You argue that no such sequence was needed, since He would immediately prove Himself, His Son, His envoy, and the Christ of God by the deeds themselves—by the evidence of miracles. I deny that this alone could serve as His credential, a credential He Himself later repudiated. After all, when He declared that many would come performing signs and mighty works—enough to mislead even the elect—and yet insisted they must not be accepted on that basis, He exposed a reckless reliance on signs and wonders, the very currency of false Christs. Consider the logic: if He chose to validate Himself, to be understood and accepted, through miracles, why deny the same grounds to others who arrive just as suddenly and without any prior authorization? If priority of arrival and priority of miraculous attestation let Him seize the faith like a bather claiming a spot in the pool, cutting off all later claimants, watch out—He may find Himself in the same predicament as those He blocks. He was discovered after the Creator, who was already known and had already worked miracles; on that precedent, no one after Him should be believed. So if you rule that the first comer who speaks first on his successors shuts the door on faith, your Christ stands pre-condemned by the very One who identifies Him as the later arrival. The sole authority to set the terms for later claimants belongs to the Creator, who could never be subsequent to anyone. Right now, as I prepare to show that the Creator produced the identical miracles you reserve exclusively for your Christ—sometimes through His servants long ago, sometimes designated for His own Christ—I can legitimately insist that your Christ ought never to have been believed on miracles alone. Those miracles could just as well be read as the Creator’s own, answering to the works He did through His servants and the promises He made in His Christ. Even if novel attestations turned up in your Christ, we would more readily conclude they belong to the same Creator, since your Christ lacks the proven track record of a victorious, ancient faith. That is why He should have come heralded by His own preaching, building faith through proclamation as well as through power. This is especially urgent because He was poised to oppose the Creator’s Christ, armed with his own signs and prophecies, shining as a rival through every kind of difference. But how can the Christ of a God never proclaimed be proclaimed? That is precisely your demand: that neither your God nor your Christ be believed—because God ought not to have remained unknown, and Christ ought to have been recognized through God.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It was once settled that the property of names belongs to the one who first proclaimed his Christ to mankind and re-named the laws. So it will also be settled that he acts with impudence when he claims many will come in his name, a name that is not his if Christ and Jesus are not the Creator's, to whom the property of names belongs. Furthermore, he ought to forbid the acceptance of those whose equal he himself is, so that the one who comes in a foreign name does so on the same basis; if not, it was his duty to prevent his disciples from the lie of the name, he who possessed his truth through the property of the name. In the end, men will come saying, 'I am the Christ,' and you will accept them, since you accepted a similar one; for neither does this man come in his own name. What then? When the Lord of names himself comes—Christ and Jesus of the Creator—will you reject him? How unjust, how iniquitous, and how unworthy of the best God, that you refuse to receive him coming in his own name, when you received another in that same name! Let us also see what signs he imposes on the times: wars, I think, and kingdom upon kingdom, nation upon nation, pestilence, famine, earthquakes, terrors, and portents from heaven—all of which suit a severe and cruel God. When he adds that these things must also happen, what kind of God does he present: a destroyer or an approver of the Creator? He confirms that the dispositions of the one whose will he enforces must be fulfilled—dispositions the best God would have removed rather than established, if they had not been his own. Yet he predicts these coming persecutions and sufferings for them, which will certainly result in martyrdom and salvation.

excerpts.citation: Origen — On First Principles Translated from Latin of Rufinus
excerpts.author: Origen
english: We hold that certain matters concerning divine promises are to be understood when we cast our understanding toward the contemplation of that eternal age which admits no end of praise, and when we contemplate its ineffable joy and blessedness.

Yet because ecclesiastical preaching also contains faith in the future judgment of God, and because the credibility of that judgment stirs people and urges them to live well and blessedly and to flee every kind of sin, and because this unmistakably shows that it lies in our power to hand ourselves over either to a praiseworthy life or to a culpable one, I consider it necessary to discuss a few things about the freedom of our will, since this question, too, is agitated by very many people not without dignity.
In order that we may more readily grasp what freedom of will is, let us inquire what the nature of will itself intends.
Of all things that are moved, some carry the causes of their movements within themselves, while others receive them from outside.
For example, all things that lack life are moved only from outside, such as stones or wood and whatever things of that sort there are, which consist solely in the condition of their matter or bodies.
We must set aside for now the question that even regards dissolution through corruption as movement, because it contributes nothing to the present purpose.
Other things, however, possess the cause of movement within themselves, such as animals or trees and all things that subsist either through natural life or through a soul.
Among these, some have thought that veins of metal should be counted, and fire too is to be regarded as having its own movement, and perhaps also the springs of water.

Now those things which have the cause of their movements within themselves, some are said to move from themselves, some from themselves; and so they distinguish things that move from themselves, which live indeed but are not animate, from things that move from themselves, namely animate beings, when fantasy, that is, a certain will or incitement, is present which has provoked and incited them to move or to be incited to something.
Finally, even in certain animals there is such a fantasy, that is, a will or sense, which by a certain natural instinct provokes and incites them to ordered and composed movements.

We see this in spiders, which are incited to the work of weaving in a most orderly way by a certain fantasy, that is, by a certain will or zeal for weaving, a natural movement undoubtedly provoking the intention of such a work, and yet the animal itself is found to have no other sense than the natural zeal for weaving, just as the bee is said to fashion honeycombs and honey from the air.

The rational animal, since it has these natural movements within itself, nevertheless possesses something more than the other animals, namely the power of reason, by which it can judge and discern concerning natural movements and reject and cast away some, and approve and accept others, so that by the judgment of this reason the movements of a human being can be directed and governed toward a praiseworthy life.

From this it follows that, since the nature of this reason which is in a human being has within itself the power of distinguishing good or evil, and once it has discerned, there is also present in it the faculty of choosing what it has approved; in choosing what is good it is praiseworthy, but in following what is base or evil it is justly judged culpable.

It should by no means escape our notice that in some mute animals a more ordered movement is found than in other animals, such as in keen dogs or warhorses, so that they appear to be moved by a certain rational sense; but this is to be believed to happen not so much by reason as by a certain incitement and natural movement, more abundantly granted for such uses.

But as we began to say, since the rational animal is such, certain things can befall us humans from outside and present themselves, whether to sight or to hearing or to other senses, which provoke and incite us to good or contrary movements.

excerpts.citation: Origen — On First Principles Translated from the Greek
excerpts.author: Origen
english: Since we are investigating matters of this magnitude, we do not rely on common accusations or the obvious evidence of what is seen; instead, we bring forward as evidence for the apparent proof of what is being said the testimonies from the writings we believe to be divine — both the so-called Old Covenant and the so-called New — and we attempt to strengthen our faith by means of a word. We have not yet discussed the writings as divine; come, then, and let us take up a few things about them in brief, setting before ourselves the considerations that move us concerning divine writings. First, before we use the writings themselves and the expressions within them, we must address the matter of Moses and Jesus Christ, the lawgiver of the Hebrews and the introducer of the saving doctrines according to Christianity.

excerpts.citation: Origen — On First Principles Translated from the Latin of Rufinus
excerpts.author: Origen
excerpts.locus: Translated from the Latin of Rufinus
english: When we discuss matters so great and weighty, human senses and ordinary understanding are not enough to entrust the heart of the matter to them, nor, so to speak, to pronounce visibly on invisible things; therefore we must bring forward the testimonies of divine Scripture to prove what we say. Since those testimonies need to carry certain and undoubted conviction — whether for what we are about to say or for what has already been said — it seems necessary first to demonstrate that the Scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Accordingly, as briefly as possible, we will also set forth evidence for this from the divine Scriptures themselves, the ones that have competently moved us to produce them: namely, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and prince of the Christian religion and doctrine.

Many lawgivers have arisen among Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers or philosophers have claimed to assert the truth; yet we recall no lawgiver who could instill a certain affection and zeal even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either willingly accept his laws or defend them with wholehearted devotion. Consequently, no one has been able to insinuate and instill the truth he perceived not only into many other foreign nations but not even into a single nation, so that his knowledge or belief would reach everyone. And indeed it cannot be doubted that lawgivers desired their laws to be observed by all people, if that were possible, and that teachers wished the truth they saw to become known to all. But knowing they could not do this at all, and that no such great virtue existed in them to move foreign nations to observe their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to attempt or begin such an undertaking, lest they be marked as imprudent in an ineffectual and unfulfillable venture.

Yet throughout the whole world, in all Greece and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and vast multitudes who, abandoning the laws of their fathers and the beings they thought were gods, have committed themselves to the observance of Moses' law and to the discipleship of Christ; and this has happened not without stirring up great hatred against them from those who venerate idols, so that they are frequently afflicted with torments and sometimes even led to death; nevertheless they embrace and guard with wholehearted affection the teaching of Christ's word. It is clear how in a short time the religion itself has grown, advancing through the punishments and deaths of its people, and through the plundering of their goods, while they endure every kind of suffering; and it is especially remarkable that not even the teachers themselves are sufficiently adequate or numerous enough: yet 'the word is preached' nonetheless 'in the whole world' (Matthew 10:18), so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and unwise' receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From this there is no doubt that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that with all power and credibility the word of Christ Jesus may prevail in the minds and souls of all. For it is evident that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that 'you will be led before rulers and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations'; and again:

excerpts.author: Origen
english: He will declare that the ecclesiastical proclamation contains the word concerning God's righteous anointing, and that this word—once it is believed to be true—also summons us to live well and to flee sin in every way. Its purpose is that, consoled by the Lord, we may take hold of what is the most necessary problem. To grasp what "self-moved" means, we must first unfold the concept itself; only when it has been accurately clarified will the matter under investigation be properly presented. Among things that move, some possess the cause of their motion within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried—wood, stones, and all matter held together merely by habit—are moved solely from outside. We may set aside the discussion of bodily locomotion for now, since it is not needed for the present subject. Animals, plants, and everything held together by nature or soul have the cause of their motion within themselves. Some say metals belong here as well, and add that fire is self-moved, perhaps also springs. Among those having the cause of motion in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves. The non-living are moved from outside themselves; the living are moved from themselves. Living things move from themselves when a fantasy arises that provokes an impulse. Again, in certain animals fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with their imaginative nature moving the impulse in an ordered way. In the spider a fantasy of weaving occurs, and an impulse follows to weave, its imaginative nature urging it to this very act, and the creature believes in nothing else beyond its own imaginative nature. In the bee the fantasy drives it to shape wax. The rational animal, however, possesses reason alongside its imaginative nature. Reason judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Because the nature of reason contains starting-points for contemplating the good and the bad, we—following those starting-points—contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad. When we give ourselves to practicing the good we are praiseworthy; when we do the opposite we are blameworthy. Yet we must not overlook that the larger part of the nature ordered toward all things is found in animals, whether to a greater or lesser degree. It is therefore near, so to speak, to the work of the rational in tracking dogs and war horses. To be subjected to this or that external thing, which stirs a fantasy in us one way or another, is admittedly not in our power. But to judge whether to use what has occurred in this way or otherwise is not the work of anyone else; it belongs to the reason within us—either working in us according to those starting-points toward impulses provoked to the good and to duty, or turning us away toward the opposite.

excerpts.locus: Argument 1. For Eight Years Gregory Has Given Up the Pra
english: An excellent thing has silence proved itself in many another person on many an occasion, and at present it befits myself, too, most especially, who with or without purpose may keep the door of my lips, and feel constrained to be silent. For I am unpractised and unskilled in those beautiful and elegant addresses which are spoken or composed in a regular and unbroken train, in select and well-chosen phrases and words; and it may be that I am less apt by nature to cultivate successfully this graceful and truly Grecian art.

Besides, it is now eight years since I chanced myself to utter or compose any speech, whether long or short; neither in that period have I heard any other compose or utter anything in private, or deliver in public any laudatory or controversial orations, with the exception of those admirable men who have embraced the noble study of philosophy , and who care less for beauty of language and elegance of expression. For, attaching only a secondary importance to the words, they aim, with all exactness, at investigating and making known the things themselves, precisely as they are severally constituted. Not indeed, in my opinion, that they: do not desire, but rather that they do greatly desire, to clothe the noble and accurate results of their thinking in noble and comely language.

Yet it may be that they are not able so lightly to put forth this sacred and godlike power (faculty) in the exercise of its own proper conceptions, and at the same time to practise a mode of discourse eloquent in its terms, and thus to comprehend in one and the same mind — and that, too, this little mind of man — two accomplishments, which are the gifts of two distinct persons , and which are, in truth , most contrary to each other. For silence is indeed the friend and helpmeet of thought and invention. But if one aims at readiness of speech and beauty of discourse, he will get at them by no other discipline than the study of words, and their constant practice.

Moreover, another branch of learning occupies my mind completely, and the mouth binds the tongue if I should desire to make any speech, however brief, with the voice of the Greeks; I refer to those admirable laws of our sages by which the affairs of all the subjects of the Roman Empire are now directed, and which are neither composed nor learned without difficulty. And these are wise and exact in themselves, and manifold and admirable, and, in a word, most thoroughly Grecian; and they are expressed and committed to us in the Roman tongue, which is a wonderful and magnificent sort of language, and one very aptly conformable to royal authority, but still difficult to me. Nor could it be otherwise with me, even though I might say that it was my desire that it should be.

english: I wonder how Celsus could place the Odrysians, Samothracians, Eleusinians, and Hyperboreans among the most ancient and wise nations, yet refuse to count the Jews as either wise or ancient, even though many writings from Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Greeks testify to their antiquity—writings I considered superfluous to reproduce here. Anyone who wishes can read Flavius Josephus’s two books on the antiquity of the Jews, where he assembles a large collection of authors bearing witness to it, and the younger Tatian’s discourse against the Greeks, which displays the most learned writers on the antiquity of the Jews and Moses. It appears, then, that Celsus speaks these things not in truth but out of a love for calumny, aiming to accuse the origin of Christianity because it is connected to the Jews. He also declares Homer’s Galactophagi, the Druids of the Gauls, and the Getae to be most wise and ancient peoples, discussing matters related to Jewish teachings—peoples of whom I do not know whether any writings survive—while he alone rejects the Hebrews, as far as he can, from both antiquity and wisdom. Again, when compiling a catalogue of ancient and wise men who benefited their contemporaries and later generations through their writings, he expelled Moses from the list of the wise. Of Linus, whom Celsus placed above those he named, neither laws nor words are brought forward that turned back and served nations; but the laws of Moses are carried by a whole nation scattered throughout the entire inhabited world. See, therefore, whether he did not openly act wickedly by excluding Moses from the catalogue of the wise. He claimed that Linus, Musaeus, Orpheus, Pherecydes, the Persian Zoroaster, and Pythagoras had received these things, committed their own doctrines to books, and preserved them until now. And he willingly forgot the myth about the so‑called gods as human‑like, a myth recorded especially by Orpheus.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: The law and the prophets have been fulfilled through paradoxes like those recorded about Jesus at his baptism — the dove and the voice from heaven. I take this as a sign of the Holy Spirit who appeared then in the form of a dove, pointing to the extraordinary things Jesus did. Celsus accuses him of learning these from Egyptians and performing them, but I will not rely on these accounts alone. It is also probable, given what Jesus' apostles accomplished, that they could not have moved people hearing new words and new teachings to abandon their ancestral traditions and accept theirs — risking dangers even to death — unless they had been backed by powers and extraordinary events. Traces of that same Holy Spirit, who appeared as a dove, are still preserved among Christians: they cast out demons, perform many healings, and perceive certain future things according to the will of the Word. Even if Celsus mocks what I am about to say, or the Jewish interlocutor he introduces, it must still be said that many have come to Christianity as if against their will, some spirit suddenly turning their governing faculty from hating the Word to dying for it, and making them think they were in a trance or a dream. We have recorded many such cases; if we wrote them down after encountering and seeing them ourselves, we would only invite broad ridicule from unbelievers, who already suppose we fabricate these things just as they imagine. But God is witness to our conscience: we want to establish the divine teaching of Jesus not through false reports, but through some varied and clear manifestation. Since the Jew expresses doubt about the written account of the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove upon Jesus, one should say to him: 'Tell me, who is speaking in Isaiah when it says, "And now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit"?' (Isaiah 48:16). The passage is ambiguous — whether the Father and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus, or the Father sent both the Christ and the Holy Spirit. The second reading is the true one. And since the Savior was sent first, then the Holy Spirit, so that the prophet's words might be fulfilled, the fulfillment of that prophecy had to be made known to later generations as well. For this reason, Jesus' disciples recorded what took place.

καὶ τὸ ἄγιον πνεῦμα ἀπέστειλαν τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἢ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπέστειλε τόν τε Χριστὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, τὸ δεύτερόν ἐστιν ἀληθές. καὶ ἐπεὶ ἀπεστάλη ὁ σωτὴρ, εἶτα τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, ἵνα πληρωθῇ τὸ εἰρημένον ὑπὸ τοῦ προφήτου, ἐχρῆν δὲ τὴν τῆς προφητείας πλήρωσιν ἐγνῶσθαι καὶ τοῖς ἑξῆς· διὰ τοῦτο ἀνέγραψαν οἱ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ τὸ γεγενημένον.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Next Celsus declares that the doctrine is barbarian in its origin — by which he means Judaism, the root from which Christianity springs. He does not, however, reproach the word for having a barbarian beginning; on the contrary, he speaks reasonably and even praises barbarians for having discovered adequate doctrines. Yet he goes on to claim that Greeks are superior when it comes to judging, confirming, and practicing toward virtue those very things barbarians first found.

From his own words we can therefore construct a defense of the truths that lie within Christianity: someone who comes to the word from Greek doctrines and disciplines would not only recognize them as true but, by putting them into practice, would also build up and complete whatever appears lacking by the standards of Greek proof, thereby establishing the truth of Christianity.

Still more must be said: there exists a proper proof of the word that is more divine than the Greek proof derived from dialectic. The apostle names this higher proof a demonstration "of spirit and power" (1 Cor 2:4). It is "of spirit" because the prophecies are sufficient to bear witness to anyone who engages them, especially concerning Christ; and it is "of power" because of the tremendous mighty works, which must be affirmed as having occurred — not only on the testimony of many other sources but also because traces of them are still preserved among those who live according to the will of the word.
