greek: Ἑξῆς βάρβαρόν φησιν ἄνωθεν εἶναι τὸ δόγμα, δηλονότι τὸν ἰουδαϊσμὸν, οὗ χριστιανισμὸς ἤρτηται. καὶ εὐγνωμόνως γε οὐκ ὀνειδίζει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀπὸ βαρβάρων ἀρχῇ τῷ λόγῳ, ἐπαινῶν ὡς ἱκανοὺς εὑρεῖν δόγματα τοὺς βαρβάρους· προστίθησι δὲ τούτοις ὅτι κρῖναι καὶ βεβαιώσασθαι καὶ ἀσκῆσαι πρὸς ἀρετὴν τὰ ὑπὸ βαρβάρων εὑρεθέντα ἀμείνονές εἰσιν Ἕλληνες. τοῦτ᾿ οὖν ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἐκ τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων εἰς ἀπολογίαν περὶ τῶν ἐν χριστιανισμῷ κειμένων, ὄντων ἀληθῶν, ὅτι ἀπὸ Ἑλληνικῶν τις δογμάτων καὶ γυμνασίων ἐλθὼν ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον οὐ μόνον κρίνοι ἂν αὐτὰ ἀληθῆ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσκήσας κατασκευάσαι ἂν καὶ τὸ δοκοῦν ἐλλιπὲς ὡς πρὸς Ἑλληνικὴν ἀπόδειξιν ἀναπληρώσαι, κατασκευάζων τὴν χριστιανισμοῦ ἀληθότητα. λεκτέον δ᾿ ἔτι πρὸς τοῦτο ὅτι ἔστι τις οἰκεία ἀπόδειξις τοῦ λόγου, θειοτέρα παρὰ τὴν ἀπὸ διαλεκτικῆς Ἑλληνικήν. ταύτην δὲ τὴν θειοτέραν ὁ ἀπόστολος ὀνομάζει ἀπόδειξιν „πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως.“ [ὡς] „πνεύματος“ μὲν διὰ τὰς προφητείας ἱκανὰς πιστοποιῆσαι τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα μάλιστα εἰς τὰ περὶ τοῦ Χριστοῦ, „δυνάμεως“ δὲ διὰ τὰς τεραστίους δυνάμεις, ἃς κατασκευαστέον γεγονέναι καὶ ἐκ πολλῶν μὲν ἄλλων καὶ ἐκ τοῦ ἴχνη δὲ αὐτῶν ἔτι σῴζεσθαι παρὰ τοῖς κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ λόγου βιοῦσι.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Jesus turned his disciples away, not from merely paying attention to magicians and those who promise to perform wonders by some method or other (the disciples had no need of that warning), but from those who proclaim themselves to be God's Christ and try, through fantasies of their own making, to lure Jesus' disciples back to themselves. He warned them in two passages. In the first he said: "If anyone tells you, 'Look, here is the Messiah!' or 'There he is!' do not believe it. False messiahs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. I have told you beforehand. So if they say to you, 'Look, he is in the wilderness,' do not go out; 'Look, he is in the inner rooms,' do not believe it. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man" (Matthew 24:23-24, 26-27). In the second he said: "Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not eat in your name and drink in your name and cast out demons in your name and do many mighty works?' And I will tell them, 'Depart from me, for you are workers of lawlessness'" (Matthew 7:22-23).

Celsus, wanting to assimilate Jesus' mighty works to the sorcery practiced among people, quotes him in these very words: "O Light and Truth, with his own voice he openly proclaims, as you also have written, that others will come to you using similar powers, evil men and sorcerers, and he names some Satan as the one devising such things." By this reasoning Celsus makes himself guilty, as though these works were not divine but the deeds of evil agents. Yet, compelled by the truth, he has disclosed both what others do and has brought his own position under scrutiny. How, then, is it not absurd to judge the one as God and the others as sorcerers on the basis of the same works? For what stronger witness could the others, who are evil, possibly invoke for themselves than these very works? Celsus himself has conceded that these things are not marks of a divine nature but tokens of certain deceivers and thoroughly wicked men.

Consider, then, whether Celsus is not clearly convicted of distorting the argument here. Jesus speaks one way about those who will perform "signs and wonders," while the Jew in Celsus's dialogue says something quite different. If Jesus had merely told his disciples to beware of those who promise great things without specifying what they claim to be, Celsus's suspicion might have had some foothold. But Jesus warns us to beware of those who promise to be "the Christ" — a claim sorcerers do not make — and he also says that some who live wickedly in his name will perform powers and cast out demons. Rather, if one must put it this way, the sorcery of those in that camp and every suspicion attached to them are exposed for what they are, while the divinity of Christ and the divinity of his disciples are affirmed. For it is possible that someone, using his name — I do not know how — may be energized by some power to appear to accomplish works similar to Christ's, and that others, in the name of Jesus, may do things resembling those of his genuine disciples.

greek: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Ἰησοῦς ἐπιστρέφων τοὺς μαθητὰς οὐχὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ [μὴ] προσέχειν ἁπαξαπλῶς γόησι καὶ τοῖς ἐπαγγελλομένοις δι᾿ οἱασδήποτε ὁδοῦ ποιεῖν τεράστια (οὐ γὰρ ἐδέοντο τούτου οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ) ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ τοῦ τοῖς ἀναγορεύουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πειρωμένοις διά τινων φαντασιῶν πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιστρέφειν τοὺς Ἰησοῦ μαθητὰς ὅπου μὲν εἶπε· „τότε ἐάν τις ὑμῖν εἴπῃ· ἰδοὺ ὧδε ὁ Χριστὸς ἢ ὧδε, μὴ πιστεύετε. ἐγερθήσονται γὰρ ψευδόχριστοι καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται καὶ δώσουσι σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα μεγάλα. ὥστε πλανᾶσθαι εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς. ἰδοὺ προείρηκα ὑμῖν. ἐὰν οὖν εἴπωσιν ὑμῖν· ἰδοὺ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ἐστὶ, μὴ ἐξέλθητε· ἰδοὺ ἐν τοῖς ταμείοις, μὴ πιστεύσητε. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ ἀστραπὴ ἐξέρχεται ἀπ᾿ ἀνατολῶν καὶ φαίνεται ἕως δυσμῶν, οὕτως ἔσται ἡ παρουσία τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου“· ὅπου δέ· „πολλοὶ ἐροῦσί μοι ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ· κύριε, κύριε, οὐ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐφάγομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου ἐπίομεν καὶ τῷ ὀνόματί σου δαιμόνια ἐξεβάλομεν καὶ δυνάμεις πολλὰς ἐποιήσαμεν; καὶ ἐρῶ αὐτοῖς· ἀποχωρεῖτε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ. ὅτι ἐστὲ ἐργάται ἀδικίας.“ ὁ δὲ Κέλσος κοινοποιῆσαι βουλόμενος τὰ τεράστια τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις γοητείαν φησὶν αὐταῖς λέξεσιν· ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια, τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει, καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε, διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν καὶ ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες, καὶ σατανᾶν τινα τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζει· ᾥστ᾿ οὐδὲ αὐτὸς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. βιαζόμενος δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπεκάλυψε καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ αὑτὸν ἤλεγξε. πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν θεὸν τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων τοὺς ἄλλους πονηροὺς ἢ τοῦτον νομιστέον αὐτῷ χρωμένους μάρτυρι; ταῦτα μέν γε καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησεν οὐχὶ θείας φύσεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπατεώνων τινῶν καὶ παμπονήρων εἶναι γνωρίσματα. ὅρα δὴ εἰ μὴ ἐν τούτοις σαφῶς ὁ Κέλσος ἐλέγχεται κακουργῶν τὸν λόγον, ἄλλο μὲν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λέγοντος περὶ τῶν ποιησόντων „σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα,“ ἄλλο δὲ τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου φάσκοντος. καὶ γὰρ εἰ μὲν ἁπλῶς τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἔλεγεν Ἰησοῦς φυλάσσεσθαι τοὺς τὰ τεράστια ἐπαγγελλομένους οὐ παρατιθέμενος, τί φήσουσιν ἑαυτοὺς εἶναι, τάχα χώραν εἶχεν ἂν ἡ ὑπόνοια αὐτοῦ· ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἀφ᾿ ὧν θέλει ἡμᾶς φυλάσσεσθαι ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐπαγγέλλονται εἶναι „ὁ Χριστὸς,“ ὅπερ οὐ ποιοῦσιν οἱ γόητες, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ βιοῦντας κακῶς φησι τινὰς δυνάμεις ποιήσειν καὶ δαίμονας ἀποβαλεῖν ἀνθρώπων· μᾶλλον δ᾿, εἰ δεῖ οὕτως εἰπεῖν, ἀποκηρύσσεται μὲν τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον ἡ γοητεία καὶ πᾶσα ἡ κατ᾿ αὐτῶν ὑπόνοια, εἰσάγεται δὲ ἡ θειότης τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θειότης τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ, ὅτι δυνατόν τινα τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ χρησάμενον καὶ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἐνεργηθέντα ὑπό τινος δυνάμεως πρὸς τὸ προσποιήσασθαι, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἴη ὁ Χριστὸς, δοκεῖν τὰ παραπλήσια ἐπιτελεῖν τῷ Χριστῷ καὶ ἄλλους τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τὰ ὡσπερεὶ παραπλήσια τοῖς γνησίοις αὐτοῦ μαθηταῖς.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Everything the Jew in Celsus's dialogue says against those who believe in Jesus can equally be turned against Moses; the result is that either the charge makes no difference, or calling Jesus' miracles magic becomes the same as calling Moses' miracles magic, since both figures can be accused of the very same crimes in the very words of that Jew. Take Christ: the Jew in Celsus cries out, "But oh light and truth," and claims Jesus openly proclaims these things, just as you yourselves have written — because "there will be others who come to you with similar powers, evil and sorcerers" (cf. Matt. 24:24). Now turn to Moses: an unbeliever could say to the Jew, whether he views Moses as an Egyptian or whoever else, "But oh light and truth, Moses openly proclaims," just as you yourselves have written — because "there will be others who come to you with similar powers, evil and sorcerers." For it is written in your law: "If a prophet or a dreamer of dreams arises among you and gives you a sign or wonder, and the sign or wonder comes true, and he says, 'Let us go after other gods, which you have not known, and let us serve them,' you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or that dreamer of dreams" (Deuteronomy 13:1–3) and what follows. The one who slanders Jesus' words says that even Satan devises such things and names them; the one who applies the same charge to Moses will say that even a prophet or a dreamer of dreams devises such things. Just as the Jew in Celsus says of Jesus that not even he himself is guiltless, since these things are not divine but the works of evil people, so the unbeliever will say to Moses, laying out the same points: not even Moses himself is guiltless, since these things are not divine but the works of evil people. The same tactic will be used against him: forced by the truth, Moses both revealed the deeds of others and refuted the charges against himself. And to the Jew who says this, one could ask: how then is it not wicked to count God as one thing and the sorcerers as another, based on the very same works? Someone could say to him, in light of the words of Moses that have been set forth: how then is it not wicked to count the prophet of God and his servant as one thing and the sorcerers as another, based on the very same works? Since Celsus, pressing the point, added to what I have applied in common the question: "What more than these things should we consider the others who are evil, or this one who uses them as a witness?" — we will add to what has been said: what more than these things, which Moses forbids obeying when they are shown with signs and wonders, should we consider those people evil, or Moses, from whom others have been accused concerning signs and wonders? Saying more to the same effect, to make the argument seem stronger, he says: "These things, indeed, he himself has acknowledged are not of a divine nature but the marks of certain deceivers and very evil people." Who then is he? You, Jew, say that Jesus is; but the one who accuses you, as being subject to the same crimes, will raise the very same accusation against Moses.

greek: Καὶ ὅλα δὲ, ἅπερ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος λέγει πρὸς τοὺς πιστεύοντας εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν, δύναται κοινοποιεῖσθαι εἰς τὴν Μωϋσέως κατηγορίαν· ὥστ᾿ ἢ μηδὲν διαφέρειν ἢ παραπλήσιον εἶναι λέγειν γοητείαν τὴν Ἰησοῦ τῇ Μωϋσέως, ἀμφοτέρων ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ λέξει τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου δυναμένων τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὑπάγεσθαι ἐγκλήμασιν. οἷον περὶ μὲν Χριστοῦ ὁ παρὰ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος λέγει· ἀλλ᾿ ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια. τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει Ἰησοῦς ταῦτα, καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε. διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν καὶ ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες· περὶ δὲ Μωϋσέως εἴποι ἂν ὁ ἀπιστῶν πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον τοῖς Μωϋσέως εἴτ᾿ Αἰγύπτιος εἴθ᾿ ὁστισοῦν· ἀλλ᾿ ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια, τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ Μωϋσῆς διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει. καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε, διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες. γέγραπται γὰρ ὑμῶν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ· „ἐὰν δὲ ἀναστῇ ἐν σοὶ προφήτης ἢ ἐνυπνιαζόμενος ἐνύπνιον καὶ δῷ σοι σημεῖον ἢ τέρας, καὶ ἔλθῃ τὸ σημεῖον ἢ τὸ τέρας, ὃ ἐλάλησε πρός σε λέγων· πορευθῶμεν καὶ ἀκολουθήσωμεν θεοῖς ἑτέροις, οὓς οὐκ οἴδατε, καὶ λατρεύσωμεν αὐτοῖς. οὐκ ἀκούσεσθε τοὺς λόγους τοῦ προφήτου ἐκείνου ἢ τοῦ ἐνυπνιαζομένου τὸ ἐνύπνιον ἐκεῖνο“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ ὁ μὲν τοὺς λόγους τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διαβάλλων φησὶ καὶ σατανᾶν τινα τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζειν, ὁ δὲ κοινοποιῶν τοῦτο πρὸς Μωϋσέα ἐρεῖ καὶ προφήτην ἐνυπνιαζόμενον τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζειν. ὥσπερ δ᾿ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖός φησι περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι ὥστε οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. οὕτως ὁ τοῖς Μωϋσέως ἀπιστῶν φήσει πρὸς αὐτὸν τὰ προειρημένα ἐκτιθέμενος τὸ αὐτό· ὥστε οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς Μωϋσῆς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. τὸ αὐτὸ δὲ ποιήσει καὶ ἐπὶ τούτου· βιαζόμενος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπεκάλυψε καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ἤλεγξεν ὁ Μωϋσῆς. λέγοντι δὲ τῷ Ἰουδαίῳ καὶ τό· πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν θεὸν τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; εἴποι τις ἂν πρὸς αὐτὸν διὰ τὰς Μωϋσέως ἐκτεθείσας λέξεις· πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν προφήτην θεοῦ καὶ θεράποντα αὐτοῦ τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; ἐπεὶ δὲ προσδιατρίβων τῷ τόπῳ ὁ Κέλσος προσέθηκεν οἷς ἐξεθέμην κοινοποιηθεῖσι καὶ τό· τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων τοὺς ἄλλους πονηροὺς ἢ τοῦτον νομιστέον αὐτῷ χρωμένους μάρτυρι; προσθήσομεν τοῖς λεγομένοις καὶ ἡμεῖς τοιαῦτα· τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων, οἷς ἀπαγορεύει πείθεσθαι Μωϋσῆς ἐπιδεικνυμένοις σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα, ἐκείνους πονηροὺς νομιστέον ἢ Μωϋσέα ἐξ ὧν ἑτέρους περὶ σημείων καὶ τεράτων διέβαλε; πλείονα δ᾿ εἰς ταὐτὸν λέγων, ἵνα δόξῃ αὔξειν τὸ ἐπιχείρημα, φησί· ταῦτα μέν γε καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησεν οὐχὶ θείας φύσεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπατεώνων τινῶν καὶ παμπονήρων εἶναι γνωρίσματα. τίς οὖν αὐτός; σὺ μὲν, ὦ Ἰουδαῖε. φῂς ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ὁ δὲ ἐγκαλῶν σοι ὡς τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐγκλήμασιν ὑποκειμένῳ τὸ αὐτὸς ἀνάξει ἐπὶ τὸν Μωϋσέα.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: After this, Celsus does not attack circumcision as a Jewish practice; instead he claims it originated with the Egyptians, trusting Egyptian testimony over Moses, who says Abraham was the first man to be circumcised. It is not Moses alone who records Abraham's name as belonging to God; many who conjure demons also invoke the phrase "the God of Abraham" in their incantations. They do this because of the name itself and the implied kinship between God and the righteous one, so they adopt the formula "the God of Abraham" even though they do not actually know who Abraham is. The same must be said of Isaac, Jacob, and Israel; these admittedly Hebrew names are scattered throughout Egyptian magical texts that promise some kind of power. The history of circumcision, which begins with Abraham and is prohibited by Jesus because he does not want his disciples to practice it, is not for interpretation now. The present moment is not for teaching on these matters but for dismantling the charges Celsus brings against the Jewish narrative, since he thinks he can more quickly disprove Christianity if he can show its Jewish origins to be false.

greek: Μετὰ ταῦτα τὸ περιτέμνεσθαι τὰ αἰδοῖα μὴ διαβαλὼν ὁ Κέλσος ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων γινόμενον, φησὶν ἀπὸ Αἰγυπτίων αὐτὸ ἐληλυθέναι, Αἰγυπτίοις μᾶλλον ἢ Μωϋσεῖ πιστεύσας, λέγοντι πρῶτον ἐν ἀνθρώποις περιτετμῆσθαι τὸν Ἀβραάμ. τοῦ δ᾿ Ἀβραὰμ τὸ ὄνομα οὐ Μωυσῆς ἀναγράφει μόνος οἰκειῶν αὐτὸν θεῷ, ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν ἐπᾳδόντων δαίμονας χρῶνται ἐν τοῖς λόγοις αὐτῶν τῷ „ὁ θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ,“ ποιοῦντες μὲν διὰ τὸ ὄνομα καὶ τὴν πρὸς τὸν δίκαιον τοῦ θεοῦ οἰκειότητα, διὸ παραλαμβάνουσι τὴν „(ὁ) θεὸς Ἀβραὰμ“ λέξιν. οὐκ ἐπιστάμενοι δὲ, τίς ἐστιν ὁ Ἀβραάμ. τὰ δ᾿ αὐτὰ λεκτέον καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ καὶ περὶ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ· ἅτινα ὁμολογουμένως Ἑβραῖα ὄντα ὀνόματα πολλαχοῦ τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις ἐπαγγελλομένοις ἐνέργειάν τινα ἐνέσπαρται μαθήμασι. τὸν δὲ λόγον τῆς περιτομῆς, ἀρξάμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ κωλυόμενον ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, μὴ βουλομένου τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ μαθητὰς τὸ αὐτὸ ποιεῖν. οὐ πρόκειται νῦν ἑρμηνεύειν. οὐ γὰρ τῆς περὶ τούτων διδασκαλίας ὁ παρὼν καιρὸς ἀλλ᾿ ἀγῶνος καθαιροῦντος τὰ φερόμενα ὑπὸ Κέλσου κατὰ τοῦ Ἰουδαίων λόγου ἐγκλήματα, οἰομένου τάχιον ψευδοποιήσειν τὸν χριστιανισμὸν, ἐὰν τῆς ἀρχῆς αὐτοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἰουδαϊκοῖς οὔσης λόγοις κατηγορῶν παραστήσῃ κἀκεῖνον ψευδῆ.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Celsus goes on to claim that those who followed Moses as their leader were merely shepherds and goatherds, deceived by rustic tricks into believing there is only one God. He ought to demonstrate how, in his view, such herdsmen could irrationally abandon the worship of the many gods. He himself claims to be able to set forth the whole crowd of Greek deities or those of other peoples, so let him produce the very substance and reality of Mnemosyne giving birth to the Muses from Zeus, or of Themis bearing the Hours, or of the ever-naked Graces existing as genuine beings. He will not succeed, for the Greek inventions that appear to be embodied from natural phenomena cannot be shown to be true gods. After all, why should Greek myths about the gods be considered truer than, say, those of the Egyptians, who in their own language know nothing of Mnemosyne as mother of the nine Muses, or of Themis as mother of the Hours, or of Eurynome as one of the Graces, or of the rest of their names? How much more effective and superior to all such fabrications is it to be persuaded by the visible order of the world to worship its Creator, who is one and the same, who breathes together with the whole cosmos, and who therefore could not have been fashioned by many creators, just as the entire heaven is not held together by many souls moving it. One soul suffices to carry the whole fixed heaven from east to west and to encompass within itself all that the world requires, all that is not self-sufficient. For every part of the world is dependent, and no part is the whole God, since God must not be incomplete, as a part is. Indeed, a deeper line of reasoning may show that, properly speaking, God is neither a part nor a whole, because a whole is composed of parts, and reason refuses to accept that the God over all could be constituted from parts, each of which cannot do what the others do.

greek: Ἑξῆς τούτοις φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι τῷ ἡγησαμένῳ σφῶν ἑπόμενοι Μωϋσεῖ αἰπόλοι καὶ ποιμένες. ἀγροίκοις ἀπάταις ψυχαγωγηθέντες ἕνα ἐνόμισαν εἶναι θεόν. δεικνύτω τοίνυν πῶς, αἰπόλων καὶ ποιμένων ἀλόγως, ὡς οἴεται, ἀποστάντων τοῦ σέβειν θεοὺς. αὐτὸς δύναται παραστῆσαι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν καθ᾿ Ἕλληνας θεῶν ἢ τοὺς λοιποὺς βαρβάρους. δεικνύτω τοίνυν ὑπόστασιν καὶ οὐσίαν Μνημοσύνης γεννώσης ἀπὸ Διὸς τὰς Μούσας. ἢ Θέμιδος τὰς Ὥρας, ἢ τὰς Χάριτας ἀεὶ γυμνὰς παραστησάτω δύνασθαι κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ὑφεστηκέναι. ἀλλ᾿ οὐ δυνήσεται τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀναπλάσματα σωματοποιεῖσθαι δοκοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν πραγμάτων δεικνύναι θεούς. τί γὰρ μᾶλλον οἱ Ἑλλήνων μῦθοι περὶ θεῶν ἀληθεῖς ἢ, φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν, οἱ Αἰγυπτίων, οὐκ εἰδότων τῇ σφῶν διαλέκτῳ Μνημοσύνην μητέρα Μουσῶν ἐννέα οὐδὲ Θέμιν Ὡρῶν οὐδὲ Εὐρυνόμην μίαν τῶν Χαρίτων οὐδὲ τὰ λοιπὰ ὀνόματα αὐτῶν; πόσῳ οὖν ἐνεργέστερον καὶ πάντων τούτων τῶν ἀναπλασμάτων βέλτιον τὸ ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων πειθόμενον τοῖς κατὰ τὴν εὐταξίαν τοῦ κόσμου σέβειν τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτοῦ ἑνὸς ὄντος ἕνα καὶ συμπνέοντος αὐτοῦ ὅλῳ ἑαυτῷ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μὴ δυναμένῳ ὑπὸ πολλῶν δημιουργῶν γεγονέναι, ὡς οὐδ᾿ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ψυχῶν συνέχεσθαι ὅλον τὸν οὐρανὸν κινουσῶν· ἀρκεῖ γὰρ μία ἡ φέρουσα ὅλην τὴν ἀπλανῆ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ἐπὶ δυσμὰς καὶ ἐμπεριλαβοῦσα ἔνδον πάντα. ὧν χρείαν ἔχει ὁ κόσμος, τὰ μὴ αὐτοτελῆ. πάντα γὰρ μέρη κόσμου, οὐδὲν δὲ μέρος ὅλου θεός· δεῖ γὰρ εἶναι τὸν θεὸν μὴ ἀτελῆ. ὥσπερ ἐστὶ τὸ μέρος ἀτελές. τάχα δὲ βαθύτερος λόγος δείξει ὅτι κυρίως θεὸς ὥσπερ οὐκ ἔστι μέρος οὕτως οὐδὲ ὅλον, ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅλον ἐκ μερῶν ἐστι· καὶ οὐχ αἱρεῖ λόγος παραδέξασθαι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν εἶναι ἐκ μερῶν. ὧν ἕκαστον οὐ δύναται ὅπερ τὰ ἄλλα μέρη.

excerpts.citation: Cyprian of Carthage — Treatises — An Address to Demetrianus An Address to Demetrianus
excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: I have often despised you, Demetrianus, because with sacrilegious mouth and impious words you have repeatedly spoken against God, who is one and true. I judged it more proper and better to spurn the ignorance of the erring in silence than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. I did not do this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: "Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words" (Proverbs 23:9). And again: "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself" (Proverbs 26:4). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our conscience and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, the Lord speaking and saying: "Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you" (Matthew 7:6). For you often came to me more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud voices you preferred to thrust your opinions forward impudently rather than listen patiently to ours. It seemed pointless to engage with you, since it would be easier and less trouble to calm the raging waves of a storm-tossed sea with shouts than to restrain your fury with reasoned words. It is surely useless labor and without effect to offer light to the blind, a discourse to the deaf, or wisdom to the brute, for the brute cannot perceive, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear. Reflecting on this, I have often held my peace and overcome the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable nor restrain the impious by religion nor calm the furious by gentleness.

But now, since you say that many complain that wars break out more frequently, that plague and famine rage, and that long spells of fair weather are broken by rains and showers, and that these are imputed to us, it is no longer right to remain silent, lest our silence begin to look not like modesty but like diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false charges, we seem to acknowledge the crime. I therefore answer you, Demetrianus, and equally those others whom you may have stirred up against us, sowing hatred against us with your slanderous words, and so making many companions for yourself from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reasoning of our words, for whoever is moved to evil by deceit will be moved all the more to good by compelling truth. You said that these things happen through us, and that all the things by which the world is now shaken and hard-pressed should be blamed on us, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this matter, because you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you ought first to know that the world has already grown old; it does not stand with the strength it once had, nor does it prevail with the vigor and power it formerly possessed. The world itself testifies to this even if we keep silent and produce no evidence from the holy Scriptures and divine preaching. The world itself now speaks and proves its own decline by the evidence of its failing elements. There is not the same abundance of rain in winter to nourish the seeds, nor the same scorching heat of the sun in summer to ripen the crops; the sown fields are not as joyful in the spring, nor is autumn as fruitful with the yield of trees. Less marble is quarried from the excavated and exhausted mountains; less wealth of silver and gold is brought forth, since the mines are now exhausted, and the poor veins dwindle and shrink day by day. The farmer is lacking in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in the court, concord in friendships, skill in the arts, discipline in morals. Do you think the substance of a declining thing can remain as great as it was when it was still new and flourishing in youth? Whatever is already near its end and verging toward the west and the extreme must diminish. Thus the sun at its setting casts its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus the moon, as its course declines, is diminished with worn horns; and the tree that was once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed by sterile old age as its branches wither. And the spring that once flowed abundantly with overflowing veins, failing with age, now barely trickles with a scant flow. This is the decree appointed for the world, this is the law of God: that all things that arise must decline, and all things that increase must grow old, the strong must become weak, the great must diminish, and when they have become weak and diminished, they must come to an end. You blame Christians because individual things diminish while the world grows old. What if the old also blamed Christians because they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as before in hearing, in stride, in keenness of sight, in strength of limbs, in vigor of organs, in bulk of members? And whereas human life once extended beyond eight or nine hundred years, now it can scarcely reach the number of a hundred. We see gray hair in children; hair falls out before it grows. Nor does life end in old age; rather it begins from old age. Thus even in its very birth, nature hastens to its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates because of the old age of the world itself, so that no one should marvel that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

latin: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.

excerpts.citation: Arnobius — Against the Nations Against the Heathen, Book I (Arnobius)
excerpts.author: Arnobius
english: I have discovered certain people who think their own opinions make them supremely wise, yet they rave, they rant, and they pronounce verdicts as if they were oracles. They claim that ever since the Christian nation appeared in the world, the earth has been ruined and the human race has been afflicted with countless evils. They even assert that the heavenly powers have abandoned their solemn duties — duties by which they once used to visit our affairs — and have been driven from the regions of the earth.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: It is therefore right, especially in a matter on which the whole plan of life turns, that every one should place confidence in himself, and use his own judgment and individual capacity for the investigation and weighing of the truth , rather than through confidence in others to be deceived by their errors , as though he himself were without understanding. God has given wisdom to all alike, that they might be able both to investigate things which they have not heard, and to weigh things which they have heard. Nor, because they preceded us in time, did they also outstrip us in wisdom; for if this is given equally to all, we cannot be anticipated in it by those who precede us. It is incapable of diminution, as the light and brilliancy of the sun; because, as the sun is the light of the eyes, so is wisdom the light of man's heart.

Wherefore, since wisdom — that is, the inquiry after truth — is natural to all, they deprive themselves of wisdom, who without any judgment approve of the discoveries of their ancestors, and like sheep are led by others. But this escapes their notice, that the name of ancestors being introduced, they think it impossible that they themselves should have more knowledge because they are called descendants, or that the others should be unwise because they are called ancestors. What, therefore, prevents us from taking a precedent from them, that as they handed down to posterity their false inventions, so we who have discovered the truth may hand down better things to our posterity?

There remains therefore a great subject of inquiry, the discussion of which does not come from talent, but from knowledge : and this must be explained at greater length, that nothing at all may be left in doubt . For perhaps some one may have recourse to those things which are handed down by many and undoubted authorities; that those very persons , whom we have shown to be no gods, have often displayed their majesty both by prodigies, and dreams, and auguries, and oracles.

And, indeed, many wonderful things may be enumerated, and especially this, that Accius Navius, a consummate augur, when he was warning Tarquinius Priscus to undertake the commencement of nothing new without the previous sanction of auguries, and the king, detracting from the credit due to his art, told him to consult the birds, and then to announce to him whether it was possible for that which he himself had conceived in his mind to be accomplished, and Navius affirmed that it was possible; then take this whetstone, he said, and divide it with a razor. But the other without any hesitation took and cut it. In the next place is the fact of Castor and Pollux having been seen in the Latin war at the lake of Juturna washing off the sweat of their horses, when their temple which adjoins the fountain had been open of its own accord.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Therefore the highest God, the parent of all, decided to transfer his religion and so sent a teacher of justice from heaven, that he might give a new law to new worshipers in him or through him — not as he had done before through a man, yet still he willed him to be born as a man so that he might exist as wholly like the highest Father. For God the Father himself, the origin and principle of all things, lacks parents; therefore Trismegistus most truly names him ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ, because he was not generated by anyone. For this reason the Son also had to be born twice, that he himself might become ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ. In his first, spiritual birth he was ἀμήτωρ, because he was begotten by God the Father alone without a mother’s role; in his second, carnal birth he was ἀπάτωρ, because he was born from a virgin’s womb without a father’s role, so that, bearing a middle substance between God and man, he might lead this fragile, weak nature of ours by the hand toward immortality. He became the Son of God through the Spirit and the son of man through flesh — that is, both God and man. God’s power shone forth in him from the works he did; man’s frailty appeared in the passion he endured — why he undertook it I will explain shortly. Meanwhile, from the prophets we learn that he was both God and man, compounded of both natures. Isaiah testifies that he was God in these words: “Egypt has been exhausted, and the trade of the Ethiopians and the Sabeans, men of stature, will come over to you and become your servants; they will walk behind you in chains, they will worship you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, though we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior. All who oppose you will be put to shame and will reverence you, and they will fall in confession” (Isaiah). Likewise Jeremiah says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned apart from him, who found every way of wisdom and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Jeremiah). Likewise David in Psalm 45: “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of equity. You loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 45). By this word he also shows his name, since, as I taught above, he was called Christ from the anointing. Then Jeremiah teaches that the same one was a man, saying: “And he is a man — who can know him?” (Jeremiah). Likewise Isaiah: “And the Lord will send them a man who will save them, and judging will heal them” (Isaiah).

latin: Summus igitur deus ac parens omnium cum religionem suam transferre uoluisset, doctorem iustitiae misit e caelo, ut nouis cultoribus nouam legem in eo uel per eum daret, non sicut ante fecerat per hominem, sed tamen nasci eum uoluit tamquam hominem, ut per omnia summo patri similis existeret. ipse enim pater deus, origo et principium rerum, quo-niam parentibus caret, ὰπάπωρ atque ὰμήτωρ a Trismegisto uerissime nominatur, quod ei nullo sit procreatus. idcirco etiam filium bis nasci oportuit, ut et ipse fieret ὰπάτωρ atque ὰμήτωρ. in prima enim natiuitate spiritali ὰμήτωρ fuit, quia sine officio matris a solo deo patre generatus est, in secunda uero carnali ὰπάτωρ fuit, quoniam sine patris officio uirginali utero procreatus est, ut mediam inter deum hominemque substantiam gerens nostram hanc fragilem inbecillamque naturam quasi manu ad inmortalitatem posset educere. factus est et dei filius per spiritum et hominis per carnem, id est et deus et homo. dei uirtus in eo ex operibus quae fecit apparuit, fragilitas hominis ex passione quam pertulit: quam cur susceperit paulo post docebo. interim et deum fuisse et hominem ex utroque genere permixtum prophetis uaticinantibus discimus. Esaias deum fuisse testatur his uerbis: fatigata est Aegyptus, et negotiatio Aethiopum et Sabain uiri alti ad te transgredientur et tui erunt serui et post te ambulabunt uincti conpedibus et adorabunt te et in te precabuntur: quoniam in te deus est, et non est deus alius praeter te. tu enim es deus, et nos nesciebamus, deus Israhel saluator. confundentur et reuerebuntur omnes qui aduersantur tibi, et cadent in confessionem. item propheta Hieremias sic ait: hic deus noster est et non deputabitur alius absque illo, qui inuenit omnem uiam prudentiae et dedit eam Iacob puero suo et Israhel dilecto sibi. post haec in terris uisus est et cum hominibus conuersatus est. item Dauid in psalmo XLEQI: thronus tuus, deus, in saecula saeculorum, uirga aequitatis uirga regni tui. dilexisti iustitiam, odio habuisti iniustitiam. propterea unxit te dominus deus tuus oleum exultationis. quo uerbo etiam nomen ostendit, siquidem, ut supra docui, ab unctione appellatus est Christus. deinde hominem fuisse eundem Hieremias docet dicens: et homo est et quis cognouit eum? item Esaias: et mittet eis dominus hominem, qui saluabit eos et iudicans sanabit eos.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Having spoken of the second birth, by which He revealed Himself to humanity in the flesh, we now turn to those marvelous works which, though they were heavenly signs of power, the Jews dismissed as sorcery. When He first began to mature, He was baptized by the prophet John in the Jordan River, that by a spiritual washing He might cleanse not His own sins — for He had none — but the sins of the flesh He had assumed. He did this so that, just as the Jews were saved through the circumcision they received, so also the Gentiles might be saved through baptism, that is, through the sprinkling of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7). This same voice had been foretold by David. And the Spirit of God descended upon Him in the form of a white dove. From that moment He began to perform mighty deeds, not by magical tricks that display nothing true or solid, but by heavenly power and authority — deeds the prophets had long ago proclaimed. These works are so numerous that no single book could contain them all. I will therefore enumerate them briefly and in general categories, without naming specific persons or places, so that I may arrive at the explanation of the meaning of His passion and cross, toward which my discourse has long been hastening.

His mighty works were what Apollo called "portentous," because wherever He went He restored the sick, the weak, and those suffering from every kind of disease to full health with a single word and in a single instant. The result was that people who had been completely paralyzed, suddenly strengthened by recovered power, picked up their own stretchers — the very beds on which they had been carried only a short time before — and carried them away. To those crippled or afflicted with defects of the feet He gave not only the ability to walk but even to run. To those whose eyes were blind in deepest darkness He restored their original sight. He loosened the tongues of the mute into speech and conversation, and to the deaf, with their ears opened, He gave hearing. He cleansed those defiled and sprinkled with stains. He did all these things not with His hands or any medicine, but with His word and command, just as the Sibyl had also predicted: "Doing all things by a word and healing every disease." Nor is it surprising that He performed wonders by a word, since He Himself is the Word of God, upheld by heavenly power and authority. It was not enough that He gave strength to the weak, soundness to the frail, and health to the sick and languishing; He also raised the dead, as if freeing them from sleep and recalling them to life. The Jews who witnessed these things charged that they were done by demonic power, even though their own secret writings contained all these events exactly as they came to pass.

coepit adolescere, tinctus est ab Iohanne propheta in Iordane flumine, ut lauacro spiritali peccata non sua, quae utique non habebat, sed carnis quam gerebat aboleret, ut quemadmodum Iudaeos suscepta circumcisione, sic etiam gentes baptismo id est purifici roris perfusione saluaret. tum uox audita de caelo est: filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. quae uox aput Dauid praedicta inuenitur. et descendit super eum spiritus dei formatus in specie columbae candidae. exinde maximas uirtutes coepit operari, non praestrigiis magicis, quae nihil ueri ac solidi ostentant, sed ui ac potestate caelesti: quae iam pridem prophetis nuntiantibus canebantur. quae opera tam multa sunt, ut unus liber ad conplectenda omnia satis non sit. enumerabo igitur illa breuiter atque generatim sine ulla quacumque iter faciebat, aegros ac debiles et omni morborum genere laborantes uno uerbo unoque momento reddebat incolumes, adeo ut membris omnibus capti receptis repente uiribus roborati ipsi lectulos suos reportarent, in quibus fuerant paulo ante delati. claudis uero ac pedum uitio adflictis non modo gradiendi, sed etiam currendi dabat facultatem. tum quorum caeca lumina in altissimis tenebris repurgabat. et haec omnia non manibus aut aliqua medella, sed uerbo ac iussione faciebat, sicut etiam Sibylla praedixerat: πάντα λόγῳ πράσσων πᾶσάν τε νόσον θεραπεύων nec utique mirum quod uerbo faceret mirabilia, cum ipse esset dei uerbum caelesti uirtute ac potestate subnixum. nec satis fuit quod uires inbecillis redderet, quod debilibus integritatem, quod aegris et languentibus sanitatem, nisi etiam mortuos suscitaret uelut e somno solutos ad uitamque reuocaret. quae uidentes tunc Iudaei daemonica potentia fieri arguebant, cum omnia sic futura ut facta sunt arcanae illorum litterae continerent.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: When Christ fulfilled all that God had willed and had foretold through His prophets many centuries before, His enemies were stirred up and, because they did not know the divine Scriptures, conspired to condemn their own God. Jesus knew this would happen and repeatedly said that He must suffer and be killed for the salvation of many; yet He withdrew with His disciples, not to avoid what He was bound to endure, but to show that in every persecution one must act in this way, so that no one may appear to have fallen through his own fault. He also foretold that one of them would betray Him. And so Judas, enticed by a reward, handed Him over to the Jews. They seized Him and brought Him before Pontius Pilate, who was then governing Syria as legate, and demanded that He be crucified, accusing Him of nothing else than saying that He is the Son of God, the King of the Jews, and because He had said, "If you destroy this temple, which was built in forty-six years, I will raise it up in three days without hands" (John 2:19), signifying His coming passion and that He would rise on the third day after being killed by the Jews — for He Himself was the true temple of God. They attacked these words as unlucky and impious. When Pilate heard this and Jesus offered no defense, Pilate declared that he found nothing in Him worthy of condemnation. But those most unjust accusers, together with the crowd they had stirred up, began to shout and to demand His cross with violent cries. Then Pilate, overcome by their clamor and by the instigation of Herod the tetrarch, who feared being driven from his kingdom, gave way; yet he himself did not pronounce sentence, but handed Jesus over to the Jews to judge Him according to their own law. They led Him away, scourged with whips, and before they crucified Him they mocked Him: they clothed Him in a purple robe, crowned Him with thorns, and saluted Him as if He were a king (John 19:2-3); they gave Him gall for food and mixed vinegar for Him to drink. After this they spat in His face and struck Him with their palms. When the executioners themselves quarreled over His garments, they cast lots for His tunic and cloak. Throughout all this He uttered no sound from His mouth, as if He were mute. Finally they suspended Him between two criminals condemned for robbery, fixing Him to the cross.

latin: Cum igitur ea quae deus fieri uoluit quaeque per prophetas suos multis saeculis ante praedixit, Christus inpleret, ob ea incitati et diuinas litteras nescientes coierunt, ut deum suum condemnarent. quod cum sciret futurum ac subinde diceret oportere se pati atque interfici pro salute multorum, secessit tamen cum discipulis suis, non ut uitaret quod necesse erat perpeti ac sustinere, sed ut ostenderet quod ita fieri oporteat in omni persecutione, ne sua quis culpa incidisse uideatur; ac denuntiauit fore ut ab uno eorum proderetur. itaque ludas praemio inlectus tradidit eum Iudaeis. at illi conprehensum ac Pontio Pilato, qui tum legatus Syriam regebat, oblatum cruci adfigi postulauerunt obicientes ei nihil aliut nisi quod diceret se filium dei esse, regem Iudaeorum; item quia dixerat: si solueritis hoc templum, quod aedificatum est annis XLVI, ego illut in triduo sine manibus resuscitabo, significans futuram breui passionem suam et se a Iudaeis interfectum tertio die resurrecturum. ipse enim fuerat uerum dei templum. has uoces eius tamquam infaustas et inpias insectabantur. quae cum Pilatus audisset et ille in defensionem sui nihil diceret, pronuntiauit nihil in eo damnatione dignum uideri. at illi iniustissimi accusatores cum populo, quem incitauerant, subclamare coeperunt et crucem eius uiolentis uocibus flagitare. tum Pontius et illorum clamoribus et Herodis tetrarchae instigatione metuentis, ne regno pelleretur; uictus est, nec tamen ipse sententiam protulit, sed tradidit eum Iudaeis, ut ipsi de illo secundum legem suam iudicarent. duxerunt igitur eum flagellis uerberatum et priusquam cruci adfigerent, inluserunt: indutum enim coloris punicei ueste ac spinis coronatum quasi regem salutarunt et dederunt ei cibum fellis et miscuerunt ei aceti potionem. post haec conspuerunt faciem eius et palmis ceciderunt. cumque ipsi carnifices de uestimentis eius contenderent, sortiti sunt inter se de tunica et pallio. et cum haec omnia fierent, nullam uocem ex ore suo, tamquam si mutus esset, emisit. tum suspenderunt eum inter duos noxios medium, qui ob latrocinia damnati erant, crucique fixerunt.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: God , therefore, the contriver and founder of all things, as we have said in the second book, before He commenced this excellent work of the world, begot a pure and incorruptible Spirit, whom He called His Son . And although He had afterwards created by Himself innumerable other beings, whom we call angels , this first-begotten, however, was the only one whom He considered worthy of being called by the divine name, as being powerful in His Father's excellence and majesty. But that there is a Son of the Most High God , who is possessed of the greatest power, is shown not only by the unanimous utterances of the prophets , but also by the declaration of Trismegistus and the predictions of the Sibyls.

Hermes, in the book which is entitled The Perfect Word , made use of these words: The Lord and Creator of all things, whom we have thought right to call God , since He made the second God visible and sensible. But I use the term sensible, not because He Himself perceives (for the question is not whether He Himself perceives), but because He leads to perception and to intelligence. Since, therefore, He made Him first, and alone, and one only, He appeared to Him beautiful, and most full of all good things; and He hallowed Him, and altogether loved Him as His own Son.

The Erythræan Sibyl, in the beginning of her poem, which she commenced with the Supreme God , proclaims the Son of God as the leader and commander of all, in these verses:— The nourisher and creator of all things, who placed the sweet breath in all, and made God the leader of all. And again, at the end of the same poem:— But whom God gave for faithful men to honour . And another Sibyl enjoins that He ought to be known :— Know Him as your God , who is the Son of God . Assuredly He is the very Son of God , who by that most wise King Solomon, full of divine inspiration, spoke these things which we have added: , God founded me in the beginning of His ways, in His work before the ages.

He set me up in the beginning, before He made the earth, and before He established the depths, before the fountains of waters came forth: the Lord begot me before all the hills; He made the regions, and the uninhabitable boundaries under the heaven. When He prepared the heaven, I was by Him: and when He separated His own seat, when He made the strong clouds above the winds, and when He strengthened the mountains, and placed them under heaven; when He laid the strong foundations of the earth, I was with Him arranging all things. I was He in whom He delighted: I was daily delighted, when He rejoiced, the world being completed.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Let us set aside the testimony of the prophets, lest the proof seem less fitting for matters that are not believed at all. Instead, let us turn to the authors whom our opponents customarily cite against us—the poets and philosophers—and call them as witnesses to the truth. From these sources we must demonstrate one God, not because they possessed a full knowledge of the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon his eyes. The poets, although they adorned the gods with songs and magnified their deeds with the highest praise, nevertheless confess again and again that all things are contained and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves—since tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God 'Protogonos,' because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him 'Phaneta,' because when nothing else yet existed, he first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Since he could not grasp this God's origin and nature in his mind, he declared that he was born from the vast air: 'Protogonos Phaethon, son of boundless air.' He had nothing further to say. Orpheus calls this God the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he founded the heavens and provided for his children, so that they might share a common dwelling and seat: 'He established an imperishable home for the immortals.' Guided by nature and reason, he therefore understood that a supreme power exists, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not say that Jupiter was the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn, nor Saturn himself, who was said to be born of heaven; yet he dared not make heaven the first god, because he saw that heaven is an element of the world, and an element needs an author. Reason thus led him to that primal God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty. Homer can give us nothing that pertains to the truth, for he wrote of human rather than divine matters. Hesiod might have, since he encompassed the genealogy of the gods in a single work; yet he contributed nothing, because he took his starting point not from the Creator God but from Chaos, a confused mass of raw and disordered matter, when he ought first to have explained whence, when, and how Chaos itself began to exist. Just as all things are ordered and fashioned by some craftsman, so this matter itself must have been made by someone. Who made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrinks from this, shuddering at the unknown truth. That song on Helicon was not poured out by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear; he came to it after meditation and preparation. Our own first poet, Vergil, was not far from the truth. Speaking of the highest God, whom he named Mind and Spirit, he wrote: 'In the beginning the spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titans' stars; and the mind, infused through every part, moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.' And lest anyone be ignorant of who this spirit is that wields such power, Vergil declared elsewhere: 'For God goes through all lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from him come the flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, and every nascent life is summoned.' Ovid also, at the start of his renowned work, confesses without disguise that the world was ordered by God, whom he calls the world's maker and the craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our poets, led by nature, had defended forever what they perceived, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth. So much for the poets. Let us turn to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictions but the investigation of truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and the first to seek natural causes, said that water is the source from which all things are born, and that God is the mind which formed all things from water. Thus he placed the material of things in moisture, and established the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as: the mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, diffused throughout, from which all living creatures receive life. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite mind that moves itself. Antisthenes allows many popular gods, but one natural God—that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes call the highest God the ether, an opinion our poet Vergil endorsed: 'Then the omnipotent Father, with fertile rains, descends into the bosom of his joyful consort, and nourishes all the great offspring, mixed with the great body.' Chrysippus names the natural power endowed with divine reason—sometimes calling it divine necessity—God; likewise, Zeno calls the natural and divine law God. The opinions of all these, though uncertain, nevertheless converge on the same point: they agree that there is one providence. Whether you call it nature, ether, reason, mind, fatal necessity, divine law, or anything else, it is the same as what we call God. Nor does the diversity of names obstruct this, since all are reduced to a single signification by their very meaning. Aristotle, although he contradicts himself and says and thinks opposing things, nevertheless testifies that one mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, defends the monarchy plainly and openly; he does not name the ether, or reason, or nature, but calls him God: 'From him this world was made perfect and wonderful.' Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many respects, frequently confesses and calls the supreme God in the books he wrote on the laws, and argues that the world is ruled by him when he disputes the nature of the gods: 'Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor obedient to it. Therefore he himself rules all nature.' Because he is God, I pass over the question of his association; nor can God himself, as we understand him, be understood in any other way than as a mind that is free and released, set apart from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Annaeus Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often does he extol the supreme God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: 'Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divinities which we individually adore and worship are suspended?' Likewise in his Exhortations: 'When he laid the first foundations of this most beautiful structure and began to arrange it so that all things might proceed under their leaders, although he himself had extended through his whole body, nevertheless God generated the ministers of his kingdom.' And how many other things he said about God, similar to our own! I defer those now, because they are more opportune in other places. For the present it is enough to show that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by the entrenched custom of perverse opinions—opinions by which they believed there are other gods, and that the things God made for human use are to be revered and worshiped as gods.

latin: Sed omittamus sane testimonia prophetarum, ne minus idonea probatio uideatur esse de his quibus omnino non creditur. ueniamus ad auctores et eos ipsos ad ueri probationem testes citemus, quibus contra nos uti solent, poetas dico ac philosophos. ex his unum deum probemus necesse est, non quod illi habuerint cognitam ueritatem, sed quod ueritatis ipsius tanta uis est, ut nemo possit esse tam caecus, quin uideat ingerentem se oculis diuinam claritatem. poetae igitur quamuis deos carminibus ornauerint et eorum res gestas amplificauerint summis laudibus, saepissime tamen confitentur spiritu uel mente una contineri regique omnia. Orpheus, qui est uetustissimus poetarum et aequalis ipsorum deorum, siquidem traditur inter Argonautas cum Tyndaridis et Hercule nauigasse, deum uerum et magnum πρωτόγονον appellat, quod ante ipsum nihil sit genitum, sed ab ipso sint cuncta generata. eundem etiam Φάνητα nominat, quod cum adhuc nihil esset, primus ex infinito apparuerit et extiterit. cuius onginem atque naturam quia concipere animo non poterat, ex aere inmenso natum esse dixit: πρωτόγονος Φαέθων περιμήϰεος ἠέρος υἱός. aliut enim amplius quod diceret non habebat. hunc ait esse omnium deorum parentem, quorum causa caelum condiderit liberisque prospexerit, ut haberent habitaculum sedemque communem: ἔϰτισεν ἀθανάτοις δόμον άϕθιτον. natura igitur et ratione ducente intellexit esse praestantissimam potestatem, caeli ac terrae conditricem. non poterat enim dicere Iouem esse principem rerum, qui erat Saturno genitus, neque ipsum Saturnum, qui caelo natus ferebatur; caelum autem tamquam deum primum constituere non audebat, quod uidebat elementum esse mundi, quod ipsum eguerit auctore. haec eum ratio perduxit ad deum illum primogenitum, cui adsignat et tribuit principatum. Homerus nihil nobis dare potuit quod pertineat ad ueritatem: qui humana potius quam diuina conscripsit. potuit Hesiodus, qui deorum generationem unius libri opere conplexus est: sed tamen nihil dedit non a deo conditore sumens exordium, sed a chao, quod est rudis inordinataeque materiae confusa congeries, cum explanare ante debuerit chaos ipsum unde quando quomodo esse aut constare coepisset. nimirum sicut ab aliquo artifice disposita ordinata effecta sunt omnia, sic ipsam materiam fictam esse ab aliquo necesse est. quis igitur hanc nisi deus fecit, cuius potestati subiacent omnia? sed refugit hoc ille, dum horret incognitam ueritatem. non enim Musarum instinctu sicut uideri uolebat in Helicone carmen illut effudit, sed meditatus uenerat ac paratus. nostrorum primus Maro non longe afuit a ueritate, cuius de summo deo, quem mentem ac spiritum nominauit, haec uerba sunt: principio caelum ac terras camposque liquentis lucentemque globum lunae Titaniaque astra spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet. ac ne quis forte ignoraret, quisnam esset ille spiritus qui tantum haberet potestatis, declarauit alio loco dicens: deum namque ire per omnis terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum; hinc pecudes armenta uiros genus omne ferarum, quemque sibi tenuis nascentem accersere uitas. Ouidius quoque in principio praeclari operis sine ulla nominis dissimulatione a deo, quem fabricatorem mundi, quem rerum opificem uocat, mundum fatetur instructum. quodsi uel Orpheus uel hi nostri quae natura ducente senserunt in perpetuum defendissent, eandem quam nos sequimur doctrinam conprehensa ueritate tenuissent. Sed hactenus de poetis. ad philosophos ueniamus, quorum grauior est auctoritas certiusque iudicium, quia noti rebus commenticiis, sed inuestigandae ueritati studuisse creduntur. Thales Milesius, qui unus e septem sapientium numero fuit quique primus omnium quaesisse de causis naturalibus traditur, aquam esse dixit ex qua nata sint omnia, deum autem esse mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit. ita materiam rerum posuit in umore, principium causamque nascendi constituit in deo. Pythagoras ita definiuit quid esset deus: animus per uniuersas mundi partes omnemque naturam commeans atque diffusus, ex quo omnia quae nascuntur animalia uitam capiunt. Anaxagoras deum esse dicit infinitam mentem quae per se ipsam moueatur: Antisthenes multos quidem esse populares deos, unum tamen naturalem id est summae totius artificem. Cleanthes et Anaximenes aethera esse dicunt summum deum, cui opinioni poeta noster adsensit: tum pater omnipotens fecundis imbribus aether coniugis in gremium laetae descendit et omnis magnus alit magno permixtus corpore fetus. Chrysippus naturalem uim diuina ratione praeditam, interdum diuinam necessitatem deum nuncupat, item Zenon naturalem diuinamque legem. horum omnium sententia quamuis sit incerta, eodem tamen spectat, ut prouidentiam unam esse consentiant. siue enim natura siue aether siue ratio siue mens siue fatalis necessitas siue diuina lex siue quid aliut dixeris, idem est quod a nobis dicitur deus. nec obstat appellationum diuersitas, cum ipsa significatione ad unum omnia reuoluantur. Anstoteles quamuis secum lpse dissideat ac repugnantia sibi et dicat et sentiat, in summum tamen unam mentem mundo praeesse testatur. Plato, qui omnium sapientissimus iudicatur, monarchian plane aperteque defendit nec aethera aut rationem aut naturam, sed ut est deum nominat: ah eo mundum hunc perfectum atque mirabilem esse fabricatum. quem Cicero secutus atque imitatus in plurimis frequenter deum confitetur ac supremum uocat in iis libris quos de legibus scripsit; ab eoque regi mundum argumentatur, cum disputat de natura deorum, hoc modo: nihil est praestantius deo. ab eo igitur mundum regi necesse est. nulli igitur est naturae oboediens aut subiectus deus. omnem ergo regit ipse naturam. quia autem sit deus, m uonsoiatione dehmt: nec uero deus ipse, qui intellegitur a nobis, alio modo intellegi potest nisi mens soluta quaedam et libera, segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens I et mouens. Annaeus quoque Seneca, qui ex Romanis uel acerrimus Stoicus fuit, quam saepe summum deum merita. laude prosequitur! nam cum de inmatura morte dissereret, non intellegis inquit auctoritatem ac maiestatem iudicis tui, rectoris orbis terrarum caelique et deorum omnium dei, a quo ista numina quae singula adoramus et colimus suspensa sunt? item in Exhortationibus: hic cum prima fundamenta molis pulcherrimae iaceret et hoc ordiretur quo neque maius quicquam nouit natura nec melius, ut omnia sub ducibus suis irent, quamuis ipse per totum se corpus intenderat, tamen ministros regni sui deus genuit. et quam multa alia de deo nostris similia locutus est! quae nunc differo, quod aliis locis opportuniora sunt. nunc satis est demonstrare summo ingenio uiros attigisse ueritatem ac paene tenuisse, nisi eos retrorsus infucata prauis opinionibus consuetudo rapuisset, qua et deos esse alios opinabantur et ea quae in usum hominis deus fecit, tamquam sensu praedita essent, pro diis habenda et colenda credebant.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: These men had no will to fabricate, nor any cunning to do so, because they were unskilled. Indeed, who could? An unlearned man cannot invent a coherent, self-consistent story when the most learned philosophers — Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus, and Zeno — contradicted one another and themselves. That is the nature of falsehoods: they cannot hold together. By contrast, the tradition these men handed down is true, so it is consistent at every point, entirely self-agreeing, and therefore persuasive, because it rests on a steady rational foundation. They did not invent this religion for profit or advantage. Their lives, both in precept and in practice, renounced pleasure and despised everything the world counts as good. They not only accepted death for their faith; they knew in advance they would die, they foretold it, and they warned that all who followed their teaching would suffer harsh and unspeakable things.

Yet the opponent affirms that Christ, driven out by the Jews, gathered a band of nine hundred men and turned bandit. Who dares challenge such authority? We are to believe it outright — perhaps some Apollo revealed it to him in a dream. Countless bandits have perished in the past and perish daily; you yourself have condemned many. Which of them, after his cross, was ever called not merely a man but a god? Perhaps you believed the story because you yourselves consecrated a murderer, Mars, as a god — something you would never have done had the Areopagites crucified him. While denying Christ’s wonders, the opponent tries to show that Apollonius performed equal or even greater feats. It is striking that he passes over Apuleius, whose many marvels are commonly recorded. Why, then, does no one worship Apollonius as a god — unless you alone, worthy of such a deity, with whom the true God will punish you for eternity? If Christ counts as a magician because he worked wonders, Apollonius is certainly the more skilled: when Domitian tried to punish him, he simply failed to appear in court. How different from Christ, who was seized and nailed to the cross. Perhaps the opponent means to charge Christ with arrogance for claiming to be God, so that Apollonius may seem more modest — though he allegedly did greater things, he did not arrogate divinity to himself.

I pass over a detailed comparison of their works now, having exposed the fraud and trickery of the magical art in the previous two books. I deny that anyone exists who does not desire above all to obtain after death what even the greatest kings crave. Why do men build magnificent tombs, erect statues, commission portraits? Why do they strive, through famous deeds or even death for their fellow citizens, to win the good opinion of posterity? Why, finally, did you choose to raise this detestable monument of your intellect, founded as it were on mud, unless you hope for immortality through the memory of your name? It is therefore foolish to suppose Apollonius did not want what he would certainly have desired if he could — for no one rejects immortality, especially when you admit that some worshiped him as a god and that his statue, under the name Hercules Alexicacus, is still honored by the Ephesians. He could not be believed a god after death, because it was established he was a man and a magician; thus he laid claim to divinity under a foreign title, since he could not and dared not do so in his own name. But our Christ could be believed God because he was no magician, and he was believed because he truly was God. I do not say this to prove Apollonius is not a god because he refused the title, but to show that we are wiser: we do not instantly ascribe divinity to marvels, as you do, who accepted a god on the strength of petty portents.

It is no wonder that you, so far removed from God’s wisdom, understand nothing of what you have read. The Jews, who from the beginning had read the prophets to whom God’s mystery was entrusted, still did not know what they were reading. Learn, then, if you have any heart: we do not believe Christ is God because he worked wonders, but because we saw that everything the prophets foretold was fulfilled in him. He passed over the wonders: we would have taken him for a magician, as you do now and the Jews did then, had not all the prophets, with one spirit, predicted beforehand that he would do those very things. And so we believe him God not so much because of his wondrous works as because of that very cross, which you lick like dogs — since the cross, too, was foretold. He did not receive the faith of divinity from his own testimony — for who can be believed when speaking of himself? — but from the testimony of the prophets, who sang long before, with one spirit, all that he did and suffered. That can never happen for Apollonius, Apuleius, or any magician.

After pouring out such delirious ravings of ignorance, after trying to uproot the truth entirely, he dared to title his books ‘Truth-loving’ — a label hostile to God. O blind heart, O mind blacker than Cimmerian darkness! He may have been a disciple of Anaxagoras, for whom snow served as ink. But it is the same blindness to call falsehood truth and to brand truth as mendacity. Clearly a crafty man sought to hide a wolf under a sheep’s skin, that with a deceitful title he might lead the reader astray. Yet grant it was ignorance, not malice: what truth have you brought us, except that you, the defender of the gods, have in the end betrayed them? You heaped praise on the highest God — confessing him King, Greatest, Maker of all, Fountain of good, Parent of all, Creator and Sustainer of the living — then you stripped your own Jupiter of his kingdom and reduced him to the rank of a servant, deprived of supreme power. Your own epilogue therefore convicts you of the error of foolish vanity. You affirm that gods exist, yet you subject them and enslave them to the very God whose religion you try to overthrow.
