latin: Afuit ergo ab his fingendi uoluntas et astutia, quoniam rudes fuerunt. aut quis possit indoctus apta inter se et cohaerentia fingere, cum philosophorum doctissimi, Plato et Aristoteles et Epicurus et Zenon, ipsi sibi repugnantia et contraria dixerint ? haec est enim mendaciorum natura, ut cohaerere non possint. illorum autem traditio quia uera est, quadrat undique ac sibi tota consentit et ideo persuadet, quia constanti ratione subfulta est. non igitur quaestus et commodi gratia religionem istam conmenti sunt, quippe qui et praeceptis et re ipsa eam uitam secuti sint, quae et uoluptatibus caret et omnia quae habentur in bonis spernit, et qui non tantum pro fide mortem subierint, sed etiam morituros esse se et scierint et praedixerint et postea uniuersos qui eorum disciplinam secuti essent acerba et nefanda passuros. ipsum autem Christum adfirmauit a Iudaeis fugatum collecta nongentorum hominum manu latrocinia fecisse. quis tantae auctoritati audeat repugnare? credamus hoc plane, nam fortasse illi hoc in somnis Apollo aliquis nuntiauit. tot semper latrones perierunt et cottidie pereunt, utique multos et ipse damnasti: quis eorum post crucem suam non dicam deus, sed homo appellatus est? uerum tu forsitan ex eo credidisti, quia uos homicidam . Martem consecrastis ut deum: quod tamen non fecissetis, si illum Ariopagitae in crucem sustulissent. idem cum facta eius mirabilia destrueret nec tamen negaret, uoluit ostendere Apollonium uel paria uel etiam maiora fecisse. mirum quod Apuleium praetermisit, cuius solent et multa et mira memorari. cur igitur, o delirum caput, nemo Apollonium pro deo colit? nisi forte tu solus, illo scilicet deo dignus, cum quo te in sempiternum uerus deus puniet. si magus Christus, quia mirabilia fecit, peritior utique Apollonius, qui ut describis cum Domitianus eum punire uellet, repente in iudicio non conparuit. quam ille qui et conprehensus est et cruci adfixus. at enim ex hoc ipso fortasse insolentiam Christi uoluit arguere, quod deum se constituerit, ut ille uerecundior fuisse uideatur, qui cum maiora faceret, ut hic putat, tamen id sibi non adrogauerit. omitto nunc ipsa opera conparare, quia in secundo et in superiore libro de fraude ac praestigiis artis magicae dixi. nego esse quemquam qui non optet in primis id sibi post mortem contingere quod etiam reges maximi concupiscunt. cur enim sibi homines sepulchra magnifica, cur statuas, cur imagines conparant? cur aliquibus claris factis aut etiam pro ciuibus morte suscepta student opiniones hominum promereri? cur denique ipse ingenii tui monumentum hoc detestabile stultitia tamquam caeno aedificatum constituere uoluisti, nisi quod inmortalitatem de memoria nominis speras? stultum igitur est id putare Apollonium noluisse quod optaret utique, si posset, quia nemo est qui inmortalitatem recuset, maxime cum eum dicas et adoratum esse a quibusdam sicut deum et simulacrum eius sub Herculis Alexicaci nomine constitutum ab Ephesiis etiam nunc honorari. non potuit ergo post mortem deus credi, quia et hominem et magum fuisse constabat, et ideo alieni nominis titulo adfectauit diuinitatem, quia suo nec poterat nec audebat. noster uero et potuit deus credi, quia magus non fuit, et creditus est, quia uere fuit. non in quit hoc dico, idcirco Apollonium non haberi deum, quia noluerit, sed ut appareat nos sapientiores esse, qui mirabilibus factis non statim fidem diuinitatis adiunximus, quam uos, qui ob exigua portenta deum credidistis. non est mirum si tu, qui a dei sapientia longe remotus es, nihil prorsus intellegis eorum quae legisti, cum Iudaei, qui a principio prophetas lectitauerant quibusque sacramentum dei fuerat adsignatum, tamen quid legerent ignorauerint. disce igitur, si quid tibi cordis est, non idcirco a nobis deum creditum, quia mirabilia fecit, sed quia uidimus in eo facta esse omnia quae nobis adnuntiata sunt uaticinio prophetarum. tecit mirabilia: magum putassemus, ut et uos nunc putatis et Iudaei tunc putauerunt, si non illa ipsa facturum prophetae omnes uno spiritu praedixissent. itaque deum credimus non magis ex factis operibusque mirandis quam ex illa ipsa cruce, quam uos sicut canes lambitis, quoniam simul et illa praedicta est. non îgitur suo testimonio — cui enim de se dicenti potest credi? —, sed prophetarum testimonio, qui omnia quae fecit ac passus est multo ante cecinerunt, fidem diuinitatis accepit, quod neque Apollonio neque Apuleio neque cuiquam magorum potuit aut potest aliquando contingere. cum igitur talia ignorantiae suae deliramenta fudisset, cum ueritatem penitus excindere conisus esset, ausus est libros suos nefarios ac dei hostes φιλαληθεῖς; adnotare. o caecum pectus, o mentem Cimmeriis ut aiunt tenebris atrorem! discipulus hic fortasse Anaxagorae fuerit, cui niues atramentum fuerunt. atquin eadem caecitas est et uero falsitatis et mendacio ueritatis nomen inponere. uidelicet homo subdolus uoluit lupum sub ouis pelle celare, ut fallaci titulo posset in retire lectorem. uerum esto, inscitia hoc, non malitia feceris: quam tandem nobis adtulisti ueritatem, nisi quod adsertor deorum eos ipsos ad ultimum prodidisti? prosecutus enim summi dei laudes, quem regem, quem maximum, quem opificem rerum, quem fontem bonorum, quem parentem omnium, quem factorem altoremque uiuentium confessus es, ademisti Ioui tuo regnum eumque summa potestate depulsum in ministrorum numerum redegisti. epilogus itaque te tuus arguit stultitiae uanitatis erroris. adfirmas enim deos esse et illos tamen subicis et mancipas ei deo cuius religionem conaris euertere.

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: Let us now turn to the divine testimonies. First, however, I will bring forward one figure who resembles the divine — on account of his immense antiquity and because the man I shall name was reckoned among the gods. In Cicero, the pontiff U. Cotta, arguing against the Stoics about religion and the variety of opinions concerning the gods, attempts, after the manner of the Academics, to render everything uncertain. He says there were five Mercuries; having enumerated four in order, he identifies the fifth as the one by whom Argus was slain, and adds that on this account he fled to Egypt and gave laws and letters to the Egyptians. The Egyptians call him Thoyth, from whom the first month of their year — that is, September — took its name. This same figure founded a city that is still called in Greek the City of Mercury, and the Pheneatae worship him religiously. Although he was a man, he was the most ancient and the most thoroughly instructed in every kind of learning, so that his knowledge of many matters and arts earned him the surname Trismegistus. He wrote many books pertaining to the knowledge of divine things, in which he asserts the majesty of the highest and singular God and addresses him by the same names we use for the Lord and Father. And lest anyone seek his name, he declared it to be anonymous — because it does not need the property of a name, owing to its very unity. His words are these: "O the one God; one, indeed, is the one who does not need a name, and he is anonymous." Therefore God does not have a name, because he is alone; nor is a proper title needed, except when a multitude demands distinction so that each person may be designated by his own mark and appellation. But for God, since he is always one, "God" is his proper name.

It remains to produce testimonies that are far more certain, drawn from the sacred and Sibylline poems. For perhaps those against whom we contend do not think poets should be believed, as if they invent empty fictions; nor philosophers, since they could have erred, being themselves men. M. Varro — than whom no one more learned ever lived, not even among the Greeks — in his books on divine matters addressed to C. Caesar the pontifex maximus, when discussing the quindecimvirs, says that the Sibylline books were not the work of a single Sibyl, but were called by one name, "Sibylline," because all women prophets were called Sibyls by the ancients, either from the name of one Delphid or from the announcing of the counsels of the gods. For the Aeolians called the gods not "Osouc" but "theos," and counsel not "boule" but "boulian." Hence the Sibyl was said to be, as it were, "theoboulia" — the counsel of God. Moreover, there were ten Sibyls, and Varro enumerates them all under the authors who wrote about each. The first was the Persian Sibyl, mentioned by Nicanor, who wrote the deeds of Alexander of Macedon. The second was the Libyan Sibyl, whom Euripides recalls in the prologue to the Lamia. The third was the Delphic Sibyl, of whom Chrysippus speaks in his book on divination. The fourth was the Cimmerian Sibyl in Italy, named by Naevius in his books on the Punic War and by Piso in his annals. The fifth was the Erythraean Sibyl, whom Apollodorus of Erythrae affirms was his fellow citizen; she prophesied to the Greeks sailing for Troy that Troy would perish and that Homer would write falsehoods. The sixth was the Samian Sibyl, about whom Eratosthenes writes in the ancient annals of the Samians that her writings were found. The seventh was the Cumaean Sibyl, named Amalthea, also called Herophile or Demophile by others. She brought nine books to King Tarquin the Elder and asked three hundred philippeos for them; the king scorned the price and mocked the woman's madness. Whereupon she burned three of the books and demanded the same price for the remaining six. Tarquin, thinking her even more insane, was moved when she burned three more and persisted at the same price, and he bought the remaining three for three hundred gold pieces. Afterwards their number was increased when the Capitol was rebuilt, and books were brought to Rome from all cities, Italian and Greek, especially from Erythrae, under the name of whatever Sibyl they were. The eighth was the Hellespontine Sibyl, born in the Troad, in the village of Marmessus near the city of Gergithus; Heraclides of Pontus writes that she lived in the times of Solon and Cyrus. The ninth was the Phrygian Sibyl, who prophesied at Ancyra. The tenth was the Tiburtine Sibyl, named Albunea, worshiped as a goddess at Tibur near the banks of the river Anio; her image is said to have been found in the whirlpool holding a book in her hand. The poems of all these Sibyls are both worn and preserved, except those of the Cumaean, whose books the Romans keep hidden, and it is not lawful for anyone but the quindecimvirs to inspect them. There are individual books for each Sibyl, but because they are inscribed with the name "Sibyl," they are believed to be the work of a single Sibyl; they are confused and cannot be discerned or assigned to each one, except for the Erythraean, who inserted her true name into her poem and declared beforehand that she would be called Erythraean, though she was born in Babylon. We too will call the Sibyl "confused" wherever we must use their testimonies. All these Sibyls, therefore, proclaim one God — especially the Erythraean, who is more famous and more highly regarded among the others. Fenestella, a most diligent writer on the fifteen men, says that when the Capitol was restored, the consul C. Curio reported to the senate that envoys should be sent to Erythrae to bring back the poems of the Sibyl that had been discovered. Accordingly P. Gabinius, M. Otacilius, and L. Valerius were sent; they brought to Rome about a thousand verses transcribed from private collections. Varro also said the same thing above. In these verses, then, that the envoys brought to Rome, we find these testimonies concerning one God: "One God, who alone rules, immense, unbegotten." That this one is the only supreme God, who made the heaven and distinguished it with lights: "But God alone is one, most high, who made the heaven, the sun, and the stars, and the moon, and the fruitful earth, and the waters of the sea." He testifies that he alone ought to be worshiped, since he alone is the builder of the world and the artificer of all things, whether of those of which it consists or those that are in it: "Honor the one who is the only ruler of the world." "Who alone is from eternity and to eternity." Likewise, another Sibyl, whoever she is, when she says she brings the voice of God to men, speaks thus:

excerpts.author: Lactantius
english: In the hidden depths of the holy writings we read that the leader of the Hebrews, together with his whole household and kin, was forced by a shortage of grain to cross into Egypt (Exodus 1:14). His descendants, after dwelling there for a long time, grew into a great nation and were crushed beneath a heavy, intolerable yoke of slavery; God struck Egypt with an incurable plague and delivered his people, leading them through the midst of the sea while the waves were split apart and driven to either side so that the people walked on dry ground (Exodus 14:13-31). When the Egyptian king tried to pursue the fugitives, the sea returned to its place and engulfed him with all his forces.

That deed, glorious and wondrous as it was, displayed God's power to humanity at that moment, yet it served only as a foreshadowing and a figure of a greater act that the same God will perform at the consummation of the ages: he will free his people from the heavy servitude of the world. In those days there was but one people of God, confined to a single nation, so only Egypt was struck; now, however, the people of God, gathered from every tongue, dwell among all nations and are oppressed by their rulers, and therefore it is necessary that all nations — that is, the whole world — be scourged by heavenly plagues so that the just and God‑fearing people may be liberated. Just as signs were given then to reveal the coming destruction of the Egyptians, so in the last days marvelous portents will appear through every element of the world, by which the imminent end of all nations will be recognized.

As the end of this age draws near, the condition of human affairs must change and deteriorate, because wickedness grows stronger, so that our present times — in which iniquity and malice have reached their highest pitch — may be judged fortunate and almost golden by comparison with that incurable evil. Justice will become so rare, and impiety, greed, and lust so rampant, that any good people who happen to exist will become prey for the wicked and will be driven away on every side by the unjust; only the wicked will be wealthy, while the good will be cast into every kind of contempt and poverty. All law will be confounded and statutes will perish; no one will possess anything except what they have seized or defended by hand, and audacity and force will rule everything. There will be no faith among men, no peace, no humanity, no shame, no truth, and consequently no security, no government, no rest from evils. The whole earth will be in turmoil, wars will rage everywhere, all nations will be armed and will attack one another; neighboring cities will fight each other, and first of all Egypt will pay the penalty for its foolish superstitions, drenched in blood as if by a river.

Then the sword will sweep across the world, cutting down everything and laying all things low like a harvest. The cause of this devastation and confusion will be that the Roman name, by which the world is now governed — my soul shudders to speak it, but I must, because it will happen — will be removed from the earth, the empire will revert to Asia, the East will dominate once more, and the West will serve. No one should be surprised if a kingdom founded with such immense strength, enlarged for so long by so many and such great men, and finally secured by such vast resources, should nevertheless collapse at some point. For nothing built by human power cannot be undone by human power, since the works of mortals are mortal. Thus other kingdoms that flourished for a long time have nonetheless perished: the Egyptians, Persians, Greeks, and Assyrians are recorded to have held dominion over the earth, and when they were all destroyed, supreme authority passed to the Romans. The more the Romans surpass all other kingdoms in greatness, the greater will be their fall, because the higher they rise, the more weight they carry toward ruin.

Seneca did not foolishly divide the history of the Roman city into ages. He said the first age was infancy under King Romulus, from whom Rome was born and, as it were, nurtured; then childhood under the subsequent kings, by whom it was enlarged and shaped by many disciplines and institutions; but when Tarquinius reigned, Rome had already begun to be, as it were, an adult, and it could not endure servitude, so it rejected the yoke of proud domination and chose to obey laws rather than kings. When its adolescence ended with the conclusion of the Punic War, it finally began to mature, its strength confirmed. After Carthage, the long‑standing rival of the empire, was destroyed, Rome stretched its hands over the whole world by land and sea until every king and nation had been subdued; then, with no more wars to fight, it misused its own power and destroyed itself. This was its first old age, when, worn out by civil wars and pressed by internal corruption, it fell back under the rule of a single emperor, as if returning to a second infancy. Having lost the liberty it had defended under Brutus's leadership and authority, it aged as though unable to sustain itself without the support of rulers. If these things are so, what remains but that destruction follows old age? And this will happen soon, as the prophecies of the prophets announce under the veil of other names so that no one may easily understand. The Sibyls, however, declare openly that Rome will perish, and indeed by the judgment of God, because it bore a name hated by God and slaughtered the people of truth, the foster child of justice. Hystaspes, the most ancient king of the Medes, from whom the river now called the Hydaspes takes its name, transmitted to posterity an admirable dream through the interpretation of a prophesying boy: he foretold long before the founding of the Trojan nation that the empire and the Roman name would be removed from the world.

latin: Est in arcanis sanctarum litterarum transcendisse in Aegyptum cogente inopia rei frumentariae principem Hebraeorum cum omni domo et cognatione. cuius posteri cum diutius in Aegypto commorantes in magnam gentem creuissent et graui atque intolerando seruitutis iugo premerentur, percussit Aegyptum deus insanabili plaga et populum suum liberauit traductum medio mari, cum discissis fluctibus et in utramque partem dimotis per siccum populus graderetur. conatusque rex Aegyptiorum profugos insequi coeunte in statum suum pelago cum omnibus copiis interceptus est. quod facinus tam clarum tamque mirabile quamuis ad praesens uirtutem dei hominibus ostenderet, tamen praesignificatio et figura maioris rei fuit, quam deus idem in extrema temporum consummatione facturus est: liberabit enim plebem suam de graui seruitute mundi. sed quoniam tunc una plebs dei et aput unam gentem fuit, Aegyptus sola percussa est, nunc autem quia populus dei ex omnibus linguis congregatus aput omnes gentes commoratur et ab his dominantibus premitur, necesse est uniuersas nationes id est orbem totum caelestibus plagis uerberari, ut iustus et cultor dei populus liberetur. et sicut tunc signa facta sunt quibus futura clades Aegyptiis ostenderetur, ita in ultimo fient prodigia miranda per omnia elementa mundi, quibus imminens exitus uniuersis gentibus intellegatur. propinquante igitur huius saeculi termino humanarum rerum statum commutari necesse est et in deterius nequitia inualescente prolabi, ut iam nostra haec tempora, quibus iniquitas et malitia usque ad summum gradum creuit, in illius tamen insanabilis mali conparatione felicia et prope aurea possint iudicari. ita enim iustitia rarescet, ita inpietas et auaritia et cupiditas et libido crebrescet, ut si qui forte tum fuerint boni, praedae sint sceleratis ac diuexentur undique ab iniustis, soli autem mali opulenti sint, boni uero in omnibus contumeliis atque in egestate iactentur. confundetur omne ius et leges interibunt. nihil quisquam tunc habebit nisi aut quaesitum aut defensum manu, audacia et uis omnia possidebunt. non fides in hominibus, non pax, non humanitas, non pudor, non ueritas erit atque ita neque securitas neque regimen neque requies a malis ulla. omnis enim terra tumultuabitur, frement ubique bella, omnes gentes in armis erunt et se inuicem obpugnabunt: ciuitates inter se finitimae proeliabuntur et prima omnium Aegyptus stultarum superstitionum luet poenas et sanguine uelut flumine operietur. tum peragrabit gladius orbem metens omnia et tamquam messem cuncta prosternens. cuius uastitatis et confusionis haec erit causa, quod Romanum nomen, quo nunc regitur orbis — horret animus dicere, sed dicam, quia futurum est — tolletur e terra et inperium in Asiam reuertetur ac rursus oriens dominabitur atque occidens seruiet. nec mirum cuiquam debet uideri, si regnum tanta mole fundatum ac tamdiu per tot et tales uiros auctum, tantis denique opibus confirmatum aliquando tamen conruet. nihil est enim humanis uiribus laboratum quod non humanis aeque uiribus destrui possit, quoniam mortalia sunt opera mortalium. sic et alia prius regna cum diutius floruissent, nihilominus tamen occiderunt. nam et Aegyptios et Persas et Graecos et Assyrios proditum est regimen habuisse terrarum: quibus omnibus destructis ad Romanos quoque rerum summa peruenit. qui quanto ceteris omnibus regnis magnitudine antistant, tanto maiore decident lapsu, quia plus habent ponderis ad ruinam quae sunt ceteris altiora. non inscite Seneca Romanae urbis tempora distribuit in aetates. primam enim dixit infantiam sub rege Romulo fuisse, a quo et genita et quasi educata sit Roma; deinde pueritiam sub ceteris regibus, a quibus et aucta sit et disciplinis pluribus institutisque formata; at uero Tarquinio regnante cum iam quasi adulta esse coepisset, seruitium non tulisse et reiecto superbae dominationis iugo maluisse legibus obtemperare quam regibus; cumque esset adulescentia eius fine Punici belli terminata, tum denique confirmatis uiribus coepisse iuuenescere. sublata enim Carthagine, quae tam diu aemula imperii fuit, manus suas in totum orbem terra marique porrexit, donec regibus cunctis et nationibus imperio subiugatis cum iam bellorum materia deficeret, uiribus suis male uteretur, quibus se ipsa confecit. haec fuit prima eius senectus, cum bellis laeerata ciuilibus atque intestino malo pressa rursus ad regimen singularis imperii reccidit quasi ad alteram infantiam reuoluta. amissa enim libertate, quam Bruto duce et auctore defenderat, ita consenuit, tamquam sustentare se ipsa non ualeret, nisi adminiculo regentium niteretur. quodsi haec ita sunt, quid restat nisi ut sequatur interitus senectutem? et id futurum breui contiones prophetarum denuntiant sub ambage aliorum nominum, ne facile quis intellegat. Sibyllae tamen aperte interituram esse Romam locuntur et quidem iudicio dei, quod nomen eius habuerit inuisum et inimica iustitiae alumnum ueritatis populum trucidarit. Hystaspes quoque, qui fuit Medorum rex antiquissimus, a quo amnis nomen accepit qui nunc Hydaspes dicitur, admirabile somnium sub interpretatione uaticinantis pueri ad memoriam posteris tradidit: sublatuiri ex orbe imperium nomenque Romanum multo ante praefatus est quam illa Troiana gens conderetur.
